# Sūrah al-Anʿām (Chapter 6) — Expanded Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Introduction to the Sūrah

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Makkan Sūrah Sent Down as One Whole**

Sūrah al-Anʿām, "The Cattle," is the sixth chapter of the Qur'an and the first long Makkan sūrah to appear in the written order of the muṣḥaf. After four lengthy Madinan chapters (al-Baqarah, Āl ʿImrān, al-Nisā', al-Mā'idah) filled with law, treaty, and communal regulation, the reader suddenly steps back in time to Makkah, to the years before the Hijrah, when the Muslims were a small and persecuted minority and the central dispute was not how to run a state but whether God is One. The sūrah's 165 verses are almost entirely devoted to that single question and to its consequences: creation, revelation, prophethood, resurrection, and the falsehood of every rival to God.

The classical sources preserve a distinctive report about its revelation. Ibn ʿAbbās and others relate that al-Anʿām came down all at once, in a single night, escorted by a great company of angels glorifying God. Al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Zamakhsharī all record versions of it:

> "Sūrat al-Anʿām was sent down all at once, accompanied by seventy thousand angels, hymning glorifications and praises." (reported by al-Ṭabarānī, al-Bayhaqī in *Shuʿab al-Īmān*, and cited by Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī at the opening of the sūrah)

The report's chain is discussed by the ḥadīth scholars and it is not of the highest grade, but the early community's sense of the sūrah is unmistakable: it is a unified, majestic proclamation of God's Oneness rather than a collection of rulings revealed piecemeal in response to events. Al-Qurṭubī adds a related report that verse 59 ("With Him are the keys of the Unseen") was honored with its own escort of angels. Whatever weight one gives these narrations, they express what any careful reader notices: al-Anʿām reads as a single sustained argument.

**Why "The Cattle"?**

The name comes from verses 136–145, where the Qur'an dismantles the pagan Arabs' invented taboos concerning livestock — animals dedicated to idols, animals whose backs were declared forbidden to ride, animals whose meat was permitted to men but forbidden to women. These verses seem at first a minor legal matter, yet they carry the whole argument of the sūrah. To forbid what God has not forbidden is to legislate in God's place; to legislate in God's place is to claim a share of His lordship. Thus the discussion of cattle is where abstract *tawḥīd* becomes concrete: whoever truly believes God alone is Lord will not accept prohibitions from any other source. The sūrah is named after the passage where its theology touches the ground.

**The Argument of the Sūrah in Outline**

The chapter moves in recognizable waves. It opens (vv. 1–3) by praising God as the Creator of the heavens, the earth, darkness, and light, and as the One who made man from clay and set his term. It then confronts the Makkans' evasions (vv. 4–11): they turn from every sign, they mock, they demand angels and written books, yet earlier generations far stronger than they were destroyed for the same obstinacy.

A series of instructions beginning with "Say" (*qul*) — a hallmark of this sūrah, occurring more than forty times — gives the Prophet ﷺ precise responses to deliver (vv. 12–73): God owns all things; He has prescribed mercy upon Himself; He alone feeds and is not fed; He holds the keys of the Unseen; He takes souls at night and returns them by day; He is Dominant over His servants. Interwoven are scenes from the Day of Resurrection in which the idolaters disown their partners and beg to be returned to the world.

The sūrah then narrates Abraham's reasoning against star-, moon-, and sun-worship (vv. 74–83), followed by the roll-call of eighteen prophets who inherited his way (vv. 84–90), and a defense of revelation against those who said "God has not sent down anything to a human being" (vv. 91–94). Verses 95–105 return to creation as evidence: the splitting of the seed, the cleaving of dawn, the stars as guides, the rain that produces gardens.

The next section (vv. 106–135) addresses the Prophet's conduct toward the deniers: do not revile their gods; know that most people on earth would lead you astray if you followed them; understand that God has appointed for every prophet enemies. Then the cattle passage (vv. 136–147) exposes the arbitrariness of pagan law, and verses 148–153 answer the excuse of predestination ("Had God willed, we would not have associated partners") before delivering the famous "Ten Commandments" of the Qur'an — a concise moral charter revealed in Makkah.

The closing section (vv. 154–165) affirms the Torah and the Qur'an as continuous revelation, warns of the Day when faith will no longer benefit a soul that did not believe before, and ends with the Prophet's declaration: "My prayer, my sacrifice, my living, and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds." The last verse names human beings *khalā'if* — successors on the earth — and states that God raised some over others in degrees in order to test them.

**A Textbook of Reasoned Monotheism**

What distinguishes al-Anʿām from other Makkan sūrahs is its method. It does not simply assert God's Oneness; it argues for it. It asks who owns the heavens and the earth. It asks who would deliver you from the darkness of land and sea if you called on Him. It points to the grain splitting underground, to sleep as a nightly death, to the arrival of the body's appointed term. It reports Abraham thinking aloud through the night sky until he says, "I do not love things that set." Ibn Taymiyyah observed that the Qur'an's proofs are *burhāniyyah* — demonstrative — and that al-Anʿām is one of the richest deposits of such proofs. Al-Rāzī's commentary on this sūrah is among the most extensive in his *Tafsīr* precisely because nearly every verse invites rational analysis.

For the modern reader this matters. Many people today assume that faith and reasoning are opposed. Al-Anʿām assumes the reverse: that a mind which honestly observes the world will find in it the fingerprints of one Maker, and that idolatry — ancient or modern — survives only by refusing to look. The sūrah's repeated command *"Say"* is therefore also an invitation to think, because each "Say" is followed by an argument that must be understood before it can be delivered.

**The Ethical Center**

Verses 151–153 deserve special mention. Ibn Masʿūd reported:

> "Whoever wishes to look at the testament of the Messenger of God ﷺ on which is his seal, let him read: 'Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you...'" (al-Tirmidhī 3070, graded ḥasan)

These verses forbid associating partners with God, mistreating parents, killing children from fear of poverty, approaching indecencies, taking life unjustly, consuming an orphan's wealth, cheating in weights and measures, speaking unjustly even about relatives, and breaking God's covenant — then conclude: "This is My path, straight, so follow it." That a Makkan sūrah, revealed before any Islamic state existed, contains so complete a moral code shows that Islam's ethics were never an afterthought to its theology. Belief in one God and just treatment of one's fellow creatures are presented as a single straight road.

**Approach of This Commentary**

The commentary that follows treats each of the 165 verses as an independent unit. For every verse it examines the Arabic vocabulary, cites relevant Qur'anic passages, brings authentic ḥadīth where they illuminate the meaning, records the views of al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Taymiyyah and others, and then reflects on the verse's logic and its application to ordinary human life. Each section carries its own bold headings that arise from the actual content of the discussion. Direct quotations from the Qur'an, ḥadīth, and the scholars are presented in blockquotes so that the reader can always distinguish the source from the explanation.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:1

> **All praise is for Allah Who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light. Yet the disbelievers set up equals to their Lord ˹in worship˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Opening with Praise, Not with Argument**

Five sūrahs of the Qur'an open with the words *al-ḥamdu lillāh* — al-Fātiḥah, al-Anʿām, al-Kahf, Saba', and Fāṭir — and al-Anʿām is the first of them after the Opening chapter. The choice is deliberate. A sūrah that will spend 165 verses arguing against idolatry does not begin by attacking idols; it begins by praising God. This teaches something about the order of the religious mind: the believer's starting point is gratitude and recognition of the One who deserves praise, and only from that ground does he turn to correct error. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the word *ḥamd* combines praise (*thanā'*) with love and reverence, and that the definite article *al-* indicates that all praise, of every kind, belongs to God by right, whether or not any creature chooses to offer it.

The linguistic scholars distinguish *ḥamd* from *shukr* (thanks). One thanks a benefactor for a specific favor received; one praises a being for what he is, whether or not one has received anything from him. By opening with *ḥamd* rather than *shukr*, the verse indicates that God deserves praise simply for being the Creator of the heavens and the earth, independent of any personal benefit the speaker has enjoyed. This is an important corrective. Many people praise God when things go well and fall silent when they do not. The verse teaches that praise is owed to the Creator as Creator, not merely as provider.

**The Two Great Pairs: Heavens and Earth, Darkness and Light**

The verse names two pairs. The first, "the heavens and the earth," covers all of physical space — the whole created realm from the highest to the lowest. The second, "darkness and light," covers the conditions under which that realm is experienced. Together they encompass everything the eye can see and the circumstances under which it sees.

There is a subtle difference in the verbs. For the heavens and the earth the Qur'an uses *khalaqa* (created); for darkness and light it uses *jaʿala* (made, appointed). Classical grammarians such as al-Zamakhsharī point out that *khalaqa* often refers to bringing a thing into being from nothing, while *jaʿala* often refers to bringing a thing into a particular state or relation. Darkness and light are not independent substances in the way the heavens and the earth are; they are conditions that arise from the arrangement of created bodies. The precision of the vocabulary reflects the precision of the reality.

Al-Ṭabarī observes that some of the earliest commentators saw in this opening an echo of how the Torah opens, where God creates the heavens and the earth and separates light from darkness (Genesis 1:1–5). The Qur'an presents itself as confirming the earlier scriptures, and it is fitting that a sūrah addressed to idolaters who claimed the heritage of Abraham should open with words that Abraham's own descendants among the People of the Book would recognize.

**Why "Darknesses" Is Plural and "Light" Is Singular**

One feature of this verse has drawn the attention of nearly every classical commentator. The Arabic reads *al-ẓulumāt wa'l-nūr* — "the darknesses and the light." Darkness is plural; light is singular. This pattern holds throughout the entire Qur'an: *ẓulumāt* is never used in the singular, and *nūr* is never used in the plural.

Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī explain the reason. Truth is one; falsehood is many. There is only one straight line between two points, but infinitely many crooked ones. There is one way to be right about God's Oneness, but countless ways to be wrong — worshipping stars, ancestors, kings, wealth, desire, or one's own opinion. Light has one source and one nature; darkness is simply the absence of light, and absences multiply wherever light is blocked. Guidance is therefore singular and unified, while misguidance fragments into sects and errors. The Qur'an states this elsewhere directly:

> "Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light" (2:257)

The consistency of the pattern across the whole Book is itself a small sign of the Qur'an's careful composition. A text assembled carelessly over twenty-three years would not maintain such a distinction without a single exception.

**The Turn: "Yet Those Who Disbelieve Ascribe Equals"**

After the majestic opening, the verse pivots with the word *thumma* — "yet," or literally "then." Grammatically, *thumma* indicates sequence, but here the commentators explain that it expresses astonishment (*istibʿād*): after all this — after God alone created the heavens, the earth, darkness and light — those who disbelieve *still* set up equals to Him. The word for "ascribe equals" is *yaʿdilūn*, from the root *ʿ-d-l*, which means to make equal or to balance. It is the same root that gives *ʿadl*, justice. The idolaters, in a bitter irony, use the faculty of equalizing — which should produce justice — to commit the greatest injustice, placing created things on the same scale as the Creator. The Qur'an calls this the gravest wrong:

> "Never associate ˹anything˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺, for associating ˹others with Him˺ is truly the worst of all wrongs" (31:13)

Note also that the verse says they ascribe equals *bi-rabbihim* — "to their Lord." It does not say "to God" in the abstract but "to their own Lord," the One who created them and sustains them. This heightens the absurdity. They are not wronging a stranger; they are equating their own Maker with stones.

**The Makkans' Own Admission**

The force of the argument depends on a fact the Qur'an records repeatedly: the Makkan idolaters did not deny that Allāh created the heavens and the earth.

> "And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will definitely say," (31:25; see also 39:38, 43:9, 43:87)

Their error was not atheism but *shirk* — associating others with God in worship, intercession, and lordship, while admitting He was the ultimate Creator. The verse presses them with their own premise. If you admit He alone created everything, on what basis do you give a share of worship to things He created? Ibn Kathīr summarizes: they acknowledge Him as Creator and then worship others alongside Him, and this is what makes their position self-contradictory.

This is a lesson in method. The Qur'an does not argue from premises its opponents reject; it argues from premises they accept and shows that their conclusions do not follow. This is the strongest form of reasoning, and it remains valid today. Many who would never bow to a stone idol nonetheless treat wealth, status, or their own desires as the true determinants of their lives, while admitting in theory that God alone controls outcomes. The verse addresses them as much as it addressed Quraysh.

**Darkness and Light as Moral Realities**

While the primary meaning of darkness and light is physical — night and day, the conditions of the created world — the commentators are unanimous that the Qur'an also intends the moral and spiritual senses. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have explained the pair as disbelief and faith, or ignorance and knowledge. Al-Qurṭubī allows both readings, noting that the physical realities are signs pointing to the spiritual ones. The same God who made night and day made the possibility of guidance and misguidance; and just as no one can create daylight by wishing for it, no one can generate true guidance from within himself without God's light.

The practical weight of this is heavy. If darkness is many and light is one, then a person who leaves the light does not simply move to an alternative position; he enters a landscape with no fixed points. The person who abandons clear guidance rarely lands in a single stable error; he drifts through many. Anyone who has watched a friend abandon principle knows this pattern: the first compromise leads to a second, and the second to a tenth, because darkness offers no place to stand.

**Praise as the Foundation of the Whole Sūrah**

Beginning with praise also sets the emotional tone for everything that follows. The sūrah will speak of the destruction of past nations, the terror of the Last Day, the idolaters' invented laws. All of this could produce a harsh, combative text. But by opening with *al-ḥamdu lillāh*, the Qur'an reminds the reader that the purpose of the argument is not victory in debate but the restoration of a right relationship — the return of praise to the One who deserves it. The Prophet ﷺ taught that praise is itself a form of worship of enormous weight:

> "Purity is half of faith, and *al-ḥamdu lillāh* fills the scale." (Muslim 223)

A person who has genuinely absorbed this first verse — who looks at the sky and the ground, at night and day, and feels praise rise in him for their Maker — has already been inoculated against the idolatry that the rest of the sūrah exposes. Praise rightly directed leaves no room for equals.

## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:2

> **He is the One Who created you from clay, then appointed a term ˹for your death˺ and another known only to Him ˹for your resurrection˺ —yet you continue to doubt!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Cosmos to the Person**

The first verse spoke of the heavens and the earth; the second turns to the human being who stands between them. This movement from the vast to the intimate is a pattern of Qur'anic argument. A person can hear that God created the universe and feel that it does not concern him personally. But when he is told that God created *him*, from clay, and has already fixed the length of *his* life, the argument becomes unavoidable. The verse addresses the listener directly: *khalaqakum* — "created *you*."

**"From Clay": The Humble Origin**

The word *ṭīn* means clay, moist earth. The Qur'an describes the origin of humanity in earth-based terms over a dozen times, with varying vocabulary that together sketches a process: *turāb* (dust, 3:59), *ṭīn* (clay, here and 7:12), *ṭīn lāzib* (sticky or viscous clay, 37:11), *ṣalṣāl min ḥama' masnūn* (dried clay from molded mud, 15:26), *ṣalṣāl ka'l-fakhkhār* (dried clay like pottery, 55:14), and *sulālah min ṭīn* (an extract of clay, 23:12). The commentators explain that the direct creation from clay refers to Adam, and that all his descendants are created "from clay" in the sense that they descend from him and that their bodies are built from the elements of the earth through the food it produces. Ibn Kathīr states that the address is to all of humanity because they are Adam's children and their origin is his origin.

The Prophet ﷺ described the connection between the earth and human variety:

> "God created Adam from a handful which He took from the whole of the earth, so the children of Adam came in accordance with the earth: among them the red, the white, the black, and those in between; the easy and the difficult; the bad and the good." (Abū Dāwūd 4693; al-Tirmidhī 2955, who graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ)

The remembrance of one's origin in clay is meant to produce humility. Every human being, whatever his rank or wealth, is made of the same material as the ground he walks on. Satan's first sin was precisely a refusal to accept this: "You created me from fire and him from clay" (7:12). Arrogance and the forgetting of one's origin are twins.

**The Two Terms**

The verse then says: *thumma qaḍā ajalan, wa ajalun musamman ʿindahu* — "then He decreed a term; and a term is appointed with Him." The word *ajal* means a fixed period or an appointed time of ending. The verse mentions it twice, and the classical commentators discussed at length whether these are one term or two.

Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Qurṭubī report the dominant view from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others: the first term is the span of each person's life in this world, ending in death; the second term, "appointed with Him," is the term of the resurrection — the interval between death and the Day of Judgment, known to God alone. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported to have said that the first is from birth to death and the second is from death to resurrection. The phrase "with Him" (*ʿindahu*) supports this reading: the Hour is a matter whose knowledge is with God exclusively, as the Qur'an states elsewhere:

> "That knowledge is only with my Lord" (7:187)

A second view, also recorded by al-Ṭabarī, takes the two terms as the term of the individual's death and the term of the whole world's ending. A third reading, from some early authorities, understands the first as the period of sleep — the daily "taking" of the soul — and the second as death, connecting this verse with 6:60 and 39:42. Al-Rāzī adds a further reflection: the first term is *decreed* (*qaḍā*) — a completed judgment — while the second is *named* (*musammā*) — it has a fixed designation, but its disclosure is withheld. All of these readings share a common point: the human being does not set his own limits. Both the end of his life and the day of his accounting have been fixed by Another.

**The Logic of Creation and Resurrection**

Why does the verse mention creation from clay and the appointed term in the same breath? Because together they form the standard Qur'anic argument for resurrection. If God brought a living, thinking human being out of lifeless clay, then bringing him back after his body has returned to clay is not harder — it is, if anything, easier from the human point of view:

> "And He is the One Who originates the creation then will resurrect it—which is even easier for Him" (30:27)

And:

> "They will be revived by the One Who produced them the first time, for He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of every created being" (36:77–79)

Al-Ṭabarī draws the parallel between this verse and 2:28: "How can you disbelieve in God when you were lifeless and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life, and then to Him you will be returned." The sequence is identical: clay (lifeless), life (first term), death, then the appointed term of return. The person who accepts the first three steps — and no one can deny his own birth and coming death — has no rational basis for rejecting the fourth.

**"Yet Still You Doubt!"**

The verse ends: *thumma antum tamtarūn* — "yet you doubt" or "then you dispute." The verb *imtarā* means to be in doubt to the point of wrangling about it. The particle *thumma* is used again as in verse 1 to express astonishment: after knowing you came from clay, after seeing death fix everyone's term without exception, you *still* doubt the resurrection?

The commentators note the nature of this doubt. It is not the honest uncertainty of someone seeking truth; it is the willful doubt of someone who does not want the conclusion. Al-Zamakhsharī observes that the Makkans doubted the resurrection while they had before their eyes the greater marvel of their own first creation. This is why the Qur'an treats such doubt as culpable rather than innocent. A person who doubts something for which he has less evidence, while accepting something for which he has more, is not following reason; he is following preference.

**Death as the Universal Teacher**

The fact that everyone's term is decreed has profound psychological consequences. The Qur'an states:

> "No soul can ever die without Allah" (3:145)

And:

> "When their time arrives, they can neither delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it" (7:34)

The Prophet ﷺ taught that a person's term is written before birth:

> "Then the angel is sent to him and he breathes the soul into him, and he is commanded with four words: to write his provision, his term, his deeds, and whether he will be wretched or happy." (al-Bukhārī 3208; Muslim 2643)

A believer who internalizes this is freed from two opposite illnesses. He is freed from paralyzing fear, because no danger can shorten a life whose length God has fixed; and he is freed from reckless arrogance, because no precaution can extend it. What remains within his power is not the length of his life but its content. This is why the Companions could enter battle with calm and also why they refused to waste a single day. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Take advantage of five before five: your youth before your old age, your health before your sickness, your wealth before your poverty, your free time before your busyness, and your life before your death." (al-Ḥākim in *al-Mustadrak*, graded ṣaḥīḥ by him and by al-Albānī)

**A Practical Reflection**

Consider how a person behaves when he knows a deadline is fixed but not disclosed. A student who knows that an examination will come but not on which day either prepares steadily or lives in denial. There is no third option. The verse describes exactly this situation: the term is fixed, and it is with God. The idolaters chose denial, dressing it up as doubt. The believer chooses preparation, and finds in it not gloom but clarity. Knowing that time is limited is what gives time its value.

The verse's structure — creation, term, appointed term, doubt — is thus a complete short sermon. It begins with where you came from, tells you where you are going, notes that the date of your final accounting is already set, and then asks, with something close to grief, why you still argue.

## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:3

> **He is the Only True God in the heavens and the earth. He knows whatever you conceal and whatever you reveal, and knows whatever you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Step of the Opening**

The first three verses of the sūrah form a compact statement of creed. Verse 1 established God as Creator of the cosmos. Verse 2 established Him as Creator of the human being and Master of his lifespan. Verse 3 now establishes that His divinity and knowledge extend everywhere and reach everything — including what is hidden within the human heart. The idolater who had somehow survived the first two arguments now faces a third: there is no corner of the universe, and no corner of the self, that lies outside God's lordship and awareness.

**"He Is God in the Heavens and on the Earth"**

This phrase — *wa huwa Allāhu fi'l-samāwāti wa fi'l-arḍ* — is unique in the Qur'an. Elsewhere the Qur'an frequently states that God *owns* what is in the heavens and the earth, or *knows* what is in them, but only here does it say that He *is God* in the heavens and on the earth. The commentators have taken care to explain what this means and what it does not mean.

Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Qurṭubī all explain that the meaning is: He is the One who is called God, worshipped as God, and obeyed as God by all who are in the heavens and on the earth. The inhabitants of the heavens — the angels — call Him God and worship Him, and the inhabitants of the earth — humans and jinn — owe Him the same. The verse asserts the universality of His divinity, not a physical location. Al-Ṭabarī paraphrases: "He is the One worshipped in the heavens and worshipped on the earth." Al-Zamakhsharī compares the structure to saying "he is the ruler in Iraq and in Syria" — meaning that his authority is recognized in both, not that he is physically present in two places at once.

This reading is confirmed by a closely parallel verse:

> "It is He Who is ˹the only˺ God in the heavens and ˹the only˺ God on the earth" (43:84)

Both verses use the same structure and both are followed by mention of God's knowledge, which suggests that the point is His universal recognition and His universal awareness. Ibn Taymiyyah, in his discussions of divine attributes, affirmed that God is above His creation in a manner befitting His majesty, while His knowledge, power, hearing, and sight encompass everything; he explained this verse in precisely that light — divinity everywhere, without confusing the Creator with created space.

**Why the Idolaters Needed to Hear This**

The pre-Islamic Arabs, like many ancient peoples, tended to divide the world into spheres of influence. There might be a supreme high god associated with the sky, and then lesser deities — al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, Manāt, and the tribal idols — who handled local matters on the earth: rain for this valley, victory for that tribe, fertility, trade, health. Their worship was essentially an arrangement of intermediaries. The verse cuts through this whole structure. There is no division of labor between heaven and earth. The same God who is God above is God below. There is no vacancy for a local deity to fill.

The modern reader may think this an ancient concern, but the pattern persists in different dress. People often affirm God in the abstract while treating the "real" forces of daily life — the economy, the doctor, the employer, luck, one's own effort — as the operative powers on the ground. The verse challenges this practical polytheism as firmly as it challenged the theoretical kind.

**"He Knows Your Secret and That Which You Make Public"**

The verse now turns to knowledge: *yaʿlamu sirrakum wa jahrakum*. The word *sirr* means what is concealed — a private thought, a hidden intention, a whispered word. *Jahr* means what is open — spoken aloud, done in public. God knows both equally; neither is clearer to Him than the other. The Qur'an repeats this in many forms:

> "Whether you speak secretly or openly—He surely knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart" (67:13–14)

> "Allah ˹even˺ knows the sly glances of the eyes and whatever the hearts conceal" (40:19)

The second of these verses is particularly penetrating. "The treachery of the eyes" refers to a glance so quick that the person beside you does not notice it. Even this is known.

The pairing of secret and public is not redundant. For a human observer, the public is knowable and the secret is not; therefore there is a strong temptation to be honest in public and otherwise in private. The verse removes the basis of that temptation. If both are equally known, the distinction between public and private conduct loses its moral significance. What matters is not who is watching but that God is always aware. This is the root of *iḥsān* as the Prophet ﷺ defined it in the ḥadīth of Gabriel:

> "*Iḥsān* is that you worship God as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He surely sees you." (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8)

**"And He Knows That Which You Earn"**

The final clause adds a third object of knowledge: *mā taksibūn* — what you earn. The verb *kasaba* is used in the Qur'an for the acquisition of deeds, good or bad, as a person acquires wealth. The metaphor is precise. A deed, once done, does not vanish; it is added to an account, like money to a ledger, and the account is fully known to God. The source commentary observes that "what you earn" refers to the deeds a person chooses and the recompense they entail.

Why is this mentioned separately from secret and public? Because secret and public describe the *state* of an action — hidden or visible — whereas "what you earn" describes its *consequence*. God knows not only what you did but what it has made of you and what it will bring you. This is a more searching knowledge. A person may do a public deed and privately know it was for show; God knows the deed, the intention, and the reward or punishment it has earned, all at once. Al-Rāzī notes that this clause introduces the idea of accountability that will dominate much of the sūrah: knowledge of deeds implies judgment upon them.

**The Structure of Complete Knowledge**

Taken together, the three clauses of the verse describe knowledge without gaps. Consider the possible ways a person might hope to escape divine notice: by being in a place beyond God's reach (refuted: He is God in the heavens and the earth); by hiding an action (refuted: He knows the secret); by acting openly but pretending it means something else (refuted: He knows what it earns). Each escape route is closed. Al-Qurṭubī remarks that the verse is thus a complete warning and a complete consolation: a warning to those who plan evil in secret, a consolation to those who do good unnoticed.

**Psychology of Being Known**

There is a common assumption that being fully known would be unbearable. In fact, the opposite is often true. The person who hides is under constant strain; he must remember his stories and manage his impressions. The person who accepts that he is fully known can stop performing. The believer who has absorbed this verse does not need an audience for his good deeds and does not fear that his quiet struggles go unrecorded. The Prophet ﷺ described the reward for the hidden deed:

> "Seven whom God will shade in His shade on the Day when there is no shade but His... and a man who gives charity and conceals it so that his left hand does not know what his right hand has spent; and a man who remembers God in private and his eyes overflow." (al-Bukhārī 660; Muslim 1031)

Two of the seven are defined by secrecy. The verse before us is what makes such secrecy meaningful: a hidden deed is hidden only from people, never from God.

**The Verse as the Close of the Opening Creed**

With verse 3 the sūrah has completed its foundational statement. God alone created everything (v. 1), God alone created you and fixed your term (v. 2), God alone is worshipped everywhere and knows everything about you (v. 3). Every argument that follows in the sūrah — against idols, against the mockery of resurrection, against invented prohibitions — will draw on these three premises. The reader who holds them firmly will find the rest of the sūrah unfolding from them as naturally as branches from a trunk.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:4

> **Whenever a sign comes to them from their Lord, they turn away from it.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Doctrine to Diagnosis**

The first three verses laid out what is true about God. Verse 4 begins to describe how the deniers respond to that truth. The shift is signaled by a change of grammatical person: the opening verses addressed the listeners directly ("created *you*," "*your* secret"), but now the Qur'an speaks about them in the third person ("come unto *them*," "*they* turned away"). Classical rhetoricians call this shift *iltifāt*, and here it functions as a kind of turning away from those who have themselves turned away. The Qur'an speaks about them rather than to them, as though presenting their case to a third party for judgment.

**What Is Meant by "Sign"?**

The word *āyah* (plural *āyāt*) is one of the most important terms in the Qur'an. Its root sense is a mark or indicator that points beyond itself to something else. The Qur'an uses it in three overlapping ways: for the verses of revelation (each verse is an *āyah*), for the phenomena of creation (the sun, the moon, rain, the alternation of night and day), and for evidentiary miracles given to prophets. The commentators understand the "signs" in this verse in all three senses. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the signs include the proofs of God's Oneness in the created order, the revealed verses of the Qur'an, and the miracles shown by the Prophet ﷺ such as the splitting of the moon.

The phrase "from among the signs of their Lord" (*min āyāti rabbihim*) is significant on two counts. First, the partitive *min* ("from among") indicates that no single sign, of whatever kind, moved them — not one out of the many. Second, the signs are attributed to "their Lord" — the One who created them and sustains them — which deepens the wrongness of their rejection. They are not ignoring a stranger's evidence; they are ignoring the messages of their own Master.

**The Habit of Turning Away**

The verse says that they *turned away* (*muʿriḍīn*). The word *iʿrāḍ* means to turn one's side (*ʿurḍ*) toward something, to present one's shoulder instead of one's face. It is the physical posture of someone who does not wish to engage. This is a specific kind of rejection. It is not the rejection of someone who examined the evidence and found it wanting; it is the rejection of someone who will not look. The Qur'an describes this posture in several places:

> "How many signs in the heavens and the earth do they pass by with indifference" (12:105)

> "Whenever Our revelations are recited to them, they turn away in arrogance as if they did not hear them, as if there is deafness in their ears" (31:7)

The verse's grammar — "never did a sign come... but that they turned away" (*wa mā ta'tīhim min āyatin... illā kānū ʿanhā muʿriḍīn*) — describes a settled pattern, not an occasional lapse. The construction *kānū* + active participle indicates a continuous state. Turning away had become their character.

**Why Signs Fail to Convince**

This verse raises an important question. If God's signs are clear, why do they not persuade? The answer the Qur'an gives, here and throughout, is that persuasion requires two things: a clear sign and a willing recipient. The sign supplies the first; the recipient must supply the second. A person who has decided in advance not to be convinced cannot be convinced by evidence, because he does not examine the evidence — he turns away from it.

Ibn Kathīr connects this verse to the broader Qur'anic teaching that the disbelievers' problem was never a shortage of proof. Al-Rāzī frames the point philosophically: the signs are causes of guidance only for those who reflect on them, and reflection is a voluntary act. The idolaters' failure was therefore a failure of will, not of intellect. This is why the Qur'an holds them responsible. One cannot be blamed for failing to understand what one could not understand, but one can be blamed for refusing to look at what one could have seen.

The same principle governs human life generally. A patient who refuses to open the test results cannot claim he was never informed. A person who avoids every conversation about his behavior cannot claim no one warned him. Turning away is itself a choice, and the person who makes it is responsible for the consequences of what he chose not to know.

**The Historical Context in Makkah**

The Quraysh were shown many signs. They heard the Qur'an, whose eloquence they themselves acknowledged in private — al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, one of their leaders, famously admitted that it was unlike any poetry or speech of men, and then publicly called it sorcery (as recorded in the commentary on 74:18–25). They witnessed the splitting of the moon:

> "The Hour has drawn near and the moon was split ˹in two˺" (54:1–2)

They knew the Prophet's ﷺ character; they had called him al-Amīn, the Trustworthy, before his mission began. Yet each sign was met with a new excuse. The pattern this verse describes was not theoretical; it was the daily experience of the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah.

**The Cross-References in the Prophetic Narratives**

The Qur'an uses almost identical language about earlier nations:

> "Whatever new reminder comes to them from the Most Compassionate, they always turn away from it" (26:5)

> "Whenever a sign comes to them from their Lord, they turn away from it" (36:46)

The repetition is intentional. By using the same words for the Quraysh that it uses for the destroyed peoples of the past, the Qur'an places the Quraysh on the same trajectory. The following verses (5–6) will make this explicit by recalling the fate of earlier generations. The turning away described in verse 4 is thus a warning sign in itself — the first symptom of a disease whose end is known.

**Turning Away in Modern Form**

The phenomenon this verse describes has not disappeared. Modern people are surrounded by the signs of creation in more detail than any previous generation — the structure of the cell, the fine-tuning of physical constants, the vastness of space, the intricacy of the human brain. Yet many manage to study these things closely without ever asking what they point to. The verse suggests that this is not a failure of information but a chosen orientation. The same data that leads one scientist to awe and worship leads another to indifference; the difference lies not in the data but in whether one is facing it or presenting one's shoulder to it.

There is also a subtler form of turning away that affects believers. A Muslim may recite verses daily and pass by the signs of creation constantly while his heart remains unmoved because he has stopped *looking*. The remedy the Qur'an prescribes is *tadabbur* — deliberate reflection:

> "Or are there locks upon their hearts" (47:24)

The verse before us is thus both an indictment of the deniers and a caution to the believers: signs are everywhere, but they benefit only the one who turns toward them.

**The Mercy Hidden in the Complaint**

Finally, notice that the verse's tone is not merely condemnatory. Its structure — "Whenever a sign comes to them from their Lord, they turn away from it." (6:4) — implies that signs *kept coming*. God did not send one sign and then leave them. He sent sign after sign, and they turned away from each. This persistence is itself a manifestation of the mercy that the sūrah will soon name explicitly: "He has taken upon Himself to be Merciful." (6:12). The complaint in verse 4 is the complaint of One who has given every opportunity and been refused every time. Understanding this makes the coming warnings of verses 5–6 feel not like cruelty but like the last words of a patient physician to a patient who would not take the medicine.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:5

> **They have indeed rejected the truth when it came to them, so they will soon face the consequences of their ridicule.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Turning Away to Active Denial**

Verse 4 described the idolaters' passive posture: turning their shoulders to every sign. Verse 5 records the next stage: *fa-qad kadhdhabū bi'l-ḥaqq* — "they have indeed denied the truth." The particle *fa* ("so," "then") marks this as the consequence of the previous verse. One who habitually refuses to look at evidence will eventually move from ignoring it to calling it false; avoidance hardens into rejection. This progression is psychologically exact. The person who will not read a letter eventually claims the letter says nothing important; the person who will not consider an argument eventually claims the argument is a lie.

The verb *kadhdhaba* (Form II of *k-dh-b*) means not merely to disbelieve but to declare something a lie — to accuse it of falsehood. The idolaters did not simply withhold assent from the Qur'an; they publicly branded it as sorcery, poetry, or fabrication. This is the specific sin the verse records.

**"The Truth When It Came unto Them"**

The object of their denial is *al-ḥaqq* — the Truth, with the definite article. The commentators identify this primarily as the Qur'an, and by extension the Prophet ﷺ who brought it and the message of God's Oneness that it contained. Al-Ṭabarī explains that it refers to the Qur'an and the Messenger who came with it. The word *ḥaqq* carries the sense of what is real, established, and rightfully owed — the opposite of *bāṭil*, what is empty and void. To call *al-ḥaqq* a lie is thus a reversal of reality itself.

The phrase "when it came unto them" (*lammā jā'ahum*) sharpens the charge. Their denial was not of some distant or abstract truth they had never encountered; it was of the truth that had arrived at their doorstep, in their own language, through a man they knew. This removes any excuse of ignorance or distance. The Qur'an makes this same point about the People of the Book:

> "Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists, when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it" (2:89)

The greater the clarity of the truth and the nearer its arrival, the graver the denial.

**"Tidings Will Soon Come to Them"**

The second half of the verse turns from their action to its consequence: *fa-sawfa ya'tīhim anbā'u mā kānū bihi yastahzi'ūn* — "so there will soon come to them the news of that which they used to mock." The word *anbā'* (singular *naba'*) means significant news, tidings of consequence. The particle *sawfa* indicates the future with a note of certainty — not "perhaps," but "it will surely come, in time."

There is a deliberate wordplay in the structure. They mocked *news* — the Prophet's ﷺ reports about resurrection, judgment, and punishment — and so *news* will come to them: not reports this time, but the actual events of which the reports spoke. The verb *istahza'a* means to ridicule, to treat as a joke. Their mockery will be answered by the arrival of the very reality they laughed at.

**What "Tidings" Are Meant: This World or the Next?**

The commentators divide over the specific referent. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī report that many early authorities understood it as a worldly punishment, specifically the defeat of the Quraysh at the Battle of Badr in the second year after the Hijrah, when the leaders who had mocked the Prophet ﷺ — Abū Jahl, ʿUtbah, Shaybah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf and others — were killed and thrown into a dry well. Ibn Kathīr inclines to this reading, noting that the verse threatens something that will come "soon" (*sawfa*) and that Badr fulfilled it within a few years of the verse's revelation. Al-Zamakhsharī allows that it may refer to punishment in this world or in the next, since both are "news" of what they mocked.

The two readings need not be opposed. The idolaters mocked both the warning of worldly destruction (like that which befell earlier nations) and the warning of the Hereafter. Both would come. Badr was the first installment; the Day of Judgment is the final one. After Badr, the Prophet ﷺ stood at the well where the bodies of the Quraysh leaders had been cast and addressed them by name:

> "O Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, O Umayyah ibn Khalaf, O ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, O Shaybah ibn Rabīʿah! Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true." (al-Bukhārī 3976; Muslim 2874)

The "news" had come to them, exactly as the verse foretold.

**The Recurring Formula**

The phrase "that which they used to mock" (*mā kānū bihi yastahzi'ūn*) is a refrain in the Qur'an, appearing in nearly identical form in more than a dozen places:

> "And the evil ˹consequences˺ of their deeds will unfold before them, and they will be overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule" (39:48)

> "˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule" (21:41)

> "Then the evil ˹consequences˺ of their deeds overtook them, and they were overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule" (16:34)

The consistency of the formula establishes a law of history: mockery of divine warnings does not cancel the warned-of event; it only ensures that the mocker meets it unprepared. Al-Rāzī observes that mockery is the lowest form of response to an argument, because it substitutes contempt for reasoning. A person who mocks has not refuted anything; he has only announced that he will not take the matter seriously. When the matter then proves real, his laughter is turned against him.

**The Psychology of Mockery**

Why did the Quraysh mock rather than argue? The Qur'an gives the answer indirectly: mockery is what one resorts to when one cannot refute but does not want to submit. It is a social weapon rather than an intellectual one. By laughing at the Prophet ﷺ, the Quraysh leaders reassured their followers that the message need not be considered. This is how entrenched interests have always dealt with inconvenient truths — not by disproving them but by making belief in them socially embarrassing.

The Qur'an notes elsewhere that the mockers themselves will be mocked:

> "Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance" (2:15)

And it warns believers against the temptation to remain in the company of mockers:

> "And when you come across those who ridicule Our revelations, do not sit with them unless they engage in a different topic" (6:68)

For a believer today, the verse offers guidance on how to respond when faith is ridiculed. The correct response is neither anxiety nor retaliation but patience grounded in certainty: the news will come. What is mocked today will be evident tomorrow. This is not a threat one makes to others; it is a fact one rests in oneself.

**The Certainty of Consequences**

The deeper principle of the verse is that denial does not alter reality. A person may deny a debt, but the debt remains. A person may laugh at a weather warning, but the storm arrives on schedule. The idolaters' denial of the truth changed nothing about the truth; it changed only their relationship to it — from potential recipients of its mercy to certain recipients of its warning. The verse does not say "they will be punished for mocking"; it says "the news of what they mocked will come to them." The consequence is not an external penalty added to their mockery; it is simply the arrival of what they mocked. Reality was always coming. Their mockery only determined how it would find them.

**The Balance Between Warning and Hope**

It should be noted that the verse speaks of what "will soon come," not of what has already been sealed. In the years between this verse's revelation in Makkah and the Battle of Badr, several of those who had mocked the Prophet ﷺ repented and embraced Islam — most famously ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who had once set out to kill him. The warning was real, but the door was open until the news actually arrived. This is characteristic of Qur'anic warnings: they are meant to change conduct, not merely to announce doom. The person who hears "tidings will soon come" and takes it seriously has, by that very act, stepped out of the category of those who mock.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:6

> **Have they not seen how many ˹disbelieving˺ peoples We destroyed before them? We had made them more established in the land than you. We sent down abundant rain for them and made rivers flow at their feet. Then We destroyed them for their sins and replaced them with other peoples.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Argument from History**

Having warned in verse 5 that "tidings will soon come," the Qur'an now supplies the evidence that such tidings do come. It appeals to history — specifically to the ruins of earlier civilizations that the Arabs knew well. The rhetorical question *a-lam yaraw* ("have they not seen / considered?") is a standard Qur'anic device for inviting the listener to reflect on something already within his knowledge. The Arabs did not need to be told that ancient peoples had perished; the remains of ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, and the cities of the Yemen lay along their trade routes. The Qur'an asks them to draw the obvious conclusion.

**"How Many a Generation"**

The word *qarn* (plural *qurūn*) is translated "generation" but carries a broader sense. Al-Qurṭubī notes that it can mean a people of a single era, or the span of time itself — a century, or a shorter period depending on usage. The Prophet ﷺ used it in the sense of an age of people: "The best of people are my *qarn*, then those who follow them, then those who follow them" (al-Bukhārī 2652; Muslim 2533). Here it refers to entire communities that flourished and then were removed. The phrase *kam min qarn* ("how many a generation") is exclamatory: not a few, not one or two, but many.

The Qur'an invokes this theme repeatedly, sometimes naming towns and sometimes generations:

> "And sufficient is your Lord as All-Aware and All-Seeing of the sins of His servants" (17:17)

> "˹Imagine˺ how many peoples We destroyed before them, who were far mightier than them" (50:36)

**"Established More Firmly Than We Have Established You"**

The heart of the verse is a comparison. The destroyed peoples were *makkannāhum fi'l-arḍ mā lam numakkin lakum* — "established on the earth in a way We have not established you." The verb *makkana* means to give a firm footing, power, and settled position. It is the root of *tamkīn*, the granting of authority and stability. The Quraysh prided themselves on their status as custodians of the Kaʿbah, their trade caravans to Syria and Yemen, and their security in the sacred precinct. The verse tells them plainly: others had more.

Note the shift in address within the verse. It began by speaking of the idolaters in the third person ("have *they* not seen") and now addresses them directly ("than We have established *you*"). This *iltifāt* brings the warning home. The comparison is not academic; it is personal. If those more powerful than you did not survive their sins, what protects you?

This addresses a specific delusion: the assumption that prosperity is proof of divine favor or of safety. The Qur'an dismantles this assumption in many places, most memorably in the words of Pharaoh, who took his rivers as evidence of his invulnerability:

> "And Pharaoh called out to his people, boasting," (43:51)

Pharaoh's rivers did not save him. The verse before us mentions rivers deliberately — "We made rivers flow beneath them" — to evoke this precedent.

**"We Sent the Sky upon Them with Abundant Rains"**

The phrase *arsalnā al-samā'a ʿalayhim midrāran* is striking. Literally, "We sent the sky upon them pouring." The word *samā'* here means rain, by the common Arabic usage in which the sky is named for what descends from it. *Midrār* is an intensive form meaning abundant, continuous flow. In the desert environment of Arabia, nothing represented prosperity more vividly than abundant rain and flowing rivers. The verse thus describes the destroyed peoples at the height of material blessing: settled, powerful, watered from above, irrigated from below.

Al-Ṭabarī explains that this description serves to show that their strength and wealth were of no avail against God's decree. Ibn Kathīr notes the pattern: God grants a people abundance, they use it in disobedience, and then He seizes them. The Qur'an describes this process in detail:

> "But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair" (6:44)

This is the phenomenon the scholars call *istidrāj* — leading someone on by degrees. Prosperity is not always a reward; sometimes it is a rope being paid out.

**"Then We Destroyed Them for Their Sins"**

The cause of destruction is stated exactly: *bi-dhunūbihim* — "for their sins." The preposition *bi* here indicates cause. They were not destroyed arbitrarily, nor because of their prosperity, nor because God's favor simply shifted. They were destroyed because of what they did. This is a statement of divine justice. The Qur'an insists on this principle without exception:

> "And your Lord ˹O Prophet˺ would never destroy a society unjustly while its people were acting rightly" (11:117)

> "We did not wrong them, rather they wronged themselves" (11:101)

The word *dhunūb* (singular *dhanb*) is a general term for sins. In the context of the sūrah, the primary sin is the one the opening verses named: ascribing equals to God, turning from His signs, and denying the truth when it came. But the ruined peoples were also known for specific wrongs — the arrogance of ʿĀd, the violence of Thamūd, the indecency of Lot's people, the fraud of Midian. Sin in belief and sin in conduct travel together.

**"And Brought into Being after Them Another Generation"**

The verse closes with a reminder that God's work does not end with destruction: *wa ansha'nā min baʿdihim qarnan ākharīn*. The verb *ansha'a* means to originate, to raise up. God removes one people and raises another in their place. This teaches two things. First, no people is indispensable; the world does not stop when a proud nation falls. Second, God is not dependent on any particular community to carry His purpose forward. The Qur'an states this as a general principle:

> "If it is His Will, He can remove you altogether, O humanity, and replace you with others" (4:133)

> "If you ˹still˺ turn away, He will replace you with another people" (47:38)

For the Quraysh, who saw themselves as the permanent center of Arabian religious and commercial life, this was a sobering thought. Within a generation of the verse's revelation, the very same Makkah would be the center of a monotheistic community, and the old order would be gone.

**The Logic of the Warning**

The verse's argument can be stated as a simple syllogism. Peoples stronger than you were destroyed for their sins. You are committing the same sins. Therefore you have no rational basis for expecting a different outcome. What made this argument compelling to its first audience was that the premises were undeniable: the ruins existed, and the Quraysh's own idolatry and mockery were public facts. The only escape from the conclusion was to abandon the sins — which is precisely what the verse aims to produce.

Al-Rāzī notes that the appeal to history is one of the Qur'an's most effective persuasive tools because it does not rely on any premise the listener might dispute. One cannot argue with a ruin.

**Ruins as Reminders**

The Islamic tradition developed a whole literature of reflection on ruins (*al-iʿtibār bi'l-āthār*). The Prophet ﷺ himself modeled this. When the Muslims passed through the ruined dwellings of Thamūd at al-Ḥijr on the way to Tabūk, he told them:

> "Do not enter upon these people who were punished unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them." (al-Bukhārī 433; Muslim 2980)

The correct response to a ruin is not tourism but reflection: these were people like us, and this is what became of them.

**Application to Individuals and Nations Today**

The verse speaks of nations, but its logic applies to individuals as well. A person may be firmly established — healthy, wealthy, respected — and imagine that his position guarantees his future. The verse reminds him that others more established than he have fallen, and that establishment is a gift with conditions. For nations, the lesson is equally direct. Modern civilizations possess power and prosperity beyond anything the ancients dreamed of; the verse's comparison ("more firmly than We have established you") is if anything more pointed now. Rain and rivers have become dams and pipelines; walled towns have become cities of glass. None of it alters the principle. Sins bring ruin; and after ruin, God raises another generation.

The verse is not a counsel of despair but a call to correction. The word "then" (*fa*) in "then We destroyed them for their sins" implies an interval — a period during which the sins accumulated and warnings were given. That interval is the space in which repentance is possible. The Quraysh were in that interval when this verse was revealed. Every reader of the verse is in that interval now.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:7

> **Had We sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ a revelation in writing and they were to touch it with their own hands, the disbelievers would still have said, “This is nothing but pure magic!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Anticipating the Demand for a Physical Scripture**

The idolaters of Makkah repeatedly demanded that the Prophet ﷺ produce a tangible, physical miracle. One of their demands was for a written book descending visibly from the sky — something they could hold and see with their eyes. The Qur'an records this request in their own words:

> "or until you have a house of gold, or you ascend into heaven—and even then we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book that we can read" (17:93)

> "If only the Quran had been sent down to him all at once" (25:32)

Verse 7 responds by describing a hypothetical scenario in which God grants precisely this demand — and then predicting the result. The rhetorical structure is a conditional: "Had We sent down..." (*wa law nazzalnā*), with the consequence "those who disbelieve would have said..." The verse is thus a diagnosis. It tells the Prophet ﷺ that the problem was never the form of the evidence; the problem was the state of the recipients.

**The Vocabulary of Tangibility**

The verse piles up details to emphasize how concrete this hypothetical book would be. *Kitāban fī qirṭās* — "a book on parchment." The word *qirṭās* refers to the material on which writing was done: papyrus, parchment, or paper. This is not a heavenly tablet perceived in a vision; it is a physical document. *Fa-lamasūhu bi-aydīhim* — "so that they touched it with their hands." Touch is the most concrete of the senses. One can doubt what one sees or hears, attributing it to illusion or imagination; but what one holds in one's hands leaves less room for such doubt. The verse describes maximum sensory certainty.

Al-Zamakhsharī draws attention to the choice of "touch" rather than "see." The Makkans had claimed that the Prophet's ﷺ experiences were the product of a disordered imagination, and that if they themselves saw something they might believe. The verse goes beyond seeing to touching, removing even the excuse that their eyes had deceived them. And still, the verse says, they would have called it sorcery.

**"This Is Naught but Manifest Sorcery"**

The predicted response is *in hādhā illā siḥrun mubīn* — "this is nothing but obvious magic." This was the standard accusation the deniers leveled at every prophet's miracle. The Qur'an records it against Moses:

> "But when Moses came to them with Our clear signs, they said ˹arrogantly˺," (28:36)

Against Jesus:

> "How I prevented the Children of Israel from harming you when you came to them with clear proofs and the disbelievers among them said," (5:110)

And against Muhammad ﷺ at the splitting of the moon:

> "Yet, whenever they see a sign, they turn away, saying," (54:2)

Why is "sorcery" the universal excuse? Because it is the one explanation that acknowledges the extraordinary nature of what was seen while denying its meaning. Calling something sorcery admits that it was beyond ordinary explanation but reassigns the cause from God to trickery. It is the perfect device for someone who cannot deny the phenomenon but refuses its implication. Al-Rāzī notes that the accusation of sorcery is thus a confession: one does not call an ordinary event magic.

**The Futility of Miracles for the Unwilling**

The central teaching of the verse is that no evidence can compel belief in a person determined not to believe. This may seem discouraging, but it is realistic and it protects against a specific error. Many people imagine that if only God gave them an undeniable sign, they would believe. The verse says that "undeniable" is not a property of signs but of hearts. A sign is denied by anyone who wishes to deny it, no matter how clear.

The Qur'an makes this explicit elsewhere:

> "still they would say," (15:14–15)

> "even if every sign were to come to them—until they see the painful punishment" (10:96–97)

Ibn Kathīr explains that these verses describe people whose obstinacy has reached the point where God's judgment against them has been sealed — not arbitrarily, but as the consequence of their own persistent refusal. They have trained themselves to disbelieve, and the training holds against any input.

**Why God Did Not Send Such a Book**

A natural question arises: if God could have sent a physical book, why did He not, even if some would reject it? The commentators give several reasons. First, as the verse itself says, it would have made no difference to the hardened. Second, verse 8 will add that granting such demands for overwhelming signs carries a consequence: when the decisive sign is given and rejected, the punishment follows immediately, with no further respite. God's withholding of the sign was therefore an act of mercy — it kept the door of repentance open. Third, the Qur'an as it was revealed — orally, in stages, in the language of its hearers — was itself a sign of a higher order than a parchment falling from the sky. A book dropping from heaven proves that something unusual happened; a book whose every verse displays unmatched eloquence, whose predictions come true, and whose teaching transforms those who accept it proves something about its Author. The Qur'an makes this point when it answers the demand for signs:

> "Is it not enough for them that We have sent down to you the Book, ˹which is˺ recited to them" (29:50–51)

**Historical Example: Those Who Saw and Denied**

The Prophet ﷺ did perform physical miracles witnessed by many: the splitting of the moon, water flowing from between his fingers, the multiplication of food, the weeping of the tree trunk. Al-Bukhārī records from Anas ibn Mālik:

> "The Prophet ﷺ was brought a vessel of water while he was at al-Zawrā', and he placed his hand in it, and water began to gush from between his fingers, and the people performed ablution." (al-Bukhārī 3572; Muslim 2279)

Yet the Makkan leaders who witnessed the moon split said, "Muhammad has bewitched us," and sent to ask travelers arriving from outside whether they had seen it — and when travelers confirmed it, they still called it sorcery. History confirmed the verse's prediction exactly. This is the empirical basis for the Qur'an's claim: it did not merely theorize that signs would be rejected; it observed them being rejected.

**The Lesson for the Prophet — and for Those Who Call to Truth**

The verse is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ ("Had We sent down unto *thee*"). Its purpose is partly consolation. The Prophet ﷺ was pained by his people's rejection and sometimes wondered whether a greater sign might win them. God tells him that it would not — that the fault lay in them and not in any deficiency of his message. This freed him from a burden he was never meant to carry. His duty was to convey clearly, not to compel results.

The same principle applies to anyone who tries to bring truth to others: a parent to a stubborn child, a teacher to a resistant student, a friend to someone in denial. There is a point beyond which more evidence does not help, because the resistance is not evidential. Recognizing this point prevents both frustration and the temptation to compromise the message in hopes of acceptance. One conveys with clarity and sincerity, then leaves the outcome to God.

**Self-Examination**

Finally, the verse invites the reader to examine his own demand for signs. When a person says, "If God showed me a miracle I would believe," he should ask honestly whether that is true — or whether he has already decided and is merely postponing the admission. The Qur'an's diagnosis is that the demand for tangible proof is often a way of avoiding the proof already present. The heavens and the earth, the rain and the rivers, the seed and the soul, are already in one's hands. A person who has touched all of these and not believed would not have believed a parchment either.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:8

> **They say, “Why has no ˹visible˺ angel come with him?” Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have certainly been settled ˹at once˺, and they would have never been given more time ˹to repent˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Demand: Send an Angel**

Verse 7 addressed the demand for a written book. Verse 8 takes up a second and equally common demand: that an angel be sent down with the Prophet ﷺ, or instead of him, to confirm his message. The Qur'an records this demand in the idolaters' own voice in several places:

> "And they say ˹mockingly˺," (25:7)

> "or until you have a house of gold, or you ascend into heaven—and even then we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book that we can read" (17:93)

> "If only a treasure had been sent down to him, or an angel had come with him" (11:12)

The demand had a surface logic. If God truly wished to send a message, why not send it through one of His heavenly servants, whose appearance would settle every doubt? A human messenger — eating, walking in the market, subject to hunger and grief — seemed to the Makkans an unlikely vessel for divine speech. The angel demand was their way of saying: give us something unmistakably supernatural.

**"The Matter Would Be Decreed"**

God's answer is severe in its brevity: *wa law anzalnā malakan la-quḍiya al-amr* — "Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided." The word *al-amr*, "the matter," here means the affair of their judgment — their punishment or destruction. The verb *quḍiya* is in the passive, meaning it would be finished, sealed, executed. *Thumma lā yunẓarūn* — "then they would not be granted respite." The verb *anẓara* means to grant delay, to give time. No delay would remain.

The commentators explain why. Al-Ṭabarī reports the understanding of the early authorities: the sending down of an angel in his true form is the kind of sign that leaves no possibility of doubt. God's established way (*sunnah*) with nations is that when such a decisive sign is given and the people still reject it, the punishment follows at once, because they have exhausted every excuse. This is the pattern in the story of Ṣāliḥ and the she-camel: the people of Thamūd demanded a sign, the camel was brought forth from the rock, they hamstrung it, and within three days they were destroyed (11:64–67). The same applied to the table sent down to the disciples of Jesus:

> "I am sending it down to you" (5:115)

Al-Zamakhsharī adds a second explanation, also recorded by al-Qurṭubī: the very sight of an angel in his true form might overwhelm and destroy human beings, whose constitution cannot bear it. The Prophet ﷺ himself, when he saw Gabriel in his true form filling the horizon, was shaken (see 53:5–10 and the ḥadīth in al-Bukhārī 4855 and Muslim 174). Ordinary people would not survive the encounter.

**Withholding the Angel as Mercy**

The verse reveals something unexpected: God's refusal to grant the idolaters' demand was an act of mercy toward them. They asked for something that would have ended their opportunity to repent. By withholding it, God kept them alive and kept the door open. This is a recurring theme in the sūrah, which will shortly declare that God "He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together for the Day of Judgment— about which there is no doubt" (6:12) and will describe how He delays punishment so that people may return.

The point deserves reflection. People often complain that God does not make Himself more obvious. The verse suggests that God's restraint is calibrated to human welfare. A sign so overwhelming that it removes all freedom would also remove all merit from belief and all possibility of gradual repentance. The measure of clarity God provides is enough to guide the sincere and enough to leave the insincere responsible — but not so much that it forecloses the future of those who might yet turn. Ibn Kathīr summarizes: had the angel been sent and they disbelieved, they would have been seized at once, as was God's way with those before them who demanded signs and then rejected them.

**The Nature of Faith and Its Testing**

Underlying this verse is a principle about the nature of faith. The Qur'an describes faith as belief in the Unseen (*al-ghayb*), and it describes this world as a place of testing:

> "˹He is the One˺ Who created death and life in order to test which of you is best in deeds" (67:2)

A test requires that the answer not be forced. If an angel stood visibly beside every prophet, faith would no longer be a moral act; it would be mere acknowledgment of the obvious, like admitting the sun is shining. The Qur'an states that on the Day of Judgment, when the Unseen becomes seen, belief will no longer be accepted:

> "Are they awaiting the coming of the angels, or your Lord ˹Himself˺, or some of your Lord" (6:158)

The angel demand was, in effect, a demand to skip the test and go straight to the answer key. The verse says that if the answer key is given, the test is over — and with it, the grading.

**"Respite" and Its Value**

The word *lā yunẓarūn* points to a great gift that is easy to overlook: time. The idolaters were living in a period of respite (*naẓrah*, *imhāl*) during which they could reconsider. Many of them used it. Among the fiercest opponents of the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah were men who later became pillars of Islam: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Khālid ibn al-Walīd, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, ʿIkrimah ibn Abī Jahl, Abū Sufyān. Had God granted the demand for an angel in the early years, none of these would have had the years they needed. The verse thus points to the real value of divine patience: not merely that punishment is delayed, but that lives are changed within the delay.

The Qur'an describes God's patience as a settled way:

> "If Allah were to punish people ˹immediately˺ for what they have committed, He would not have left a single living being on earth" (35:45)

**Angels in Human Experience**

It should be noted that angels did appear to the Prophet ﷺ and, on occasion, to others — but in human form. Gabriel came as a man to teach the Companions their religion, in the famous ḥadīth in which he sat with his knees against the Prophet's ﷺ knees and asked about Islam, faith, and excellence (Muslim 8). He appeared to Mary "as a well-proportioned man" (19:17). The angels came to Abraham and Lot as guests. In each case they took human form precisely so that the encounter would be bearable and the test would remain intact. Verse 9 will make this the explicit answer to the angel demand.

**The Principle Applied**

For the reader today, the verse warns against a particular kind of bargaining with God: "If You do this, then I will believe / obey / repent." Such bargains misunderstand the relationship. God has already provided what is needed for belief. To demand more is not to seek certainty but to postpone commitment — and to demand it in the form of an overwhelming sign is to ask, without realizing it, for the end of one's own respite. The wise person uses the time he has rather than demanding proof that would end it.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:9

> **And if We had sent an angel, We would have certainly made it ˹assume the form of˺ a man—leaving them more confused than they already are.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Completing the Answer to the Angel Demand**

Verse 8 explained one reason why an angel was not sent: it would have sealed the matter and ended the respite. Verse 9 adds a second, subtler point. Even if God had chosen to send an angel as a messenger, He would have had to send him in human form — and then the idolaters would be no better off than they were with a human prophet. Their demand, examined closely, defeats itself.

**"We Would Have Sent Him as a Man"**

The verse says *wa law jaʿalnāhu malakan la-jaʿalnāhu rajulan* — "had We made him [the messenger] an angel, We would have made him a man." Al-Ṭabarī explains the necessity: human beings cannot look upon angels in their true form and survive the sight, nor would they be able to receive teaching from beings so unlike themselves. God's wisdom in sending messengers is that they should be of the same kind as those they address, so that they can be seen, heard, followed, and imitated. The Qur'an makes this point directly:

> "Had there been angels walking the earth, well settled, We would have surely sent down for them an angel from heaven as a messenger" (17:95)

The logic is exact. Angels for angels, humans for humans. A messenger must be an example, and one cannot follow the example of a being whose nature one does not share. If an angel does not eat, sleep, feel hunger, suffer loss, or face temptation, how could his conduct model patience under hunger, or restraint under temptation, or gratitude in loss? The human messenger's humanity is not a weakness of the message; it is a requirement of it.

The Qur'an emphasizes this repeatedly regarding the Prophet ﷺ:

> "I am only a man like you, ˹but˺ it has been revealed to me that your God is only One God" (18:110)

> "We never sent any messenger before you ˹O Prophet˺, who did not eat food and go about in market-places" (25:20)

The very features the Makkans found disqualifying — eating, walking in markets — are named as features of *all* messengers.

**"Thus Obscuring for Them That Which They Themselves Obscure"**

The final clause is one of the most compressed in the sūrah: *wa la-labasnā ʿalayhim mā yalbisūn*. The verb *labasa* (in this form) means to confuse, to make obscure, to cover something so that it is not clearly recognized. It is related to *libās*, clothing — the idea is of covering something so that its true nature is hidden. The verse says: had We sent an angel in human form, We would have confused them in the same way they confuse themselves.

The commentators explain the meaning. If an angel came in the form of a man, the idolaters would look at him and say, "This is only a man like us" — precisely what they said about Muhammad ﷺ. They would be back where they started, and their confusion would be compounded, because now they could not tell whether the human figure before them was a man or an angel. Their demand, granted, would produce more obscurity rather than less. Al-Qurṭubī adds a further dimension: the leaders of the idolaters, who deliberately confused their followers about the Prophet ﷺ, would then have a new tool — "see, even this supposed angel is only a man" — and the confusion they spread would be reinforced.

The phrase "that which they themselves obscure" (*mā yalbisūn*) places responsibility where it belongs. The idolaters were the original source of confusion. They confused their followers by calling the Qur'an poetry and the Prophet ﷺ a sorcerer; they confused themselves by refusing to look at clear signs. God's sending an angel in human form would not create new confusion; it would only give their existing confusion something further to feed on. The verse can be read as: "We would have left them in the confusion they had chosen."

**Divine Wisdom in the Form of Revelation**

This verse reveals a principle about how God communicates with humanity. He does not bypass the human condition; He works within it. Revelation comes in human language, through human messengers, in ways that human faculties can receive. This is not a limitation on God but a mercy toward human beings. The Qur'an says of itself:

> "We have not sent a messenger except in the language of his people to clarify ˹the message˺ for them" (14:4)

Ibn Kathīr draws the connection: just as the message must be in the people's language, the messenger must be of the people's kind. Anything else would fail the purpose of communication.

There is an analogy in ordinary teaching. A child learns from a teacher who was once a child, who remembers what confusion feels like, who can sit at the child's level. A teacher who had never been a child and could not understand the child's difficulties would be less effective, not more, however brilliant. The human prophet is the teacher who has walked the road.

**The Prophet's Humanity as Evidence, Not Obstacle**

The Makkans thought that the Prophet's ﷺ ordinary humanity counted against his claim. The Qur'an turns this around. The fact that an ordinary, unlettered man from among them, whose life they had watched for forty years, suddenly began to produce speech of unmatched eloquence, containing knowledge of previous nations he had never studied and predictions that came true, was itself the sign. The Qur'an makes this argument:

> "Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you" (10:16)

His humanity was the control condition that made the miracle of the Qur'an visible. Had he been an angel, the eloquence would have been unremarkable. Because he was a man, it was a proof.

**The Self-Defeating Nature of Insincere Demands**
