The deeper teaching of verses 7–9 taken together is that insincere demands for evidence are structurally self-defeating. The Makkans asked for a book; a book would have been called sorcery. They asked for an angel; an angel would have ended their respite, or, in human form, would have looked like a man and been rejected on the same grounds as the man. There is no configuration of evidence that satisfies someone who does not want to be satisfied. This is why the Qur'an so often shifts from providing signs to examining the condition of the one who demands them.

For anyone who works with people — parents, teachers, counselors, leaders — this is a familiar dynamic. There are objections that seek an answer and objections that seek to avoid one. The first kind is satisfied by information; the second kind generates a new objection for every answer given. Discernment between the two is essential. The Qur'an models this discernment: it answers the demand for signs with an analysis of the demand itself.

**A Note on Angels in Human Form**

The verse's premise — that angels sent to humans take human form — is confirmed throughout the Qur'an and the ḥadīth. Gabriel appeared to Mary "Then We sent to her Our angel, ˹Gabriel,˺ appearing before her as a man, perfectly formed" (19:17). The angels who visited Abraham were taken by him for travelers and offered a roasted calf (11:69–70). The angels who came to Lot appeared as handsome young men, provoking the wickedness of his people (11:77–78). Gabriel came to the Prophet ﷺ in the form of a man to teach the Companions, and sometimes in the form of the Companion Diḥyah al-Kalbī. In each case the human form was necessary for the interaction and left the human observers free to recognize or fail to recognize what they were seeing. The verse simply states the principle that underlay all these events.

**Trusting God's Choice of Means**

The verse invites a posture of trust regarding how God has chosen to guide. He chose a human messenger, a recited book, and a gradual revelation, not because He could not do otherwise but because this was the wise way for beings like us. The one who accepts guidance in the form God actually sent it, rather than demanding a form of his own invention, is the one who receives it. The one who insists on his own conditions receives, in the words of the verse, only more of the confusion he has already chosen.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:10

> **˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Consolation Through Precedent**

After exposing the idolaters' evasions in verses 7–9, the Qur'an turns to console the Prophet ﷺ. The mockery he faced was not new, and its outcome was not uncertain. The verse opens with an emphatic construction — *wa la-qad istuhzi'a bi-rusulin min qablik* — "and indeed, messengers before you were surely mocked." The particles *la* and *qad* together give strong confirmation: this has truly and certainly happened before.

The Prophet ﷺ was a human being with human feelings. The Qur'an elsewhere records that the rejection of his people grieved him deeply:

> "Now, perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death over their denial, if they ˹continue to˺ disbelieve in this message" (18:6)

> "We certainly know that what they say grieves you ˹O Prophet˺" (6:33)

Knowing that Noah, Abraham, Moses, and every prophet before him had been mocked placed his suffering within a pattern. A person who suffers alone suffers more than one who knows that others have walked the same road and come through it. The verse gives the Prophet ﷺ company across the centuries.

**"Messengers" — Not One but Many**

The indefinite plural *rusul* ("messengers") without further specification indicates that mockery was the common lot of the prophets, not an exception. The Qur'an confirms this in a sweeping statement:

> "No messenger ever came to them without being mocked" (36:30)

The stories bear this out. Noah's people mocked him as he built the ark on dry land (11:38). Abraham's people mocked his rejection of their idols and threw him into the fire (21:68). Hūd was called a fool (7:66). Ṣāliḥ was called bewitched (26:153). Shuʿayb was told that his prayer must have taught him to interfere with their wealth (11:87). Moses was called a "A magician or a madman" (51:39). Each of these accounts, known to the Prophet ﷺ through revelation, formed the background of this verse.

**The Vocabulary of Mockery**

The verse uses two related verbs. *Istuhzi'a* means to be ridiculed or made an object of scorn. *Sakhira* (in *alladhīna sakhirū minhum*, "those who scoffed at them") is a near-synonym with a slightly more active sense of contemptuous derision. Both describe treating a person or a message as laughable, unworthy of serious engagement. The pairing of the two words may indicate the thoroughness of the mockery: from casual dismissal to deliberate scorn.

Mockery occupies a specific place in the psychology of rejection. It is what one does when one cannot argue but does not wish to concede. It shifts the ground from truth to status: the mocker positions himself as superior, and the audience as sharing his superiority, so that agreement with the mocked person becomes socially costly. It is thus a tool of social control disguised as humor. The Quraysh leaders used it deliberately, as al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith did when he followed the Prophet's ﷺ gatherings with his own entertainments to draw people away.

**"Beset by That Which They Used to Mock"**

The second half of the verse describes the outcome: *fa-ḥāqa bi'lladhīna sakhirū minhum mā kānū bihi yastahzi'ūn*. The verb *ḥāqa* means to surround, encompass, close in upon — to befall someone inescapably. It is a strong word. The thing they mocked did not merely arrive; it surrounded them so that there was no exit.

The commentators note the precision of "that which they used to mock." The mockers laughed at the warnings of punishment; punishment surrounded them. They laughed at the promise of divine intervention; divine intervention came. The instrument of their downfall was the very thing they had treated as a joke. This exactness is a form of justice: each is met by what he chose to deny. The Qur'an repeats this formula about the mockers of the past, using the same verb *ḥāqa*:

> "Indeed, on the Day it overtakes them, it will not be averted from them, and they will be overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule" (11:8)

> "Then the evil ˹consequences˺ of their deeds overtook them, and they were overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule" (16:34; also 39:48; 40:83; 45:33; 46:26)

**The Historical Fulfillment for the Quraysh**

For the Makkan mockers, the fulfillment came in stages. The most prominent mockers — described in a famous group of five in the commentaries on 15:95 ("Indeed, We are sufficient for you against the mockers") — each met his end in the years before Badr, according to the reports collected by Ibn Isḥāq: al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wā'il, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth, al-Aswad ibn al-Muṭṭalib, and al-Ḥārith ibn Qays. Then at Badr the remaining leaders — Abū Jahl and others — fell. The Prophet's ﷺ address to their bodies in the well (al-Bukhārī 3976; Muslim 2874) marked the moment when what they mocked closed in on them.

Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse, though revealed in Makkah when the Muslims were weak and the mockers powerful, spoke of the mockers' fate as an accomplished fact for earlier nations and as a settled certainty for the present ones. This was itself a test of faith for the Companions: to believe, in the years of weakness, that the pattern would hold.

**The Law Behind the Pattern**

Why does mockery of prophets consistently end this way? The answer lies in what mockery is. To mock a warning is to refuse to prepare for what it warns of. The person who laughs at the fire alarm does not put out the fire; he is simply in the building when it burns. The mockers of the prophets were not punished by some arbitrary decree unrelated to their mockery; their mockery was the very mechanism by which they excluded themselves from the safety the prophets offered. The warning was the door; the mockery was the refusal to walk through it.

This has practical implications for anyone tempted to treat serious matters lightly. Ridicule feels like power because it lets one dismiss without engaging. But it is a false power, because the thing dismissed continues to exist. Al-Rāzī observes that the verse is a warning to the Quraysh delivered in the form of a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ: by telling him what happened to earlier mockers, God tells them what awaits.

**The Prohibition of Mockery for Believers**

The Qur'an's condemnation of mockery is not limited to mockery of prophets. Believers are forbidden to mock one another:

> "Do not let some ˹men˺ ridicule others, they may be better than them, nor let ˹some˺ women ridicule other women, they may be better than them" (49:11)

The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "It is enough evil for a man that he despises his Muslim brother." (Muslim 2564)

The connection to the verse before us is that mockery, wherever it appears, springs from the same root: a false sense of superiority that substitutes contempt for understanding. The person who mocks a prophet and the person who mocks his neighbor share a disposition, even if the gravity of the two acts differs enormously.

**How to Bear Being Mocked**

For a believer who is mocked for his faith, the verse offers a method. First, recognize that this is the ancient experience of the best of humanity — the prophets themselves. Second, understand that mockery is not refutation; it leaves the truth intact. Third, trust that the outcome is with God and does not require retaliation. The Prophet ﷺ modeled this. When the people of Ṭā'if drove him out with stones and mockery, and the angel of the mountains offered to crush them, he replied:

> "Rather, I hope that God will bring forth from their descendants those who will worship God alone and not associate anything with Him." (al-Bukhārī 3231; Muslim 1795)

The verse assured him that the mockers would be encompassed; his own response was to hope for their children. This is the balance the verse teaches: certainty about the justice of the outcome, without personal bitterness in the meantime.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:11

> **Say, “Travel throughout the land and see the fate of the deniers.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First "Say" of the Sūrah**

This verse contains the first of the many commands *qul* ("Say") that characterize Sūrah al-Anʿām. The word occurs more than forty times in this chapter, more than in any other sūrah of comparable length. Each *qul* hands the Prophet ﷺ a specific response to deliver to the idolaters, and together they form a kind of manual of prophetic argument. The first of them is not a statement of doctrine but an invitation to investigate: go and look for yourselves.

**"Journey upon the Earth"**

The command *sīrū fi'l-arḍ* — "Similar situations came to pass before you, so travel throughout the land and see the fate of the deniers" — appears in this exact form in several verses (3:137; 16:36; 27:69; 29:20; 30:42), and in the interrogative form *a-fa-lam yasīrū fi'l-arḍ* ("Have the deniers not travelled through the land to see what was the end of those ˹destroyed˺ before them") in others (12:109; 22:46; 30:9; 35:44; 40:21, 82; 47:10). The repetition marks it as a central Qur'anic method. The Qur'an does not ask for blind acceptance of its claims about the fate of past nations; it asks its listeners to verify them empirically.

The verb *sāra* means to travel, to move through a place. The Arabs were a traveling people. The Quraysh in particular were traders whose caravans went north to Syria and south to Yemen — journeys mentioned in Sūrah Quraysh (106:2). Along these routes lay the ruins of destroyed peoples: the rock-cut dwellings of Thamūd at al-Ḥijr in the north, the remains of the peoples of Lot near the Dead Sea, the ruins of Saba' and the collapsed Ma'rib dam in the south. The command to travel was therefore not asking them to do anything unfamiliar; it was asking them to pay attention to what they already passed.

Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse establishes the legitimacy — even the merit — of travel undertaken for reflection and learning. Travel is not merely for trade or pleasure; it can be an act of worship when its purpose is to draw lessons from what one sees.

**"Behold How the Deniers Fared in the End"**

The object of the journey is *thumma unẓurū kayfa kāna ʿāqibat al-mukadhdhibīn* — "Persist in your ways, for I ˹too˺ will persist in mine" The word *ʿāqibah* means the final outcome, the end result, what a thing comes to. The Qur'an is especially concerned with endings. A nation may prosper for centuries; the question is how it ends. A person may flourish for decades; the question is his *ʿāqibah*. This word will recur in the sūrah (6:135) as the key measure by which lives and communities are evaluated.

The verse specifies "the deniers" (*al-mukadhdhibīn*) — those who called the truth a lie, the same word used in verse 5. This is the link between the passage's abstract warnings and the concrete evidence. Verse 5 said they denied; verse 6 said earlier generations were destroyed; verse 10 said mockers were encompassed by what they mocked; and now verse 11 says: go and see it for yourselves. The argument has moved from assertion to invitation to verify.

**The Empirical Method of the Qur'an**

This verse deserves attention for what it reveals about the Qur'an's approach to belief. It does not merely command; it points to evidence and invites examination. The evidence here is historical and archaeological — the remains of civilizations. The listener is expected to see, reason, and conclude. This is why the classical scholars regarded reflection (*naẓar*) and drawing lessons (*iʿtibār*) as obligations of the intellect, not optional exercises. Al-Rāzī observes that the verse contains a command to reason from the visible to the invisible: from the ruins one sees to the divine law of consequences one cannot see directly.

The Qur'an makes the goal of such travel explicit elsewhere:

> "Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind" (22:46)

The instrument of seeing, in this verse, is not the eye but the heart. Many people pass by ruins and see only stones. The one who "beholds" in the Qur'anic sense sees the people who built them, the warnings they received, the choice they made, and the end they met.

**What the Ruins Teach**

The specific lesson of the ruins is stated across the Qur'an's narratives of destroyed peoples. They were strong (6:6). They were prosperous. They had messengers sent to them. They denied. They were destroyed. And in each case the Qur'an notes that their strength, wealth, and buildings did not save them:

> "Their messengers came to them with clear proofs" (30:9)

The pattern is stated with such regularity that it amounts to a law of history in the Qur'anic view: no civilization survives persistent denial of God and persistent injustice. This is not because God is vindictive but because denial and injustice are self-destructive; they corrode the moral foundations on which any society rests. The ruins are the visible record of this corrosion reaching its conclusion.

**The Prophet's Own Practice**

The Prophet ﷺ practiced what this verse commands. On the expedition to Tabūk in the ninth year after the Hijrah, the army passed through al-Ḥijr, the dwellings of Thamūd. He covered his face with his cloak, hastened his mount, and instructed the Companions:

> "Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves unless you are weeping, lest what befell them befall you." (al-Bukhārī 3380; Muslim 2980)

He also told them not to drink from the wells of Thamūd or use their water for cooking, but to use only the well from which Ṣāliḥ's she-camel had drunk. His conduct shows the correct posture toward such places: not curiosity or pride in one's own superiority, but humility and fear of sharing the fate of those who dwelt there.

**Travel as Education**

The command to travel has been understood by Muslim scholars through the centuries as encouragement to see the world with a purpose. The great Muslim travelers — Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Baṭṭūṭah, and countless students who journeyed for knowledge — cited such verses as their warrant. Travel widens the mind, exposes one to the diversity of God's creation, and, when undertaken reflectively, deepens one's sense of the transience of human power. A person who has seen the ruins of many empires is less likely to be intoxicated by the current one.

**Application in a Modern Setting**

Today, the "journey upon the earth" can be taken literally — the ruins of Petra, Palmyra, the pyramids, Persepolis, and countless other sites are accessible — but it can also be taken through history books, museums, and documentaries, which bring the record of the past to those who cannot travel. The verse's demand is not the physical movement itself but the reflection it enables. A person who reads the history of a fallen empire and asks "why did it fall?" and "am I making the same mistakes?" is obeying the verse.

The modern world tends to view the past as a story of progress, with each age superior to the last. The verse suggests a different lens: the past as a series of warnings. Every fallen civilization once believed itself permanent. The command to "behold how the deniers fared in the end" asks us to hold that fact steadily in view — not to become fearful, but to become honest about what actually preserves a people and what actually destroys it.

**The Tone of the Command**

Note that the verse does not say "tell them they will be destroyed." It says "tell them to go and look." This is a dignified form of argument. It treats the opponent as capable of reason and invites him to reach the conclusion on his own. It also removes the argument from the realm of the Prophet's ﷺ personal claim and places it in the realm of public, verifiable fact. Anyone could travel; anyone could see. The verse thus embodies a confidence that the truth can withstand examination — a confidence that runs throughout Sūrah al-Anʿām.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:12

> **Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “To whom belongs everything in the heavens and the earth?” Say, “To Allah!” He has taken upon Himself to be Merciful. He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together for the Day of Judgment— about which there is no doubt. But those who have ruined themselves will never believe.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question the Prophet Answers Himself**

The verse contains two commands to "Say." In the first, the Prophet ﷺ is told to pose a question: "To whom belongs what is in the heavens and the earth?" In the second, he is told to answer it himself: "To God." This structure — question followed immediately by the questioner's own answer — is used in Arabic rhetoric when the answer is so obvious that the opponent cannot dispute it, and the speaker answers on his behalf to move the argument forward. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that the Prophet ﷺ was to answer before they could, because the answer was already established in their own minds and there was no other possible reply.

The Makkan idolaters, as noted at verse 1, acknowledged that Allāh was the Creator and Owner of the heavens and the earth:

> "If you ask them ˹O Prophet˺ who created the heavens and the earth, they will certainly say," (39:38)

The question is therefore not seeking information; it is establishing a shared premise from which the rest of the verse's argument will follow. If everything belongs to God, then He alone has authority over it, He alone can be relied upon, and He alone determines its end.

**"Whatsoever Is in the Heavens and on the Earth"**

The phrase *mā fi'l-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* uses *mā* ("what," "whatsoever"), which in Arabic typically refers to non-rational things, though it can encompass all. The commentators note that this comprehensive form includes every being and every thing — the stars, the angels, the mountains, the seas, the animals, human beings, and the idols the Makkans worshipped, which were themselves carved from stones that belong to God. The argument against idolatry is contained in the very phrasing: whatever you worship besides God is itself something that belongs to God. One does not petition a possession instead of its owner.

**"He Has Prescribed Mercy for Himself"**

The next clause is one of the most important theological statements in the Qur'an: *kataba ʿalā nafsihi al-raḥmah* — "He has written mercy upon Himself." The verb *kataba* means to write, and by extension to prescribe, ordain, or make binding. When used with *ʿalā* ('upon'), it indicates obligation: something written upon someone is required of him. The Qur'an uses this form for religious duties: "Fasting is prescribed for you—as it was for those before you—so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺" (2:183). Here, astonishingly, God uses it of Himself. He has made mercy obligatory — upon Himself.

The phrase appears only twice in the Qur'an, both times in this sūrah (here and at 6:54). No other attribute is described this way. God does not say He has "prescribed justice upon Himself" or "prescribed power upon Himself," though He is just and powerful. Mercy alone is singled out as a self-imposed commitment. The commentators draw the conclusion that mercy holds a unique and supreme place among the divine attributes as they relate to creation.

The ḥadīth literature confirms and expands this. The Prophet ﷺ reported:

> "When God created the creation, He wrote in His Book — and it is with Him above the Throne — 'Indeed My mercy prevails over My wrath.'" (al-Bukhārī 3194; Muslim 2751)

Another version reads:

> "Indeed My mercy has preceded My wrath." (Muslim 2751)

Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "God has one hundred parts of mercy. He sent down one part among the jinn, mankind, animals, and insects; by it they show compassion to one another, by it they show mercy to one another, and by it the wild beast shows tenderness to her young. And God has held back ninety-nine parts of mercy with which He will show mercy to His servants on the Day of Resurrection." (Muslim 2752; al-Bukhārī 6000)

**What Self-Obligation Means for God**

This clause raises a theological question the scholars addressed with care. God is absolutely free; nothing binds Him from outside. What does it mean, then, that He "prescribed" mercy upon Himself? The answer is that the obligation is self-imposed and flows from His own nature. Nothing compelled Him; He chose, as an expression of who He is, to make mercy the governing principle of His dealings with creation. Ibn Taymiyyah discussed this in his treatment of divine promises: God's commitments to Himself are absolutely reliable, not because any external law constrains Him but because He does not go back on His word. The Qur'an states:

> "You will certainly gather all humanity for the ˹promised˺ Day—about which there is no doubt" (3:9)

The source commentary observes a further point: for God to prescribe mercy upon Himself, mercy must already be essential to His nature. A being not merciful by nature would not choose to bind himself to mercy. The self-obligation is thus evidence of the essential attribute. God is *al-Raḥmān*, the Most Merciful, in His very essence; the prescribing is the expression of that essence in action.

**Why Mercy Is Mentioned Here**

In the flow of the sūrah, the mention of mercy at this point serves a specific purpose. Verses 4–11 have described the idolaters' denial and mockery and warned of destruction. A listener might ask: if they are so guilty, why does God delay their punishment? The answer is the mercy He has prescribed upon Himself. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī explain that this is why the punishment does not fall immediately: God gives respite so that people may repent and believe. The delay that the idolaters took as evidence of the emptiness of the threat was in fact the operation of divine mercy.

Al-Zamakhsharī offers a broader reading: the mercy God has prescribed includes His undertaking to guide human beings to knowledge of His Oneness, through signs in creation and through messengers. Both readings are complementary. God's mercy is manifest in sending guidance and in delaying punishment for those who reject it, so that they may yet accept.

**"He Will Surely Gather You on the Day of Resurrection"**

The verse continues: *la-yajmaʿannakum ilā yawmi'l-qiyāmati lā rayba fīh*. The emphatic form *la-yajmaʿanna* (with the *lām* of oath and the heavy *nūn* of emphasis) is as strong as Arabic grammar permits: "He will most certainly gather you." The verb *jamaʿa* means to gather or collect. On the Day of Resurrection all humanity, from Adam to the last person born, will be gathered in one place for judgment.

The placement of this clause immediately after the mention of mercy is significant. Mercy explains the delay; but the delay is not indefinite. There will be a gathering. The two truths belong together. God is merciful in giving time; He is just in ensuring that the time ends in an accounting. Neither truth cancels the other. A person who takes only the mercy becomes complacent; a person who takes only the judgment becomes despairing. The verse holds them in balance.

"In which there is no doubt" (*lā rayba fīh*) is a phrase used of the Day of Resurrection in several places (3:9, 3:25, 4:87, 22:7, 40:59, 45:26) and of the Qur'an itself in 2:2. The word *rayb* means unsettling doubt. The Day is not open to reasonable doubt; whatever uncertainty people feel about it is, as verse 2 said, culpable disputation rather than honest inquiry.

**"Those Who Have Lost Their Souls"**

The verse ends: *alladhīna khasirū anfusahum fa-hum lā yu'minūn* — "those who have lost themselves, they do not believe." The verb *khasira* is commercial: to lose in a transaction, to suffer a deficit. The object of the loss is *anfusahum* — their own selves, their own souls. This is the ultimate loss. A merchant may lose his goods and recover; a person who loses himself has nothing left with which to recover. The Qur'an uses this image repeatedly:

> "The ˹true˺ losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on Judgment Day" (39:15)

Two readings of the sentence are recorded. Al-Zamakhsharī reads it as cause and effect: because they have ruined themselves by ascribing partners to God, turning from His signs, and mocking His messenger, they do not believe — their unbelief is the fruit of their self-destruction. Al-Ṭabarī records a reading in which "those who have lost their souls" describes those who will be gathered on the Day: they will be gathered, and among them are those who lost themselves and did not believe. Both readings converge on the same warning: unbelief is not a neutral intellectual position; it is a transaction in which a person trades his own soul for nothing.

**The Balance of Mercy and Judgment in Human Life**

The verse gives believers a framework for understanding their own situation. Every day of life is a day of the mercy God has prescribed upon Himself — a day in which repentance is possible, in which sins can be erased, in which one can improve. And every day brings the gathering closer. The two truths together produce the right disposition: hope without complacency, seriousness without despair. The Prophet ﷺ described the effect of properly understanding God's mercy and justice:

> "If the believer knew what punishment God has, none would hope for His Paradise; and if the disbeliever knew what mercy God has, none would despair of His Paradise." (Muslim 2755)

**Mercy as the Foundation of Trust**

Finally, the verse's statement that God has prescribed mercy upon Himself is the foundation of every believer's confidence in approaching Him. One does not approach an arbitrary power with any hope; one approaches a power that has committed itself to mercy with every hope. This is why the believer can repent after sin, return after straying, and pray after neglect: not because he deserves to be received, but because the One he approaches has bound Himself to receive. The verse is thus not merely a doctrine to be affirmed but the ground on which the whole religious life stands.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:13

> **To Him belongs whatever exists in the day and night. And He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Completing the Statement of Ownership**

Verse 12 declared that to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth — ownership described by *place*. Verse 13 now adds that to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day — ownership described by *time*. Between the two verses, the totality of existence is covered along both of its axes. There is nothing anywhere, and nothing at any time, that falls outside God's dominion. This is a characteristic Qur'anic completeness: the argument leaves no gap through which a rival claim might enter.

**"All That Dwells in the Night and in the Day"**

The verb *sakana* means to be still, to rest, to dwell, to settle. The phrase *mā sakana fi'l-layli wa'l-nahār* has been understood in two ways by the commentators. Al-Ṭabarī explains that *sakana* here means to be contained within — everything that exists within the night and the day, that is, everything that exists in time. Since night and day encompass all time, this means everything that exists at all. On this reading, the verse is a general statement of God's ownership of all temporal beings.

A second reading takes *sakana* in its specific sense of resting or being still, so that the verse refers to everything that finds rest in the night — creatures that sleep — and by implication everything that moves in the day. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the mention of stillness implies its opposite, movement, by a figure of speech common in Arabic in which one of two opposites stands for both. Al-Zamakhsharī suggests that stillness was mentioned rather than movement because the still things are more numerous, or because stillness is a greater blessing to creatures than movement, since every creature seeks rest.

Both readings agree on the conclusion: all creatures, whether they are resting or moving, whether in darkness or in light, belong to God. Nothing escapes His ownership by hiding in the night or by being busy in the day.

**Night and Day as Signs**

The Qur'an frequently pairs night and day as signs of God's power and mercy:

> "And He is the One Who causes the day and the night to alternate, ˹as a sign˺ for whoever desires to be mindful or to be grateful" (25:62)

> "So We made the sign of the night devoid of light, and We made the sign of the day ˹perfectly˺ bright, so that you may seek the bounty of your Lord and know the number of years and calculation ˹of time˺" (17:12)

> "Imagine if Allah were to make the night perpetual for you until the Day of Judgment, which god other than Allah could bring you sunlight" (28:71)

The alternation of night and day is so regular that people cease to notice it, yet the entire rhythm of human life — work and rest, waking and sleep, the counting of days and years — depends on it. The verse invites the listener to consider that the One who owns the night and the day owns him also, since his whole existence unfolds within them.

**Connection to the Opening Verse**

Verse 1 of the sūrah stated that God "made the darknesses and the light." Verse 13 returns to this theme in a new key. Night and day are the darkness and light of daily experience. What verse 1 stated as an act of creation, verse 13 states as a fact of ownership. God did not merely set night and day in motion and step back; whatever exists within them remains His at every moment. This closes off a subtle form of idolatry: the idea that God created the world but does not govern its ongoing details, leaving room for other powers to operate. The verse says no. The night belongs to Him, and so does everything in it; the day belongs to Him, and so does everything in it.

**"And He Is the Hearing, the Knowing"**

The verse closes with two divine names: *al-Samīʿ al-ʿAlīm*. God is the All-Hearing and the All-Knowing. The pairing is deliberate and connects to what preceded it. If God owns everything in the night and the day, then He hears what is said in the darkness of night as clearly as what is said in the light of day, and He knows what happens in the stillness of sleep as fully as what happens in the activity of waking.

The name *al-Samīʿ* is from the root *s-m-ʿ*, to hear. God's hearing encompasses every sound, every whisper, every unspoken plea. The Qur'an says:

> "And He is with you wherever you are." (57:4)

> "Indeed, ˹it is˺ We ˹Who˺ created humankind and ˹fully˺ know what their souls whisper to them, and We are closer to them than ˹their˺ jugular vein" (50:16)

ʿĀ'ishah reported an incident that illustrates the reach of divine hearing. A woman named Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah came to the Prophet ﷺ to complain about her husband, speaking so quietly that ʿĀ'ishah, in the same room, could not hear all she said — and God revealed the opening of Sūrat al-Mujādilah: "Indeed, Allah has heard the argument of the woman who pleaded with you ˹O Prophet˺ concerning her husband, and appealed to Allah" (58:1). ʿĀ'ishah remarked:

> "Praise be to God, whose hearing encompasses all voices. The woman who disputed came to the Prophet ﷺ and was speaking to him while I was in a corner of the house, and I could not hear what she said, and God revealed: 'God has heard...'" (al-Bukhārī, *Kitāb al-Tawḥīd*, chapter heading; al-Nasā'ī 3460; Ibn Mājah 188)

The name *al-ʿAlīm* is from the root *ʿ-l-m*, knowledge. God knows all things — past, present, future, actual and possible, manifest and hidden. Verse 3 already stated that He knows the secret and the public and what each person earns. Verse 13 seals the section with the same reminder.

**Why Hearing and Knowing Are Named Here**

The choice of these two names at this point is instructive. The context is the idolaters' mockery (verses 5, 10) and their demands for signs (verses 7–9). The verse quietly reminds them: everything you said in your gatherings at night, every plan you made, every joke at the Prophet's ﷺ expense, was heard. Every intention behind your demands was known. There is a note of warning in the names, but there is also a note of comfort for the Prophet ﷺ and the believers: the One who owns the night and the day hears the prayers of the persecuted and knows their suffering.

Al-Rāzī observes that the two names together answer any hope of concealment. One might hide an action from human sight by doing it at night; one might hide a word from human hearing by whispering. But to the Hearing, the Knowing, night and whisper are as open as day and shout.

**The Structure of the Two Verses Together**

Verses 12 and 13 form a single argument, closing the quotation opened by "Say" in verse 12. The Prophet ﷺ is to say, in effect: "Everything belongs to God — in every place and at every time. He has committed Himself to mercy. He will gather you for judgment. Those who ruin themselves do not believe. And He hears and knows everything." Each element supports the others. Ownership establishes His right to judge; mercy explains His patience; the gathering guarantees the outcome; hearing and knowledge ensure that the judgment will be accurate. The idolaters are left with no ground on which to stand: they cannot deny His ownership, cannot escape His judgment, and cannot conceal anything from His knowledge.

**Practical Implications of the Night**

There is a specific application of this verse to the believer's life. The night, in Islamic practice, is a time of special nearness to God. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains, and says: 'Who is calling upon Me, that I may answer him? Who is asking Me, that I may give him? Who is seeking My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?'" (al-Bukhārī 1145; Muslim 758)

The verse's statement that "to Him belongs what dwells in the night" gives this practice its foundation. The night is not an empty time when God's attention is elsewhere; it belongs to Him as fully as the day. The believer who rises in the last part of the night is not calling into a void; he is calling to the Hearing, the Knowing, who owns that hour and everything in it.

Conversely, the verse warns against using the night as cover for wrongdoing. The Prophet ﷺ described people who do good deeds by day and then, in the privacy of night, violate God's limits, and said that God would render their deeds like scattered dust (Ibn Mājah 4245, graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Albānī). The night hides nothing from the One who owns it.

**Stillness and Trust**

Finally, the verse's mention of 'dwelling' or 'resting' carries a gentle teaching. Every creature seeks rest, and rest is possible only where there is security. The verse tells the believer that whatever rests in the night rests in God's ownership and under His knowledge. This is the basis of the peace with which a believer can sleep: not because the night is safe in itself, but because the night belongs to the One who never sleeps. The Throne Verse says of Him: "Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him" (2:255). Creatures rest; their Owner watches. The believer entrusts himself to that watching, and finds in it a stillness that the idolater, with his many gods and no real guardian, never knew.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:14

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Will I take any guardian other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, Who provides for all and is not in need of provision?” Say, “I have been commanded to be the first to submit and not be one of the polytheists.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Refusing the Invitation to Compromise**

The Makkan leaders, according to the reports gathered by al-Ṭabarī and others, at various times invited the Prophet ﷺ to a compromise: acknowledge their gods, and they would acknowledge his; or return to the religion of his forefathers, and they would enrich and honor him. This verse gives his answer. It is framed as a rhetorical question — *a-ghayra Allāhi attakhidhu waliyyan* — "Shall I take other than God as a protector?" — with the answer so obvious that no explicit "no" is needed.

The word *walī* is central. It means a protector, guardian, patron, ally — the one to whom a person turns for help and whose authority he accepts. In pre-Islamic Arabia, a person without a *walī* was defenseless; tribal protection was survival. The idolaters' gods were, in their minds, *awliyā'* — patrons who protected them and interceded for them. The verse asks: how could I take as patron anything other than the One who originated the heavens and the earth? The question turns the concept of patronage back on itself. A patron must be more powerful than the one he protects. What could be more powerful than the Creator?

**"The Originator of the Heavens and the Earth"**

The divine name *Fāṭir* is used here. It comes from the root *f-ṭ-r*, whose basic meaning is to split, cleave, or break open. From this comes the sense of originating something by bringing it forth as though splitting it from nothing. The name always appears in the Qur'an in the phrase *Fāṭir al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ*, "Originator of the heavens and the earth" (12:101; 14:10; 35:1; 39:46; 42:11).

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that he did not fully grasp the meaning of *fāṭir* until two Bedouins came to him disputing over a well, and one of them said, "*Anā faṭartuhā*" — "I originated it," meaning "I was the first to dig it." (This report is cited by al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr.) The word thus carries the sense of being the very first to bring something into being, with no precedent.

The same root gives *fiṭrah*, the primordial nature on which God creates every human being:

> "So be steadfast in faith in all uprightness ˹O Prophet˺—the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people" (30:30)

The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Every child is born upon the *fiṭrah*; then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian." (al-Bukhārī 1385; Muslim 2658)

The connection is meaningful. The One who originated the heavens and the earth also originated the human soul with an innate recognition of Him. To take another as protector is thus not only irrational in view of the cosmos but a betrayal of one's own original nature.

**"Who Feeds and Is Not Fed"**

The verse then adds a second description: *wa huwa yuṭʿimu wa lā yuṭʿam* — "and He feeds and is not fed." This phrase does two things at once. It affirms God's provision: every creature that eats is fed by Him. And it affirms His independence: He needs nothing from anyone. Together they define the difference between the Creator and every possible rival. Anything that needs to be fed is dependent, and what is dependent cannot be the ultimate protector.

The Qur'an makes this argument explicitly regarding Jesus and Mary:

> "The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger" (5:75)

To eat is to need; to need is to be a creature. The argument applies equally to the idols of Makkah, which their worshippers "fed" with offerings, and to any object of devotion that must be sustained by its devotees.

The Qur'an also states God's independence from provision as the very purpose of creation being worship and not service to His need:

> "I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me" (51:56–58)

Ibn Kathīr records that the Prophet ﷺ, after a meal, would say:

> "Praise be to God who feeds and is not fed, who has favored us and guided us and given us food and drink, and every good trial He has tried us with." (Ibn Kathīr, citing Aḥmad; a similar wording is in al-Bukhārī 5459: "Praise be to God, abundant, good, blessed praise, not sufficed, not bid farewell, not dispensed with, our Lord")

The phrase "who feeds and is not fed" thus passed from the verse into the daily devotions of the Muslims, reminding them at every meal of the difference between the Provider and the provided.

**Why "Protector" and "Feeder" Belong Together**

The verse pairs the concept of *walī* with the concept of feeding. This is not accidental. In the tribal world of Arabia, the patron was expected to provide for those under his protection; the relationship of protection was also a relationship of sustenance. The verse argues that the only true patron is the only true provider. A god that must be fed cannot feed you; a god that must be protected cannot protect you. The idols were fed by their worshippers and guarded by them from theft and damage. The relationship was upside down: the worshippers were the patrons of their gods. The verse asks the Prophet ﷺ to expose this inversion.

**"I Was Commanded to Be the First of Those Who Submit"**

The second "Say" gives the positive counterpart: *innī umirtu an akūna awwala man aslam* — "I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit." The word *aslama* means to submit, to surrender oneself, to give oneself over entirely. It is the verb from which *Islām* and *Muslim* derive. The Prophet ﷺ does not merely decline the idolaters' gods; he declares his own total submission to God, and he declares it as a command he has received, not a choice he has made on his own initiative.

The commentators offer several readings of "first." Al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī and others explain that he was the first of his own people and generation to submit to God through this revelation, thus leading by example. Al-Ṭabarsī and others suggest "first" in rank — the foremost among those who submit. Others note that he was the first because he alone received the revelation and was therefore the first to embrace it. The readings converge on the idea that the Prophet ﷺ is not asking his people to do something he has not himself done. He submitted first; he calls them to follow.

The phrase echoes what Moses said after witnessing God's manifestation:

> "I turn to You in repentance and I am the first of the believers" (7:143)

And it will be repeated near the end of this sūrah (6:163), where the Prophet ﷺ is again told to say, "I am the first of those who submit."

**The Logic of Being First**

Why should the leader be the first to submit? Because a call to submission that the caller has not himself answered is hollow. The Prophet's ﷺ authority came not from birth, wealth, or power but from the fact that he lived what he preached before anyone else did. The Qur'an condemns the opposite pattern:

> "Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture" (2:44)

The principle is general. Every parent, teacher, and leader who wishes to guide others must first submit to the standard he sets. The child watches whether the parent prays; the student watches whether the teacher is honest. "First of those who submit" is the description of every credible guide.

**"And Be Not among the Idolaters"**

The verse closes with a direct address to the Prophet ﷺ, outside the quotation: *wa lā takūnanna min al-mushrikīn* — "and do not be among the idolaters." The emphatic form (*lā takūnanna*, with the heavy *nūn*) makes the prohibition absolute.

This raises a question the commentators address. The Prophet ﷺ was never an idolater and never would be. Why is he prohibited from it? Several answers are given. Al-Qurṭubī explains that the address, though directed to the Prophet ﷺ, is intended for his community: they are the ones who might be tempted toward *shirk*, and the prohibition reaches them through him. Al-Rāzī adds that even for the Prophet ﷺ, the reminder serves to strengthen his refusal of the idolaters' invitations to compromise and to make clear that no negotiation on this point is possible. Others note that such addresses show the gravity of the matter: if even the Prophet ﷺ, who is beyond temptation on this point, is reminded, how much more must ordinary believers be on guard.

The Qur'an uses the same form elsewhere:

> "It has already been revealed to you—and to those ˹prophets˺ before you—that if you associate others ˹with Allah˺, your deeds will certainly be void and you will truly be one of the losers" (39:65)

**The Application Today**

The verse's question — "Shall I take a protector other than God?" — is not confined to carved idols. Anything a person relies upon as his ultimate security, anything he fears losing more than he fears God's displeasure, anything he serves in the expectation that it will save him, functions as a *walī*. For some it is wealth; for others, status, a powerful patron, a political system, or one's own cleverness. The verse offers a simple test: does this thing feed, or is it fed? Does it sustain me, or do I sustain it? Everything other than God fails the test. Only the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who feeds and is not fed, can be a protector in the full sense — and the Prophet's ﷺ answer, "I was commanded to be the first of those who submit," is the answer every believer is invited to make his own.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:15

> **Say, “I truly fear—if I were to disobey my Lord—the torment of a tremendous Day.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prophet Confesses His Own Accountability**

The previous verse ended with the command to the Prophet ﷺ not to be among the idolaters. This verse gives the reason he never could be: he fears the consequence of disobeying his Lord. The statement is remarkable because it places the Prophet ﷺ himself under the same law of accountability as everyone else. He does not say "I am exempt because I am a prophet." He says, in effect, "If I were to disobey, I would be punished, and I fear that punishment."

This confession serves several purposes at once. It shows the idolaters that the Prophet ﷺ is not claiming a special status that lifts him above divine judgment. It demonstrates that his refusal of their compromise is not stubbornness but fear of God. And it models for the believers the correct relationship to divine command: obedience grounded in reverent awe.

**The Vocabulary of Fear**

The verb used is *akhāfu*, from *khawf*, fear. This is distinct from other Qur'anic words for fear such as *khashyah* (reverent awe rooted in knowledge of the one feared) and *taqwā* (protective wariness). *Khawf* is the ordinary word for fear of a harm one expects. The Prophet ﷺ speaks plainly: he fears the punishment.

The object of fear is *ʿadhāba yawmin ʿaẓīm* — "the punishment of a tremendous Day." The word *ʿaẓīm* means great, mighty, immense. The Qur'an frequently describes the Day of Judgment with this adjective, and describes its punishment with it as well. To fear the punishment of that Day is a sign of understanding its reality. One does not fear what one does not believe in.

The condition is *in ʿaṣaytu rabbī* — "if I disobey my Lord." The word *ʿaṣā* means to rebel, to refuse obedience. Note the possessive: "*my* Lord." The Prophet ﷺ speaks of his relationship with God in personal terms. He is not describing a distant lawgiver but the One who created him, sustains him, and has the right to command him.

**Knowledge and Fear Go Together**

The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "By God, I am the most knowledgeable of God among you and the most fearful of Him." (al-Bukhārī 6101; Muslim 2356)

And in another wording:

> "I am the most God-fearing of you and the most knowing of you of what I should avoid." (al-Bukhārī 20)

The connection between knowledge and fear is a principle stated in the Qur'an:

> "servants, only the knowledgeable ˹of His might˺ are ˹truly˺ in awe of Him" (35:28)

The more one knows of God's majesty, justice, and power, the more one fears displeasing Him. This is not the fear of a slave before a cruel master but the awe of one who understands what is at stake. The idolaters mocked the warnings of punishment precisely because they did not know God; the Prophet ﷺ feared them because he knew Him best. The verse thus contrasts two conditions: the knowledgeable person who fears and the ignorant person who mocks.

**Why This Is Not Contradicted by the Prophet's Forgiveness**

A question arises: the Prophet ﷺ was promised forgiveness — "so that Allah may forgive you for your past and future shortcomings, perfect His favour upon you, guide you along the Straight Path," (48:2). Why then does he fear? The scholars give several answers. First, the fear is conditional: "*if* I disobey." The condition is hypothetical; the Prophet ﷺ would not disobey, but the statement makes clear that were anyone — even he — to do so, the consequence would follow. Second, the verse establishes the principle of the universality of divine justice, which admits no exceptions by rank. Third, the Prophet ﷺ was the model for his community; his expression of fear teaches them to fear. Fourth, and most deeply, fear and hope are companions in the believer's heart, and the promise of forgiveness does not extinguish fear but refines it into a fear of falling short of what God deserves.

Al-Qurṭubī notes that this verse is a rebuke to anyone who imagines that piety or status removes the need for caution. If the Messenger of God ﷺ declares his fear, no one after him can claim to be beyond it.

**The Balance of Fear and Hope**

Islamic spirituality has always insisted on holding fear (*khawf*) and hope (*rajā'*) in balance. Fear without hope leads to despair; hope without fear leads to complacency. The Qur'an describes the righteous as those who combine both:

> "They abandon their beds, invoking their Lord with hope and fear, and donate from what We have provided for them" (32:16)

> "They abandon their beds, invoking their Lord with hope and fear, and donate from what We have provided for them" (32:16)

The Prophet ﷺ described the two as the wings of the believer. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb reportedly said that if it were announced that all people would enter Paradise except one, he would fear that he was that one; and if it were announced that all would enter the Fire except one, he would hope that he was that one. This is the disposition the verse teaches: never so secure that one grows careless, never so afraid that one gives up.

The verse's placement in the sūrah is significant. Verse 12 declared that God has prescribed mercy upon Himself. Verse 15, three verses later, declares that the Prophet ﷺ fears the punishment of a tremendous Day. The two are not in tension; they are the two poles between which the believer's heart moves. Mercy is the reason to hope; the Day is the reason to fear. A person who has absorbed both verses has the right posture toward God.

**The Function of Fear in Moral Life**

Modern culture often treats fear of divine punishment as a primitive motive, inferior to love or duty. This misunderstands the role of fear. Fear is what protects us from harm we cannot yet see. The person who fears fire does not touch it; the person who fears illness takes precautions; the person who fears financial ruin saves. Fear of God is of this kind: it is a rational response to the reality of judgment, and it protects the soul from harm as ordinary fear protects the body.

Moreover, the Prophet's ﷺ fear was not a fear that paralyzed him but one that guided him. It did not make him anxious or miserable; it made him careful, upright, and steady. The same is true of any believer who fears God rightly. Such fear is not a cloud over life but a fence along a cliff — it marks the edge so that one can walk freely everywhere else.

An analogy the tradition has used is that of a person walking through a path with thorns and pitfalls. His caution is not misery; it is intelligence. He watches his steps, gathers his garment, and reaches the end unharmed. The one who strides carelessly, mocking the caution of others, is the one who falls. The Prophet's ﷺ statement of fear is the statement of a man who sees the path clearly.

**A Message to the Idolaters**

Addressed to the Makkans, the verse carries an implicit argument. They had invited the Prophet ﷺ to compromise, perhaps imagining that his refusal was mere pride or a bid for power. He tells them: I refuse because I fear my Lord. This removes any suspicion of worldly motive. A man who fears God more than he desires wealth or honor cannot be bought. The Quraysh had already tried. When ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah offered him wealth, leadership, and marriage in exchange for abandoning his message, the Prophet ﷺ responded by reciting the opening of Sūrah Fuṣṣilat until ʿUtbah begged him to stop (recorded by Ibn Isḥāq and cited by Ibn Kathīr). The verse before us is the theological expression of that refusal.

**The Universal Standard**

The greatest lesson of the verse is that no one is above the law of God — not even the one who brought the law. In a world where power and position routinely purchase exemption from accountability, the Prophet's ﷺ public declaration that he too would be punished for disobedience is a foundation of justice. The Qur'an makes the same point about the prophets generally:

> "We would have certainly seized him by his right hand," (69:44–47)

A religion whose prophet fears God's judgment is a religion in which no one may claim immunity. This is why Islam has historically resisted the elevation of any human being to a status beyond accountability. The Prophet ﷺ himself set the standard: "Truly I fear the punishment of a tremendous Day should I disobey my Lord."

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:16

> **Whoever is spared the torment of that Day will have certainly been shown Allah’s mercy. And that is the absolute triumph.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Other Side of Fear**

Verse 15 spoke of fearing the punishment of the tremendous Day. Verse 16 immediately describes the alternative: being spared from it. The two verses are inseparable. Having named the thing to be feared, the Qur'an now names the thing to be hoped for, and it describes escape from punishment as an act of divine mercy and as the greatest possible success. The structure prevents the previous verse from being heard as a message of terror alone. Fear was named so that one might seek what this verse describes.

**"Whosoever Is Spared on That Day"**

The verb *yuṣraf* is passive: "it is turned away from him" or "he is turned away from it." Two readings existed among the early reciters. One reads *man yuṣraf ʿanhu* — "whoever it [the punishment] is turned away from." The other reads *man yaṣrif* — "whoever He [God] turns it away from." Both readings convey the same meaning: the punishment does not simply fail to reach the person; it is actively diverted from him by God. The verb *ṣarafa* means to turn, avert, divert. Punishment is pictured as something with a trajectory, which would reach everyone unless diverted.

This picture is important. The default condition of a human being, considering his sins and shortcomings, is one that merits some measure of divine displeasure. Escape from punishment is not automatic; it requires that God turn the punishment aside. This is why the verse attributes the sparing to mercy rather than to desert.

**"He Has Certainly Been Merciful unto Him"**

The phrase *fa-qad raḥimah* is emphatic: "then He has indeed shown him mercy." The commentators stress that the verse does not say "he has earned his escape" or "his deeds have saved him" but "God has shown him mercy." Al-Zamakhsharī observes that this indicates that salvation on that Day is fundamentally a matter of divine mercy, even for those whose deeds were good, because no one's deeds are sufficient to purchase escape from divine judgment if God were to reckon strictly.

The Prophet ﷺ stated this explicitly:

> "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said, "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said, "Not even I, unless God envelops me in His mercy and grace." (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816)

This ḥadīth does not mean that deeds are irrelevant; the Qur'an repeatedly promises reward for righteous deeds. It means that deeds are the means by which one seeks mercy, not a price by which one buys it. The relationship between a servant and his Lord is not commercial. Whatever good a person does, he does with faculties God gave him, in a life God granted, guided by a revelation God sent. The deed itself is a gift; the reward is a further gift. The verse's insistence on mercy protects against the spiritual disease of believing oneself entitled to salvation.

**Connection to "He Has Prescribed Mercy for Himself"**

Verse 12 declared that God has prescribed mercy upon Himself. Verse 16 shows that mercy in operation at the decisive moment. The mercy God committed Himself to is not merely mercy in this life — delaying punishment, sending guidance, providing sustenance — but mercy on the Day itself, when it will make the difference between ruin and triumph. This fulfills the ḥadīth quoted at verse 12, in which God "held back ninety-nine parts of mercy with which He will show mercy to His servants on the Day of Resurrection" (Muslim 2752).

**"That Is the Manifest Triumph"**

The verse ends: *wa dhālika al-fawzu al-mubīn* — "and that is the clear success." The word *fawz* means to attain what one seeks and escape what one fears — victory in both senses at once. *Mubīn* means clear, evident, unmistakable. The Qur'an uses *fawz* with various adjectives for salvation in the Hereafter: *al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm* (the great triumph), *al-fawz al-kabīr* (the mighty triumph), and *al-fawz al-mubīn* (the manifest triumph). The verse states the essence of success:

> "Every soul will taste death" (3:185)

The phrase "drawn away from the Fire" in 3:185 uses a related verb (*zuḥziḥa*) and expresses the same idea as verse 16: being removed from the trajectory of punishment.

**Redefining Success**

The verse offers a definition of success that stands against the definitions most people live by. In ordinary usage, success means wealth, position, recognition, comfort. The Qur'an does not deny that these are good in their place, but it refuses to call them *fawz*. Real success is measured on the Day when everything else is stripped away. A person who had every worldly success and is not spared on that Day has not succeeded; a person who had nothing in this world and is spared has attained the manifest triumph.

This redefinition has practical consequences. It determines what a person will sacrifice for what. If success is worldly, one sacrifices principle for gain; if success is being spared on that Day, one sacrifices gain for principle. The Quraysh offered the Prophet ﷺ every worldly success; the verse tells us what he was measuring by instead.

**The Word "Manifest"**

Why is the triumph called "manifest" or "clear"? Several reasons suggest themselves. First, it is clear in the sense of being unmistakable — no one who attains it will doubt that he has succeeded, and no one who misses it will be able to pretend he has not failed. In this world, success and failure are often ambiguous; a person may appear successful and be miserable, or appear to fail and be at peace. On that Day the ambiguity ends. Second, it is clear in the sense of being visible to all: the Qur'an describes the people of Paradise with faces that are radiant (75:22; 80:38–39) and the people of the Fire with faces that are dark (3:106; 80:40–41). Third, it is clear in the sense of being complete — a success that leaves nothing further to seek.

**Why Escape Alone Is Called Triumph**

Notice that the verse does not mention Paradise explicitly. It says that merely being spared from punishment is the manifest triumph. Al-Rāzī reflects on this: the removal of harm is itself a supreme good, prior to the attainment of any benefit. A person threatened with a terrible punishment who learns he has been spared feels relief greater than any pleasure could give. The verse begins with this most basic form of success and leaves the further reward — Paradise and the vision of God — to be described elsewhere. It emphasizes how serious the danger is by treating escape from it as sufficient cause for calling the outcome triumph.

There is also a lesson in humility here. The believer does not approach the Day demanding reward; he approaches it hoping to be spared. Whatever he receives beyond that is grace upon grace.

**The Practical Disposition**

The verse cultivates a specific disposition: earnest seeking of God's mercy through obedience, combined with awareness that the outcome depends on Him. This is not fatalism; the Qur'an is explicit that deeds matter and that God does not waste the work of any worker (3:195). It is rather the recognition that one's deeds are offered to God as a petition for mercy, not presented to Him as a bill for payment. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to ask for salvation in exactly these terms:

> "O God, I ask You for Paradise and seek refuge in You from the Fire." (Abū Dāwūd 792; Ibn Mājah 910; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

The simplicity of this supplication reflects the verse's teaching: what one truly needs is to be spared and to be admitted, and both are asked of God as gifts.

**Reading Verses 15 and 16 Together**

The two verses form a complete lesson. The Prophet ﷺ fears the punishment of the Day (v. 15). Whoever is spared that punishment has received mercy and attained the clear triumph (v. 16). Fear and hope; danger and rescue; the tremendous Day and the manifest success. A person who has understood both verses knows what to fear, what to hope for, and where to turn for the outcome he hopes for. This is the whole of the religious life in two sentences.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:17

> **If Allah touches you with harm, none can undo it except Him. And if He touches you with a blessing, He is Most Capable of everything.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Foundation of Reliance**

This verse states a principle upon which the entire Islamic concept of trust in God (*tawakkul*) rests: all harm and all benefit are in God's hand alone. No creature can remove what God has sent, and no creature can withhold what God has decreed. The verse is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ in the singular ("touch *thee*"), but the commentators agree that its application is universal; every human being stands in exactly the relationship it describes.

The verse continues the sūrah's demolition of idolatry from a new angle. Verses 12–14 argued from ownership and provision: God owns everything and feeds everyone. Verse 17 argues from power over outcomes: God alone controls what happens to you. If that is so, then turning to any other being for protection or benefit is not merely disobedient but useless.

**The Vocabulary of "Touch"**

The verb *massa* means to touch — a light contact, as distinct from striking or seizing. The Qur'an uses it for both harm and good coming to a person: *yamsaska bi-ḍurr* (touches you with harm) and *yamsaska bi-khayr* (touches you with good). The choice of this gentle verb is instructive. Even severe affliction is described as a "touch" from God's perspective — a reminder that what seems overwhelming to the creature is a light matter to the Creator, and that it can be lifted as easily as it was laid. Al-Rāzī notes that the use of *massa* for both harm and good suggests that both come to the human being from outside, from God, and are not generated by the person himself.

The word *ḍurr* means harm, hurt, adversity — illness, loss, poverty, grief. The word *khayr* means good in the broadest sense — health, wealth, safety, happiness, guidance. The two together encompass everything that can happen to a person.

**"None Can Remove It Save He"**

The first half of the verse states: *fa-lā kāshifa lahu illā huwa* — "there is no remover of it except Him." The word *kāshif* is an active participle from *kashafa*, to uncover, lift, remove. Harm is pictured as something laid upon a person like a covering, and only God can lift it. The exclusive construction — negation followed by exception — is the strongest form of restriction in Arabic. It admits no partner in the removal of harm.

This has an immediate bearing on the idolaters' practice. They turned to their idols in times of drought, illness, and danger. The verse tells them that their idols cannot lift the smallest affliction. The Qur'an makes the same point about all false objects of worship:

> "Or if He willed ˹some˺ mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy" (39:38)

> "But those ˹false gods˺ you call besides Him can neither help you nor even themselves" (7:197)

Even the Prophet ﷺ is told to declare that he has no such power over himself:

> "If I had known the unknown, I would have benefited myself enormously, and no harm would have ever touched me" (7:188)

**"Should He Touch Thee with Goodness, He Is Powerful over All Things"**

The second half of the verse has a subtly different structure. For harm, it says "none can remove it save He." For good, it says "He is Powerful over all things." Why the difference? Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī both note that the parallel expression — "none can withhold it save He" — is stated in the Qur'an elsewhere:

> "And whatever He withholds, none but Him can release it" (35:2)

Here, however, the Qur'an chooses to conclude with the general statement of power. This has the effect of encompassing both halves: He who is powerful over all things can both remove harm and bestow good, can both withhold good and send harm. The statement of comprehensive power covers every case, so that the listener does not imagine any exception on either side.

There may also be a note of encouragement in the phrasing. When harm comes, the verse comforts: only God can lift it, so turn to Him. When good comes, the verse reminds: He who sent it is powerful over all things — able to increase it, sustain it, or take it away — so remain grateful and do not become complacent.

**Divine Power and Human Effort**

A question naturally arises: if only God removes harm, what is the role of medicine, effort, and precaution? The Islamic tradition answers clearly. Means (*asbāb*) are themselves created by God and commanded by Him; using them is obedience, not a rival to reliance. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Seek treatment, O servants of God, for God has not sent down a disease without sending down a cure for it." (Abū Dāwūd 3855; al-Tirmidhī 2038; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

And when a man asked whether he should tie his camel or trust in God, the Prophet ﷺ replied:

> "Tie it, and trust in God." (al-Tirmidhī 2517, graded ḥasan)

The verse does not deny the efficacy of means; it denies their independence. The doctor treats, but God cures. The farmer plants, but God grows. The soldier fights, but God grants victory. Means are the channel through which God's decree often flows, and the believer uses them fully while knowing that their effect depends entirely on God. The error the verse corrects is the belief that the means themselves are the source — which is the same error as idolatry in a different dress.

**The Psychology of Trust**

The verse produces a specific inner state in the person who absorbs it. He is freed from two anxieties. First, he no longer fears creatures, because he knows they cannot harm him unless God permits. The Prophet ﷺ taught the young Ibn ʿAbbās:

> "Know that if the whole nation gathered to benefit you with something, they would not benefit you except with something God had already written for you; and if they gathered to harm you with something, they would not harm you except with something God had already written against you. The pens have been lifted and the pages have dried." (al-Tirmidhī 2516, graded ṣaḥīḥ)

Second, he no longer despairs in affliction, because he knows the One who sent it can lift it. The person who believes his suffering is caused by blind chance or by enemies beyond his reach has no one to turn to. The person who believes it came from God has the One to turn to who can remove it.

This is not passivity. A person who trusts God works, plans, seeks treatment, and defends himself — but he does so without the frantic anxiety of one who believes everything depends on his own control, and without the bitterness of one who believes he is the victim of forces that answer to no one.

**Affliction as Something God "Touches" You With**

There is a further consolation in the verse's attribution of affliction to God. If affliction came from a source indifferent or hostile to us, it would be meaningless suffering. But if it comes from God — the One who has prescribed mercy upon Himself (v. 12) — it comes with purpose. The Qur'an and ḥadīth are clear that affliction, for the believer, is a means of purification and elevation:

> "No fatigue, nor disease, nor sorrow, nor sadness, nor hurt, nor distress befalls a Muslim, even if it were the prick of a thorn, but that God expiates some of his sins for it." (al-Bukhārī 5641; Muslim 2573)

The same hand that touches with harm is the hand that removes it and the hand that rewards patience under it. The believer's response to affliction is therefore not "why me?" but "what is being asked of me, and to whom do I turn?"

**Connection to Mercy**

The source commentary notes that this verse must be read with verse 12 ("He has prescribed mercy upon Himself") and with 7:156 ("My mercy encompasses all things"). The God who holds all harm and all good in His hand is not a capricious power but One who has committed Himself to mercy. This transforms the meaning of the verse from a statement of raw omnipotence into a statement of trustworthy omnipotence. The believer does not merely acknowledge that God controls everything; he rejoices in it, because he knows who God is.

**The Prophet as the First Addressee**

Finally, the verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ directly. He was, at the time of this revelation, under enormous pressure in Makkah — mocked, threatened, and boycotted. The verse tells him that none of this can harm him beyond what God permits, and that whatever good comes to him is from God's power. This grounded his steadfastness. It also demonstrated to his followers, watching him, what reliance on God looks like in practice: calm under threat, gratitude in ease, and constant turning to the One who touches with both.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:18

> **He reigns supreme over His creation. And He is the All-Wise, All-Aware.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Culmination of the Argument from Sovereignty**

This short verse completes a sequence that began at verse 12. God owns everything in space (v. 12) and time (v. 13); He originates, feeds, and is not fed (v. 14); He is the One to be feared and the One whose mercy saves (vv. 15–16); He alone sends harm and good (v. 17). Verse 18 gathers all of this into a single declaration of absolute sovereignty: *wa huwa al-qāhiru fawqa ʿibādih* — "He is the Dominant above His servants." Everything the preceding verses described flows from this one fact.

**The Name al-Qāhir**

The divine name *al-Qāhir* comes from the root *q-h-r*, which means to subdue, overpower, prevail over, compel. A *qāhir* is one whose authority cannot be resisted. The Qur'an also uses the intensive form *al-Qahhār*, "the All-Subduing," six times, typically in contexts affirming God's Oneness against multiple lords:

> "Allah—the One, the" (12:39)

> "Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Supreme" (13:16)

The form *al-Qāhir* in the present verse appears twice in the Qur'an, both in Sūrah al-Anʿām (here and at 6:61). The name indicates that all creatures are under God's compulsion in the sense that none can escape His decree, none can resist His will, and none can avoid His judgment. Al-Ṭabarī explains the meaning: all things are humbled before Him, subject to His authority, and made lowly beneath His majesty. Al-Zamakhsharī adds that it conveys that everything is subservient to His power and under His disposal.

**"Above His Servants"**

The phrase *fawqa ʿibādih* — "above His servants" — has been discussed by the scholars in two dimensions. First, *fawqa* (above) indicates the exaltedness of God's authority: He is above all in rank, power, and majesty, as a king is "above" his subjects. Second, the early scholars and Ibn Taymiyyah affirmed that God is also above His creation in the sense of His transcendence and highness (*ʿuluww*) in a manner befitting His majesty, without likening Him to created things and without asking "how." Ibn Kathīr and the majority of the classical exegetes note both meanings without contradiction: God is above His servants in majesty and authority, and He is exalted above them in His transcendence. The verse's context — subduing power — makes the sense of authority primary, but the affirmation of God's highness is consistent with the rest of the Qur'an:

> "They fear their Lord above them, and do whatever they are commanded" (16:50)

> "the Most Compassionate, ˹Who is˺ established on the Throne" (20:5)

**Why "Servants"?**

The verse does not say "dominant over creation" but "dominant over His *servants*" (*ʿibād*). The word *ʿabd* (plural *ʿibād*) means servant or slave — one who belongs to another. The choice of this word makes a point: all human beings, including those who deny God and worship idols, are His servants in the sense that they belong to Him and are under His power, whether they acknowledge it or not. The idolaters who thought they had other patrons were, in reality, God's servants all along — subdued by His decree, fed by His provision, and moving toward His judgment. The verse thus reminds them of a fact about themselves: whatever they call themselves, they are *ʿibād*.

The Qur'an distinguishes between servitude by compulsion, which is universal, and servitude by choice, which is worship:

> "There is none in the heavens or the earth who will not return to the Most Compassionate in full submission" (19:93)

Every being comes to God as a servant. The believer's distinction is that he chooses to be what he already is.

**Subduing Power Paired with Wisdom and Awareness**

The verse could have ended with "He is the Dominant over His servants." Instead it adds: *wa huwa al-ḥakīmu al-khabīr* — "and He is the Wise, the Aware." The pairing is not decorative. Power without wisdom is tyranny; power without awareness is blind force. By joining *al-Qāhir* to *al-Ḥakīm* and *al-Khabīr*, the verse declares that God's overwhelming power is exercised with perfect wisdom and perfect knowledge. Nothing He decrees is arbitrary; nothing He does is uninformed.

*Al-Ḥakīm* comes from the root *ḥ-k-m*, whose meanings include judgment, wisdom, and the restraint of something to prevent error (a *ḥakamah* is the bit of a horse's bridle). God's wisdom means that He puts everything in its proper place and that all His actions serve purposes, whether or not creatures perceive them.

*Al-Khabīr* comes from the root *kh-b-r*, which refers to knowledge of the inner reality of things, of what is hidden beneath the surface. A *khabīr* is an expert who knows a matter from inside. God is aware of the inner state of every servant — his intentions, his weaknesses, his secret thoughts — and this awareness informs His dealings with him.

Al-Rāzī draws out the significance: the verse first affirms God's total power, which might frighten; then it affirms His wisdom and awareness, which reassure. His power is not the power of an indifferent force but of a Being who knows each servant intimately and disposes of him wisely. This is why the believer can submit to God's dominance without resentment. One submits gladly to power that is wise and aware; one submits resentfully only to power that is blind.

**The Meaning for the Idolaters**

For the Makkans, the verse delivered a final blow to the logic of their religion. They believed that their idols had some measure of independent power — to intercede, to protect, to bring rain or victory. The verse says that God is dominant *above* all His servants, which includes any being they might worship: angels, jinn, ancestors, or celestial bodies. Whatever they turned to was itself subdued under God. To seek the favor of the subdued rather than the Subduer is irrational. The Qur'an makes this point in its account of Abraham, later in this sūrah, who rejected star, moon, and sun because each was subject to setting — that is, subject to a power above it.

**The Meaning for the Believer**

For the believer, the verse is a source of both awe and peace. Awe, because he stands under a power that cannot be resisted and a knowledge that cannot be deceived. Peace, because that power is wise and that knowledge is caring. The believer does not have to wonder whether his affairs are in competent hands; they are in the hands of the One who is dominant over everything and wise in everything. Whatever befalls him has passed through that wisdom.

This is also the antidote to fear of other human beings. Tyrants, oppressors, and enemies may seem powerful, but they are among God's servants over whom He is dominant. Their power is borrowed and limited; His is inherent and absolute. The Qur'an says of Pharaoh, the archetype of human power, that he was "among the corrupters" and was drowned. The believer who understands verse 18 measures every human power against the divine and finds it small.

**Application to the Inner Life**

There is a further, subtler application. A person's own desires, habits, and passions can seem to dominate him — he feels unable to change, subdued by his own nature.
