The verse reminds him that God is dominant above him and therefore above his desires as well. The One who subdues all things can subdue the servant's own lower self, if the servant turns to Him. The Prophet ﷺ frequently prayed:

> "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." (al-Tirmidhī 2140; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

The heart is turned by the One who is dominant over it. This gives hope to anyone struggling with himself: the power that can change him is not his own limited will but the will of *al-Qāhir*, to whom he can appeal.

**Closing the First Section of the Sūrah**

With verse 18, the sūrah's opening movement reaches its summit. From praise of the Creator (v. 1) to the declaration of His absolute dominance, wisdom, and awareness (v. 18), the argument has established everything needed for what follows. The next verse will turn to the question of testimony — who bears witness to the truth of the Prophet's ﷺ message — and the answer will draw on all that has been established here. The God who is dominant over His servants and aware of all things is the ultimate Witness, and His testimony outweighs every human denial.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:19

> **Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Who is the best witness?” Say, “Allah is! He is a Witness between me and you. And this Quran has been revealed to me so that, with it, I may warn you and whoever it reaches. Do you ˹pagans˺ testify that there are other gods besides Allah?” ˹Then˺ say, “I will never testify ˹to this˺!” ˹And˺ say, “There is only One God. And I totally reject whatever ˹idols˺ you associate with Him.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verse of Four "Says"**

This verse contains four commands to "Say" — more than any other verse in the sūrah. Each *qul* introduces a distinct move in a compact but complete argument about testimony. The idolaters had demanded witnesses to the truth of the Prophet's ﷺ claim. According to a report cited by al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī and others, some of the Makkans said to him, "Who bears witness that you are the Messenger of God? The Jews and Christians deny you." The verse answers with the highest possible witness.

**"What Thing Is Greatest as Testimony?"**

The first question is *ayyu shay'in akbaru shahādatan* — "what thing is greatest in testimony?" The word *shahādah* means testimony, witness, the declaration of what one has seen or knows. In any dispute, the value of testimony depends on the witness: his knowledge of the facts, his truthfulness, and his freedom from bias. The question asks the listener to consider: whose testimony is the most reliable of all?

The use of *shay'* ("thing") rather than *man* ("who") has been noted by the grammarians. It is a general question that includes every possible witness — human, angelic, or divine — so that the answer, when given, is seen to exclude all competitors.

**"God Is Witness between You and Me"**

The Prophet ﷺ answers his own question, as in verse 12: *qul Allāhu shahīdun baynī wa baynakum* — "Say: God is Witness between me and you." The answer is unanswerable. No witness knows more than God, none is more truthful, and none is more free from bias. And God's testimony to the Prophet's ﷺ truth was given in the form of the Qur'an itself — a book whose eloquence, knowledge, and effect no human being could produce. The divine name *al-Shahīd*, the Witness, appears in many verses:

> "Sufficient is Allah as a Witness between me and you" (29:52)

> "Allah is sufficient as a Witness between me and you, as is whoever has knowledge of the Scripture" (13:43)

Al-Qurṭubī explains the logic. When a person is asked "who testifies for you?" and answers "God," he is making the strongest possible claim — and also the most dangerous one, for if he is lying, he has invoked the greatest of witnesses against himself. The Prophet's ﷺ willingness to call God as his witness is itself evidence of his sincerity. A liar might invoke God once in a moment of desperation; no liar builds his whole life and message on the claim that God testifies for him, with the Qur'an daily challenging his opponents to produce its like.

**Jesus and Hūd Calling God to Witness**

The Qur'an records earlier prophets making the same appeal. Jesus, questioned by God on the Day of Judgment about the claims made for him, will say:

> "And I was witness over them as long as I remained among them" (5:117)

And the Prophet Hūd told his people:

> "I call Allah to witness, and you too bear witness, that I ˹totally˺ reject whatever you associate" (11:54–55)

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stands in this line. To call God as witness is the prophetic response to a people who will not accept human testimony.

**"This Qur'an Has Been Revealed unto Me, That I May Warn You and Whomsoever It May Reach"**

The verse now specifies the content of God's testimony: *wa ūḥiya ilayya hādhā al-Qur'ānu li-undhirakum bihi wa man balagh* — "and this Qur'an has been revealed to me so that I may warn you by it and whomever it reaches." The Qur'an is the testimony; the warning is its purpose.

The phrase *wa man balagh* — "and whomever it reaches" — is one of the most important statements of the universality of the Qur'anic message. The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to warn not only the Makkans in front of him but everyone the Qur'an would ever reach, in every place and time. Al-Ṭabarī explains: whoever the Qur'an reaches is warned by it, and the Prophet ﷺ is a warner to him even if he never met him. Ibn Kathīr cites the ḥadīth:

> "Convey from me, even if one verse." (al-Bukhārī 3461)

And the Prophet's ﷺ declaration in the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah:

> "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, no one of this nation hears of me — neither Jew nor Christian — and then dies without believing in that with which I was sent, except that he will be among the inhabitants of the Fire." (Muslim 153)

The early scholars understood from this verse that the reaching of the Qur'an to a person is what establishes the proof (*ḥujjah*) against him. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī said: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as though he has seen the Prophet ﷺ." Everyone who reads the Qur'an today is among "whomever it reaches" and is directly addressed by this verse.

**"Do You Truly Bear Witness That There Are Other Gods beside God?"**

The third question turns from the Prophet's ﷺ testimony to the idolaters': *a-innakum la-tashhadūna anna maʿa Allāhi ālihatan ukhrā* — "do you indeed testify that with God there are other gods?" The construction is interrogative with heavy emphasis (*a-innakum la-*), conveying disbelief and challenge. It asks them to state, on the record, whether they are prepared to testify to this. The implication is that a rational person would hesitate. The idolaters had no evidence for other gods — no revelation, no proof, no rational argument. Their whole position rested on inherited custom. The question exposes the emptiness of their testimony beside the fullness of God's.

**"I Bear No Such Witness"**

The Prophet's ﷺ answer is uncompromising: *qul lā ashhad* — "Say: I do not bear witness." Whatever they might testify, he will not join them. This is a public, absolute dissociation. It leaves no room for the kind of compromise the Makkans had proposed — mutual recognition of gods — and it sets the standard for every believer: one does not testify to what one knows to be false, whatever the social cost.

**"He Is Only One God, and I Am Quit of What You Associate"**

The fourth 'Say' delivers the positive creed and the final dissociation: *qul innamā huwa ilāhun wāḥidun wa innanī barī'un mimmā tushrikūn* — "There is only One God. And I totally reject whatever ˹idols˺ you associate with Him" (6:19). The particle *innamā* is restrictive: 'He is *only*' — nothing else, no other god. The word *barī'* means innocent, free, disavowing — the same word Abraham will use at 6:78 ("O my people! I totally reject whatever you associate ˹with Allah in worship˺" (6:78)) and that the Qur'an uses at the opening of Sūrat al-Tawbah for the dissociation from the idolaters (9:1). The Prophet ﷺ takes his stand exactly where Abraham stood: alone against his people's gods, declaring the One and disowning the many.

**The Structure of the Argument**

The four "Says" form a complete legal proceeding. First, the standard of evidence is established: the greatest witness. Second, the witness is named and his testimony presented: God, through the Qur'an. Third, the opposing party is asked to present its testimony: do you truly testify to other gods? Fourth, the verdict is delivered: He is One, and I am free of what you associate. The verse moves with the clarity of a courtroom and leaves the idolaters' case without a witness.

**Testimony as the Core of Islam**

The verse's focus on testimony (*shahādah*) is not incidental. The declaration by which a person enters Islam is called the *shahādah*: "I bear witness that there is no god but God, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God." Both parts are present in this verse: God is the sole witness and the sole God; Muhammad ﷺ is the one to whom the Qur'an was revealed as a warner. The verse thus contains, in argumentative form, the two testimonies that constitute the faith.

Why is faith framed as testimony rather than merely as belief? Because testimony is public, binding, and consequential. A witness stakes his integrity on what he declares. To bear witness to God's Oneness is to commit oneself publicly to living by it. The Prophet's ﷺ "I bear no such witness" and "I am free of what you associate" are declarations that shaped his life and defined his relationship to his society. The believer's *shahādah* is meant to do the same.

**Warning as an Act of Mercy**

Finally, note that the purpose of the Qur'an is stated as warning (*li-undhirakum*). Warning is often perceived as harsh. But a warning is given only to those one wishes to save. One does not warn an enemy of a danger; one warns a friend, a child, a neighbor. The Qur'an's warning to the idolaters and to "whomever it reaches" is an expression of the mercy God prescribed upon Himself in verse 12. The Prophet ﷺ was a warner because he cared about the outcome for those he warned. Every reader who encounters the Qur'an is, by that encounter, someone God has chosen to warn — which is to say, someone God has chosen to reach.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:20

> **Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him ˹to be a true prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Those who have ruined themselves will never believe.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Witness: The People of the Book**

Verse 19 established God as the greatest witness to the Prophet's ﷺ truth. Verse 20 introduces a supporting witness of a different kind: the People of the Book, the Jews and Christians who possessed earlier revelation. The verse states that they *recognize* the Prophet ﷺ and his message. This addresses the idolaters' claim, recorded in the reports on verse 19, that the People of the Book did not testify for him. The Qur'an replies: they recognize him, whether or not they admit it publicly.

The verse is nearly identical to 2:146, which appears in connection with the change of the *qiblah*. Its repetition here, in a Makkan sūrah addressed primarily to idolaters, shows that the argument from the earlier scriptures was part of the Prophet's ﷺ case from the beginning.

**"Those unto Whom We Gave the Book"**

The phrase *alladhīna ātaynāhum al-kitāb* is the Qur'an's standard designation for the Jews and Christians. It emphasizes that their scripture was given by God — a fact that carries an obligation. Having received revelation, they were in a position to recognize new revelation from the same source. The Torah and the Gospel, as the Qur'an describes them, contained descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ to come:

> "˹They are˺ the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel" (7:157)

> "And ˹remember˺ when Jesus, son of Mary, said," (61:6)

The People of the Book were therefore expected to be the first to recognize the Prophet ﷺ, and the sincere among them did.

**"Recognize It as They Recognize Their Own Children"**

The analogy is deliberately chosen for its force. Nothing is more certain to a parent than the identity of his own child. A father does not need evidence to know his son; recognition is immediate and beyond doubt. The verb *ʿarafa* means to know by recognition — to identify something already familiar. It is different from *ʿalima*, to know by learning. The People of the Book did not need to learn who the Prophet ﷺ was; they recognized him from what they already had.

The object "it" (*hu*) has been read in two ways by the commentators. Al-Ṭabarī and others take it to refer to the Prophet ﷺ himself, whose description they found in their scriptures. Others take it to refer to the Qur'an, or to the truth of the message generally. The readings are complementary: recognizing the Prophet ﷺ and recognizing the truth of what he brought are one recognition.

**Historical Testimony**

The Islamic sources preserve accounts of Jewish and Christian scholars who testified to this recognition. The most famous is ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, the leading rabbi of Madinah, who embraced Islam upon meeting the Prophet ﷺ. In the commentary on 2:146, Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī report that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb asked ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām about this verse, and he replied:

> "O ʿUmar, I recognized him when I saw him as I recognize my own son — and my recognition of Muhammad is stronger, because I have no doubt that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, whereas concerning my son, I do not know what his mother may have done."

Whether or not every detail of this report is established, it captures the meaning the early community understood.

There is also the testimony of Waraqah ibn Nawfal, the elderly Christian cousin of Khadījah, who upon hearing the Prophet's ﷺ account of the first revelation said:

> "This is the Nāmūs [the angel of revelation] whom God sent down to Moses. Would that I were young and strong; would that I were alive when your people drive you out." (al-Bukhārī 3; Muslim 160)

And the Negus of Abyssinia, a Christian king, upon hearing Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib recite from Sūrat Maryam, wept and said that this and what Jesus brought came from the same source (reported by Ibn Isḥāq and Aḥmad). These figures represent the recognition the verse describes.

**Recognition Is Not the Same as Acceptance**

The verse says they recognize; it does not say they all believe. This distinction is essential and is made explicit in 2:146:

> "Those to whom We gave the Scripture know him as they know their own sons. But indeed, a party of them conceal the truth while they know it."

Recognition is a matter of knowledge; acceptance is a matter of will. Many of the People of the Book knew the Prophet ﷺ was who he claimed to be and refused to follow him for reasons of pride, position, tribal loyalty, or fear of losing their standing. The Qur'an describes some of them as motivated by envy:

> "Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them" (2:109)

This teaches an important lesson about the nature of unbelief. It is often not a failure of knowledge but a failure of will. A person can know the truth and refuse it. The Qur'an holds such a person more accountable, not less, because he cannot plead ignorance.

**"Those Who Have Lost Their Souls, They Do Not Believe"**

The second sentence repeats verse 12's ending: *alladhīna khasirū anfusahum fa-hum lā yu'minūn*. In verse 12 the phrase described the idolaters; here it applies equally to those People of the Book who recognized and refused. The two groups differed enormously in knowledge — one had scripture and one did not — but they shared the same outcome: self-ruin through refusal of the truth.

The repetition also serves a structural purpose. It brackets the section from verse 12 to verse 20. The section began with God's ownership, mercy, and gathering, and ended with the testimony of God and the recognition of the People of the Book; at both ends, the same verdict is pronounced on those who refuse: they have lost themselves. Al-Zamakhsharī reads the phrase here as covering both the idolaters and the concealing People of the Book: whoever, from either group, has ruined himself by rejection does not believe.

**Why "Losing One's Soul" Is the Right Description**

The metaphor of loss is exact. Every person is given a soul as a capital to trade with. He may invest it in truth and gain eternal profit, or he may spend it on falsehood and lose everything. The person who recognizes the truth and refuses it has made the worst possible transaction: he had the goods in his hand and threw them away. The Qur'an describes the Day when such a person will realize his loss:

> "They will hide ˹their˺ remorse when they see the torment" (10:54)

Ibn Kathīr comments that "losing one's soul" is the ultimate failure, because a person may lose wealth and recover it, or lose health and regain it, but a soul lost to eternal punishment has no recovery.

**The Broader Lesson about Knowledge and Faith**

The verse invites a hard question that every reader should ask himself: is there any truth I recognize and refuse to act upon? The People of the Book are the case study, but the pattern is universal. A person may recognize that a habit is destroying him and continue it. He may recognize that a belief is false and hold it for the comfort of his community. He may recognize an obligation and evade it. In each case, the recognition makes the refusal worse, not better. The verse teaches that knowledge without submission is a form of self-ruin.

Conversely, the verse honors the sincere among the People of the Book — those who recognized and followed. The Qur'an praises them:

> "Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it — they are believers in it. And when it is recited to them, they say, 'We have believed in it; indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed we were, before it, Muslims.' Those will be given their reward twice for what they patiently endured." (28:52–54)

Recognition followed by acceptance is rewarded twice; recognition followed by refusal is counted as loss of the soul. The knowledge was the same; the will made the difference.

**The Relevance of the Verse Today**

The verse's claim — that the earlier scriptures contain recognition of the Prophet ﷺ — remains a live topic. Muslim scholars have pointed to passages in Deuteronomy 18:18 (the prophet like Moses from among the brethren of Israel), Deuteronomy 33:2 (the Lord coming from Sinai, rising from Seir, and shining from Mount Paran — the region of Makkah), and the Gospel of John's promise of the Paraclete (John 14–16), among others. Whatever one makes of specific texts, the Qur'anic claim is that the sincere reader of the earlier scriptures would find the Prophet ﷺ described, and history records that many did.

For the Muslim reader, the verse also carries a warning against the complacent assumption that possessing scripture guarantees guidance. The People of the Book possessed scripture and many still refused. Possessing the Qur'an is likewise no guarantee unless it is accompanied by the willingness to submit to what it says.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:21

> **Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rhetorical Superlative of Wrong**

The verse opens with a question that expects the answer 'no one': *wa man aẓlamu mimman* — "Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His signs?" (6:21). This formula appears some fifteen times in the Qur'an and always identifies the gravest categories of wrongdoing. It is used for those who fabricate lies against God (6:93, 6:144, 11:18, 18:15, 61:7), for those who deny God's signs (6:157, 18:57, 32:22), for those who do both together (7:37, 10:17, 29:68, 39:32), for those who prevent God's name from being mentioned in the mosques (2:114), and for those who conceal testimony they have from God (2:140). The verse before us names two offenses and places them at the summit of injustice.

**The Meaning of Ẓulm**

The word *ẓulm*, translated "wrong," has a precise meaning in Arabic: to place something where it does not belong, to take something from its rightful place, to fall short of giving what is due or to exceed proper bounds. Justice (*ʿadl*) is putting each thing in its place; *ẓulm* is its violation. Understanding this definition clarifies why the two offenses in the verse are the greatest wrongs. To fabricate a lie against God is to attribute to Him what does not belong to Him; to deny His signs is to strip from Him the acknowledgment that is His due. Both are misplacements at the highest possible level — concerning the Creator Himself. The Prophet ﷺ described the highest form of *ẓulm*:

> "The gravest of sins is that you set up a rival to God while He created you." (al-Bukhārī 4477; Muslim 86)

**"Fabricates a Lie against God"**

The phrase *iftarā ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban* uses the verb *iftarā*, from *f-r-y*, which means to cut or fashion, and by extension to invent, to make up. A fabrication (*firyah*) is a lie manufactured deliberately. To fabricate a lie *against God* is to attribute to Him something He did not say, command, or permit — to speak on His behalf without authority.

The commentators identify several forms this took among the Makkans. First, the claim that God had partners — daughters (the angels), intercessors (the idols), or associates in lordship. Second, the claim that their idolatrous practices were divinely sanctioned. The Qur'an records them saying exactly this:

> "We found our forefathers doing it and Allah has commanded us to do it" (7:28)

Third, the invented dietary prohibitions that this sūrah will address at length (6:136–145), in which they declared certain cattle forbidden and attributed the prohibition to God:

> "Have you seen that which Allah has sent down for you as a provision, of which you have made some lawful and some unlawful" (10:59)

Al-Rāzī notes that the phrase may also cover the false religious claims of the People of the Book, though the Makkan context makes the idolaters the primary referents.

**Why Fabricating against God Is the Worst Lie**

All lies are wrong, but lying about God has a unique gravity. A lie about a person injures that person and misleads those who hear it; a lie about God corrupts the very source of truth and misleads people about the ultimate reality on which their eternal destiny depends. Moreover, it is an usurpation. Only God has the right to declare what is lawful and unlawful, what pleases Him and what angers Him. The one who invents such declarations has seated himself in God's place. The Qur'an treats this as a form of taking a lord besides God:

> "They have taken their rabbis and monks as well as the Messiah, son of Mary, as lords besides Allah, even though they were commanded to worship none but One God" (9:31)

When ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, a former Christian, objected that they did not worship their scholars, the Prophet ﷺ explained:

> "Did they not make lawful for you what God had forbidden, and you made it lawful; and forbid for you what God had permitted, and you made it forbidden?" He said, "Yes." He said, "That is your worship of them." (al-Tirmidhī 3095, graded ḥasan)

The verse therefore has a permanent application. Anyone who says "God has commanded" or "God has forbidden" without knowledge, whether from cultural habit, personal preference, or the desire to control others, falls under its warning. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire." (al-Bukhārī 110; Muslim 3)

If lying about the Prophet ﷺ carries this penalty, lying about God carries no less.

**"Or Denies His Signs"**

The second offense is *kadhdhaba bi-āyātih* — "denies His signs." Where fabrication *adds* falsehood to religion, denial *subtracts* truth from it. The two are opposite errors that lead to the same destination. One says of God what He did not say; the other refuses what He did say. Together they exhaust the ways of corrupting one's relationship to revelation.

As discussed at verse 4, the "signs" include the verses of revelation, the miracles of prophets, and the phenomena of creation. To deny them is to call the truth a lie — the same verb *kadhdhaba* used in verse 5.

Al-Qurṭubī observes that the two offenses are frequently found together in the same person. The Makkans who invented false religious practices also denied the Prophet's ﷺ revelation. This is not accidental. One who has invested in fabricated religion must deny the true one, because the true one exposes the fabrication. The person who has built his life on a lie about God is threatened by God's truth and therefore rejects it.

**"Surely the Wrongdoers Will Not Prosper"**

The verse concludes with a categorical judgment: *innahu lā yufliḥu al-ẓālimūn* — "indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper." The verb *aflaḥa* is the same used in the call to prayer (*ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ*, "come to success"). Its root sense is to cleave or split — as a farmer splits the earth — and from this comes the meaning of achieving what one seeks, of success and lasting good. The *fallāḥ* is the farmer whose labor bears fruit. To "prosper" in the Qur'anic sense is to attain the fruit of one's efforts in both worlds.

The wrongdoers will not attain this. Al-Rāzī explains that they will not find what they seek in either this world or the next: in this world, their fabrications and denials bring no true peace or security; in the next, they bring punishment. The Qur'an uses this formula for disbelievers generally:

> "The disbelievers will never succeed" (28:82; also 23:117)

And it contrasts them with those who do succeed:

> "It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful" (2:5)

**The Logic of Non-Prosperity**

Why is it certain that the fabricator and the denier will not prosper? Because prosperity in any real sense requires alignment with reality. A farmer who plants against the seasons does not harvest; a builder who ignores the properties of materials sees his building fall. The one who fabricates lies about God and denies His signs has built his entire life against the deepest reality there is. Whatever temporary gains he makes — power, wealth, the approval of his tribe — rest on a foundation that will give way. The verse states not merely that God will punish him but that his project cannot succeed, because it is at war with the truth.

There is also a psychological dimension. The person who has lied about God must maintain the lie, and maintenance costs effort. He must suppress the signs he encounters, avoid reflection, silence questioners, and defend his invention against every challenge. This is the opposite of the peace and openness that mark genuine prosperity of the soul. The Qur'an describes the constriction of the chest that accompanies rejection of guidance (6:125). The fabricator's life is one of constant defense; the believer's is one of rest in the truth.

**A Mirror for the Believer**

The verse is addressed to the idolaters, but it holds up a mirror to everyone. The believer must guard against the subtler forms of both offenses. He fabricates against God when he asserts religious rulings he has not verified, attributes his own preferences to divine command, or claims certainty about God's will in matters God has left open. He denies God's signs when he ignores the evidence of creation, neglects the Qur'an, or refuses to accept a truth because of its inconvenience. The distance between the idolater and the believer is real, but the verse's warning applies across it: the one who wishes to prosper must neither add to God's religion nor subtract from it.

The safe course was described by the Prophet ﷺ:

> "I have left among you two things; you will not go astray as long as you hold to them: the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger." (al-Muwaṭṭa', *mursal*; strengthened by al-Ḥākim and others)

To hold to what God actually revealed, neither fabricating nor denying, is the whole of the verse's positive instruction.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:22

> **˹Consider˺ the Day We will gather them all together then ask those who associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺, “Where are those gods you used to claim?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Verdict to the Scene**

Verse 21 pronounced that the wrongdoers will not prosper. Verse 22 begins to show what that non-prosperity looks like by transporting the listener to the Day of Judgment. This is a characteristic Qur'anic technique: after stating a principle, it dramatizes the principle by depicting its consequences at the moment when they become undeniable. The idolaters, who mocked resurrection (v. 5, v. 29), are made to see themselves standing in it.

The verse opens with *wa yawma naḥshuruhum jamīʿan* — "and the Day We gather them all together." The verb *ḥashara* means to gather, assemble, drive together — as one drives a herd. It is the standard word for the assembling of all creatures for judgment, and the Day itself is called *Yawm al-Ḥashr*. The word *jamīʿan* ("all together," "every one") emphasizes that no one is missing: the idolaters, the prophets who warned them, the partners they worshipped, and all witnesses will be present in one assembly.

**"Then We Shall Say to Those Who Ascribed Partners"**

The speaker on that Day is God Himself: *thumma naqūlu li'lladhīna ashrakū* — "then We will say to those who associated." The word *ashrakū* comes from *sh-r-k*, to share or associate. A *sharīk* is a partner; *shirk* is the act of assigning partners to God in His divinity, lordship, or worship. Those who did so are addressed directly, without intermediary. In this life they avoided God's message, turned from His signs (v. 4), and mocked His Messenger (v. 10). On that Day there is no avoidance; the One they neglected speaks to them, and they must answer.

**"Where Are Those Partners Whom You Claimed?"**

The question is *ayna shurakā'ukum alladhīna kuntum tazʿumūn* — "where are your partners whom you used to claim?" Every word is chosen for effect.

*Ayna* — "where?" — is a question of location, and it implies absence. One asks "where is it?" of something that ought to be present and is not. The partners were supposed to intercede for their worshippers, to stand beside them in time of need. The question exposes their absence at the moment of greatest need.

*Shurakā'ukum* — "*your* partners" — attributes the partners to the idolaters, not to God. They were never God's partners in reality; they were only the idolaters' partners in imagination. The possessive marks them as the idolaters' own invention.

*Kuntum tazʿumūn* — "you used to claim" — uses the verb *zaʿama*, which in Arabic carries the connotation of a claim without proof, an assertion that is doubtful or false. The Arabs said "*zaʿama*" when reporting something they did not vouch for. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that *zaʿamū* ("they claim") is a poor mount for a man — meaning that basing one's speech on unverified claims is dangerous (Abū Dāwūd 4972). God's use of this verb on the Day of Judgment is a final verdict on the idolaters' theology: it was all *zaʿm* — baseless assertion.

**The Question Is Not for Information**

God knows where the partners are; He knows they never had any power. The question is what the rhetoricians call *taqrīʿ* and *tawbīkh* — rebuke and reproach through interrogation. It forces the idolaters to confront the emptiness of their belief by asking them to produce what they cannot produce. Al-Ṭabarī explains: the question is asked to shame them and to make manifest the falsehood of what they worshipped, since the partners will not be able to benefit them or even to appear on their behalf.

There is a form of teaching in this. A person who has been told a thousand times that his belief is false may still cling to it; but when he is asked, at the decisive moment, to point to the object of his belief and cannot, the falsehood becomes self-evident. The Day of Judgment is described in the Qur'an as the Day when all hidden things are tested (86:9) and when every claim is measured against reality.

**Parallel Scenes in the Qur'an**

The Qur'an depicts this interrogation in several places, each adding a detail:

> "Then on the Day of Judgment He will humiliate them and say," (16:27)

> "˹Watch for˺ the Day He will call to them," (28:62)

> "And it will be said to them," (26:92–93)

> "Where are those ˹idols˺ you used to associate" (40:73–74)

The last passage anticipates the response in verses 23–24 of the present sūrah: confronted with the absence of their partners, the idolaters will deny having worshipped them at all. In other passages, they call on their partners and receive no answer (28:64), or their partners disown them (10:28). Every version shows the same result: the partners are useless when it matters.

**The Idolaters' Own Expectations**

The force of the question depends on what the idolaters had believed their partners would do. The Qur'an records their expectation:

> "These are our intercessors with Allah" (10:18)

> "We worship them only so they may bring us closer to Allah," (39:3)

They expected intercession — that on the Day of Judgment their gods would plead for them. The question "where are your partners?" is addressed exactly to this expectation. The intercessors are absent. The nearness they promised is nowhere. The idolaters stand alone before the One they neglected.

**The Universal Application**

The verse's warning is not confined to those who worshipped carved images. Anyone who relies on something other than God as his ultimate security, and expects it to save him at the decisive moment, will face the same question. The wealthy man who trusted his wealth, the powerful man who trusted his position, the proud man who trusted his own cleverness — each will be asked, in effect, "where is that which you claimed?" And each will find it absent. The Qur'an describes this moment for the one who trusted wealth:

> "And their wealth will be of no benefit to them when they tumble ˹into Hell˺" (92:11)

> "My wealth has not benefited me" (69:28–29)

The modern reader may not bow to idols, but he may still have "partners" — things he relies on as if they held the keys to his fate. The verse asks him to consider now, while there is time, whether these things will be present when he needs them most.

**The Gathering as Consolation for the Oppressed**

The verse begins with the gathering of all together. For the persecuted believers in Makkah — who watched the idolaters prosper while they suffered — this was a promise. There would be a Day when everyone stood in the same assembly, when the powerful could not escape and the weak could not be silenced, and when God Himself would address the wrongdoers. Justice deferred is not justice denied. The Prophet ﷺ described that Day:

> "The people will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked, uncircumcised." ʿĀ'ishah asked, "O Messenger of God, men and women together, looking at one another?" He said, "O ʿĀ'ishah, the matter will be too severe for them to look at one another." (al-Bukhārī 6527; Muslim 2859)

In that severity, every rank of this world is dissolved. The only thing that will matter is the answer to God's question.

**The Mercy in the Warning**

Finally, the verse is revealed *now*, in this world, before the Day it describes. This is itself mercy. God tells the idolaters in advance what He will ask them, so that they may prepare an answer — or rather, so that they may abandon the partners before the question comes. A judge who reveals his question ahead of the trial is giving the defendant every chance. The idolaters of Makkah heard this verse and could still choose. So can every reader.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:23

> **Their only argument will be: “By Allah, our Lord! We were never polytheists.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Idolaters' Only Reply**

When God asks, "Where are your partners whom you claimed?" (v. 22), the idolaters must respond. Verse 23 reports what they will say — and it is not what one might expect. They do not point to their partners; they cannot. They do not plead for mercy; that would require admitting guilt. Instead, they deny that they were ever idolaters at all: "By God, our Lord, we were not idolaters."

The verse opens with *thumma lam takun fitnatuhum illā an qālū* — "then their *fitnah* will be nothing but that they said..." The word *fitnah* is difficult to render with one English word. Its root meaning is the testing of gold by fire to separate pure from impure. From this it comes to mean a trial, a test, a temptation, discord, and — in the present verse — the response one gives under trial, one's plea or excuse. Al-Ṭabarī reports several understandings from the early authorities: that *fitnah* here means their answer (*jawāb*), their excuse (*maʿdhirah*), or their argument (*ḥujjah*). Qatādah said it means "their plea." Al-Zamakhsharī suggests that the word is used with a touch of irony: the whole outcome of their lifelong *fitnah* — their infatuation with idols — reduces to this single desperate sentence.

Another reading, also recorded by al-Ṭabarī, takes *fitnah* in the sense of trial or test: when they are tested on that Day, the only thing they will produce is a denial. Either way, the verse describes the poverty of their defense.

**The Oath: "By God, Our Lord"**

They swear: *wa'llāhi rabbinā* — "by God, our Lord." The irony is severe. In their lifetime, they had assigned partners to God; now, in their moment of desperation, they swear by Him alone and call Him "our Lord." The oath reveals what they always knew. When every fabricated god has vanished, the One remains, and even the liar swears by Him. The Qur'an noted this pattern in this life as well: when the idolaters were in peril at sea, they called on God alone, and when He delivered them, they returned to their partners (10:22–23; 29:65). On the Day of Judgment, the peril is absolute, and the instinct is the same — but this time there is no return to shore.

Some commentators note that "our Lord" (*rabbinā*) can also be read as a vocative — "O our Lord" — as if they were addressing Him in supplication while swearing by Him. Either reading conveys the same thing: at the end, the idolaters acknowledge the Lord they had denied.

**"We Were Not Idolaters"**

The claim itself, *mā kunnā mushrikīn*, is a flat falsehood. They spent their lives as idolaters, defended idolatry, persecuted those who abandoned it, and mocked the Prophet ﷺ for opposing it. Now they say they never did it. How can this be?

The commentators offer several explanations, and they are complementary. First, terror. Confronted with the Fire, a person will say anything that might postpone it, even a lie so obvious that it cannot succeed. Al-Rāzī notes that the plea is the product of fear, not repentance, and therefore of no value. Second, self-deception carried to its conclusion. The idolaters had told themselves throughout life that their partners were legitimate intercessors, not rivals to God. On some level they may believe their own denial: "We did not associate partners with God; we merely sought nearness through intermediaries." The verse records this as a lie, because the reality of what they did was *shirk*, whatever they called it. Third, a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, cited by Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī, connects this verse to a later scene: when the idolaters see that only those who worshipped God alone are being forgiven, they will say, 'Come, let us deny,' and they will say, "By Allah, our Lord! We were never polytheists." (6:23). At that point God will seal their mouths, and their hands and feet will testify against them (36:65). Their denial is thus the last desperate maneuver before the truth is forced out of their own limbs.

**The Psychology of Denial**

This verse is a profound observation about how human beings handle guilt. When a person has done wrong and is confronted with it beyond any possibility of defense, the response is often not confession but denial — even absurd denial. The child caught with the broken vase says "I didn't do it." The official caught in corruption says "I have never taken a bribe." The denial is not a calculated strategy; it is a reflex of a self that cannot bear to acknowledge what it has become.

The Qur'an shows that this reflex persists even into the Hereafter, where denial is useless. This tells us something important: character is not changed by circumstance. A person who lied his whole life will lie at the Judgment. The habits formed here are the habits carried there. This is why the Qur'an repeatedly urges honesty with oneself now, while it can still change something:

> "Be mindful of Allah, and say what is right" (33:70)

And why the Prophet ﷺ warned:

> "Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness, and wickedness leads to the Fire. A man continues to lie and seek to lie until he is written with God as a liar." (al-Bukhārī 6094; Muslim 2607)

The one "written as a liar" is the one whose lying has become his nature. Verse 23 shows such a person at the end.

**Contrast with the Believer's Confession**

The Qur'an contrasts the idolaters' denial with the posture God loves: acknowledgment and repentance. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to say every morning:

> "O God, You are my Lord; there is no god but You. You created me and I am Your servant... I acknowledge to You Your blessing upon me, and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." (al-Bukhārī 6306)

"I acknowledge my sin" is the exact opposite of "we were not idolaters." The believer confesses now, in this world, where confession opens the door of forgiveness. The idolater denies then, in the next world, where denial closes it. The difference between the two is not that one sinned and the other did not, but that one admitted it and the other refused.

**Why Their Denial Cannot Succeed**

The verse implicitly points to the futility of lying before God. The One they are lying to is the One who knows their secret and their public (v. 3) and hears everything (v. 13). To deny idolatry before Him is like denying a theft to a person who watched it happen and holds the recording. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the following verse (24) will describe the lie's exposure, and other verses describe how their own bodies will contradict them:

> "on the Day their tongues, hands, and feet will testify against them for what they used to do" (24:24)

> "On this Day We will seal their mouths, their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will testify to what they used to commit" (36:65)

The lie is not merely useless; it compounds the offense. They lied against God in this world by inventing partners (v. 21); now they lie against themselves by denying it (v. 24). The two lies bracket their whole existence.

**Lessons for the Reader**

Three lessons emerge. First, the greatest danger of habitual sin is that it forms a character that cannot repent even when repentance is the only hope. Second, the instinct to swear by God when everything else has failed proves that knowledge of Him was always present beneath the denial; no one is truly ignorant of Him. Third, the honest confession of one's wrongs, made now, is the greatest gift a person can give himself, because the alternative — denial at the Judgment — is described in this verse, and it is hopeless.

The verse's opening word, *thumma* ("then"), also carries a note of the pathetic. After the gathering, after the question, after a lifetime of arrogant idolatry, *then* — this is all they have: an oath and a lie. The contrast between the confidence of the idolaters in Makkah, mocking and threatening, and the quavering denial of the same men on that Day, is the sermon of the verse.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:24

> **See how they will lie about themselves and how those ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**God Directs the Prophet's Attention**

The verse opens with the command *unẓur* — "look," "behold," "consider." It is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and through him to every listener. God invites attention to the spectacle of verse 23: the idolaters swearing, by God, that they were never idolaters. The command to look implies that there is something instructive in the scene — a lesson to be drawn. The Qur'an uses this form in several places to mark a moment of exposure:

> "See how they fabricate lies against Allah—this alone is a blatant sin" (4:50)

> "So they have gone so ˹far˺ astray that they cannot find the ˹Right˺ Way" (17:48)

The tone is one of grave astonishment. Here are people who spent their lives lying about God and now, standing before Him, lie about themselves.

**"How They Lie against Themselves"**

The phrase *kayfa kadhabū ʿalā anfusihim* — "how they lied against themselves" — is precise. In verse 21 they were described as fabricating lies *against God*. Now they lie *against themselves*. The two are connected. A person who begins by lying about God ends by lying about himself, because the lie about God distorts his whole relationship to reality, including his understanding of who he is and what he has done.

There is also a sense in which the lie is "against" themselves because it harms them. In Arabic, to do something *ʿalā* someone is to do it to his detriment. Their lie in verse 23 does not help them; it condemns them further. They are, in the most literal sense, their own worst witnesses. Al-Ṭabarī explains: they lied against themselves by denying what they had done, and the lie became further evidence against them.

Al-Zamakhsharī notes a subtle point: in this world, a lie sometimes benefits the liar — he escapes blame, gains advantage, protects his position. In the Hereafter, no lie benefits. The idolaters' denial is thus the purest form of lying: a lie with no possible gain, uttered only because lying had become their nature.

**"That Which They Used to Fabricate Has Forsaken Them"**

The second half of the verse: *wa ḍalla ʿanhum mā kānū yaftarūn* — "and lost to them is what they used to invent." The verb *ḍalla* means to go astray, to be lost, to vanish. Applied to a thing, it means that thing has gone missing, wandered off, become unavailable. The object is *mā kānū yaftarūn* — "what they used to fabricate" — that is, the partners they invented, the intercessors they imagined, the false religion they constructed.

Everything the idolaters built has "gone astray from them." The gods they served are nowhere. The intercession they counted on does not materialize. The whole apparatus of their religion has evaporated at the moment of need. The Qur'an uses this same phrase repeatedly of the false gods on the Day of Judgment:

> "Whatever ˹idols˺ they used to invoke besides Allah will fail them" (41:48)

> "Where are those ˹idols˺ you used to associate" (40:73–74)

> "They will have certainly ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them" (7:53; 10:30; 11:21; 16:87; 28:75)

**The Dual Nature of "Forsaking"**

The commentators observe that the fabrications forsake them in two ways. First, ontologically: the gods never existed as gods; on the Day of Judgment, this non-existence becomes plain. What was never real cannot be present. Second, in the case of partners that were real beings — angels, jinn, or righteous humans whose images were worshipped — those beings will actively disown their worshippers:

> "And when the polytheists see their associate-gods, they will say," (16:86)

> "Those ˹gods˺ will deny their worship and turn against them" (19:81–82)

Even Satan, who led them into idolatry, will disown them:

> "So do not blame me" (14:22)

**The Fate of Every Fabrication**

The verse states a law: whatever is fabricated will forsake its fabricator. This is not merely an eschatological claim; it describes the nature of falsehood. A fabrication has no independent existence; it is sustained only by the will of the one who fabricates it and the agreement of those who accept it. Withdraw the will and the agreement, and it collapses. On the Day of Judgment, all wills are subdued and all agreements dissolved before the truth. The fabrication has nothing left to stand on.

This applies in this world as well, though less completely. Lies are eventually exposed; false reputations crumble; invented ideologies fail when tested against reality. The idolaters of Makkah experienced this even before the Day of Judgment: within a generation, their idols were broken, their invented prohibitions abolished, and their religion forgotten. The three hundred and sixty idols around the Kaʿbah were toppled on the day of the Conquest while the Prophet ﷺ recited:

> "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished" (17:81)

The gods forsook their worshippers in Makkah in the year 8 AH, before they forsook them at the Judgment.

**The Lesson of the Vanishing**

For the believer, the verse teaches where to invest. Only what is real endures; only what is true will be present at the end. The Qur'an contrasts the fate of the false with the permanence of the true:

> "Everything is bound to perish except He Himself" (28:88)

> "Whatever you have will end, but whatever Allah has is everlasting" (16:96)

A person who builds his security on fabricated gods, whatever their modern form — an ideology, a status, a possession, a self-image — should expect the verse's outcome: at the moment of need, it will not be there. A person who builds on God builds on the only foundation that does not vanish. This is not merely pious counsel; it is a statement of fact about what lasts.

**The Structure of Verses 22–24**

Taken together, the three verses form a complete short drama. The gathering (v. 22a); the question, "Where are your partners?" (v. 22b); the desperate denial, "We were not idolaters" (v. 23); the exposure of the denial and the disappearance of the partners (v. 24). The idolaters end where the sūrah began them: without an argument, without a witness, and without a god. Every stage of the drama was foreseen and described to them in advance, in a Makkan sūrah, while they still had the power to change its ending.

**The Kindness in "Behold"**

Finally, the command "behold" is directed to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, not to the idolaters. It invites those who still have time to look at the end of those who do not. This is the function of all the Qur'an's descriptions of the Hereafter: they are shown to the living so that the living may choose differently. The scene of the idolaters lying against themselves and being forsaken by their fabrications is placed before the reader as a warning and a mercy. The reader who looks, and learns, and turns to the One who will not forsake him, has received the verse's purpose.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:25

> **There are some of them who ˹pretend to˺ listen to your recitation ˹of the Quran˺, but We have cast veils over their hearts—leaving them unable to comprehend it—and deafness in their ears. Even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them. The disbelievers would ˹even˺ come to argue with you, saying, “This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but ancient fables!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Listening without Hearing**

The verse returns from the scene of the Judgment to the present situation in Makkah, and describes a particular group among the idolaters: those who *listen* to the Prophet ﷺ but do not receive what they hear. *Wa minhum man yastamiʿu ilayk* — "and among them are those who listen to you." The verb *istamaʿa* means to listen attentively, to lend an ear. These people were not absent from the Prophet's ﷺ recitations; they attended them. Yet the listening produced nothing.

Al-Zamakhsharī and others report that the verse was revealed concerning leaders of the Quraysh such as Abū Sufyān, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, ʿUtbah and Shaybah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and Abū Jahl, who came to hear the Prophet ﷺ recite the Qur'an. In one well-known account, Abū Jahl, Abū Sufyān, and al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq each secretly went out at night to listen to the Prophet ﷺ reciting in his house, each unaware of the others; they met on the road at dawn and agreed not to do it again lest their followers be affected — and each returned the next two nights (reported by Ibn Isḥāq). They heard; they were moved; and they refused. The verse describes exactly this condition.

**"Coverings over Their Hearts"**

God says: *wa jaʿalnā ʿalā qulūbihim akinnatan an yafqahūh* — "and We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it." The word *akinnah* (singular *kinān*) means a cover, sheath, or veil — something that encloses and conceals, like the sheath of an arrow or the husk of a fruit. The heart (*qalb*) in Qur'anic usage is the organ of understanding, not merely of emotion; it is where comprehension and conviction occur. A covered heart cannot grasp what is presented to it.

The verb *faqiha* means to understand deeply, to comprehend the meaning and purpose of a thing, not merely its surface. It is the root of *fiqh*, the science of understanding the law. The covered hearts hear the words of the Qur'an but do not attain *fiqh* of it — they do not penetrate to its meaning.

**"And in Their Ears a Deafness"**

The verse adds: *wa fī ādhānihim waqran* — "and in their ears a heaviness." The word *waqr* means a weight or load; applied to the ear, it means a heaviness that impairs hearing — deafness or dullness. This is not physical deafness; these people heard the sounds of the recitation clearly enough to be affected by them. It is a deafness of reception. The words enter the ear but do not pass to the heart.

The Qur'an uses these two images — covered hearts and heavy ears — together in several places (17:46; 18:57; 41:5), and it also speaks of a seal on hearts and hearing (2:7) and a veil over eyes. Each describes the same condition from a different angle: the faculties of perception are intact, but the pathway from perception to understanding is blocked.

**The Question of Divine Agency**

The verse says that *God* placed the coverings. This has raised one of the most discussed questions in Qur'anic theology: if God prevents them from understanding, how can they be blamed for not understanding? The classical commentators approached this from several directions, and the fuller Qur'anic picture resolves the tension.

Al-Rāzī records that some scholars read the verse as straightforward evidence that guidance and misguidance are from God alone, and that the covering represents an innate disposition. But he also records the objection: this would seem to contradict God's statement that He does not burden a soul beyond its capacity (2:286), and it would hand the disbelievers an excuse. Al-Rāzī's own resolution, shared by al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, and the majority, is that the covering is a *consequence* of the disbelievers' own prior choices. They turned away from the signs (v. 4), denied the truth (v. 5), and mocked (v. 10); as a result of this persistent refusal, God left them to it and confirmed them in the state they had chosen. The Qur'an states this sequence explicitly elsewhere:

> "So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate" (61:5)

> "We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance" (6:110)

> "This is how Allah seals the heart of every arrogant tyrant" (40:35)

In each case, the human act comes first, and the divine sealing follows as its consequence. The covering is not an arbitrary imposition on innocent people; it is the settled state of people who spent years refusing to understand until refusal became their nature. God, as Creator of all things including human states, is the one who brings this settled state into being — but He brings it into being in response to what they themselves chose. Al-Qurṭubī adds that the verse may simply describe their condition figuratively: their refusal to benefit put them in the same position as one whose heart is literally covered.

Ibn Taymiyyah discussed this in terms of God's justice and wisdom: God guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills, but His will is not arbitrary; He guides those who seek guidance and misguides those who prefer misguidance, and He does not wrong anyone. The person under the covering is not someone who wanted to understand and was prevented; he is someone who did not want to understand and was given what he wanted.

**"Were They to See Every Sign, They Would Not Believe"**

The verse continues: *wa in yaraw kulla āyatin lā yu'minū bihā* — "Yet, whenever they see a sign, they turn away, saying," This confirms the diagnosis of verses 7–9. The problem is not the quantity or quality of evidence; it is the state of the receiver. A person with a covered heart could witness every miracle and remain unmoved. The Makkans saw the moon split and called it sorcery (54:1–2). They heard the Qur'an and called it poetry. The verse says that no additional sign would change this, because signs work on the heart, and their hearts were closed.

**"When They Come to Thee, They Dispute with Thee"**

Their listening does not lead to belief; it leads to argument: *ḥattā idhā jā'ūka yujādilūnak* — "until, when they come to you, they dispute with you." The verb *jādala* means to argue, to wrangle, to contend. The commentators note that this describes the actual purpose of their listening. They came not to learn but to find material for objection. This is a familiar type: the person who attends a lecture only to prepare his rebuttal, who reads a book only to find what he can attack. Such a person hears every word and understands none, because understanding requires openness and he came closed.

**"Fables of Those of Old"**

The verse ends by recording their objection: *in hādhā illā asāṭīr al-awwalīn* — "this is nothing but the tales of the ancients." The word *asāṭīr* (singular *usṭūrah*) means legends, myths, written tales — from the root *s-ṭ-r*, to write in lines. The charge was that the Qur'an's accounts of past nations were merely old stories that the Prophet ﷺ had collected and rewritten. This objection is attributed to al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith in particular, who had traveled to Persia, learned the tales of Rustam and Isfandiyār, and told the Quraysh that Muhammad's ﷺ stories were no different from his own.

The Qur'an records this objection in nine places (6:25; 8:31; 16:24; 23:83; 25:5; 27:68; 46:17; 68:15; 83:13), showing how central it was to the Makkan resistance. The response is implicit throughout the Qur'an: the accounts of past nations contained knowledge the Prophet ﷺ could not have obtained — details unknown to the Arabs, corrections of errors in the existing traditions, and a consistent moral argument that no collection of legends possesses. And the Qur'an contains far more than narratives: law, theology, argument, and prophecy that no "fable" could supply. The charge of "fables" was itself an admission that they could not refute the content and had to attack its source.

**What This Verse Teaches about Receptivity**

The verse is a diagnosis of a spiritual disease, and understanding it helps the reader avoid it. The disease begins with turning away, progresses through denial and mockery, and ends with a heart that cannot receive even when it listens. The cure is at the beginning, not the end: to turn toward the signs while the heart is still open. The Qur'an describes the receptive heart:

> "Surely in this is a reminder for whoever has a ˹mindful˺ heart and lends an attentive ear" (50:37)

"Who listens while he is present" — with his heart engaged, not merely his ear. This is the opposite of the listeners in verse 25, whose ears were present and whose hearts were absent.

For the believer, the verse is a caution. One can attend every gathering, hear every sermon, read every verse, and remain unchanged, if one comes to dispute rather than to receive. The Companion Ibn Masʿūd said that when he heard "O you who have believed," he would listen carefully, because either a command was coming that he must obey or a prohibition that he must avoid. That is listening with the heart. The verse before us describes the alternative, and its end.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:26

> **They turn others away from the Prophet and distance themselves as well. They ruin none but themselves, yet they fail to perceive it.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Two-Sided Rejection**

The verse describes the Makkan leaders' response to the Qur'an in two verbs: *wa hum yanhawna ʿanhu wa yan'awna ʿanhu* — "and they forbid [others] from it, and they [themselves] keep away from it." The two verbs are nearly identical in sound — *yanhawna* and *yan'awna* — differing by a single letter. This phonetic pairing gives the phrase a memorable ring in Arabic and underlines that the two actions belong together.

The first verb, *nahā ʿan*, means to forbid, to prohibit, to turn others away from something. The Makkan leaders actively prevented people from hearing the Prophet ﷺ. They stationed themselves at the entrances to Makkah during the pilgrimage season to warn arriving tribes against him. They made noise during his recitation:

> "Do not listen to this Quran but drown it out so that you may prevail" (41:26)

They persecuted those who accepted the message, boycotted the Prophet's ﷺ clan, and tried to silence the Qur'an in every way available to them.

The second verb, *na'ā ʿan*, means to distance oneself, to go far from something. Not only did they prevent others; they themselves kept away. They did not merely fail to accept; they actively distanced themselves. Al-Ṭabarī explains the pairing: they combined two evils — misguiding others and being misguided themselves. This is the complete profile of the obstinate leader: he is lost, and he ensures that those who follow him are lost too.

**The Alternative Interpretation: Abū Ṭālib**

A number of classical commentators — al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī — record an interpretation attributed to some early exegetes in which the verse refers to the Prophet's ﷺ uncle Abū Ṭālib. On this reading, *yanhawna ʿanhu* means "they forbid [harm] from him" — that is, they protect the Prophet ﷺ — while *yan'awna ʿanhu* means "they keep away from [accepting] him." Abū Ṭālib, according to the majority of Sunni historians, protected the Prophet ﷺ for years against the Quraysh but did not himself embrace Islam. The verse would then describe his paradoxical position.

The source commentary raises a significant objection to this reading, and it deserves consideration. The verse concludes that these people "destroy none but themselves." Protecting the Prophet ﷺ was a meritorious act, not a self-destructive one. Moreover, the verse falls within a long passage condemning the Makkan idolaters generally, and the plural "they" fits that broader group better than a single individual. Ibn Kathīr himself, after recording the Abū Ṭālib interpretation, notes that the more general reading — that the verse describes the idolaters who forbid others from following the Prophet ﷺ and themselves keep away — is stronger and fits the context. Shiite exegetes reject the Abū Ṭālib reading for a different reason, holding that he did embrace Islam. On balance, the general reading is preferred, while acknowledging that the tradition preserves the other.

**"They Destroy None but Themselves"**

The verse's judgment on their conduct: *wa in yuhlikūna illā anfusahum* — "and they destroy none but themselves." The verb *ahlaka* means to destroy, ruin, cause to perish. The restriction *in... illā* ("not... except") is emphatic. Whatever they intend by forbidding and keeping away — to destroy the Prophet's ﷺ mission, to protect their own position, to preserve their ancestral religion — the actual effect is limited to one target: themselves.

This is one of the Qur'an's recurring assurances. Human opposition cannot harm God, cannot harm His religion, and cannot ultimately harm His Messenger; it can only harm the opposer. The Qur'an says of those who plot against the truth:

> "And the disbelievers made a plan ˹against Jesus˺, but Allah also planned —and Allah is the best of planners" (3:54)

> "You will find no change in the way of Allah, nor will you find it diverted ˹to someone else˺" (35:43)

> "Then they will be defeated and the disbelievers will be driven into Hell," (8:36)

The Makkan leaders spent their wealth, their energy, their influence, and eventually their lives fighting the Qur'an. The Qur'an survived; they did not. Their forbidding did not stop a single sincere seeker from finding the truth, and their keeping away did not diminish the truth by a hair. All the destruction they caused fell on themselves.

**Why Opposition to Truth Is Self-Destructive**

There is a logic behind this assurance. Truth does not depend on human acceptance for its reality; it is what it is regardless. A person who opposes truth is opposing something that will not yield. The result is not that the truth is damaged but that the opposer exhausts himself against an immovable object. He wastes his life, corrupts his character, and arrives at the Judgment as an enemy of what he could have embraced. The idolaters who forbade the Qur'an did not reduce its truth; they only excluded themselves from its benefit.

There is also the specific harm of leading others astray. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Whoever calls to misguidance will have upon him sin like the sins of those who follow him, without that reducing their sins in the least." (Muslim 2674)

The leader who forbids others from the truth bears not only his own loss but a share of theirs. The verse says they destroy "none but themselves," and this is true in the sense that the truth is unharmed; but the destruction they bring on themselves is compounded by every person they turned away.

**"Though They Are Unaware"**

The verse ends: *wa mā yashʿurūn* — "and they perceive not." The verb *shaʿara* means to perceive, sense, be aware — it is the root of *shiʿr*, poetry, originally the perception of subtle things. The idolaters did not perceive that their opposition was destroying them. They believed they were winning: defending their gods, protecting their status, silencing a troublemaker. They could not see that every act of forbidding and keeping away was a stroke against their own souls.

This lack of awareness is itself a symptom of the covered heart described in verse 25. A person whose heart is veiled cannot perceive his own condition; he mistakes ruin for success and loss for gain. The Qur'an describes this self-deception in the strongest terms:

> "Shall we inform you of who will lose the most deeds" (18:103–104)

The tragedy of the idolaters was not only that they were destroying themselves but that they did not know it. Had they known, they might have stopped. The verse thus functions as an announcement: this is what you are doing, even though you cannot see it.

**Application: The Two Errors and Their Modern Forms**

The verse identifies two distinct failures — preventing others from truth and distancing oneself from it — and both have modern forms. The first is committed by anyone who uses influence to keep others from hearing or considering the truth: parents who forbid their children from learning about their religion, media that ridicules faith to make it socially untenable, authorities who suppress religious teaching. The second is committed by anyone who, without necessarily obstructing others, simply keeps himself at a distance — never reading the Qur'an, never attending a gathering, never allowing himself to be in a position where the truth might reach him. The verse's warning covers both: neither harms the truth; both harm the one who does them.

For the believer, the verse has a positive counterpart. If forbidding others from truth and keeping away from it destroy the self, then calling others to truth and drawing near to it build the self. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Whoever calls to guidance will have reward like the rewards of those who follow him, without that reducing their rewards in the least." (Muslim 2674)

The same principle that makes obstruction self-destructive makes invitation self-enriching.

**The Consolation for the Prophet**

Finally, the verse consoled the Prophet ﷺ in his distress. He saw the Makkan leaders blocking his message, turning away the tribes, persecuting his followers. It appeared that they were succeeding. God told him: they are destroying only themselves. The mission would not fail; the obstructors would. Within a decade, those same leaders were dead or defeated, and the tribes they had turned away were entering Islam in crowds. The verse's assurance was proven in his own lifetime — and it remains an assurance for everyone who conveys truth against opposition.

## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:27

> **If only you could see when they will be detained before the Fire! They will cry, “Oh! If only we could be sent back, we would never deny the signs of our Lord and we would ˹surely˺ be of the believers.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"If Thou Couldst See"**

The verse begins with *wa law tarā* — "and if you could see" — a construction the Qur'an uses to open a window onto a scene of the Hereafter. The conditional has no stated consequence: "If you could see... [you would see something terrible]." The omission of the consequence is a rhetorical device (*ḥadhf al-jawāb*) that leaves the horror to the imagination, as when a person says "if you had seen what I saw..." and trails off. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the unstated consequence is more powerful than any stated one could be.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the vision is meant for every listener. The Qur'an frequently transports its audience to the Day of Judgment in this way so that the future becomes vivid enough to influence present choices.

**"Arraigned before the Fire"**

The scene is *idh wuqifū ʿalā al-nār* — "when they are made to stand before the Fire." The verb *waqafa* in this form means to be stopped, halted, made to stand — as a defendant is made to stand before a court. The preposition *ʿalā* ("upon" or "before") has been read in several ways by the commentators: standing at the edge of the Fire, looking into it; standing above it on the bridge; or standing "upon" it in the sense of being placed within it. Al-Ṭabarī records all these possibilities. The image in any case is of people held in place, forced to confront what they denied, unable to look away or leave.

The word *al-nār*, "the Fire," is the Qur'an's most common name for Hell. Those who mocked its mention in this life (v. 5, v. 10) now stand before its reality.

**The Wish: "Would That We Were Sent Back!"**

Their words are *yā laytanā nuraddu* — "oh, would that we were returned!" The particle *layta* expresses a wish for something impossible or unattainable — the wish of regret. The verb *nuraddu* is passive: "we are returned," sent back to the world. This is the wish of every person who realizes too late what he should have done. The Qur'an records this wish repeatedly:

> "It is only a ˹useless˺ appeal they make" (23:99–100)

> "If only you could see the wicked hanging their heads ˹in shame˺ before their Lord, ˹crying" (32:12)

> "We will do good, unlike what we used to do" (35:37)

The last passage contains God's answer to the wish: you had enough time, and you were warned. The wish to return is the wish for a second chance that was already given — every day of life was that chance.

**The Promise: "We Would Not Deny... We Would Be Believers"**

They continue: *wa lā nukadhdhiba bi-āyāti rabbinā wa nakūna min al-mu'minīn* — "and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers." Note that they now call Him "our Lord" (*rabbinā*) and His signs "the signs of our Lord" — the very signs they had called fables (v. 25). The terror of the Fire has produced, in an instant, the acknowledgment they refused for a lifetime.

Al-Ṭabarī records two grammatical readings of this clause. In the reading adopted by most reciters, the verbs are in the subjunctive after *fa* or with the sense of consequence: "would that we were returned, then we would not deny... and we would be believers." In another reading, the verbs are in the indicative and the wish extends over all three clauses: "would that we were returned, and that we had not denied, and that we were among the believers." The source commentary notes that the first reading fits better with verse 28, which responds to their promise of future belief by declaring it a lie: "even if they were sent back, they would return to what they were forbidden."

**The Nature of Their Regret**

The commentators examine the quality of this regret closely. Is it repentance? Al-Rāzī answers no. It is a wish born of fear, not of love for the truth. A person who says "I would believe" only when standing before the Fire is not expressing a change of heart; he is expressing a desire to escape pain. Genuine repentance is turning to God out of recognition of His right and one's own wrong; this is turning from the Fire out of terror. The two can look similar but are fundamentally different, and God, who knows the secret and the public (v. 3), distinguishes them perfectly.

This distinction is essential for understanding why the wish is not granted. God is not withholding mercy from sincere penitents; He is refusing to accept as repentance what is not repentance. The Qur'an states the principle:

> "However, repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying, and then cry," (4:18)

Repentance at the moment of certain death, or after it, is not repentance; it is capitulation.

**Why the Return Is Not Granted**

There is also a matter of justice and coherence. The world is the place of testing; the Hereafter is the place of recompense. If people could return from the Hereafter after seeing its reality, the test would be void. Everyone would believe after seeing the Fire; belief would no longer be a free choice but a forced conclusion. The whole structure of moral responsibility depends on the finality of death. The verse's poignancy comes from the fact that the wish is impossible — and it was always going to be impossible, which is why the warning was given now.

There is also, as verse 28 will state, the matter of their sincerity. God knows that even if they were returned, they would return to their old ways. The wish is not merely impossible; it is dishonest.

**The Value of the Present Moment**

The verse's deepest teaching is about time. The idolaters in the Fire wish for what every living person already possesses: a life in the world in which belief is possible. The gift they beg for is the gift the reader holds in his hands. Every day of life is an answer to the prayer "would that we were sent back" — an answer given before the prayer is made. The person who understands this does not waste the day.

The Prophet ﷺ described the regret of even the righteous over unused time:

> "There is no one who dies but that he regrets. If he was a doer of good, he regrets that he did not do more; and if he was a doer of evil, he regrets that he did not stop." (al-Tirmidhī 2403, graded weak by some but with supporting meaning in other texts)

And he taught his community to use the present:

> "Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a traveler on the road." Ibn ʿUmar used to say: "When evening comes, do not expect morning; and when morning comes, do not expect evening. Take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death." (al-Bukhārī 6416)

**Believing before Seeing**

The verse also highlights the essence of faith: belief in what is unseen. The idolaters would believe after seeing the Fire — but that is not faith, it is sight. Faith is to believe on the basis of evidence and revelation before the reality is forced upon one. The Qur'an opens its description of the righteous with exactly this quality:

> "Who believe in the unseen." (2:3)

The believer's distinction is that he does now, freely, what the idolater will wish to have done when it is too late. He has seen the same signs; he has heard the same warnings; the difference is that he responded while the response still counted.

**Looking at the Scene with the Prophet**

Finally, the verse invites the Prophet ﷺ and the reader to *look* — 'if you could see.' The purpose is not to gloat over the damned but to be sobered by their fate and moved to prevent it in oneself and others. The Prophet ﷺ, who was described as "He is concerned by your suffering, anxious for your well-being, and gracious and merciful to the believers" (9:128), would have looked at this scene with sorrow. The believer who reads it should feel the same: sorrow for those who wasted their chance, gratitude for the chance still in hand, and urgency to use it.

## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:28

> **But no! ˹They only say this˺ because the truth they used to hide will become all too clear to them. Even if they were to be sent back, they would certainly revert to what they were forbidden. Indeed they are liars!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**God's Response to the Wish**

Verse 27 recorded the idolaters' wish to be sent back and their promise to believe. Verse 28 is God's response, and it opens with *bal* — "nay," "rather," "on the contrary." This particle corrects a false impression. The idolaters presented their wish as a sincere desire for faith; God says: no, that is not what is happening. What is happening is that the truth they concealed has been exposed, and their promise is a lie.

**"It Has Now Become Clear to Them What They Used to Hide"**

The phrase *badā lahum mā kānū yukhfūna min qabl* — "there has appeared to them what they used to hide before" — has been read in several complementary ways by the commentators.

Al-Ṭabarī explains that what they hid were their evil deeds, committed in secret in this world, now manifested before them in the Hereafter. The Day of Judgment is described as the Day when "on the Day all secrets will be disclosed" (86:9), when every hidden thing is brought into the open:

> "And the record ˹of deeds˺ will be laid ˹open˺, and you will see the wicked in fear of what is ˹written˺ in it" (18:49)

Al-Rāzī offers additional readings. What they hid may be their *shirk* itself — as in verses 23–24, where they tried to deny it — now made manifest so that denial is impossible. Or it may be the knowledge, which the leaders of Makkah privately possessed, that the Prophet ﷺ was truthful. They hid this from their followers and, to some degree, from themselves. On the Day of Judgment, the truth they suppressed becomes unavoidable.

Al-Zamakhsharī records a further possibility: the verse may refer to the hypocrites, who hid their disbelief beneath a show of faith, or to the People of the Book, who hid their recognition of the Prophet ﷺ. The source commentary notes that these readings fit less well with the Makkan context, which is addressed to the pagan idolaters. But the underlying principle holds for all: on that Day, everything hidden is revealed, and the wish to return is uttered by people who now see the truth they spent their lives covering.

**Why This Undermines Their Wish**
