The connection between "it has become clear to them what they hid" and their wish to return is subtle but crucial. They say they would believe if returned. God says: your desire to return is not a desire for faith; it is the shock of seeing your own concealed reality exposed. You are not converted; you are caught. The distinction matters because a person who is merely caught will, when the pressure lifts, return to what he was. And that is exactly what the next clause says.

**"Even If They Were Sent Back, They Would Return"**

*Wa law ruddū la-ʿādū li-mā nuhū ʿanhu* — "and if they were returned, they would surely go back to what they were forbidden." The verb *ʿāda* means to return to a former state or practice. The phrase "what they were forbidden" (*mā nuhū ʿanhu*) refers to *shirk*, denial, and mockery — everything the Prophet ﷺ had warned them against.

This is a statement of divine knowledge about what would happen under a hypothetical condition. God knows not only what has happened and what will happen but what would happen if things were otherwise. The theologians call this knowledge of the conditional (*ʿilm al-shar ṭī*), and the Qur'an affirms it in several places:

> "˹But˺ even if He had made them hear, they would have surely turned away heedlessly" (8:23)

The verse tells us that the idolaters' character was fixed by their own choices to such a degree that even the experience of the Fire would not permanently alter it. Returned to the world, with its temptations, its social pressures, and the fading of memory, they would revert.

**The Psychology of Reversion**

This claim is psychologically credible. Human beings are notoriously prone to return to their patterns once a crisis passes. The patient who swears he will change his habits after a heart attack often does not. The person who resolves to reform during a disaster forgets the resolve when the disaster ends. The Qur'an describes exactly this pattern with regard to the idolaters at sea:

> "But when He delivers you ˹safely˺ to shore, you turn away" (17:67)

> "But as soon as He delivers them ˹safely˺ to shore, they associate ˹others with Him once again˺" (29:65)

If the fear of drowning produces only temporary faith, the fear of the Fire would produce the same. The character formed over a lifetime is not undone by a moment of terror. This is why the Qur'an insists on transformation *now*, through repeated choices, rather than on a single dramatic conversion under pressure.

**The Theological Dimension**

Al-Rāzī notes that some scholars used this verse in discussions of divine decree: the idolaters' disbelief was known to God and written before their creation, and even a second life would not change it. Others emphasized that the verse describes the consequence of the idolaters' own settled character, not an external compulsion. The two views converge on the same practical point: what a person will do is a function of who he has become, and who he has become is the result of his own choices. God's foreknowledge does not force the choice; it knows it. The verse is not saying "they cannot change because God decreed it" but "they would not change, and God knows it, because that is who they made themselves."

**"Truly They Are Liars"**

The verse concludes with a flat judgment: *wa innahum la-kādhibūn* — "and indeed they are liars." The emphasis (*inna* + *la*) is strong. Their promise to believe if returned is a lie — not a well-meant resolution that would later fail, but a falsehood at the moment of utterance. They do not truly intend to believe; they intend to escape. God, who knows the secret and the public, exposes the lie.

This connects to verse 23, where they lied by saying "we were not idolaters," and to verse 24, where they "lied against themselves." The idolaters are shown lying at every stage: lying about God in this world (v. 21), lying about their past at the Judgment (v. 23), and lying about their future (v. 28). The label "liars" is the summary of a lifetime and beyond.

**The Lesson: Sincerity Is Tested in Freedom**

The verse teaches that the value of faith lies in its freedom. Belief extracted by the sight of the Fire is worthless because it is not chosen; it is compelled. God wants faith that is offered when the alternative is available — faith that costs something, that is chosen over comfort and conformity. The idolaters' promise fails this test completely. Had they returned, the cost would have reappeared and the choice would have gone the same way.

For the reader, this raises a searching question: is my faith of the kind that would survive if the fear that supports it were removed? Or is it a bargain struck under pressure? The Qur'an praises those whose faith is steady in ease and hardship alike:

> "but if they are afflicted with a trial, they relapse ˹into disbelief˺, losing this world and the Hereafter" (22:11)

The one who worships "on an edge" is the one who would revert if returned. The one whose faith is rooted is the one who does not need the Fire to remind him.

**The Finality of the Verse**

Verses 27 and 28 together close the door on the fantasy of a second chance. The wish to return is understood, recorded, and refused — not out of cruelty but because it is a lie and because the world was already the second chance, and the third, and the thousandth. Every sunrise the idolaters saw in Makkah was a return of the kind they would later beg for. This is the verse's final teaching: you are already where they wish to be. Act accordingly.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:29

> **They insisted, “There is nothing beyond this worldly life and we will never be resurrected.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Creed of the Denier Stated Plainly**

After showing the idolaters at the Judgment, the Qur'an returns to what they said in this life, so that the contrast between their confidence then and their terror later stands out. Their creed is stated in a single sentence: *in hiya illā ḥayātunā al-dunyā wa mā naḥnu bi-mabʿūthīn* — "there is nothing but our worldly life, and we are not going to be resurrected."

The grammar is emphatic. *In... illā* ("nothing but") restricts existence to this life alone. *Mā naḥnu bi-mabʿūthīn*, with the emphatic *bi*, is a strong denial: "we are certainly not going to be raised." This is not tentative doubt; it is a confident assertion of materialism.

Several commentators note that the verse can be read as continuing verse 28: "if they were sent back, they would return to what they were forbidden" — *and they would say* "there is nothing but our worldly life." On this reading, the verse describes what they would say upon return, confirming that their character is unchanged. Al-Ṭabarī allows both readings: it may describe what they said in the world, or what they would say if returned. Either way, the creed is the same.

**The Word "Dunyā"**

The word *dunyā* is a feminine elative from the root *d-n-w*, meaning "near" or "low." *Al-ḥayāt al-dunyā* is "the nearer life" or "the lower life" — the life that is close at hand and beneath the higher life to come. The word itself carries the Qur'anic judgment that this life is not the whole of reality; it is the nearer portion of a longer existence. The idolaters used the term without accepting its implication. By saying "there is nothing but *al-dunyā*," they were using a word that presupposes an *ākhirah* (a "later" life) to deny that there is one.

**Denial of Resurrection as the Core Error**

The Qur'an records this denial in many places, often in the idolaters' own voices:

> "Once we are dead and reduced to dust and bones, will we really be resurrected" (23:82–83)

> "There is nothing beyond our first death, and we will never be resurrected" (44:35)

> "Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected, then you will certainly be informed of what you have done" (64:7)

> "When we are reduced to bones and ashes, will we really be raised as a new creation" (17:49)

The denial of resurrection was, for the Makkans, the crux of their rejection of the message. Belief in God as Creator they could accept; belief that God would raise the dead and judge them they found intolerable, because it made every action consequential. Al-Rāzī observes that the denial of resurrection is the root from which all other forms of heedlessness grow: if there is no accounting, there is no reason to restrain desire, to accept moral limits, or to heed a prophet.

**Why the Makkans Denied Resurrection**

Their objection was partly intellectual and partly moral. Intellectually, they could not conceive how decayed bones and scattered dust could be reassembled into living persons. The Qur'an answers this objection repeatedly by pointing to the first creation (36:78–79), to the revival of dead earth by rain (41:39), and to the ease of repetition compared to origination (30:27). Morally, the denial served their interests. A people devoted to tribal pride, accumulation of wealth, and the exploitation of the weak had every reason to reject a doctrine that would hold them accountable. The Qur'an exposes this motive:

> "We are ˹most˺ capable of restoring ˹even˺ their very fingertips" (75:3–5)

The denial of resurrection, in other words, is often not a conclusion reached by reasoning but a preference dressed as reasoning. The person who wishes to continue in sin needs a worldview in which sin has no lasting consequence.

**The Modern Form of This Creed**

The verse describes an ancient belief that has become, in some circles, a modern orthodoxy. "There is nothing but this life" is the working assumption of much of contemporary culture, whether stated explicitly as materialist philosophy or lived implicitly as the pursuit of pleasure, achievement, and possession as though nothing else existed. The Qur'an's response to this position was formulated fourteen centuries ago and remains applicable.

First, the position is not the conclusion of evidence but the absence of it: no one has demonstrated that death ends everything; the claim is an assertion. Second, it contradicts the universal human sense of justice, which demands that wrongs unaddressed in this life be addressed somewhere. If a tyrant dies comfortably in old age and his victims die in torment, and there is nothing further, then justice is a fiction — a conclusion most people cannot honestly accept. Third, it leaves the extraordinary fact of human consciousness, moral awareness, and longing for meaning without explanation. The Qur'an says:

> "Did you then think that We had created you without purpose, and that you would never be returned to Us" (23:115)

Fourth, and most simply, the One who created life from clay (v. 2) is manifestly able to recreate it. To admit the Creator and deny the resurrection is incoherent.

**The Consequences of This Creed**

The verse is placed between two scenes of the Judgment (vv. 27–28 and v. 30), so that the creed is surrounded by its refutation. The literary structure makes the point: "there is nothing but this life," they said — and here they are, standing before their Lord. The denial did not prevent the resurrection; it only ensured they arrived at it unprepared.

The Qur'an also describes the effect of this creed on conduct. Those who believe there is nothing but this life tend to become "the people of the left," whose lives are marked by heedless indulgence:

> "They used to ask ˹mockingly˺," (56:45–47)

The connection between denial of resurrection and moral collapse is not accidental. Belief in accountability is the foundation of restraint; remove it, and restraint becomes irrational.

**The Believer's Counter-Creed**

Against "there is nothing but our worldly life," the Qur'an sets the believer's confession:

> "And the next life is certainly far better for you than this one" (93:4)

> "even though the Hereafter is far better and more lasting" (87:16–17)

And the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "By God, this world in comparison to the Hereafter is nothing but as if one of you dipped his finger in the sea; let him see what it brings back." (Muslim 2858)

The believer does not deny this life or its goods; he places them in proportion. This life is real, but it is *dunyā* — the nearer, lower portion. The Hereafter is the larger reality toward which it points. Living by this proportion is the whole difference between the believer and the denier, and the verse before us states the denier's position so that the believer can see clearly what he has rejected.

**A Note of Sorrow**

Finally, one senses in the verse a note of divine sorrow at the smallness of the deniers' vision. To say "there is nothing but this life" is to shrink existence to a few decades of eating, competing, and dying. The Qur'an offers an existence that begins in clay and continues eternally, in which every deed matters and every soul is known. The idolaters chose the smaller story. The verse records their choice, and the following verse records where it led.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:30

> **But if only you could see when they will be detained before their Lord! He will ask ˹them˺, “Is this ˹Hereafter˺ not the truth?” They will cry, “Absolutely, by our Lord!” He will say, “Then taste the punishment for your disbelief.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Window onto the Judgment**

Verse 27 opened with "If you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire." Verse 30 uses the identical opening — *wa law tarā idh wuqifū* — but with a decisive change: not "before the Fire" but *ʿalā rabbihim*, "before their Lord." The progression is deliberate. In verse 27 they confronted the punishment; in verse 30 they confront the Judge. The Fire is terrible, but standing before the Lord one denied is the more profound reckoning.

The phrase "their Lord" is pointed. The verse could have said "before God"; it says "before *their* Lord" — the One who created them, sustained them, sent them signs, and whom they denied while calling His message "fables of the ancients" (v. 25). They are made to stand before the One they belonged to all along.

**"Is This Not the Truth?"**

God's question is *a-laysa hādhā bi'l-ḥaqq* — "is this not the truth?" The demonstrative *hādhā* ("this") refers to the resurrection, the Judgment, and everything the prophets warned of — all that the idolaters had denied in verse 29 with the words "we shall not be resurrected." Now the resurrection is not a prediction but their present experience, and God asks them to confirm what they see.

The question is not for information. It is what the rhetoricians call a question of *taqrīr* — a question that compels acknowledgment. It forces the deniers to state, with their own mouths, the truth they spent their lives denying. There is a form of justice in this. They mocked the resurrection publicly; they must affirm it publicly. Al-Ṭabarī explains that God asks them in order to rebuke them and to establish the proof against them from their own words.

**"Yea, Indeed, by Our Lord!"**

Their answer: *qālū balā wa rabbinā* — "they say: Yes, by our Lord!" The particle *balā* is the specific Arabic word for affirming a negative question — "yes, it is the truth." They add an oath: "by our Lord." This is the same oath they swore in verse 23, when they lied ("by God, our Lord, we were not idolaters"). Now they swear the truth. The contrast is instructive. In verse 23 they swore falsely to escape; in verse 30 they swear truthfully because escape is impossible and the truth is inescapably before them.

Their acknowledgment is complete. Every doubt is gone. Those who said "there is nothing but our worldly life" now say "yes, by our Lord, this is the truth." The Qur'an describes this moment of certainty in several places:

> "If only you could see the wicked hanging their heads ˹in shame˺ before their Lord, ˹crying" (32:12)

"We are now certain" — but certainty acquired after the Judgment is worthless as faith, because it is no longer belief in the Unseen. It is sight.

**"Then Taste the Punishment for Having Disbelieved"**

God's reply is *fa-dhūqū al-ʿadhāba bi-mā kuntum takfurūn* — "then taste the punishment because of what you used to deny." The *fa* ("then") marks the consequence: having admitted the truth, they now receive what denial of it earned.

The verb *dhāqa* — "taste" — is used for punishment in more than two dozen verses. The choice of this word is meaningful. Taste is the most intimate and undeniable of the senses; one cannot be mistaken about what one tastes, and one cannot taste at a distance. The Qur'an says that the deniers will *taste* the punishment because their knowledge of it will be experiential and immediate, the exact opposite of the abstract mockery with which they treated it in this world. Al-Rāzī notes the connection: they treated the warning as a mere story; they will know its reality as one knows the taste of food in one's mouth.

The phrase *bi-mā kuntum takfurūn* — "because of what you used to disbelieve in" or "because you used to disbelieve" — states the cause. The punishment is not arbitrary. It is the earned consequence of a lifetime of denial. The verb *kafara*, from which *kufr* derives, means originally to cover — a farmer who covers the seed is a *kāfir* in the old poetic usage. To disbelieve is to cover over the truth, to bury the evidence one has been shown. The punishment is for this covering.

**The Parallel in Sūrat al-Aḥqāf**

An almost identical passage appears in 46:34:

> "And the Day those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: 'Is this not the truth?' They will say, 'Yes, by our Lord.' He will say, 'Then taste the punishment for what you used to deny.'"

And a related exchange occurs between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire:

> "The residents of Paradise will call out to the residents of the Fire," (7:44)

The repetition of this scene across the Qur'an emphasizes its certainty and its lesson: the truth will be acknowledged by everyone eventually; the only question is whether one acknowledges it in time to benefit.

**The Idolaters' Own Words Testify**

This verse completes a sequence in which the idolaters' own speech convicts them. In verse 29 they said, "we shall not be resurrected." In verse 30 they say, "yes, by our Lord, this is the truth." Their earlier denial and later confession are placed one verse apart so that the reader hears both. The Qur'an does not need to argue against them; it lets them argue against themselves. The Day of Judgment is, among other things, the day when every person's own words and deeds are set before him as witnesses.

**Tasting in This World**

The source commentary notes that the Qur'an also speaks of "tasting" consequences in this world through forms of atonement — for breaking oaths, violating the sanctity of pilgrimage, or other transgressions (5:95; 59:15; 64:5; 65:9). The principle is the same: experience teaches what argument could not. A person who "tastes" the consequences of a small transgression in this life, through the discipline of expiation, is being trained to understand that consequences are real — so that he does not have to learn it in the way described in verse 30.

**Learning from the Scene**

The verse is shown to the living. Its purpose is to make the moment of "yes, by our Lord" occur now rather than then. Every person will eventually stand before his Lord and acknowledge the truth; the verse offers the chance to acknowledge it now, while acknowledgment is faith rather than forced admission. The Prophet ﷺ described the difference between the two states:

> "Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him; and whoever hates to meet God, God hates to meet him." (al-Bukhārī 6507; Muslim 2683)

The believer who has already said "yes, my Lord, this is the truth" in his lifetime meets his Lord as one returning home. The denier meets Him as one caught. The verse is placed before the reader so that he may choose which meeting will be his.

**The Justice of "Because of What You Used to Deny"**

Finally, the verse affirms that punishment is proportioned to conduct. The idolaters are not punished for being human, for being ignorant, or for failing to reach a standard beyond them. They are punished "because of what you used to deny" — for a specific, chosen, persistent act of covering the truth they were shown. God's statement of the cause is itself an act of justice; He does not punish without explaining why. This transparency is a mercy even in judgment, and it is the reason no one on that Day will be able to say "I did not know why this is happening to me."

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:31

> **Losers indeed are those who deny the meeting with Allah until the Hour takes them by surprise, then they will cry, “Woe to us for having ignored this!” They will bear ˹the burden of˺ their sins on their backs. Evil indeed is their burden!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict of Loss**

The verse opens with a completed judgment: *qad khasira alladhīna kadhdhabū bi-liqā' Allāh* — "lost indeed are those who denied the meeting with God." The particle *qad* with the perfect verb indicates that the loss is certain and already effective. The word *khasira*, as discussed at verse 12, is a commercial term: to suffer a loss in a transaction, to come out with less than one put in. Those who deny the meeting with God have made the worst trade possible; they invested a life and received ruin.

**"The Meeting with God"**

The phrase *liqā' Allāh* — "the meeting with God" — is one of the Qur'an's most important expressions for the Hereafter. It describes the Day of Judgment not merely as an event but as an encounter: the creature will meet his Creator. The Qur'an uses this phrase repeatedly:

> "Those who deny the meeting with God have lost, until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly..." (this verse)

> "Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, being pleased and content with this worldly life, and who are heedless of Our signs," (10:7–8)

> "So whoever hopes for the meeting with their Lord, let them do good deeds and associate none in the worship of their Lord" (18:110)

The concept of "meeting" makes the Hereafter personal. It is not an abstract accounting but a coming face to face with the One who created you, watched you, and knows everything you did. To deny this meeting is to live as though one will never have to look into the eyes of the One to whom one owes everything. The verse says such people have lost — because they have organized their whole lives around a falsehood.

**"Until, When the Hour Comes upon Them Suddenly"**

The verse continues: *ḥattā idhā jā'athumu al-sāʿatu baghtatan* — "until, when the Hour comes to them suddenly." The word *al-sāʿah* ("the Hour") is the Qur'an's term for the moment of resurrection and judgment. The word *baghtatan* means suddenly, unexpectedly, without warning. This adverb appears with the Hour in many verses (7:187; 12:107; 21:40; 22:55; 43:66; 47:18).

The suddenness is essential to the verse's warning. The deniers of the meeting with God lived as though the Hour would never come — or at least, not yet. They deferred, postponed, and assumed there was time. Then it came without notice. The Prophet ﷺ described the suddenness:

> "The Hour will be established while two men have spread out their cloth between them, and they will not be able to buy or sell it or fold it up. The Hour will be established while a man has milked his camel and is taking the milk away, and he will not be able to drink it. The Hour will be established while a man is repairing his watering trough, and he will not be able to water from it. The Hour will be established while a man has raised his morsel to his mouth, and he will not be able to eat it." (al-Bukhārī 6506; Muslim 2954)

For the individual, death is his personal Hour, and it too comes suddenly. Most people do not know the day of their death. The verse applies at both levels: the universal Hour and the personal one.

**"Alas for Us, That We Neglected It!"**

Their cry at that moment: *yā ḥasratanā ʿalā mā farraṭnā fīhā* — "And warn them ˹O Prophet˺ of the Day of Regret, when all matters will be settled, while they are ˹engrossed˺ in heedlessness and disbelief" The word *ḥasrah* means a grief so intense that it leaves one helpless — the regret of a person who sees clearly what he lost and knows he cannot recover it. The Qur'an names the Day of Judgment "the Day of Regret" (*Yawm al-Ḥasrah*, 19:39) because of this feeling.

The verb *farraṭa* means to neglect, to fall short, to fail to do what should have been done — with a connotation of having let something slip away through carelessness. The pronoun *fīhā* ("in it") is understood by the commentators to refer either to the Hour (they neglected preparation for it), to the worldly life (they neglected to use it well), or to the matter generally. All amount to the same thing: they had time and did not use it.

Al-Rāzī, cited in the source commentary, describes this regret with a penetrating analysis. It is not the regret of a person who tried and failed; it is the regret of a person who realizes he squandered the very faculties given to him for the purpose of succeeding. God gave them intellect to recognize the truth, senses to perceive the signs, and time to act — and they wasted all of it. Al-Rāzī uses the commercial metaphor: it is like a merchant who not only fails to make a profit but loses the borrowed capital as well. The capital was the soul, the life, the faculties; all were given on loan; all were lost.

**"They Will Bear Their Burdens upon Their Backs"**

The verse then describes their condition: *wa hum yaḥmilūna awzārahum ʿalā ẓuhūrihim* — "and they carry their burdens on their backs." The word *wizr* (plural *awzār*) means a heavy load, and by extension a sin — because sin weighs on the soul. The image of the sinner carrying his sins on his back is vivid and appears elsewhere:

> "Let them bear their burdens in full on the Day of Judgment as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge" (16:25)

> "Yet they will certainly ˹be made to˺ carry their own burdens, as well as other burdens along with their own" (29:13)

Al-Ṭabarī explains that the burdens are their sins themselves, made manifest and heavy. Other commentators, as the source notes, understand the burden as the divine wrath earned by those sins, or as the very warnings and reminders they refused, which now weigh on them as evidence of their neglect (compare 20:100–101, where the one who turns from the Reminder "Whoever turns away from it will surely bear the burden ˹of sin˺ on the Day of Judgment,").

There is a physical logic to the image. In this life, sins can seem weightless — a lie, a betrayal, an act of oppression, a mockery of the truth — none of them feels heavy at the moment of commission. On the Day of Judgment their true weight is felt. Ibn Masʿūd said that the believer sees his sins as though he were sitting beneath a mountain that might fall on him, while the wicked man sees his sins as a fly passing his nose that he brushes away (al-Bukhārī 6308). The verse describes the moment when the fly becomes the mountain.

**"Behold! Evil Is That Which They Bear!"**

The verse concludes with an exclamation: *a-lā sā'a mā yazirūn* — "unquestionably, evil is what they bear!" The particle *a-lā* is used for emphasis and calling attention. The verb *sā'a* ("how evil!") is a verb of blame. The load they carry is not merely heavy; it is evil — it will not be set down at a resting place but will drag them to the Fire.

**The Contrast with the Believer's Burden**

The Qur'an offers a counter-image. The believer also carries something, but it is different in kind:

> "But whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done good, they will have the highest ranks" (20:75)

> "Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold" (6:160)

Where the denier's burden weighs him down, the believer's deeds lift him up. Both are the accumulated results of a life; the difference lies in what was accumulated.

**The Lesson: Prepare for the Meeting**

The verse's central term is "the meeting with God," and its central warning is about neglect. The person who believes in the meeting prepares for it, as one prepares for any important encounter — by getting one's affairs in order, by making amends, by bringing what will be well received. The person who denies it makes no preparation and is caught by the suddenness of the Hour with nothing but the weight of his sins. The Prophet ﷺ was asked when the Hour would come, and he asked the questioner:

> "What have you prepared for it?" (al-Bukhārī 6167; Muslim 2639)

This is the question the verse poses. Not "when will the Hour come?" but "what have you prepared?" The one who has prepared does not fear its suddenness; the one who has not will cry, "Alas for us." The verse describes the second so that the reader will become the first.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:32

> **This worldly life is no more than play and amusement, but far better is the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter for those mindful ˹of Allah˺. Will you not then understand?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Diagnosis Behind the Denial**

The previous verses described people who denied the meeting with God and said "there is nothing but our worldly life." Verse 32 addresses the root of that error by stating what this world actually is. The deniers treated worldly life as the whole of reality; the verse declares it "nothing but play and diversion" in comparison with what follows. The correction is not merely theological but a reordering of value.

**"Play and Diversion"**

The two words are *laʿib* and *lahw*. *Laʿib* is play — activity engaged in for its own amusement, without lasting result, as children play. *Lahw* is diversion or distraction — anything that occupies attention and turns it away from what matters, from the root *l-h-w*, to be diverted or heedless. The two together describe an existence in which people are busy and absorbed but produce nothing that lasts and are distracted from what does.

Al-Rāzī explains the sense in which the world is "play": play involves a kind of delusion in which the inner reality of things is hidden behind their outward appearance. Children playing at war or commerce take their game seriously and may weep or rejoice over it, but the adult sees that nothing real has been won or lost. Similarly, the pursuits people take most seriously in this world — wealth, position, rivalry, display — are, from the standpoint of eternity, a kind of children's game. The wealth is left behind; the position dissolves; the rivalry is forgotten.

The source commentary rightly notes that the verse does not condemn play as such. Play is permissible in Islam; the Prophet ﷺ raced with ʿĀ'ishah and permitted the Abyssinians to perform with spears in the mosque. The verse's point is comparative: much of what the world holds most weighty is, in relation to the Hereafter, as insubstantial as play. The Qur'an makes the same comparison with more detail:

> "And in the Hereafter there will be either severe punishment or forgiveness and pleasure of Allah, whereas the life of this world is no more than the delusion of enjoyment" (57:20)

> "But the Hereafter is indeed the real life, if only they knew" (29:64)

The last verse states the point sharply: the Hereafter is "*the* life" — the real one. This world, by comparison, barely qualifies.

**"Better Indeed Is the Abode of the Hereafter for Those Who Are Reverent"**

The verse continues: *wa la'l-dāru al-ākhiratu khayrun li'lladhīna yattaqūn* — "and surely the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are God-conscious." The word *dār* means abode, dwelling, home — a place of settled residence. This world is not called a *dār* in this verse; only the Hereafter is. The implication is that this world is a passage, a temporary stopping place, while the Hereafter is home.

The comparative *khayr* ("better") is used in Arabic sometimes to mean "better than" and sometimes simply "good" in an absolute sense. The commentators note that here it may carry both: the Hereafter is better than this world, and it is absolutely good.

The qualification "for those who are reverent" (*li'lladhīna yattaqūn*) is crucial. The Hereafter is not better for everyone; for the deniers described in the preceding verses it is worse than anything they experienced here. It is better for those who have *taqwā* — the protective awareness of God that guards a person from what harms him. *Taqwā*, from the root *w-q-y* (to protect, shield), is like the care of a person walking through a path full of thorns: he gathers his garment and watches his step. The one who lives this way finds the Hereafter better; the one who strides carelessly finds it a place of regret.

**Why This Comparison Is True**

The verse's claim can be reasoned through. Consider duration. This life is a few decades at most; the Hereafter is without end. A rational person weighs the temporary against the permanent and prefers the permanent, as anyone would prefer a permanent home to a night in a rented room. Consider quality. The best pleasures of this world are mixed with fatigue, anxiety, illness, loss, and the knowledge that they will end; the pleasures of Paradise are described as unmixed and unending:

> "No fatigue will touch them there, nor will they ever be asked to leave" (15:48)

Consider certainty. Worldly goods can be lost at any moment; the reward of the Hereafter, once granted, is secure. On every axis of comparison, the Hereafter is better — for those who qualify for its good.

**"Do You Not Understand?"**

The verse ends with a question: *a-fa-lā taʿqilūn* — "will you not then use your reason?" The verb *ʿaqala* means to understand, to reason, to bind (as one binds a camel; the intellect "binds" a person from folly). The question implies that the preference for this world over the Hereafter is not merely a spiritual failing but an intellectual one. It is irrational to prefer the smaller, shorter, less certain good to the greater, longer, guaranteed one. Anyone who used his reason would see this.

The Qur'an frequently connects faith with reason in this way. It does not ask people to believe against their intellect but to use their intellect properly. The denier of the Hereafter has not out-reasoned the believer; he has failed to reason at all about the most important question. The Prophet ﷺ described the intelligent person:

> "The intelligent one is he who takes account of himself and works for what comes after death, and the incapable one is he who follows his desires and merely hopes in God." (al-Tirmidhī 2459, graded ḥasan by him; others regard the chain as weak, though the meaning is confirmed by the Qur'an)

Intelligence, in this definition, is not cleverness in worldly affairs but the wisdom to prepare for what lasts.

**Living the Comparison**

What does it mean to live by this verse? Not to abandon the world — Islam forbids monasticism and commands earning, marrying, building, and caring for others. It means to hold the world in proportion: to use it without being used by it, to enjoy its lawful goods without mistaking them for the goal, and to make every worldly activity serve the Hereafter. The Companions were merchants, farmers, soldiers, and rulers; they were not detached from the world, but they were detached from its illusions. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is reported to have said: "The world is departing, and the Hereafter is approaching, and each has children; so be children of the Hereafter and not children of the world."

The Prophet ﷺ described his own relationship to it:

> "What have I to do with this world? I am in this world only like a rider who seeks shade under a tree, then departs and leaves it." (al-Tirmidhī 2377, graded ṣaḥīḥ)

The rider enjoys the shade; he does not mistake it for home.

**The Psychological Freedom of This View**

Understanding the world as play and diversion, in the Qur'anic sense, is liberating rather than depressing. The person who believes this world is everything must win at it; every loss is catastrophic, every rival a threat, every failure a diminishment of his entire existence. The person who believes this world is a passage can lose without despair, compete without hatred, and fail without collapse, because his real stake is elsewhere. The Qur'an describes this equanimity:

> "˹We let you know this˺ so that you neither grieve over what you have missed nor boast over what He has granted you" (57:23)

This equanimity is not indifference; it is the calm of someone who knows what matters.

**Connection to the Sūrah's Argument**

In the flow of Sūrah al-Anʿām, this verse addresses the deniers' error at its foundation. They mocked the Prophet ﷺ, demanded signs, denied resurrection, and would beg for return — all because they valued this world above everything. Verse 32 tells them that the thing they valued was play, and the thing they mocked was the real abode. If they could see this — if they would use their reason — the whole structure of their denial would fall. The verse thus offers the cure for the disease that the preceding thirty verses diagnosed.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:33

> **We certainly know that what they say grieves you ˹O Prophet˺. It is not your honesty they question—it is Allah’s signs that the wrongdoers deny.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**God Acknowledges the Prophet's Grief**

After thirty-two verses arguing with the idolaters, the sūrah turns to the Prophet ﷺ himself with words of intimate comfort. *Qad naʿlamu innahu la-yaḥzunuka alladhī yaqūlūn* — "We certainly know that what they say grieves you." The emphatic construction (*qad naʿlamu*, *innahu*, *la-yaḥzunuka*) makes the acknowledgment full and explicit. God does not merely know the Prophet's ﷺ grief in the abstract; He states it to him, so that the Prophet ﷺ knows he is seen.

The verb *ḥazina* means to grieve, to be sorrowful. The Prophet ﷺ was not indifferent to his people's rejection. He loved them, wished for their salvation, and was wounded by their mockery, their accusations of sorcery and madness, and their calling the revelation "fables of the ancients." The Qur'an records his grief in several places and repeatedly consoles him:

> "Now, perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death over their denial, if they ˹continue to˺ disbelieve in this message" (18:6)

> "Perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death over their disbelief" (26:3)

> "Indeed, We ˹fully˺ know what they conceal and what they reveal" (36:76)

This verse is distinctive among the consolations. As the source commentary observes, it is the only place where the Prophet ﷺ is comforted specifically by being told that the rejection is not personal.

**"It Is Not Thee That They Deny"**

The heart of the verse: *fa-innahum lā yukadhdhibūnak* — "indeed, they do not deny you." At first this seems to contradict the plain facts; the Makkans called the Prophet ﷺ a liar constantly. The commentators resolve the apparent contradiction by drawing on what the Makkans themselves knew and said.

Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī point out that the Prophet ﷺ was known among the Quraysh as *al-Amīn*, the Trustworthy, before his mission. In forty years of life among them he had never been known to lie. When he first called them publicly from Mount Ṣafā and asked, "If I told you that horsemen were in the valley about to attack you, would you believe me?" they answered, "Yes, we have never known you to lie" (al-Bukhārī 4770; Muslim 208). Their denial was therefore not of his personal truthfulness, which they could not honestly dispute, but of the message itself.

There is a well-known report, recorded by al-Tirmidhī and al-Ḥākim and cited by Ibn Kathīr in the commentary on this verse, that Abū Jahl said to the Prophet ﷺ:

> "We do not call you a liar, but we deny what you have brought." Upon which God revealed: "Indeed, they do not deny you, but it is the signs of God that the wrongdoers reject." (al-Tirmidhī 3064; graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Ḥākim, with discussion of its chain)

Similarly, when al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq privately asked Abū Jahl whether Muhammad ﷺ was truthful, Abū Jahl reportedly replied that he was, but that the clan of Hāshim already had the honor of feeding the pilgrims and providing water, and if they now claimed prophethood too, the clan of Makhzūm could never match them. The rejection was tribal pride, not honest disbelief.

**The Grammatical Readings**

Two readings of *lā yukadhdhibūnak* exist among the reciters. The majority read the intensive form *yukadhdhibūna* (they do not call you a liar). Nāfiʿ and al-Kisā'ī read *lā yukdhibūnak*, from the Form IV verb, which was explained by the linguists as "they do not find you a liar" — that is, they do not find any lie in you when they examine your speech. Both readings converge on the meaning that the Prophet's ﷺ personal honesty was not the issue.

**"Rather, It Is the Signs of God That the Wrongdoers Reject"**

The verse relocates the denial: *wa lākinna al-ẓālimīna bi-āyāti Allāhi yajḥadūn* — "but the wrongdoers reject the signs of God." The verb *jaḥada* is significant. It does not mean simply to disbelieve; it means to deny something one knows to be true, to reject with the tongue what the heart has recognized. The Qur'an uses this verb of Pharaoh's people:

> "And, although their hearts were convinced the signs were true, they still denied them wrongfully and arrogantly" (27:14)

This is precisely the diagnosis: the Makkans knew, and rejected anyway. Their *juḥūd* was not ignorance but willful denial. The verse calls them *al-ẓālimūn* — the wrongdoers — because, as discussed at verse 21, *ẓulm* is to put a thing out of its rightful place. They took the truth they recognized and placed it in the category of falsehood.

The shift from "you" to "the signs of God" also lifts the burden from the Prophet ﷺ in a second way. If the rejection were of him, it would be his problem to solve. Since the rejection is of God's signs, it is God's matter, and God will deal with it. The Prophet's ﷺ task was to convey; the response to rejection was not his responsibility.

**The Deeper Principle: Attitude toward the Messenger Reflects Attitude toward God**

The verse implies a principle stated elsewhere in the Qur'an: how one treats God's Messenger reveals how one relates to God.

> "Surely those who pledge allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ are actually pledging allegiance to Allah" (48:10)

> "If you ˹sincerely˺ love Allah, then follow me" (3:31)

> "Whoever obeys the Messenger has truly obeyed Allah" (4:80)

The Messenger is transparent to the message. To accept him is to accept God's word; to reject him is to reject God's word. The Makkans could not separate the two, however much they claimed to admire his character. Their professed respect for his honesty, combined with their rejection of his message, was incoherent — a man who is honest in everything cannot be lying about the one thing that matters most. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that this incoherence exposes the depth of their obstinacy: they were reduced to affirming his truthfulness and denying his truth at the same time.

**The Psychology of Personal Rejection**

The verse addresses a universal human vulnerability. When our sincere efforts are refused, we tend to take it personally. A parent whose child rejects his advice feels rejected as a parent; a teacher whose student fails to learn feels a failure as a teacher; a person who shares a truth and is mocked feels mocked himself. This personalization compounds the pain and can distort judgment — leading either to despair or to a compromise of the message in hope of being accepted.

The verse offers the Prophet ﷺ — and every believer who calls to truth — a way out. The rejection is not of you; it is of the truth you carry. You are not diminished by it. Your worth does not depend on their acceptance. Your job is faithfully to deliver; their job is to respond; and the One whose signs are rejected will handle the consequences. This separation is not a way of avoiding responsibility but of locating it correctly. The Prophet ﷺ remained fully responsible for conveying with clarity, patience, and compassion; he was never responsible for the outcome.

**Comfort without Flattery**

Notice how the comfort is given. God does not tell the Prophet ﷺ that the Makkans will soon believe, or that his grief is misplaced, or that everything will be easy. He tells him the truth about the situation: their rejection is of God's signs, and they are wrongdoers. This is comfort grounded in clarity, not in false hope. It allows the Prophet ﷺ to grieve without being crushed and to continue without being deceived. Verse 34 will add the further comfort of precedent — all messengers were denied and all were helped — and verse 35 will gently correct any temptation to force the outcome.

**The Wrongdoers' Loss**

Finally, the verse's description of the deniers as *al-ẓālimūn* shows who is actually harmed. The Prophet ﷺ grieved, but his grief was for them, not for himself. They were the ones rejecting God's signs, and they were the ones who would bear the consequence. The verse gently redirects the Prophet's ﷺ sorrow: grieve, if you must, for them — not because they have wronged you, but because they have wronged themselves.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:34

> **Indeed, messengers before you were rejected but patiently endured rejection and persecution until Our help came to them. And Allah’s promise ˹to help˺ is never broken. And you have already received some of the narratives of these messengers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Consolation of Company**

Verse 33 told the Prophet ﷺ that the rejection was not of him personally. Verse 34 extends the comfort in a different direction: he is not the first to suffer this, and those who suffered before him were vindicated. *Wa la-qad kudhdhibat rusulun min qablik* — "and messengers before you were certainly denied." The passive verb and the indefinite plural indicate that this was the general experience of the prophets, not an occasional misfortune.

This verse takes up the theme of verse 10 ("messengers were mocked before you") and develops it. There, the emphasis was on the mockers' fate; here, the emphasis is on the messengers' response and their eventual relief. The Prophet ﷺ is invited to see himself as one of a long line — Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Abraham, Lot, Shuʿayb, Moses, Jesus — every one of them denied, every one of them patient, every one of them helped.

**"They Bore Patiently Their Being Denied and Persecuted"**

*Fa-ṣabarū ʿalā mā kudhdhibū wa ūdhū* — "so they were patient over being denied and harmed." Two forms of suffering are named: *takdhīb* (being called a liar) and *adhā* (being harmed, injured, persecuted). The first is verbal and psychological; the second is physical and social. The messengers endured both.

The verb *ṣabara* — to be patient, to persevere, to hold firm — is one of the central virtues of the Qur'an. Its root meaning is to restrain or confine; *ṣabr* is the restraint of the self from despair, complaint, and abandonment of duty under pressure. It is not passive resignation but active endurance: the prophets did not stop preaching when denied; they continued. Noah preached for nine hundred and fifty years (29:14). Moses returned to Pharaoh again and again. The patience the verse describes is the patience of persistence.

The Qur'an mentions specific examples of the messengers' patience under harm:

> "On the Day they see what they have been threatened with, it will be as if they had only stayed ˹in this world˺ for an hour of a day" (46:35)

> "We have certainly sent messengers before you ˹O Prophet˺ and blessed them with wives and offspring" (13:38)

Moses said to his people, when Pharaoh's oppression intensified:

> "Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah ˹alone˺" (7:128)

**"Till Our Help Came to Them"**

The patience had an end: *ḥattā atāhum naṣrunā* — "until Our help came to them." The word *naṣr* means help, support, victory — specifically, the aid that brings triumph. The verse states as historical fact that divine help did come to the earlier messengers. Noah was saved and his deniers drowned; Abraham was delivered from the fire; Moses was brought through the sea and Pharaoh was destroyed; Lot was taken out before the cities were overturned.

The Qur'an states this as a general law:

> "Our Word has already gone forth to Our servants, the messengers," (37:171–173)

> "I and My messengers will certainly prevail" (58:21)

> "We certainly help Our messengers and the believers, ˹both˺ in this worldly life and on the Day the witnesses will stand forth ˹for testimony˺—" (40:51)

The help may come in this world, in the form of deliverance or victory, or it may be deferred to the Hereafter, but it always comes. The word *ḥattā* ("until") tells the Prophet ﷺ something important about the timing: the help comes at the end of the patience, not the beginning. There is an interval of suffering, and the interval is not a sign that help has failed; it is the space in which patience is exercised and proven.

**"None Alters the Words of God"**

*Wa lā mubaddila li-kalimāti Allāh* — "and there is no changer of the words of God." This clause anchors the promise. The reason the Prophet ﷺ can be certain of help is that God has spoken, and what God has spoken cannot be altered by any power. The commentators offer several understandings of "the words of God" here, and they are complementary.

Al-Thaʿlabī and others take "the words of God" as the Qur'an itself: no one can alter it, and its promises will therefore stand. Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī take it as God's promise of victory to His messengers: it is decreed and cannot be reversed. Al-Rāzī also records a reading in which "the words of God" refers to His decree for all things, including the disbelief of those who disbelieve — which nothing the Prophet ﷺ does can change. On all these readings, the point for the Prophet ﷺ is the same: the outcome is not in the hands of the deniers, and it is not in his own hands; it is in God's decree, which is fixed.

The phrase recurs in the Qur'an:

> "For them is good news in this worldly life and the Hereafter" (10:64)

> "Recite what has been revealed to you from the Book of your Lord" (18:27)

> "The Word of your Lord has been perfected in truth and justice" (6:115)

**"There Has Already Come unto Thee Some Tidings of the Messengers"**

The verse concludes: *wa la-qad jā'aka min naba'i al-mursalīn* — "and there has certainly come to you some account of the messengers." By this point in the Makkan period, the Prophet ﷺ had received many of the Qur'anic narratives of the earlier prophets — the sūrahs of Hūd, Yūnus, Maryam, Ṭā Hā, al-Shuʿarā', al-Qaṣaṣ and others, with their accounts of Noah, Abraham, Moses, and the rest. The verse points him to these as evidence: you have seen in these accounts how the messengers were denied, how they endured, and how God helped them. The same pattern will hold for you.

The word *naba'* (news of consequence) is the same word used in verse 5 ("tidings will soon come to them"). The news of the messengers is not merely edifying; it is the record of a divine pattern that applies to the present.

**The Pattern as a Source of Certainty**

There is a logical structure to the consolation. If the law "messengers are denied, endure patiently, and are helped" held for every previous case, and the Prophet ﷺ is a messenger of the same God with the same message, then the law will hold for him. The narratives of past prophets are not merely stories but data points establishing a regularity. The Qur'an frequently invokes God's "way" (*sunnat Allāh*) as unchanging:

> "way, already long established ˹in the past˺" (48:23)

For the Prophet ﷺ in the years of Makkan persecution, this was the foundation of his steadfastness. He did not endure blindly; he endured knowing how the story ends.

**The Application for Every Believer**

The verse's teaching extends beyond the prophets. Anyone who stands for truth, calls to good, or lives by principle will face some form of denial and harm. The verse provides the method: patience — active, persistent, uncomplaining — until God's help comes. And it provides the ground: God's words do not change; His promise to support those who support His cause stands.

The Prophet ﷺ taught Ibn ʿAbbās this principle in words that echo the verse:

> "Know that victory comes with patience, relief with distress, and ease with hardship." (Aḥmad 2803; graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Albānī)

The order matters: patience first, then victory. The believer who expects the victory without the patience has misunderstood the pattern. The believer who understands it can endure the interval without despair, because he knows the interval is not the end.

**Patience Is Not Passivity**

A final clarification: the patience the verse commends is not withdrawal from effort. The messengers continued to preach, argue, warn, and call while they were patient. Patience is what sustained their effort, not what replaced it. For the Prophet ﷺ, the years of Makkan patience were years of relentless activity — teaching, traveling to Ṭā'if, meeting the tribes at the pilgrimage, sending Companions to Abyssinia, and finally emigrating to Madinah. The help came, at Badr and afterward, to a man who had never stopped working. The verse promises help to those who are patient in the struggle, not to those who wait for it idly.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:35

> **If you find their denial unbearable, then build—if you can—a tunnel through the earth or stairs to the sky to bring them a ˹more compelling˺ sign. Had Allah so willed, He could have guided them all. So do not be one of those ignorant ˹of this fact˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Consolation, with a Correction**

Verses 33 and 34 comforted the Prophet ﷺ with the truths that the rejection was not personal and that all messengers were denied and then helped. Verse 35 adds a third element, and it is a gentle but firm correction of any wish, however well-intentioned, to force the outcome. The Prophet ﷺ loved his people and longed for their guidance. The verse acknowledges this longing — *wa in kāna kabura ʿalayka iʿrāḍuhum*, "and if their turning away is hard for you" — and then shows him the limits of what he can do.

The word *kabura* means to be great, heavy, burdensome. Their *iʿrāḍ* — their turning away (the same word used of them in verse 4) — weighed on him heavily. God does not dismiss this weight; He names it and addresses it.

**The Impossible Challenge**

The verse continues: *fa-in istaṭaʿta an tabtaghiya nafaqan fi'l-arḍi aw sullaman fi'l-samā'i fa-ta'tiyahum bi-āyah* — "then if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky, and bring them a sign..." The word *nafaq* means a tunnel or underground passage (the same root gives *munāfiq*, hypocrite — one who has a hidden exit). *Sullam* means a ladder or stairway. The image is of the Prophet ﷺ digging through the earth or climbing to the heavens to retrieve some sign so overwhelming that the deniers would have to believe.

The conditional is understood by all commentators as unfulfillable. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that the Prophet ﷺ obviously cannot do these things, and the point of proposing them is to make clear that even if he could, and even if he brought the sign, it would not achieve what he hopes. The unstated conclusion (*jawāb al-shar ṭ*) is "then do so" — but with the implication "and it would make no difference," as verses 7, 25, and 37 have already established.

The rhetorical form is what the Arabs call *taʿjīz* — demonstrating incapacity. It is like telling someone consumed with an impossible worry, "If you can reach the moon and bring it down, go ahead" — not as mockery, but to show him that the thing he wishes for is beyond his power and therefore not his burden.

**"Had God Willed, He Would Have Gathered Them All to Guidance"**

The verse then states the decisive truth: *wa law shā'a Allāhu la-jamaʿahum ʿalā al-hudā* — "and if God had willed, He would have gathered them all upon guidance." Guidance is in God's hand, not the Prophet's ﷺ. God could have created human beings such that all of them believed, or He could have compelled belief by overwhelming signs. He did not. The Qur'an states this in many places:

> "Had your Lord so willed, He would have certainly made humanity one single community ˹of believers˺, but they will always ˹choose to˺ differ—" (11:118)

> "Had your Lord so willed ˹O Prophet˺, all ˹people˺ on earth would have certainly believed, every single one of them" (10:99)

> "Had Allah willed, they would not have been polytheists" (6:107)

The phrase *jamaʿahum ʿalā al-hudā* — "gathered them upon guidance" — pictures God bringing all humanity together on one path. This is within His power. That He has not done so is a matter of His wisdom, not His inability.

**The Theological Question**

This verse, like others of its kind, became a locus of theological discussion, and the source commentary summarizes the two main tendencies. Some theologians read the verse as evidence that God creates human acts and decrees each person's guidance or misguidance directly, so that what the Prophet ﷺ wishes for is simply not what God has willed. Others, including al-Zamakhsharī and, in a more nuanced way, al-Rāzī, read it as meaning that God *could* have compelled all humanity to guidance, but chose not to, because compelled belief is not the belief He seeks. On this reading, the verse affirms human freedom: God willed that people should choose, and the consequence of that will is that some choose wrongly.

The mainstream Sunni position, articulated by Ibn Taymiyyah and others, holds both truths together. God's will encompasses everything that happens, including human choices; nothing occurs outside His will. At the same time, God has given human beings real will and holds them accountable for how they use it. The two are not contradictory, because God's will is not coercion; He wills that human beings should have the capacity to choose, and He wills to create their choices according to what they themselves choose. The verse's function in its context is practical, not metaphysical: it tells the Prophet ﷺ that the guidance of his people is God's business, and he should not torment himself as though it were his.

**"So Be Not among the Ignorant"**

The verse ends with a striking admonition: *fa-lā takūnanna min al-jāhilīn* — "so do not be among the ignorant." The emphatic form makes it a strong prohibition. How can the Prophet ﷺ, the most knowledgeable of God's creatures, be warned against ignorance?

The commentators explain carefully. *Jahl* in Arabic is not merely lack of knowledge but also acting in a way contrary to knowledge — impetuousness, emotional excess, behaving as though one did not know what one knows. The pre-Islamic era is called the *Jāhiliyyah* not because the Arabs were uneducated but because they acted from passion rather than wisdom. To be "among the ignorant" here would mean to allow grief over the deniers to override what the Prophet ﷺ knew: that guidance is from God, that he was sent to convey and not to compel, and that the outcome is in God's hands. Al-Qurṭubī explains: do not be like one who does not know that God's will governs guidance, and who therefore exhausts himself with sorrow over what he cannot change.

The verse is thus not an accusation but a protection. It anticipates a real temptation — to let compassion become anguish, and anguish become a kind of forgetfulness of God's sovereignty — and it forbids it before it takes hold. The same form of address appears elsewhere as a means of instructing the community through the Prophet ﷺ:

> "and do not be one of those who deny Allah" (10:95)

No one imagined that the Prophet ﷺ would deny God's signs; the address strengthens him and teaches others.

**The Limits of Responsibility**

The central lesson of this verse is about the boundary between what a person is responsible for and what he is not. The Prophet ﷺ was responsible for conveying the message with clarity, patience, and compassion. He was not responsible for making people accept it. The Qur'an states this division repeatedly:

> "But if you turn away, then he is only responsible for his duty and you are responsible for yours" (24:54)

> "You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills, and He knows best who are ˹fit to be˺ guided" (28:56)

The second verse was revealed concerning the Prophet's ﷺ uncle Abū Ṭālib, whom he loved and urged to say the *shahādah* on his deathbed, without success. Even his own uncle's guidance was not in his power.

This boundary is a mercy for everyone who cares about others. Parents cannot make their children righteous; teachers cannot make their students wise; friends cannot make each other believe. Each can convey, model, urge, and pray. None can decide for another. The person who forgets this boundary either despairs when others do not respond or tries to coerce them — both of which the verse implicitly forbids. The person who accepts it can care deeply, work tirelessly, and still sleep at night, because he knows the outcome was never his to control.

**The Compassion behind the Correction**

It is important to read this verse in the tone the context demands. It is not a rebuke of the Prophet's ﷺ compassion; it is a protection of it. God knows that the Prophet's ﷺ grief comes from love, and He does not ask him to stop loving. He asks him to remember, in his love, that God loves these people more than he does, knows them better than he does, and has given them the freedom that makes their choice meaningful. The Prophet ﷺ is to be a warner, not a savior; the saving is God's. Understanding this let him continue his mission for another decade and more, through every rejection, without breaking — and it lets every believer who shares his compassion do the same.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:36

> **Only the attentive will respond ˹to your call˺. As for the dead, Allah will raise them up, then to Him they will ˹all˺ be returned.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Who Actually Responds**

Verse 35 told the Prophet ﷺ that guidance is in God's hands and that he should not torment himself over the deniers. Verse 36 explains the mechanism: a message is answered only by those capable of hearing it. *Innamā yastajību alladhīna yasmaʿūn* — "only those who hear respond." The restrictive particle *innamā* ("only") limits response to a specific group: those who hear.

The verb *istajāba* means to answer a call, to respond positively to a summons. It is the word used for God's answering of prayer (*istajāba li-duʿā'ihi*) and for a person's answering God's call. The verb *samiʿa* — "hear" — is used here in its full sense: not merely to receive sound but to take in, to attend, to accept. Arabic, like English, uses "hear" for both: one may say "I heard you" meaning "I received the sound" or "I heard you" meaning "I understood and accept."

**The Deaf Hearers**

The verse implies that not everyone who hears, hears. The Makkan leaders described in verse 25 listened to the Prophet ﷺ — attentively, even secretly, night after night — and did not "hear" in the sense of this verse. The Qur'an makes this distinction explicit:

> "Some of them listen to what you say, but can you make the deaf hear even though they do not understand" (10:42)

> "Nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs and walk away" (27:80)

> "Do not be like those who say," (8:21–22)

The last passage is striking: the worst creatures are "the deaf and dumb who do not use reason" — not the physically impaired, but those who have ears and will not hear. The verse before us tells the Prophet ﷺ that his call will be answered by the genuine hearers, and that he should not expect a response from the deaf.

**What Makes Someone Able to Hear**

The source commentary notes that "those who hear" are understood as those to whom God has given the capacity to hear and understand the call. This connects to the discussion at verse 25 about the covered hearts. But the Qur'an also makes clear what a person can do to become a hearer: he can approach the message with openness rather than hostility, reflect rather than dispute, and seek the truth rather than defend a position. The Qur'an describes the receptive hearer:

> "those who listen to what is said and follow the best of it" (39:18)

The one who "listens and follows the best" is a hearer. The one who listens in order to argue (verse 25: "they come to you to dispute") is not. The difference lies in the posture of the heart, which is within a person's power to adjust, though its ultimate opening is from God.

**"As for the Dead, God Will Resurrect Them"**

The second half of the verse: *wa'l-mawtā yabʿathuhum Allāh* — "and the dead, God will raise them." The commentators offer two readings, both of which fit the context.

Al-Ṭabarī reads "the dead" as the disbelievers considered from the perspective of their physical death: they will die, God will resurrect them, and they will be judged for their refusal. On this reading, the verse says: those who hear respond now; as for those who do not, leave them — God will raise them from their graves and settle their account. This reading fits the following clause, "and to Him they will be returned."

Al-Rāzī, al-Ājurrī (Aj), and many others read "the dead" as a description of the disbelievers themselves in their present state: they are spiritually dead — dead in heart, dead to truth, dead to the signs. Their deafness is a symptom of their deadness. The Prophet ﷺ cannot make the dead hear; only God can give life. On this reading, "God will raise them" means that God alone can bring the spiritually dead to life — and if He wills, He will. The Qur'an uses the image of death and life for disbelief and faith explicitly:

> "Can those who had been dead, to whom We gave life and a light with which they can walk among people, be compared to those in complete darkness from which they can never emerge" (6:122)

> "Respond to Allah and His Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life" (8:24)

The second verse uses the same verb, *istajāba* ("respond"), as the verse before us, and links it to life. Responding to the call is life; failing to respond is death.

**Both Readings Together**

The two readings converge on a single lesson for the Prophet ﷺ. Some people are alive to the truth and will respond to it; others are dead to it and will not respond, however clearly it is presented. The Prophet's ﷺ task is to call; the living will answer. The dead are not his responsibility — either God will give them life, or God will raise them for judgment. In neither case is their present unresponsiveness a failure on the Prophet's ﷺ part.

There is also a note of hope in the second reading. If the disbelievers are "dead," and God "will raise them," then their state is not necessarily final. God raises the dead. Many who were spiritually dead in Makkah — ʿUmar, Khālid, ʿIkrimah, Abū Sufyān — were brought to life. The Prophet ﷺ could not do it; God did. The verse thus tells him both to leave the outcome to God and to know that God's power over the dead is real.

**"And unto Him They Shall Be Returned"**

The verse concludes: *thumma ilayhi yurjaʿūn* — "then to Him they will be returned." Every person, hearer and deaf alike, living and dead, returns to God. This is the Qur'an's most frequent closing formula, and here it seals the argument. The Prophet ﷺ need not resolve everything in this world; there is a return, and at the return all accounts are settled.

**The Practical Wisdom of the Verse**

This verse teaches a discipline of effort that is valuable far beyond its original setting. Anyone who teaches, counsels, parents, or leads will encounter two kinds of people: those who hear and those who do not. The natural temptation is to invest most heavily in the unresponsive — to argue with them, chase them, compromise for them — while taking the responsive for granted. The verse redirects this. The call is made to all; the response comes from those who hear; and the rest are left to God without bitterness. This is not giving up on people; it is recognizing that one cannot give life to the dead and should not be crushed by failing to.

The Prophet ﷺ practiced this. He conveyed to everyone — to Abū Jahl as to Abū Bakr — but he did not measure his success by Abū Jahl's response. He gathered the hearers, taught them, built them into a community, and let God deal with the deaf. The result was a community strong enough, when God's help came, to change the world.

**The Personal Question**

Finally, the verse asks the reader which category he is in. Am I among those who hear — who receive the message with an open heart and respond to it — or among the deaf, who hear the sound and reject the meaning? The answer is not fixed. The Qur'an's constant call is to become a hearer:

> "those who listen to what is said and follow the best of it" (39:17–18)

And the Prophet ﷺ prayed against the alternative:

> "O God, I seek refuge in You from knowledge that does not benefit, from a heart that does not humble itself, from a soul that is not satisfied, and from a supplication that is not answered." (Muslim 2722)

A heart that does not humble itself is a heart that does not hear. The verse describes the consequence; the prayer seeks the cure.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:37

> **They ask, “Why has no ˹other˺ sign been sent down to him from his Lord?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Allah certainly has the power to send down a sign”—though most of them do not know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Demand Returns**

The idolaters' demand for a sign is raised once more: *wa qālū law lā nuzzila ʿalayhi āyatun min rabbih* — "and they say: Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" The particle *law lā* here expresses a demand or reproach — "why not?" — with the implication that the absence of the demanded sign proves the falsity of the claim. This is the same objection that verses 7–9 addressed regarding a written book and an angel, and that verse 25 addressed regarding the covered hearts. The Qur'an records the demand in many places (2:118; 7:203; 10:20; 13:7, 27; 20:133), showing how persistently it was raised.

The word "sign" (*āyah*) in their mouths meant a specific kind of miracle — something spectacular and coercive, like turning Mount Ṣafā into gold, or making a spring gush in Makkah, or bringing God and the angels before them face to face (17:90–93). They did not count the Qur'an as a sign, nor the splitting of the moon, nor the innumerable signs of creation. They wanted a sign of their own specification.

**"Surely God Has the Power to Send Down a Sign"**

The Prophet ﷺ is instructed to answer: *qul inna Allāha qādirun ʿalā an yunazzila āyah* — "Say: Indeed God is able to send down a sign." The answer does two things at once. It affirms God's power absolutely: He can send any sign at any time. And it declines to promise that He will. The demanded sign is not withheld because God cannot produce it; it is withheld because God, in His wisdom, has chosen not to. The distinction is crucial. The idolaters framed the absence of the sign as evidence of impotence; the answer reframes it as an exercise of wisdom.

The Qur'an makes the reason for withholding explicit elsewhere:

> "And We gave Thamûd the shecamel as a clear sign, but they wrongfully rejected it" (17:59)

> "If We willed, We could send down upon them a ˹compelling˺ sign from the heavens, leaving their necks bent in ˹utter˺ submission to it" (26:4)

The second verse confirms the answer in verse 37: God *could* send a sign that would compel submission. He does not, because compelled submission is not what He seeks, and because — as verse 8 established — a decisive sign followed by rejection brings immediate destruction. Withholding the sign is thus, as al-Rāzī and Ibn Kathīr observe, a form of mercy and respite.

**Why the Qur'an Is the Sign**

The source commentary rightly emphasizes that the Prophet's ﷺ true sign was the Qur'an itself. Every prophet was given a miracle suited to his time. Moses came to a people skilled in magic and was given the staff and the hand that surpassed all magic. Jesus came to a people skilled in medicine and was given healing of the born-blind and the leper and the raising of the dead. Muhammad ﷺ came to a people whose highest art was eloquence, and he was given a Book whose eloquence no one could match. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "There was no prophet among the prophets but that he was given signs because of which people believed in him. But what I have been given is a revelation which God revealed to me, and I hope that I will have the most followers among them on the Day of Resurrection." (al-Bukhārī 4981; Muslim 152)

The Qur'an's challenge to produce something like it was issued repeatedly and never met:

> "And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true" (2:23–24)

The Qur'an is a superior sign to a spectacular miracle in several respects. A miracle is witnessed once, by those present, and afterward known only by report; the Qur'an is present in every generation, available to every person, and can be examined directly. A miracle compels wonder but does not teach; the Qur'an both proves and instructs. A miracle can be dismissed as sorcery by those who did not see it; the Qur'an's challenge stands open to all. The idolaters' demand for a sign was made by people already holding the greatest sign in their hands.

**The Signs Around and Within**

Beyond the Qur'an, the source commentary notes the Qur'an's insistence that signs of God's power and care are everywhere for those who look:

> "How many signs in the heavens and the earth do they pass by with indifference" (12:105)

> "We will show them Our signs in the universe and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that this ˹Quran˺ is the truth" (41:53)

The rain, the seed, the alternation of night and day, the design of the body, the bond between spouses — each is called an *āyah*. The idolaters lived surrounded by signs and demanded a sign. This is the pattern verse 4 described: no sign came to them but that they turned from it.

**"But Most of Them Know Not"**

The verse concludes: *wa lākinna aktharahum lā yaʿlamūn* — "but most of them do not know." What do they not know? Several things, according to the commentators. They do not know that God's withholding of the sign is mercy, not weakness. They do not know that the sign they demand would seal their destruction if they rejected it. They do not know that the Qur'an is a greater sign than what they ask for. And they do not know, most fundamentally, the nature of God's wisdom in dealing with His creatures — that He sends signs according to His purposes, not according to human demands.

The word "most" (*akthar*) is characteristic of the Qur'an's fairness. It does not say all of them; some among the Makkans did know, or came to know. But the majority were in ignorance — not the ignorance of the uneducated but the ignorance of those who have not reflected on what is before them.

**The Logic of Withholding**

The verse's teaching can be reasoned through. Consider what would happen if God granted every demand for a sign. First, the demands would never end; each satisfied demand would generate a new one, as Pharaoh's people responded to each of Moses' signs by asking for another and calling each one magic. Second, faith would cease to be faith; it would become mere acknowledgment of the coercively obvious, without merit or freedom. Third, as verse 8 stated, those who rejected after the decisive sign would be destroyed at once, and the respite in which repentance occurs would end. Withholding the sign is therefore not a failure to provide evidence — the evidence is abundant — but a refusal to provide the specific kind of evidence that would destroy the purpose of the test.

An analogy: a teacher who gave students the answer key before the examination would produce perfect scores and no learning. The examination's purpose requires that the answers be discoverable through effort but not handed over on demand. The signs God has given — the Qur'an, creation, the prophets' character, the fulfillment of predictions — are discoverable by anyone who looks. The sign the idolaters demanded was the answer key.

**Application: The Modern Demand**

The demand for a sign has not disappeared. It appears today as "if God exists, why doesn't He show Himself?" or "I would believe if I saw a miracle." The Qur'an's answer is the same: God is able, and God has chosen the form of evidence suited to a test of free beings. The evidence is present — in the Qur'an, in creation, in conscience, in the lives of those transformed by faith — and the one who demands a different kind of evidence should ask himself whether he is seeking truth or seeking an excuse. Verse 37's closing phrase applies: most of those who make the demand do not know what they are asking for, or what its granting would cost them.

For the believer, the verse is a reminder that faith is meant to be a response to sufficient evidence, not to overwhelming compulsion — and that the sufficiency is already in his hands.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:38

> **All living beings roaming the earth and winged birds soaring in the sky are communities like yourselves. We have left nothing out of the Record. Then to their Lord they will be gathered all together.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Sign in the Creatures**

The idolaters asked for a sign (v. 37). Verse 38 answers by pointing to signs they had never considered: the animals crawling on the earth and the birds flying in the sky. Every one of them, the verse says, belongs to a community like the human community. The implication is that the world is full of signs of God's ordering, knowledge, and care — one need only look at the nearest creature. The idolaters demanded a spectacle while surrounded by the miracle of living beings, each organized into its kind, each provided for, each known to God.

**"No Creature That Crawls upon the Earth, Nor Bird That Flies upon Its Wings"**

The word *dābbah* (from *dabba*, to move slowly, to crawl or walk) refers to any creature that moves on the earth — land animals of every kind. The word *ṭā'ir* means a flying thing, a bird. The phrase "flies with its two wings" (*yaṭīru bi-janāḥayhi*) has drawn comment: birds obviously fly with their wings, so why mention it? The commentators explain that it is added for emphasis and precision, to exclude figurative uses of "flying" (as the Arabs said of a swift horse or a rumor that it "flew") and to make clear that literal birds are meant. It may also draw attention to the wings themselves as a sign of design — the marvel of flight, which no human being could accomplish until very recently and which every sparrow performs without thought.

Together, land creatures and birds represent the whole animal kingdom as visible to the desert Arab — those below, on the earth, and those above, in the air. The Qur'an frequently uses such pairs to indicate totality.

**"Communities Like Yourselves"**

The verse's central and most remarkable claim: *illā umamun amthālukum* — "but they are communities like you." The word *ummah* (plural *umam*) is one of the Qur'an's most important terms. It usually denotes a community defined by a shared way of life or religion — the *ummah* of Muhammad ﷺ, the *ummah* of each prophet.
