The Qur'an says that every *ummah* has had a messenger (10:47; 16:36; 35:24). To apply this word to animals is to say something significant about them.

The commentators explored what this likeness consists of, and the source commentary surveys their views. At the most basic level, Ibn Kathīr and others note that animals are, like human beings, creatures (*khalq*) of God, and that they are, like human beings, recipients of His provision and mercy:

> "There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah" (11:6)

> "How many are the creatures that cannot secure their provisions" (29:60)

Al-Rāzī considers this reading too thin. If the verse merely meant that animals are creatures, the use of the weighty term *ummah* would be pointless. He and al-Thaʿlabī suggest a deeper likeness: animals are aware of God and glorify Him. The Qur'an states this of all created things:

> "There is not a single thing that does not glorify His praises—but you ˹simply˺ cannot comprehend their glorification" (17:44)

> "Do you not see that Allah is glorified by all those in the heavens and the earth, even the birds as they soar" (24:41)

The second verse is striking: "each has *known* its prayer and its glorification." The birds are not merely metaphorically praising God; they know what they are doing. The verse before us, read with 24:41, describes animal communities as beings in conscious relationship with their Creator.

Al-Rāzī goes further still. Reading this verse together with 10:47 — "And for every community there is a messenger." (10:47) — he suggests that animal communities may in some way receive divine direction suited to their nature. The Qur'an says God "revealed" to the bee (16:68), and the ant in the story of Solomon is shown speaking, warning her community, and displaying knowledge (27:18). The likeness is thus not merely biological but, in a manner appropriate to each kind, spiritual.

**What the Likeness Teaches about God**

The verse's primary purpose in context is to display the extent of God's knowledge and governance. If every creature on land and in the air belongs to an ordered community, is provided for, and is known to God individually, then God's knowledge and care are limitless. The One who governs the communities of ants and sparrows will not fail to govern, know, and judge the community of human beings. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī draw exactly this conclusion: the verse should increase the listener's certainty in his own resurrection and reckoning, since the God who keeps account of every bird will surely keep account of every person.

**What the Likeness Teaches about Ethics**

The source commentary draws a further conclusion that deserves emphasis. If animals are communities in relationship with their Creator, created to glorify Him, then they possess an inherent dignity that human beings must respect. The Qur'an affirms that God has made the natural world serviceable to humanity (14:32; 16:14; 31:20), but service is not license for cruelty or waste. The Prophet ﷺ established this ethic in numerous ḥadīths:

> "A woman was punished because of a cat which she imprisoned until it died. She entered the Fire because of it, for she neither fed it nor gave it water when she confined it, nor did she let it eat from the creatures of the earth." (al-Bukhārī 3318; Muslim 2242)

> "While a man was walking on a road, he became very thirsty and found a well. He descended into it, drank, and came out. Then he saw a dog panting and eating mud from thirst. The man said, 'This dog has reached the same state of thirst that I had reached.' So he descended into the well, filled his shoe with water, held it in his mouth, climbed out, and gave the dog water. God thanked him and forgave him." They said, "O Messenger of God, is there a reward for us in animals?" He said, "In every living creature there is a reward." (al-Bukhārī 2363; Muslim 2244)

> "God has prescribed excellence in all things. So when you kill, kill well; and when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade and let him spare suffering to the animal he slaughters." (Muslim 1955)

The Prophet ﷺ forbade using animals as targets, branding them on the face, overburdening them, and taking the young of birds from their nests to distress the mother. Each of these rulings flows from the vision of verse 38: the animals are communities whose Lord is our Lord.

**"We Have Neglected Nothing in the Book"**

Between the description of the animal communities and the statement of their gathering, the verse inserts a parenthetical: *mā farraṭnā fi'l-kitābi min shay'* — "We have not neglected anything in the Book." The verb *farraṭa* — the same used in verse 31 for the deniers' neglect — here is negated of God: He neglects nothing.

The commentators differ on "the Book." Al-Thaʿlabī and many others take it as the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ*), the record in which God has written the destiny and details of every creature. On this reading, the verse says that every animal community, every bird, every individual creature is recorded in God's register — nothing is omitted. This fits the surrounding context of divine knowledge and gathering.

Al-Rāzī and others take "the Book" as the Qur'an. On this reading, the verse says that the Qur'an contains, in principle, all the guidance human beings need. This does not mean that the Qur'an lists every fact or every legal ruling; it means, as the source commentary explains, that it contains the foundations from which all necessary knowledge of religion is derived, including the authority of the Prophet's ﷺ Sunnah, of scholarly consensus, and of sound reasoning. The Qur'an states of itself:

> "And We have sent down to you the Book as clarification for all things and as guidance and mercy and good tidings for the Muslims." (16:89)

Both readings are sound and both fit the verse. God's register omits nothing; God's revelation omits nothing needed.

**"They Shall Be Gathered unto Their Lord"**

The verse ends: *thumma ilā rabbihim yuḥsharūn* — "then to their Lord they will be gathered." The verb *ḥashara* is the standard term for the gathering of humanity for judgment (as in verse 22). Its use for the animals raises the question of whether animals are resurrected.

The commentators differ, as the source notes. Some (recorded by al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr) understand the gathering as death — the animals are gathered to their end. Others take it as literal resurrection. Several ḥadīths support the latter. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "You will certainly render the rights to their owners on the Day of Resurrection, until the hornless sheep is given retribution from the horned sheep." (Muslim 2582)

And Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī and al-Thaʿlabī cite the report that after God settles the accounts among the animals, He will command them to become dust, at which point the disbeliever will say, "I wish I were dust" (78:40). The Qur'an also lists among the events of the Last Day:

> "and when wild beasts are gathered together," (81:5)

The weight of evidence favors a real gathering, in which justice is done even among the animals, before they are returned to dust. This confirms the verse's teaching: God's justice is so complete that it extends to the sheep, and the human being who imagines his own wrongs will be overlooked is deceived.

**An Interpretive Aside**

The source commentary records that Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah took the beasts and birds as figures for types of human beings who have come to resemble animals in character, and that the philosopher Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī developed sophisticated arguments for the resurrection of all creatures. These readings need not displace the literal one; the Qur'an frequently carries layered meanings, and the literal sense — real animals, real communities, real gathering — is primary.

**The Sign Answered**

Returning to the context: the idolaters demanded a sign. This verse gives them one that surrounds them. Every ant colony, every flock, every creature moving on the ground or flying overhead is a community ordered by God, provided for by God, recorded by God, and destined for God. The one who cannot see a sign in this would not see one in a mountain of gold. And the one who does see it is moved to two things at once: certainty in the God who governs all life, and reverence for the fellow communities with whom he shares the earth.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:39

> **Those who deny Our signs are ˹wilfully˺ deaf and dumb—lost in darkness. Allah leaves whoever He wills to stray and guides whoever He wills to the Straight Way.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Returning to the Deniers**

Verse 38 displayed the signs in the animal communities. Verse 39 describes what happens to those who deny such signs: *wa'lladhīna kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā ṣummun wa bukmun fi'l-ẓulumāt* — "and those who deny Our signs are deaf and mute, in darknesses." The verse does not say they *will become* deaf and mute, but that they *are* — the denial and the disability are simultaneous, or rather the disability describes the denial.

**Deaf, Mute, in Darkness**

Three conditions are named. *Ṣumm* (plural of *aṣamm*) — deaf: they do not hear the truth, as verses 25 and 36 described. *Bukm* (plural of *abkam*) — mute: they do not speak the truth, cannot confess it, cannot ask about it sincerely. *Fi'l-ẓulumāt* — in darknesses: they do not see the truth; they move through existence without light. The plural *ẓulumāt* recalls verse 1 of the sūrah, where God "made the darknesses and the light" — darknesses many, light one. The deniers are in the many darknesses because they have refused the one light.

The Qur'an uses these images in combination elsewhere:

> "They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺" (2:18)

> "˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding" (2:171)

In those verses, blindness is named explicitly. Here, "in darknesses" takes its place — and it is a stronger image. A blind person in a lit room is still surrounded by light he cannot see; a person in darkness has no light around him at all. The deniers are not merely unable to perceive; they are in an environment without illumination, because they have turned from the source of it.

**Why These Faculties?**

Hearing, speech, and sight are the faculties by which a human being receives truth, articulates it, and perceives it. The Qur'an says that God gave these faculties for exactly this purpose and holds people accountable for them:

> "And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers while you knew nothing, and gave you hearing, sight, and intellect so perhaps you would be thankful" (16:78)

> "Indeed, all will be called to account for ˹their˺ hearing, sight, and intellect" (17:36)

The deniers had intact ears, tongues, and eyes. But with respect to the truth, they were as though deprived of all three. The verse's judgment is that faculties unused for their purpose are, in the relevant sense, absent. A person who has ears and will not hear the truth is deaf to it, whatever his physical condition.

**"Whomsoever God Will, He Leads Astray"**

The second half of the verse states the sovereign source of guidance and misguidance: *man yasha'i Allāhu yuḍlilhu wa man yasha' yajʿalhu ʿalā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm* — "whom God wills, He sends astray; and whom He wills, He places on a straight path." This is one of the verses most discussed in Islamic theology, and the source commentary summarizes the classical positions with care.

The Qur'an states in many places that God guides and misguides according to His will (7:155; 14:4; 16:93; 35:8; 74:31). It also states in many places that God misguides specifically the wrongdoers, the transgressors, and those who have already chosen disbelief:

> "Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many" (2:26)

> "This is how Allah leaves every transgressor and doubter to stray—" (40:34)

> "So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate" (61:5)

The two sets of verses must be read together. God's will is sovereign and encompasses all things; nothing happens outside it. And God's will is not arbitrary; He misguides those who have chosen the path of transgression and guides those who seek guidance. The first set of verses affirms His sovereignty; the second explains the wisdom by which that sovereignty operates.

**The Theological Debate in Brief**

The source commentary notes the two major schools. The Muʿtazilites, represented in al-Zamakhsharī's commentary, held that God's "leading astray" means withholding His special favor (*luṭf*) from those who have rejected it, or naming as astray those who have gone astray, or leading them away from Paradise in the Hereafter — never directly creating disbelief in them, since that would be unjust. The Ashʿarites, represented in al-Rāzī's commentary, held that God creates all acts, including human acts, and that guidance and misguidance are ultimately His creation, though human beings "acquire" (*kasb*) their acts and are accountable for them.

The position of the early scholars and of Ibn Taymiyyah, which many regard as the most balanced, affirms both divine sovereignty and human responsibility without reducing one to the other. God creates everything, including human choices; and human beings genuinely choose, and are justly held to account, because God creates their choices in accordance with their own wills. God guides those who turn toward Him and leaves astray those who turn away — and both the turning and its consequence occur within His will. The verse before us is thus not a statement that God arbitrarily damns some and saves others, but a statement that the source of all guidance and all misguidance is God, and that no one is guided or misguided except by His will — which is always wise and always just.

**The Practical Import in Context**

Whatever the metaphysical details, the verse's function in its place is clear and practical. It follows a series of consolations to the Prophet ﷺ (verses 33–37) and a demonstration of God's all-encompassing knowledge (verse 38). Its message to him is: do not despair over the deaf and mute in darkness; guidance is not yours to give. God places whom He wills on the straight path. Your task is to call; the outcome is His. The verse thus continues the theme of verses 35–36 and prevents the Prophet ﷺ from either despair or the illusion that more effort on his part would compel belief.

Its message to the deniers is different: your deafness, muteness, and darkness are not accidents. You chose to deny, and God has confirmed you in what you chose. The remedy is not to demand more signs but to turn — and the One who leads astray is the One who guides, and He guides whoever turns to Him sincerely.

**The Straight Path**

The verse's final phrase, *ṣirāṭin mustaqīm* — 'a straight path' — is the same expression the believer asks for seventeen times a day in al-Fātiḥah: "Guide us along the Straight Path," (1:6). The prayer is addressed to God because, as this verse states, He is the One who places people upon it. No one walks the straight path by his own power alone; he walks it because God has placed him on it and keeps him on it. This is why the believer never ceases to ask for guidance, however long he has been guided. The Prophet ﷺ himself prayed constantly:

> "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." (al-Tirmidhī 2140, graded ṣaḥīḥ)

The image of a path is itself instructive. A path is straight when it leads directly to its destination without deviation. The straight path is the shortest, safest route to God. The darknesses in which the deniers wander have no path at all — only directionless movement. To be placed on the straight path is to be given not merely light but direction: to know where one is going and how to get there.

**Hope Within the Verse**

Finally, the verse holds both halves together: God misguides, and God guides. The person who reads only the first half despairs; the person who reads only the second grows complacent. Read together, they produce the right posture: fear of being among those left astray, hope of being among those placed on the path, and constant turning to the One who does both. The deaf and mute in darkness are not beyond His reach; He who placed them in darkness can bring them out, and He has done so for countless people who once denied. The verse describes the present state of the deniers without sealing their future — and it reminds every believer that his own guidance is a gift held in trust, to be asked for daily and never presumed upon.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:40

> **Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Imagine if you were overwhelmed by Allah’s torment or the Hour—would you call upon any other than Allah ˹for help˺? ˹Answer me˺ if your claims are true!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**An Argument from the Idolaters' Own Instincts**

The verse opens a new argument, and it is one of the most psychologically penetrating in the sūrah. Instead of telling the idolaters what to believe, it asks them to observe what they already believe at the deepest level — what they would actually do in a moment of extremity. *Qul a-ra'aytakum* — "Say: Have you considered yourselves?" or "Tell me about yourselves." The phrase *a-ra'aytakum* is an idiom of inquiry that draws the listener's attention to himself and demands an honest answer. The Prophet ﷺ is to make the idolaters look inward.

**The Two Scenarios**

Two situations are proposed: *in atākum ʿadhābu Allāhi aw atatkumu al-sāʿah* — "if the punishment of God came to you, or the Hour came to you." The first, as al-Ṭabarī explains, refers to a worldly catastrophe of the kind that destroyed earlier nations — a flood, a wind, an earthquake, a plague, a defeat. The second is the Hour itself, the end of the world and the onset of the Judgment. Both are situations in which every human resource has failed and only a higher power can help.

**"Would You Call upon Anyone Other Than God?"**

The question: *a-ghayra Allāhi tadʿūna* — "is it other than God you would call?" The word order in Arabic places "other than God" first, for emphasis: "Is it *other than God* whom you would call?" The expected answer is no. When the wave is towering over the boat, when the earth is shaking, when the plague is at the door, the idolaters would not call on al-Lāt or al-ʿUzzā. They would call on Allāh.

The Qur'an documents this repeatedly, drawing on the idolaters' own experience at sea:

> "But when He delivers you ˹safely˺ to shore, you turn away" (17:67)

> "But when He delivers them ˹safely˺ to shore, only some become relatively grateful" (31:32)

> "If You save us from this, we will certainly be grateful" (10:22–23)

The Makkans were traders who crossed the Red Sea to Abyssinia and knew storms. They knew exactly what they did in a storm. The verse holds up a mirror.

**"If You Are Truthful"**

The verse closes with the condition: *in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — "if you are truthful." This phrase challenges the idolaters to be honest. Their public position was that their gods had power. Their private conduct in crisis showed that they did not believe it. The verse asks: which is the truth? If you are truthful about what you really believe, you will admit that in the moment of terror you turn to God alone. And if that is so, your idolatry in times of ease is a lie you tell yourselves.

Al-Zamakhsharī observes that the challenge is unanswerable. If they say "we would call on our gods," they lie, and their own experience convicts them. If they say "we would call on God," they concede the argument. Either way, the point is made.

**The Structure of the Argument**

The argument can be laid out. Premise one: in a moment of ultimate danger, a person calls on whatever he truly believes can save him. Premise two: in such moments, the idolaters call on God alone, not on their partners. Conclusion: the idolaters truly believe that God alone can save them, and their partners cannot. Corollary: their worship of partners in ordinary times is not based on belief in the partners' power but on habit, social pressure, and self-deception.

This argument is powerful because it does not rely on any premise the idolaters can dispute. It relies on their own conduct, which they cannot deny. It is the same method the sūrah used at verse 12 (asking to whom the heavens and earth belong) and will use again at verses 63–64: appeal to what the opponent already knows and let his own knowledge convict him.

**The Fiṭrah Revealed**

The verse exposes what Islamic theology calls the *fiṭrah* — the innate disposition toward recognizing the One God. The Prophet ﷺ said that every child is born on the *fiṭrah* (al-Bukhārī 1385; Muslim 2658). Layers of culture, habit, and false teaching can be laid over it, but the *fiṭrah* remains beneath, and in moments when the layers are stripped away — moments of terror, of confrontation with death — it speaks. The idolater at sea, crying "O Allāh," is the *fiṭrah* speaking through the layers. The verse asks the idolaters to listen to that voice and to recognize it as the truth about themselves.

This has been observed across cultures and ages. People who profess no faith pray in emergencies. Soldiers under fire, patients before surgery, parents at a child's sickbed — the reflex to call on a higher power appears where the constructed self collapses. The Qur'an does not treat this reflex as weakness; it treats it as evidence. In crisis, the human being knows whom to call.

**The Ethical Challenge**

There is also an ethical dimension. To worship one thing in ease and another in distress is a form of hypocrisy toward oneself. It means living a lie in the good times and telling the truth only when forced. The verse invites the idolaters to align their ordinary lives with the truth they confess in extremity — to worship in ease the One they call on in fear. This is the essence of sincerity (*ikhlāṣ*): consistency between what one believes at the deepest level and what one does at the surface.

The believer is called to the same consistency in a different form. He may never have worshipped an idol, but he may have trusted his wealth, his connections, or his own competence in ordinary times and remembered God only in crisis. The verse asks him, too, to be truthful: if he would call on God alone in the storm, why does he rely on other things in the calm?

**The Punishment and the Hour as Realities**

Note that the verse presents the punishment of God and the Hour as real possibilities, not hypotheticals for the sake of argument. The idolaters mocked both (vv. 5, 29). The verse assumes their reality and asks what the idolaters will do when they arrive. This is an implicit warning wrapped in an argument: these things are coming, and when they come, you will call on God — so why not call on Him now, while calling is worship rather than desperation?

**Connection to Verse 41**

The verse ends with a question; verse 41 supplies the answer. "Nay, but it is upon Him that you would call." The two verses form one argument, and the answer is stated by God on the idolaters' behalf — because God knows what they would do better than they know themselves.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:41

> **No! He is the only One you would call. And if He willed, He could remove the affliction that made you invoke Him. Only then will you forget whatever you associate with Him ˹in worship˺.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**God Answers on Their Behalf**

Verse 40 asked whether the idolaters would call on anyone other than God in the moment of catastrophe. Verse 41 answers: *bal iyyāhu tadʿūn* — "Nay, Him alone you would call." The particle *bal* corrects any pretense that they might call on their partners. The pronoun *iyyāhu* is placed before the verb for exclusive emphasis — "Him *alone*," not merely "Him." This is the same construction as *iyyāka naʿbudu* in al-Fātiḥah, "You alone we worship." In the moment of truth, the idolaters' worship becomes what it should always have been: directed to God alone.

The verse states this as fact, not speculation. God knows what they would do. And, as the preceding verses noted, their own history at sea confirms it.

**"He Would Remove That Which Had Caused You to Call upon Him"**

The verse continues: *fa-yakshifu mā tadʿūna ilayhi* — "and He would remove that for which you call upon Him." The verb *kashafa*, as at verse 17, means to lift, uncover, remove — as one lifts a covering from something. The affliction that drove them to call is pictured as something laid upon them, and God lifts it.

This clause makes an important point about God's response. He does not merely receive their desperate call; He answers it. The idolaters who call on God in the storm are delivered from the storm. This is documented in the sea passages: "But when He delivers them ˹safely˺ to shore, only some become relatively grateful" (29:65; 31:32; 17:67). God's mercy extends even to those who call on Him only in extremity. The Qur'an says:

> "Who responds to the distressed when they cry to Him, relieving ˹their˺ affliction, and ˹Who˺ makes you successors in the earth" (27:62)

The word "desperate" (*al-muḍṭarr*) describes exactly the state of verse 40: a person with no other recourse. God answers such a person — not because he deserves it, but because He has prescribed mercy upon Himself (v. 12).

**"If It Be His Will"**

The removal is qualified: *in shā'a* — "if He wills." God is not obligated to remove every affliction called upon Him. He removes what He wills, when He wills, according to His wisdom. Sometimes the affliction is removed; sometimes it is not, because it serves a purpose the sufferer does not see; sometimes it is the punishment itself, and no call will avert it. The qualification preserves God's freedom and prevents the verse from being read as a mechanical guarantee.

Al-Rāzī notes that the phrase also refutes the idea that the idolaters' call has any power of its own. The removal of harm is God's act, done by His will. The one who calls is not commanding God but petitioning Him, and the petition is granted by grace. This is why the believer's supplication is always accompanied by submission to God's decision:

> "Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly" (7:55)

**"You Would Forget Whatever Partners You Had Ascribed unto Him"**

The verse's final clause is its sharpest: *wa tansawna mā tushrikūn* — "and you would forget what you associate." In the moment of crisis, the partners are not merely set aside; they are *forgotten*. The verb *nasiya* means to forget entirely, to have something slip from the mind. When the wave is towering, no one thinks of al-Lāt. The idols do not even enter consciousness. This is a profound observation. It is not that the idolaters deliberately choose God over their partners in the crisis; it is that the partners vanish from the mind altogether, as though they had never existed — because at the level of the *fiṭrah* they never did.

Al-Zamakhsharī draws out the implication: the forgetting shows that the partners were never truly believed in. What one truly believes in is what one remembers in the moment of need. The idolaters remembered God and forgot everything else, which reveals the actual structure of their belief beneath the layers of custom. The Qur'an makes the same point about the partners on the Day of Judgment, when they "go astray" from their worshippers (v. 24): the partners are absent at the critical moment, both in this world's crises and in the next world's reckoning.

**The Complete Argument of Verses 40–41**

The two verses, taken together, establish that the idolaters' own hearts testify to God's exclusive lordship. In crisis, they call on Him alone; He alone responds; and their partners are forgotten. The lesson is drawn implicitly: why not live in ordinary times according to what you know in extraordinary ones? Why give worship in ease to things you forget in fear?

This argument was extremely effective in its original setting, and it remains effective. It does not require the listener to accept any premise on authority. It asks him only to be honest about himself. The person who has ever prayed in an emergency knows the truth of verse 41 from the inside.

**The Return to Partners after Deliverance**

The verse describes the moment of crisis, but the Qur'an also describes what typically follows: once delivered, the idolaters return to their partners.

> "But as soon as He delivers them ˹safely˺ to shore, they associate ˹others with Him once again˺" (29:65)

> "Whenever someone is touched by hardship, they cry out to Us, whether lying on their side, sitting, or standing" (10:12)

This pattern — sincerity in crisis, forgetfulness in ease — is one of the most consistent observations about human nature in the Qur'an. It is not confined to pagan Arabs. It describes the person who makes solemn vows during an illness and forgets them upon recovery, the person who promises to change during a disaster and reverts when the disaster passes. Verse 41 shows the moment of sincerity; the Qur'an elsewhere shows the relapse; and the combined lesson is that the moment of sincerity was the truth, and the relapse is the lie.

**Gratitude as the Proper Response**

The verse implies what the correct response to deliverance should be. If God alone was called and God alone delivered, then God alone deserves the gratitude — and gratitude expressed not merely in words but in a life realigned around the truth that the crisis revealed. The Qur'an describes the one who does this:

> "When one is touched with hardship, they cry out to their Lord, turning to Him ˹alone˺" (39:8)

The verse condemns the forgetting and the setting up of equals afterward. The alternative — remembering, and remaining upon the sincerity of the crisis — is what God asks. The Prophet ﷺ taught the believer to make his gratitude permanent:

> "Recognize God in ease, and He will recognize you in hardship." (al-Tirmidhī 2516; Aḥmad 2803; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

The one who recognizes God in ease is not caught off guard in hardship, and does not have to be reminded by terror of what he should have known all along.

**The Mercy in God's Answering**

Finally, the verse reveals something about God that the idolaters had not appreciated: He answers even those who ignore Him in ordinary times. He does not say, "You forgot Me in your ease; I will forget you in your distress." He removes the affliction "if He wills" — and He frequently wills it, out of the mercy He has prescribed upon Himself. This generosity is itself an argument. A God who answers the desperate call of an idolater is a God who deserves to be called upon always, and served always, and thanked always. The verse shows His mercy in operation and asks the idolaters to draw the obvious conclusion.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:42

> **Indeed, We have sent messengers before you ˹O Prophet˺ to other people who We put through suffering and adversity ˹for their denial˺, so perhaps they would be humbled.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Returning to the Pattern of History**

After the argument from the idolaters' instincts in crisis (vv. 40–41), the sūrah returns to the lessons of earlier nations, first raised at verse 6. This time the focus is not on their destruction but on the process that preceded it: God sent messengers, and He sent hardship, and both were meant to produce humility. *Wa la-qad arsalnā ilā umamin min qablika* — "and We certainly sent [messengers] to communities before you." The verb *arsalnā* ("We sent") has its object understood: messengers. The emphatic *la-qad* confirms that this happened repeatedly and certainly.

The word *umam* (communities) is the plural of *ummah*, the same term applied to animal communities in verse 38. Here it refers to the human peoples to whom prophets were sent. The verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ (*min qablik*, "before you") and continues the theme of verse 34: your situation is not new; here is what happened before.

**"We Seized Them with Misfortune and Hardship"**

*Fa-akhadhnāhum bi'l-ba'sā'i wa'l-ḍarrā'i* — "so We seized them with adversity and hardship." The verb *akhadha* means to take, to seize — a firm grip. The two nouns are frequently paired in the Qur'an. *Ba'sā'* (from *ba's*, hardship, might, war) is generally understood by the commentators — al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī — as external hardship: poverty, loss of wealth, straitened circumstances, famine. *Ḍarrā'* (from *ḍarr*, harm) is understood as bodily affliction: illness, pain, physical suffering. Together they cover the two main forms of worldly trial: what happens to one's possessions and what happens to one's body.

The Qur'an mentions the pair as tests that reveal character:

> "It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺" (2:177)

> "We tested them with prosperity and adversity, so perhaps they would return ˹to the Right Path˺" (7:168)

**"That They Might Humble Themselves"**

The purpose is stated: *laʿallahum yataḍarraʿūn* — "that perhaps they would humble themselves." The verb *taḍarraʿa* means to humble oneself, to plead in lowliness, to supplicate with earnest submission. It comes from a root meaning to be lowly or weak (as a young animal is weak), and it describes the posture of one who has abandoned pretension and turns to God in need. The Qur'an commands this posture in prayer:

> "Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly" (7:55)

The verse therefore reveals the purpose of hardship: it is not sent primarily to punish but to break the illusion of self-sufficiency and open the heart. When a person is prosperous and healthy, he easily imagines himself independent. When wealth fails or illness strikes, the illusion cracks, and the truth — that he depends entirely on God — becomes visible. Hardship is designed to produce the recognition that verses 40–41 described: the turning to God alone.

**Hardship as Mercy**

This reframing of hardship is one of the Qur'an's most important teachings. Suffering is not evidence of God's absence or displeasure; it is often His instrument for bringing people back. The commentators compare it to the discipline of a caring physician or father — unpleasant in the moment, corrective in intent. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī develop this image at verse 44: God alternates hardness and gentleness with His creatures as a wise parent does with a child, seeking to form character.

The Prophet ﷺ taught that affliction is a sign of God's attention, not His abandonment:

> "When God wills good for His servant, He hastens his punishment in this world; and when He wills evil for His servant, He withholds his sins from him until He requites him for them on the Day of Resurrection." (al-Tirmidhī 2396, graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ)

> "The greatest reward comes with the greatest trial. When God loves a people, He tests them. Whoever is content will have contentment, and whoever is displeased will have displeasure." (al-Tirmidhī 2396; Ibn Mājah 4031; graded ḥasan)

The messengers were sent, and hardship accompanied them, because the two together are more effective than either alone. The messenger explains the meaning of the hardship; the hardship opens the heart to the messenger. The Qur'an describes this pairing in the story of Moses and Pharaoh's people:

> "people with famine and shortage of crops so they might come back ˹to their senses˺" (7:130)

**The Two Possible Responses**

Hardship presents a fork. One road is *taḍarruʿ* — humbling oneself, turning to God, recognizing one's dependence. The other, which verse 43 will describe, is hardening — resisting the lesson, blaming circumstances, and continuing as before. The hardship is the same; the response differs. This is the essence of a test: it does not create character but reveals it, and it offers an opportunity to change it.

The Qur'an describes the wrong response in several places:

> "If We give people a taste of Our mercy then take it away from them, they become utterly desperate, ungrateful" (11:9–10)

In both prosperity and adversity, this person fails: he despairs in hardship and boasts in ease. The one who passes the test is described immediately after:

> "It is they who will have forgiveness and a mighty reward" (11:11)

**Psychology of Humbling**

There is a psychological wisdom in the verse. Human beings are built to notice change. A person who has always had enough does not think about provision; a person who loses it thinks of nothing else. A person who has always been healthy takes his body for granted; a person who falls ill discovers how much depends on things he never controlled. Hardship, by removing what was assumed, makes visible what was invisible. This is why the Qur'an can say that hardship is sent "that they might humble themselves": it does not force humility, but it creates the conditions in which humility becomes obvious.

Modern people sometimes respond to suffering by asking, "Why would a good God allow this?" The verse suggests a different question: "What is this meant to show me?" The first question treats suffering as an accusation against God; the second treats it as a message from Him. The second question is the one that leads somewhere.

**Application to the Individual**

Though the verse speaks of nations, its logic applies to individuals. Every person encounters *ba'sā'* and *ḍarrā'* — financial loss, illness, grief. The verse tells him what they are for. If he responds with *taḍarruʿ* — turning to God in humility, examining his life, seeking forgiveness — the hardship has done its work. If he responds by hardening — with bitterness, blame, or defiance — he has failed the test and, as verse 43 warns, opened himself to worse.

The Companions understood this. When afflicted, they examined themselves. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: "Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account." The habit of reading hardship as a message, and responding to it with humility, is the practical fruit of this verse.

**The Verse as Consolation to the Prophet**

Finally, the verse continues to console the Prophet ﷺ. God had sent messengers before him, and He had accompanied their missions with hardships intended to humble their peoples. This tells the Prophet ﷺ that the Makkans' current circumstances — including the drought and famine that struck Makkah during his mission, recorded in the ḥadīth literature (al-Bukhārī 1007) — are part of a divine method, not a sign that anything has gone wrong. God is working on the Makkans as He worked on earlier nations. Whether they humble themselves or harden is their choice, and the following verses describe both outcomes.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:43

> **Why did they not humble themselves when We made them suffer? Instead, their hearts were hardened, and Satan made their misdeeds appealing to them.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Lament Over a Missed Opportunity**

The verse opens with *fa-law lā* — "if only," "why did they not" — a particle that combines reproach with regret. God had sent hardship precisely so that they might humble themselves (v. 42); this verse laments that they did not. *Fa-law lā idh jā'ahum ba'sunā taḍarraʿū* — "if only, when Our might came upon them, they had humbled themselves." The word *ba's* here refers to the hardship God sent — His severity, His striking power. The verb *taḍarraʿū* is the same as in verse 42: to humble oneself, to plead in lowliness.

The tone is significant. God does not say merely "they did not humble themselves"; He says "if only they had." This is the language of One who wished for their good and was refused. It confirms what the sūrah has stated in other ways: God's sending of hardship was not vindictive but corrective, and their failure to respond grieved — if one may use the word — the One who sent it.

**"But Rather Their Hearts Hardened"**

*Wa lākin qasat qulūbuhum* — "but their hearts hardened." The verb *qasā* means to become hard, dry, unyielding — as stone is hard, or as earth becomes hard when it has not received rain. The heart, in the Qur'an, is meant to be soft: responsive to truth, moved by warning, tender toward God. A hardened heart is one that no longer responds. The Qur'an describes this condition in several places:

> "Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers" (2:74)

> "They distorted the words of the Scripture and neglected a portion of what they had been commanded to uphold" (5:13)

> "Has the time not yet come for believers" (57:16)

The last verse describes how hardening occurs: "a long period passed over them." Hardness is not usually sudden. It is the accumulation of ignored warnings, unheeded reminders, and repeated refusals, until the heart loses its capacity to respond.

**Why Hardship Sometimes Hardens Rather Than Softens**

The verse raises an important question. Hardship was sent to humble; why did it harden instead? The answer lies in the nature of tests. A test does not determine the response; it reveals and intensifies the disposition already present. A heart inclined toward God responds to hardship by turning to Him more; a heart inclined away responds by resenting Him more. The same fire that softens wax hardens clay.

The commentators note that the hardening was the people's own doing, though God is said to have "They distorted the words of the Scripture and neglected a portion of what they had been commanded to uphold" in other verses (5:13) — because God creates the consequences of human choices. They chose to resist; the resistance hardened them; God brought the hardening into being as the just result. The Qur'an holds them accountable because the initial choice was theirs.

There is a further psychological mechanism. When a person suffers and refuses to see the suffering as a message, he must find another explanation. He blames chance, blames enemies, blames the weather. Each such explanation is a small act of denial, and each denial adds a layer to the heart's covering. Over time, the layers become a shell. This is how hardship, meant to open, ends up closing — not because of the hardship itself, but because of the interpretation the person chose to place on it.

**"And Satan Made All They Used to Do Seem Fair unto Them"**

*Wa zayyana lahumu al-shayṭānu mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — "and Satan made attractive to them what they used to do." The verb *zayyana* means to adorn, to beautify, to make something appear fair and appealing. Satan's method is not usually to make evil look evil and invite people to it; it is to make evil look good. He presents idolatry as loyalty to ancestors, injustice as strength, mockery of prophets as wit, and stubbornness as principle. The one deceived does not think he is doing wrong; he thinks he is doing well.

The Qur'an describes this tactic as Satan's declared strategy:

> "For allowing me to stray I will surely tempt them on earth and mislead them all together," (15:39)

> "For Satan has made their deeds appealing to them—hindering them from the ˹Right˺ Way and leaving them unguided—" (27:24)

And it notes that this deception is also, in part, a human tendency:

> "Are those whose evil-doing is made so appealing to them that they deem it good ˹like those who are rightly guided˺" (35:8)

The source commentary lists many verses in which this self-deception appears (2:212; 3:14; 6:108, 122, 137; 8:48; 9:37; 10:12; 13:33; 16:63; 27:4; 29:38; 40:37; 41:25; 47:14). The pattern is so pervasive that it may be called the fundamental mechanism of moral failure: not choosing evil knowing it to be evil, but being brought to see evil as good.

**The Connection between Hardening and Adornment**

The two clauses of the verse are linked. A hardened heart is precisely one that has lost the ability to see its own deeds clearly. When the heart is soft, a person feels the wrongness of his wrong; conscience pricks him; warnings reach him. When the heart hardens, the sensitivity is gone, and into the vacuum Satan brings his adornment. The person now sees his deeds as fair because he has lost the faculty that would show them as foul. Hardening makes adornment possible; adornment confirms the hardening. The two reinforce each other in a downward spiral.

This is why the Qur'an places such importance on keeping the heart soft — through remembrance of God, recitation of the Qur'an, reflection on death, and companionship with the righteous. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Do not talk too much without remembrance of God, for much talk without remembrance of God hardens the heart, and the furthest of people from God is the one with a hard heart." (al-Tirmidhī 2411, graded weak by some; the meaning is confirmed by other texts)

And he prescribed the remedy: when a man complained to him of hardness of heart, he told him to stroke the head of an orphan and feed the poor (Aḥmad 7576; graded ḥasan). The acts of mercy soften what neglect has hardened.

**The Verse as Diagnosis**

The verse offers a complete diagnosis of how a people arrives at destruction. First, they are warned by messengers and tested by hardship (v. 42). Second, they refuse to humble themselves (v. 43a). Third, their hearts harden (v. 43b). Fourth, Satan adorns their deeds so they cannot see their wrongness (v. 43c). Fifth — as verse 44 will describe — they forget the warning entirely, prosperity returns, and they are seized suddenly. Each stage follows from the previous one, and the whole sequence begins with a single refusal at the moment of hardship.

**The Lesson for the Present**

For the individual, the verse is a warning about the moment of hardship. That moment is a fork. To respond with humility — turning to God, examining oneself, asking forgiveness — is to take the road that leads to softness, clarity, and mercy. To respond with resistance is to take the road that leads to hardness, self-deception, and eventually to what verse 44 describes. The choice is made in the moment of hardship, but its consequences unfold long afterward.

The verse's opening "if only" suggests that the alternative was always available. The people of earlier nations could have humbled themselves; God wished that they would. That they did not was their choice, not their fate. The same is true of everyone who reads the verse: the moment of hardship is an invitation, and the invitation can be accepted.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:44

> **When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Stage of the Pattern**

Verses 42 and 43 described the sending of hardship and the failure to humble. Verse 44 describes what comes after: forgetting, prosperity, exultation, sudden seizure, and despair. This is one of the most sobering verses in the Qur'an, because it describes a divine method that reverses ordinary expectations. One might expect that after people harden against hardship, God would send more hardship. Instead, He sends ease — and the ease is the prelude to destruction.

**"When They Forgot That Whereof They Had Been Reminded"**

*Fa-lammā nasū mā dhukkirū bihi* — "so when they forgot what they had been reminded of." The commentators give two complementary readings of what they forgot. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī take it as the lesson of the hardship: they forgot what the affliction should have taught them about their dependence on God. Al-Ṭabarī takes it as the message of the messengers: they forgot the warning they had been given. Both readings describe the same failure. The reminder — whether delivered through a prophet's words or through the hard experience of suffering — was set aside and no longer shaped their conduct.

The verb *nasiya* (to forget) is used deliberately. They did not consciously reject the reminder; they let it slip. This is the ordinary way in which people fail: not by dramatic renunciation but by quiet forgetting. The resolve made during the illness fades after the recovery; the prayer offered in the storm is forgotten on the shore. The Qur'an treats such forgetting as culpable, because the reminder was clear and the forgetting was a choice to stop attending to it.

**"We Opened unto Them the Gates of All Things"**

*Fataḥnā ʿalayhim abwāba kulli shay'* — "We opened upon them the doors of everything." The image is of gates being thrown open and every kind of good pouring through: wealth, health, security, abundance, ease. The hardship of verse 42 is lifted; the people who hardened under it now enjoy prosperity beyond what they had before.

Why would God do this? The commentators offer two explanations, which the source commentary presents as alternatives but which may operate together. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī see it as a continuation of the divine pedagogy: having tried severity, God now tries gentleness, as a wise father alternates between firmness and kindness to reach a stubborn child. If hardship did not humble them, perhaps abundance will make them grateful. This gives them one more chance.

Al-Ṭabarī reads it as *istidrāj* — leading on by degrees. Having refused the warning, they are given prosperity that confirms them in their delusion, draws them deeper into worldliness, and makes the eventual seizure more complete. The Qur'an describes this method explicitly:

> "We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend" (68:44–45)

> "As for those who deny Our signs, We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend" (7:182)

The Prophet ﷺ articulated the principle in a ḥadīth cited by Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī at this verse:

> "When you see that God gives a servant of the world what he loves despite his disobedience, that is only *istidrāj*." Then he recited: "So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened upon them the doors of everything..." (Aḥmad 17311; graded ḥasan by al-Albānī)

**"Till, As They Exulted in What They Were Given"**

*Ḥattā idhā fariḥū bi-mā ūtū* — "until, when they rejoiced in what they were given." The verb *fariḥa* means to rejoice, exult, be delighted — and in the Qur'an it often carries the connotation of arrogant exultation, the joy of one who thinks his good fortune is his own doing or his own due. The Qur'an says:

> "Surely Allah does not like the prideful" (28:76)

> "Surely Allah does not like the prideful" (28:76, addressed to Qārūn)

The prosperity had its predictable effect on hardened hearts. Instead of gratitude, it produced exultation. They read their abundance as proof that they were right — that their way of life was blessed, that the warnings were baseless, that whatever gods or methods they relied on were working. This is the delusion the source commentary notes: the prosperity confirmed to them that their deeds were "fair" (v. 43), because success seemed to vindicate them.

**"We Seized Them Suddenly"**

*Akhadhnāhum baghtatan* — "We seized them suddenly." The verb *akhadha* (to take, seize) is the same used in verse 42 for the seizure with hardship; this time the seizure is final. The adverb *baghtatan* (suddenly, unexpectedly) is the same used of the Hour in verse 31. The destruction comes without warning, at the height of the exultation.

The suddenness is essential. Had the destruction come gradually, they might have repented, or at least prepared. Coming suddenly, at the peak of their prosperity, it catches them entirely unready. The Qur'an describes this pattern with several destroyed peoples: Pharaoh's people, drowning at the moment of their pursuit; the people of Lot, overturned at dawn; the people of Shuʿayb, seized by the cry while in their homes. In every case the end came as a shock.

**"Whereupon They Came to Despair"**

*Fa-idhā hum mublisūn* — "and at once they were in despair." The word *mublis* comes from *ablasa*, to be silenced by despair, to be dumbfounded, to lose all hope and have no argument left. Al-Ṭabarī and others note that this root is connected to the name *Iblīs*, the Devil, so called because he despaired of God's mercy after his refusal to prostrate to Adam. The people described in this verse share Iblīs's condition: cut off, silenced, hopeless. Al-Rāzī observes that their despair is intensified by the contrast with their previous ease, just as Iblīs's fall was made worse by the height from which he fell.

The word also conveys the sense of being unable to speak in one's own defense. At the moment of seizure, they have nothing to say. The excuses, the arguments, the mockery — all are gone. There is only silence.

**The Full Sequence**

Verses 42–44 form a complete account of how nations are destroyed. Hardship is sent to humble; it is resisted and hardens; prosperity is sent as a final test or as a lure; it produces exultation instead of gratitude; and destruction falls suddenly. The sequence has repeated throughout history, and the Qur'an presents it as a law of God's dealing with peoples (*sunnat Allāh*). The Makkans, when this verse was revealed, were somewhere in the middle of it. They had been warned; they had experienced hardship; they had not humbled themselves. The verse told them what would follow if they continued.

**The Detachment the Verses Teach**

The source commentary rightly identifies the overall effect of these verses: they teach detachment from both adversity and prosperity. Adversity is not evidence of God's rejection; it may be His most direct call. Prosperity is not evidence of God's approval; it may be His most dangerous test. Neither state reveals one's standing with God; only one's response to each state reveals it. The believer therefore neither despairs in hardship nor exults in ease. He meets both with the same posture — humility, gratitude, and attentiveness to what God is asking.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz is reported to have said, on being told that a certain man's affairs had all gone well: "Then he is in danger." He understood this verse. The Prophet ﷺ himself, when he was given abundance after long hardship, responded not with exultation but with increased worship, standing in prayer until his feet swelled, and saying, "Should I not be a grateful servant?" (al-Bukhārī 4837; Muslim 2820). That is the response prosperity is meant to produce, and it is the opposite of what verse 44 describes.

**A Warning to the Prosperous**

For the modern reader, the verse speaks directly to societies and individuals enjoying unprecedented abundance. "The gates of all things" have been opened as never before. The verse asks: what has been the response? Gratitude and humility, or exultation and forgetting? It does not say that prosperity is evil; it says that prosperity given to those who have forgotten God's reminder is a precursor to something else. The one who reads this verse in comfort should read it with attention, and should ask himself which stage of the sequence he is in.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:45

> **So the wrongdoers were utterly uprooted. And all praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Completion of the Sequence**

Verse 44 ended with the sudden seizure of the exultant people and their despair. Verse 45 records the finality of their end: *fa-quṭiʿa dābiru al-qawmi alladhīna ẓalamū* — "so the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off." The verb *quṭiʿa* (passive of *qaṭaʿa*) means to be cut, severed. The word *dābir* means the rear, the last part, the tail end of something — and by extension, the root and remnant. To cut off the *dābir* of a people is to eliminate them entirely, down to the last trace, so that nothing of them remains as a people. Al-Rāzī explains: they were uprooted completely.

The Qur'an uses this expression for other destroyed peoples:

> "So We saved him and those with him by Our mercy and uprooted those who denied Our signs" (7:72, of the people of Hūd)

> "Those ˹sinners˺ will be uprooted in the morning" (15:66, of the people of Lot)

> "Will to establish the truth by His Words and uproot the disbelievers" (8:7)

The phrase indicates not merely defeat but extinction as a community. ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot — these are known today only through the records of their destruction. Their cities are ruins; their lineages are ended; their names survive only as warnings.

**"The People Who Did Wrong"**

The destroyed are identified by their character: *al-qawm alladhīna ẓalamū* — "the people who did wrong." This is the third time in a few verses that the term *ẓulm* has appeared (vv. 21, 33, and here). It identifies the cause of destruction. They were not destroyed for being weak, for being foreign, or for any arbitrary reason; they were destroyed for *ẓulm* — for placing things where they did not belong, for wronging God by associating partners with Him and wronging others by injustice and wronging themselves by refusing guidance.

The Qur'an is consistent on this point. Destruction follows wrongdoing; it does not fall on the righteous:

> "And your Lord ˹O Prophet˺ would never destroy a society unjustly while its people were acting rightly" (11:117)

> "Your Lord would never destroy a society until He had sent to its capital a messenger, reciting Our revelations to them" (28:59)

The second verse adds a crucial condition: destruction comes only after a messenger has been sent. The people who were cut off had been warned. This is why the verse can conclude with praise.

**"Praise Be to God, Lord of the Worlds!"**

The verse ends with a formula that might seem startling after the description of a people's extermination: *wa'l-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi'l-ʿālamīn* — "and praise be to God, Lord of the worlds." Why praise God for destruction?

The commentators give several answers, and they build on one another. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarsī explain that the praise is for God's justice and for His many merciful efforts to guide these people before their destruction. He sent messengers; He sent hardship to humble them; He sent ease to test them; He gave them respite and reminders. Only after every means had been exhausted and refused did He cut them off. The praise is for the completeness of His mercy before the judgment, and for the perfect justice of the judgment when it came.

Al-Zamakhsharī adds that the praise is also for the relief of the earth from wrongdoers. When a tyrannical people is removed, the oppressed are freed, the land is cleansed, and the way is cleared for a better generation (recall verse 6: "and We brought into being after them another generation"). The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "When a wicked person dies, the servants, the land, the trees, and the animals are relieved of him." (al-Bukhārī 6512; Muslim 950)

Ibn Kathīr notes further that the praise teaches the believers how to respond when God destroys the enemies of truth: not with gloating or triumph in their own strength, but with praise of God, whose power and justice accomplished it. The Prophet ﷺ, after the victory at Badr and after the Conquest of Makkah, responded not with celebration of his own might but with prostration and praise.

**Praise as the Frame of the Sūrah**

The formula "All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds" (1:2) also connects this verse to the opening of the sūrah, which began "All praise is for Allah Who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light" (6:1). The sūrah opened with praise for creation; here it praises God for justice in history. Both are aspects of the same Lord. He who creates also governs; He who brings peoples into being also removes them when they have exhausted their opportunity. Praise is owed for both, because both flow from perfect wisdom.

The full formula, *al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi'l-ʿālamīn*, is of course the opening of al-Fātiḥah, recited in every unit of every prayer. The believer who says it daily is affirming what verse 45 affirms: that God is worthy of praise in all His acts, including those that seem severe. This is a mature form of faith. It does not praise God only for what pleases; it praises Him for what is right.

**The Justice in "Cutting Off"**

The severity of the verse should not obscure its justice. Consider what the destroyed peoples had done. They had rejected messengers who came with clear proofs. They had responded to hardship with hardened hearts. They had responded to ease with arrogant exultation. They had oppressed the weak, persecuted the believers, and mocked the warnings. Every opportunity had been given and refused. At some point, continued respite ceases to be mercy and becomes complicity with oppression. God's cutting off of such a people is what justice requires when mercy has been exhausted.

The Qur'an also notes that the righteous among such peoples were saved. Noah and those with him, Hūd and the believers, Lot and his family (except his wife), Ṣāliḥ and his followers — in every account, the messenger and the faithful are delivered before the destruction falls. The "last remnant" that is cut off is the remnant of "the people who did wrong," not of the whole population indiscriminately.

**The Lesson for the Makkans and for Us**

For the Quraysh who first heard this verse, it was the conclusion of an argument that began at verse 42. They were being told: this is the pattern; you are in it; here is where it ends. Within a decade, the leadership that had rejected the Prophet ﷺ was cut off at Badr and afterward — not the whole people of Makkah, many of whom embraced Islam, but the hardened core of the opposition. The pattern held.

For every reader, the verse is a reminder that history is moral. Peoples rise and fall not only through economic or military causes but through their response to truth and their treatment of one another. The verse does not deny secondary causes; it names the primary one: *ẓulm*. And it teaches the correct response to witnessing the fall of the unjust — not gloating, not fear, but praise to the Lord of the worlds, whose justice does not sleep and whose mercy precedes every judgment.

**Ending on Praise**

Finally, there is a literary and spiritual wisdom in ending this dark passage with praise. Verses 42–45 have described a descent: hardship, hardening, delusion, prosperity, exultation, seizure, despair, extinction. A reader could be left in gloom. The closing praise lifts the eyes from the ruins to the One who governs all things wisely. It reminds the reader that the story of the wrongdoers is not the whole story, that above their fall stands a Lord who is worthy of praise, and that praise — not despair — is the believer's final word on every event.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:46

> **Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Imagine if Allah were to take away your hearing or sight, or seal your hearts—who else other than Allah could restore it?” See ˹O Prophet˺ how We vary the signs, yet they still turn away.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second "Consider Yourselves"**

The verse uses the same opening as verse 40 — *qul a-ra'aytum* — "Say: Have you considered?" Once again the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to make the idolaters look at themselves, this time not at what they would do in a crisis but at what they possess and could lose. The question is designed to strip away the assumption of self-sufficiency and reveal dependence on God at the most intimate level: the faculties by which one perceives and understands.

**"Were God to Take Away Your Hearing and Your Sight and Seal Your Hearts"**

*In akhadha Allāhu samʿakum wa abṣārakum wa khatama ʿalā qulūbikum* — "if God took your hearing and your sight and set a seal upon your hearts." Three faculties are named. Hearing (*samʿ*, in the singular, as always in the Qur'an) and sight (*abṣār*, in the plural) are the two primary senses by which a person receives information from the world. The heart (*qalb*) is the seat of understanding, by which a person makes sense of what the senses bring. To lose all three is to be cut off from reality entirely — deaf, blind, and uncomprehending.

The verb *akhadha* (to take) for hearing and sight indicates their removal; the verb *khatama* (to seal) for the heart indicates its closing. A sealed heart, like a sealed vessel, receives nothing and gives nothing out. The Qur'an speaks of God sealing hearts in several places (2:7; 4:155; 9:87, 93; 45:23), always in reference to those who have persistently rejected the truth.

Note the order: hearing, sight, heart. This is the standard Qur'anic order for these faculties (16:78; 17:36; 32:9; 67:23), and it may reflect the sequence of knowledge: one hears reports, sees for oneself, and then understands with the heart. The verse threatens the loss of all three stages at once.

**"What God Other Than God Would Restore Them unto You?"**

*Man ilāhun ghayru Allāhi ya'tīkum bih* — "what god other than God would bring them to you?" The question expects the answer "none." The idolaters worshipped many gods; the verse asks which of them could give back a sense that God had taken. Could al-Lāt restore sight? Could Hubal unseal a heart? The idolaters knew the answer. Their gods could not do these things because their gods could do nothing.

The argument parallels verse 17 ("if God touches you with affliction, none can remove it save He") and verse 41 ("Him alone you would call"). Each approaches the same truth from a different direction: God alone controls harm and benefit; God alone is called upon in extremity; God alone could restore what He has taken. The Qur'an uses this form of question elsewhere:

> "Imagine if Allah were to make the night perpetual for you until the Day of Judgment, which god other than Allah could bring you sunlight" (28:71–72)

> "Or if He willed ˹some˺ mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy" (39:38)

**The Gift of the Senses**

The verse implicitly reminds the listener of what he has. Hearing, sight, and understanding are so constant that they are taken for granted. A person does not thank God for his eyesight each morning; he simply sees. The verse asks him to imagine losing it — and losing hearing and understanding at the same time — and then to ask who could give it back. The exercise produces two things: a sudden awareness of how much one has received, and a sudden awareness of how completely one depends on the Giver.

The Qur'an frequently names these faculties as gifts requiring gratitude:

> "And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers while you knew nothing, and gave you hearing, sight, and intellect so perhaps you would be thankful" (16:78)

> "He is the One Who brought you into being and gave you hearing, sight, and intellect" (67:23)

The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to say every morning:

> "O God, grant me health in my body; O God, grant me health in my hearing; O God, grant me health in my sight. There is no god but You." (Abū Dāwūd 5090; graded ḥasan by al-Albānī)

The prayer reflects exactly the concern of the verse: hearing and sight are God's to give and God's to take, and their continuance is a mercy to be asked for daily.

**Physical and Spiritual Faculties Together**

The verse can be read on two levels, and the commentators read it on both. Physically, it speaks of the literal senses and the literal capacity to understand. Spiritually, it speaks of the faculties by which one perceives truth — the hearing that receives revelation, the sight that sees the signs, the heart that understands. Verses 25 and 39 have already described the idolaters as spiritually deaf, mute, and in darkness. Verse 46 warns that God, who has already allowed these spiritual faculties to be impaired in them by their own choice, could also take their physical faculties — and then who would help?

The two levels reinforce each other. The person who has lost spiritual sight is in the more serious condition, because spiritual blindness leads to eternal loss, while physical blindness leads only to worldly hardship. The Qur'an says:

> "Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind" (22:46)

The one who fears losing his eyes should fear far more losing his heart.

**"Behold How We Vary the Signs"**

The verse turns to the Prophet ﷺ: *unẓur kayfa nuṣarrifu al-āyāt* — "look how We diversify the signs." The verb *ṣarrafa* means to turn something in various directions, to present it in different forms, to vary it. God does not present His proofs in one form only; He varies them — sometimes as arguments from creation, sometimes as histories of past nations, sometimes as questions about the listener's own instincts, sometimes as parables, sometimes as warnings, sometimes as promises. This variation is itself a mercy, because different people are moved by different approaches, and the same person may be reached by one form when another failed.

The phrase appears elsewhere in the sūrah (6:65, 6:105) and in the Qur'an generally (7:58; 17:41; 46:27). It draws attention to the pedagogy of revelation. The Qur'an is not a monotone; it approaches the human being from every side.

**"Yet Still They Turn Away"**

The verse concludes: *thumma hum yaṣdifūn* — "then they turn away." The verb *ṣadafa* means to turn aside, to avert oneself, to turn away with the whole body. It is a stronger word than the *iʿrāḍ* of verse 4; it suggests a deliberate, complete turning of the back. The commentators note that the word is used only three times in the Qur'an, all in this sūrah (here, and twice in verse 157), where it describes the most stubborn form of rejection.

The pairing of "We vary the signs" with "they turn away" makes a point about responsibility. God has done everything on His side: He has presented proofs in every form. The failure is entirely on the side of the recipients, who turn from each form as it is presented. This is the culmination of the sūrah's argument about signs: the problem was never a shortage of evidence but a settled refusal to receive it.

**The Practical Exercise**

The verse offers a practical exercise that anyone can perform. Close your eyes and imagine never opening them. Cover your ears and imagine never hearing again. Imagine your mind losing its grip on meaning. Then ask: who gave me these faculties, and who could restore them? The honest answer is the beginning of gratitude, and gratitude is the beginning of worship. The idolaters were asked to perform this exercise and turned away. The reader is asked to perform it and — one hopes — to respond as the verse intends: with recognition that everything he perceives, and the very capacity to perceive it, is a gift from the One God who alone could take it and alone could return it.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:47

> **Ask, “Imagine if Allah’s punishment were to overwhelm you with or without warning—who would be destroyed other than the wrongdoers?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third "Consider Yourselves"**

For the third time in a short span (vv. 40, 46, 47), the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to say *a-ra'aytakum* — "Have you considered?" The repetition builds a rhythm of self-examination. Verse 40 asked whom they would call in catastrophe; verse 46 asked who could restore their senses; verse 47 asks who would be destroyed if God's punishment came. Each question is unanswerable except in a way that undermines the idolaters' position.

**"Suddenly or Openly"**

The punishment is described as coming *baghtatan aw jahratan* — "suddenly or openly." The commentators explain the pair as covering the two ways a punishment may arrive. Al-Zamakhsharī says *baghtatan* means unexpectedly, as at night while people sleep, and *jahratan* means openly, in broad daylight, seen approaching before it strikes. Al-Rāzī summarizes: with or without warning. The pair thus encompasses every mode of arrival. Whether it comes in darkness or in light, whether it gives a moment's notice or none, the question that follows applies.

The Qur'an describes both modes in the histories of past nations. The people of Lot were seized at dawn, suddenly (15:66, 73). The people of ʿĀd saw the punishment approaching as a cloud they mistook for rain (46:24) — it came openly, and they still did not recognize it. Neither the suddenness nor the openness saved anyone who was destined for destruction.

**"Would Any Be Destroyed Save the Wrongdoing People?"**

The question: *hal yuhlaku illā al-qawmu al-ẓālimūn* — "would any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?" The expected answer is no. The verse asserts a principle: divine punishment targets wrongdoers. It is not random; it is not indiscriminate; it falls on those who have earned it by *ẓulm*.

This is the fourth appearance of *ẓulm* and its derivatives in the section (vv. 21, 33, 45, 47). The consistent identification of the punished as "wrongdoers" establishes the moral logic of destruction: it is a consequence of conduct, not an accident of fate.

**The Question of Collective Punishment**

The source commentary raises a genuine difficulty. The verse says only wrongdoers would be destroyed, yet the Qur'an's accounts of worldly destruction — the flood, the overturning of Sodom, the wind that destroyed ʿĀd — describe entire peoples being wiped out. How are these reconciled?

Several considerations resolve the tension. First, in every account, the messenger and the believers who followed him were delivered before the destruction. Noah and those in the ark; Lot and his daughters; Hūd and the believers; Ṣāliḥ and the faithful; Shuʿayb and his followers — all were saved. The destruction fell on those who remained, who were, by definition, those who had rejected. The "whole people" who were destroyed was the whole people who did wrong.

Second, the Qur'an acknowledges that worldly trials may touch the righteous along with the wicked when the righteous have failed to oppose the wrong:

> "Beware of a trial that will not only affect the wrongdoers among you" (8:25)

Zaynab bint Jaḥsh asked the Prophet ﷺ, "Shall we be destroyed while there are righteous among us?" He replied:

> "Yes, when wickedness becomes abundant." (al-Bukhārī 3346; Muslim 2880)

This ḥadīth indicates that a society in which wickedness prevails and the righteous do not resist may be struck as a whole. But the righteous who are struck in such a case are not "destroyed" in the sense of the verse; their worldly death is not their ruin.

Third — and this is al-Rāzī's resolution — the verse speaks of destruction (*halāk*) in the full sense, which is ruin in both worlds. The righteous who die in a worldly calamity are not "destroyed"; they die as martyrs or as tested believers and receive their reward with God, as verse 48 will describe. The wrongdoers who die in the same calamity are destroyed, because they lose both this world and the next. The same physical event is destruction for one and transition for the other. ʿĀ'ishah asked the Prophet ﷺ about an army that would be swallowed by the earth while containing people who were not part of its purpose, and he said:

> "They will be swallowed together, then resurrected according to their intentions." (al-Bukhārī 2118; Muslim 2884)

The event is the same; the outcome is determined by what each person was.

**The Argument's Force Against the Idolaters**

The verse's rhetorical purpose was to turn the idolaters' own admission against them. They would concede, if honest, that divine punishment falls on wrongdoers. The unstated conclusion is: and you are the wrongdoers. You have ascribed partners to God (v. 1), turned from His signs (v. 4), denied the truth (v. 5), mocked the Messenger (v. 10), and fabricated lies against God (v. 21). If punishment came, who would it strike? The question answers itself.

This is an invitation to self-assessment before the fact. The idolaters were asked to imagine the punishment and to identify its targets. If they identified themselves — as honesty required — they were being given the chance to change before the punishment arrived. The verse is thus, like all the Qur'an's warnings, a form of mercy: it describes the outcome so that the outcome may be avoided.

**Divine Justice as a Source of Security for the Righteous**

The verse also comforts the believers. In Makkah they were a persecuted minority, and they might have feared that any divine punishment on the city would sweep them away with the idolaters. The verse assures them that God's punishment discriminates: it destroys wrongdoers. Whatever happens to their bodies, their souls are safe. This is why the Companions could face persecution and warfare without terror: they knew that the destruction God sends does not ruin the righteous.

The Qur'an makes this security explicit in the following verse: "Whoever believes and does good, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve" (6:48).

**Application: Fearing the Right Thing**

The verse teaches the believer what to fear and what not to fear. He should not fear the punishment of God as though it might fall on him arbitrarily; it falls on wrongdoers, and if he is not among them, it is not aimed at him. He should fear *becoming* a wrongdoer — because that, and only that, is what makes a person a target. The fear is redirected from the event to the cause. This is a healthier and more productive fear. It leads not to anxiety about what might happen but to vigilance about what one is doing.

The ordering of the three "consider yourselves" questions also has a lesson. First, whom do you call on in crisis (v. 40)? Second, who could restore what only God gives (v. 46)? Third, who would be destroyed if God's punishment came (v. 47)? The first two establish God's exclusive power; the third establishes His exclusive justice. Together they describe a God who alone can help and who punishes only the guilty — a God who deserves to be worshipped alone, and who can be trusted completely by those who do.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:48

> **We have sent messengers only as deliverers of good news and as warners. Whoever believes and does good, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Defining the Messenger's Role**

After a series of warnings about destruction, the verse steps back to state the essential function of every messenger: *wa mā nursilu al-mursalīna illā mubashshirīna wa mundhirīn* — "and We do not send the messengers except as bringers of good news and as warners." The restrictive construction (*mā... illā*) limits their role to these two functions. Messengers are not sent to compel, to rule by force, to perform wonders on demand, or to guarantee outcomes. They are sent to announce good news and to warn.

The word *mubashshir* comes from *bushrā*, good news — the announcement of something joyful to come. The word *mundhir* comes from *indhār*, warning — the announcement of danger so that it may be avoided. The two together describe the whole of prophetic communication: here is what awaits those who believe and do good; here is what awaits those who reject and do wrong. Choose.

The pairing appears throughout the Qur'an (2:119, 213; 4:165; 5:19; 17:105; 18:56; 25:56; 33:45; 34:28; 35:24; 48:8). It is the Qur'an's standard definition of prophethood.

**Why Both Functions Are Necessary**

A messenger who only warned would drive people to despair; a messenger who only brought good news would leave them complacent. Human beings are moved by both hope and fear, and a message that engages only one leaves half the person unaddressed. The Prophet ﷺ was instructed to balance the two:

> "Inform My servants ˹O Prophet˺ that I am truly the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful," (15:49–50)

He told his Companions when sending them out:

> "Give good news and do not repel; make things easy and do not make them difficult." (al-Bukhārī 69; Muslim 1734)
