This balance is the reason the sūrah, after its warnings about destruction (vv. 42–47), immediately turns to good news (v. 48). The reader who has been sobered by the fate of the wrongdoers is now shown the alternative.

**The Limit of Responsibility**

The verse's restriction also defines the limit of the messenger's responsibility, continuing the theme of verses 33–36. The messenger conveys the good news and the warning; whether people accept is not his to control. This is stated explicitly elsewhere:

> "But if you turn away, then Our Messenger" (64:12)

> "You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺" (88:21–22)

For the Prophet ﷺ, grieving over the Makkans' rejection, this was a liberation. For every believer who calls others to good, it is the same: convey clearly, and leave the rest to God.

**"Whosoever Believes and Makes Amends"**

The verse then states the outcome for those who respond: *fa-man āmana wa aṣlaḥa* — "so whoever believes and reforms." Two conditions are named. The first is *īmān*, faith — inward belief in God, His messengers, His books, His angels, the Last Day, and the decree. The second is *iṣlāḥ*, from the root *ṣ-l-ḥ* — to set right, to reform, to make good. The verb *aṣlaḥa* means to put things in order: to correct one's conduct, repair what one has damaged, and act rightly going forward.

The pairing of belief and reform is characteristic of the Qur'an, which almost never mentions faith without deeds. The source commentary notes that verse 48 names both inward faith and outward righteousness, while verse 49 names both inward denial and outward iniquity. Faith and works are not separable; each is the natural expression of the other. A faith that produces no reform is questionable, and a reform without faith lacks its foundation. The Qur'an states the combined condition for salvation repeatedly:

> "Indeed, those who believe and do good will have the Gardens of Paradise as an accommodation," (18:107)

The choice of *aṣlaḥa* rather than the more common *ʿamila al-ṣāliḥāt* (did righteous deeds) is notable. *Aṣlaḥa* implies correction — setting right what was wrong. It suits a verse addressed to people who had been in error and were being invited to change. The one who believes *and reforms* is the one who not only accepts the truth but repairs the damage of his previous rejection.

**"No Fear Shall Come upon Them, Nor Shall They Grieve"**

The promise: *fa-lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn* — "Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve" This formula appears more than a dozen times in the Qur'an as the description of the saved (2:38, 62, 112, 262, 274, 277; 3:170; 5:69; 7:35, 49; 10:62; 43:68; 46:13). It describes freedom from the two afflictions that trouble the human soul: fear (*khawf*), which concerns the future, and grief (*ḥuzn*), which concerns the past.

The commentators explain the two precisely. Fear is anxiety about what may come — punishment, loss, the unknown. Grief is sorrow over what has passed — missed opportunities, losses suffered, wrongs done. The believers who reform are freed from both. They do not fear the future because their end is secure; they do not grieve the past because their sins are forgiven and their losses will be compensated.

The primary reference of the formula is to the Hereafter: on the Day of Judgment, when others tremble and lament, the believers will be secure. But the commentators also note that the promise begins in this world. The believer who trusts God's promise and has set his life right already experiences a measure of freedom from fear and grief that others lack. The Qur'an describes God's friends:

> "There will certainly be no fear for the close servants of Allah, nor will they grieve" (10:62–64)

**The Psychology of Security**

The promise of "no fear and no grief" speaks to a deep human need. Most people live under the weight of both: anxiety about what may happen and regret about what has happened. Neither can be resolved by worldly means, because the future is beyond control and the past is beyond change. The only resolution is trust in One who controls the future and forgives the past. The verse offers exactly this. The believer who has reformed has handed his future to God and had his past erased by Him; there is nothing left to fear and nothing left to grieve.

This is not a promise of a life without difficulty. Believers suffer illness, loss, and persecution like anyone else. The promise is that these difficulties do not produce the fear and grief that overwhelm others, because the believer sees them within a framework in which nothing is wasted and everything is ultimately well. The Prophet ﷺ described this state:

> "How wonderful is the affair of the believer, for all his affairs are good, and this is not for anyone except the believer. If something good happens to him, he is grateful, and that is good for him; and if something bad befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him." (Muslim 2999)

**The Structure of Verses 48–49**

Verse 48 states the messengers' function and the reward of those who respond rightly. Verse 49 will state the fate of those who respond wrongly. Together they present the two outcomes that the messengers announce — the good news and the warning — in the form of a promise and a threat. The listener is placed at the fork and shown both roads clearly. This is the whole of the prophetic method: not compulsion but clear presentation of consequences, and the freedom to choose.

**Application**

For the believer, the verse asks two things: believe and reform. Belief is the foundation; reform is the evidence and the fruit. The one who has both may claim the promise — not with arrogance, but with humble hope. For the one still outside faith, the verse offers a simple invitation: the messenger has brought good news and warning; the good news is for whoever believes and sets his life right; and the good news is freedom from fear and grief forever.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:49

> **But those who deny Our signs will be afflicted with punishment for their rebelliousness.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Other Fork of the Road**

Verse 48 described the outcome for those who believe and reform: no fear, no grief. Verse 49 describes the outcome for those who do the opposite: *wa'lladhīna kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā yamassuhumu al-ʿadhābu bi-mā kānū yafsuqūn* — "and those who deny Our signs, the punishment will touch them because of what they used to do of transgression." The two verses form a matched pair, and their symmetry is instructive. Belief plus reform leads to security; denial plus transgression leads to punishment. The inward and the outward are named in both cases.

**"Those Who Deny Our Signs"**

The inward failure is *takdhīb* — calling the signs false. This is the verb that has recurred throughout the sūrah (vv. 5, 21, 27, 31, 39) and is the opposite of the *īmān* of verse 48. To deny God's signs is to reject the evidence He has provided: the verses of revelation, the miracles of prophets, and the phenomena of creation. It is the inward stance of refusal.

**"The Punishment Shall Befall Them"**

*Yamassuhumu al-ʿadhāb* — "the punishment will touch them." The verb *massa* (to touch) is the same used in verse 17 for God touching a person with affliction or good. Its use here is a kind of understatement: the punishment will "touch" them — as though a light contact, when in reality it is the Fire. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that *mass* is sometimes used in the Qur'an for severe experiences, to convey that even a light touch of this punishment is unbearable. The Qur'an says of the Fire:

> "If they were touched by even a breath of your Lord" (21:46)

If a mere breath (*nafḥah*) is enough to produce this cry, the full "touch" is beyond description.

**"For the Iniquity They Committed"**

The cause is stated: *bi-mā kānū yafsuqūn* — "because of what they used to do of *fisq*." The preposition *bi* indicates causation: the punishment is *because of* their conduct. The word *fisq* comes from a root meaning to go out, to depart — the Arabs used it of a date breaking out of its skin. In religious usage, *fisq* is departing from obedience to God, transgressing His limits, going outside the bounds of what He has commanded. A *fāsiq* is one who has left the path of obedience.

The verb is in the imperfect (*yafsuqūn*) with *kānū*, indicating continuous, habitual action: "they used to persistently transgress." The punishment is for a settled pattern of conduct, not an occasional lapse.

**The Symmetry of Faith-and-Deeds and Denial-and-Deeds**

The source commentary draws attention to the theological significance of the pairing. Verse 48 names *belief* (inward) and *reform* (outward). Verse 49 names *denial* (inward) and *transgression* (outward). The Qur'an consistently treats the inward and outward as inseparable. One's inner state determines one's conduct, and one's conduct reveals and reinforces one's inner state.

This has several implications. First, faith is not merely a mental assent that can coexist with any conduct; it produces reform. Second, transgression is not merely a behavioral problem that can coexist with any belief; it flows from and feeds denial. Third, judgment is rendered on the whole person — what he believed and what he did — not on either in isolation. The Qur'an says:

> "Every soul will be detained for what it has done," (74:38)

**Justice in the Statement of Cause**

The verse does not say merely "they will be punished." It says they will be punished "because of what they used to do." This is characteristic of the Qur'an's insistence on divine justice. Punishment is always tied to cause. The Qur'an states the principle in the strongest terms:

> "And your Lord will never wrong anyone" (18:49)

> "And if it is a good deed, He will multiply it many times over and will give a great reward out of His grace" (4:40)

> "This is ˹the reward˺ for what your hands have done" (3:182)

Ibn Kathīr and other commentators note that stating the cause of punishment serves both justice and instruction. It is just because it shows that no one is punished except for what he did. It is instructive because it shows the listener what to avoid. The verse is thus both a verdict and a warning: this is what happens to those who deny and transgress; do not be among them.

**Why the Two Are Linked**

The connection between denying signs and transgressing limits is not arbitrary. A person who denies that God has spoken has no reason to obey what God has said. Denial of the signs removes the foundation of obedience. Conversely, a person who wishes to transgress has a motive to deny the signs, because acknowledging them would make his transgression inexcusable. The Qur'an observes this dynamic:

> "When is this Day of Judgment" (75:5–6)

The question about the Day is not a sincere inquiry; it is a way of dismissing the Day so that the sinning may continue. Denial serves transgression, and transgression entrenches denial. The verse names both because both are present in the person it describes.

**The Mercy Implicit in the Pair**

Verses 48 and 49 together are an act of mercy, because they lay out the consequences of both choices *in advance*. The messengers are sent as bringers of good news and warners (v. 48); these two verses are the good news and the warning in their briefest form. No one who hears them can claim not to have known. The Qur'an says that this advance notice is precisely why no one will have an excuse:

> "˹All were˺ messengers delivering good news and warnings so humanity should have no excuse before Allah after ˹the coming of˺ the messengers" (4:165)

**Application**

For the reader, the verse invites a simple inventory. What is my inward stance toward God's signs — acceptance or denial? What is my outward conduct — within His limits or outside them? The two questions are really one, because the answers correlate. The one who finds denial and transgression in himself should hear the verse as a warning and turn; the one who finds belief and reform should hear verse 48 as a promise and be grateful. Either way, the pair of verses has done what the messengers were sent to do: it has brought good news and given warning, and left the choice where God placed it — in the hands of the one who hears.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:50

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I do not say to you that I possess Allah’s treasuries or know the unseen, nor do I claim to be an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me.” Say, “Are those blind ˹to the truth˺ equal to those who can see? Will you not then reflect?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prophet Defines His Own Claim**

The idolaters had raised a series of objections rooted in their expectations of what a messenger from God should be. He should have wealth and power (17:90–91). He should know the future (7:187; 10:48). He should be an angel, not a man who eats and walks in markets (25:7). This verse instructs the Prophet ﷺ to answer all of these at once by stating precisely what he does and does not claim. It is a declaration of the limits of prophethood, and it is notable for its honesty: the Prophet ﷺ is told to disclaim powers rather than to assert them.

The words are almost identical to those spoken by Noah to his people:

> "treasuries or know the unseen, nor do I claim to be an angel, nor do I say that Allah will never grant goodness to those you look down upon" (11:31)

The repetition shows that this is the prophetic posture across history. Every messenger was a human being who disclaimed divine powers and pointed only to the revelation he had received.

**"I Do Not Say That with Me Are the Treasuries of God"**

*Lā aqūlu lakum ʿindī khazā'inu Allāh* — "I do not say to you that with me are the treasuries of God." The word *khazā'in* (singular *khizānah*) means storehouses, treasuries — the places where wealth and provision are kept. The "treasuries of God" are His stores of provision, from which He gives to whom He wills:

> "There is not any means ˹of sustenance˺ whose reserves We do not hold, only bringing it forth in precise measure" (15:21)

The Prophet ﷺ disclaims control over these. He cannot make anyone rich, cannot produce gold from the mountain, cannot end a famine by his own power. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī explain that this answers the idolaters' demand for worldly wonders and their objection that a true prophet would be wealthy and powerful. The Prophet ﷺ is not a dispenser of provision; that is God's role alone.

**"Nor Do I Know the Unseen"**

*Wa lā aʿlamu al-ghayb* — "and I do not know the unseen." The *ghayb* is everything hidden from human perception: the future, the contents of hearts, the timing of the Hour, what happens beyond the reach of the senses. Knowledge of the *ghayb* belongs to God alone:

> "None in the heavens and the earth has knowledge of the unseen except Allah" (27:65)

> "With Him are the keys of the unseen—no one knows them except Him" (6:59)

The Prophet ﷺ knew of the unseen only what God revealed to him:

> "˹He is the˺ Knower of the unseen, disclosing none of it to anyone," (72:26–27)

The disclaimer answers the demand to foretell the Hour and the objection that a true prophet would know all hidden things. It also protects the community from a dangerous error: attributing to the Prophet ﷺ, or to any human, independent knowledge of the unseen. When ʿĀ'ishah heard someone claim that the Prophet ﷺ knew what would happen tomorrow, she said: "Whoever tells you that he knows what will be tomorrow has lied, and then she recited, 'No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow'" (al-Bukhārī 4855; Muslim 177, in the ḥadīth of the three matters). The Prophet's ﷺ own life confirmed the disclaimer: he did not know of the slander against ʿĀ'ishah until revelation cleared her; he did not know the outcome of battles before they were fought.

**"Nor Do I Say That I Am an Angel"**

*Wa lā aqūlu lakum innī malak* — "So whoever hopes for the meeting with their Lord, let them do good deeds and associate none in the worship of their Lord" This answers the objection addressed in verses 8–9. The Prophet ﷺ makes no claim to be other than human. He is, as the Qur'an says repeatedly, "a man like you" (18:110; 41:6) to whom revelation has come. The disclaimer is not a weakness in his position but its strength: a human messenger can be followed, imitated, and understood in a way an angel could not.

**"I Follow Only That Which Is Revealed unto Me"**

Having disclaimed three things, the Prophet ﷺ affirms one: *in attabiʿu illā mā yūḥā ilayy* — "I follow only what is revealed to me." This is the whole of his claim. He is not a source of provision, knowledge of the unseen, or angelic power; he is a recipient and follower of revelation. Everything he teaches comes from what God has sent down. His authority rests entirely on this.

The statement has two edges. Against the idolaters, it says: do not judge me by standards I never claimed; judge the revelation I bring. For the believers, it says: the Prophet ﷺ himself follows revelation, so you must follow it too; and what he teaches is not personal opinion but what God has revealed. The Qur'an confirms this:

> "Nor does he speak of his own whims" (53:3–4)

**"Are the Blind and the Seer Equal?"**

The second "Say" shifts from disclaimer to argument: *qul hal yastawī al-aʿmā wa'l-baṣīr* — "Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?" The question expects "no." The blind and the seeing are not equal; one perceives reality and the other does not. The comparison is between those who see the truth of the revelation and those who are blind to it. The commentators are unanimous that spiritual sight is meant, as the Qur'an says:

> "Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind" (22:46)

The question appears in the same form elsewhere (11:24; 13:16; 35:19; 40:58), and a parallel question asks:

> "Are those who know equal to those who do not know" (39:9)

The point in context is this: the Prophet ﷺ does not claim treasuries, unseen knowledge, or angelic nature — but he does claim to see. He has received revelation and follows it; he perceives the truth about God, the world, and the Hereafter. The idolaters, for all their wealth and status, are blind to these things. The two are not equal, and the difference is not in worldly power but in perception of reality.

**"Will You Not, Then, Reflect?"**

The verse ends: *a-fa-lā tatafakkarūn* — "˹They are˺ those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth ˹and pray˺," The verb *tafakkara* means to reflect, to ponder, to turn a matter over in the mind. The Qur'an calls for reflection constantly (3:191; 16:44; 30:8; 45:13), and here it asks the idolaters to think about the difference between the blind and the seeing and to ask which they are.

The appeal to reflection is significant after the disclaimers. The Prophet ﷺ does not ask to be believed because of power or wonders; he asks the listener to think. This is the confidence of one who knows that honest reflection leads to the truth. The idolaters demanded compulsion; the Prophet ﷺ offered reasoning.

**The Honesty of the Disclaimer**

There is a lesson in the verse for anyone who represents truth. The Prophet ﷺ did not overstate his powers to win followers. He said plainly what he was not. This honesty was itself evidence of his truthfulness — a fraud would claim more, not less. The Companions were taught by this example to be truthful about the limits of their knowledge; Ibn Masʿūd said that when a person is asked about what he does not know, he should say, "I do not know." The verse models this integrity at the highest level.

**Following Revelation as the Standard**

Finally, the verse establishes the standard by which all religious claims are to be measured: revelation. The Prophet ﷺ followed what was revealed to him; the believer follows what the Prophet ﷺ conveyed. Neither treasuries nor unseen knowledge nor angelic status is the basis of religious authority — only the Book of God and the guidance of the one to whom it was revealed. This is the foundation of the whole Islamic approach to knowledge, and it is stated here in a single phrase: "I follow only what is revealed to me."

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:51

> **Warn with this ˹Quran˺ those who are awed by the prospect of being gathered before their Lord—when they will have no protector or intercessor besides Him—so perhaps they will be mindful ˹of Him˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command to Warn, and Its Target**

After defining what the Prophet ﷺ is and is not (v. 50), the verse turns to what he is to do: *wa andhir bihi* — "and warn by it." The pronoun "it" refers to the Qur'an, as Ibn Kathīr and the majority of commentators explain — the revelation the Prophet ﷺ has just said he follows. His task is to warn, and his instrument is the Book.

The command specifies a particular audience: *alladhīna yakhāfūna an yuḥsharū ilā rabbihim* — "those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord." The verse does not say "warn everyone"; it says warn those who fear the gathering. This is a striking focus, because the previous verses addressed the deniers who mocked the resurrection. Here the Prophet ﷺ is told to direct his warning toward those who take it seriously.

**Who Are "Those Who Fear"?**

Al-Zamakhsharī records three possibilities, and they may all be intended. First, the Muslims — believers who accept the resurrection and fear God's judgment, but who are deficient in their works and need the warning to move them to greater obedience. Second, the People of the Book — Jews and Christians who believed in the Day of Judgment but had not yet accepted the Prophet ﷺ; their existing belief in the gathering made them receptive to warning about it. Third, those among the idolaters who, despite their public denial, harbored a hidden fear of the reckoning — the ones whose *fiṭrah* still spoke — and who might therefore be reached.

What unites all three is receptivity. A warning benefits only someone who can take it seriously. The person who fears the gathering will hear a warning about the gathering; the person who mocks it will not. The verse therefore instructs the Prophet ﷺ in an economy of effort that the sūrah has been developing since verse 36 ("only those who hear will respond"): direct the warning toward those in whom it can take root.

This does not mean the deniers were not warned; the entire sūrah is addressed to them. It means that the warning's *purpose* — producing *taqwā* — is achieved in those who fear. The Qur'an says elsewhere:

> "You can only warn those who follow the Reminder and are in awe of the Most Compassionate without seeing Him" (36:11)

> "Your duty is only to warn whoever is in awe of it" (79:45)

**The Value of Fear**

The verse identifies fear of the gathering as the quality that makes a person warnable. This says something positive about fear. In much modern thinking, fear is considered a negative emotion to be overcome. The Qur'an treats fear of God and of the Judgment as a virtue — the beginning of wisdom, the ground of *taqwā*. The person who fears the gathering is not a coward; he is a realist. He knows he will stand before his Lord, and he takes that knowledge seriously. This fear is what motivates him to prepare, to seek forgiveness, to avoid what will harm him. The Qur'an praises it:

> "And whoever is in awe of standing before their Lord will have two Gardens" (55:46)

> "Surely those who tremble in awe of their Lord," (23:57–61)

**"They Have, apart from Him, No Protector and No Intercessor"**

The verse then describes the situation of those gathered: *laysa lahum min dūnihi waliyyun wa lā shafīʿ* — "they have, besides Him, no protector and no intercessor." The word *walī* (protector, guardian, patron) appeared at verse 14; *shafīʿ* (intercessor) is one who pleads on another's behalf. On the Day of Gathering, no one will have any protector or intercessor apart from God.

This statement has two functions. First, it is part of the warning: when you stand before your Lord, you will have no one to shield you and no one to plead for you except by His leave. The idolaters believed their gods would intercede (10:18; 39:3); this verse removes that hope. Second, it clarifies the doctrine of intercession. The verse does not deny intercession absolutely; it denies intercession "apart from Him" — that is, independent of His permission. The Qur'an teaches that intercession exists but only by God's leave and for those He approves:

> "Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission" (2:255)

> "They do not intercede except for whom He approves, and they tremble in awe of Him" (21:28)

> "On that Day no intercession will be of any benefit, except by those granted permission by the Most Compassionate and whose words are agreeable to Him" (20:109)

The Prophet's ﷺ intercession on the Day of Judgment, affirmed in many authentic ḥadīths (al-Bukhārī 4712; Muslim 194), falls within this framework: it is granted by God, for whom He wills, and is thus not "apart from Him" but through Him. The source commentary notes the report from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq that the Qur'an itself is an intercessor for those who live by it, which aligns with the ḥadīth:

> "Recite the Qur'an, for it will come on the Day of Resurrection as an intercessor for its companions." (Muslim 804)

In all cases, the intercession derives from God's permission. There is no independent power that can stand between a person and his Lord.

**Why This Makes the Warning Effective**

The knowledge that there is no protector or intercessor apart from God is what makes the fear of the gathering serious. If a person believed he could rely on a patron to shield him or a friend in high places to plead for him, the gathering would hold less terror. Knowing that he will stand alone, with only God's mercy between him and the consequences of his deeds, he takes preparation seriously. The verse thus adds to the warning the fact that makes the warning bite.

**"That They Might Be Reverent"**

The purpose is stated: *laʿallahum yattaqūn* — "that perhaps they may have *taqwā*." This is the goal of all warning. *Taqwā*, from the root *w-q-y* (to protect, to shield), is the protective awareness that keeps a person from harm — the vigilance of one walking through a thorny path who gathers his garment and watches his steps. The warning is not meant to produce paralysis or despair but *taqwā*: careful, alert, protective conduct.

The relationship between fear and *taqwā* is worth noting. Fear is the emotion; *taqwā* is the behavior it produces. A person who fears the gathering and responds by guarding himself against sin has converted fear into *taqwā*. A person who fears and does nothing has fear without benefit. The verse aims at the conversion: warn those who fear, so that their fear becomes protective conduct.

**The Wisdom of Directed Warning**

For anyone who teaches or calls to good, the verse offers a method. Identify those in whom the message can take root — those who already have some seriousness about the ultimate questions — and invest in them. This is not elitism; the call is open to all. It is realism about where the fruit will grow. The Prophet ﷺ conveyed to everyone, but he built his community from those who feared the gathering. They became the vessels through whom the message reached the world.

**Application to the Believer**

For the believer, the verse is both description and instruction. Description: you are among "those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord," and the Qur'an's warnings are addressed to you — not to make you despair but to make you careful. Instruction: know that you have no protector or intercessor apart from Him, so make your preparation directly with Him — through repentance, obedience, and the seeking of His mercy — rather than relying on anyone or anything else to stand between you and your Lord. The fear the verse names is a gift; used rightly, it produces the *taqwā* that is the goal of all revelation.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:52

> **˹O Prophet!˺ Do not dismiss those ˹poor believers˺ who invoke their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. You are not accountable for them whatsoever, nor are they accountable for you. So do not dismiss them, or you will be one of the wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Occasion of Revelation**

This verse was revealed in response to a specific incident, recorded by al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Wāḥidī, and others. A group of prominent Quraysh — the reports name al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis, ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn, and others among the tribal nobility — came to the Prophet ﷺ and indicated that they might be willing to sit with him and hear his message, but that they were unwilling to sit alongside his poorer followers: Bilāl the freed Abyssinian slave, ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, Ṣuhayb the Byzantine, Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt, Ibn Masʿūd, and others of low social standing. They asked him to send these followers away, or at least to have them moved to the back, so that the nobles would not be seen in their company.

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, who was among the poor believers at the time, narrated the incident:

> "We were six with the Prophet ﷺ, and the idolaters said to him, 'Drive these away so that they will not be insolent toward us.' I was there, along with Ibn Masʿūd, a man from Hudhayl, Bilāl, and two men whose names I do not recall. Something entered the heart of the Messenger of God ﷺ, as God willed, and he spoke to himself about it. Then God revealed: 'And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, desiring His Face.'" (Muslim 2413)

Some reports indicate that the Prophet ﷺ, hoping to win the nobles to Islam and thereby bring their tribes with them, was inclined to accommodate the request temporarily — perhaps to ask the poor believers to withdraw when the nobles came, and to teach them at another time. The verse was revealed to forbid this absolutely.

**"Drive Not Away"**

*Wa lā taṭrudi* — "and do not drive away." The verb *ṭarada* means to expel, to chase off, to send away with contempt. It is a harsh word, used for driving off an animal or an unwanted person. Its use here conveys how the nobles' request would have been experienced by the poor believers: not as a temporary arrangement but as being cast out. The prohibition is emphatic and unconditional.

**"Those Who Call upon Their Lord Morning and Evening, Desiring His Face"**

The people who must not be driven away are described not by their social status but by their spiritual practice: *alladhīna yadʿūna rabbahum bi'l-ghadāti wa'l-ʿashiyyi yurīdūna wajhah* — "those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His Face." The verse redefines who matters. The nobles measured worth by lineage and wealth; God measures it by devotion.

"Morning and evening" is understood by al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī as referring to the prescribed prayers at their times, or to constant remembrance of God throughout the day, or to both. The expression conveys constancy — these people are in continuous relationship with their Lord, from the beginning of the day to its end.

"Desiring His Face" (*yurīdūna wajhah*) is the Qur'an's expression for pure sincerity. It means seeking God Himself — His pleasure, His nearness, and, as al-Rāzī notes, the vision of Him in the Hereafter — not seeking anything worldly through worship. Ibn Kathīr explains it as sincerity of intention. The phrase appears elsewhere in praise of the righteous:

> "We feed you only for the sake of Allah, seeking neither reward nor thanks from you" (76:8–9)

> "pleasure, establish prayer, donate from what We have provided for them—secretly and openly—and respond to evil with good" (13:22)

By describing the poor believers this way, the verse elevates them above the nobles who despised them. Bilāl, calling on his Lord morning and evening and seeking only His Face, outranks any chieftain who seeks only status.

**"Naught of Their Reckoning Falls upon Thee"**

*Mā ʿalayka min ḥisābihim min shay'in wa mā min ḥisābika ʿalayhim min shay'* — "nothing of their account is upon you, and nothing of your account is upon them." The commentators offer two readings of whose "reckoning" is meant, as the source commentary details.

On one reading, "their reckoning" refers to the poor believers. Some of the Quraysh had suggested that the poor followed the Prophet ﷺ not from sincerity but for food and shelter. The verse responds: their inner motives are not your responsibility to assess; you judge by what is apparent, and God judges the heart. This echoes the principle that "No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another" (6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38). The Prophet ﷺ was not accountable for the sincerity of his followers, nor were they accountable for his.

On the other reading, which al-Zamakhsharī finds more plausible, "their reckoning" refers to the nobles. The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ: you are not responsible for whether these nobles accept Islam. Their account is with God. You should not be so anxious for their conversion that you would wrong your sincere followers to achieve it. Both readings converge on the same instruction: the Prophet ﷺ should not calculate on the basis of who might be won or who might be insincere; he should honor those who sincerely worship and leave all reckonings to God.

**"Such That Thou Shouldst Drive Them Away and Thus Become One of the Wrongdoers"**

The verse concludes with a stark consequence: *fa-taṭrudahum fa-takūna min al-ẓālimīn* — "that you should drive them away and thus be among the wrongdoers." Driving away sincere worshippers to accommodate the arrogant would be *ẓulm* — placing a thing out of its rightful place. It would be placing status above sincerity, and that inversion is precisely the injustice the sūrah has been condemning since verse 1.

The source commentary raises the natural question: how could the Prophet ﷺ have been inclined toward something that the verse calls wrongdoing? Al-Rāzī's answer is careful. The Prophet's ﷺ intention was entirely good — to facilitate the nobles' entry into Islam, which would bring their tribes with them and strengthen the Muslim community. He did not intend to demean his followers, and he could have continued teaching them separately. His inclination was toward a strategic accommodation, not toward injustice. God corrected the inclination before it became action, and the correction itself demonstrates the Prophet's ﷺ perfect responsiveness to revelation. The verse does not record a sin; it records a guidance that prevented a mistake.

**The Parallel with Noah**

The Qur'an records that Noah faced the identical demand and refused it:

> "Their judgment is with my Lord, if you had any sense" (26:111–114)

> "But I can see that you are a people acting ignorantly" (11:29)

The consistency across prophets shows that this is a principle of God's religion, not a circumstance of one moment. The nobles of every age have made the same demand, and every prophet has given the same answer.

**The Related Passages**

Two other passages address the same issue. Sūrat al-Kahf commands:

> "And patiently stick with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure" (18:28)

And Sūrat ʿAbasa gently reproves the Prophet ﷺ for turning his attention to a wealthy Makkan while the blind ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm sought his instruction (80:1–10). In all three cases, the lesson is identical: the measure of a person is his sincerity toward God, not his standing among people, and the one who calls to God must never rank people by worldly status.

**The Social Revolution in the Verse**

This verse struck at the foundation of the Arabian social order. In pre-Islamic Makkah, lineage was everything. A freed Abyssinian slave was not a person of consequence; a chieftain of Tamīm was. The verse declares that in God's sight the ranking is reversed when the slave calls on his Lord sincerely and the chieftain does not. This principle would be stated in general form later:

> "Surely the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous among you" (49:13)

And the Prophet ﷺ would declare it in his Farewell Sermon:

> "O people, your Lord is one and your father is one. There is no superiority of an Arab over a non-Arab, nor of a non-Arab over an Arab, nor of a white over a black, nor of a black over a white, except by *taqwā*." (Aḥmad 23489; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

The verse before us is where this principle was first defended in practice — at the cost of potentially losing the allegiance of powerful men.

**The Aftermath**

The Prophet ﷺ obeyed. He did not drive away the poor believers. And the reports add that after the verse was revealed, he would sit with them until they rose to leave, and he would say, "Praise be to God who did not cause me to die until He commanded me to be patient with a people from my community" (recorded by Ibn Kathīr). Bilāl became the *mu'adhdhin* of Islam; Ibn Masʿūd became one of its greatest scholars; ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, and Khabbāb became pillars of the community. The nobles who had demanded their removal either eventually embraced Islam on equal terms or were forgotten.

**The Lesson for Every Community**

The temptation the verse addresses recurs in every generation. Religious communities are tempted to court the wealthy and prominent, to make the poor and unlettered feel less welcome, to measure success by the status of those attracted rather than the sincerity of those gathered. The verse forbids this absolutely. The one who calls to God must honor those who seek God's Face, whatever their station, and must never trade their dignity for the approval of those who seek only their own.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:53

> **In this way We have tested some by means of others, so those ˹disbelievers˺ may say, “Has Allah favoured these ˹poor believers˺ out of all of us?” Does Allah not best recognize the grateful?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Divine Purpose behind Social Difference**

The verse opens with *wa kadhālika* — "and thus" — connecting it to the incident of verse 52. The nobles' contempt for the poor believers was not a random social fact; it was part of a divine design. *Fatannā baʿḍahum bi-baʿḍ* — "We tested some of them by means of others." The verb *fatana*, as discussed at verse 23, comes from the testing of metal by fire. God tests people by placing them in relation to one another — rich alongside poor, powerful alongside weak, early believers alongside late — and observing how each responds to the other.

The Qur'an states this principle in several places:

> "We have made some of you a trial for others" (25:20)

> "He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth and elevated some of you in rank over others, so He may test you with what He has given you" (6:165)

> "But He does ˹this only to˺ test some of you by means of others" (47:4)

Al-Ṭabarī explains the general meaning: differences in wealth and status are a trial for everyone. The strong are tested in how they treat the weak; the weak are tested in their patience and trust in God. Neither condition is a reward or a punishment in itself; each is an examination.

**The Test in Its Specific Setting**

In the context of verse 52, the test had a precise form. The prominent Makkans were tested by the humble status of the Prophet's ﷺ followers. To accept Islam, they would have to sit beside Bilāl and Ibn Masʿūd, to accept that these men had preceded them in faith, and — as al-Rāzī notes — to accept instruction from those they had always considered beneath them. This required them to abandon the equation of spiritual worth with social rank, an equation on which their whole self-understanding rested. Most of them failed the test at first; some passed it later.

At the same time, al-Rāzī observes, the poor believers were also tested. They watched the wealthy idolaters prosper while they themselves suffered persecution, hunger, and contempt. Their test was to remain steadfast without envy, to trust that God's distribution was wise, and not to conclude from worldly appearances that God had favored their oppressors.

**"Are These the Ones Whom God Has Graced among Us?"**

The verse quotes the question the test produces: *a-hā'ulā'i manna Allāhu ʿalayhim min bayninā* — "Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favor from among us?" The verb *manna* means to bestow a favor graciously. The question drips with contempt when spoken by the nobles: *these* — slaves, foreigners, the poor — are the ones God has chosen over *us*, the lords of Quraysh? The incredulity reveals the assumption being tested: that God's favor should track worldly status.

The source commentary notes that the question could also be asked in the opposite direction, by the poor believers about the wealthy idolaters: are *these* — the arrogant, the persecutors — the ones God has favored with wealth and security, while we suffer? Both groups, looking at the other, might ask the same question with different emotions. The verse's ambiguity may be deliberate: the test runs in both directions, and each group must learn that worldly condition does not indicate divine favor.

The Qur'an records the same reaction from the elites of every prophet's people:

> "The disbelieving chiefs of his people said," (11:27)

**"Does God Not Know Best Those Who Are Thankful?"**

The verse answers the question with another: *a-laysa Allāhu bi-aʿlama bi'l-shākirīn* — "Is not God most knowing of the thankful?" The answer, of course, is yes. God knows who is truly grateful, and He bestows His favor on the basis of that knowledge, not on the basis of lineage or wealth. If He has graced Bilāl with faith, it is because He knows Bilāl's gratitude. The nobles' incredulity reflects their ignorance, not any error in God's choice.

The word "thankful" (*shākirīn*) is significant. Gratitude is the response to favor; the one who receives faith and is grateful for it has demonstrated that he deserved to receive it. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the poor believers, receiving the greatest favor — guidance — responded with gratitude, worship, and steadfastness, while the nobles, receiving worldly favor, responded with arrogance and denial. God knew which group would be thankful, and He gave the greater gift accordingly.

This principle is stated elsewhere:

> "And thus We have tested some of them through others, that they might say... Does God not know best the thankful?" (this verse)

> "If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more" (14:7)

**The Reversal of Worldly Ranking**

The verse continues the social revolution begun in verse 52. Human beings rank one another by what is visible: wealth, ancestry, power, appearance. God ranks by what is invisible to human beings but perfectly known to Him: sincerity, gratitude, *taqwā*. The two rankings frequently diverge, and the divergence is itself the test. The one who insists on the human ranking, and refuses to accept God's, has failed. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "God does not look at your forms or your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds." (Muslim 2564)

And he described the reversal:

> "Shall I not inform you about the people of Paradise? Every weak and oppressed person; if he swore by God, God would fulfill his oath. Shall I not inform you about the people of the Fire? Every harsh, arrogant, and proud person." (al-Bukhārī 4918; Muslim 2853)

**The Logic of Testing through Others**

Why does God test people through one another rather than in isolation? Because character is revealed in relationship. A person alone cannot demonstrate generosity, patience with others, humility, or justice. These virtues exist only in relation to other people, and they are tested precisely when the other person is different from oneself — poorer or richer, weaker or stronger, earlier or later in faith. A society without differences would be a society without most of the tests that form character. The verse thus explains not only the specific incident in Makkah but the general structure of human society: its inequalities are, among other things, the arena of moral examination.

This does not mean inequality is to be celebrated or left unaddressed. Islam commands the wealthy to give, the strong to protect, and the community to care for its weak. The test for the strong is precisely whether they do these things. The verse does not justify contempt for the poor; it condemns it as a failure of the test.

**Application**

The verse asks every reader two questions. First: when I see someone of lower standing than myself favored by God with faith, knowledge, or righteousness, do I respond like the Makkan nobles — "*these* people?" — or do I recognize that God knows best whom to favor? Second: when I see someone of higher standing than myself prospering while I struggle, do I conclude that God has favored them and neglected me, or do I trust that worldly condition is a test and not a verdict? The one who passes both tests has understood the verse. The one who fails either has fallen into the trap it describes.

**The Consolation for the Poor Believers**

Finally, the verse was a direct consolation to Bilāl, ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, Khabbāb, Ibn Masʿūd, and the others whom the nobles had asked the Prophet ﷺ to drive away. God Himself declared that He knew them to be among the thankful, and that His favor to them was not an error the nobles could correct. Within a few years, these men were leading prayers, commanding respect, and teaching the very tribes whose chiefs had despised them. God knew best.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:54

> **When the believers in Our revelations come to you, say, “Peace be upon you! Your Lord has taken upon Himself to be Merciful. Whoever among you commits evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺ then repents afterwards and mends their ways, then Allah is truly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Prohibition to Positive Command**

Verse 52 forbade the Prophet ﷺ from driving away the sincere believers. Verse 54 commands what he should do instead: welcome them with peace and with the good news of God's mercy. *Wa idhā jā'aka alladhīna yu'minūna bi-āyātinā fa-qul salāmun ʿalaykum* — "and when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: Peace be upon you." The contrast with the nobles' demand could not be sharper. The nobles wanted these people expelled; God commands that they be greeted with the greeting of Paradise.

**Who Comes, and Why the Greeting**

The people who come are described as "those who believe in Our signs" — the same believers of verse 52 who call on their Lord morning and evening, now identified by their faith. The Prophet ﷺ is to receive them with *salām*. Several reports about the verse's occasion are recorded, and they are complementary. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī note that it may continue the incident of verse 52, instructing the Prophet ﷺ to honor the poor believers with greeting rather than dismissal. They also record that it may refer to those believers, said to include ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who had initially advised the Prophet ﷺ to accommodate the nobles' request and then regretted it; the verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to greet them with peace and assure them of forgiveness. Al-Ṭabarī records a third report: a group of believers came confessing serious sins they had committed, and the Prophet ﷺ was silent until this verse was revealed, instructing him to greet them and give them hope.

All three occasions share a theme: believers approaching the Prophet ﷺ in some state of need — whether marginalized, regretful, or burdened by sin — and being received with peace and mercy.

**"Peace Be upon You"**

*Salāmun ʿalaykum* is the greeting of Islam, and its use here has deep roots. The Qur'an presents it as the greeting of the people of Paradise (7:46; 14:23; 16:32; 39:73; 56:26), the greeting of the angels to the righteous (13:23–24; 16:32), and a formula of blessing upon the prophets (37:79, 109, 120, 130, 181). When the Prophet ﷺ greets the believers with it, he is receiving them as the people of Paradise are received. Al-Rāzī notes that the greeting is itself a form of honor, and that God's command to offer it to the poor believers publicly reversed the humiliation the nobles had tried to impose.

The Prophet ﷺ taught the greeting as a means of spreading love among believers:

> "You will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not tell you of something which, if you do it, you will love one another? Spread peace among yourselves." (Muslim 54)

The verse is, among other things, the Qur'anic foundation of this practice.

**"Your Lord Has Prescribed Mercy for Himself"**

The Prophet ﷺ is to say: *kataba rabbukum ʿalā nafsihi al-raḥmah* — "your Lord has written mercy upon Himself." This is the second occurrence of this extraordinary phrase in the sūrah; the first was at verse 12. There it was stated to the idolaters as an explanation of God's patience. Here it is stated to the believers as the ground of their hope. The same mercy that delays the punishment of the deniers guarantees the forgiveness of the repentant.

Note the possessive: "*your* Lord" — the Lord of these humble believers. The phrase is intimate and reassuring. The One who has bound Himself to mercy is your own Lord, and His mercy is for you.

The ḥadīth literature confirms the meaning, as discussed at verse 12:

> "When God created the creation, He wrote in His Book, which is with Him above the Throne: 'My mercy prevails over My wrath.'" (al-Bukhārī 3194; Muslim 2751)

Ibn Kathīr, at this verse, cites the ḥadīth of Muʿādh ibn Jabal, which expresses the same self-binding of God in a different form:

> The Prophet ﷺ said, "O Muʿādh, do you know what is the right of God over His servants?" I said, "God and His Messenger know best." He said, "That they worship Him and not associate anything with Him." Then he said, "Do you know what is their right over God if they do that?" I said, "God and His Messenger know best." He said, "That He not punish them." (al-Bukhārī 2856; Muslim 30)

God owes nothing to anyone; yet He has made it a "right" of His servants that He not punish those who worship Him alone. This is the same self-obligation the verse describes.

**"Whosoever among You Does Evil in Ignorance"**

The content of the prescribed mercy is then specified: *annahu man ʿamila minkum sū'an bi-jahālatin* — "that whoever among you does evil in ignorance." The phrase "in ignorance" (*bi-jahālah*) has been discussed extensively by the commentators, particularly at 4:17 ("Repentance is accepted by God only for those who do wrong in ignorance and then repent soon after"). The early authorities — Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah, Mujāhid, and others — explained that "in ignorance" does not mean without knowing the act is wrong, for then it would not be a sin requiring repentance. It means that every act of disobedience is, in a sense, committed in a state of *jahālah* — a moment when the person acts against what he knows, when passion or heedlessness overrides knowledge. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: "Every sin a servant commits, he commits in ignorance." Ibn ʿAbbās explained: "It is because of his ignorance that he commits the sin, whether it be deliberate or not."

On this understanding, "in ignorance" is not a restriction that excludes deliberate sinners from mercy; it is a description of the condition of every sinner at the moment of sin. The verse therefore offers mercy to all who sin — which is everyone — on the condition that follows.

**"And Thereafter Repents and Makes Amends"**

*Thumma tāba min baʿdihi wa aṣlaḥa* — "then repents after it and reforms." Two conditions. First, *tawbah* — repentance, from the root *t-w-b*, to return. To repent is to turn back to God from the sin, with regret for it, abandonment of it, and resolve not to return to it. Second, *iṣlāḥ* — reform, setting right, the same word used at verse 48. Repentance is inward turning; reform is the outward correction that proves the turning was real. A person who says he has repented but continues in the same conduct has not repented; a person who repents and reforms has fulfilled the condition.

The word *thumma* ("then," "thereafter") indicates that repentance may come after an interval. The door does not close immediately after the sin. The Qur'an says elsewhere that repentance is accepted until death approaches (4:18), and the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "God accepts the repentance of His servant as long as his soul has not reached his throat." (al-Tirmidhī 3537, graded ḥasan)

**"He Is Truly Forgiving, Merciful"**

The verse concludes: *fa-annahu ghafūrun raḥīm* — "then indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful." Two divine names. *Ghafūr* comes from *ghafara*, to cover, to shield — as a helmet (*mighfar*) covers the head. God's forgiveness covers the sin so that it no longer harms the sinner. *Raḥīm* is the intensive form of mercy — the One who is continually and abundantly merciful. The pairing tells the repentant sinner not merely that he may be forgiven but that forgiveness and mercy are God's settled attributes, expressed toward whoever turns to Him.

**The Structure of the Verse as Consolation**

The verse moves through a complete arc of reassurance. It begins with welcome (peace be upon you). It establishes the foundation (God has bound Himself to mercy). It acknowledges the reality of sin (whoever does evil in ignorance). It specifies the way back (repents and reforms). And it concludes with the guarantee (He is Forgiving, Merciful). A believer burdened by his failures, hearing this from the Prophet ﷺ, receives everything he needs: acceptance, hope, a method, and a promise.

**The Prophet as the Voice of Divine Mercy**

The verse instructs the Prophet ﷺ to be the one who delivers this message. This shaped his character and his community. He was not a harsh judge of sinners but the announcer of God's mercy to them. When a young man came to him asking permission to commit fornication, he did not expel him but reasoned with him gently and prayed for him (Aḥmad 22211). When a Bedouin urinated in the mosque, he stopped the Companions from rebuking him harshly and had water poured over the spot (al-Bukhārī 220). When a man confessed a sin and asked for punishment, he told him that his prayer had already expiated it (al-Bukhārī 526). This was the Prophet ﷺ living out verse 54.

**The Balance with Verse 12**

The two occurrences of "He has prescribed mercy upon Himself" in this sūrah, at verses 12 and 54, address two audiences and produce two effects. For the deniers, the mercy is a reason for their continued respite and a reason to turn before it ends. For the believers, the mercy is a reason for hope after every fall and a reason never to despair. The same attribute, stated in the same words, functions as warning and as comfort — because mercy is one, and its reception depends on the state of the one who hears of it.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:55

> **This is how We make Our signs clear, so the way of the wicked may become distinct.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Statement of Method**

This short verse pauses the argument to comment on the argument itself. *Wa kadhālika nufaṣṣilu al-āyāt* — "and thus We detail the signs." The verb *faṣṣala* means to separate into parts, to set out in detail, to make distinct — as a butcher separates joints or a jeweler sets stones individually. God does not present His signs as an undifferentiated mass; He details them, distinguishing one from another and presenting each clearly.

The phrase occurs four times in this sūrah (here, 6:97, 6:98, 6:126) and in many other places (7:32, 52, 174; 9:11; 10:5, 24; 11:1; 13:2; 30:28; 41:3). Its recurrence indicates that the Qur'an is conscious of its own method: it is a Book of detailed exposition, in which the proofs of God's Oneness and the truth of His Messenger are laid out one by one, from every angle, so that no honest reader can claim they were unclear. The preceding verses have exemplified this: arguments from creation (vv. 1–3), from history (vv. 6, 10–11, 42–45), from the idolaters' own instincts (vv. 40–41, 46–47), from the nature of prophethood (vv. 48–50), and from social justice (vv. 52–54). Each is a sign detailed.

**"That the Way of the Guilty May Be Made Clear"**

The stated purpose: *wa li-tastabīna sabīlu al-mujrimīn* — "and so that the way of the criminals may become clear." The word *sabīl* means a road, a path, a way. The word *mujrim* comes from *jarama*, to cut — a *jurm* is a crime, an offense that cuts one off from what is right. The *mujrimūn* are the guilty, the criminals, those who have committed the offense of denying God and His signs.

The purpose is striking. One might expect the verse to say "that the way of the righteous may be made clear." Instead it says the way of the guilty. Why? The commentators give several reasons. First, clarity about the wrong path is necessary to avoid it. A traveler who knows only where the safe road lies but not where the dangerous ones diverge from it will still be lost; he needs to recognize the wrong turnings. The Qur'an details the signs so that the believers can see exactly where the guilty went astray — what they said, what they demanded, how they responded to hardship and ease — and avoid those turnings.

Second, by making the way of the guilty clear, the Qur'an removes their excuse. When the arguments have been detailed and the guilty still reject them, it becomes evident that their rejection is not from lack of clarity but from obstinacy. Their path is exposed as a choice. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī explain that the exposition of signs serves to distinguish truth from falsehood so plainly that the guilty stand revealed.

Third, there is an implicit contrast. When the way of the guilty is clear, the way of the righteous is clear by contrast. Light is known by darkness; the straight road by the crooked. In the reading of some reciters, the verse reads *li-tastabīna sabīla al-mujrimīn* with the verb addressed to the Prophet ﷺ — "so that you [Muhammad] may clearly see the way of the guilty" — which gives the Prophet ﷺ discernment of who his real opponents are and what motivates them.

**The Value of Recognizing Error**

The verse teaches a principle that runs through Islamic learning: knowledge of falsehood is part of knowledge of truth. The scholars said, "I learned evil not for evil's sake, but to guard against it; for whoever does not know evil will fall into it." Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān said:

> "People used to ask the Messenger of God ﷺ about good, but I used to ask him about evil, fearing that it would reach me." (al-Bukhārī 3606; Muslim 1847)

The Qur'an details the signs so that the way of the guilty is clear; the believer studies it so that he recognizes the way of the guilty when he encounters it — in the arguments of deniers, in the temptations of his own soul, and in the pressures of society.

**Why Detail Is Necessary**

The verse's emphasis on detailing (*tafṣīl*) answers an objection sometimes raised against religious teaching: why so much repetition, so many arguments, so many angles on the same point? The verse answers: because clarity requires it. A single argument may be missed, misunderstood, or dismissed. Many arguments, approaching from every direction, leave no room for honest misunderstanding. The Qur'an says of itself:

> "˹It is˺ a Book whose verses are perfectly explained—a Quran in Arabic for people who know," (41:3)

> "We have surely set forth in this Quran every ˹kind of˺ lesson for people, but humankind is the most argumentative of all beings" (18:54)

The detailing is a mercy toward the sincere, who are given every help toward understanding, and a proof against the obstinate, who are left with no excuse.

**The Contrast with the Guilty's Method**

There is an implicit contrast between God's method and the method of the guilty. God details His signs — He explains, argues, provides evidence, invites reflection. The guilty do not argue; they mock (v. 5, v. 10), turn away (v. 4), demand impossible signs (v. 7–8, v. 37), call the truth fables (v. 25), and make noise to drown it out (41:26). The Qur'an's patient exposition stands against their refusal to engage. The verse thus vindicates the Qur'an's approach: where the guilty offer only denial, God offers detailed proof.

**Where This Verse Sits in the Sūrah**

The verse closes a section (vv. 33–54) largely devoted to the Prophet's ﷺ relationship with his people: his grief, the consolations, the definitions of his role, and the incident of the poor believers. It marks a transition to a new series of "Say" commands (vv. 56–66) in which the Prophet ﷺ will make his final, uncompromising declaration to the idolaters. Before that declaration, the verse states that everything preceding has been a detailed exposition designed to make the guilty's path unmistakable. The declarations that follow are addressed to people who have been shown everything and can no longer plead ignorance.

**Application**

For the reader, the verse invites gratitude for the Qur'an's method. God has not left the truth vague or the falsehood obscure; He has detailed both. The one who reads with attention will find that every form of denial has been anticipated and answered, and that every path of error has been marked. This is a gift. It means that no sincere seeker need be lost; the roads have been mapped, and the dangerous ones have been labeled. The verse asks only that one read the map — and, having seen the way of the guilty clearly, take the other road.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:56

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I have been forbidden to worship those you invoke besides Allah.” Say, “I will not follow your desires, for I then would certainly be astray and not one of those ˹rightly˺ guided.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Declaration of Non-Negotiable Separation**

After fifty-five verses of argument, consolation, and exposition, the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to make an unequivocal declaration: *qul innī nuhītu an aʿbuda alladhīna tadʿūna min dūni Allāh* — "Say: I have been forbidden to worship those whom you call upon besides God." There is no more room for the compromise the Makkans kept proposing. The Prophet ﷺ states his position as a matter of divine prohibition, not personal preference.

The passive verb *nuhītu* — "I have been forbidden" — is significant. The Prophet ﷺ does not say "I refuse" or "I choose not to"; he says he has been *forbidden*. The prohibition comes from God. This removes the matter from the realm of negotiation entirely. One can negotiate with a person's choices; one cannot negotiate with a command he has received from above. The Makkans were, in effect, asking him to disobey God, and he tells them plainly that this is what they are asking.

**"Those Whom You Call upon apart from God"**

The objects of the forbidden worship are described as *alladhīna tadʿūna min dūni Allāh* — "those you call upon besides God." The verb *daʿā* (to call upon, to invoke, to pray to) is the essence of worship in the Qur'an; the Prophet ﷺ said, "Supplication is worship" (Abū Dāwūd 1479; al-Tirmidhī 2969, graded ṣaḥīḥ). To call upon something is to worship it. The Makkans called upon their idols for rain, victory, children, and intercession. The Prophet ﷺ is forbidden from any share in this.

The phrase *min dūni Allāh* — "besides God," "apart from God," "to the exclusion of God" — is the Qur'an's standard expression for objects of worship that are set alongside or in place of God. It covers not only stone idols but anything called upon as a source of help independent of Him: angels, jinn, saints, ancestors, or celestial bodies.

**"I Will Not Follow Your Caprices"**

The second "Say": *qul lā attabiʿu ahwā'akum* — "Say: I will not follow your desires." The word *ahwā'* is the plural of *hawā*, which means inclination, passion, whim, caprice — the desire of the lower self unguided by revelation or reason. In the Qur'an, *hawā* is consistently the opposite of guidance:

> "Have you seen ˹O Prophet˺ the one who has taken their own desires as their god" (25:43)

> "And do not follow ˹your˺ desires or they will lead you astray from Allah" (38:26)

> "So if they fail to respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires" (28:50)

By calling the Makkans' religion *ahwā'*, the verse makes a diagnosis. Their idolatry was not based on revelation, proof, or reason; it was based on inherited whim — on what their fathers had done, on what suited their interests, on what their passions preferred. The plural form ("desires") points to the fragmented nature of such religion: each tribe, each clan, each person following his own inclination, with no unifying truth. This recalls the plural "darknesses" of verse 1.

The Qur'an repeatedly warns the Prophet ﷺ against following the desires of those who reject revelation (2:120, 145; 5:48–49; 6:150; 13:37; 42:15; 45:18). These warnings are not because he was inclined to do so, but because they establish the principle for his community: revelation, not human desire, is the measure of religion.

**"For Then I Would Have Gone Astray"**

The Prophet ﷺ gives the reason: *qad ḍalaltu idhan wa mā anā min al-muhtadīn* — "I would then have gone astray, and I would not be among the guided." The verb *ḍalla* means to lose the way, to wander from the path. The consequence of following human desire in religion is not a different but equally valid path; it is loss of the path altogether. The Prophet ﷺ states this of himself hypothetically: were he to follow their desires, he — even he — would be astray.

This is a striking admission of the universal principle. Guidance is not a personal possession that one retains regardless of conduct; it is a state of being on the right path, and one leaves that state the moment one follows desire instead of revelation. The Prophet ﷺ is on the path because he follows what is revealed to him (v. 50); he would leave it if he followed anything else. The same is true of everyone.

**The Structure of the Two Refusals**

The verse contains two refusals that correspond to two levels of compromise. The first refuses worship of their gods — the most direct form of compromise. The second refuses following their desires — a subtler form, in which one might not worship the idols outright but might accommodate the idolaters' preferences in how the religion is presented or practiced. The Makkans had offered both kinds of deal: "worship our gods for a year and we will worship yours" (the occasion of Sūrat al-Kāfirūn), and "soften your message about our gods and our fathers." The verse refuses both.

The two refusals are the foundation of religious integrity. A community that will not worship false gods but will bend its teaching to suit the desires of the powerful has failed the second test even if it passed the first. The verse requires both: no worship of what is called upon besides God, and no following of desires in the shaping of religion.

**Parallel Declarations**

The Qur'an contains several parallel declarations that the Prophet ﷺ was instructed to make:

> "I do not worship what you worship," (109:1–6)

> "If you are in doubt of my faith, then ˹know that˺ I do not worship those ˹idols˺ you worship instead of Allah" (10:104)

> "I have been forbidden to worship those ˹idols˺ you worship besides Allah, since clear proofs have come to me from my Lord" (40:66)

The last of these is almost identical to the present verse and adds the reason: "once the clear proofs have come to me." The prohibition is not arbitrary; it follows from the clarity of the evidence.

**The Courage of the Declaration**

It is worth remembering the circumstances. The Prophet ﷺ was in Makkah, a persecuted man with a small following, facing the united power of the Quraysh. They controlled the city, the trade, the sanctuary, and the social order. They had offered him wealth, leadership, and marriage into the noblest families if he would compromise. The declaration in this verse — "I have been forbidden... I will not follow your desires" — was made from a position of total worldly weakness. It required a certainty that came not from calculation but from knowing what God had commanded.

This is a model for every believer who faces pressure to compromise. The pressure may be social, professional, familial, or cultural. The verse teaches the response: state clearly what God has forbidden, decline to follow the desires of those who reject His guidance, and understand that any compromise is not a small adjustment but a step off the path.

**The Two Categories Named**

The verse ends by dividing humanity into two: those who have gone astray (*ḍāllūn*) and those who are guided (*muhtadūn*). These are the categories of al-Fātiḥah — "the path of those You have favored, not of those who have earned wrath nor of those who go astray." There is no third category of those who follow desires and are also guided. The one who follows revelation is guided; the one who follows desire is astray. The Prophet ﷺ places himself, by God's command, firmly in the first category, and declares that the only way to remain there is to refuse the second.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:57

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Indeed, I stand on a clear proof from my Lord—yet you have denied it. That ˹torment˺ you seek to hasten is not within my power. It is only Allah Who decides ˹its time˺. He declares the truth. And He is the Best of Judges.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"I Stand upon a Clear Proof from My Lord"**

Having declared what he refuses (v. 56), the Prophet ﷺ now declares what he stands on: *qul innī ʿalā bayyinatin min rabbī* — "Say: Indeed I am upon a clear proof from my Lord." The word *bayyinah* means a clear evidence, a manifest proof, something that makes a matter plain beyond doubt. The preposition *ʿalā* ("upon") pictures the proof as ground beneath the feet — the Prophet ﷺ is standing on solid evidence, not on inherited custom or personal preference.

This claim is made by several prophets in the Qur'an when confronting their peoples:

> "Consider if I stand on a clear proof from my Lord and He has blessed me with a mercy from Himself, which you fail to see" (11:28, Noah)

> "Consider if I stand on a clear proof from my Lord and He has blessed me with a mercy from Him" (11:63, Ṣāliḥ)

> "Consider if I stand on a clear proof from my Lord and He has blessed me with a good provision from Him" (11:88, Shuʿayb)

Al-Ṭabarī explains that the claim asserts the prophet's own certainty about the truth of what he brings. The Prophet ﷺ is not hesitant or unsure; he stands on clear proof — the revelation itself, its inimitable eloquence, its confirmation of earlier scriptures, its fulfilled predictions, and the evidences of God's Oneness in creation that it points to. The contrast with the "desires" of verse 56 is deliberate: they follow whim; he stands on proof.

**"And You Have Denied Him"**

*Wa kadhdhabtum bih* — "and you have denied it/Him." The pronoun may refer to the clear proof, to the Lord, or to the Qur'an; the commentators allow all three, and the meaning converges. The Makkans denied the proof, and in doing so denied the One who sent it. The verse places the two positions side by side: I stand on proof; you stand on denial. There is no middle ground, and the verse does not pretend there is.

**"That Which You Seek to Hasten Is Not within My Power"**

*Mā ʿindī mā tastaʿjilūna bih* — "I do not have that which you seek to hasten." The verb *istaʿjala* means to seek to hurry something, to demand it come quickly. The Makkans, in their mockery, demanded that the punishment the Prophet ﷺ warned of should come at once, if it was real. The Qur'an records this demand:

> "If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or overcome us with a painful punishment" (8:32)

> "When will this threat come to pass if what you say is true" (10:48)

> "And Allah will never fail in His promise" (22:47)

The demand was not sincere. It was a way of saying: "Your threats are empty; if they were real, prove it now." The Prophet ﷺ is instructed to answer: the punishment is not in my hands. I did not claim to control it; I claimed to warn of it. Its timing is God's decision. This continues the disclaimers of verse 50: he does not have the treasuries of God, does not know the unseen, is not an angel — and does not control the punishment.

**"Judgment Belongs to God Alone"**

*In al-ḥukmu illā lillāh* — "the judgment is not but for God." This is one of the Qur'an's most consequential phrases. The word *ḥukm* means judgment, decree, decision, rule, authority. The restrictive construction (*in... illā*) makes the statement exclusive: judgment belongs to God and to none other. In the immediate context, as al-Zamakhsharī notes, the judgment concerns when and whether the punishment falls — this is God's decision, not the Prophet's ﷺ and not the Makkans'. But the phrase has a general scope, and it became a foundational principle in Islamic thought: ultimate authority in law and decree belongs to God alone. The same phrase appears in the mouth of Joseph:

> "He has commanded that you worship none but Him" (12:40)

And later in this sūrah: "Should I seek a judge other than Allah while He is the One Who has revealed for you the Book ˹with the truth˺ perfectly explained" (6:114). The source commentary notes that this verse serves as a Qur'anic basis for the sovereignty of divine rather than human law — a principle that must be understood correctly. It does not mean that no human being may make any decision; the Prophet ﷺ and his successors judged between people constantly. It means that the ultimate source of legitimate law and authority is God, and that human judgment is legitimate only insofar as it accords with His.

The phrase was later misused by the Khārijites, who raised it against ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib when he accepted human arbitration. ʿAlī's response has become famous: 'A word of truth by which falsehood is intended.' The truth of the phrase is absolute; its misapplication to reject all human judgment was a distortion. Correctly understood, 'judgment belongs to God alone' means that God's decree governs all things, His law is the standard of right, and no human authority may override it — while human beings are still commanded to judge justly according to what He has revealed (4:58; 5:49).

**"He Relates the Truth"**

*Yaquṣṣu al-ḥaqq* — "He relates the truth." The verb *qaṣṣa* means to narrate, to relate, to follow a trace — it is the root of *qiṣaṣ*, stories. God relates the truth: in the Qur'an, He tells what is real about Himself, the world, past nations, and the future. His account is the true account. There is an alternative reading, noted by al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, and al-Zamakhsharī, in which the verb is *yaqḍī al-ḥaqq* — "He decrees the truth" — which fits the context of judgment. Both readings are sound; God both narrates what is true and decrees what is just.

**"And He Is the Best of Deciders"**

*Wa huwa khayru al-fāṣilīn* — "and He is the best of those who decide." The verb *faṣala* means to separate, to distinguish, to decide between — the same root as *tafṣīl* (detailing) in verse 55. A *fāṣil* is one who separates truth from falsehood and gives a decisive judgment between disputants. God is the best of such judges because His knowledge is complete, His justice is perfect, and His decision is final. Al-Ṭabarī explains that He will decide between the Prophet ﷺ and those who reject him, and between truth and falsehood, and His decision will be the right one.

The Qur'an uses parallel expressions:

> "He is the Best of Judges" (7:87; 10:109; 11:45)

> "Is Allah not the most just of all judges" (95:8)

**The Verse as a Whole**

The verse moves through a complete position statement. I stand on clear proof. You have denied. The punishment you mockingly demand is not mine to send. The decision is God's alone. He relates the truth and decides best. Each clause answers a Makkan objection: to their claim that he follows fancy, he says he stands on proof; to their mockery of the punishment, he says it is not his to hasten; to their implicit claim that they are the arbiters, he says judgment is God's; to any doubt about the outcome, he says God is the best of deciders.

**Living by "Judgment Belongs to God"**

For the believer, the phrase "judgment belongs to God alone" has a daily application that goes beyond questions of law and politics. It means accepting God's decree in one's own life — the timing of provision, the outcome of efforts, the length of trials — as the decision of the best of deciders. It means not demanding that God act on one's own schedule, as the Makkans demanded punishment on theirs. And it means submitting one's opinions and desires to what He has revealed, recognizing that His account is the true one even when it contradicts what one would prefer. The Prophet ﷺ modeled this: standing on clear proof, refusing compromise, and leaving every outcome to the judgment of God.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:58

> **Say ˹also˺, “If what you seek to hasten were within my power, the matter between us would have already been settled. But Allah knows the wrongdoers best.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Following the Thread from Verse 57**

Verse 57 stated that the punishment the Makkans mockingly demanded was "not within my power." Verse 58 develops this with a hypothetical: *qul law anna ʿindī mā tastaʿjilūna bihi la-quḍiya al-amru baynī wa baynakum* — "Say: If I had that which you seek to hasten, the matter would have been decided between me and you." The phrase "the matter would be decided" (*quḍiya al-amr*) is the same used in verse 8 regarding the sending of an angel: it means the affair would be concluded, the punishment would fall, and there would be no further respite.

The verse thus says two things at once. To the Makkans: you should be grateful that the punishment is not in my hands, because if it were, given your persistent denial and mockery, it would have fallen already. To the Prophet ﷺ and the believers: the delay is not because the Prophet ﷺ is weak or the threat empty, but because the matter is in God's hands and God's wisdom governs its timing.

**The Human Limit and the Divine Wisdom**

The commentators — al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī among them — explain the logic. A human being, however patient, has limits. The Prophet ﷺ had endured years of mockery, persecution of his followers, insults to his person, and rejection of the clearest proofs. Had the power of punishment been in human hands, even the most forbearing human would have used it by now. That it has not fallen is evidence that it rests with One whose patience exceeds any human's — One who "has prescribed mercy upon Himself" (v. 12) and who delays punishment so that people may repent.

This is a subtle answer to the Makkans' mockery. They said: if the punishment were real, it would have come. The verse says: it has not come *precisely because* it is real and is controlled by the Real Judge, whose wisdom you do not understand. Had it been controlled by a human — even by the Prophet ﷺ — you would have been destroyed. The delay is a mercy, and you are mocking the mercy that keeps you alive.

The Qur'an states this principle directly:

> "If Allah were to punish people ˹immediately˺ for what they have committed, He would not have left a single living being on earth" (35:45)

> "Your Lord is the All-Forgiving, Full of Mercy" (18:58)
