**The Prophet's Character Reflected**

There is also something revealing about the Prophet's ﷺ character in this verse. The verse does not say "if I had the power I would spare you"; it says "the matter would be decided." This is not vindictiveness. It is an honest acknowledgment that a human being confronting such obstinacy would bring the matter to its just conclusion. That the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to say this shows the completeness of his submission: he does not claim a patience greater than God's, nor does he pretend that the Makkans' conduct does not merit punishment. He simply states that the decision is not his — and in doing so, he implicitly commends the greater patience of the One whose it is.

At the same time, the Prophet's ﷺ actual conduct showed that his desire for the Makkans was mercy, not destruction. When the angel of the mountains offered to crush the people of Ṭā'if, he declined (al-Bukhārī 3231; Muslim 1795). When he conquered Makkah, he forgave the very people who had persecuted him. The verse states a hypothetical about power; the Prophet's ﷺ life showed that even had he possessed it, his inclination was toward forbearance.

**"And God Knows Best the Wrongdoers"**

The verse concludes: *wa Allāhu aʿlamu bi'l-ẓālimīn* — "and God knows best the wrongdoers." This is the fifth use of *ẓālim* in the passage (vv. 21, 33, 45, 47, and here). The phrase does several things.

First, it explains why God's timing is wiser than any human's would be. God knows the wrongdoers perfectly — He knows which of them will eventually repent and which will never repent, which will die in unbelief and which will embrace faith after years of opposition. He delays the punishment because He knows that among the wrongdoers are those who will turn. A human being, seeing only present conduct, would strike; God, seeing the whole trajectory, waits. Many of the Makkans who mocked in the year this verse was revealed became devout Muslims within a decade. Had the matter been "decided" then, they would have been lost.

Second, the phrase is a warning. God knows the wrongdoers — knows them by name, knows their deeds, knows their secret thoughts. The delay is not forgetfulness. When the term ends, the punishment will fall on exactly those who deserve it, and none will be missed.

Third, it identifies the Makkans by their category. The Prophet ﷺ has just said "between me and you"; the verse now names "you" as "the wrongdoers." They are not neutral skeptics; they are people committing *ẓulm* — placing things out of their rightful place, and above all placing partners alongside God.

**The Wisdom of Delay in Human Life**

The verse offers a lesson that extends beyond its context. Human beings often wish for immediate consequences — for wrongdoers to be punished at once, for justice to be swift and visible. When it is not, they doubt whether justice exists. The verse teaches that the delay of consequences is not the absence of justice but the operation of a wisdom greater than the human wish for immediacy. God knows who will change; He knows what purposes are served by the interval; He knows the full account of each person. The believer learns to trust this timing rather than demanding his own.

This is also a lesson about restraint for those who hold power. The Prophet ﷺ, had he possessed the power to punish, would have "decided the matter." That he did not possess it, and that God withheld the punishment, is presented as better. The lesson for anyone with power over others is that the ability to punish is not the same as the wisdom to know when punishment serves the good. The best of deciders (v. 57) delays; those with lesser knowledge should be even more cautious.

**The Balance of the Passage**

Verses 56–58 form a unit in which the Prophet ﷺ states his position with total clarity and total humility. Clarity: I am forbidden to worship your gods; I stand on clear proof; you have denied. Humility: the punishment is not mine; judgment is God's; if the matter were in my hands it would be decided, but it is not. The Prophet ﷺ claims everything for the truth and nothing for himself. This combination — uncompromising about the message, humble about one's own role — is the model for every believer who represents the truth to others.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:59

> **With Him are the keys of the unseen—no one knows them except Him. And He knows what is in the land and sea. Not even a leaf falls without His knowledge, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth or anything—green or dry—but is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**One of the Great Verses of Divine Knowledge**

This verse is among the most celebrated in the Qur'an. Al-Qurṭubī records a report that it was sent down with an escort of twelve thousand angels of its own, distinct from the angels who accompanied the sūrah as a whole. Whatever weight one gives that report, it reflects the reverence with which the early community regarded the verse. It is the most complete single statement in the Qur'an of God's knowledge — extending from the greatest hidden realities to the smallest visible particulars — and it follows naturally from verse 58's closing words: "God knows best the wrongdoers." How well does He know? The verse answers.

**"With Him Are the Keys of the Unseen"**

*Wa ʿindahu mafātiḥu al-ghayb* — "and with Him are the keys of the Unseen." The word *mafātiḥ* is the plural of *miftaḥ* (key) or *maftaḥ* (treasury, storehouse); the commentators read both meanings. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, and al-Zamakhsharī gloss it as the keys to the storehouses (*khazā'in*) of the Unseen — the treasuries from which all things are brought into being according to God's decree. The image is of locked chambers containing everything hidden — the future, the destinies of creatures, the secrets of hearts — and God alone holding the keys.

The word *ghayb* (Unseen) encompasses everything beyond ordinary human perception: God Himself, the angels, the future, the inner states of others, the time of death, the Hour, and the realities of the next world. This is the only verse in the Qur'an that speaks of the *keys* of the Unseen, though many verses affirm that God alone knows it (6:50; 10:20; 27:65).

The Prophet ﷺ explained the phrase in a well-known ḥadīth:

> "The keys of the Unseen are five, which none knows but God: none knows what will happen tomorrow but God; none knows what is in the wombs but God; none knows when it will rain but God; no soul knows in what land it will die; and none knows when the Hour will be established but God." Then he recited: "Indeed, God has knowledge of the Hour and sends down the rain and knows what is in the wombs. And no soul perceives what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul perceives in what land it will die. Indeed, God is Knowing and Aware." (31:34; al-Bukhārī 4627, 4697)

These five represent the categories of the Unseen most pressing to human beings: the future in general, the mystery of life's beginning, the sustenance on which life depends, the place of life's end, and the end of all things. Each is a key held by God alone. Modern science has extended human knowledge of some of these — weather forecasting, imaging of the womb — but not to the level of certain knowledge the ḥadīth denies to creatures; and the fundamental point, that the future and the decree are God's, stands untouched.

**"None Knows Them but He"**

*Lā yaʿlamuhā illā huwa* — "none knows them but He." The exclusive construction denies knowledge of the Unseen to every creature — every prophet, every angel, every jinn. What creatures know of it, they know only by God's disclosure:

> "˹He is the˺ Knower of the unseen, disclosing none of it to anyone," (72:26–27)

This verse is the scriptural basis for rejecting every claim to independent knowledge of the hidden: fortune-telling, astrology, divination, and any assertion that a saint or scholar knows the future by his own power. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Whoever goes to a fortune-teller and asks him about something and believes him, his prayer will not be accepted for forty days." (Muslim 2230)

The source commentary notes that the phrase *mafātiḥ al-ghayb* was adopted as the title of al-Rāzī's great commentary and of a work by Mullā Ṣadrā — in the sense of works that unlock difficult truths. The verse's own sense, however, is that the ultimate keys are with God alone.

**"And He Knows What Is on Land and Sea"**

Having affirmed God's knowledge of the Unseen, the verse turns to the seen: *wa yaʿlamu mā fi'l-barri wa'l-baḥr* — "and He knows what is on the land and in the sea." Land and sea together represent the whole visible earth. God's knowledge is not confined to hidden things; He knows every visible thing too — every creature on every continent, every fish in every ocean, every grain of sand and drop of water.

**"No Leaf Falls but That He Knows It"**

*Wa mā tasquṭu min waraqatin illā yaʿlamuhā* — "and not a leaf falls but that He knows it." This is the verse's most memorable image. Consider the number of trees on earth, the number of leaves on each, the number that fall in every moment across the planet. No human mind can begin to count them. God knows each one: when it falls, where it falls, why it falls, and where it comes to rest. The image was chosen because a falling leaf is the very type of the insignificant event — something no one notices, records, or cares about. If God knows this, He knows everything.

**"Nor Any Seed in the Dark Recesses of the Earth"**

*Wa lā ḥabbatin fī ẓulumāti al-arḍ* — "nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth." A leaf falls in the open, where at least it could in principle be seen. A seed buried in the earth is in total darkness — hidden from every eye, in a place no light reaches. God knows it: its location, its condition, whether it will sprout or rot. The phrase "darknesses of the earth" (using the plural *ẓulumāt*, as in verse 1) conveys the deepest possible concealment. Nothing is hidden by darkness from the One who made darkness.

**"Nor Anything Moist or Dry"**

*Wa lā raṭbin wa lā yābisin* — "nor anything moist nor dry." This pair is a merism — two opposites that together encompass everything. Every physical thing is either moist or dry; the pair thus covers all matter. The living and the dead, the growing and the withered, the fresh and the desiccated — all are known.

**"But That It Is in a Clear Book"**

*Illā fī kitābin mubīn* — "but that it is in a clear Book." All of this — the Unseen, the land and sea, every leaf, every seed, every moist and dry thing — is recorded. The commentators identify the "clear Book" as the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ*), in which God has written all things (85:22), or as an expression for God's knowledge itself (al-Zamakhsharī). The Qur'an connects God's knowledge with a written record in several places:

> "There is no activity you may be engaged in ˹O Prophet˺ or portion of the Quran you may be reciting, nor any deed you ˹all˺ may be doing except that We are a Witness over you while doing it" (10:61)

> "There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah" (11:6)

The image of the Book adds to the idea of knowledge the idea of permanence. God's knowledge is not fleeting awareness; it is fixed, recorded, and retrievable. Nothing is forgotten.

**The Theological Weight of the Verse**

The source commentary notes that this verse became a central proof text against the claim, made by some philosophers influenced by Aristotle, that God knows only universals — general categories — and not particulars. The verse could not be more explicit: God knows *this* leaf, *this* seed, *this* particular thing. Al-Ghazālī, in his critique of the philosophers, made this one of the three points on which he declared their position to be outside Islam. A God who knew only universals could not judge individuals, answer individual prayers, or be aware of individual suffering. The verse affirms a God who knows every particular — and this is the God to whom one can pray, before whom one will be judged, and by whom every deed is seen.

**Why This Knowledge Matters Practically**

Al-Ṭabarī draws the practical conclusion: if God knows every falling leaf, He certainly knows every human act, however small or hidden. This is the verse's function in context. The Makkans mocked, demanded punishment, and thought their deeds unobserved. The verse tells them that the One they mock knows the leaf and the seed; He knows them. And for the believer, the verse is the ground of a profound security: nothing he suffers goes unnoticed, nothing he does in secret goes unrecorded, and nothing that concerns him is outside the knowledge of the One who holds the keys.

The Prophet ﷺ taught the young Ibn ʿAbbās to live by this awareness:

> "Be mindful of God, and He will protect you. Be mindful of God, and you will find Him before you. If you ask, ask of God; if you seek help, seek help from God. Know that if the whole nation gathered to benefit you, they would not benefit you except with what God had written for you." (al-Tirmidhī 2516)

"What God had written" — the clear Book of this verse. To know that everything is written, and that the Writer knows every leaf, is to be freed from anxiety about what others can do and from the illusion that anything one does is hidden.

**The Reach from the Greatest to the Smallest**

Finally, notice the movement of the verse. It begins with the keys of the Unseen — the highest and most hidden realities. It descends to land and sea — the visible world. It descends further to a single leaf, then to a buried seed, then to any moist or dry thing. And it ends by gathering all of this into a Book. The structure conveys that there is no scale at which God's knowledge fails. From the destiny of the universe to the fall of a leaf in a forest no one will ever visit, everything is known, and known perfectly. This is what it means to say that the keys are with Him.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:60

> **He is the One Who calls back your souls by night and knows what you do by day, then revives you daily to complete your appointed term. To Him is your ˹ultimate˺ return, then He will inform you of what you used to do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Sleep as a Daily Death**

Verse 59 established the totality of God's knowledge. Verse 60 brings that knowledge to the most intimate level of human experience — the daily cycle of sleeping and waking — and finds in it a proof of resurrection. *Wa huwa alladhī yatawaffākum bi'l-layl* — "˹It is˺ Allah ˹Who˺ calls back the souls ˹of people˺ upon their death as well as ˹the souls˺ of the living during their sleep" The verb *tawaffā* is the standard Qur'anic verb for taking a soul at death (as in 39:42 and 32:11). Its use here for sleep is deliberate and instructive: sleep is a kind of death.

The commentators explain the likeness. In sleep, as in death, the outward senses cease to function; the limbs are still; awareness of the world departs. Al-Rāzī notes that only the inner life of the soul continues. The Qur'an makes the parallel explicit in another verse:

> "Then He keeps those for whom He has ordained death, and releases the others until ˹their˺ appointed time" (39:42)

This verse describes two kinds of "taking": the taking at death, from which there is no return to this world, and the taking in sleep, from which God releases the soul each morning. Both are His act. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to recognize this every night and morning:

> When he went to bed, he would say: "In Your name, O God, I die and I live." And when he woke, he would say: "Praise be to God who gave us life after He caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection." (al-Bukhārī 6312, 6324)

The morning prayer uses the word *nushūr* — resurrection — for waking. The Prophet ﷺ lived the analogy of this verse daily.

**"And He Knows What You Commit by Day"**

*Wa yaʿlamu mā jaraḥtum bi'l-nahār* — "and He knows what you earned by day." The verb *jaraḥa* literally means to wound; in usage it means to earn or acquire, particularly of deeds — perhaps because a deed leaves a mark, like a wound. God knows what each person does in his waking hours. This clause links verse 60 to verse 59: the One who knows every leaf knows every deed.

The pairing of night and day recalls verse 13 ("to Him belongs what dwells in the night and the day"). At night He takes the soul; by day He knows its actions. There is no hour in which a person is outside His governance or His knowledge.

**"Then by Day He Resurrects You"**

*Thumma yabʿathukum fīhi* — "then He raises you in it [the day]." The verb *baʿatha* is the standard verb for resurrection from the dead (as in *yawm al-baʿth*, the Day of Resurrection). Its use for waking completes the analogy: sleep is death, waking is resurrection. Every morning is a small resurrection, performed by God for every sleeper on earth.

**The Argument for Resurrection**

The analogy is not merely poetic; it is an argument. The Makkans denied resurrection, saying "there is nothing but our worldly life" (v. 29) and asking how bones and dust could be brought back. The verse answers: consider what you experience every night and every morning. Your consciousness is withdrawn; your body lies as if dead; and then consciousness is returned and you rise. The One who does this daily can certainly do it finally. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī draw exactly this conclusion: if God can suspend waking consciousness in sleep and restore it in the morning, He can suspend it permanently in death and restore it at the resurrection. The mechanism is the same; only the interval differs.

The Qur'an uses the same form of argument with rain and dead earth:

> "And it is Allah Who sends the winds, which then stir up ˹vapour, forming˺ clouds, and then We drive them to a lifeless land, giving life to the earth after its death" (35:9)

And with the sleepers of the Cave, whom God caused to sleep for three hundred years and then raised, "promise ˹of resurrection˺ is true and that there is no doubt about the Hour" (18:21). Sleep, rain, and the sleepers are all instances of God bringing what appeared dead back to life — rehearsals, within this world, of the resurrection the deniers reject.

**"That a Term Appointed May Be Fulfilled"**

*Li-yuqḍā ajalun musammā* — "so that a specified term may be fulfilled." The daily resurrection of waking continues until the appointed term — the lifespan decreed for each person — is completed. This echoes verse 2 ("then He decreed a term, and a term is appointed with Him"). Each morning God returns the soul for one more day toward the total He has fixed. When the term is complete, the taking in sleep becomes the taking in death, and there is no further waking in this world.

The source commentary notes that the Qur'an assigns an appointed term to individuals (7:34), communities (10:49), and all created phenomena (13:2; 31:29; 35:13). This is the doctrine of *qadar* — God's measuring out of all things, including their duration. Each waking is a reminder that the term is not yet complete; each sleep is a reminder that it might be.

**"Then unto Him Shall Be Your Return"**

*Thumma ilayhi marjiʿukum* — "then to Him is your return." After the term is fulfilled, after the final taking, comes the return to God. The verse traces the whole arc: sleep, waking, the appointed term, death, return. Nothing in the cycle happens outside God's control, and the cycle ends with Him.

**"And He Shall Inform You of That Which You Used to Do"**

*Thumma yunabbi'ukum bi-mā kuntum taʿmalūn* — "So whoever will be given their record in their right hand will read it ˹happily˺ and will not be wronged ˹even by the width of˺ the thread of a date stone" The verb *nabba'a* means to inform, to give news — from *naba'*, tidings of consequence. At the return, God will tell each person what he did. This is the account, the presentation of deeds. The Qur'an describes it in the form of a book placed in the hand (17:71; 69:19, 25) and in the form of the deeds themselves being brought forward (99:6–8). The phrase occurs in many verses (5:105; 9:94, 105; 10:23; 29:8; 31:15; 39:7; 62:8).

The connection to the verse's middle clause is precise. "He knows what you earn by day" — during life. "He will inform you of what you used to do" — after death. The knowledge accumulated in this life is disclosed in the next. Nothing done in the waking hours is lost; all of it is known, recorded, and reported back.

**The Spiritual Rhythm of Sleep and Waking**

The source commentary notes that the mystical commentators (Aj) saw in the cycle of sleeping and waking a figure for the alternation of spiritual states — contraction (*qabḍ*) and expansion (*basṭ*), withholding and giving — that characterizes the path to God. Every believer experiences times when God seems near and times when He seems distant, times of spiritual vitality and times of dryness. The verse suggests that both are His act, both are within His knowledge, and both are moving toward the return. Just as one does not despair at night because morning is coming, one need not despair in spiritual contraction because expansion follows.

**The Daily Practice the Verse Invites**

The verse turns two of the most ordinary human experiences — falling asleep and waking up — into occasions of remembrance. Falling asleep, the believer entrusts his soul to the One who takes it, knowing he may not receive it back. The Prophet ﷺ taught:

> "When you go to your bed, perform ablution as you would for prayer, then lie on your right side and say: 'O God, I have submitted my face to You, entrusted my affair to You, and sought refuge in You... If you die that night, you die upon the *fiṭrah*.'" (al-Bukhārī 247; Muslim 2710)

Waking, the believer thanks the One who returned it, knowing that the return is a new grant of time toward the appointed term. Between the two, he lives knowing that "He knows what you earn by day." The whole day is thus framed by awareness of God: surrendered to Him at night, received from Him in the morning, watched by Him in between.

A person who lives this way has, without any great effort, absorbed the verse's teaching about resurrection. He does not need to argue about whether bones can be reassembled; he has experienced, thousands of times, the return of consciousness to a body that lay as if dead. He knows the One who does this can do it once more.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:61

> **He reigns supreme over all of His creation, and sends recording-angels, watching over you. When death comes to any of you, Our angels take their soul, never neglecting this duty.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"He Is Dominant over His Servants"**

The verse opens with a repetition of the phrase from verse 18: *wa huwa al-qāhiru fawqa ʿibādih* — "Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Supreme" The name *al-Qāhir* comes from *qahara*, to overpower, to subdue, to have irresistible mastery. The intensive form *al-Qahhār* appears in six verses (12:39; 13:16; 14:48; 38:65; 39:4; 40:16). The phrase "above His servants" expresses transcendence and supremacy — God is not one power among others but the power over all.

The repetition of the phrase is not idle. In verse 18 it followed the statement that God alone removes harm and grants good (v. 17). Here it follows the statement that He takes souls in sleep and raises them by day (v. 60) and introduces the statement that He takes them in death. In both places, the phrase asserts that God's mastery over human beings is complete: their life, their consciousness, their death — all are in His grip. Al-Rāzī, commenting on the sequence of verses 59–61, describes the divine knowledge and power they express as an ocean without a shore: the mind that tries to encompass them finds no boundary.

**"And He Sends Guardians over You"**

*Wa yursilu ʿalaykum ḥafaẓah* — "and He sends over you guardians." The word *ḥafaẓah* is the plural of *ḥāfiẓ*, one who guards, preserves, keeps. These are angels, and the commentators identify two functions for them, both attested in the Qur'an.

First, they guard human beings from harm. The Qur'an says:

> "For each one there are successive angels before and behind, protecting them by Allah" (13:11)

Ibn ʿAbbās explained that these angels protect a person from what has not been decreed for him; when the decree comes, they withdraw. Every person is surrounded by unseen guardians who prevent countless harms of which he is never aware.

Second, they record human deeds. The Qur'an speaks of "noble recorders" (82:10–12) and describes two angels receiving every word:

> "As the two recording-angels— ˹one˺ sitting to the right, and ˹the other to˺ the left—note ˹everything˺," (50:17–18)

> "They know whatever you do" (82:10–12)

Al-Rāzī notes the tradition that there are two recording angels for each person, one for good deeds and one for bad. The word *ḥafaẓah* in this verse encompasses both the protecting and the recording function; both are forms of "keeping."

**Why Record What God Already Knows?**

A natural question, addressed by al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī: if God knows every leaf that falls (v. 59), why does He need angels to record human deeds? The answer is that the recording is not for God's benefit but for human beings'. First, knowing that one's deeds are being written by angels — beings who are present, observant, and incorruptible — is a powerful restraint on wrongdoing and a powerful encouragement to good. Second, on the Day of Judgment, the written record will be presented as evidence, so that no one can deny what he did (17:13–14; 18:49). The record establishes the justice of the verdict in a form even the accused must acknowledge. Third, the presence of the angels honors the human being: his life is worth recording, every word of it.

**"Till, When Death Comes unto One of You"**

*Ḥattā idhā jā'a aḥadakum al-mawt* — "until, when death comes to one of you." The guardians accompany a person throughout life. At its end, death comes — not as an accident but as an appointed event that "comes." Verse 60 spoke of the daily taking in sleep; this verse speaks of the final taking. The transition from guardianship to death is seamless: the same divine governance that watched over the person in life now brings his life to its end.

**"Our Messengers Take Him"**

*Tawaffathu rusulunā* — "Our messengers take him." Here "messengers" (*rusul*) refers to angels, as it does in 22:75 ("God chooses messengers from among the angels and from among the people"). The Qur'an elsewhere speaks of a single angel of death:

> "Then to your Lord you will ˹all˺ be returned" (32:11)

Tradition names this angel ʿIzrā'īl, though the name does not appear in the Qur'an or the most authentic ḥadīth. The plural here, "Our messengers," is reconciled by al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī with the singular in 32:11 by the explanation that the angel of death has assistants who act under his command. Together they extract the soul; he oversees the process. The Qur'an confirms that multiple angels are present at death, treating the righteous and the wicked differently:

> "Enter Paradise for what you used to do" (16:32)

> "If only you could see when the angels take the souls of the disbelievers, beating their faces and backs, ˹saying,˺" (8:50)

The Prophet ﷺ described the process in detail in the long ḥadīth of al-Barā' ibn ʿĀzib: the angels of mercy come to the believer with shrouds from Paradise, and the angel of death says, "O good soul, come out to forgiveness and pleasure from God," and the soul flows out like a drop from a waterskin; while the angels of punishment come to the disbeliever, and his soul is dragged out like a skewer through wet wool (Aḥmad 18534; Abū Dāwūd 4753).

**"And They Neglect Not Their Duty"**

*Wa hum lā yufarriṭūn* — "and they do not fall short." The verb *farraṭa* means to neglect, to be remiss, to fail in one's duty. The angels who take souls do not miss anyone, do not come early or late, do not take the wrong person, do not fail in any detail of their commission. Death arrives exactly when decreed, for exactly the person decreed, and the angels execute it perfectly.

The phrase carries a sobering implication. No one escapes. No fortress, no wealth, no medicine, no precaution delays the angels by a moment once the term is complete:

> "Wherever you may be, death will overcome you—even if you were in fortified towers" (4:78)

And it carries a reassuring implication. Death does not come by chance or error. The believer who fears an untimely or accidental death may rest in the knowledge that the angels do not fall short — they come only when God sends them.

**The Whole Span of Life in One Verse**

The verse encompasses a human life from its beginning to its end. God is master over the person (his existence is in God's hand). Guardians accompany him (his life is protected and recorded). Death comes (his term is fulfilled). Messengers take him (his soul is received). Nothing is neglected (the whole process is exact). Together with verse 60, which covered the daily cycle, and verse 62, which will describe the return to God, the passage gives a complete picture of the human being's situation: he lives, sleeps, wakes, is watched, dies, and returns, at every stage in the grip of the Dominant One.

**The Believer's Response**

How should one live in light of this verse? Ibn Kathīr and the early commentators draw the natural conclusion: with awareness that one is watched and recorded, and with preparation for the messengers who will come without fail. The Prophet ﷺ was asked which believers are the most intelligent, and he replied:

> "Those who remember death most often and are best prepared for what comes after it. Those are the intelligent ones." (Ibn Mājah 4259)

A person who knows that guardians record his every word will guard his words. A person who knows that the messengers will not be a moment late will not postpone repentance. And a person who knows that the One above him is the Dominant will not fear any power below Him. The verse describes reality; the believer aligns himself with it.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:62

> **Then they are ˹all˺ returned to Allah— their True Master. Judgment is His ˹alone˺. And He is the Swiftest Reckoner.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The End of the Journey**

Verse 61 ended with the angels taking the soul at death. Verse 62 describes what follows: *thumma ruddū ilā Allāhi mawlāhumu al-ḥaqq* — "then they are returned to God, their true Master." The verb *radda* means to return, to send back. The passive form — "they are returned" — emphasizes that this is not the soul's own movement but God's act: the soul is brought back to Him as a thing is brought back to its owner.

This is the destination toward which the entire passage (vv. 59–62) has been moving. God knows all things (v. 59). He takes souls in sleep and returns them (v. 60). He guards, records, and finally takes them in death (v. 61). And now the taken souls are brought back to Him for judgment (v. 62). The sequence traces the arc of every human life and ends where the Qur'an always ends: with the return to God.

**"Their True Master"**

The word *mawlā* is rich in meaning. From the root *w-l-y* (nearness, following, authority), it denotes a master, a protector, a patron, a lord — and, in other contexts, a client, a freed slave, or an ally. In relation to God, *mawlā* means the Master who owns, protects, and has authority over His servants. The Qur'an calls God the *mawlā* of the believers (2:286; 3:150; 8:40; 22:78; 47:11; 66:2).

The adjective *al-ḥaqq* — "the True," "the Real" — distinguishes God from every other claimant to mastery. Verse 61 called human beings God's "servants" (*ʿibād*); this verse calls God their "true Master." The point is pointed: the Makkans had taken idols as their masters, called upon them, and served them. Those were false masters, who could neither help nor harm. At death, every soul is returned not to the false masters it served but to the true Master who owned it all along. The idols vanish; the reality remains. The Qur'an says of the Day of Judgment:

> "Then and there every soul will face ˹the consequences of˺ what it had done" (10:30)

The verbal parallel with the present verse is exact, and the conclusion — "lost from them is whatever they used to invent" — makes explicit what this verse implies.

**"Surely Judgment Is His"**

*A-lā lahu al-ḥukm* — "Unquestionably, His is the judgment." The particle *a-lā* is an emphatic call to attention: take heed, know for certain. This is the second affirmation in the passage that judgment belongs to God (after v. 57, "judgment belongs to God alone"). There the phrase was spoken in the context of the Makkans' demand for punishment; here it is placed at the moment of the soul's return. When the soul stands before its true Master, the only judgment that matters is His. No advocate, no intercessor without His permission, no appeal to any other authority.

Al-Ṭabarī explains that on that Day, God alone will judge between His creatures, and none will share in His judgment. The Qur'an describes the Day as one when "˹It is˺ the Day no soul will be of ˹any˺ benefit to another whatsoever, for all authority on that Day belongs to Allah ˹entirely˺" (82:19) and when "True authority on that Day will belong ˹only˺ to the Most Compassionate" (25:26).

**"And He Is the Swiftest of Reckoners"**

*Wa huwa asraʿu al-ḥāsibīn* — "and He is the swiftest of those who take account." The word *ḥāsib* comes from *ḥasaba*, to count, to compute, to reckon — the root of *ḥisāb*, the accounting of deeds. God is the swiftest reckoner. The commentators explain the swiftness in several ways.

First, the reckoning is swift because God does not need to compute. He knows the total of every person's deeds already; the "reckoning" is the disclosure of a sum that has never been in doubt. A human accountant must add figures one by one; God knows the result instantly.

Second, the reckoning is swift because God reckons all creatures simultaneously. Billions of human beings and jinn, each with a lifetime of deeds, are all judged together, and the judgment of one does not delay the judgment of another. The Qur'an says God will bring all of them together in a single moment (36:53), and the commentators note that God reckons all creation in the time it takes to milk a ewe — or less.

Third, the reckoning is swift in that it is near. The Qur'an frequently pairs the swiftness of reckoning with its imminence: "Surely Allah is swift in reckoning" (2:202; 3:19, 199; 5:4; 13:41; 14:51; 24:39; 40:17). What seems distant to the heedless is, from God's perspective and in the scale of eternity, at hand. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "I and the Hour have been sent like these two" — and he held up his index and middle fingers together. (al-Bukhārī 6504; Muslim 2951)

**The Two Sides of the Divine Names**

The source commentary notes that the Qur'an describes God as both "the Swiftest Reckoner" (6:62) and "swift in punishment" (6:165; 7:167). It also describes Him as "Forgiving, Merciful" (as in the very same verse 6:165). The swiftness of His reckoning is a warning to the wrongdoer, who will not be able to delay or evade the account; and it is a comfort to the wronged, who will not have to wait indefinitely for justice. The same attribute functions differently depending on where one stands.

**The Logic of the Passage: vv. 59–62**

These four verses form one of the Qur'an's most complete meditations on God's relationship to the human being. Read together, they answer the question implied by the Makkans' mockery: who is this God whose punishment you demand and whose Messenger you reject? He is the One who holds the keys of the Unseen and knows every leaf. He is the One who takes your soul every night and returns it every morning. He is the Dominant One who guards you, records you, and will take you at death without fail. And He is the true Master to whom you will be returned for a judgment that is His alone and a reckoning that is swift. Against this, the idols are nothing, and the mockery is folly.

**The Practical Orientation**

For the believer, the verse answers the most basic question about direction. Where am I going? To God, my true Master. Who will judge me? He alone. How long until the account? Swiftly — sooner than I imagine. The answers reorder priorities. A person who knows he is returning to his true Master will not waste his loyalty on false ones. A person who knows the judgment is God's alone will not be paralyzed by the judgments of people, nor will he imagine that pleasing people is sufficient. And a person who knows the reckoning is swift will not postpone his preparation.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb used to say: "Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account, and weigh your deeds before they are weighed for you." This is the practical response to "He is the swiftest of reckoners": to reckon oneself now, while the account can still be corrected, before the swift reckoning that admits no correction.

**"True Master" as Consolation**

Finally, the phrase "their true Master" holds a consolation that the passage's severity might obscure. To be returned to one's true Master is to come home. For the soul that served God in life, the return is not to a stranger or a tyrant but to the One it loved and longed for. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him." (al-Bukhārī 6507; Muslim 2683)

The believer's death is a return to the true Master who guarded him, recorded his good deeds, and waited for him. The verse describes a judgment, but for those who prepared for it, the judgment is the meeting they hoped for.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:63

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who rescues you from the darkest times on land and at sea? He ˹alone˺ you call upon with humility, openly and secretly: “If You rescue us from this, we will be ever grateful.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Returning to the Argument from Distress**

After the sublime passage on divine knowledge and death (vv. 59–62), the sūrah returns to an argument it used in verses 40–41: the appeal to what human beings do when they are in real danger. *Qul man yunajjīkum min ẓulumāti al-barri wa'l-baḥr* — "Say: Who saves you from the darknesses of the land and the sea?" The question is rhetorical, and its answer is one the Makkans themselves knew.

**"The Darkness of Land and Sea"**

The plural *ẓulumāt* (darknesses) appears again, as in verses 1 and 59. Here it refers to the terrors of travel: being lost in the desert at night, without stars or landmarks; being caught at sea in a storm, in the darkness of night and cloud and towering waves. Al-Ṭabarī explains that "darknesses" here means the hardships and terrors of these situations, for the Arabs called any severe distress a darkness. Land and sea together cover the whole field of human travel and, by extension, of human vulnerability. The Makkans were traders; their caravans crossed the desert to Syria and Yemen, and their ships and those they traded with crossed the Red Sea. They knew these darknesses firsthand.

**"When You Call upon Him Humbly and in Secret"**

*Tadʿūnahu taḍarruʿan wa khufyah* — "you call upon Him humbly and secretly." The word *taḍarruʿ* denotes humble, abject supplication — the pleading of one who has no power and knows it; it was used in verses 42–43 of the humility God sought from the nations He tested. The word *khufyah* means secretly, quietly, in the privacy of the heart. In extreme danger, people call on God in both ways: aloud with tears and inwardly with a silent plea.

The pairing appears in a well-known command:

> "Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly" (7:55)

What the Qur'an commands as the manner of prayer, human beings do naturally when in peril. The verse points out that the idolaters, who in ordinary times invoked their idols, invoked God alone — humbly and inwardly — when the storm came. The Qur'an records this repeatedly:

> "But when He delivers you ˹safely˺ to shore, you turn away" (17:67)

> "But as soon as He delivers them ˹safely˺ to shore, they associate ˹others with Him once again˺" (29:65)

> "But when He delivers them ˹safely˺ to shore, only some become relatively grateful" (31:32)

**"If He Saves Us from This, We Shall Surely Be among the Thankful"**

The verse quotes the vow made in distress: *la-in anjānā min hādhihi la-nakūnanna min al-shākirīn* — "if He saves us from this, we will surely be among the grateful." The construction is a solemn oath, with emphatic particles (*la-in... la-nakūnanna*). In the moment of terror, the human being promises God everything: if You save me, I will be grateful, I will worship You alone, I will change my life. The vow is sincere at the moment it is made. The verse's implicit point — made explicit in the next verse — is what happens to it afterward.

Note that the vow is stated in the third person: "if *He* saves us." The commentators observe that the speakers are not addressing God directly but speaking to one another about Him — or that the verse reports the content of their plea. Either way, the object of the plea is unmistakably God — not Hubal, not al-Lāt, not al-ʿUzzā. In extremity, the idols are forgotten.

**The Argument's Force**

The argument is the same as in verses 40–41, and it deserves to be stated plainly. The idolaters claimed that their idols were worthy of worship alongside God. But their own behavior in crisis revealed what they actually believed: that only God could save them. When the danger was real, they did not divide their prayer among many gods; they called on One, humbly and inwardly, and vowed gratitude to Him alone. Their crisis-behavior was a confession of pure monotheism.

This is a form of argument that appeals not to premises the idolater might dispute but to his own conduct, which he cannot dispute. He has done this. He has been in the darkness of the sea and called on God alone. The verse asks him only to be consistent — to acknowledge in calm what he confessed in the storm.

**The Spiritual Function of Distress**

Al-Rāzī reflects on why God allows such distress. Distress strips away pretense. In ordinary times a person can maintain illusions about his own power, his gods, and his independence. In the storm, the illusions fail, and he discovers what he really knows: that he is helpless and that only God can save him. Distress is thus a teacher. It produces, in a few moments, the humility and sincerity that years of comfort fail to produce. The believer who understands this does not resent the darknesses of land and sea; he recognizes them as occasions when the heart is cleared of everything false and turned entirely to God.

The Prophet ﷺ taught his community a supplication for exactly such moments — the prayer of Jonah in the darkness of the whale:

> "The supplication of Dhū al-Nūn when he called from within the whale: 'There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers.' No Muslim ever supplicates with it for anything but that God answers him." (al-Tirmidhī 3505, graded ṣaḥīḥ)

Jonah's prayer is the model of the humble, secret call from darkness. It contains pure monotheism ("there is no god but You"), glorification, and confession of one's own fault. It is what verse 63 describes, spoken rightly.

**An Inner Reading**

The source commentary notes that mystical commentators (Aj) read the "darkness of the land" as the perils of the outward path — the Sharīʿah, where one may be lost in the letter of the law without its spirit — and the "darkness of the sea" as the perils of the inward path — the Ṭarīqah, where one may drown in states and experiences without the anchor of the law. In both, one is saved only by God. Whatever one makes of this reading, it captures a truth: the dangers of the spiritual life, like those of physical travel, are dangers from which only God delivers, and the traveler on either road must call on Him humbly and in secret.

**The Verse as a Mirror**

The verse invites the reader to remember his own darknesses — the illness, the accident, the moment of fear when everything else fell away and he called on God alone. It asks him what he vowed then and whether he kept it. The idolaters of Makkah are not the only ones who make promises in the storm and forget them on the shore. The verse holds up the moment of extremity as the moment of truth and asks that the rest of life be lived in its light.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:64

> **Say, “˹Only˺ Allah rescues you from this and any other distress, yet you associate others with Him ˹in worship˺.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer to the Question**

Verse 63 asked, "Who delivers you from the darkness of land and sea?" Verse 64 gives the answer the idolaters knew but would not state: *qul Allāhu yunajjīkum minhā wa min kulli karb* — "Say: God delivers you from it and from every distress." The Prophet ﷺ is instructed to answer the question himself, because the idolaters, though they know the answer, will not confess it in public. He speaks the truth their conduct has already admitted.

**"From This and from Every Distress"**

The verse extends the scope. Verse 63 spoke of the darkness of land and sea — specific perils of travel. Verse 64 says God delivers "from it and from every *karb*." The word *karb* means distress, grief, anguish — from a root meaning to tighten, to constrict, as grief constricts the chest. God is the deliverer not only from storms and desert but from every kind of affliction: illness, poverty, fear, sorrow, oppression, the anguish of the heart. The generalization is important. The idolaters might concede that God saves from the sea but imagine that lesser troubles were handled by lesser powers. The verse denies this. Every deliverance from every distress is His.

The Qur'an names God as the one who removes distress in several places:

> "Who responds to the distressed when they cry to Him, relieving ˹their˺ affliction, and ˹Who˺ makes you successors in the earth" (27:62)

> "And ˹remember˺ when Noah had cried out to Us earlier, so We responded to him and delivered him and his family from the great distress" (21:76)

> "We delivered him and his family from the great distress," (37:76, of Noah; 37:115, of Moses and Aaron)

The Prophet ﷺ taught a supplication for distress that names its source:

> "The words of distress: There is no god but God, the Magnificent, the Forbearing. There is no god but God, Lord of the mighty Throne. There is no god but God, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth and Lord of the noble Throne." (al-Bukhārī 6346; Muslim 2730)

Every clause of this supplication is a declaration of God's exclusive divinity. The remedy for distress is the confession that the idolaters make in the storm and abandon on the shore.

**"Yet You Ascribe Partners unto Him"**

*Thumma antum tushrikūn* — "then you associate [partners with Him]." The particle *thumma* ("then") marks the sequence and the shocking contrast. God delivers you; *then* you associate partners with Him. The very people who were saved from the storm by calling on God alone, and who vowed gratitude, return to their idols once the danger is past. This is the broken vow of verse 63.

The Qur'an describes this pattern with a consistency that suggests it is a permanent feature of human nature:

> "Whenever someone is touched by hardship, they cry out to Us, whether lying on their side, sitting, or standing" (10:12)

> "But when He delivers you ˹safely˺ to shore, you turn away" (17:67)

> "But as soon as He gives them a taste of His mercy, a group of them associates ˹others˺ with their Lord ˹in worship˺," (30:33)

The source commentary notes also 7:189–190, where a couple pray to God for a sound child and then, when it is granted, attribute partners to Him in what He has given. The pattern is the same: sincere monotheism in need, association in ease.

**The Anatomy of Ingratitude**

Why do human beings behave this way? The commentators and the Qur'an itself suggest several reasons. First, forgetfulness: the intensity of the crisis fades, and with it the intensity of the recognition it produced. Second, the return of the illusion of self-sufficiency: once safe, a person feels in control again and forgets that his safety was granted. Third, social pressure: on the shore, the idolater rejoins a community that worships idols, and its expectations reassert themselves. Fourth, the desire to avoid the implications: to acknowledge that God alone saved him would require him to abandon his idols, his ancestors' religion, and his social position — so he explains away the crisis-moment as panic rather than insight.

The verse addresses all of these by stating the matter plainly. *God* delivered you. Not your skill, not your luck, not your idols. And the deliverance was not limited to that crisis; He delivers from every distress. Your association of partners with Him is therefore not a reasonable position you hold in calm; it is a betrayal of what you knew in the storm.

**The Word "Associate"**

The verb *tushrikūn* (from *shirk*, to share, to associate) is the Qur'an's precise term for the idolaters' error. They did not deny God; they *shared* His rights with others. This verse shows why *shirk* is so grave. It is not an innocent theological mistake; it is ingratitude to the One who saves. The person who is rescued from drowning and then thanks a stone has not merely erred; he has wronged his rescuer. This is why the Qur'an calls *shirk* "Never associate ˹anything˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺, for associating ˹others with Him˺ is truly the worst of all wrongs" (31:13) and why God has said He will forgive anything but it (4:48, 116).

**Gratitude as the Test**

Verse 63 ended with the vow: "we will surely be among the thankful." Verse 64 shows the vow broken. The pair thus makes gratitude (*shukr*) the test of sincerity. Anyone can call on God in extremity. The question is whether one remains grateful — that is, remains monotheist, remains obedient, remains conscious of dependence — when the extremity passes. The Qur'an says that few pass this test:

> "˹Only˺ a few of My servants are ˹truly˺ grateful" (34:13)

The Prophet ﷺ modeled the alternative. When ʿĀ'ishah asked why he prayed until his feet swelled when God had forgiven him everything, he said:

> "Should I not be a grateful servant?" (al-Bukhārī 4837; Muslim 2820)

Gratitude was not, for him, a response to crisis but a permanent state — the fulfilment, in calm and in security, of the vow that others make only in the storm.

**Living the Verse**

The verse is a call to consistency. It asks the reader to identify the God he calls on when everything else fails, and to worship that God — and only that God — when everything is well. It asks him to remember his deliverances: the illness that passed, the danger averted, the grief that lifted. Each was from God. Each was from "every distress." And each obliges him to the gratitude he promised. The idolaters returned to their idols; the believer's task is to return, instead, to the One who saved him, and to keep returning, so that the vow of the storm becomes the practice of the shore.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:65

> **Say, “He ˹alone˺ has the power to unleash upon you a torment from above or below you or split you into ˹conflicting˺ factions and make you taste the violence of one another.” See how We vary the signs, so perhaps they will comprehend.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Deliverance to Warning**

Verse 64 declared that God delivers from every distress. Verse 65 states the corollary: the One who delivers is also the One who can afflict. *Qul huwa al-qādiru ʿalā an yabʿatha ʿalaykum ʿadhāban* — "Say: He is the Able One, to send upon you a punishment." The name *al-Qādir* (the Able, the Powerful) is placed with the definite article — He is *the* One with power. Those who forget Him after deliverance and return to their idols should remember that the same power that saved them can be turned against them.

**"From above You or from beneath Your Feet"**

*Min fawqikum aw min taḥti arjulikum* — "from above you or from beneath your feet." The verse names two directions of punishment. The commentators, including Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatādah as recorded by al-Ṭabarī, give examples of each from the history recounted in the Qur'an. From above: the flood that drowned Noah's people, the stones rained on Lot's people, the cry (*ṣayḥah*) that seized Thamūd, the wind that destroyed ʿĀd. From beneath: the earthquake that shook Midian, the swallowing of Qārūn and his house into the earth (28:81), the drowning of Pharaoh from beneath.

Some early authorities read the phrase in a second, social sense: "from above you" meaning from your rulers and elites, and "from beneath your feet" meaning from your slaves and the lower classes — that is, punishment through the tyranny of those above or the rebellion of those below. Both readings are recorded, and both express the same truth: punishment can come from any direction, and no direction is safe.

The Qur'an uses similar spatial language elsewhere:

> "And had they observed the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to them from their Lord, they would have been overwhelmed with provisions from above and below" (5:66)

> "Do you feel secure that the One Who is in heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you up as it quakes violently" (67:16–17)

**"Or to Confound You as Factions"**

*Aw yalbisakum shiyaʿan* — "or to confuse you into sects." The verb *labasa* means to mix, to confuse, to cover one thing with another — the root of the "confusion" in verse 9 (*la-labasnā ʿalayhim*) and verse 82 (*lam yalbisū*). *Shiyaʿ* is the plural of *shīʿah*, a faction, a party, a group of followers. The third form of punishment is internal: God may cause a people to fragment into hostile factions, each following its own leaders and hating the others.

This is a subtler punishment than fire from the sky, but the Qur'an treats it as no less severe. Division is a torment. It destroys trust, paralyzes cooperation, turns neighbors into enemies, and makes a community incapable of any common good. The Qur'an warns repeatedly against it:

> "And hold firmly to the rope of Allah and do not be divided" (3:103)

> "And do not be like those who split ˹into sects˺ and differed after clear proofs had come to them" (3:105)

> "˹like˺ those who have divided their faith and split into sects, each rejoicing in what they have" (30:32)

> "So We let hostility and enmity arise between them until the Day of Judgment, and soon Allah will inform them of all they have done" (5:14)

**"And Make You Taste the Might of One Another"**

*Wa yudhīqa baʿḍakum ba'sa baʿḍ* — "and make some of you taste the violence of others." *Ba's* means might, violence, the harm of war. This is the natural consequence of factionalism: civil war, in which a people becomes its own punisher. No external enemy is needed; God lets the factions destroy each other. Of all the punishments in the verse, this is the one that requires the least intervention and yet produces the most lasting harm.

**The Prophet's Prayer and Its Answer**

The most important report about this verse is one recorded by Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī from several chains. The Prophet ﷺ prayed for his community to be spared each of the three punishments named in the verse, and Gabriel informed him of the outcome:

> Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ reported that the Messenger of God ﷺ came one day from the heights of the city, and when he passed the mosque of Banū Muʿāwiyah, he entered and prayed two units, and we prayed with him. He supplicated to his Lord at length, then turned to us and said: "I asked my Lord for three things. He granted me two and refused me one. I asked my Lord not to destroy my community by famine, and He granted it to me. I asked Him not to destroy my community by drowning, and He granted it to me. And I asked Him not to make their violence be among themselves, and He refused me that." (Muslim 2890)

In the version Ibn Kathīr cites at this verse, when "from above you" was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said, "I seek refuge in Your face"; when "from beneath your feet" was revealed, he said, "I seek refuge in Your face"; and when "or to confound you as factions and make you taste the might of one another" was revealed, he said, "This is lighter" — or, in another version, he was told that this was not lifted from his community (al-Bukhārī 4628 records the first part of this).

The meaning is sobering. The Muslim community has been spared the collective annihilating punishments that destroyed earlier nations — no flood, no stones from the sky, no earthquake wiping out the whole *ummah*. But it has not been spared internal division and mutual violence. The history of the community, from the civil wars of the first century to the present, confirms this. The Prophet ﷺ foresaw it and warned of it:

> "When the sword is drawn among my community, it will not be lifted from them until the Day of Resurrection." (Abū Dāwūd 4252; al-Tirmidhī 2202)

And he foretold the multiplication of sects:

> "The Jews split into seventy-one sects, and the Christians into seventy-two, and my community will split into seventy-three sects, all of them in the Fire except one." They said, "Which is it, O Messenger of God?" He said, "That which I and my Companions are upon." (Abū Dāwūd 4596; al-Tirmidhī 2641)

**Division as Punishment, Difference as Mercy**

The source commentary is careful to distinguish between the sectarian division condemned in this verse and the legitimate diversity of scholarly opinion that Islamic tradition has honored. The report often quoted, "The difference of my community is a mercy," is not established as a ḥadīth, though its content — that legitimate differences of legal interpretation are a mercy and a facilitation — was affirmed by scholars such as al-Suyūṭī and reflected in the community's acceptance of multiple schools of law. The difference is clear: scholarly diversity on secondary questions, held with mutual respect and within shared fundamentals, is a mercy; factionalism that breaks the community into hostile parties, each anathematizing the others and shedding their blood, is the punishment of this verse.

**"Behold How We Vary the Signs"**

*Unẓur kayfa nuṣarrifu al-āyāt* — "look how We diversify the signs." The verb *ṣarrafa* means to turn about, to present in varied forms — the same verb as in verse 46. God presents His signs from many angles: creation, history, the daily cycle of sleep, deliverance from distress, and now the warning of punishment. Each is a different approach to the same truth.

**"That They May Understand"**

*Laʿallahum yafqahūn* — "that perhaps they may understand." The verb *faqiha* means to understand deeply, to grasp the inner meaning — the root of *fiqh*. The variety of signs is aimed at producing not mere acknowledgment but real comprehension. A person who understands this verse grasps that his safety from every direction — above, below, and within — is held by God alone, and that the deliverance he enjoys is a grant, not a right.

**The Verse in Muslim Self-Understanding**

Few verses have shaped Muslim reflection on their own history more than this one. The community has been spared the fate of ʿĀd and Thamūd; it has not been spared the fate of tearing itself apart. Every Muslim who laments the divisions of the *ummah* is lamenting the fulfilment of this verse's third clause and of the Prophet's ﷺ unanswered prayer. The response the verse calls for is not despair but understanding (*fiqh*): to recognize division as a punishment, to refuse to participate in it, to hold fast to the rope of God together, and to treat every brother in faith as someone whose blood, wealth, and honor are sacred — as the Prophet ﷺ declared in his final sermon.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:66

> **Still your people ˹O Prophet˺ have rejected this ˹Quran˺, although it is the truth. Say, “I am not a keeper over you.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Thy People Have Denied It"**

After the sequence of signs — divine knowledge, sleep and death, deliverance from distress, the warning of punishment — the verse records the response: *wa kadhdhaba bihi qawmuka* — "and your people have denied it." The object "it" refers to the Qur'an, or to the punishment just warned of, or to the whole of what the Prophet ﷺ has brought; the commentators allow each, and the meaning converges. Despite everything, the Quraysh have denied.

The phrase "your people" (*qawmuka*) is intimate and painful. These are not strangers; they are the Prophet's ﷺ own tribe, his kinsmen, the people among whom he grew up and who had called him al-Amīn, the Trustworthy. Their denial was a personal wound, as verse 33 acknowledged ("We know that what they say grieves you"). The verse names the denial without softening it.

**"Though It Is the Truth"**

*Wa huwa al-ḥaqq* — "and they deny what came afterwards, though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures" Three words that place the denial in its proper light. Their denial does not make the message doubtful; the message is the truth, and their denial is simply false. The Qur'an frequently affirms its own truth against those who reject it (2:91; 10:108; 13:1; 34:6; 47:2), and the affirmation here serves as consolation to the Prophet ﷺ: you are not the one in error.

The phrase also implies the gravity of their position. To deny what is false is harmless; to deny what is true is to set oneself against reality. The Quraysh were not rejecting an opinion; they were rejecting the truth about God, themselves, and their destiny. The consequences of such rejection do not depend on whether they acknowledged it.

**"Say: I Am Not a Guardian over You"**

*Qul lastu ʿalaykum bi-wakīl* — "Say: I am not over you a guardian." The word *wakīl* means one entrusted with the affairs of another — a guardian, a trustee, an agent responsible for outcomes. The Prophet ﷺ is instructed to disclaim this role. He is not responsible for making them believe, not accountable for their choice, and not empowered to compel them. His duty was to convey the message clearly; theirs is to respond; and God's is to judge.

This disclaimer appears in many verses addressed to the Prophet ﷺ:

> "Whoever obeys the Messenger has truly obeyed Allah" (4:80)

> "Indeed, there have come to you insights from your Lord" (6:104)

> "The truth has surely come to you from your Lord" (10:108)

> "Have you seen ˹O Prophet˺ the one who has taken their own desires as their god" (25:43)

> "Surely We have revealed to you the Book ˹O Prophet˺ with the truth for humanity" (39:41)

The repetition establishes a principle central to the Islamic understanding of prophethood and of religious responsibility generally. The Prophet ﷺ is a messenger, warner, and bringer of good news (v. 48). He is not a guardian who answers for the choices of others.

**Why This Disclaimer Matters**

The disclaimer serves several purposes. First, it relieves the Prophet ﷺ of a burden he could not bear. If he were responsible for the belief of his people, their denial would be his failure — and this thought was tormenting him, as verses 33–35 showed. The verse tells him: this is not your failure, because it was never your responsibility. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the Prophet's ﷺ task was to convey; the acceptance or rejection lay with the hearers and the outcome with God.

Second, it protects human freedom. If the Prophet ﷺ were a guardian with power to compel, faith would not be a choice, and the whole structure of moral responsibility would collapse. The Qur'an insists that faith must be freely chosen: "Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood" (2:256); "Whoever wills let them believe, and whoever wills let them disbelieve" (18:29). The Prophet's ﷺ role as conveyor, not guardian, is the precondition of this freedom.

Third, it places the Prophet ﷺ correctly in relation to God. God alone is *al-Wakīl* — the Trustee over all things (3:173; 4:81; 6:102; 11:12; 33:3, 48; 39:62). No creature shares this role. For the Prophet ﷺ to claim guardianship over people's hearts would be to claim a divine prerogative. His disclaimer is an act of *tawḥīd*.

**The Distinction between Conveying and Compelling**

The verse draws the line that every teacher, parent, preacher, and reformer must learn. One is responsible for conveying the truth clearly, sincerely, and completely. One is not responsible for whether it is accepted. The Qur'an states this to the Prophet ﷺ directly:

> "But if they turn away, then your duty ˹O Prophet˺ is only to deliver ˹the message˺ clearly" (16:82)

> "Whether We show you ˹O Prophet˺ some of what We threaten them with, or cause you to die ˹before that˺, your duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺" (13:40)

> "If you persist in denial, so did ˹many˺ communities before you" (29:18)

Understanding this distinction is a matter of both psychological health and theological correctness. Psychologically, the person who believes he is responsible for others' choices will be crushed by their refusals, will resort to pressure and manipulation, or will give up entirely. The person who understands that his responsibility ends with clear conveyance can persist patiently, without despair and without coercion. Theologically, the belief that one can or must control others' faith usurps God's role and denies human freedom.

**Not an Excuse for Indifference**

The disclaimer must not be misread. "Now, perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death over their denial, if they ˹continue to˺ disbelieve in this message" does not mean "Are those whose evil-doing is made so appealing to them that they deem it good ˹like those who are rightly guided˺" The Prophet ﷺ cared intensely — so intensely that God had to restrain his grief (18:6; 26:3; 35:8). The disclaimer concerns responsibility and power, not concern. One may — must — care deeply about others' guidance while recognizing that one cannot produce it. The combination of intense care and clear recognition of one's limits is the prophetic model. Indifference and coercion are the two failures it avoids.

**The Verse's Place in the Passage**

Verses 56–67 form a series of "Say" commands in which the Prophet ﷺ states his position with finality: I will not worship your gods; I stand on clear proof; judgment is God's; He knows all; He takes you in sleep and death; He delivers you and can punish you. Verse 66 records that his people denied all this, affirms that it was the truth regardless, and closes with the Prophet ﷺ stepping back from any claim to control the outcome. He has said what he was sent to say. The rest is between them and God. Verse 67 will add the final word: every tiding has its appointed time, and they will come to know.

**The Consolation within the Verse**

Beneath its apparent severity, the verse is a mercy to the Prophet ﷺ. It acknowledges his pain ("your people have denied"), affirms his rightness ("it is the truth"), and lifts from his shoulders a weight he was never meant to carry ("you are not a guardian over them"). Every sincere caller to God who has watched loved ones refuse the truth knows this pain and needs this consolation. The verse offers it: convey, care, pray — and leave the outcome to the One who alone is Guardian.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:67

> **Every ˹destined˺ matter has a ˹set˺ time to transpire. And you will soon come to know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Short Verse with a Long Reach**

Verse 67 is brief, but it closes the entire section that began with verse 56 and leaves the deniers with a statement that answers every one of their demands and mockeries. *Li-kulli naba'in mustaqarr* — "for every tiding there is a settled place." The word *naba'* means news, tidings — specifically news of weight and consequence, not trivial information (it is the root of *nabī*, prophet, the one who brings momentous news). The word *mustaqarr* means a place or time of settling, of coming to rest, of being established — from *qarra*, to settle, to be fixed. Verse 98 will use the same word for the human being's "place of settlement."

**"For Every Tiding There Is a Fixed Setting"**

The meaning, as al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr explain, is that every piece of news the Qur'an conveys — every promise, every threat, every prediction — has an appointed time and place at which it will be realized. The news of the punishment has a fixed time. The news of the Prophet's ﷺ victory has a fixed time. The news of the resurrection has a fixed time. None of them is empty; each is settled and will arrive when its moment comes.

This answers the Makkans' central mockery. They said: you warn us of punishment, but it does not come; you speak of resurrection, but we see no sign of it; where is what you promise? The verse replies: every tiding has its settled time. The absence of the event now is not evidence that it will not occur; it is evidence only that its time has not yet come. The Qur'an says the same in different words:

> "term. When their" (7:34)

> "And Allah will never fail in His promise" (22:47)

> "So do not be in haste against them, for indeed We are ˹closely˺ counting down their days" (19:84)

**The Principle of Appointed Times**

The verse states in general form a principle the sūrah has stated in several specific forms: the appointed term of life (v. 2), the appointed term of nations (v. 6), the appointed term fulfilled by daily waking (v. 60), and the timing of punishment held by God alone (vv. 57–58). The world runs on God's schedule, not on the deniers' demands. Everything He has announced will occur at exactly the moment He has fixed — not a moment sooner, to satisfy the mockers' challenge, and not a moment later, to let them escape.

This principle has an important implication for understanding prophecy generally. The truth of a prophetic announcement is not tested by its immediate fulfilment but by its fulfilment at the appointed time. The Prophet ﷺ announced things that came true within months (the Muslims' victory at Badr), within years (the conquest of Makkah), within decades (the fall of Persia and Byzantium), within centuries (the spread of Islam to the ends of the earth), and things that remain future (the signs of the Hour). Each had, and has, its *mustaqarr*.

**"And Soon You Shall Know"**

*Wa sawfa taʿlamūn* — "and you will come to know." The particle *sawfa* indicates the future, often with a sense of certainty and sometimes of threat. The verb "know" is stated without an object, which broadens it: you will know the truth of what you denied, the reality of the punishment you mocked, the certainty of the resurrection you dismissed, and the error of the position you took.

The phrase is a recurring Qur'anic close to arguments with deniers:

> "˹But˺ soon they will know, when they face the punishment, who is far astray from the ˹Right˺ Way" (25:42)

> "Each ˹of us˺ is waiting, so keep waiting" (20:135)

> "So enjoy yourselves, for soon you will know." (16:55; 30:34)

> "You will soon come to know" (102:3–4)

The tone is not vindictive but certain. The verse does not describe the Prophet ﷺ threatening; it describes reality informing. Knowledge will come — through the events of history, through death, and through resurrection — and when it comes, the question of who was right will no longer be a matter of debate.

**The Verse as the Prophet's Rest**

Verse 66 told the Prophet ﷺ that he was not a guardian over his people. Verse 67 tells him what he can rest on: the outcome is fixed and certain. He need not force the issue, need not answer every taunt, need not despair when the punishment does not arrive on the mockers' timetable. Every tiding has its settled place. His task was to convey it; its fulfilment is guaranteed by the One who sent it. This is a profound source of calm for anyone who represents truth in a hostile environment: the truth does not need to be defended by anxiety; it needs only to be stated, and time will vindicate it.

**The Verse and the Sūrah's Fulfilment**

The source commentary notes that the phrase "for every tiding there is a fixed setting" was fulfilled with respect to the Makkans themselves within a few years. Those who mocked the warning of punishment tasted it at Badr, where the chiefs of Quraysh — Abū Jahl, ʿUtbah, Shaybah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf — were killed. Those who lived saw the Prophet ﷺ enter Makkah in triumph and stand at the Kaʿbah as the idols were toppled. They came to know. And the greater knowing — at death and resurrection — awaits all who deny, as the verse promised.

**Application: Patience and Certainty**

For the believer, the verse teaches two things. First, patience with the timing of God's promises. One does not know when a given tiding will be fulfilled, but one knows that it has a settled place. Prayers are answered at the appointed time; relief comes at the appointed time; justice is done at the appointed time. The believer's part is not to hasten but to trust.

Second, the certainty that one will know. Everything now debated, disputed, doubted, or denied will become known — not as opinion but as experienced fact. The believer lives now in the light of what he will know then. He arranges his life around the tidings whose fulfilment is settled, rather than around the passing appearances that the deniers mistake for permanent reality. "Soon you shall know" is, for him, not a threat but a promise: what he believed on the basis of evidence he will one day see with his eyes, and the seeing will confirm the believing.

**Closing the Section**

With this verse the great series of "Say" commands (vv. 56–67) comes to rest. The Prophet ﷺ has declared his refusal of idolatry, his standing on clear proof, God's exclusive judgment, God's total knowledge, God's power over life and death, His deliverance and His power to punish, the denial of his people, his own limited role, and now the certainty of the outcome. Nothing remains to be said to the obstinate. The next verse turns from what to say to them to how to conduct oneself around them: when they mock the signs, turn away until they change the subject.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:68

> **And when you come across those who ridicule Our revelations, do not sit with them unless they engage in a different topic. Should Satan make you forget, then once you remember, do not ˹continue to˺ sit with the wrongdoing people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Speech to Conduct**

The preceding verses instructed the Prophet ﷺ in what to *say* to the deniers. This verse instructs him in how to *behave* around them when they turn to mockery. *Wa idhā ra'ayta alladhīna yakhūḍūna fī āyātinā* — "and when you see those who plunge into [vain talk about] Our signs." The shift from declaration to conduct is natural: once everything has been said and the response is derision, the remaining question is how to preserve one's dignity and one's faith in the presence of those who scoff.

**The Verb *Khāḍa***

The verb *khāḍa* literally means to wade into water, to plunge in. Applied to speech, it means to plunge into a subject recklessly, to engage in idle, mocking, or irreverent talk — to splash about in a matter without seriousness or respect. Al-Rāzī is precise on this point: *khawḍ* means talk that is disrespectful and disparaging, not sincere inquiry. The verse is not forbidding discussion of the Qur'an, nor honest questions, nor scholarly debate about its meaning; it is forbidding participation in sessions where the signs of God are mocked, ridiculed, and treated as a game. The Qur'an uses the same verb for the idle talk of those in Hell, who confess: "We used to indulge ˹in falsehood˺ along with others," (74:45), and for the deniers who "play" (*yalʿabūn*) in their vain talk (6:91; 9:65; 43:83; 52:12; 70:42).

The Makkan setting was concrete. The Quraysh held gatherings in which they mocked the Qur'an, invented objections to it, ridiculed the resurrection, and made sport of the Prophet ﷺ and his followers. When he passed such a gathering, or found himself in one, what should he do?

**"Turn Away from Them till They Engage in Other Discourse"**

*Fa-aʿriḍ ʿanhum ḥattā yakhūḍū fī ḥadīthin ghayrih* — "then turn away from them until they plunge into some other talk." The instruction is measured. It does not say "fight them," "curse them," or "never speak to them again." It says turn away — withdraw from the conversation, leave the gathering, or at minimum disengage — *until* the subject changes. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that once they move to another topic, one may rejoin them. The prohibition is not against the people as such but against sitting through the mockery.

The wisdom is several-fold. First, sitting silently through mockery of God's signs implies acquiescence and lends the mockery an audience. Second, the believer's presence exposes him to the corrosive effect of ridicule, which weakens faith by degrees even when it does not persuade. Third, remaining in such a session compromises the believer's dignity: he becomes a spectator to the derision of what he holds most sacred. Fourth, withdrawal is itself a form of protest — a silent testimony that this speech is unacceptable.

The Qur'an gives the same instruction in Madīnah, and extends it to all believers:

> "He has already revealed to you in the Book that when you hear Allah" (4:140)

The Madinan verse adds the reason: "you would then be like them." Voluntary participation in a gathering of mockery makes one a party to it.

**"And If Satan Should Cause Thee to Forget"**

*Wa immā yunsiyannaka al-shayṭān* — "But Satan made him forget to mention Joseph to his master, so he remained in prison for several years" The verse anticipates that one may forget the instruction — may find oneself in such a gathering without realizing it, or may be drawn into a conversation that turns to mockery without noticing the shift. Forgetting is attributed to Satan, as elsewhere in the Qur'an: the companion of Joseph in prison forgot to mention him to the king because "Satan made him forget" (12:42), and the hypocrites are those whom "Satan has taken hold of them, causing them to forget the remembrance of Allah" (58:19).

That the verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ and speaks of Satan making him forget raised questions for some commentators, since the Prophet ﷺ was protected from Satan's dominion. The resolutions offered are that the address, though grammatically to the Prophet ﷺ, is meant for his community; or that forgetting is a natural human incident that Satan may exploit without exercising any real power over the Prophet ﷺ; or that even prophets may be subject to the attempt at whispering, which God then effaces, as in 22:52. What is clear is the practical rule: forgetting is excused, but the moment one remembers, one must act.

**"Then Once Thou Hast Remembered, Sit Not"**

*Fa-lā taqʿud baʿda al-dhikrā maʿa al-qawmi al-ẓālimīn* — "then do not sit, after the remembrance, with the wrongdoing people." The instruction is precise: the obligation begins at the moment of remembering. Before that, there is no blame, for God does not hold anyone responsible for what he forgets; the Prophet ﷺ said, "God has excused my community for mistake, forgetfulness, and what they are coerced into" (Ibn Mājah 2045). After remembering, however, remaining seated is a choice, and the choice must be to leave.

The mockers are named "the wrongdoing people" (*al-qawm al-ẓālimīn*) — the sixth use of the root in this stretch of the sūrah. Mocking God's signs is a form of *ẓulm*: placing what deserves reverence in the position of a joke.
