**Does the Verse Apply to Believers Too?**

Al-Ṭabarī records reports connecting this verse to the factions mentioned in verse 65, and concluding that the warning applies not only to idolaters but to believers who engage in fruitless and divisive wrangling about religion. On this reading, a believer should also withdraw from Muslim gatherings in which religion is treated as a subject for point-scoring, mockery of other Muslims, or contentious dispute for its own sake. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "No people went astray after having been guided except that they were given to disputation." Then he recited: "They did not present it to you except for argument. But they are a people prone to dispute." (43:58; al-Tirmidhī 3253)

And he promised:

> "I guarantee a house in the outskirts of Paradise for one who leaves off arguing even when he is in the right." (Abū Dāwūd 4800)

**Not a Prohibition on Thought**

As al-Rāzī stresses, this verse has sometimes been misused to forbid all discussion of religious questions and to require a purely literal, unreflective approach to scripture. This is a misreading. The Qur'an constantly commands reflection (*tadabbur*, *tafakkur*) on its verses and on creation, invites questions, and models argument. What the verse forbids is *khawḍ* — disrespectful plunging, mockery, irreverent play. The distinction between sincere inquiry and mocking talk is usually obvious from tone and intention, and the believer is expected to recognize it.

**Contemporary Forms of the Gathering**

The gatherings of the Quraysh have modern equivalents that make this verse more relevant, not less. Media, online forums, comment threads, entertainment, and social circles routinely host mockery of religion, of God, of prophets, and of sacred things — sometimes as deliberate provocation, more often as casual background noise. The verse's rule applies: one is not required to police the world, but one is required not to sit as a willing audience to derision of what one holds sacred. "Turn away until they change the subject" translates, in the digital age, to closing the tab, leaving the thread, changing the channel, or steering the conversation — and, when one forgets and finds oneself absorbed, leaving as soon as one remembers.

**Dignity without Aggression**

Finally, the verse models a posture that is neither aggressive nor servile. The believer does not attack the mockers, but neither does he flatter them by staying. He withdraws with dignity and returns when the talk is decent. This posture preserved the Prophet's ﷺ standing in Makkah and preserved his followers' faith; it remains the right posture wherever the signs of God are treated with contempt.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:69

> **Those mindful ˹of Allah˺ will not be accountable for those ˹who ridicule it˺ whatsoever—their duty is to advise, so perhaps the ridiculers will abstain.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question the Verse Answers**

Verse 68 commanded withdrawal from gatherings where God's signs are mocked. A question naturally arises: if a believer does find himself among such people — before he remembers, or because circumstances require it — does he share in their guilt? Will the reckoning of the mockers fall on him by association? Verse 69 answers: *wa mā ʿalā alladhīna yattaqūna min ḥisābihim min shay'* — "and nothing of their reckoning is upon those who are God-fearing."

**"Their Reckoning Falls Not upon Those Who Are Reverent"**

The word *ḥisāb* (reckoning, account) refers to the accounting of the mockers' deeds on the Day of Judgment. The verse says that no part of it — *min shay'*, "anything at all" — falls on the *muttaqīn*, those who guard themselves against God's displeasure. Each is accountable for himself. This is a restatement of the principle already given in verse 52 concerning the poor believers ("nothing of their account is upon you, and nothing of your account is upon them") and stated as a general law throughout the Qur'an:

> "No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another" (6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38)

Al-Ṭabarī explains that the verse reassures the believers who have been near such gatherings: they are not judged for what others said. If they withdrew as commanded, or if they were present only until they remembered, no share of the mockers' sin attaches to them. This relieves the anxiety that a sensitive conscience might feel about having been in the company of wrongdoers.

**The Reports on the Occasion**

Some early commentators record that when 4:140 or this verse's instruction became known, some Muslims said: "If we withdraw every time they mock, we will never be able to sit in the Sacred Mosque or perform circumambulation, for they mock everywhere." Ibn ʿAbbās and others explained that this verse came as an accommodation: the believers were not held accountable for the mockers' talk, provided they remained conscious of God and did what they could — including admonishing the mockers. The verse thus balances verse 68's strictness with a recognition of the believers' constrained situation in Makkah.

**"But a Reminder"**

*Wa lākin dhikrā* — "but a reminder." The clause is elliptical, and the commentators supply the sense: but upon the believers is [the duty of] reminding; or, but [the believers should offer] a reminder. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that the believers should not merely leave the mockers but should also express their disapproval and admonish them — remind them of God, of the seriousness of what they mock, and of the consequences. Withdrawal alone is passive; the verse adds an active duty.

This is the balance the Qur'an consistently strikes. Verse 68 said turn away; verse 69 says but remind. The believer is not to be complicit, but neither is he to be silent when a word might help. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Whoever among you sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then with his heart — and that is the weakest of faith." (Muslim 49)

Withdrawal is the disapproval of the heart made visible; reminding is the correction of the tongue. In Makkah, correction by the hand was not possible; the verse commands what was.

**"That They Might Be Reverent"**

*Laʿallahum yattaqūn* — "that perhaps they may become God-fearing." The purpose of the reminder is reforming the mockers. The believer reminds not to score points or vent frustration but in the hope that the mockers will come to *taqwā*. This hope is not naïve; many of the Quraysh who mocked the Qur'an in the early years became its most devoted servants later. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Khālid ibn al-Walīd, ʿIkrimah ibn Abī Jahl, and Abū Sufyān all mocked before they believed. The reminder that seemed futile at the time was a seed that later bore fruit.

The verse uses the same verb for the believers ("those who are reverent," *yattaqūn*) and for the hoped-for state of the mockers ("that they may be reverent," *yattaqūn*). The believers already possess what the mockers lack; the reminder is the means by which what one group has may reach the other. This is the essence of *daʿwah*: not condemnation from a height but the extension of a good one possesses to those who do not yet have it.

**The Structure of Verses 68–69**

Read together, the two verses form a complete guide to conduct among those who mock religion. Withdraw from the mockery (68a). If you forget and find yourself present, leave as soon as you remember (68b). Do not fear that their sin will attach to you if you are God-conscious (69a). But do not merely leave — remind them (69b), in the hope that they may change (69c). The sequence moves from self-protection to reassurance to active good, and it anticipates every question a conscientious believer might raise.

**Taqwā as the Protective Condition**

The verse's protection is conditioned on *taqwā*. It is "those who are reverent" who bear nothing of the mockers' account. *Taqwā* is what distinguishes the believer who finds himself in a hostile gathering from the mocker beside him: the same room, the same conversation, but one heart guarding itself against God's displeasure and the other reveling in ridicule. The external situation is shared; the internal state is not; and it is the internal state that determines the account. This is why the Qur'an insists that God "You love them but they do not love you, and you believe in all Scriptures" (3:119; 5:7) — the reckoning follows the heart, not the seating arrangement.

At the same time, *taqwā* is not merely an inner feeling; it manifests in conduct. The person of *taqwā* will, in fact, withdraw when he remembers, and will, in fact, remind when he can. The verse's protection belongs to those whose God-consciousness produces the behavior verse 68 commanded, not to those who claim inner disapproval while remaining comfortable spectators.

**Application to Mixed Environments**

Few believers today live in purely Muslim environments. Workplaces, schools, families, and public spaces bring them into constant contact with people who may mock or dismiss what they hold sacred. This verse frees them from two errors. The first error is scrupulous withdrawal from all such environments, out of fear that mere proximity to wrongdoers stains one's own record; the verse says it does not, if one is God-conscious and does what is required. The second error is silent complicity — sitting through everything, saying nothing, and calling it tolerance; the verse commands a reminder. Between the two lies the prophetic path: presence with integrity, withdrawal from active mockery, and a word of reminder offered in hope.

**The Hope at the End**

The verse ends not with a threat but with a hope: "that they might be reverent." This is characteristic of the Qur'an's treatment of even its harshest opponents. The door is left open. The reminder is offered. The possibility of *taqwā* is affirmed even for those who currently mock. The believer who remembers this will remind with gentleness rather than contempt, because he is not pronouncing a verdict but extending an invitation.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:70

> **And leave those who take this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere play and amusement and are deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life. Yet remind them by this ˹Quran˺, so no one should be ruined for their misdeeds. They will have no protector or intercessor other than Allah. Even if they were to offer every ˹possible˺ ransom, none will be accepted from them. Those are the ones who will be ruined for their misdeeds. They will have a boiling drink and painful punishment for their disbelief.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Widening the Circle**

Verse 68 concerned those who mock the signs of God in conversation. Verse 70 widens the instruction to a broader category: *wa dhari alladhīna ittakhadhū dīnahum laʿiban wa lahwan* — "and leave those who have taken their religion as play and diversion." The command *dhar* ("leave," "let be") is the same used in verse 91 ("leave them to play at their vain discourse") and elsewhere. It means to disengage, not to pursue them, not to wear oneself out over them — while, as the verse goes on to say, still reminding them.

**"Who Take Their Religion to Be Play and Diversion"**

The pair *laʿib* and *lahw* was used in verse 32 to describe the life of this world. Here it describes the way certain people hold their religion. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī list several kinds of people covered by the phrase: those who do not take religious matters seriously at all; those whose religion is itself mere folly, such as idolatry; those who decide religious questions by whim and desire; those who turn religious festivals and rites into mere occasions for amusement; and those who use religion as an instrument for worldly ends — power, wealth, status. In each case, religion has been made into something to be played with rather than something to be lived by.

The phrase "*their* religion" is significant. Even idolaters had a religion; they performed rites, made pilgrimage, invoked deities. But they held it as play — as tribal custom, spectacle, and social occasion, without any serious reckoning with the God it supposedly concerned. The Qur'an describes their circumambulation of the Kaʿbah as "nothing but whistling and clapping" (8:35). This is religion as *lahw*.

The Qur'an says of these people on the Day of Judgment:

> "Today We will ignore them just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs and for rejecting Our revelations" (7:51)

**"And Who Are Deluded by the Life of This World"**

*Wa gharrat'humu al-ḥayātu al-dunyā* — "and whom the life of this world has deceived." The verb *gharra* means to deceive by false appearance, as a mirage deceives. The world presents itself as permanent, sufficient, and worth all one's attention; it is none of these. Those who take religion as play do so because they have been taken in by this appearance. The two attitudes are connected: seriousness about the world produces frivolity about religion, and vice versa. The Qur'an warns repeatedly against this deception (6:130; 31:33; 35:5; 45:35; 57:20).

**"But Remind Them with It"**

*Wa dhakkir bih* — "and remind with it" — that is, with the Qur'an (al-Rāzī). As in verse 69, disengagement does not mean abandonment. The believer leaves them to their play but continues to remind them with the Book. The Qur'an itself is the reminder (*dhikr*, *tadhkirah*), and its recitation and explanation are the means by which those deluded by the world may be awakened.

**"Lest Any Soul Be Delivered to Ruin Because of What It Has Earned"**

*An tubsala nafsun bi-mā kasabat* — "lest a soul be given over to destruction for what it earned." The verb *ubsila* is rare and forceful; it means to be handed over, pledged, or delivered up to ruin — as a hostage is delivered or a pledge forfeited. The soul that has earned ruin by its deeds is handed over to the consequences. The image is of a debt come due: what the soul "earned" (*kasabat*) through its heedless play is now collected.

This clause gives the reason for the reminder. One reminds because the alternative is that souls perish. The urgency of *daʿwah* comes from the reality of what is at stake.

**"It Has No Protector apart from God, nor Any Intercessor"**

*Laysa lahā min dūni Allāhi waliyyun wa lā shafīʿ* — "They worship besides Allah others who can neither harm nor benefit them, and say," This formula appeared in verse 51, where it was the reason for warning those who fear the gathering. Here it describes the condition of the ruined soul: no one to protect it from God's judgment, no one to plead on its behalf. The idolaters believed their idols would intercede for them (10:18; 39:3); the verse strips that hope away. Intercession exists, but only by God's permission and only for those He approves (2:255; 21:28), and it is not available to those who died in disbelief.

**"Though It Should Offer Every Kind of Ransom, It Shall Not Be Accepted"**

*Wa in taʿdil kulla ʿadlin lā yu'khadh minhā* — "and if it should offer every ransom, it will not be accepted from it." The word *ʿadl* here means an equivalent, a ransom, something offered in exchange. On that Day, no exchange is possible. The Qur'an repeats this many times:

> "Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another" (2:48)

> "Indeed, if each of those who disbelieve then die as disbelievers were to offer a ransom of enough gold to fill the whole world, it would never be accepted from them" (3:91)

> "If every wrongdoer were to possess everything in the world, they would surely ransom themselves with it" (10:54)

The Prophet ﷺ described the exchange God will propose:

> "It will be said to the person of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection: 'If you had everything on earth, would you ransom yourself with it?' He will say, 'Yes.' God will say: 'I asked of you something much easier than that while you were in the loins of Adam — that you not associate anything with Me — but you insisted on associating others with Me.'" (al-Bukhārī 3334; Muslim 2805)

**"Those Are the Ones Delivered to Ruin for That Which They Have Earned"**

The verse repeats the verb *ubsilū* and the phrase "for what they earned," emphasizing that the ruin is self-inflicted. No one is delivered to destruction arbitrarily; each is handed over to what his own deeds have purchased.

**"A Drink of Boiling Liquid and a Painful Punishment"**

*Lahum sharābun min ḥamīmin wa ʿadhābun alīm* — "But those who disbelieve will have a boiling drink and a painful punishment for their disbelief" *Ḥamīm* is water heated to the extreme. The image appears in many descriptions of Hell (10:4; 18:29; 37:67; 38:57; 40:72; 44:46–48; 47:15; 56:54, 93; 78:25) and contrasts with the cool, pure drinks of Paradise (37:45–47; 76:5–6, 17–18, 21; 83:25–28). The person who was "deluded by the life of this world" and drank its pleasures is given, in the next, a drink that torments. The connection is not arbitrary: what was taken as play is repaid with what admits no play.

**"For Having Disbelieved"**

*Bi-mā kānū yakfurūn* — "because of what they used to disbelieve." The verse closes by naming the root of the ruin: disbelief, sustained over time (*kānū* — "they used to"). The play, the delusion, the failure to take religion seriously — all of these were expressions of disbelief, and it is disbelief that earns the end described.

**The Report about Abū Bakr's Son**

Al-Zamakhsharī records a report from some pious commentators that this verse was revealed concerning the attempt by a son of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq — before the son's own conversion — to draw his father back to idolatry. If so, the verse would have addressed a believer facing pressure from a family member who treated religion as play; the instruction would be to leave him to his play while continuing to remind him. Verse 71 has also been linked to the same setting.

**On Abrogation**

Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī note that some scholars considered this verse's non-confrontational command ("leave them") to have been abrogated by later Madinan verses commanding fighting against the idolaters (9:5). The better view, held by many, is that there is no abrogation here: the verse establishes a permanent principle about how to deal with those who mock religion — disengage and remind — which remains valid regardless of the political circumstances that later permitted armed defense. "Leave them" describes the posture of the caller to God toward the frivolous; it is not a ruling about warfare that a later ruling could replace.

**The Verse's Two Movements**

The verse has two movements. The first (leave them, but remind them) is instruction to the believer. The second (lest a soul be ruined... boiling drink... painful punishment) is the content of the reminder itself. The believer is told what to do and given the very words with which to do it. Anyone who reads verse 70 aloud to one who treats religion as play has delivered the reminder the verse commands.

**Religion as Play in Every Age**

The verse's description of religion held as "play and diversion" is one of the Qur'an's most enduring diagnoses. Religion can become play through spectacle without substance, through ritual without remembrance, through festivals without fear of God, through debate for entertainment, through the use of religious identity for political or social advantage, and through the casual, ironic detachment that treats the sacred as one more consumer preference. In each case the remedy is the same: to remember that the reckoning is real, that no ransom will be accepted, and that what one plays with now will be answered for. The verse leaves the frivolous to their play — and leaves them the reminder, in case they should wake.

## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:71

> **Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Should we invoke, other than Allah, those ˹idols˺ which cannot benefit or harm us, and turn back to disbelief after Allah has guided us? ˹If we do so, we will be˺ like those disoriented by devils in the wilderness, while their companions call them to guidance, ˹saying˺, ‘Come to us!’ Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Allah’s guidance is the ˹only˺ true guidance. And we are commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rhetorical Refusal**

The verse returns to the form of "Say" and gives the believers' answer to those who would draw them back to idolatry. *Qul a-nadʿū min dūni Allāhi mā lā yanfaʿunā wa lā yaḍurrunā* — "Say: Shall we call upon, besides God, what neither benefits us nor harms us?" The question is rhetorical, and its form — a question rather than a flat refusal — invites the hearer to see the absurdity for himself. Should we abandon the One who saves from every distress (v. 64) for things that can do nothing at all?

**"That Which Neither Benefits nor Harms"**

This is the Qur'an's standard characterization of idols, repeated in many verses (5:76; 10:18, 106; 13:16; 20:89; 21:66; 22:12; 25:55; 26:71–73). The characterization is exact. A being worthy of worship must be able to do something for or against the worshipper; otherwise, worship is pointless. The idols could do neither. Abraham put the same question to his people:

> "Do you then worship—instead of Allah—what can neither benefit nor harm you in any way" (21:66)

The Qur'an illustrates the futility with two images:

> "The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger" (2:171)

> "But those ˹idols˺ the pagans invoke besides Him ˹can˺ never respond to them in any way" (13:14)

The second image is especially vivid: a thirsty man holding his open palms toward water and expecting it to rise to his mouth. This is the prayer of the idolater — an act whose form is petition but whose object cannot respond.

**"And Be Turned Back on Our Heels after God Has Guided Us"**

*Wa nuraddu ʿalā aʿqābinā baʿda idh hadānā Allāh* — "And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you" To turn on one's heels is to retreat, to go back the way one came. The phrase describes apostasy — returning to the ignorance from which God's guidance had brought one out (2:143; 3:144, 149). The verse frames the choice starkly: to return to idolatry after guidance is not a lateral move between equally valid options but a retreat from light into the darkness one had escaped.

The phrase "after God has guided us" carries a note of gratitude and of horror. Gratitude: God guided us; we did not guide ourselves. Horror: how could we throw away what He gave?

**"Like One Bewildered, Seduced by Satans on the Earth"**

The verse then offers a parable of the apostate: *ka'lladhī istahwat'hu al-shayāṭīnu fi'l-arḍi ḥayrān* — "like one whom the satans have lured away on the earth, bewildered." The verb *istahwā* means to entice, to lure, to draw away by appealing to desire (*hawā*). The satans — jinn in the service of Iblīs, or human beings who do his work (2:14, 102; 6:112, 121; 26:221) — have lured this person off the road, and now he wanders *ḥayrān*: confused, lost, not knowing which way to turn. Al-Rāzī reads "on the earth" figuratively: lured into a pit, a place from which he cannot see the way.

The image draws on the Arabs' experience of the desert, where a traveler lured off the track by a mirage, a false light, or the voice of a ghoul (the *ghūl* of Arab lore, which called travelers to their deaths) would wander until he perished. The apostate is like this traveler: seduced by desires, lost among the satans' voices, with no direction.

**"Though He Has Companions Who Call Him to Guidance, 'Come to Us!'"**

*Lahu aṣḥābun yadʿūnahu ilā al-hudā i'tinā* — "he has companions who call him to guidance: 'Come to us!'" The bewildered traveler is not without help. His companions — his fellow travelers, those who know the road — are calling to him, telling him where safety lies. But he does not respond; the satans' seduction holds him. The pathos of the image is that rescue is available and refused.

The commentators identify the "companions" as the sincere believers who call the wavering person back to faith. Al-Rāzī connects this to the report about Abū Bakr and his son: if verse 70 concerned the son trying to draw the father to idolatry, this verse may reflect the father calling the son to guidance. Whatever the specific occasion, the figure is universal: every person tempted toward disbelief has, somewhere, voices calling him back, and the question is which voice he follows.

A minority reading, recorded by al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī, takes the "companions" as the idolaters and the "guidance" they offer as their own false guidance; but the majority reading, in which the companions are the sincere and the guidance is real, fits the parable better and is followed here.

**"Indeed, the Guidance of God Is the True Guidance"**

The second "Say" gives the resolution: *qul inna hudā Allāhi huwa al-hudā* — "Say: Indeed, the guidance of God — that is the guidance." The construction is emphatic and exclusive: God's guidance is *the* guidance; there is no other. The phrase occurs also in 2:120 and 3:73. Al-Rāzī and al-Bayḍāwī explain that every path other than the one God has laid out, however it may be called "guidance" by those who follow it, leads astray. The bewildered traveler in the parable had many voices calling to him; only one of them knew the way.

This is the answer to the apostate's confusion. He is *ḥayrān*, bewildered, because he has lost the criterion by which to distinguish true guidance from false. The verse restores it: God's guidance is the guidance. Return to it, and the bewilderment ends.

**"And We Are Commanded to Submit to the Lord of the Worlds"**

*Wa umirnā li-nuslima li-rabbi al-ʿālamīn* — "and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds." The verb *aslama* means to submit, to surrender, to give oneself over — the root of *islām* and *muslim*. The believers' answer to the invitation to idolatry is that they are under command: they have been ordered to submit to the Lord of all worlds, and they cannot obey a rival summons. This echoes the Prophet's ﷺ "I have been forbidden" in verse 56. The believers' position is defined by command, not preference, and this makes it non-negotiable.

The phrase "Lord of the worlds" (*rabb al-ʿālamīn*) — the second phrase of al-Fātiḥah — situates the command in its proper scale. The idolaters invited the believers to submit to local, tribal gods that could not benefit or harm. The believers answer that they submit to the Lord of everything that exists. The disproportion is the argument.

**The Verse as a Whole**

The verse moves from question (shall we call on what cannot help?) to consequence (and retreat from guidance?) to image (like a traveler lured into the wilderness, deaf to his companions' calls) to resolution (God's guidance is the guidance) to commitment (we are commanded to submit). It is a complete answer to apostasy: the rational absurdity of it, the loss it entails, the psychological state it produces, the truth it abandons, and the obligation it violates.

**The Practical Portrait**

The parable in this verse is one of the Qur'an's most psychologically acute pictures of losing faith. The person does not usually decide, in a clear moment, to abandon God. He is *lured* — drawn gradually by desires, by voices that flatter or frighten, by the satans of his environment — until he finds himself bewildered, not knowing what he believes or where he stands. And all the while there are companions calling: "Come to us!" — the believer friend, the family member, the scholar, the verse remembered from childhood. The verse asks the bewildered one to hear those voices, and it gives the believer who calls a model for how to call: not with contempt for the lost, but with the urgent, hopeful cry of a companion who sees a friend wandering toward danger.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:72

> **establish prayer, and be mindful of Him. To Him you will all be gathered together.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Completing the Commission**

Verse 71 ended with "we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds." Verse 72 continues the sentence and completes the list of what the believers have been commanded: *wa an aqīmū al-ṣalāta wa'ttaqūh* — "and [we have been commanded] to establish the prayer and to be mindful of Him." The grammatical shift from "that we submit" (first person) to "establish the prayer" (imperative) reflects the content of the command as it was received: God said, "Establish the prayer and fear Me," and the believers report that they were so commanded.

Three commands are thus given as the substance of the believers' obligation: submit (*aslama*), establish prayer (*aqāma al-ṣalāh*), and be reverent (*ittaqā*). Together they form a compact summary of the religion.

**Al-Rāzī's Analysis of the Three Commands**

Al-Rāzī offers an elegant reading of why these three are singled out. Human action, he notes, falls into three categories: acts of the heart, acts of the limbs, and acts of omission — refraining from what is forbidden. The verse names the best of each. Submission (*islām*), together with faith, is the best act of the heart: the inward surrender of the will to God. Prayer is the best act of the limbs: the bodily worship that combines standing, bowing, prostration, and recitation, and that the Prophet ﷺ called "the pillar of the religion." Reverence (*taqwā*) is the best act of omission: the fear and mindfulness of God that restrains one from sin. Thus the verse, in three words, encompasses the whole of a righteous life — inner surrender, outer worship, and protective restraint.

**"To Perform the Prayer"**

The word *aqīmū* means literally "make stand," "establish," "set upright." The Qur'an almost never says simply "pray"; it says "establish the prayer," which implies performing it properly, regularly, with its conditions and its inner presence, and maintaining it as a standing institution in one's life and community. The prayer referred to is the canonical prayer (*ṣalāh*), which by the time of this Makkan verse was already the central act of Muslim worship, and which was fixed at five daily prayers at the Night Journey.

That prayer is named as the second commandment, immediately after submission, signals its rank. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is prayer, and its peak is striving in the way of God." (al-Tirmidhī 2616)

And:

> "Between a man and disbelief and idolatry is the abandonment of prayer." (Muslim 82)

For the believers in Makkah, surrounded by idolaters who called them back to their old religion, prayer was the daily, physical enactment of their refusal. Five times a day they turned away from the idols and prostrated to the Lord of the worlds. To "establish the prayer" was to establish, in the body, the answer given in verse 71.

**"And to Reverence Him"**

*Wa'ttaqūh* — "and fear Him," "be mindful of Him," "guard yourselves with respect to Him." The concept of *taqwā* has been discussed at several points in this sūrah (vv. 32, 51, 69). Its root meaning is protection: to place a shield between oneself and what one fears. *Taqwā* toward God is the constant awareness of His presence, His commands, and His prohibitions, which functions as a shield against sin. The Qur'an calls it the best provision (2:197) and the criterion of nobility (49:13).

Placing *taqwā* immediately after prayer is instructive. Prayer without *taqwā* — ritual without mindfulness — is a body without a soul. The Qur'an says that prayer "Indeed, ˹genuine˺ prayer should deter ˹one˺ from indecency and wickedness" (29:45), but only prayer performed with the reverence that carries over into the rest of life. The command to establish prayer and be reverent binds the ritual to the ethical.

**"It Is unto Him That You Shall Be Gathered"**

*Wa huwa alladhī ilayhi tuḥsharūn* — "and He is the one to whom you will be gathered." The verse concludes, as the sūrah so often does, with the return to God. The verb *ḥashara* means to gather, to assemble — the technical term for the assembling of all creatures on the Day of Judgment (*yawm al-ḥashr*). The construction is emphatic: it is to *Him* — not to the idols, not to anyone else — that all will be gathered.

The clause provides the reason for the three commands. Why submit to God, pray to Him, and fear Him? Because it is to Him that one will be gathered. The idols will not be there to receive their worshippers; God will be there to receive everyone. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the verse motivates obedience by reminding the hearer of the destination: prepare for the meeting with the One before whom you will stand.

The gathering has been mentioned already in this sūrah (v. 22, v. 38, v. 51) and will recur (v. 128). Its repetition keeps the hearer oriented. Every command, every argument, every warning is framed by the fact of the gathering.

**The Answer to Apostasy, Completed**

Verses 71–72 together are the believers' complete response to those who would draw them back to idolatry. Shall we call on what cannot help? Shall we retreat after guidance, like a bewildered traveler ignoring his companions' calls? No: God's guidance is the guidance, and we are commanded to submit, to pray, to fear Him — and it is to Him we will be gathered. Every element of the response is grounded in reality: the impotence of the idols, the value of guidance, the command of God, and the certainty of the gathering. Against this, the idolaters' invitation has nothing to offer but the tug of desire and the pull of custom.

**The Verse as a Daily Program**

Beyond its polemical setting, verse 72 gives the believer a program for every day. Submit — renew the surrender of the will each morning. Establish the prayer — five times, properly, with presence. Be reverent — carry the awareness of God into every transaction, every word, every private moment. Remember the gathering — let the day be lived in the light of the meeting toward which it moves. A person who does these four things has done what the verse commands, and has, in al-Rāzī's terms, perfected the acts of the heart, the limbs, and restraint.

**Why the Verse Ends Here**

The next verse (73) will turn from the believers' commitment to the description of the One to whom they have committed: the Creator of the heavens and the earth, whose Word is truth, whose is the sovereignty on the Day of the trumpet. The sequence is deliberate. Having declared "we are commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds," the sūrah now describes that Lord, so that the submission is not to an abstraction but to a God whose attributes make submission the only rational response.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:73

> **He is the One Who created the heavens and the earth in truth. On the Day ˹of Judgment˺ He will say, ‘Be!’ And there will be! His command is truth. All authority is His ˹alone˺ on the Day the Trumpet will be blown. He is the Knower of all—seen or unseen. And He is the All-Wise, All-Aware.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Describing the Lord of the Worlds**

Verses 71–72 declared the believers' submission to "the Lord of the worlds." Verse 73 describes Him. *Wa huwa alladhī khalaqa al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍa bi'l-ḥaqq* — "and He is the one who created the heavens and the earth in truth." The verse gathers, in a single sentence, God's creative power, His creative Word, His sovereignty over the end of the world, His knowledge, and His wisdom. It is a compact creed, and it sets up the Abraham narrative that follows (vv. 74–83), in which the Creator of the heavens and earth is contrasted with the celestial bodies that His people worshipped.

**"Created the Heavens and the Earth in Truth"**

The phrase *bi'l-ḥaqq* — "in truth," "with truth," "He is the One Who made the sun a radiant source and the moon a reflected light, with precisely ordained phases, so that you may know the number of years and calculation ˹of time˺" — recurs in many verses about creation (10:5; 14:19; 15:85; 16:3; 29:44; 30:8; 39:5; 44:39; 45:22; 46:3; 64:3). It denies that creation is arbitrary, playful, or pointless:

> "We did not create the heavens and the earth and everything in between for sport" (21:16)

> "We have not created the heavens and earth and everything in between without purpose—as the disbelievers think" (38:27)

> "˹They are˺ those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth ˹and pray˺," (3:191)

To create "in truth" means to create with purpose, according to wisdom, in a way that corresponds to reality and leads to a just end. Al-Rāzī adds that it implies the creation is good — a real, purposeful order, not an illusion or an accident. This contrasts with the view of the deniers, who treat the world as a place for play (v. 32) with no reckoning at its end (v. 29). If the world was created in truth, it was created for an outcome, and that outcome is the gathering (v. 72) and the judgment.

**"On the Day He Says 'Be!' and It Is"**

*Wa yawma yaqūlu kun fa-yakūn* — "and the day He says 'Be,' and it is." The creative command *kun* ("Be!") appears in eight verses (2:117; 3:47, 59; 6:73; 16:40; 19:35; 36:82; 40:68). It expresses the absolute ease and immediacy of God's creation: He does not labor, does not need materials or time; He commands, and the thing exists. The formula is the Qur'an's definitive statement of divine omnipotence.

Al-Ṭabarī explains that "the Day" here is the Day of Resurrection — the day on which God will say "Be" to the dead, and they will rise. The word "day" links this clause to the following one about the trumpet. God created the world with "Be"; He will resurrect it with "Be." The Qur'an makes the parallel explicit:

> "The One Who created you the first time" (17:51)

> "All it takes, when He wills something ˹to be˺, is simply to say to it" (36:82)

The verse thus answers the deniers' doubt about resurrection by pointing to the mode of the first creation. The One whose Word brought the heavens and earth into being needs only the same Word to bring the dead back.

**"His Word Is the Truth"**

*Qawluhu al-ḥaqq* — "His Word is the truth." Whatever God says is true, and whatever He says "Be" to, is. His Word does not fail, does not deceive, and does not describe a reality other than the one it produces. Al-Ṭabarī notes an alternative reading of the opening clause — that God created the heavens and earth *by* the Truth, that is, by His Word — which harmonizes with this phrase: His Word is the Truth, and by it all things were made.

The source commentary notes that this verse was cited in the theological debate over whether God's Speech is eternal or created. Those who held it eternal argued that if all things are created by God's Word, the Word must precede creation and therefore cannot itself be created. The point is subtle and the debate was long, but the verse's plain sense is clear: God's Word is truth, and by it He creates.

**"Sovereignty Is His on the Day When the Trumpet Is Blown"**

*Wa lahu al-mulku yawma yunfakhu fi'l-ṣūr* — "˹Beware of˺ the Day the Trumpet will be blown, and We will gather the wicked on that Day blue-faced ˹from horror and thirst˺" The *ṣūr* is the horn or trumpet whose blowing heralds the end of the world and the resurrection. The Qur'an mentions it in many verses (18:99; 20:102; 23:101; 27:87; 36:51; 39:68; 50:20; 69:13; 74:8; 78:18). Sūrah 39:68 describes two blasts: at the first, all in the heavens and earth fall dead except whom God wills; at the second, all rise and stand looking on. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "How can I be at ease when the bearer of the horn has put it to his mouth, bent his forehead, and inclined his ear, waiting for the command to blow?" The Companions asked, "What should we say?" He said, "Say: God is sufficient for us, and the best disposer of affairs; upon God we rely." (al-Tirmidhī 2431, 3243)

God's sovereignty is absolute at all times, but on the Day of the trumpet it is manifest without rival. Every earthly kingship, every idol's supposed power, every human claim to authority is gone. The Qur'an says:

> "Who does all authority belong to this Day" (40:16)

The phrase answers the idolaters' hope that their gods might help them at the end. On that Day there is one Sovereign.

**"Knower of the Unseen and the Seen"**

*ʿĀlimu al-ghaybi wa'l-shahādah* — "And you will be returned to the Knower of the seen and unseen, then He will inform you of what you used to do" This pairing occurs frequently (9:94, 105; 13:9; 23:92; 32:6; 39:46; 59:22; 62:8; 64:18). It expresses the totality of God's knowledge, already elaborated in verse 59: the hidden (the future, the hearts, the realities beyond perception) and the manifest (everything observable). No sphere is closed to Him. On the Day of the trumpet, this knowledge is the basis of a judgment from which nothing is concealed.

**"And He Is the Wise, the Aware"**

*Wa huwa al-ḥakīmu al-khabīr* — "and He is the Wise, the Aware." The pair closes the sūrah's first verse cluster (v. 18) and reappears here. *Al-Ḥakīm* is the One whose every act is placed rightly, according to perfect wisdom. *Al-Khabīr* is the One who knows the inner reality of things, as one who has tested them. The two names together assure the hearer that the creation "in truth," the Word, the sovereignty, and the knowledge are all exercised wisely and with complete awareness. Nothing in creation or judgment is arbitrary.

**The Verse as Preface to Abraham**

The verse's emphasis on the Creator of the heavens and the earth prepares the ground for Abraham's argument in verses 74–79, which ends with "I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth." Abraham's people worshipped stars, moon, and sun — created things within the heavens. The verse states, before the story begins, who actually created those heavens. The reader thus knows the answer before Abraham reaches it, and watches him arrive at the truth the verse has already declared.

**The Verse as Creed**

Read on its own, verse 73 is a complete confession of faith: God is the purposeful Creator; His Word is truth and creates by command; He alone will reign at the end; He knows all things hidden and manifest; He is wise and aware. Each element answers a specific error — that the world is meaningless, that God cannot resurrect, that others share His authority, that deeds go unseen, that events are random. A believer who holds this verse in mind has a settled foundation from which the confusions of the world cannot shake him, and a clear picture of the Lord to whom he has been commanded to submit.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:74

> **And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said to his father, Ȃzar, “Do you take idols as gods? It is clear to me that you and your people are entirely misguided.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pericope of Abraham (vv. 74–83)**

With this verse the sūrah turns from argument to narrative. The next ten verses recount Abraham's confrontation with his father and his people over idolatry, and his reasoning from the setting of star, moon, and sun to the Creator of the heavens and the earth. The story is not a digression. It dramatizes, in the life of the patriarch whom the Quraysh claimed as their ancestor and the founder of their sanctuary, the very argument the sūrah has been making: that *tawḥīd* is evident to anyone who sincerely contemplates the created order, and that idolatry — including the idolatry of one's own father and people — must be rejected when the truth becomes clear. For the Makkans, the story was a rebuke: their revered ancestor had broken with his father's religion for exactly the reason Muhammad ﷺ was asking them to break with theirs.

The Abraham narratives appear in many sūrahs (2:124–141, 258–260; 14:35–41; 19:41–50; 21:51–73; 26:69–104; 29:16–27; 37:83–113; 43:26–28; 60:4–6). This passage is distinctive in its focus on the celestial argument.

**"When Abraham Said to His Father, Azar"**

*Wa idh qāla Ibrāhīmu li-abīhi Āzar* — "when Abraham said to his father, Ȃzar" (6:74). This is the only place in the Qur'an where the name Āzar appears. The Bible names Abraham's father Terah (Genesis 11:26). The commentators offer several reconciliations. Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Rāzī record that Āzar may have been a second name or a title of Terah; that it may have been the name of the idol he served, so that Abraham was addressing him by his idol's name in reproach; or that it was a descriptive term meaning 'crooked' or 'erring.' Others, including some cited by al-Rāzī and al-Ṭūsī, held that Āzar was Abraham's paternal uncle, called 'father' in the broad Arabic usage that includes uncles (as in 2:133, where Ishmael is counted among Jacob's 'fathers' though he was his uncle).

The uncle theory was driven partly by a theological concern: some held that a prophet's ancestors could not have been idolaters, citing the report "Their mothers bore them through hardship upon hardship, and their weaning takes two years" It was also driven by the observation that Abraham's disavowal of his father in 9:114 seemed hard to square with the Qur'anic command to maintain kindness toward disbelieving parents (31:14–15). Al-Rāzī, however, concludes that the plainest reading of this and other verses is that Āzar was Abraham's actual father and was an idolater — and this is the view of the majority. Indeed, the Qur'an elsewhere records Abraham's tender but firm addresses to "my father" (19:42–45) and his prayer for him (26:86; 60:4), which would lose their poignancy if the man were merely an uncle. The tension with 9:114 is resolved within that verse itself: Abraham prayed for his father only because of a promise he had made, and when it became clear to him that his father was an enemy of God, he dissociated himself.

**"Do You Take Idols for Gods?"**

*A-tattakhidhu aṣnāman ālihah* — "do you take idols as gods?" The word *aṣnām* (sg. *ṣanam*) refers to carved images, statues representing deities. The question is incredulous and confrontational. Abraham does not begin with tactful preliminaries; he names the practice and questions it directly. The interrogative form ("do you take...?") invites his father to hear the absurdity in the statement of his own belief.

The reproach is sharpened by the report, recorded by al-Ṭabarī and others, that Āzar was not merely a worshipper but a maker of idols — a craftsman who carved the very gods he served. Abraham's question thus carries a further edge: you take as gods the things you yourself have made? The Qur'an elsewhere records Abraham's argument on exactly this point:

> "when it is Allah Who created you and whatever you do" (37:95–96)

**"Truly I See You and Your People in Manifest Error"**

*Innī arāka wa qawmaka fī ḍalālin mubīn* — "indeed I see you and your people in clear error." Abraham extends the judgment from his father to the whole community. The error is *mubīn* — clear, evident, manifest. Idolatry is not a subtle mistake that requires elaborate refutation; it is an obvious error that anyone who looks honestly can see.

The verb "I see" (*arā*) is significant. Abraham does not say "I have been told" or "I believe"; he says "I see." His rejection of idolatry is based on perception — the perception of reality that the following verses will describe. He looks at the idols and sees things that cannot see; he looks at the heavens and sees things that set; and he concludes that neither can be the Lord.

**The Courage and Its Cost**

The confrontation was not without cost. The Qur'an records that Āzar responded with a threat:

> "If you do not desist, I will certainly stone you ˹to death˺" (19:46)

And Abraham's people cast him into the fire (21:68–69; 37:97). The son who told his father "I see you in manifest error" did so knowing what it would cost, and paid it. For the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions in Makkah, who were breaking with their own fathers and facing expulsion and violence for it, the example was direct.

**How Abraham Spoke to His Father**

Though this verse gives the confrontation in its sharpest form, the fuller account in Sūrat Maryam shows the tenderness with which Abraham addressed his father. Four times he says 'O my father' (*yā abati*), a form of gentle address. He reasons with him: "Why do you worship what can neither hear nor see, nor benefit you at all?" (19:42). He appeals to him: "I have certainly received some knowledge which you have not received, so follow me and I will guide you to the Straight Path." (19:43). He fears for him: "I truly fear that you will be touched by a torment from the Most Compassionate" (19:45). And when his father threatens him, he responds: "Peace be upon you! I will pray to my Lord for your forgiveness. He has truly been Most Gracious to me." (19:47). The manifest-error judgment of this verse and the tenderness of that passage are not in conflict; together they show that one may be uncompromising about the truth and gentle with the person.

**The Lesson for Sons and Fathers**

The verse establishes a principle that the Qur'an states as law elsewhere: there is no obedience to a parent in disobedience to God, though kindness to parents remains obligatory even when they are disbelievers (29:8; 31:15). Abraham did not obey his father's religion; he did not cease to be his son. He rejected the idols and still prayed for him. This balance — refusal of the error, preservation of the bond as far as possible — is the model for every believer whose family holds to what God has forbidden.

**"Manifest Error" and the Sūrah's Theme**

The phrase *ḍalāl mubīn* ties Abraham's story to the sūrah's central contrast between guidance and misguidance (vv. 39, 56, 71). Abraham "sees" the error and, in the following verses, is shown the truth. The sequence — recognition of error, then reception of guidance — is the path the sūrah invites the Makkans to walk. They too could see, if they looked honestly, that their idols were in manifest error; and they too could receive what Abraham received.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:75

> **We also showed Abraham the wonders of the heavens and the earth, so he would be sure in faith.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Divine Initiative**

Verse 74 showed Abraham rejecting idolatry on the basis of what he "saw." Verse 75 reveals the source of that seeing: *wa kadhālika nurī Ibrāhīma malakūta al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* — "and thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth." The subject is God. Abraham's clarity was not merely his own achievement; God showed him. This is crucial for understanding the celestial argument that follows (vv. 76–78): whatever Abraham's reasoning, it took place within a divine showing, and its conclusion was a divine gift.

The word *kadhālika* ("thus," "in this way") connects the showing to the preceding verse: just as Abraham saw his people's error, so God showed him the truth. Recognition of falsehood and reception of truth went together.

**The Word *Malakūt***

*Malakūt* is an intensive form of *mulk* (dominion, kingdom, sovereignty). It appears four times in the Qur'an (6:75; 7:185; 23:88; 36:83) and denotes the inner reality of God's sovereignty — the kingdom as it truly is, in its full dependence on its King. To be shown the *malakūt* of the heavens and the earth is to see not merely the physical heavens and earth but their nature as a dominion: contingent, governed, held in being by One who is not part of them.

Sūrah 7:185 asks, "Have they ever reflected on the wonders of the heavens and the earth, and everything Allah has created, and that perhaps their end is near" — implying that the *malakūt* is available, in some degree, to anyone who looks. Sūrah 36:83 says, "So glory be to the One in Whose Hands is the authority over all things, and to Whom ˹alone˺ you will ˹all˺ be returned" Abraham was shown this dominion; the invitation to look into it stands for all.

**Two Interpretations of the Showing**

The commentators offer two understandings, which are not mutually exclusive.

The first, held by Ibn Kathīr and developed by al-Rāzī, is that God showed Abraham the dominion by opening his inner sight to the significance of what everyone can see. The heavens and the earth are visible to all; but most people see them without perceiving their dependence on a Creator, veiled by habit, distraction, and attachment to the world. When Abraham rejected his father's idolatry (v. 74), he attained a clarity that allowed him to see, with the eye of the intellect, what the phenomena signify. The Qur'an says that God gave Abraham "sound judgment" (*rushd*) beforehand (21:51), and that anyone who reflects on the heavens and earth with sincerity should arrive at their Maker (10:101; 34:9). On this view, the showing is the illumination of reason.

The second, recorded by Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭūsī, and al-Zamakhsharī from early authorities, is that God granted Abraham a miraculous vision: the heavens were opened to him so that he saw their levels up to the Throne, and the earth was cleaved so that he saw to its depths. Some reports add that he saw the deeds of people and began to pray against the sinners, until God told him to stop, for He is more merciful to His servants than Abraham. On this view, the showing was a revelatory experience granted to a prophet.

Al-Rāzī suggests a synthesis: any thoughtful monotheist may perceive proofs of God in creation, but Abraham experienced the divine self-manifestation in creation to a degree reserved for the greatest prophets — the degree the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ sought when he prayed, "O God, show me things as they truly are." The showing was both rational and revelatory: reason illuminated by grace to a prophetic intensity.

**"That He Might Be among Those Possessing Certainty"**

*Wa li-yakūna min al-mūqinīn* — "and that he might be among those who have certainty." The word *yaqīn* (certainty) denotes knowledge free of doubt — knowledge so firm that it is not shaken by objection or circumstance. The Qur'an speaks of levels of certainty: the certainty of knowledge (*ʿilm al-yaqīn*), the certainty of sight (*ʿayn al-yaqīn*), and the certainty of direct experience (*ḥaqq al-yaqīn*) (102:5–7; 56:95; 69:51). Abraham was raised to certainty by what he was shown.

Al-Rāzī notes that certainty is typically attained after a period of reflection in which doubts are raised and resolved; the process is what produces the firmness. The verses that follow (76–78), in which Abraham considers and rejects successive candidates for lordship, may be read as this process — or as the demonstration of a certainty already attained. Al-Rāzī also allows the reading "And the everlasting good deeds are far better with your Lord in reward and in outcome": God showed him the dominion as a reward for the sincerity he already possessed. Both readings honor the same truth: sincerity and certainty reinforce each other, and God increases in guidance those who accept it (19:76; 47:17).

**The Purpose of Certainty**

Why was certainty necessary? Because Abraham was about to confront his father, his people, and their king; to be thrown into the fire; to leave his homeland; to be commanded to sacrifice his son. None of this could be borne on the basis of opinion. It required certainty — the kind that made him say, in the fire, "God is sufficient for me, and He is the best disposer of affairs" (as reported in al-Bukhārī 4563). The showing of the dominion was the foundation on which everything else in Abraham's life stood.

The same holds for every believer in proportion. Faith that will withstand pressure, loss, and doubt must be grounded in more than inherited assumption. It must be, in some degree, *seen* — through reflection on the signs God has spread through creation and revelation, and through the experience of His answering, providing, and guiding. The verse invites the believer to seek what Abraham was given: not blind conviction but certainty that comes from being shown.

**Abraham's Certainty and the Later Request**

A reader may recall that this same Abraham later asked God to show him how He gives life to the dead, and when God asked, "Do you not believe?" (2:260), he replied, "Yes I do, but just so my heart can be reassured." (2:260). This is not a contradiction of the certainty described here. Abraham's request was not for belief he lacked but for the higher certainty of sight added to the certainty of knowledge. The showing of the dominion gave him certainty; the showing of resurrection brought that certainty to rest. The believer's relationship with God is one of increasing certainty, and each level is a gift.

**The Verse's Role in the Passage**

Verse 75 stands between Abraham's rejection of idolatry (v. 74) and his celestial argument (vv. 76–78). It functions as the hinge that tells the reader how to understand what follows: whatever form Abraham's words about star, moon, and sun take, they are spoken by one whom God has shown the dominion and made certain. He is not groping toward a conclusion he does not yet hold; he is, at minimum, demonstrating — and perhaps also recalling the process by which he came to know — that nothing that sets can be the Lord. The reader has been told the end before the argument begins.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:76

> **When the night grew dark upon him, he saw a star and said, “This is my Lord!” But when it set, he said, “I do not love things that set.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Scene**

*Fa-lammā janna ʿalayhi al-layl* — "so when the night covered him." The verb *janna* means to cover, to conceal, to enclose — it is the root of *jinn* (hidden beings), *jannah* (a garden enclosed by foliage), *janīn* (the fetus hidden in the womb), and *majnūn* (one whose reason is veiled). Night enclosed Abraham; in the darkness a star appeared. *Ra'ā kawkaban* — "he saw a star." The commentators, including Ibn Kathīr and al-Jalālayn, identify the star as Venus (*al-Zuhrah*), the brightest, though the text does not name it. The narrative moves from the least bright celestial body (a star) to the moon to the sun, in ascending order of brilliance, so that the argument builds toward the strongest possible candidate and still concludes against it.

**"This Is My Lord!"**

*Qāla hādhā rabbī* — "he said: This is my Lord." This is the sentence that has occupied the commentators. How could Abraham — a prophet, one whom God had just shown the dominion of the heavens and earth and made certain (v. 75) — say of a star, "This is my Lord"?

Two principal interpretations are recorded, and a third that reconciles them.

**First Interpretation: The Argument of a Debater**

According to Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, and many others, Abraham did not make the statement in earnest. He was engaging his people in argument, and he began by voicing their own position — as a skilled debater adopts an opponent's premise in order to demolish it. His people worshipped celestial bodies (or idols representing them); Abraham said, in effect, "Let us suppose this star is my Lord" — and then let its setting refute the supposition. Al-Ṭabarī records the reading that the words were spoken with incredulity or irony: "*This* is my Lord?!" On this view, the sequence of star, moon, and sun is a staged demonstration, each step exposing the inadequacy of the object that his people revered.

Support for this reading comes from the context: Abraham has already denounced idolatry as manifest error (v. 74) and been shown the dominion (v. 75). It also matches his method elsewhere. In 21:51–67, he breaks the idols and, when asked, says "And indeed, We had granted Abraham sound judgment early on, for We knew him well ˹to be worthy of it˺" forcing his people to confront the absurdity themselves. In 37:88–89, he glances at the stars and says "I am sick," a strategic utterance that lets him remain behind and act against the idols. Abraham's characteristic approach is to lead his opponents to see their error through their own premises. The celestial argument fits.

**Second Interpretation: The Seeker's Path**

According to al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭūsī, al-Suyūṭī, and others, the passage recounts a genuine process of reasoning by which Abraham, before his prophethood, arrived at the knowledge of God's Oneness. Many of these commentators connect the passage to a story about Abraham's early life: that the king (identified by some as Nimrod) had dreamed of a boy who would overthrow him and ordered all male infants killed; that Abraham's mother hid him in a cave, where he grew up in isolation; and that when he first emerged and saw the sky, he sought his Lord among its lights, saying of each in turn "this is my Lord" until each set, and concluding that his Lord was beyond them all.

The source commentary notes that this story has no basis in the Qur'anic or Biblical accounts and appears to blend elements from other narratives (the infancy of Moses, the Cave). It raises its own difficulty: a prophet identifying a star with God, even briefly, would be a form of *shirk*. Those who hold this interpretation answer that Abraham was a young child at the time, before the age of responsibility and before his prophethood, so no fault attaches. And they note that even on this reading, the process was not purely human: God "showed him the dominion" (v. 75) and later calls the discourse "Our argument which We gave to Abraham" (v. 83). The reasoning was divinely guided.

**The Reconciliation**

The two readings may be joined. Abraham may have been staging a rhetorical demonstration for his people, and the demonstration may have retraced a path of reflection that he had genuinely walked earlier — a path that began in wonder at the heavens and ended in certainty regarding *tawḥīd*. The words "this is my Lord" would then be both a debater's move and an honest recollection of a question once asked. What is certain, on any reading, is where the process ends: in the declaration of verse 79, "I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth." The passage is about arriving at *tawḥīd*, and the Qur'an calls it God's argument.

**"But When It Set, He Said, 'I Love Not Things That Set'"**

*Fa-lammā afala qāla lā uḥibbu al-āfilīn* — "but when it set, he said: I do not love those that set." The verb *afala* means to set, to disappear below the horizon, to vanish. The star that shone in the night sinks and is gone. Abraham's response is not a technical argument but an expression of the heart: *I do not love* things that set.

The phrasing is deliberate and profound. Abraham does not say "this cannot be my Lord because it changes" — though that argument is implied and was developed by the theologians (what changes is contingent; what is contingent needs a cause; the Lord is the cause of all and therefore does not change). He says "I do not love." The relationship with the Lord is a relationship of love, and love cannot be given to what disappears. A lord who sets abandons his worshipper; he is not there when needed; he is subject to a cycle he does not control. The heart that seeks its Lord seeks One who is always present. The star, however beautiful, fails this test.

**The Logic of Setting**

Behind the expression of the heart lies an argument that al-Rāzī and others draw out. Setting is a form of change and of absence. Whatever changes is governed by something other than itself — by the laws that govern its motion. Whatever is governed is not the Governor. Whatever is absent for part of the time cannot be the sustainer of all things at all times. Therefore nothing that sets can be the Lord. The argument applies to every created thing, for everything created is subject to change, but the celestial bodies are the most telling case because they are the most sublime of visible things. If even they fail, everything below them fails a fortiori.

**The Star as the First Step**

The star is the first and weakest candidate. Its setting is the first refutation. The passage will repeat the pattern with the moon and the sun, each greater than the last, so that the argument cannot be dismissed as applying only to minor lights. By the end, every visible glory of the heavens has been tested and found wanting, and only the Creator of the heavens remains.

**The Sufi Reading**

The source commentary records that Sufi commentators read the passage as a map of spiritual ascent. Each celestial body represents a station of understanding; each setting represents the seeker's realization that the station is limited and must be transcended. For al-Qushayrī, the star is the intellect that first apprehends truth through demonstrative proof; its setting is the recognition that proof alone does not satisfy. The moon is knowledge grown clearer; the sun is the light of direct knowledge (*maʿrifah*). And Abraham's progression is from seeing created things through God, to seeing them for God, to the effacement of all things in God. This reading does not displace the literal sense; it draws out a pattern the literal sense contains: that the heart passes through lesser lights on its way to the Light.

**What the Verse Teaches**

The verse teaches, first, that the heart is made for a Lord who does not set — and that every attachment to what sets will end in the disappointment Abraham voices. Wealth sets; health sets; power, youth, and human beings all set. To love them as lords is to love what will leave. Second, it teaches a method: to test every candidate for one's ultimate devotion by asking whether it sets. Third, it teaches that this reasoning was given to Abraham as a gift and a proof, and is available to anyone who looks at the night sky with the same honesty.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:77

> **Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, “This one is my Lord!” But when it disappeared, he said, “If my Lord does not guide me, I will certainly be one of the misguided people.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Candidate**

*Fa-lammā ra'ā al-qamara bāzighan* — "then when he saw the moon rising." The word *bāzigh* means rising, emerging, breaking forth — used of a heavenly body as it appears over the horizon with its light. The moon is greater and brighter than the star; its rising is more impressive; it dominates the night sky. If the argument of verse 76 could be dismissed by saying that a mere star is obviously too small to be Lord, the moon presents a stronger case. Abraham says again: *hādhā rabbī* — "this is my Lord." The same words, the same test, a greater object.

**"But When It Set"**

*Fa-lammā afala* — "but when it set." The moon too sets. For all its brilliance and dominance, it follows the same course as the star: it rises, it traverses the sky, it sinks below the horizon and is gone. It also waxes and wanes, growing from a sliver to fullness and back to nothing. The commentators note that Abraham's people included astrologers, who believed the celestial bodies exerted influence when waxing and lost it when waning. Al-Rāzī observes that the moon's cycle should therefore have been especially persuasive to them: a lord whose power comes and goes with a monthly cycle is no lord.

**The Change in Abraham's Response**

Here the pattern varies. After the star set, Abraham said, "I do not love things that set" — a statement of principle. After the moon sets, he says: *la-in lam yahdinī rabbī la-akūnanna min al-qawmi al-ḍāllīn* — "if my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who are astray." The response has deepened. It is no longer only a rejection of the failed candidate; it is a turning toward the true Lord with a confession of need.

Notice the phrase "my Lord" (*rabbī*). Abraham has just said of the moon, "this is my Lord," and it has set. Now he says, "if my Lord does not guide me" — and the "my Lord" here cannot be the moon, which has just been dismissed. It is the true Lord, the one he is seeking, whom he addresses even before he has named Him. The verse thus shows Abraham already oriented toward the real God in the very midst of the demonstration. This supports the reading that he was never sincerely attributing lordship to the moon: the "my Lord" who guides is distinct from the "my Lord" who set.

**"If My Lord Does Not Guide Me"**

The conditional sentence expresses a fundamental truth of the sūrah: guidance is from God alone. Verse 71 declared, "the guidance of God is the true guidance." Verse 39 said, "whomever God wills He sends astray, and whomever He wills He places on a straight path." Here Abraham — the father of the prophets, the friend of God, the one shown the dominion of the heavens — says that without God's guidance he would be among the lost. If Abraham needed guidance, everyone needs it. No degree of intellect, sincerity, or spiritual capacity exempts a person from dependence on God for the finding of the way.

The Prophet ﷺ taught this dependence in his prayers:

> "O God, I ask You for guidance, piety, chastity, and sufficiency." (Muslim 2721)

And in the prayer he taught ʿAlī: "O God, guide me and set me straight" (Muslim 2725). The most guided of human beings prayed for guidance daily. Abraham's statement in this verse is the same posture.

**The Rhetorical Function toward His People**

Al-Rāzī notes that the statement also served Abraham's argument against his people. By saying "if my Lord does not guide me, I will be among the astray," he was implicitly describing their condition. They had not been guided; they were among the astray — and the proof was that they worshipped what sets. Abraham's confession of his own dependence on guidance was a mirror held up to those who imagined they needed none.

**Progression in the Three Responses**

The three responses to the three settings form a progression. After the star: "I do not love things that set" — the negative principle. After the moon: "if my Lord does not guide me, I will be among the astray" — the turn toward the true Lord and the confession of need. After the sun (v. 78): "O my people, I am free of what you associate" — the public declaration. The movement is from private insight to personal petition to public witness. It is the natural sequence of conviction: one first sees what is false, then turns to the One who is true, then declares the truth to others.

**Why the Moon Fails**

The moon fails for the same reason the star failed, and the repetition is the point. Greater size and brightness do not change the essential fact: it sets. The argument is not about magnitude but about nature. Anything that appears and disappears, waxes and wanes, rises and sets, is governed and not the Governor. To worship the moon because it is greater than a star is to miss the point entirely; what disqualifies both is what they share.

This has a direct application to the way people rank their idols. Someone may reject a crude idol as obviously unworthy while devoting himself to a more impressive one — wealth over trinkets, a powerful nation over a village chief, an ideology over a superstition. The verse says: the moon is more impressive than the star, and it sets just the same. What is created remains created, however grand.

**The Vulnerability in the Verse**

There is a striking humility in this verse. In the midst of a demonstration whose conclusion he knows, Abraham gives voice to the vulnerability every seeker feels: the fear of being lost. "If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the astray." This is not weakness; it is accuracy. The one who does not fear going astray has not understood how easy it is. The one who knows his dependence on God's guidance holds on to it more tightly. Abraham's certainty (v. 75) and his confessed dependence (v. 77) are two sides of one relationship: he is certain *because* he depends, and he depends *because* he knows that certainty is a gift and not an achievement.

**Toward the Sun**

The moon has set. One candidate remains — the greatest of all visible lights, the sun. The argument will reach its climax there, and with it Abraham's break with his people.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:78

> **Then when he saw the sun shining, he said, “This must be my Lord—it is the greatest!” But again when it set, he declared, “O my people! I totally reject whatever you associate ˹with Allah in worship˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Greatest Candidate**

*Fa-lammā ra'ā al-shamsa bāzighatan qāla hādhā rabbī hādhā akbar* — "then when he saw the sun rising, he said: This is my Lord; this is greater." The sun is the culmination. It is incomparably brighter than star or moon; it banishes them all; it gives light, warmth, and life; it was the supreme deity of many ancient peoples. Abraham adds a phrase not used for the previous two: *hādhā akbar* — "this is greater." If anything in the visible cosmos could claim lordship, it is the sun.

The commentators note a grammatical detail. *Shams* (sun) is feminine in Arabic, yet Abraham says *hādhā* (masculine "this") rather than *hādhihi*. Al-Zamakhsharī and others explain that the masculine refers to the underlying concept — "this [luminous thing], this [object]" — or that Abraham deliberately avoided the feminine to prevent his people from hearing "she is my Lord," which would have struck them as ascribing femininity to God. The detail shows the care with which every word in the passage is chosen.

**"But When It Set"**

*Fa-lammā afalat* — "but when it set." Even the sun sets. The greatest of all visible lights, the giver of day, sinks below the horizon every evening and leaves the world in darkness. The argument is now complete. The three brightest bodies in the heavens — the ones Abraham's people considered the most powerful of the seven they worshipped (Ibn Kathīr) — have all been tested by the same criterion and have all failed. There is nothing left in the sky to try.

**Why the Sun's Setting Is Decisive**

Al-Ṭūsī draws out the implication for his people's stone idols. If the celestial bodies — which move across the heavens, shine with their own light, and seem so sublime — are disqualified by their setting, then stone images, which cannot even move, are disqualified all the more. The celestial argument is thus not a digression from the confrontation over idols (v. 74) but its foundation: Abraham refutes the highest objects of worship in order to make the refutation of the lowest self-evident. Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī add that the idols may themselves have represented celestial deities, so the argument struck at the root of the whole system.

**"O My People! Truly I Am Quit of the Partners You Ascribe"**

*Qāla yā qawmi innī barī'un mimmā tushrikūn* — "he said: O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate." With the sun's setting, Abraham turns from the sky to his people and makes his declaration. The word *barī'* means free, clear, innocent, disassociated — from the root *b-r-'* that gives *barā'ah*, the formal disavowal that opens Sūrah 9. Abraham declares himself quit of everything they associate with God: the star, moon, and sun; the idols; all of it.

The declaration marks the transition from demonstration to witness. Until now, Abraham has been reasoning — for his people's benefit, or in recollection of his own path. Now he states the conclusion publicly and personally: I am free of your *shirk*. The address "O my people" is both intimate and final; he speaks as one of them and, in the same breath, separates himself from what defines them.

The same disavowal is recorded from Abraham in other passages:

> "˹Remember, O Prophet˺ when Abraham declared to his father and his people," (43:26–27)

> "You already have an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people," (60:4)

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was instructed to say the same in verse 19 of this sūrah ("I call Allah to witness, and you too bear witness, that I ˹totally˺ reject whatever you associate"), and Hūd said it to ʿĀd (11:54). The words of disavowal are the shared inheritance of the prophets.

**The Argument's Structure as a Whole**

Verses 76–78 form a single argument in three stages, and its structure deserves to be stated. The criterion: whatever sets cannot be the Lord. The test: applied to the star, the moon, and the sun in ascending order. The result: all set; therefore none is the Lord. The conclusion: the Lord is the One who made them and does not set — which verse 79 will state. The argument is inductive in its form (three cases) and deductive in its force (the criterion applies to every created thing). It is an argument that anyone can follow, that requires no special learning, and that leads inexorably to *tawḥīd*.

Al-Rāzī draws an important lesson from the passage's very existence. If religious truth were self-evident, Abraham would not have needed to argue. If it could rest on blind imitation, his people would have been right to follow their fathers. The passage shows that truth in religion is neither obvious without reflection nor validly inherited without examination; it must be reached by sincere and objective reflection on clear proofs drawn from the created order. This is why God gave Abraham an argument (v. 83) and not merely a command.

**Reason and Revelation in the Passage**

The passage is often cited as the Qur'an's clearest example of rational argument for God's Oneness. This is correct, with the qualification that verse 75 has already supplied: the reasoning took place within a divine showing, and verse 83 calls the argument "Ours." Reason and revelation are not opposed here; revelation illuminates reason, and reason, so illuminated, arrives at what revelation teaches. The Qur'an's consistent position is that the honest use of reason confirms *tawḥīd* — which is why it constantly commands reflection — and that the same reason, when clouded by desire and imitation, fails to reach it. Abraham's reason was clear because God showed him; his people's was clouded because they clung to their fathers' ways.

**What Sets in Human Life**

The application of the passage extends far beyond astronomy. Every person has candidates for lordship — things he treats as ultimate, that he serves, loves, fears, and orients his life around. The verse's criterion applies to all of them: does it set? Career sets. Beauty sets. Health, reputation, wealth, nations, movements, and the people one loves — all rise and set. Some are stars, some moons, some suns; the greatest of them is still *āfil*, one that sets. Abraham's declaration is the only sane response to this recognition: I am free of what you associate. Not because created things are worthless — the sun is a magnificent gift — but because none of them is the Lord, and to treat them as such is to love what will leave.

**Toward the Turning of the Face**

The disavowal in this verse is the negative half of Abraham's confession. He has said what he is free of. Verse 79 will give the positive half: to whom he has turned. The two together — *barā'ah* from all that sets, *ḥanīfiyyah* toward the Creator — constitute the *tawḥīd* that the whole sūrah has been arguing for, now spoken by the ancestor whose religion the Makkans claimed to follow.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:79

> **I have turned my face towards the One Who has originated the heavens and the earth—being upright—and I am not one of the polytheists.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Positive Confession**

Verse 78 gave the negative: "I am quit of the partners you ascribe." Verse 79 gives the positive: *innī wajjahtu wajhiya li'lladhī faṭara al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍa ḥanīfan wa mā anā min al-mushrikīn* — "Indeed, I have turned my face toward the One who originated the heavens and the earth, inclining to truth, and I am not of those who associate."
