The two verses together form the complete declaration of *tawḥīd*: negation of all false objects of worship, affirmation of the true One. This is the structure of the *shahādah* itself — "no god" (negation) "but God" (affirmation) — and Abraham's words are its earliest and fullest model.

**"I Have Turned My Face"**

The verb *wajjaha* means to direct, to orient, to turn toward; *wajh* is the face. To turn one's face toward something is to direct one's whole attention and being to it — the face being the seat of perception, identity, and honor. Al-Rāzī explains that the phrase means to orient one's entire self toward the worship and obedience of God, not merely to look in a direction. The same expression appears in other verses:

> "Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord" (2:112)

> "So if they argue with you ˹O Prophet˺, say," (3:20)

> "Whoever fully submits themselves to Allah and is a good-doer, they have certainly grasped the firmest hand-hold" (31:22)

> "So be steadfast in faith in all uprightness ˹O Prophet˺—the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people" (30:30)

The turning of the face is the outward expression of *islām* — the surrender of the self. In prayer, the believer literally turns his face toward the Kaʿbah, which Abraham built; the physical turning enacts the inner one Abraham describes.

**"Toward Him Who Created the Heavens and the Earth"**

The object of the turning is described not by a name but by an act: *alladhī faṭara al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* — "the One who originated the heavens and the earth." The verb *faṭara* means to split, to cleave, to bring forth from nothing — to originate. It is the verb of verse 14 ("So be steadfast in faith in all uprightness ˹O Prophet˺—the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people") and the root of *fiṭrah*, the primordial nature on which human beings are created (30:30). Abraham turns not to anything *in* the heavens — star, moon, or sun — but to the One who *made* the heavens. This is the resolution of the celestial argument. Everything in the sky sets; the One who made the sky does not. The argument moved through created lights to their uncreated Source.

The description is a direct answer to the worship of celestial bodies: you worship the heavens' contents; I worship the heavens' Maker. It is also the answer that verse 73 prepared ("He it is Who created the heavens and the earth in truth") and that verse 1 opened the sūrah with. The sūrah's first words and Abraham's confession converge.

**"As a Ḥanīf"**

*Ḥanīfan* — "as a ḥanīf," "inclining to truth." The word *ḥanīf* is one of the Qur'an's key religious terms. Its root (*ḥ-n-f*) means to incline, to turn away from one thing toward another. A *ḥanīf* is one who turns away from all false religion toward pure monotheism — who inclines from the crooked to the straight. In pre-Islamic Arabia, the term was used for a small number of individuals who rejected idolatry and sought the religion of Abraham without belonging to Judaism or Christianity.

The Qur'an uses *ḥanīf* predominantly of Abraham (2:135; 3:67, 95; 4:125; 6:161; 16:120, 123) and of the pure monotheism he embodied (22:31; 30:30; 98:5). The most pointed statement is:

> "Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was one inclining toward truth, a Muslim. And he was not of the polytheists." (3:67)

For the Makkans, the word carried weight. They claimed Abraham as their ancestor and the founder of their sanctuary. The verse tells them what Abraham's religion actually was: *ḥanīfiyyah*, the turning of the face to the Creator alone, free of all association. Their idolatry was not the religion of Abraham but its negation. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was commanded to follow "Surely my Lord has guided me to the Straight Path, a perfect way, the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists" (6:161; 16:123), and he described his mission as the restoration of that religion: "I have been sent with the tolerant *ḥanīfiyyah*" (Aḥmad 22291).

**"And I Am Not of the Idolaters"**

*Wa mā anā min al-mushrikīn* — "and I am not of those who associate." The verse closes by restating the negation, so that the positive confession is framed on both sides by the rejection of *shirk*. Abraham says it in verse 78 ("I am quit of what you associate") and again here ("I am not of the idolaters"). The repetition is emphatic: there is no residue of association in his turning. The face is turned entirely and only toward the Creator.

The phrase also appears in 3:67, 16:120, and 16:123 as the defining mark of Abraham, and the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to say it in 6:161–163. It became the phrase by which the community defined itself against the idolatry around it.

**Abraham's Prayer of Opening**

The Prophet ﷺ incorporated this verse into his prayer. When he began the ritual prayer, he would say, after the opening *takbīr*:

> "I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth, as a *ḥanīf*, and I am not of the idolaters. Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my living, and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds; no partner has He. With this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims. O God, You are the King; there is no god but You. You are my Lord and I am Your servant..." (Muslim 771)

The opening of this supplication is verse 79; its continuation is verses 162–163 of this sūrah. Every prayer the Prophet ﷺ began with these words was a renewal of Abraham's confession — the turning of the face, five times a day, toward the One who made the heavens and the earth. The believer who learns this opening supplication makes Abraham's words his own.

**The Structure of the Confession**

Verse 79 contains, in a single sentence, the essential elements of monotheistic faith. An act of will: "I have turned my face." An object: "Him who originated the heavens and the earth." A disposition: "as a *ḥanīf*." And an exclusion: "I am not of the idolaters." Will, object, disposition, exclusion — the anatomy of *tawḥīd*. Each element is necessary. Without the act of will, faith is mere opinion. Without the right object, it is idolatry. Without the disposition of *ḥanīfiyyah*, it is unstable, liable to incline back. Without the exclusion, it is *shirk* dressed as faith.

**The Culmination of the Sūrah's Argument**

This verse is, in a sense, the destination toward which the sūrah's first seventy-eight verses have been traveling. The sūrah opened with the Creator of the heavens and the earth (v. 1) and the idolaters who set up equals to Him. It argued from creation, from history, from the idolaters' own instincts, from the nature of prophethood, and from God's knowledge and power. Now it presents, in narrative, the man who followed that argument to its conclusion and spoke it: I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth. What the sūrah has been arguing, Abraham did. The Makkans are invited to do the same — not as a novelty, but as a return to the religion of their father.

**The Verse for the Individual**

For the individual believer, verse 79 is a sentence to be said and meant. It may be said in the opening of prayer, as the Prophet ﷺ said it. It may be said in the morning, as an orientation for the day. It may be said in moments when other lords — the stars, moons, and suns of one's own life — rise and demand allegiance. Each time, it does what Abraham's saying of it did: it turns the face away from what sets and toward the One who does not. That turning is the whole of religion, and the verse gives it words.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:80

> **And his people argued with him. He responded, “Are you arguing with me about Allah, while He has guided me? I am not afraid of whatever ˹idols˺ you associate with Him—˹none can harm me,˺ unless my Lord so wills. My Lord encompasses everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. Will you not be mindful?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The People Respond**

Abraham has made his declaration (vv. 78–79). Now his people push back: *wa ḥājjahu qawmuh* — "and his people argued with him." The verb *ḥājja* (from *ḥujjah*, argument, proof) means to contend with arguments, to dispute. The confrontation is no longer one-sided. Having heard Abraham disavow their gods, the people marshal their case against him.

The Qur'an does not record their arguments here, but the commentators — al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī — reconstruct them from parallel passages. They argued from tradition: "We found our forefathers worshipping them" (21:53; 43:23). They argued from incredulity: "Indeed, this is something totally astonishing" (38:5). And they argued from fear: they threatened that their gods would harm him for his insolence — a threat implied by Abraham's response, which is largely about fear. This last was the standard weapon of idolatrous peoples; Hūd's people said the same: "All we can say is that some of our gods have possessed you with evil" (11:54).

**"Do You Dispute with Me Concerning God, When He Has Guided Me?"**

*Qāla a-tuḥājjūnnī fi'llāhi wa qad hadān* — "he said: Do you argue with me about God, when He has guided me?" Abraham's first response is astonishment. He has been guided by God Himself — shown the dominion of the heavens and the earth (v. 75), given certainty. How do they imagine that their disputation will move one in this condition? The question exposes the asymmetry: they argue from custom and threat; he speaks from guidance. Al-Rāzī notes that Abraham is not refusing to argue — he goes on to argue at length — but is pointing out that their arguments cannot touch what God has established in him.

The phrase "concerning God" (*fi'llāh*) also carries a note of reproach. The subject of dispute is God — His Oneness, His right to exclusive worship. To dispute about this, when the evidence has been displayed across the heavens, is to dispute about the most evident of matters.

**"I Fear Not the Partners You Ascribe unto Him"**

*Wa lā akhāfu mā tushrikūna bih* — "and I do not fear what you associate with Him." This answers the threat. His people warned that their gods would harm him; Abraham replies that he does not fear them. The reason is the one given throughout the sūrah: the idols can neither benefit nor harm (vv. 17, 71). To fear them is to attribute to them a power they lack. Abraham's fearlessness is not bravado; it is the logical consequence of his understanding. One does not fear a stone.

This fearlessness is one of the marks of *tawḥīd*. The idolater lives in fear of many things — of his gods' anger, of omens, of spirits, of the powers he has set up. The monotheist fears One. The Qur'an says:

> "So do not fear them" (3:175)

> "Is Allah not sufficient for His servant" (39:36)

The second verse describes exactly Abraham's situation, and the situation of the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah: threatened with the wrath of idols, and answered by the sufficiency of God.

**"Save as My Lord Wills"**

*Illā an yashā'a rabbī shay'an* — "unless my Lord should will something." Abraham qualifies his fearlessness with a recognition of God's absolute will. Al-Rāzī explains: Abraham fears nothing from the idols themselves; but if some harm were to come to him, it would come only by God's will — as a test, or for a wisdom of His — and not by any power of the idols. The exception thus reinforces the principle rather than weakening it. Even harm that appears to come from a created source comes only by God's permission. This is the doctrine the Prophet ﷺ taught Ibn ʿAbbās: "If the whole nation gathered to harm you, they could not harm you except with what God had written against you" (al-Tirmidhī 2516).

The qualification also displays Abraham's precision and humility. He does not claim invulnerability; he claims that the only source of what befalls him is his Lord. This is the confidence of one who knows where power lies, not of one who thinks himself beyond harm.

**"My Lord Encompasses All Things in Knowledge"**

*Wasiʿa rabbī kulla shay'in ʿilman* — "my Lord encompasses all things in knowledge." The verb *wasiʿa* means to be wide enough to contain, to encompass. God's knowledge encompasses everything — a truth the sūrah stated with unforgettable particularity in verse 59. Abraham invokes it here as the foundation of his trust: whatever happens to him will happen within the knowledge of his Lord, according to His wisdom. Nothing can come from the idols or from his people that God does not know and has not permitted. The phrase appears in similar form in 20:98, 40:7, and 65:12, and its fullest expression is in the Throne Verse: "He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them, but no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺" (2:255).

**"Will You Not, Then, Remember?"**

*A-fa-lā tatadhakkarūn* — "will you not then take heed?" The verb *tadhakkara* means to remember, to be reminded, to take a lesson — from *dhikr*. Abraham ends with an appeal. He does not curse his people or dismiss them; he asks them to remember. What should they remember? What they already know in their *fiṭrah*: that the One who made the heavens is the Lord, that what sets is not divine, that stones cannot harm. The truth is not foreign to them; it is buried under custom and fear, and it needs only to be recalled.

The Qur'an frequently ends arguments with this appeal (cf. 6:152; 7:3; 10:3; 11:24, 30; 16:17; 23:85; 27:62; 32:4; 37:155; 45:23; 69:42). It presumes that the hearer has the capacity to recognize truth and needs only to be reminded of it. This is a respectful form of argument: it treats the opponent as a rational being capable of remembering, not as an enemy to be crushed.

**The Verse as a Model for Debate**

Verse 80 shows how a person of guidance responds to hostile argument. He does not become defensive; he notes calmly that he has been guided. He does not respond to threats with fear or counter-threats; he states that he fears only God. He does not claim more than he knows; he qualifies his confidence with submission to God's will. He grounds his position in God's attributes — here, His knowledge. And he ends with an invitation to remember rather than a condemnation. The Prophet ﷺ, facing the Quraysh with the same arguments and threats, was given this model, and every believer who must defend his faith is given it too.

**Fear and Its Objects**

The verse's deepest teaching concerns fear. What a person fears reveals what he believes has power over him. Abraham's people feared their gods, and their fear was the proof of their *shirk*: they attributed to created things a power that belongs to God. Abraham feared God alone, and his fearlessness before the idols was the proof of his *tawḥīd*. The question the verse puts to every reader is: what do you fear? Loss of wealth, disapproval of people, the power of the strong, the malice of enemies, omens, fate? Every fear of a created thing as an independent power is a trace of association. The remedy is the one Abraham states: my Lord encompasses all things in knowledge; nothing befalls me but what He wills; therefore I fear Him, and Him alone.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:81

> **And how should I fear your associate-gods, while you have no fear in associating ˹others˺ with Allah—a practice He has never authorized? Which side has more right to security? ˹Tell me˺ if you really know!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Turning the Threat Around**

Verse 80 recorded Abraham's people threatening him with the wrath of their gods, and his reply that he does not fear them. Verse 81 develops the reply into a counter-argument that reverses the positions: *wa kayfa akhāfu mā ashraktum wa lā takhāfūna annakum ashraktum bi'llāhi mā lam yunazzil bihi ʿalaykum sulṭānan* — "and how should I fear what you associate, while you do not fear that you have associated with God that for which He has sent down to you no authority?"

The structure is a comparison of fears. You want me to fear your idols. But consider what *you* are doing: you have set up partners to the Creator of the heavens and the earth — the One who actually holds all power — and you do this without any fear. Which of us is behaving irrationally? I decline to fear things that cannot harm; you decline to fear the One who can. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī explain that Abraham expresses astonishment that they could expect him to fear helpless idols while they themselves are fearless in committing the gravest offense against the only Being worth fearing.

**"For Which He Has Sent Down to You No Authority"**

The word *sulṭān* means authority, warrant, proof — the power of a valid argument or a divine sanction. Abraham's point is that their *shirk* rests on nothing. God has sent no revelation authorizing the worship of partners; there is no proof from reason; there is only inherited custom. The Qur'an makes this charge repeatedly:

> "These ˹idols˺ are mere names that you and your forefathers have made up—a practice Allah has never authorized" (53:23)

> "Yet they worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and of which they have no knowledge" (22:71)

> "Or have We sent down to them an authority which attests to what they associate ˹with Him˺" (30:35)

The phrase appears in 7:33 and 7:71, 12:40, and elsewhere as the Qur'an's standing demand: produce your proof. Idolatry, in every form, has never been able to produce it. It rests on assertion, tradition, and desire, not on any authority God has given.

**"So Which of the Two Parties Has Greater Right to Security?"**

*Fa-ayyu al-farīqayni aḥaqqu bi'l-amn* — "so which of the two groups is more deserving of security?" Abraham now poses the decisive question. Two parties stand facing each other: one that worships the Creator alone and fears Him alone, and one that worships created things without authority and fears everything but Him. Which of the two has a right to feel secure — secure from divine punishment, secure in the truth of its position, secure in the face of what is coming?

The word *amn* means security, safety, freedom from fear. It is the opposite of *khawf*, fear, and the two words frame the whole exchange. Abraham's people tried to instill fear in him; he asks who actually has grounds for security. The answer, given in verse 82, is obvious once the question is posed correctly.

**"If You Know"**

*In kuntum taʿlamūn* — "if you know." The conditional is a challenge and an invitation. If you have knowledge, answer the question — and the honest answer condemns your position. The phrase also implies that they do have the knowledge to answer, if they would only consult it. As in verse 80's "will you not remember?", Abraham appeals to a capacity his people possess but do not use.

**The Logic of the Argument**

The argument in verses 80–81 is a reductio. Assume the idolaters' premise: that their gods have power and are to be feared. Then they should fear, above all, the Creator of those gods and of everything else. But they do not fear Him; they associate partners with Him freely. So they do not really believe that power is to be feared — or, if they do, they are inconsistent, fearing the lesser and not the greater. Either way, their demand that Abraham fear their idols is incoherent. The only coherent position is Abraham's: fear the One who has all power, and fear nothing else.

The argument also exposes the psychological reality of idolatry. Idolaters are typically anxious — fearful of omens, of angering this or that deity, of curses and spirits. Yet they are strangely fearless about the one thing that should concern them: their relationship with the true God. Abraham's question forces this inversion into the open. Fear is misplaced; security is claimed where it is least warranted.

**Security as the Fruit of Tawḥīd**

The verse establishes a theme that verse 82 will conclude: *tawḥīd* produces security, and *shirk* produces fear. This is not merely a claim about the afterlife; it is observable in this life. The person who knows that one God holds all things, who fears Him alone, and who has no partners to placate, lives with a settled heart. The person who has scattered his devotion and his fear among many powers lives with a divided and anxious one. The Qur'an states the general principle:

> "those who believe and whose hearts find comfort in the remembrance of Allah" (13:28)

Abraham's question — which party has greater right to security? — is the question every person must answer about his own life. The one who has placed his trust in what cannot fail has security; the one who has placed it in what sets has none.

**The Two Parties Then and Now**

The "two parties" (*al-farīqayn*) of the verse were, in the first instance, Abraham and his people. In the sūrah's context, they were the Prophet ﷺ with his followers and the Quraysh. The Quraysh threatened the Muslims with the anger of their gods and with worldly ruin; the Muslims stood on *tawḥīd* without worldly power. Which party had greater right to security? History answered within a generation: the party of *tawḥīd* triumphed, and the gods of Quraysh were reduced to rubble. But the deeper answer is not historical; it is the one verse 82 gives, and it holds regardless of worldly outcomes.

**Abraham's Rhetorical Mastery**

Al-Rāzī observes that the Qur'an presents Abraham as the master of argument — the prophet who breaks idols and then tells his people to ask the largest of them who did it (21:63), who confounds the king by asking him to bring the sun from the west (2:258), and who here turns his people's threat into a question they cannot answer. This mastery is not ornamental. It shows that the truth can be defended by reason, that argument has a place in religion, and that the prophets used it. Verse 83 will confirm that this argument was God's gift to Abraham and the means by which He raised him in rank.

**The Verse as a Question for the Reader**

Abraham's question has lost none of its edge. To anyone who fears the loss of worldly things more than he fears God, who placates powers and people while neglecting the One who holds all power, who lives anxiously among his "partners" while feeling secure about his standing with God — the verse asks: which of the two parties has greater right to security? And it adds, quietly: if you know.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:82

> **It is ˹only˺ those who are faithful and do not tarnish their faith with falsehood who are guaranteed security and are ˹rightly˺ guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer**

Verse 81 asked which of the two parties has greater right to security. Verse 82 answers: *alladhīna āmanū wa lam yalbisū īmānahum bi-ẓulmin ulā'ika lahumu al-amnu wa hum muhtadūn* — "those who believe and do not clothe their faith with wrongdoing — for them is security, and they are guided." Whether the words are Abraham's conclusion or God's confirmation of it, the commentators differ; the majority read them as the continuation of Abraham's speech, and the translation so renders them. Either way, they are the verdict on the question.

**"Who Do Not Obscure Their Belief through Wrongdoing"**

The verb *labasa* means to mix, to confuse, to cover one thing with another — the same verb used in verse 9 ("We would have confused for them what they confuse") and verse 65 ("confound you as factions"). Here it means to clothe or mix faith with *ẓulm* — to have faith but to overlay it with wrongdoing so that it is obscured. The condition for security is faith that is *not* so mixed.

The word *ẓulm* is the key. As discussed at verse 21, it means putting a thing in other than its proper place, and the sūrah has used it repeatedly for the idolaters. Its most general sense includes every kind of wrongdoing. Read in that general sense, the verse would seem to say that security belongs only to those whose faith is unmixed with any sin at all — a standard no one meets.

**The Companions' Alarm and the Prophet's Explanation**

This is exactly how the Companions first understood it, and they were alarmed. The report is recorded by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Ṭabarī:

> When the verse "Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing" was revealed, it was hard on the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, and they said, "Which of us has not wronged himself?" The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "It is not as you suppose. It is only as Luqmān said to his son: 'O my son, do not associate anything with God; indeed, association is a great wrongdoing (*ẓulm ʿaẓīm*).'" (31:13; al-Bukhārī 32, 3360, 4776; Muslim 124)

The Prophet ﷺ thus interpreted the *ẓulm* of this verse as *shirk* specifically, using the Qur'an to explain the Qur'an. The security and guidance promised belong to those who believe and do not mix their faith with association of partners with God. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī affirm this as the correct meaning. It fits the context exactly: the whole exchange between Abraham and his people has been about *shirk*, and the "two parties" of verse 81 were distinguished by whether they associated partners with God.

**Why Shirk Is the Ẓulm That Voids Security**

The Prophet's ﷺ explanation is not a softening of the verse; it identifies the precise wrong at issue. *Shirk* is the *ẓulm* that touches faith itself, because it places a created thing in the position that belongs to God alone — the ultimate misplacement. Other sins wrong oneself or others; *shirk* wrongs the relationship with God at its root, and it is the one sin the Qur'an says God will not forgive if one dies upon it (4:48, 116). Faith mixed with *shirk* is not merely imperfect faith; it is faith contradicted at its foundation. Faith mixed with lesser sins remains faith, though diminished, and the sinner remains within the sphere of security and guidance even as he needs repentance.

Al-Rāzī records a broader reading in which the verse commends those who join faith with good works generally, and this is not wrong as a description of the ideal; but the Prophet's ﷺ interpretation fixes the threshold. What voids security is *shirk*; what perfects it is the avoidance of all wrongdoing.

**"It Is They Who Have Security"**

*Ulā'ika lahumu al-amn* — "those — for them is security." The emphatic construction (*ulā'ika*, "those [and no others]") marks the believers as the party that has the right to security Abraham asked about. What kind of security? Security from eternal punishment, first of all — the fear that hangs over the idolater is lifted from the monotheist. Security in this life as well: the settled heart of one who fears one Lord and no partners. And security in the truth of one's position: the believer stands on ground that will not give way.

The Qur'an elsewhere connects security with faith:

> "There will certainly be no fear for the close servants of Allah, nor will they grieve" (10:62–64)

**"And They Are Rightly Guided"**

*Wa hum muhtadūn* — "and they are the guided." Security and guidance go together. The one who has *tawḥīd* is on the straight path; the one on the straight path has security, because the path leads where it promises. The idolaters, whatever their worldly power, have neither: they are astray, and their sense of security is false.

**The Report on the Marks of Security**

Ibn Kathīr records a report in which the Prophet ﷺ described those who have security and guidance by their conduct: "those who are thankful when they receive, patient when they are denied, seek forgiveness when they have done wrong, and forgive when they have been wronged." Whatever the grade of the report, its content describes how the security of *tawḥīd* manifests in character. The person secure in God is grateful in ease, patient in hardship, repentant in failure, and forgiving toward others — because his relationship with God is settled and he is not anxiously seeking security from creatures.

**The Verse in Islamic Theology**

This verse, with the Prophet's ﷺ explanation, became a foundational text in Islamic theology on the relationship between faith and sin. It established that sins short of *shirk* do not expel a person from faith or from the promise of eventual security — against the Khārijites, who held that major sins made one an unbeliever. And it established that *shirk* does void faith and forfeit security — against any laxity that would treat association as a minor matter. The mainstream position is drawn from this verse and the ḥadīth explaining it: the believer who sins remains a believer, under God's threat and eligible for His forgiveness; the one who associates has mixed his faith with what destroys it.

**Abraham's Argument Complete**

With this verse, Abraham's exchange with his people concludes. He was asked to fear the idols; he asked who deserves security; he answered that security belongs to those who believe without *shirk*. The argument moved from the celestial bodies (vv. 76–78) to the confession of the Creator (v. 79) to the dispute over fear (vv. 80–81) to the verdict on security (v. 82). It is, from beginning to end, an argument for *tawḥīd* — and the next verse will call it God's own.

**Security as a Present Reality**

Finally, the verse describes a present state, not only a future reward: "for them *is* security." The believer who has purified his faith from association has security now — in the midst of the Makkan persecution, in the fire into which Abraham was cast, in every circumstance where the powers of this world threaten. The security is not the absence of danger; it is the presence of a relationship that no danger can touch. Abraham in the fire said, "God is sufficient for me, and He is the best disposer of affairs," and the fire was made cool. The security of the verse is that sentence, lived.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:83

> **This was the argument We gave Abraham against his people. We elevate in rank whoever We please. Surely your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**God Claims the Argument**

The Abraham pericope closes with a divine comment on all that preceded: *wa tilka ḥujjatunā ātaynāhā Ibrāhīma ʿalā qawmih* — "and that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people." The word *ḥujjah* means an argument, a proof, a decisive case that establishes a claim and silences opposition. The demonstrative *tilka* ("that") points back to what has just been recounted. Al-Rāzī notes that it may refer to the argument about fear and security (vv. 80–82), to the celestial argument (vv. 76–78), or — most naturally — to both, the entire reasoning by which Abraham refuted idolatry.

What is striking is the possessive: "*Our* argument." God claims the reasoning as His own. Abraham voiced it, but God gave it. This settles the interpretive question that has hovered over the passage. Whatever Abraham's words about star, moon, and sun meant, they were part of an argument God had given him. His reasoning was not autonomous speculation that happened to reach the right answer; it was a proof bestowed by the One who "showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth" (v. 75). Reason, in the Qur'an's view, is itself a gift, and its sound use is guided.

**"Which We Gave unto Abraham"**

The verb *ātaynā* ("We gave") is the verb of bestowal. The argument was a gift, like the prophethood, the certainty, and the progeny that follow (v. 84). This teaches that clarity of thought about God — the ability to see through falsehood and articulate truth — is among the greatest gifts God grants, on a level with the other blessings the passage lists. One should ask for it, as the Prophet ﷺ asked: "O God, show me the truth as truth and grant me to follow it, and show me falsehood as falsehood and grant me to avoid it."

**"Against His People"**

The argument was given *ʿalā qawmih* — "against his people." A *ḥujjah* is directed at an opponent; it is meant to establish a case against someone. God armed Abraham for a specific confrontation with specific people, and the argument was fitted to them: to astrologers and star-worshippers, an argument from the setting of stars; to those who threatened him with idols, an argument about who truly deserves fear. The Qur'an elsewhere shows Abraham with other arguments fitted to other opponents — the king who claimed to give life and death (2:258), the idol-worshippers who could not deny that their images do not speak (21:63–65). The lesson is that the defense of truth is not one-size-fits-all; it meets each error where it stands.

**The Qur'an's View of Argument**

The source commentary draws attention to a broader point that al-Rāzī makes forcefully. Some literalists disparaged the use of reasoned argument in religion, holding that one should simply accept revelation without rational defense. Al-Rāzī cites this verse against them: God Himself gave Abraham an argument, called it His own, and — as the next clause says — raised Abraham in rank *by means of it*. Argument is therefore not foreign to religion; it is a divine gift and a means of elevation. The Qur'an commands the Prophet ﷺ to "Invite ˹all˺ to the Way of your Lord with wisdom and kind advice, and only debate with them in the best manner" (16:125), condemns disputing "˹Still˺ there are some who dispute about Allah without knowledge, guidance, or an enlightening scripture," (22:8), and declares that "Had it been His Will, He would have easily imposed guidance upon all of you" (6:149). Reason, rightly used and rightly grounded, is a servant of faith.

**Why Abraham, and Why Here**

Al-Rāzī also observes that the Qur'an regularly invokes Abraham in the context of the Prophet's ﷺ disputes with the Makkans — as it does in this sūrah — because Abraham was the one figure all parties revered. The idolatrous Arabs honored him as their ancestor and the builder of their sanctuary; the Jews and Christians honored him as their patriarch. To show Abraham arguing for pure *tawḥīd* against idolatry was to confront the Makkans with the founder of their own tradition rejecting what they practiced. And to show him as neither Jew nor Christian but a *ḥanīf* (v. 79; 3:67) was to answer the exclusivist claims made by the People of the Book (2:135, 140; 3:65–68). Abraham is thus the Qur'an's model of argument and the chief witness in its arguments.

**"We Raise in Degrees Whomsoever We Will"**

*Narfaʿu darajātin man nashā'* — "We raise in degrees whom We will." The word *darajāt* (degrees, ranks, steps) appears in many contexts. The commentators list the possibilities: degrees of worldly provision and power (6:165; 43:32); degrees of reward for virtue (4:95–96; 9:20; 46:19); degrees of knowledge and wisdom (12:76; 58:11); and degrees among the prophets (2:253). Al-Rāzī reads the clause in context: God raised Abraham in rank *by virtue of the argument* He gave him. The one who is given understanding of truth and the ability to defend it is elevated thereby. This connects to 58:11: "Allah will elevate those of you who are faithful, and ˹raise˺ those gifted with knowledge in rank"

The phrase "whom We will" reminds the hearer that elevation is by God's choice. Abraham did not earn his rank by lineage or power; God chose him, guided him, gave him the argument, and raised him. This echoes verse 53 ("Does God not know best those who are thankful?") and anticipates verse 124 ("God knows best where to place His message"). Rank in God's sight follows His knowledge of who deserves it, not human expectations.

**"Truly Thy Lord Is Wise, Knowing"**

*Inna rabbaka ḥakīmun ʿalīm* — "indeed, your Lord is Wise, Knowing." The two names explain the raising in degrees. God raises whom He wills — but His will is wise (*ḥakīm*) and informed by complete knowledge (*ʿalīm*). He knows who is fit for elevation, and He elevates according to wisdom. The pairing forestalls any suggestion of arbitrariness: the choice of Abraham, the giving of the argument, and the raising in rank were all acts of wisdom grounded in knowledge.

The address "*thy* Lord" turns to the Prophet ﷺ. The same Lord who gave Abraham his argument and raised him is Muhammad's ﷺ Lord; He has given him the Qur'an — the argument against the Makkans — and will raise him as He raised Abraham. The verse thus closes the Abraham story by linking it to the Prophet's ﷺ situation: what God did for the father, He is doing for the son.

**The Structure of Verses 74–83**

The pericope has a clear architecture. Confrontation with the father (v. 74). Divine showing (v. 75). The three settings (vv. 76–78). The confession (v. 79). The people's dispute and Abraham's reply (vv. 80–81). The verdict on security (v. 82). God's claim of the argument and Abraham's elevation (v. 83). It moves from the rejection of falsehood, through the demonstration of truth, to the confession of faith, to its defense, to its reward. It is a complete account of how a human being comes to *tawḥīd*, holds it against opposition, and is honored for it — and God signs it as His own.

**What the Reader Takes from the Pericope**

The believer takes from these ten verses several permanent lessons. That *tawḥīd* can be seen by anyone who looks honestly at what sets and what does not. That the rejection of falsehood, even a father's, is required when truth is clear. That certainty is a gift to be sought. That one's confession must be both negative (free of what you associate) and positive (turned toward the Creator). That fear belongs to God alone and security follows from that. That argument in defense of truth is a divine gift and a means of elevation. And that the whole of this was given to Abraham — and through the Qur'an, to everyone who reads.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:84

> **And We blessed him with Isaac and Jacob. We guided them all as We previously guided Noah and those among his descendants: David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron. This is how We reward the good-doers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reward of Abraham**

Having declared that it raises whom it wills in degrees (v. 83), the sūrah now describes how God raised Abraham: through his progeny. *Wa wahabnā lahu Isḥāqa wa Yaʿqūb* — "and We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob." The verb *wahaba* means to give freely, as a gift — the root of *al-Wahhāb*, the Bestower. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī explain that these were granted to Abraham as a reward for his obedience and sincerity after he had left his people and his homeland for God's sake. The man who was willing to lose his father and his people for *tawḥīd* was given a line of prophets in return.

The Qur'an records this gift in the context of Abraham's emigration:

> "As I distance myself from ˹all of˺ you and from whatever you invoke besides Allah, I will ˹continue to˺ call upon my Lord ˹alone˺, trusting that I will never be disappointed in invoking my Lord" So when he had left them and those they worshipped other than God, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and each of them We made a prophet. (19:48–49)

> "And We blessed him with Isaac ˹as a son˺ and Jacob ˹as a grandson˺, as an additional favour—making all of them righteous" (21:72)

Isaac was the son granted to Abraham and Sarah in their old age (11:71; 51:28–30); Jacob was Isaac's son, given "in addition" (*nāfilah*) — a grandson promised alongside the son, so that Abraham saw two generations of prophets before his death.

**"Each We Guided"**

*Kullan hadaynā* — "each We guided." The gift was not merely of children but of guided children. Verses 84–90 are, in fact, a passage about guidance: the word recurs, and the passage ends with "those are the ones God has guided; so follow their guidance" (v. 90). Abraham's reward was that the guidance God gave him (v. 75, v. 80) was continued in his line. This is the fulfillment of the principle stated in verse 83: God raises in degrees whom He wills, and He raised Abraham by making him the father of prophets.

**"And We Guided Noah Before"**

*Wa Nūḥan hadaynā min qabl* — "and Noah We guided before." The verse reaches back beyond Abraham to Noah, the first of the great messengers, who lived long before him. Noah's inclusion serves several purposes. It shows that guidance did not begin with Abraham; it is a continuous stream from the earliest times. It sets the pattern that Abraham followed: Noah too stood alone against his people, argued with them, and was rejected by most (11:25–48; 71:1–28). And it establishes the genealogy that follows, since the prophets named next are described as Noah's progeny.

**"And among His Progeny"**

*Wa min dhurriyyatih* — "and from his progeny." The pronoun most naturally refers to Noah, the nearest antecedent, though most of the figures named are also Abraham's descendants. The phrase introduces a list of eight prophets across a vast span of history.

**The Eight Named**

*Dāwūd* — David: king and prophet, recipient of the Psalms, to whom the mountains and birds were subjected and iron was made soft (21:79–80; 34:10–11; 38:17–26). The Qur'an notes his repentance and his exemplary worship; the Prophet ﷺ said the most beloved prayer to God is the prayer of David, who slept half the night, prayed a third, and slept a sixth (al-Bukhārī 1131).

*Sulaymān* — Solomon, David's son: given a kingdom unlike any other, command over the wind and the jinn, understanding of the speech of birds (27:15–44; 34:12–14; 38:30–40). Al-Ṭabarī notes that his inclusion after his father reflects both descent and prophetic succession.

*Ayyūb* — Job: the model of patience under affliction, who lost wealth, family, and health and did not cease to call on his Lord until God restored all (21:83–84; 38:41–44). He is said to be a descendant of Isaac through Esau (al-Ṭabarī). The Qur'an says of him: "We truly found him patient" (38:44).

*Yūsuf* — Joseph: son of Jacob, whose story fills the twelfth sūrah — the "best of stories" (12:3) — and who embodies chastity, forgiveness, and trust in God through betrayal, prison, and power.

*Mūsā* and *Hārūn* — Moses and Aaron: the brothers sent to Pharaoh, deliverers of the Children of Israel, recipients of the Torah. Moses is the most frequently mentioned prophet in the Qur'an, and his narratives span many sūrahs (2:49–74; 7:103–155; 20:9–99; 26:10–67; 28:3–47, among others). Aaron was given to Moses as a helper in answer to his prayer (20:29–36).

**The Order of the List**

The names are not in chronological order (Joseph preceded Moses; Job's era is uncertain; David and Solomon came long after Moses). The commentators suggest that the ordering is thematic rather than temporal. Al-Rāzī notes that the list gathers figures who exemplify different forms of God's favor: David and Solomon were given kingship with prophethood; Job was given patience in affliction; Joseph was given both trial and authority; Moses and Aaron were given the mission against tyranny. The point is not history but the range of God's guidance — that it has been given to kings and to sufferers, to those raised high and those cast low, and that all of them are one family of faith.

**"Thus Do We Recompense the Virtuous"**

*Wa kadhālika najzī al-muḥsinīn* — "and thus do We reward the doers of good." The word *muḥsin* comes from *iḥsān* — excellence, doing what is beautiful, worshipping God "as if you see Him" (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8). The prophets named were *muḥsinūn*, and their reward — guidance, prophethood, honor, and blessed progeny — is the pattern of how God rewards excellence. Al-Ṭabarī explains that they were recompensed because they were patient and obedient in times of trial. Noah endured nine hundred and fifty years of rejection; Abraham the fire and the exile; Job the loss of everything; Joseph the well and the prison; Moses the confrontation with Pharaoh. The reward followed the trial.

The phrase "thus do We recompense" implies continuation. God's way with the *muḥsinūn* has not changed. The believer who does what is beautiful, and endures with patience, is under the same law of recompense as the prophets, in his measure.

**The Passage as Consolation to the Prophet**

For the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in Makkah, this list was a genealogy of his own situation. Each of these prophets had been rejected by his people, had endured hardship for the truth, and had been vindicated and honored by God. The list assured him that he stood in a line — that the pattern of trial followed by reward that God established with Noah and Abraham would hold with him. And it prepared for verse 90's command: "those are the ones God has guided; so follow their guidance."

**Guidance as Inheritance and as Gift**

The verse holds together two truths. Guidance runs in Abraham's line — his sons and grandsons were prophets, and the honor of his house was his reward. Yet each is said to have been guided by God individually ("each We guided"), and verse 87 will note that not all their relatives were chosen. Guidance is not automatically inherited by blood; it is given by God to whom He wills, and Abraham's family was honored because God chose to place it there. The Quraysh, who claimed Abraham's blood but not his faith, were reminded that the inheritance that matters is the guidance, not the lineage — a point the Prophet ﷺ made when he said, "Whoever is slowed by his deeds will not be hastened by his lineage" (Muslim 2699).

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:85

> **Likewise, ˹We guided˺ Zachariah, John, Jesus, and Elias, who were all of the righteous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Group**

The list of prophets continues: *wa Zakariyyā wa Yaḥyā wa ʿĪsā wa Ilyās* — "and Zachariah, John, Jesus, and Elias." Where verse 84 gathered figures associated with kingship, deliverance, and endurance, verse 85 gathers four prophets whose common feature, according to the commentators, is asceticism and devotion — men of the sanctuary, the wilderness, and the pure life, remote from worldly power. Al-Rāzī suggests that the groupings across verses 84–86 reflect different modes of prophetic excellence, so that the whole range of righteousness is represented.

**Zachariah**

*Zakariyyā* — Zachariah, the priest and guardian of Mary, the father of John. His story is told in 3:37–41, 19:2–15, and 21:89–90. Its center is a prayer: an old man with a barren wife, seeing the provision God gave to Mary in her sanctuary, asks his Lord for an heir, and is granted John. The Qur'an preserves the tenderness of his supplication:

> "Surely my bones have become brittle, and grey hair has spread across my head, but I have never been disappointed in my prayer to You, my Lord" (19:4)

Zachariah is the prophet of hope against evidence — of asking for what seems impossible and receiving it. His inclusion here, after the great kings and deliverers, reminds the reader that guidance is found in the quiet prayer of an old man as much as in the parting of the sea.

**John**

*Yaḥyā* — John the Baptist, son of Zachariah, given a name no one had borne before (19:7). The Qur'an describes him with singular praise: "as well as purity and compassion from Us" (19:12–14). He was "Allah gives you good news of ˹the birth of˺ John who will confirm the Word of Allah and will be a great leader, chaste, and a prophet among the righteous" (3:39). John is the model of youthful piety, chastity, and reverence, and tradition records his martyrdom at the hands of a tyrant. The Prophet ﷺ met him in the second heaven during the Night Journey, alongside Jesus (al-Bukhārī 3887).

**Jesus**

*ʿĪsā* — Jesus, son of Mary: the Word of God cast to Mary and a spirit from Him (4:171), born without a father, who spoke in the cradle, healed the blind and the leper, raised the dead by God's permission, and was given the Gospel (3:45–59; 5:110–118; 19:16–36). The Qur'an honors him as one of the five Messengers of Firm Resolve and clears him of the divinity attributed to him: "The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger" (5:75). His inclusion in a list of prophets descended from Noah and Abraham places him firmly within the line of human prophets and monotheistic guidance.

**A Point of Lineage**

Ibn Kathīr and al-Jalālayn note a significant implication. The verse continues the list begun in verse 84 as the "progeny" of Noah (and Abraham). Jesus had no human father; his descent from Noah and Abraham therefore runs through his mother, Mary. The verse thus establishes that progeny (*dhurriyyah*) may be reckoned through the female line. This point was of importance to those — Shīʿah and many Sunnīs alike — who held the Prophet's ﷺ descendants in particular esteem, since all of his descendants come through his daughter Fāṭimah; al-Ṭabarī and others record that this verse was cited as precedent. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others also used it to affirm that the grandsons of the Prophet ﷺ are truly his "sons," as the Prophet ﷺ himself said of al-Ḥasan: "This son of mine is a master" (al-Bukhārī 2704).

**Elias**

*Ilyās* — Elias, or Elijah, mentioned also in 37:123–132, where he calls his people away from the worship of Baʿl: "Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers" (37:125–126). The commentators offer several identifications: some report that he was a descendant of Aaron (al-Ṭabarī, al-Jalālayn); others identify him with Idrīs (19:56–57; 21:85), though the majority hold them distinct. What is clear from Sūrah 37 is his mission: a prophet who confronted a people that had turned to a false god, and whose people rejected him, "He was truly one of Our faithful servants" (37:132). His story is the pattern of Abraham's and Muhammad's ﷺ, and his placement in this list is a further link between the Prophet ﷺ and his predecessors.

**"Each Was among the Righteous"**

*Kullun min al-ṣāliḥīn* — "who were all of the righteous" (6:85). The word *ṣāliḥ* — righteous, sound, upright — describes one whose faith and conduct are in order. The Qur'an uses it as a summary of prophetic character: Abraham prayed, "Bless me with righteous offspring" (37:100), and he himself was "We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous" (2:130; 16:122). Solomon asked to be admitted "by Your mercy among Your righteous servants" (27:19). Joseph prayed to die a Muslim and be joined "with the righteous" (12:101).

That prophets — who held the highest ranks of humanity — are described simply as "among the righteous" teaches two things. First, righteousness is the essential thing, and prophethood is built upon it; the prophets were prophets *because* they were righteous, not righteous because they were prophets. Second, the category of "the righteous" is one that ordinary believers may enter. The Qur'an promises that "the prophets, the people of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous—what honourable company" (4:69). The prophets are the head of the company; the righteous believer belongs to it.

**The Diversity of the Righteous**

The four prophets of this verse were very different men: an aged priest, a young ascetic, a wonder-working messenger born of a virgin, a fiery reformer against Baʿl. They lived in different centuries and faced different trials. Yet the verse describes them with one phrase. Righteousness has one essence — soundness of faith and conduct before God — and many forms. The reader who cannot be a king like David or a deliverer like Moses may still be righteous like Zachariah, who prayed in his sanctuary and was heard.

**The Verse in the Prophet's Situation**

For the Prophet ﷺ, this verse named four predecessors whose experiences mirrored his own in particular ways: Zachariah, whose prayer was answered against all expectation; John, who was killed for his integrity; Jesus, whose people rejected and plotted against him; Elias, who called a people back from a false god and was heeded by only a few. Each had walked the road the Prophet ﷺ was walking. And each was "among the righteous" — the company in which God had placed him, and the company to which he was calling the Quraysh.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:86

> **˹We also guided˺ Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot, favouring each over other people ˹of their time˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Group**

The list of prophets concludes: *wa Ismāʿīla wa'l-Yasaʿa wa Yūnusa wa Lūṭā* — "and Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot." With these four, the passage has named eighteen prophets across verses 84–86 (with Abraham himself, and Muhammad ﷺ as the addressee, the count of prophets named in the passage's scope reaches twenty). The commentators observe that this third group is again thematically united: each of the four was a prophet whose mission involved a journey, an exile, or a foreign people — Ishmael settled in the valley of Makkah, Elisha succeeded Elijah in a troubled land, Jonah went to Nineveh, and Lot left Abraham's company for the cities of the plain.

**Ishmael**

*Ismāʿīl* — Ishmael, Abraham's firstborn, the son of Hagar, whom Abraham settled with his mother in the barren valley of Makkah at God's command (14:37), and with whom Abraham raised the foundations of the Kaʿbah:

> "And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺" (2:127)

The Qur'an describes Ishmael as "He was truly a man of his word, and was a messenger and a prophet" (19:54–55). He is the son whom, according to the majority of Muslim scholars, Abraham was commanded to sacrifice (37:102–107), and who submitted with the words, "O my father, do as you are commanded; you will find me, if God wills, of the steadfast." The source commentary notes that 19:54 calls him both messenger (*rasūl*) and prophet (*nabī*) — terms with a technical distinction: a messenger brings a new law or scripture or founds a community, while the broader category of prophet includes all whom God sends to warn and guide, whether or not with a new law.

Ishmael's placement in this list carried direct force for the Makkans. He was their ancestor, the co-builder of the sanctuary they guarded, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was his descendant. The verse reminded them that the religion of the Kaʿbah was Ishmael's religion — *tawḥīd* — and that the Prophet ﷺ was calling them back to it.

**Elisha**

*Al-Yasaʿ* — Elisha, the successor of Elijah. He is mentioned only here and in 38:48, where he is named with Ishmael and Dhū al-Kifl as "among the excellent" (*al-akhyār*). The Qur'an gives no narrative of him; the commentators record that he was a prophet to the Children of Israel who inherited Elijah's mission. His inclusion, without elaboration, teaches that not every prophet's story is told — the Qur'an says, "We have told you the stories of some of them, while others We have not" (40:78) — and that being among God's favored does not require fame.

**Jonah**

*Yūnus* — Jonah, "decree, and do not be like ˹Jonah,˺ the Man of the Whale, who cried out ˹to Allah˺, in total distress" (68:48), *Dhū al-Nūn* (21:87). He was sent to Nineveh, left his people in anger before God's permission, was swallowed by the great fish, and called out from the darkness: "There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except You. Glory be to You! I have certainly done wrong." (21:87). God answered him and delivered him, and his people — uniquely among those the Qur'an mentions — believed en masse when they saw the signs of punishment approaching, and the punishment was lifted (10:98; 37:139–148).

Jonah's story teaches that a prophet may err in judgment and be corrected, that repentance from the depths is heard, and that a whole people may be saved by turning to God before it is too late. The Prophet ﷺ said, "No one should say that I am better than Jonah son of Mattā" (al-Bukhārī 3412; Muslim 2376) — a caution against disparaging a prophet on account of his trial. And he taught Jonah's prayer as the supplication that God never fails to answer (al-Tirmidhī 3505).

**Lot**

*Lūṭ* — Lot, the nephew of Abraham, who believed in him and emigrated with him (29:26), and was sent to the cities of the plain whose people practiced what no people had practiced before them (7:80–84; 11:77–83; 15:57–77; 26:160–173; 27:54–58; 29:28–35; 54:33–38). He was saved with his family, except his wife, when the cities were overturned. Lot's inclusion here, immediately after the Abraham narrative, connects the two: the man who left his father for God (Abraham) was joined by a nephew who left his people for God (Lot), and both were counted among the favored.

**"Each We Favored above the Worlds"**

*Wa kullan faḍḍalnā ʿalā al-ʿālamīn* — "and each We preferred over the worlds." The verb *faḍḍala* means to prefer, to give excellence or precedence to. The phrase "above the worlds" (*ʿalā al-ʿālamīn*) is understood by al-Ṭabarī and most commentators as meaning above all the people of their own times — each prophet was the most excellent human being of his age. The same phrase is used of the Children of Israel as a community (2:47, 122; 7:140), where it also refers to their era. The verse thus declares that in each generation, God's favored ones were the prophets, whatever the world thought of them at the time.

This was a pointed message in Makkah, where the "favored" were held to be the wealthy and powerful, and where the Prophet ﷺ and his followers were regarded as nobodies. The verse said: in every age, the ones God actually favored were the prophets and those with them — usually persecuted, usually few, and always vindicated.

**The Whole List, vv. 84–86**

The eighteen names of verses 84–86, together with Abraham, form the Qur'an's longest continuous list of prophets in one passage (the other extended list is 4:163). The commentators note the deliberate structure: three verses, three closing phrases ("thus do We recompense the virtuous"; "each was among the righteous"; "each We favored above the worlds"), and three groupings. Whatever the thematic principle, the cumulative effect is to display the breadth and continuity of God's guidance: from Noah to Jesus, across kings and ascetics, deliverers and exiles, the famous and the barely mentioned, one stream of *tawḥīd* runs through history, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stands at its end as its heir.

**"Favored" and the Recompense of Trial**

Each of the four prophets in this verse endured a particular trial: Ishmael the sacrifice and the barren valley; Elisha the burden of a fallen people; Jonah the belly of the fish; Lot the depravity of his city and the loss of his wife. Their "favor above the worlds" was not exemption from trial but excellence within it. This is the consistent teaching of the passage, stated in verse 84's closing phrase and confirmed here: the recompense of the virtuous is not a life without hardship but honor before God, in this world and the next, earned through patience in hardship.

**The Example for the Believer**

The believer reading this list is not a prophet, but he is invited into the company. The Qur'an says that those who obey God and His Messenger will be "And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be in the company of those blessed by Allah" (4:69). To read these names is to remember one's family — the family of faith that stretches back to Noah — and to draw from their examples what one's own trial requires: the submission of Ishmael, the quiet fidelity of Elisha, the repentance of Jonah, the steadfastness of Lot among a corrupt people. And it is to remember that the world's estimate of who is favored has always been wrong, and God's has always been right.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:87

> **And ˹We favoured˺ some of their forefathers, their descendants, and their brothers. We chose them and guided them to the Straight Path.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Extending the Circle**

Having named eighteen prophets by name (vv. 84–86), the verse now widens the circle without naming: *wa min ābā'ihim wa dhurriyyātihim wa ikhwānihim* — "and from among their fathers and their descendants and their brothers." Beyond those listed, there were others — ancestors, offspring, and kinsmen of the named prophets — whom God also chose and guided. The three categories cover the family in every direction: backward (fathers), forward (progeny), and sideways (brethren). Guidance ran through the whole kinship network of the prophets, though not to every member of it.

**The Partitive "From Among"**

The preposition *min* ("from among," "some of") is significant, and al-Jalālayn draws out its implication: *some* of their fathers, progeny, and brethren were chosen — not all. The families of the prophets included disbelievers. Abraham's father was an idolater (v. 74). Noah's son drowned in the flood, refusing to board the ark (11:42–43). Lot's wife was destroyed with her people (7:83; 66:10). Jacob's sons plotted against their brother Joseph before their repentance. Being related to a prophet was no guarantee of guidance. The verse honors the many in the prophets' families who were chosen while quietly acknowledging that others were not.

This teaches a fundamental principle: guidance is not transmitted by blood. God 'chooses' whom He guides, and His choice is not bound by lineage. The Qur'an stated this to Abraham directly when he asked about his descendants: "My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers." (2:124). The Quraysh, who prided themselves on descent from Abraham and Ishmael, were being told that this descent conferred nothing if they rejected the guidance those ancestors brought.

**"We Chose Them"**

*Wa'jtabaynāhum* — "We chose them and guided them to the Straight Path" (6:87). The verb *ijtabā* means to select, to choose out, to gather to oneself — from a root meaning to collect. God selected these individuals from among their families and gathered them to Himself. Al-Ṭabarī explains that to be 'chosen' here means to be chosen for God's religion, for the conveying of His messages, or — in a further sense — singled out for His love. The verb is used elsewhere of God's election of prophets: "Then his Lord chose him ˹for His grace˺, accepted his repentance, and guided him ˹rightly˺." (20:122, of Adam); "He ˹Who˺ has chosen you" (22:78, of the Muslim community).

Divine choice is a recurring theme of the sūrah. Verse 53 asked whether God does not know best the thankful; verse 83 said He raises in degrees whom He wills; verse 124 will say He knows best where to place His message. The verse here applies the theme to the families of the prophets: from among them, God chose.

**"And Guided Them unto a Straight Path"**

*Wa hadaynāhum ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm* — "and We guided them to a straight path." This is the phrase of al-Fātiḥah — *ṣirāṭ mustaqīm* — the path the believer asks to be shown seventeen times a day in prayer. The verse tells him who has walked it: the prophets and those chosen from their families. When he asks for "the path of those You have favored," these are the ones he means. The Qur'an confirms this in 4:69: "the prophets, the people of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous—what honourable company"

The path is described as *mustaqīm* — straight, upright, without crookedness. There is one such path, and all the prophets walked it. This is the Qur'an's insistence on the unity of revealed religion: Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad ﷺ did not bring different religions but one religion — submission to the one God — in different laws suited to different times. The verse describes them all as guided to a single straight path, and verse 90 will command the Prophet ﷺ to follow that same guidance.

**Choice and Guidance Together**

The verse pairs two divine acts: choosing (*ijtibā'*) and guiding (*hidāyah*). God chose them, and He guided them. The order matters. Choice precedes guidance; God's election of a person is the cause of that person's being guided, not its result. This is the Qur'an's consistent teaching on the priority of grace: "Whatever you ˹believers˺ spend in charity, it is for your own good—as long as you do so seeking the pleasure of Allah" (2:272); "You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills, and He knows best who are ˹fit to be˺ guided" (28:56). At the same time, God's choice is not arbitrary; it follows His knowledge of who is fit (v. 83: "your Lord is Wise, Knowing"; v. 124: "God knows best where to place His message"). Choice and guidance together express the truth that the guided cannot take credit for their guidance and yet were not chosen at random.

**The Balance between Family and Individual**

The verse holds two truths in balance. On one side, the prophets' families were the soil in which guidance grew: God chose from among their fathers, progeny, and brethren, and the concentration of prophets in Abraham's line was real. Righteous families produce righteous children more often than not; the environment of faith, the example of parents, and the prayers of the pious for their descendants all matter. Abraham prayed for his offspring (2:128; 14:35–40), and his prayers were answered across generations. On the other side, each individual was chosen individually, and some in the same families were not. Family gives opportunity; it does not give guarantee. Each person must receive the guidance for himself.

This balance addresses a perennial error in two forms. One form is the assumption that a good lineage or religious family suffices — the error of the Quraysh, and of anyone who rests on ancestral piety. The other is the despair of one who comes from a family without faith and assumes he cannot be chosen — but Abraham came from an idolater's house. The verse says: God chose from among the families of the prophets, and He chooses whom He wills. Neither presumption nor despair is warranted.

**The Verse for the Community**

Al-Ṭabarī's gloss that "chose" may mean "singled out for His love" gives the verse a warmth that its structure might hide. God did not merely appoint these people to a function; He gathered them to Himself in love. The straight path is the path of those God loves. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to seek this love: "O God, I ask You for Your love, and the love of those who love You, and the love of every deed that brings me closer to Your love" (al-Tirmidhī 3235). To be among those God has "chosen and guided to a straight path" is the highest thing a human being can hope for, and the verse names the company one hopes to join.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:88

> **This is Allah’s guidance with which He guides whoever He wills of His servants. Had they associated others with Him ˹in worship˺, their ˹good˺ deeds would have been wasted.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Naming What Has Been Described**

Verses 84–87 recounted the prophets whom God guided. Verse 88 names what they received: *dhālika hudā Allāh* — "that is the guidance of God." The demonstrative *dhālika* points back to everything the preceding verses described — the guidance given to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Noah, and all the rest. It was not their own achievement; it was God's guidance. This connects to the sūrah's repeated insistence that guidance belongs to God (v. 71: "the guidance of God is the true guidance"; v. 77: Abraham's "if my Lord does not guide me").

**"With Which He Guides Whomsoever He Will among His Servants"**

*Yahdī bihi man yashā'u min ʿibādih* — "He guides whoever He wills of His servants" (6:88). The phrase "He guides whoever He wills" occurs many times in the Qur'an (2:142, 213, 272; 10:25; 14:4; 16:93; 22:16; 24:46; 28:56; 35:8; 39:23; 42:52; 74:31). It affirms that guidance is a divine act and a divine prerogative. No one is guided by his own power, and no one — not even a prophet — can guide another by his own power. The prophets were guided because God willed to guide them; the same is true of every believer since.

The phrase "among His servants" (*min ʿibādih*) is a reminder that all — prophets and ordinary believers, guided and astray — are God's servants. Guidance does not change one's status as a servant; it perfects it. The prophets were the most perfect servants, not something more than servants.

**The Doctrine of Guidance**

The affirmation that God guides whom He wills raised a question the theologians debated at length: if guidance is God's will, what of human responsibility? The Qur'an's own answer, spread across many verses, is that God's will to guide is not arbitrary but responsive to the servant's state. He guides "Indeed, Allah leaves to stray whoever He wills, and guides to Himself whoever turns to Him—" (13:27; 42:13), "As for those who struggle in Our cause, We will surely guide them along Our Way" (29:69), and those who 'believe' (10:9; 22:54); He does not guide "the wrongdoing people" (2:258; 5:51), "˹such˺ disbelieving people" (2:264), or "the rebellious people" (5:108; 9:24). The servant's turning, striving, and believing are themselves enabled by God — yet they are real acts for which he is accountable. God's will and human choice operate at different levels: He wills to guide the one who seeks, and the seeking is both the servant's act and God's gift. The verse affirms the divine side of this relationship; other verses affirm the human side; the whole Qur'an holds both.

**"But Were They to Ascribe Partners unto God"**

*Wa law ashrakū* — "and if they had associated partners [with God]." The pronoun "they" refers to the prophets just named. The conditional is counterfactual: they did not associate, and the verse does not suggest they might have. It states what *would* have followed if they had, in order to establish a principle that applies to everyone.

**"All That They Were Doing Would Have Come to Naught"**

*La-ḥabiṭa ʿanhum mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — "surely what they used to do would have been rendered void for them." The verb *ḥabiṭa* means to be nullified, to become void, to come to nothing — used of a camel that eats poisonous herbage and swells up and dies, its apparent fullness being in fact its ruin. Deeds that are "*ḥabiṭ*" are deeds that seemed substantial but count for nothing.

The principle is stark: had even the prophets associated partners with God, all their good deeds — their worship, their patience, their teaching, their sacrifices — would have been erased. If this holds for the prophets, it holds a fortiori for everyone else. The Qur'an states the same to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ personally:

> "It has already been revealed to you—and to those ˹prophets˺ before you—that if you associate others ˹with Allah˺, your deeds will certainly be void and you will truly be one of the losers" (39:65)

> "Whoever associates others with Allah ˹in worship˺ will surely be forbidden Paradise by Allah" (5:72)

**Why Shirk Nullifies Everything**

Why does *shirk* have this uniquely destructive effect? Because all good deeds derive their value from being done for God. A prayer is valuable because it is worship of God; charity is valuable because it is given for God's sake; patience is valuable because it is endurance in submission to God. If the doer associates partners with God, the foundation on which every deed rested is removed. The deeds are not merely diminished; they lose the very thing that made them deeds of worth. This is the logic of verse 82: faith mixed with *shirk* is not partially valid faith but faith contradicted at its root.

The Prophet ﷺ conveyed God's own statement of the principle:

> God, Blessed and Exalted, says: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in needing no partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his association." (Muslim 2985)

**The Warning's Direction**

The verse's counterfactual about the prophets serves as a warning to two audiences. To the Makkans: you honor Abraham and Ishmael, and you have their blood; but if even they had associated partners with God, their deeds would have been void — so what of your circumambulations, your feeding of pilgrims, and your maintenance of the sanctuary, all done in the midst of *shirk*? The Qur'an says elsewhere that the idolaters' maintenance of the mosque counts for nothing: "It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while they openly profess disbelief" (9:17). And to the believers: no rank, no achievement, no history of service protects against the nullifying power of *shirk*. If the prophets themselves were under this law, no one is above it.

**The Severity and the Mercy**

The verse's severity is real, but it should be understood together with the mercy that surrounds it in the sūrah. God has prescribed mercy upon Himself (vv. 12, 54). He forgives all sins for those who repent (39:53). He forgives everything except *shirk* to whom He wills, and *shirk* itself to whoever repents of it before death (4:48; 25:68–70). The verse does not say that a person who once associated is lost; it says that association, persisted in, voids deeds. The Companions who had been idolaters before Islam were told that Islam wipes out what came before it (Muslim 121). The severity is against the state of *shirk*, not against the person who has left it.

**Guidance and Its Opposite in One Verse**

The verse holds together the greatest gift and the greatest loss. The first half describes God's guidance, given to the prophets and to whom He wills. The second half describes what would nullify even that: association of partners. The juxtaposition teaches that guidance is not a possession that, once received, is secure regardless of what one does with it. It is held on the condition of *tawḥīd*. The prophets held it perfectly; the believer holds it as best he can; and the one thing that would take it entirely is the one thing the whole sūrah has been warning against.

**The Practical Vigilance**

For the believer, the verse instills vigilance against *shirk* in all its forms — not only the worship of idols, which few are tempted by, but the subtler forms the Prophet ﷺ warned of: showing off in worship, which he called "the lesser *shirk*" (Aḥmad 23630); swearing by other than God (al-Tirmidhī 1535); attributing outcomes to created causes as if they acted independently (al-Bukhārī 846, on attributing rain to the stars); and trusting in amulets and omens (Aḥmad 17422). Each is a small crack in the foundation on which all deeds rest. The verse's warning about the prophets is meant to make the believer guard that foundation as the most precious thing he has.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:89

> **Those were the ones to whom We gave the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood. But if these ˹pagans˺ disbelieve in this ˹message˺, then We have already entrusted it to a people who will never disbelieve in it.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Gifts**

The verse returns to the prophets named in verses 84–86 and specifies what God gave them: *ulā'ika alladhīna ātaynāhumu al-kitāba wa'l-ḥukma wa'l-nubuwwah* — "those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, judgment, and prophethood." Three gifts, in ascending intimacy with God.

*Al-Kitāb* — the Book: scripture, revealed guidance in written or preserved form. Not every prophet received a scripture of his own, but the prophets as a body were the recipients and custodians of God's Books — the Scrolls of Abraham, the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel — and each was sent within a scriptural tradition. The word here may be read collectively: the prophets were the people of the Book in the truest sense.

*Al-Ḥukm* — judgment: al-Ṭabarī explains this as either the knowledge of the Book and its rulings — the ability to understand and apply scripture — or the sound intellect and wisdom that grant a prophet profound understanding. The Qur'an speaks of God giving *ḥukm* to Lot (21:74), David and Solomon (21:79), Moses (26:21; 28:14), and John "And We granted him wisdom while ˹he was still˺ a child," (19:12). It is the discerning wisdom that turns knowledge into right decision. The parallel expression "the Book and wisdom" (*al-ḥikmah*) appears in many verses (2:129, 151; 3:81, 164; 4:54, 113; 62:2), and the two terms overlap.

*Al-Nubuwwah* — prophethood: the office itself, the being chosen by God to receive revelation and convey it. This is the highest of the three, for it is the direct relationship with God from which the other two flow.

The three together describe complete religious authority: revealed text, wise understanding, and divine commission. The prophets had all three; no one after them has the third, and this is why the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is the Seal.

**"So If They Do Not Believe in Them"**

*Fa-in yakfur bihā hā'ulā'* — "so if these disbelieve in them." The pronoun "these" (*hā'ulā'*) shifts the reference to the Prophet's ﷺ contemporaries — the Makkans, who were hearing the sūrah recited. "Them" (*bihā*) refers to the three gifts — the Book, judgment, and prophethood — now embodied in the Qur'an and in Muhammad ﷺ. The verse thus makes a transition: from the prophets of the past, who were given these things, to the present recipients of the same things, and to the people who reject them.

The conditional ("if these disbelieve") describes the actual situation: the Quraysh were rejecting the Book and the Prophet ﷺ. The verse contemplates their rejection and states what follows from it.

**"We Have Entrusted Them to a People Who Will Not Disbelieve in Them"**

*Fa-qad wakkalnā bihā qawman laysū bihā bi-kāfirīn* — "then We have already entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them." The verb *wakkala* means to entrust, to commit to someone's charge — the root of *wakīl* (guardian, trustee; cf. v. 66). God has entrusted the Book, judgment, and prophethood to a people who will believe in them, guard them, and carry them forward. The rejection of the Quraysh will not cause the message to fail; it has been placed in safe hands.

Who are these people? The commentators offer several identifications. Al-Jalālayn: the Emigrants and the Helpers — the Makkans who believed and the Madinans who received them. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Ṭūsī: the Helpers of Madīnah specifically, who would embrace the Prophet ﷺ when his own city rejected him. Al-Ṭūsī also records: the prophets themselves, who all believed in one another and in the revelation each brought. Others include the angels, or all believers to the end of time. The readings are complementary. The verse announces, in Makkah, that the message has a people — and the years that followed identified them: the Companions who emigrated, the Anṣār who welcomed, and every generation since that has preserved the Qur'an and followed the Prophet ﷺ.

The Qur'an makes the same announcement in Madīnah:

> "Whoever among you abandons their faith, Allah will replace them with others who love Him and are loved by Him" (5:54)

> "If you ˹still˺ turn away, He will replace you with another people" (47:38)

**The Independence of the Truth from Its Rejecters**

The verse's central teaching is that the truth does not depend on any particular audience accepting it. The Quraysh imagined that their rejection was decisive — that if the leaders of Makkah refused Muhammad ﷺ, his mission would come to nothing. The verse tells them that God has already provided for the message's survival. It will be carried by others. Their refusal harms only themselves.

This principle is stated for the Prophet's ﷺ consolation as much as for the Makkans' warning. He had grieved over his people's denial (vv. 33–35). The verse assures him: the Book, judgment, and prophethood you carry are not in danger. Whether Quraysh believe or not, God has entrusted them to a people who will. The Prophet's ﷺ task was to convey; the message's future was in God's hands and would be secured through whomever He chose.

**The Fulfilment**

History bore out the verse with precision. The Quraysh as a body rejected the Prophet ﷺ for thirteen years and drove him from Makkah. The Helpers of Madīnah — a people who had no tribal obligation to him — received him, pledged to defend him, and became the base from which the religion spread.
