Within a decade, the message the Quraysh had rejected was carried by an *ummah*; within a century, from Spain to India. And the Quraysh themselves, in the end, joined the people to whom the message had been entrusted — not as its custodians but as latecomers to it. The verse had told them, at the moment of their rejection, exactly what would happen.

**The Continuing Trust**

The verse also describes a continuing reality. In every generation, the Book, judgment, and prophethood are entrusted to "a people who will not disbelieve in them" — the community that memorizes the Qur'an, studies its meaning, follows the Prophet ﷺ, and transmits all of this to the next generation. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "There will not cease to be a group of my community manifest upon the truth, unharmed by those who forsake them, until the command of God comes." (Muslim 1920)

To be among this people is a trust (*wakālah*). The believer who receives the Qur'an receives it as something entrusted, to be guarded and passed on. The verse's word for what God did — *wakkalnā*, "We entrusted" — makes every believer a trustee.

**Reading the Verse Today**

Whenever the message of the prophets is rejected — by a society, a generation, a family, or a powerful class — this verse applies. The rejection is real and painful, but it is not decisive. God has entrusted His guidance to those who will not reject it, and He raises them up where and when He wills. The one who conveys the truth and sees it refused should remember the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah, hearing this verse, not knowing yet who the "people" would be — and should trust, as he did, that they exist and that God will bring them.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:90

> **These ˹prophets˺ were ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah, so follow their guidance. Say, “I ask no reward of you for this ˹Quran˺—it is a reminder to the whole world.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command That the List Was Leading To**

Verses 84–89 named eighteen prophets, described their guidance, their election, and the gifts they received. Verse 90 delivers the point of the whole passage: *ulā'ika alladhīna hadā Allāhu fa-bi-hudāhumu'qtadih* — "those are the ones God has guided, so follow their guidance." The demonstrative *ulā'ika* gathers all the prophets named; the imperative *iqtadih* commands the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to take them as his models.

The verb *iqtadā* means to follow as an example, to pattern oneself after — a *qudwah* is a model or exemplar. The command is not "follow them" but "follow *their guidance*" (*bi-hudāhum*). The distinction is precise. The prophets brought different laws suited to their times and peoples; the Prophet ﷺ is not commanded to adopt the Torah's rulings or the Gospel's specific dispensation. He is commanded to follow the guidance they shared: *tawḥīd*, patience under rejection, trust in God, uprightness, and steadfast conveying of the message. The final *-h* on *iqtadih* is a pausal letter that gives the word weight and finality, as though the whole passage comes to rest on it.

**The Prophet as Heir of All the Prophets**

The command establishes something important about Muhammad ﷺ. He is the heir and the culmination of the prophetic line. He was told to model himself on Noah's endurance, Abraham's *ḥanīfiyyah*, Job's patience, Joseph's forgiveness, Moses' courage, David's devotion, Jesus' compassion, and the qualities of all the rest. The Prophet ﷺ himself said: "I am the most worthy of Jesus son of Mary in this world and the next; the prophets are paternal brothers — their mothers are different but their religion is one" (al-Bukhārī 3443; Muslim 2365). Because he followed the guidance of all, his community is commanded to follow him, and in following him follows them all. The Qur'an says: "If you ˹sincerely˺ love Allah, then follow me" (3:31).

The scholars drew a jurisprudential principle from this verse: that the laws of previous prophets, insofar as they are confirmed by the Qur'an and not abrogated, may be followed by this community (*sharʿ man qablanā sharʿun lanā*). The verse's command to follow the guidance of the prophets was cited as support, alongside the Prophet's ﷺ practice of following, for example, the Abrahamic rites of pilgrimage and the fast of ʿĀshūrā' as observed by Moses.

**The Consolation in the Command**

For the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah, the command was also a consolation. The prophets whose guidance he was told to follow had all been rejected by their peoples. Following their guidance meant, among other things, enduring what they endured with the trust they showed. If his people mocked him, so had Noah's; if they threatened him, so had Abraham's; if they conspired against him, so had Jesus'. He was walking a road that had been walked by the best of humanity, and the road led where theirs had led.

**"I Ask Not of You Any Reward for It"**

*Qul lā as'alukum ʿalayhi ajran* — "I do not ask you for a payment for this ˹message˺" Having been told to follow the prophets, the Prophet ﷺ is told to say what every prophet said. The disclaimer of reward is the signature of the true messenger, repeated by Noah (11:29; 26:109), Hūd (11:51; 26:127), Ṣāliḥ (26:145), Lot (26:164), Shuʿayb (26:180), and Muhammad ﷺ himself (38:86; 42:23). Sūrah 36 makes it a criterion by which to recognize a true messenger: "Follow those who ask no reward of you, and are ˹rightly˺ guided" (36:21).

The disclaimer answers a suspicion the Makkans harbored: that the Prophet ﷺ sought wealth, power, or status through his preaching. He asks nothing — no fee for the Qur'an, no tribute for guidance, no position for himself. This was borne out by his life: he died with his armor pawned to a Jew for barley (al-Bukhārī 2916), having refused the mountains of Makkah turned to gold (al-Tirmidhī 2347). A message brought at no charge by one who could have demanded any price is a message brought for God's sake alone.

The principle has a wider application. Those who teach the Qur'an and call to God should not make the message a means of worldly gain. The scholars permitted a livelihood for those devoted to teaching, on the model of the Companions who were provided for, but they warned sternly against selling religion — against tailoring the message to those who pay, or preaching for status and applause. The Prophet's ﷺ "I ask no reward" is the standard.

**"It Is Naught but a Reminder for the Worlds"**

*In huwa illā dhikrā li'l-ʿālamīn* — "It is certainly We Who have revealed the Reminder, and it is certainly We Who will preserve it" The "it" is the Qur'an. It is called *dhikrā* — a reminder, a remembrance — because it brings to mind what human beings already know in their *fiṭrah* and have forgotten: their Creator, their purpose, their return. The Qur'an calls itself *dhikr* and *dhikrā* many times (15:9; 16:44; 21:50; 38:1; 43:44; 68:52; 81:27).

The phrase "for the worlds" (*li'l-ʿālamīn*) is a claim of universality. Al-Rāzī notes that the Qur'an's message is not limited to the Arabs or to any people; it is a reminder for all — humanity and jinn, in every land and every age. The same phrase closes 12:104, 38:87, 68:52, and 81:27. It distinguishes the Qur'an from the previous scriptures, which were addressed to particular communities, and it corresponds to the Prophet's ﷺ description of himself as "sent to all people" (al-Bukhārī 335; Muslim 521) and "a mercy to the worlds" (21:107).

There is a pointed contrast within the verse. The Prophet ﷺ asks nothing from the Makkans; the Qur'an offers everything to the worlds. He takes no reward; he gives a reminder to all creation. The direction of benefit is entirely from the message to its hearers, and the Makkans who rejected it were rejecting a gift.

**Why "Reminder" and Not "Instruction"**

The choice of *dhikrā* over words meaning teaching or instruction reflects the Qur'an's understanding of the human condition. Human beings are not blank slates needing to be informed of God for the first time; they are creatures who knew Him in the primordial covenant (7:172), whose nature inclines to Him (30:30), and who have forgotten. The Qur'an reminds. This is why its arguments — from creation, from history, from the storm at sea — work by appeal to what the hearer already senses. Abraham's "will you not remember?" (v. 80) is the whole method.

**The Verse as Closure**

Verse 90 closes the great central section on prophethood (vv. 74–90). It began with Abraham's confrontation with his father and ends with the command to follow the guidance of Abraham and all the prophets, delivered without charge as a reminder to the worlds. Everything between — the setting of the celestial bodies, the dispute over fear, the list of the guided, the warning against *shirk*, the entrusting of the message to a believing people — has been building to this: the Prophet ﷺ is the heir of all the prophets, and his Book is the reminder for all the worlds. The Makkans who claimed Abraham's blood were being offered Abraham's guidance, from Abraham's heir, at no cost. The next verse will turn to those who denied that God had sent anything to anyone.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:91

> **And they have not shown Allah His proper reverence when they said, “Allah has revealed nothing to any human being.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who then revealed the Book brought forth by Moses as a light and guidance for people, which you split into separate sheets—revealing some and hiding much? You have been taught ˹through this Quran˺ what neither you nor your forefathers knew.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Allah ˹revealed it˺!” Then leave them to amuse themselves with falsehood.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Failing to Measure God**

*Wa mā qadarū Allāha ḥaqqa qadrih* — "and they did not estimate God with the estimate due to Him." The verb *qadara* means to measure, to assess, to appreciate the magnitude of something. The phrase means that they failed to grasp God's greatness — they held a conception of Him so diminished that they could say what follows. The same phrase opens 22:74 and 39:67, the latter continuing: "They have not shown Allah His proper reverence—when on the Day of Judgment the ˹whole˺ earth will be in His Grip, and the heavens will be rolled up in His Right Hand" To fail to measure God rightly is the root of every theological error, and the verse identifies a specific instance.

**"God Has Not Sent Down Aught to Any Human Being"**

*Idh qālū mā anzala Allāhu ʿalā basharin min shay'* — "when they said: God has not sent down anything to any human being." This is a denial of revelation as such — not merely of the Qur'an but of the very possibility that God communicates with human beings. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the statement fails to appreciate God's majesty, and al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zamakhsharī add that it fails to appreciate His mercy: a God who created human beings and then left them without guidance would be neither as great nor as merciful as He is. The one who thinks God would not send down guidance has measured Him too small.

**Who Said It?**

The commentators differ over the speakers. Several — al-Jalālayn, al-Wāḥidī — record that a group of Jews, or specifically a rabbi named Mālik ibn al-Ṣayf, came to debate with the Prophet ﷺ and in the heat of argument said, "God has not sent down anything to any human being." When the Prophet ﷺ asked, "Not even to Moses?", the man was caught, and the verse was revealed. Al-Ṭabarī, however, judges it more likely that the speakers were the Makkan idolaters, since the sūrah is Makkan and its dominant concern is the idolaters, and since the Jews as a body did not deny that God reveals to human beings. The verse's own argument — "who sent down the Book that Moses brought?" — works against either audience: against the Jews, it exposes a contradiction with their own scripture; against the idolaters, who acknowledged Moses as a prophet of the People of the Book, it exposes a denial they could not consistently maintain. Verse 92 will note the possibility that this verse is Madinan.

**"Say: Who Sent Down the Book That Moses Brought?"**

*Qul man anzala al-kitāba alladhī jā'a bihi Mūsā* — "Say: Who sent down the Book that Moses brought?" The Prophet ﷺ answers the denial with a question about a fact no one in Arabia disputed: that Moses brought the Torah. If God has never sent anything to a human being, where did the Torah come from? The Jews revered it as revealed; the Christians accepted it; even the idolaters knew of it and respected the People of the Book for possessing it. The denial of all revelation collapses against the one revelation everyone acknowledged.

**"As a Light and a Guidance for Mankind"**

*Nūran wa hudan li'l-nās* — "a light and a guidance for people." The Torah is honored with two of the Qur'an's highest descriptions of revelation. Light dispels darkness and allows one to see; guidance shows the way. The same pair is applied to the Torah in 5:44 ("Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light") and to the Gospel in 5:46. The Qur'an does not disparage the earlier scriptures; it affirms their divine origin and their value, and it accuses their custodians — not the books — of concealment and alteration. This honoring of the Torah in the very verse that argues against the deniers is characteristic: the Qur'an's argument for revelation includes the previous revelations, all of which came from the same God.

**"Which You Make into Parchments That You Display, While Hiding Much"**

*Tajʿalūnahu qarāṭīsa tubdūnahā wa tukhfūna kathīran* — "you make it into parchments that you show, while you conceal much." The word *qirṭās* (pl. *qarāṭīs*) means a sheet of writing material — papyrus, parchment, paper. The Torah had been written out on separate sheets, some of which were displayed and read publicly while much was hidden. The Qur'an charges the custodians of the Torah with selective disclosure in several places (2:42, 140, 146, 159, 174; 3:71, 187; 5:15). Al-Ṭabarī and others record that what was concealed included the descriptions of the coming Prophet ﷺ and certain legal rulings, such as the penalty of stoning, which the Jews of Madīnah tried to hide until the Prophet ﷺ had the Torah brought and the passage was found (al-Bukhārī 3635; Muslim 1699).

Al-Ṭabarī notes and prefers an alternative reading — *yajʿalūnahu... yubdūnahā... yukhfūna* — in the third person: "which *they* make into parchments *they* display, while hiding much." On this reading the Prophet ﷺ is speaking to the idolaters *about* the Jews, not to the Jews directly; the argument runs: you say God has sent nothing to anyone, yet you know the People of the Book have a Book from Moses, which they write on parchments. Both readings are transmitted; the sense is the same.

**"And You Were Taught That Which You Knew Not, Neither You nor Your Fathers"**

*Wa ʿullimtum mā lam taʿlamū antum wa lā ābā'ukum* — "and you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers." The commentators offer several addressees. If addressed to the Jews, it means that the Torah taught them what they had not known (Ibn ʿAjībah), or that the Qur'an has now taught them things not in the Torah (al-Zamakhsharī). If addressed to the Arabs, it means that the Qur'an has brought them knowledge — of God, of the prophets, of the previous nations, of the Hereafter — that neither they nor their ancestors possessed. Al-Ṭabarī allows that it may address the believers. In every case, the clause is a further proof of revelation: the knowledge you now have, which you did not have and could not have acquired by your own means, came from somewhere — and that somewhere is what you deny.

**"Say: Allāh"**

*Quli'llāh* — "Say: God." The Prophet ﷺ asked, "Who sent down the Book that Moses brought?" Now he is instructed to answer his own question with a single word. The answer is so obvious that no one can dispute it, and the deniers cannot bring themselves to say it — so the Prophet ﷺ says it for them, as he did in verses 12 and 64. The one-word answer carries enormous weight: it names the One who sent the Torah and, by implication, the One who sent the Qur'an, and it exposes the denial of revelation as a denial of what everyone knows.

The Sufi commentators — Ibn ʿAjībah, al-Sulamī — heard in this command a general instruction: say "Allāh," inwardly and outwardly, in every situation; let His Name be the answer to every question and the refuge from every distraction; and leave all else. Whatever the merits of this extension, it captures the verse's movement: from the noise of denial to the single, sufficient Name.

**"Then Leave Them to Play at Their Vain Discourse"**

*Thumma dharhum fī khawḍihim yalʿabūn* — "then leave them in their vain talk, playing." After the answer has been given, the Prophet ﷺ is to leave them. The words *khawḍ* (plunging into idle talk) and *laʿib* (play) are the words of verses 68 and 70. The deniers' discourse about revelation is not a serious inquiry that deserves further engagement; it is play. Having stated the truth in one word, the Prophet ﷺ need not wrestle with them further. This is the same posture the sūrah has taught since verse 68: state the truth clearly, then disengage from mockery.

**The Argument's Force**

The verse's argument deserves restatement, because it is a model of economy. The denial: God has sent nothing to any human. The counter-question: then who sent the Torah? The evidence that the Torah exists and is revered: you write it on parchments and display it. The evidence that revelation has taught what could not otherwise be known: you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew. The answer: God. The conclusion: leave them. In six clauses, a universal denial of revelation is refuted by appeal to a fact the deniers themselves acknowledged. This is *ḥujjah* in the sense of verse 83 — an argument that closes the matter.

**What It Means to Measure God Rightly**

The verse opened by saying that the deniers did not measure God with His true measure. The implication is that the affirmation of revelation is part of measuring Him rightly. A God worthy of the name — the Creator of the heavens and the earth, the Knower of every leaf, the One who has prescribed mercy upon Himself — would not leave His creatures without a word. To deny revelation is to imagine a God too indifferent or too remote to speak, and such a God is not the God the sūrah has been describing. The believer measures God rightly when he expects His guidance, receives it with gratitude, and recognizes, in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an, the voice of the One who does not leave His servants in the dark.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:92

> **This is a blessed Book which We have revealed—confirming what came before it—so you may warn the Mother of Cities and everyone around it. Those who believe in the Hereafter ˹truly˺ believe in it and guard their prayers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Torah to the Qur'an**

Verse 91 argued from the Torah that God does send down revelation. Verse 92 turns to the present revelation: *wa hādhā kitābun anzalnāhu mubārak* — "and this is a Book We have sent down, blessed." The demonstrative "this" (*hādhā*) points to the Qur'an being recited. Having established that God sent the Torah to Moses, the verse now says: and this, too, is from Him. The parallel is exact — the same verb (*anzala*, "sent down") is used for both Books — and the implication is that the one who accepts the first has no consistent ground for rejecting the second.

**"A Blessed Book"**

*Mubārak* — blessed, full of *barakah*. The root *b-r-k* denotes abundant, enduring, and increasing good — the blessing that grows rather than diminishes. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī explain that the Qur'an is called blessed because of the vast benefit it contains for humanity: guidance in this life, salvation in the next, healing for hearts, and reward for every letter recited. The Qur'an applies the word to itself in 21:50, 38:29, and 44:3 ("a blessed night"), and the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Whoever recites a letter from the Book of God has a good deed for it, and the good deed is multiplied tenfold. I do not say that *alif-lām-mīm* is one letter; rather *alif* is a letter, *lām* is a letter, and *mīm* is a letter." (al-Tirmidhī 2910)

This is *barakah* in its precise sense: good that multiplies.

**"Confirming That Which Came Before It"**

*Muṣaddiqu alladhī bayna yadayh* — "He has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book in truth, confirming what came before it, as He revealed the Torah and the Gospel" The Qur'an confirms the previous scriptures — the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel — in their essential message: the Oneness of God, the sending of prophets, the moral law, and the Hereafter. This is a central Qur'anic theme, stated in many places (2:41, 89, 91, 97, 101; 3:3, 50, 81; 4:47; 5:46, 48; 10:37; 12:111; 35:31; 46:12, 30; 61:6). It positions the Qur'an not as a rival to earlier revelation but as its continuation and completion — the same God, speaking again, confirming what He said before and correcting what had been altered.

The confirmation also serves as evidence. A Book that came from an unlettered man in Arabia and agreed in substance with scriptures he had never read — while correcting details in ways the People of the Book could not refute — bears the marks of a common source. Verse 91 asked who sent the Torah; verse 92 says the Qur'an confirms it; the two together argue that the same Sender sent both.

**"That Thou Mayest Warn the Mother of Cities and Those around Her"**

*Wa li-tundhira umma al-qurā wa man ḥawlahā* — "Surely the first House ˹of worship˺ established for humanity is the one at Bakkah—a blessed sanctuary and a guide for ˹all˺ people" *Umm al-Qurā* — the Mother of Cities — is Makkah. The commentators give several reasons for the title. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Rāzī, and al-Zamakhsharī note that the Kaʿbah at its center was the first house of worship established for humanity (3:96); that Makkah was, by some accounts, the first city; and that it was the direction of prayer and the destination of pilgrimage for the surrounding towns, so that people gathered to it as children to a mother. Al-Rāzī and al-Bayḍāwī also record the tradition that the earth was spread out from beneath the Kaʿbah — an image, whatever its literal status, of Makkah's spiritual primordiality.

"Those around her" (*man ḥawlahā*) may refer to the Arabian Peninsula or, as al-Rāzī holds, to the whole world — since the Qur'an is "a reminder for the worlds" (v. 90). The verse names the immediate audience (Makkah), then extends outward without limit. The mission begins at the center and radiates.

The word "warn" (*tundhir*) recalls verse 19 ("that I may warn you thereby and whomever it reaches") and the definition of the Prophet's ﷺ role in verse 48. The Qur'an is a Book of warning first — it awakens people to the reality of judgment — and its blessing is inseparable from its warning.

**"Those Who Believe in the Hereafter Believe in It"**

*Wa'lladhīna yu'minūna bi'l-ākhirati yu'minūna bih* — "and those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it." The verse identifies who accepts the Qur'an: those who believe in the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the connection: belief in the reality of the Day of Judgment is the foundation of religious seriousness. One who believes that he will stand before God and answer for his deeds will take a Book that warns of that Day seriously; one who denies the Hereafter has no reason to. The Makkans' rejection of the Qur'an was rooted in their denial of resurrection (v. 29): a message about accountability is meaningless to those who deny it.

The verse thus explains, without polemic, why some believe and some do not. The variable is not intelligence or lineage but the orientation toward the Hereafter. This is a diagnostic tool of enduring value: resistance to revelation is very often resistance to accountability, and the argument for the Qur'an begins with the argument for the Day.

**"And They Are Mindful of Their Prayers"**

*Wa hum ʿalā ṣalātihim yuḥāfiẓūn* — "and they guard their prayers." The verb *ḥāfaẓa* means to guard, to maintain, to keep watch over. Those who believe in the Hereafter and in the Qur'an are marked by their care for prayer: its times, its conditions, its regularity, its inner presence. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that prayer is the pillar of the religious life, and belief that does not issue in prayer is suspect.

The connection between the three — belief in the Hereafter, belief in the Book, and guarding of prayer — is organic. Belief in the Hereafter makes one receptive to the Book; the Book commands prayer; prayer keeps belief in the Hereafter alive by turning one toward God five times a day. Remove any one and the others weaken. The Qur'an's first description of the God-fearing in Sūrat al-Baqarah has the same structure: "who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them," (2:3–4).

The Prophet ﷺ made prayer the criterion between faith and its absence:

> "The covenant between us and them is prayer; whoever abandons it has disbelieved." (al-Tirmidhī 2621; al-Nasā'ī 463)

Al-Rāzī cites this ḥadīth and notes, with the majority of scholars, that it refers most strictly to one who abandons prayer while denying its obligation; but the ḥadīth's severity — and the verse's placement of prayer alongside belief — shows how central prayer is to what it means to believe.

**The Verse as a Portrait of the Believer**

In its closing clause, the verse paints the believer in three strokes: he believes in the Hereafter, he believes in the Qur'an, and he guards his prayer. This is a compact description of the person the sūrah has been addressing and forming. He takes the future seriously, he takes the Book seriously, and he takes his daily meeting with God seriously. Against him stands the person of verse 91, who denies that God has sent anything to anyone, and the person of verse 70, who takes his religion as play. The verse invites the hearer to decide which portrait is his.

**A Possible Madinan Origin**

Some commentators note that this verse — along with verse 91 — may have been revealed in Madīnah, given its engagement with the People of the Book, and inserted here by the Prophet's ﷺ instruction. Al-Zamakhsharī mentions verses 20, 23, 91, 93, 114, 141, and 151–153 as possibly Madinan. Whether or not that is so, the verse's placement is fitting: after the argument from the Torah (v. 91), the affirmation of the Qur'an as its confirmation follows naturally, and the description of those who believe in it completes the contrast with those who deny.

**The Blessing That Confirms and Warns**

The verse holds together three functions of the Qur'an that might seem to pull apart: it is blessed (a gift), it confirms (a continuity), and it warns (a summons). A Book that only blessed would be comfort without demand; one that only confirmed would be repetition without newness; one that only warned would be threat without mercy. The Qur'an is all three. It comes as a blessing, it stands in the line of all God's Books, and it wakes the Mother of Cities and everyone around her to the Day for which they were created.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:93

> **Who does more wrong than the one who fabricates lies against Allah or claims, “I have received revelations!”—although nothing was revealed to them—or the one who says, “I can reveal the like of Allah’s revelations!”? If you ˹O Prophet˺ could only see the wrongdoers in the throes of death while the angels are stretching out their hands ˹saying˺, “Give up your souls! Today you will be rewarded with the torment of disgrace for telling lies about Allah and for being arrogant towards His revelations!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Kinds of Fabricator**

Verse 91 dealt with those who deny that God reveals anything. Verse 93 deals with the opposite error: those who falsely claim revelation for themselves or who belittle it. *Wa man aẓlamu mimmani'ftarā ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban* — "Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His signs" The rhetorical question is the Qur'an's formula for the gravest wrong (6:21, 144; 7:37; 10:17; 11:18; 29:68; 61:7). Here it introduces three offenders.

The first fabricates a lie against God in general — inventing false doctrines, false prohibitions, false gods, and attributing them to Him. This was the idolaters' characteristic sin, exemplified in their food taboos, which they claimed were God's commands (vv. 136–140, 143–144).

The second says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him — the false prophet. Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, and others record that the verse was understood to refer to Musaylimah of Yamāmah, the "Liar," who claimed prophethood in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime and produced crude imitations of the Qur'an, and to al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī of Yemen, who did the same. Both were destroyed within a short time — al-Aswad killed before the Prophet's ﷺ death, Musaylimah at the Battle of Yamāmah under Abū Bakr.

The third says, "Whenever Our revelations are recited to them, they challenge ˹you˺," — one who claims that the Qur'an is merely human composition and that he could produce its equal. The Qur'an records this boast from the Makkans: "This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but ancient fables" (8:31). The verse answers the boast by classifying it with the gravest wrongs.

**The Report about Ibn Abī Sarḥ**

Al-Wāḥidī and al-Zamakhsharī record that the verse was also connected with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ, who served for a time as a scribe of revelation. According to the report, as the Prophet ﷺ dictated a verse ending in a description of God, Ibn Abī Sarḥ anticipated the ending — suggesting "So Blessed is Allah, the Best of Creators" (23:14) — and when the Prophet ﷺ confirmed that this was indeed the revealed wording, the scribe concluded that he too could receive revelation. He apostatized, returned to Makkah, and rejoined Islam only at the conquest, when ʿUthmān interceded for him. He later served as a governor under ʿUthmān. The report is instructive as an example of how a coincidence can be misread by a mind inclined to self-exaltation, and how the claim "I could produce the like" arises.

Al-Ṭabarī and al-Jalālayn note that whatever the specific occasions, the verse is general: it condemns every claim to false revelation and every boast of being able to match the Qur'an.

**Why These Are the Greatest Wrong**

Why does the Qur'an rank fabrication against God as the greatest *ẓulm*? Because it corrupts the source of all guidance. A person who steals or lies to another harms a fellow creature; a person who invents a revelation, or attributes falsehood to God, poisons the well from which everyone drinks. Those who follow the false prophet are led astray; those who accept the invented prohibition bind themselves with what God never commanded; those who believe the Qur'an is human composition lose the guidance it offers. The harm is not to one person but to everyone who relies on the fabricator's word, and the offense is against the Truth itself.

**"If Thou Couldst See When the Wrongdoers Are in the Throes of Death"**

*Wa law tarā idhi'l-ẓālimūna fī ghamarāti al-mawt* — "and if you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death." The verse shifts abruptly from the description of the offense to a vision of its consequence. The word *ghamarāt* (sg. *ghamrah*) means overwhelming depths — the floods of water that close over a drowning man. The wrongdoers are pictured in the depths of death, overwhelmed, as the verses on the angels of death (vv. 61–62) described.

The phrase "if you could see" (*law tarā*) has appeared in verses 27 and 30 and will appear again; it invites the hearer to witness, in imagination, a scene from beyond the veil, and it leaves the apodosis unstated — "you would see something terrible" — because words fail.

**"And the Angels Stretch Forth Their Hands"**

*Wa'l-malā'ikatu bāsiṭū aydīhim* — "and the angels are stretching out their hands." The angels of death extend their hands toward the dying wrongdoers. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the stretching may be to seize the souls, to strike, or to torment — as 8:50 describes: "if you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieved, striking their faces and their backs." The image contrasts with the gentle taking of the believer's soul described in the ḥadīth of al-Barā' (Aḥmad 18534): for the believer, the angels come with fragrant shrouds and the soul flows out easily; for the disbeliever, the soul is dragged out like a skewer through wet wool.

**"Yield Up Your Souls!"**

*Akhrijū anfusakum* — "bring out your souls!" The command is harsh and mocking. The soul of the wrongdoer clings to the body, refusing to leave, dreading what awaits; the angels demand it. Some commentators read the command as an expression of the soul's extraction by force — "get your souls out," as one says to a debtor who withholds what he owes.

**"This Day Shall You Be Recompensed with the Punishment of Humiliation"**

*Al-yawma tujzawna ʿadhāba al-hūn* — "today you are recompensed with the punishment of humiliation." The word *hūn* means humiliation, disgrace, abasement. The punishment fits the crime. The fabricator exalted himself — claiming revelation, claiming to match God's Word, claiming to speak for God; his recompense is abasement. "This day" refers to the moment of death and what follows in the grave, or to the Day of Judgment which the dying already perceive as imminent; the commentators allow both, and the verse deliberately collapses the distance between death and judgment.

**"For Having Spoken Untruth against God, and for Waxing Arrogant against His Signs"**

*Bi-mā kuntum taqūlūna ʿalā Allāhi ghayra al-ḥaqqi wa kuntum ʿan āyātihi tastakbirūn* — "It is not for you to be arrogant here" Two crimes are named as the grounds of the punishment. The first is the fabrication already described: speaking untruth about God. The second is *istikbār* — arrogance, considering oneself too great to submit. This is the sin of Iblīs (2:34; 7:13; 38:74–75) and the characteristic attitude of the deniers toward God's signs (7:40, 133; 10:75; 23:45–46; 39:59; 45:31).

The two crimes are linked. It is arrogance that leads a person to claim revelation for himself, to boast that he could match the Qur'an, or to invent religion; and it is arrogance that prevents him from submitting to the signs God actually sent. The fabricator and the mocker share a single root: the refusal to be small before God.

**The Verse's Structure**

The verse moves from crime to punishment with a speed that mirrors the suddenness of death. One moment the fabricator is confident, inventing, boasting; the next he is in the depths of death, with the angels' hands stretched toward him and their voices demanding his soul. There is no interval for reconsideration. This is why the verse is placed here: after the arguments for revelation (vv. 91–92), it warns those who would respond to revelation not with denial but with counterfeit — and it shows where the counterfeit leads.

**The Contemporary Relevance**

False claims to revelation did not end with Musaylimah. Every age has produced those who claim divine inspiration for their own words, who found sects on private "revelations," or who assert that scripture is merely human and that they could write as well. The verse's classification stands: these are among the gravest wrongs, because they corrupt the channel of guidance. And the verse's warning stands: the confidence of the fabricator lasts only until the angels stretch out their hands.

**The Contrast with the True Prophet**

The verse also sharpens, by contrast, the picture of the true Prophet ﷺ that the sūrah has drawn. He said only what was revealed to him (v. 50); he asked no reward (v. 90); he claimed no power over the unseen or over punishment (vv. 50, 57–58); he was commanded to follow the guidance of the prophets before him (v. 90). He fabricated nothing, claimed nothing beyond his commission, and was humble before God's signs. The fabricator is his exact opposite, and the fabricator's end is the exact opposite of what awaits the one who conveyed the truth without addition.

## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:94

> **˹Today˺ you have come back to Us all alone as We created you the first time —leaving behind everything We have provided you with. We do not see your intercessors with you—those you claimed were Allah’s partners ˹in worship˺. All your ties have been broken and all your claims have let you down.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Address after Death**

Verse 93 left the wrongdoers in the throes of death, with the angels demanding their souls. Verse 94 follows them beyond: God Himself addresses them. *Wa laqad ji'tumūnā furādā kamā khalaqnākum awwala marrah* — "and you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time." The address is in the past tense — "you have come" — as though the arrival has already happened, which, from God's perspective, it has. The verse is one of the Qur'an's most powerful evocations of the soul's condition at the moment it stands before its Maker.

**"Now You Have Come unto Us Alone"**

The word *furādā* is the plural of *fard*, single, solitary, alone. Each soul comes to God by itself. The commentators draw out the several dimensions of this solitude.

First, the solitude of the crowd. The Day of Resurrection is a day of universal gathering, yet every person will feel utterly alone in it — absorbed in his own fate, unable to attend to anyone else (19:95: "And each of them will return to Him on the Day of Judgment all alone"; 80:34–37: "on that Day every person will flee from their own siblings,").

Second, the solitude of stripping. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that they come without the worldly means, wealth, associates, and children they had relied on. Al-Rāzī adds that these were the things that gave them status and protection in life; at death, all are gone. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Three things follow the dead person: his family, his wealth, and his deeds. Two return, and one remains. His family and wealth return, and his deeds remain." (al-Bukhārī 6514; Muslim 2960)

Third, the solitude of origin. "As We created you the first time" — each person entered the world alone, naked, possessing nothing (al-Jalālayn). The verse says that he leaves it the same way. The whole apparatus of possessions, alliances, and titles accumulated in between was temporary scaffolding, and it comes down.

**"And You Have Left behind That Which We Had Bestowed upon You"**

*Wa taraktum mā khawwalnākum warā'a ẓuhūrikum* — "leaving behind everything We have provided you with" (6:94). The verb *khawwala* means to grant possession, to bestow as a favor. Everything the wrongdoers owned was 'bestowed' — it was never theirs by right but lent. And now it is "behind their backs" (2:101), in the world they have left, useless to them. The image of leaving things behind one's back recurs in the Qur'an for what people abandon or neglect (2:101; 3:187; 11:92).

Al-Rāzī draws a contrast that gives the verse its practical edge. Worldly goods are left behind, and the connection between a person and what he acquired is severed. But what a person 'sends forth' — knowledge of God, virtue, good deeds — is not left behind; it goes ahead of him and meets him. The Qur'an says: "Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will find it with Allah far better and more rewarding." (73:20). The wrongdoers in this verse sent nothing forth; they invested everything in what would be left behind, and they arrive with nothing.

**"We See Not with You Your Intercessors"**

*Wa mā narā maʿakum shufaʿā'akumu alladhīna zaʿamtum annahum fīkum shurakā'* — "They worship besides Allah others who can neither harm nor benefit them, and say," The idolaters had justified their worship of idols by claiming that these were intercessors who would plead for them with God (10:18; 39:3). God now asks: where are they? They are not present. No idol, no false deity, no imagined partner has come to stand beside its worshipper.

The word *zaʿamtum* ("you claimed," "you alleged") is the Qur'an's word for baseless assertion. The partners existed only in the claim. At the moment when intercession would matter, the claim is exposed as empty. Verse 22 anticipated this: "Where are your partners whom you used to claim?" And verse 51 stated that there is no intercessor apart from God. The idolaters had built their security on intercessors who never existed; they discover this alone, before God.

**"Now the Bond between You Has Been Severed"**

*Laqad taqaṭṭaʿa baynakum* — "˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off" The verb *taqaṭṭaʿa* is intensive: torn apart, severed completely. The bond between the idolaters and their idols, between the followers and their leaders, between the worshipper and the partners he claimed — all cut. The Qur'an describes this severing from several angles: the leaders disowning their followers (2:166–167), Satan disowning those who obeyed him (14:22), the false gods denying that they were worshipped (10:28–29; 16:86–87; 28:63), and the friends of this world becoming enemies (43:67). Everything that connected people in *shirk* is dissolved, and each stands alone.

**"And That Which You Once Claimed Has Forsaken You"**

*Wa ḍalla ʿankum mā kuntum tazʿumūn* — "and lost from you is what you used to claim." The verb *ḍalla* — the root of *ḍalāl*, going astray — means here to be lost, to vanish, to fail. What they claimed (*tazʿumūn*, the same verb) — the partners, the intercession, the whole structure of their religion — has gone astray from them, disappeared, left them in the lurch. The verse ends where verse 24 ended: "lost from them is what they used to invent."

**The Anatomy of the Verse**

The verse strips the wrongdoer of four things in sequence. His company: he comes alone. His possessions: left behind. His intercessors: not present. His connections: severed. What remains is the soul as it was created — alone, with nothing — standing before the One who created it. This is the meaning of "as We created you the first time." Death returns a person to the bare condition of his origin, and everything that seemed to add to that condition is revealed as borrowed.

**Why the Verse Is Placed Here**

The verse follows the condemnation of fabricators (v. 93) and precedes a new sequence of signs from creation (vv. 95–99). Its function is to bring the section on revelation and its deniers to its terminus. Those who denied that God sends anything to human beings (v. 91), those who took religion as play (v. 70), those who fabricated lies against God (v. 93) — all of them arrive at this moment. The verse shows what all their positions come to when the accessories are removed. Then, having shown the end, the sūrah returns to the beginning: the grain, the dawn, the stars, the single soul — the signs that should have led them to God before they had to meet Him alone.

**The Verse for the Living**

The verse is addressed to the dead, but it is recited to the living, and its purpose is to let them see now what they will otherwise see too late. The Prophet ﷺ said that the intelligent person is "the one who takes account of himself and works for what comes after death" (al-Tirmidhī 2459). To take account in light of this verse is to ask: what will remain with me when I come alone? Not the wealth — it stays behind. Not the connections — they are severed. Not the false securities — they were never real. Only what was sent forth: faith, deeds, knowledge of God. The verse invites the living to invest in what will not be left behind.

**Alone, but Not Abandoned**

Finally, the solitude the verse describes is the solitude of the *wrongdoer*, who has cut himself off from God by his *shirk* and finds, at death, that he has no one. The believer also comes alone in the sense of bringing no worldly companions — but he does not come to a stranger. He comes to the "true Master" of verse 62, whose mercy he trusted, whose Book he followed, whose prayer he guarded. For him, arriving alone is arriving home. The verse's terror is reserved for those who built on what would be severed, and its implicit invitation is to build on what will not.

## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:95

> **Indeed, Allah is the One Who causes seeds and fruit stones to sprout. He brings forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living. That is Allah! How can you then be deluded ˹from the truth˺?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Returning to the Signs**

After the vision of the wrongdoer alone before God (v. 94), the sūrah returns to the created order and opens a new series of signs (vv. 95–99). The turn is deliberate. Having shown where denial ends, the Qur'an points again to the evidence that should prevent it — evidence lying in every field and orchard. *Inna Allāha fāliqu al-ḥabbi wa'l-nawā* — "Indeed, God is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone."

**"The Cleaver of the Grain and the Fruit Stone"**

The word *fāliq* comes from *falaqa*, to split, to cleave — the root of *al-falaq*, the daybreak that splits the night (113:1), and the sea parted for Moses (26:63). God splits the *ḥabb* — the grain, the seed of cereals — and the *nawā* — the stone or pit of the date and other fruits. Every seed buried in the earth is hard, dry, sealed, apparently lifeless. Then it splits, and from the crack emerges a shoot that will become a stalk of wheat or a date palm. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the splitting of the seed is the coming forth of life from what seemed dead, and that this is why the verse continues as it does.

The image was chosen with care. The seed is the humblest of things — a grain a person might scatter without noticing, a stone he spits out after eating a date. Yet within it is a process no human power can initiate or replicate: the breaking open of a closed shell and the emergence of a living plant, with roots reaching down and shoot reaching up, each knowing its direction. The verse says that God is the One who does this, in every seed, in every field, in every season. The source commentary notes that the divine name *al-Fāṭir*, "the Originator" (v. 14), is also derived from a root meaning to split; to originate is to cleave open the nothing and bring forth the something.

**"He Brings Forth the Living from the Dead"**

*Yukhriju al-ḥayya min al-mayyit* — "He brings out the living from the dead." The living plant from the dead seed is the immediate reference, and it is the sign the verse presents to the eye. But the phrase reaches further. God brings forth the living human being from the lifeless drop; He brought forth Adam from clay; He will bring forth the resurrected from the dust of the grave. Each is an instance of life emerging from what has no life, and the seed is the daily demonstration that God does this.

**"And He Is the One Who Brings Forth the Dead from the Living"**

*Wa mukhriju al-mayyiti min al-ḥayy* — "You bring forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living" The reverse movement is equally His. From the living plant comes the dead seed; from the living animal, the lifeless egg; from the living human being, the corpse. Death is not an accident that befalls life from outside; it is brought forth from life by the same God who brought life from death. The Qur'an pairs these movements in several places (3:27; 10:31; 30:19), and behind them stand two divine names: *al-Muḥyī*, the Giver of Life (30:50; 41:39), and *al-Mumīt*, the Bringer of Death.

Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī observe that the two movements describe a cycle visible everywhere in creation: seed to plant to seed, egg to bird to egg, drop to human to dust. The cycle is the signature of a single Governor who controls both directions. No one else brings life from death or death from life; the idols certainly do not.

**The Cycle as Argument for Resurrection**

The Makkans' central objection to the Qur'an was the resurrection: how can the dead be brought back? The verse answers with what they saw every planting season. The seed they buried was dead by every appearance; it split, and life came out. If God does this with every grain, why should He not do it with human beings? The Qur'an makes the argument explicit elsewhere:

> "And it is Allah Who sends the winds, which then stir up ˹vapour, forming˺ clouds, and then We drive them to a lifeless land, giving life to the earth after its death" (35:9)

> "When they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land and then cause rain to fall, producing every type of fruit" (7:57)

Islamic theology named the two movements *mabda'* (origin) and *maʿād* (return): the coming forth of creatures from God and their return to Him. The verse's two clauses correspond to these. God brought the living from the dead at the origin; He brings the dead from the living at the end of earthly life; and He will bring the living from the dead again at the return. The seed enacts the whole doctrine in miniature.

**The Spiritual Dimension**

The commentators, including Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by al-Ṭabarī, also read the verse spiritually. God brings forth the believer from the disbeliever — a living heart from a dead one — as He brought Abraham from Āzar and many Companions from idolatrous parents. And He brings forth the disbeliever from the believer — a dead heart from a living one — as Noah's son came from Noah. Faith is life and disbelief is death, and God alone controls the passage between them. This reading does not replace the physical one; it extends it. The same power that splits the seed splits the hardened heart and brings faith from it.

**"That Is God"**

*Dhālikumu Allāh* — "that is God." The demonstrative gathers everything just described — the splitting of seeds, the bringing forth of life and death — and identifies its Author. This is God: not an abstraction, not a distant first cause, but the One doing these things now, in every seed in the earth. The idolaters knew the name *Allāh*; the verse tells them what the name refers to. The phrase recurs in verse 102 and in 10:3, 10:32, 35:13, 39:6, and 40:62, always following a description of God's acts in creation and always with the same force: the God you must worship is the One who does *this*.

**"How, Then, Are You Perverted?"**

*Fa-annā tu'fakūn* — "so how are you turned away?" The verb *ufika* (passive) means to be turned aside, deflected, perverted from the right course — as a person is turned from a road by a lie or a delusion (*ifk* means a lie, a slander). The question is one of astonishment. If this is God — the One who splits the seed and brings life from death — how can you be turned away from Him to stones that do nothing? The question appears in 10:34, 35:3, 40:62, and elsewhere, always with the same sense: given the evidence, your turning away is inexplicable.

The passive voice is significant. The idolaters *are turned* — by custom, by their leaders, by the satans of verse 71, by their own desires. They did not reason their way to idolatry; they were deflected into it. The verse invites them to notice the deflection and turn back.

**The Verse as a Practice of Seeing**

The verse teaches the believer a way of looking at the world. When he sees a sprout breaking the soil, he sees God splitting the seed. When he sees a harvest, he sees the living brought from the dead. When he sees a death, he sees the dead brought from the living by the same Hand. The world becomes legible as a continuous act of God — not a machine running on its own but a creation being created, moment by moment. The Qur'an's frequent command to "look" (*unẓur*) at creation is a command to see it this way. The one who sees it so cannot be turned away; the one who has been turned away has stopped seeing.

## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:96

> **He causes the dawn to break, and has made the night for rest and ˹made˺ the sun and the moon ˹to travel˺ with precision. That is the design of the Almighty, AllKnowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Cleaving**

Verse 95 named God the Cleaver of the grain and the fruit stone. Verse 96 names Him *fāliqu al-iṣbāḥ* — "Cleaver of the daybreak." The same participle, *fāliq*, is used, and the parallel is intended. As God splits the sealed seed to bring forth the shoot, He splits the darkness of night to bring forth the dawn. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī explain the image: the first light of morning appears as a crack in the blackness, a line of white along the horizon that widens until the darkness is broken and the day emerges. The Arabs called this first light "˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall" (2:187). The verse says that God is the One who makes that crack.

The word *iṣbāḥ* is a verbal noun meaning the coming of morning, the breaking of day. Some readers took it as a plural of *ṣubḥ* — 'the dawns' — in which case God is the Cleaver of every dawn that has ever broken. Either way, the reference is to a phenomenon that every person on earth witnesses every day and that no one can produce. The Qur'an swears by it: 'By the dawn' (89:1); and its last chapter but one begins, "I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak" (113:1) — *rabb al-falaq*, using the same root.

**The Two Cleavings Together**

The pairing of seed and dawn is instructive. Both are emergences of something from what conceals it: life from the hard shell, light from the darkness. Both happen quietly, by no visible agency, with perfect regularity. Both are so ordinary that people cease to notice them, and both are — on reflection — beyond any power but God's. The Qur'an juxtaposes them so that the reader who has become numb to one may be awakened by the other. And both connect to the sūrah's opening verse, which spoke of God's creation of "the darknesses and the light."

**"He Has Made the Night for Repose"**

*Wa jaʿala al-layla sakanan* — "and He has made the night a rest." The word *sakan* comes from *sakana*, to be still, to be calm, to dwell — the root of *sakīnah* (tranquility) and *maskan* (dwelling). Night is made as a stillness in which creatures rest. The Qur'an mentions this mercy in many places (10:67; 25:47; 27:86; 28:73; 40:61; 78:9–10), sometimes pairing it with the day as a time of seeking livelihood.

The verse treats the alternation of night and day not as a mere astronomical fact but as a provision. Night is *for* rest — it was made with human need in view. The darkness that the idolaters might fear, or the deniers dismiss as mere absence of light, is a designed gift: a time when activity ceases, the body recovers, and the soul withdraws into the daily death of sleep that verse 60 described. A world without night would be a world without rest, and the verse asks the hearer to recognize the rest as given.

**"And the Sun and the Moon for Reckoning"**

*Wa'l-shamsa wa'l-qamara ḥusbānan* — "and the sun and the moon as a reckoning." The word *ḥusbān* is from *ḥasaba*, to count, to calculate — the root of *ḥisāb* (v. 62). The sun and moon are made as instruments of reckoning: their regular motions allow human beings to count days, months, and years, to fix the times of prayer and fasting and pilgrimage, and — as al-Rāzī notes — to determine direction, including the direction of the *qiblah*. The Qur'an says the same in 10:5 — "He is the One Who made the sun a radiant source and the moon a reflected light, with precisely ordained phases, so that you may know the number of years and calculation ˹of time˺." (10:5) — and 17:12, and it speaks of "The sun and the moon ˹travel˺ with precision" (55:5).

The word *ḥusbān* also carries the sense of exactness. The motions of sun and moon are not approximate; they are calculated so precisely that eclipses can be predicted centuries ahead. This precision is the sign. Objects of such regularity are not gods acting by will — Abraham's argument (vv. 76–78) — but instruments made by One who set them in their courses for the benefit of His creatures.

**The Contrast with the Idolaters' View**

Abraham's people worshipped the sun and moon; the Makkans venerated celestial bodies through their idols; the Sabians of Arabia prayed to the stars. The verse quietly dismantles this. The sun and moon are not lords; they are timekeepers. They were made — *jaʿala*, "He made" — for a purpose defined by their Maker and serving His creatures. To worship what was made as a clock is to mistake the instrument for the Craftsman. This is the same reduction the Qur'an applies to every idol: it strips the false god of its assumed majesty by naming its actual function.

**"Such Is the Decree of the Mighty, the Knowing"**

*Dhālika taqdīru al-ʿazīzi al-ʿalīm* — "that is the determination of the Mighty, the Knowing." The word *taqdīr* comes from *qadara*, to measure, to determine — the root of *qadar*, God's decree that measures all things. The regularity of night and day, sun and moon, is a *taqdīr*: a measured ordinance, laid down and maintained by God. Nothing in it is accidental; every rising and setting is determined.

The two names that close the verse are precisely suited. *Al-ʿAzīz*, the Mighty, is the One whose power holds the sun and moon in their courses and whom nothing can resist. *Al-ʿAlīm*, the Knowing, is the One whose knowledge designed the courses with the precision that makes reckoning possible. Might without knowledge would produce force without order; knowledge without might would produce design without execution. The heavens display both, and the verse names both. The same pairing closes 36:38: "That is the design of the Almighty, All-Knowing"

**The Verse and Daily Life**

Verse 96 covers the whole of a day: the dawn that opens it, the night that closes it, and the sun and moon that mark its passage. It asks the hearer to see each as God's act. The believer who wakes at dawn sees the Cleaver of the daybreak at work and prays the dawn prayer, which the Qur'an says is "witnessed" (17:78). He works by the sun and rests by the night, and recognizes both as provisions. He reckons his months by the moon — Ramaḍān, the pilgrimage, the sacred months — and knows the reckoning is God's gift. The most ordinary structures of time are, for the one who sees rightly, a continuous sign.

**From the Earth to the Heavens**

The sequence of verses 95–97 moves the eye upward. Verse 95 looked at the ground: the seed splitting in the soil. Verse 96 looks at the horizon and the sky: the dawn breaking, the sun and moon in their courses. Verse 97 will look at the night sky: the stars by which travelers find their way. The signs are arranged from the nearest and smallest to the farthest and grandest, and at every level the same conclusion presses: this is God's doing — how, then, are you turned away?

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:97

> **And He is the One Who has made the stars as your guide through the darkness of land and sea. We have already made the signs clear for people who know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Stars as Guides**

*Wa huwa alladhī jaʿala lakumu al-nujūma li-tahtadū bihā fī ẓulumāti al-barri wa'l-baḥr* — "and He is the one who made for you the stars, that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land and the sea." Verse 96 spoke of the sun and moon as instruments of temporal reckoning; verse 97 speaks of the stars as instruments of spatial orientation. Al-Rāzī notes the complementarity: when the sun and moon are absent — on a moonless night in the desert or on the open sea — the stars remain, and by them the traveler finds his direction.

The Arabs were expert star-navigators. Caravans crossed the desert by night to avoid the heat, steering by the Pole Star and the constellations; sailors on the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean did the same. The verse names a skill on which their lives depended and identifies its foundation as God's provision: He *made* the stars *for you*, that you might be guided. The Qur'an mentions this function also in 16:16: "Also by landmarks and stars do people find their way"

**"For You"**

The phrase *lakum* — "for you" — is significant. The stars, which the idolaters and the Sabians worshipped, were made *for* human beings, as a service to them. This inverts the relationship the star-worshippers imagined. They served the stars; the verse says the stars serve them. What is made for one's use is not one's lord. Here again, as with the sun and moon in verse 96, the Qur'an demotes a false object of worship by naming its actual purpose.

The Qur'an is precise about the purposes of the stars. Qatādah, as recorded by al-Bukhārī in the heading to his chapter on the stars, said: "God created these stars for three purposes: as adornment for the sky, as missiles against the devils, and as signs by which to be guided. Whoever claims anything else about them has erred, forfeited his share, and burdened himself with what he has no knowledge of." The third purpose is this verse's; the first two are 67:5 and 37:6–7. The claim of astrology — that the stars govern human destinies — is what Qatādah dismissed.

**"Amid the Darkness of Land and Sea"**

The phrase *ẓulumāt al-barr wa'l-baḥr* — "the darknesses of the land and the sea" — was used in verse 63 for the perils from which people call on God. Here it refers, in the first place, to the literal darkness of night in the desert and on the ocean, where there are no landmarks and one can wander until one dies. Al-Ṭabarī records also the reading that the darknesses are figurative: the moral and intellectual darkness of error and misguidance. On this reading, the verse points beyond the physical stars to the guidance that God provides for the soul lost in the darkness of ignorance — the prophets and the revelation, which are, in the Qur'an's imagery, lights (5:15; 42:52; 64:8). The traveler who steers by the stars is a figure of the believer who steers by revelation.

The source commentary suggests that on this figurative reading, the sun, moon, and stars of verses 96–97 may represent degrees of spiritual illumination — as they did in Abraham's ascent (vv. 76–78). The sun of direct knowledge, the moon of reflected knowledge, and the stars of the scattered lights that guide when the greater lights are hidden. The Qur'an frequently invokes the three together (12:4; 7:54; 16:12; 22:18; 55:5–6), always as creatures subservient to God's command.

**Guidance Physical and Spiritual**

The verb *tahtadū* — "that you may be guided" — is the verb of *hidāyah*, the sūrah's most persistent concern (vv. 35, 39, 56, 71, 77, 80, 82, 84, 87, 88, 90). Its use here for physical navigation ties the physical to the spiritual. God has made provision for both. He set the stars so that the body may find its way through the desert; He sent the prophets and the Book so that the soul may find its way through life. The one who thanks God for the first and ignores the second has recognized the lesser guidance and refused the greater.

**"We Have Expounded the Signs"**

*Qad faṣṣalnā al-āyāt* — "We have detailed the signs." This is the phrase of verse 55, discussed there. The signs — the seed, the dawn, the night, the sun and moon, the stars — have been set out one by one, each explained, each distinct. God has not left the evidence in a heap; He has arranged it. The phrase appears twice in three verses (here and v. 98) and again in v. 126, emphasizing that this section of the sūrah is a deliberate exposition.

**"For a People Who Know"**

*Li-qawmin yaʿlamūn* — "for a people who know." Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabrisī explain: for those who possess intellect and use it, who reflect correctly, who reason from what the senses perceive to what the mind grasps, and from the seen to the unseen. The signs are detailed for everyone, but they are *received* by those who know — who bring to them a mind willing to follow the evidence. The next verse will close with "for a people who understand" (*yafqahūn*), and the pair marks the two capacities the signs require: knowledge (grasping the facts) and understanding (grasping their meaning).

The phrase is an implicit rebuke. The Makkans knew the stars intimately — they steered by them and named them. They had the knowledge. What they lacked was the willingness to follow it to its conclusion: that the One who made the stars for their guidance is the One who deserves their worship. Knowledge that stops at use and refuses meaning is knowledge that has not been completed.

**The Stars and the Argument from Design**

The verse is one of the Qur'an's clearest statements of what later thought called the argument from providence: the created order is arranged for the benefit of human beings, and this arrangement points to an arranger who intended their benefit. The stars are visible from the earth, fixed enough to be reliable, bright enough to be seen — and they happen to be exactly what a creature traveling the earth's surface at night would need. The verse does not say this is coincidence; it says God made them *for you*. The believer who steers by a star and knows who placed it there has completed the argument that the star-worshipper and the materialist, in their opposite ways, leave unfinished.

**From Reckoning to Guidance**

The three verses 95–97 have moved from the earth (seed) to the sky (dawn, sun, moon) to the depths of the night sky (stars), and from the emergence of life to the measurement of time to the finding of direction. Each is a domain of human dependence — food, time, travel — and each is a domain of God's provision. Verse 98 will complete the series by turning to the human being himself: the single soul from which all were brought forth, and the two stations through which every soul passes. The signs outside lead to the sign within.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:98

> **And He is the One Who originated you all from a single soul, then assigned you a place to live and another to ˹be laid to˺ rest. We have already made the signs clear for people who comprehend.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sign Within**

After the seed, the dawn, the sun and moon, and the stars, the sūrah turns the eye inward: *wa huwa alladhī ansha'akum min nafsin wāḥidah* — "He is the One Who produces gardens—both cultivated and wild — and palm trees, crops of different flavours, olives, and pomegranates— similar ˹in shape˺, but dissimilar ˹in taste˺" The signs in the world outside lead to the sign that each hearer carries in his own existence. The verb *ansha'a* means to originate, to bring into being, to cause to grow — used of God's producing of creatures and gardens (6:141; 23:78; 56:35).

**"From a Single Soul"**

*Min nafsin wāḥidah* — "Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women" The phrase opens Sūrat al-Nisā' ("O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate and dispersed from both of them many men and women," 4:1) and recurs in 7:189 and 39:6. The single soul is Adam, from whom all humanity descends. Every human being who has ever lived — of every race, language, and land — traces back to one origin. This is the Qur'anic basis for the unity of humankind and for the equality the Prophet ﷺ proclaimed in his final sermon: "Your Lord is one, and your father is one; there is no superiority of an Arab over a non-Arab... except by piety."

As a sign, the single origin has a particular force. From one soul, God has brought forth billions — each distinct in face, voice, fingerprint, and character, yet all of one kind. The multiplication of the one into the many, with unity of nature and diversity of individuals, is a display of creative power that no human agency approaches. And it is a display the hearer cannot dismiss as remote, because he is one of the many.

**"And Then a Dwelling Place and a Repository"**

*Fa-mustaqarrun wa mustawdaʿ* — "then a place of settlement and a place of deposit." The two words are the verse's center, and the commentators have explained them in several ways, all of which the source commentary reviews.

*Mustaqarr* comes from *qarra*, to settle, to be fixed — the word used in verse 67 for the "fixed setting" of every tiding. *Mustawdaʿ* comes from *wadaʿa*, to deposit, to entrust for safekeeping — a *wadīʿah* is a thing left in trust. The two words are paired also in 11:6: "There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah"

The most common interpretation, held by Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Zamakhsharī, is that the *mustaqarr* is the womb, where the human being settles and is formed, and the *mustawdaʿ* is the loins of the father, where he is deposited before conception. On this reading, the verse traces the human being from his origin in Adam through the stations of his coming-to-be: deposited in the father, settled in the mother, brought forth into the world. Ibn ʿAbbās and others are reported to have held this view.

A second interpretation, recorded by al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī, takes the *mustaqarr* as the womb and the *mustawdaʿ* as the grave. The womb is where the soul enters the earthly world; the grave is where it is deposited to await resurrection. This reading fits the passage's theme of life and death, creation and return (v. 95), and pictures the two thresholds of human existence.

A third, also in al-Ṭabarī, takes the *mustaqarr* as one's dwelling on earth and the *mustawdaʿ* as one's ultimate place with God. Al-Rāzī reverses this: the *mustawdaʿ* is the earthly home, which is a temporary deposit always subject to change, and the *mustaqarr* is the Hereafter, which is permanent.

**Reading the Interpretations Together**

The source commentary observes that the interpretations, taken together, describe a single journey. The human being is deposited in the loins, settled in the womb, brought into the world where he dwells for a time, deposited in the grave, and finally settled in his permanent abode. At every stage he is either in a temporary keeping or in a settled place, and every temporary keeping gives way to another until the final settlement. The two words thus contain a whole anthropology: the human being is a traveler between stations, never fully at home until the last.

There is a further nuance in the Arabic. Some readers voweled the first word as *mustaqirr* (active participle: "one who settles") rather than *mustaqarr* (place of settling), giving the sense: "some of you are settled [in the womb/on earth], and some are deposited [in the loins/in the grave]." The variant reinforces the picture: at any moment, humanity is distributed across the stations, some here and some there, all in God's knowledge and disposal.

**The Sign of One's Own Coming-to-Be**

The verse asks each hearer to consider his own existence as evidence. He did not exist; he was deposited as a drop; he was settled in a womb and formed there without any action of his own; he was brought out into light. The Qur'an returns to this argument repeatedly (22:5; 23:12–14; 75:37–40; 76:2; 86:5–7), because it is the argument closest to home. The one who denies that God can raise the dead must explain how God — or anything — brought *him* from nothing through these stations. The Qur'an says: "Do ˹such˺ people not remember that We created them before, when they were nothing" (19:67). And: "Were they not ˹once˺ a sperm-drop emitted" (75:36–40).

**"We Have Expounded the Signs for a People Who Understand"**

*Qad faṣṣalnā al-āyāti li-qawmin yafqahūn* — "We have detailed the signs for a people who understand." Verse 97 ended with "for a people who know" (*yaʿlamūn*); this verse ends with "for a people who understand" (*yafqahūn*). The verb *faqiha* means to understand deeply, to grasp the inner sense — the root of *fiqh*. Al-Rāzī explains that the signs are for those willing to understand, or endowed by God with the power of understanding. Al-Ṭabrisī adds that the repeated references to God's expounding of the signs are an encouragement to contemplation.

The shift from knowing to understanding may correspond to the shift in subject. The stars (v. 97) are known — their positions, their uses. One's own origin (v. 98) must be understood — the fact of having been brought from a single soul through hidden stations is not observed but grasped by reflection. The first requires knowledge of the world; the second requires understanding of oneself. The Qur'an calls for both, and the sign of one's own existence is the one that most requires the deeper faculty.

**The Passage Completed**

Verses 95–98 form a unit: the seed and the stone (life from death in the earth), the dawn and the night and the sun and moon (light and time in the heavens), the stars (guidance across the earth), and the single soul with its stations (the human being himself). The movement is from the ground beneath one's feet to the sky above one's head to the self within. At each point the verse says, in effect, "He is the one who did this." And at the end it says: the signs have been detailed for those who know and understand. What remains is for the hearer to be among them. Verse 99 will add the final and most abundant sign — rain, and the vegetation it brings forth — before the sūrah returns to the idolaters' errors about God.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:99

> **And He is the One Who sends down rain from the sky—causing all kinds of plants to grow—producing green stalks from which We bring forth clustered grain. And from palm trees come clusters of dates hanging within reach. ˹There are˺ also gardens of grapevines, olives, and pomegranates, similar ˹in shape˺ but dissimilar ˹in taste˺. Look at their fruit as it yields and ripens! Indeed, in these are signs for people who believe.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Culminating Sign**

The series of signs that began with the splitting of the seed (v. 95) ends with the fullest picture of vegetable life in the sūrah: rain falling, plants sprouting, grain forming, dates hanging, orchards of grapes, olives, and pomegranates ripening. *Wa huwa alladhī anzala min al-samā'i mā'an* — "and He is the one who sends down water from the sky." The verse gathers into a single sweep the entire process by which the earth feeds its inhabitants, and it asks the hearer to look.

**Water from the Sky**

God's sending down of rain is one of the Qur'an's most frequently invoked signs. It revives the dead earth (16:65; 22:63; 29:63; 30:24; 43:11), provides drink (15:22), purifies (8:11), and — as here — brings forth crops and fruit (2:22; 14:32; 16:10–11; 20:53; 23:18–19; 31:10; 35:27; 39:21; 50:9–10; 78:14–16). Verse 141 of this sūrah will return to the same theme in similar language. For the Arabs, rain was not a routine event but a matter of survival; a year without it meant famine. That God sends it, and no one else, was the most direct evidence of their dependence on Him — evidence the Prophet ﷺ pressed when he warned against attributing rain to the stars (al-Bukhārī 846; Muslim 71).

**From "He" to "We"**

The source commentary draws attention to a shift in person. The verse begins in the third person — "He it is who sends down water" — and then shifts to the first person plural: "thereby *We* bring forth the shoot of every plant." The commentators find meaning in the shift. The third person, describing the sending of water from above, evokes God's transcendence; the first person, describing the bringing forth of each plant, evokes His immanence — His direct, intimate involvement in every sprout that breaks the soil. God is above the heavens sending the rain and present in every seed receiving it. The grammar enacts the theology.

**The Sequence of Growth**

The verse traces the process stage by stage. *Fa-akhrajnā bihi nabāta kulli shay'* — "and We bring forth by it the growth of every thing": the first green shoot of every kind of plant. *Fa-akhrajnā minhu khaḍiran* — "then We bring forth from it greenery": the growing plant. *Nukhriju minhu ḥabban mutarākiban* — "from which We bring forth grain, piled up": the ear of wheat or barley, with its kernels packed closely in rows. The word *mutarākib* means stacked, one upon another, and describes exactly how grain sits on the ear.

The repetition of "We bring forth" (*akhrajnā*, *nukhriju*) three times insists that each stage is God's act. The shoot does not produce the greenery by itself; the greenery does not produce the grain by itself. At each transition, the verse says *We*. This is the Qur'an's consistent rejection of the view that nature runs itself: what appears as an autonomous process is a continuous divine action.

**The Date Palm**

*Wa min al-nakhli min ṭalʿihā qinwānun dāniyah* — "and from the date palm, from its spathe, clusters hanging low." The *ṭalʿ* is the sheath or spathe in which the palm's flowers form; the *qinwān* are the clusters of dates; *dāniyah* means near, low-hanging, within reach. The image is of a palm heavy with ripe fruit, its clusters bending down toward the hand. The source commentary notes that this suggests both abundance (the clusters are heavy) and ease (they are accessible) — the same image used for the fruit of Paradise, "shade will be right above them, and its fruit will be made very easy to reach" (55:54; 69:23; 76:14). The date palm was the tree of Arabia, and the Prophet ﷺ compared the believer to it: a tree whose leaves do not fall and which gives fruit in every season (al-Bukhārī 61).

**Gardens of Grapes, Olives, and Pomegranates**

*Wa jannātin min aʿnābin wa'l-zaytūna wa'l-rummān* — "and olives and" Three further fruits, each mentioned elsewhere as examples of God's provision (grapes: 16:67; 36:34; 80:28; olives: 80:29; 95:1; pomegranates: 55:68). The grape gives food, drink, and raisins; the olive gives oil for food and light — "His light is like a niche in which there is a lamp, the lamp is in a crystal, the crystal is like a shining star, lit from ˹the oil of˺ a blessed olive tree, ˹located˺ neither to the east nor the west, whose oil would almost glow, even without being touched by fire" (24:35); the pomegranate is a fruit of the Garden (55:68). The list moves from the staple (grain) to the sustaining (dates) to the delightful (grapes, olives, pomegranates), covering the range of what the earth offers.

**"Like unto One Another and Yet Not Alike"**

*Mushtabihan wa ghayra mutashābih* — "resembling and not resembling." The phrase is the verse's intellectual center. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Jalālayn explain: the plants resemble one another in some respects — leaves, form, manner of growth — yet differ in others — taste, color, scent, use. Two trees may look nearly identical and bear fruit that is entirely different. Or, as the phrase is also read: the fruits resemble one another in appearance yet differ in flavor.

The source commentary connects this to the theme of unity and multiplicity that runs through the passage. One water falls on one soil and produces an endless diversity of plants and fruits (cf. 13:4: "watered with one water, yet We make some of them exceed others in taste"). One soul was the origin of billions of distinct human beings (v. 98). The principle is the same: a single Source produces a multiplicity that is unified in kind and diversified in individuals. The unity points to one Creator; the diversity points to His wisdom and will. Neither a blind force nor a plurality of gods could produce this pattern of coherent variety.

**"Look upon Their Fruits, as They Grow and Ripen!"**
