*Unẓurū ilā thamarihi idhā athmara wa yanʿih* — "look at its fruit when it bears fruit, and at its ripening." The command is direct: look. Not merely at the fruit, but at the *process* — the bearing and the ripening. The verse asks for attention to change over time: the small hard green thing becoming the sweet full ripe thing, by a transformation that no farmer performs and no one fully understands. The Qur'an's command to "look" (*unẓur*) is the foundation of what Islamic thought called *tafakkur* — contemplation of creation as a means of knowing the Creator. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Reflect on the creation of God, and do not reflect on God's essence" (reported by al-Bayhaqī in *Shuʿab al-Īmān*, with weakness in its chain but sound in meaning).

**"Truly in That Are Signs for a People Who Believe"**

*Inna fī dhālikum la-āyātin li-qawmin yu'minūn* — "indeed in that are signs for a people who believe." The three previous verses closed with "a people who know" (v. 97), "a people who understand" (v. 98), and now "Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller" The progression is deliberate. Knowledge grasps the facts; understanding grasps their meaning; belief responds to the meaning with faith. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the believers are the ones who actually benefit from the signs, because their hearts are open to what the signs indicate; the disbelievers, whose hearts are sealed (v. 46; 2:26), see the same fruits and draw no conclusion. The signs are objectively present for everyone; they are subjectively received by those who believe.

Al-Bayḍāwī specifies what the signs indicate: God's Oneness (one water, one process, one Governor), His Power (life from dead earth), and His Wisdom (the ordered diversity of the produce). These are precisely the three attributes the sūrah has been arguing for since its first verse.

**The Passage as a Whole: vv. 95–99**

The five verses form one of the Qur'an's great meditations on creation. They move from the seed in the earth to the dawn in the sky, from the sun and moon to the stars, from the single soul to the rain and its harvest. At each step they name God as the doer and call on a faculty — knowledge, understanding, belief — to receive the sign. The passage answers, without polemic, the errors the sūrah has been confronting: the idols do none of this; the celestial bodies are instruments, not gods; the denier of resurrection sees resurrection every spring. It is placed immediately before the verses on the jinn and the "offspring" falsely attributed to God (vv. 100–101), so that the reader, having seen what God actually does, may judge how absurd it is to attribute to Him partners and children.

**The Practice of Looking**

The verse's command remains in force. The believer who eats a date, presses an olive, or watches a vine set fruit is commanded to look — to see the rain that fell, the shoot that emerged, the transformation that ripened, and the God who did each part. This is not sentimental nature-appreciation; it is an act of worship, because it completes the sign by acknowledging its Author. The Qur'an says of those who do this: "˹They are˺ those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth ˹and pray˺," (3:191). The verse gives them the whole orchard to look at, and asks only that they see.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:100

> **Yet they associate the jinn with Allah ˹in worship˺, even though He created them, and they falsely attribute to Him sons and daughters out of ignorance. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they claim!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Creator's Works to the Creature's Errors**

Verses 95–99 displayed what God does: splits the seed, cleaves the dawn, sets the stars, brings forth humanity from one soul, sends rain and raises harvests. Verse 100 turns to what human beings do in response: *wa jaʿalū lillāhi shurakā'a al-jinn* — "and they have made the jinn partners to God." The juxtaposition is the argument. After such evidence of a single all-powerful Creator, they set up as His partners beings He created.

**"They Make the Jinn Partners unto God"**

The jinn are a class of created beings, made from smokeless fire (55:15; 15:27), invisible to human beings under normal conditions, possessed of free will and therefore accountable, and including both believers and disbelievers (72:1–15). Satan (Iblīs) is of the jinn (18:50). The Arabs of the Prophet's ﷺ time both feared and venerated them: they sought their protection when camping in wild places (72:6), made offerings to them, and consulted soothsayers who claimed contact with them.

How did they make the jinn 'partners'? Al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, and others list the forms. By worshipping or venerating them directly. By obeying their whisperings — following the promptings of the satans in matters of religion, as verse 121 will describe — "Surely the devils whisper to their ˹human˺ associates to argue with you" (6:121) — which the Qur'an classes as a form of worship: "Did I not command you, O Children of Adam, not to follow Satan, for he is truly your sworn enemy" (36:60). And by asserting a kinship between God and the jinn — the Qur'an records that the Makkans "have also established a ˹marital˺ relationship between Him and the jinn" (37:158), imagining, in some accounts, that the angels were daughters of God by jinn mothers.

Al-Rāzī also reads the verse as encompassing the dualist view of the Zoroastrians, who posited a god of light who creates good and a god of darkness who creates evil — a doctrine that makes an evil power a co-creator with God. Any belief that gives a spiritual being an independent share in creating, governing, or deserving worship falls under the verse.

**"Though He Created Them"**

*Wa khalaqahum* — "and He created them." Three words that dismantle the whole error. The jinn are creatures. Whatever powers they have — invisibility, speed, the ability to whisper — were given them by God, and they remain subject to Him in every respect. Abraham's argument against the celestial bodies (vv. 76–78) applies here: what is created cannot be the Creator's partner. The verse's structure places the fact of their creation immediately after the fact of their being taken as partners, so that the contradiction is unmistakable.

The pronoun in "created them" may refer to the jinn or to the idolaters themselves; on the second reading, the sense is: they attribute partners to the God who created *them* — the very people making the attribution. Both readings hold, and both expose the absurdity.

**"And Falsely Attribute Sons and Daughters to Him"**

*Wa kharaqū lahu banīna wa banātin bi-ghayri ʿilm* — "and they have fabricated for Him sons and daughters without knowledge." The verb *kharaqa* means to tear, to rend, to cut through — and by extension to invent, to fabricate out of nothing, to make a false claim. The word conveys violence to the truth: they *tore out* sons and daughters for God from their own imaginations.

The sons and daughters refer to two errors the Qur'an addresses repeatedly. The attribution of sons: the Christian doctrine that Jesus is the Son of God (5:17, 72; 9:30; 19:35), and the claim recorded of some Jews that Ezra was a son of God (9:30). The attribution of daughters: the Arab idolaters' belief that the angels — and the goddesses al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, and Manāt — were God's daughters (16:57; 37:149–153; 43:16–19; 52:39; 53:19–27). The Qur'an notes the particular perversity of the second: the Arabs, who despised daughters for themselves and buried them alive, assigned daughters to God (16:57–59; 53:21–22: "Do you ˹prefer to˺ have sons while ˹you attribute˺ to Him daughters").

**"Without Any Knowledge"**

*Bi-ghayri ʿilm* — "without knowledge." The attribution rests on nothing: no revelation, no proof, no evidence — only inherited assertion and imagination. This is the Qur'an's recurring charge against *shirk*: it is a claim about God made without any basis in knowledge (v. 81: "for which He has sent down to you no authority"; 10:68; 22:71; 53:28: "And surely assumptions can in no way replace the truth").

The phrase also marks the contrast with the preceding verses. The signs of creation were "for a people who know" (v. 97), "who understand" (v. 98), "who believe" (v. 99). The attribution of partners and children is "without knowledge." Knowledge leads to *tawḥīd*; ignorance produces *shirk*. The verse places the two side by side.

**"Glory Be to Him!"**

*Subḥānahu* — "glory be to Him," "exalted is He." The word *subḥān* comes from *sabbaḥa*, to declare free of imperfection — to glorify God by denying of Him everything unworthy. It is the word the Qur'an reaches for whenever offspring or partners are attributed to God (2:116; 4:171; 10:68; 17:43; 19:35; 21:26; 39:4). To say *subḥānahu* after such a claim is to reject the claim as a defect in one's conception of God and to reaffirm His perfection.

**"Exalted Is He above That Which They Ascribe"**

*Wa taʿālā ʿammā yaṣifūn* — "and He is high above what they describe." The verb *taʿālā* means to be exalted, to be far above. God is above having partners, above having children, above every description that falls short of Him. Al-Jalālayn glosses the phrase simply: He is above having offspring. The same closing occurs in 6:100, 23:91, and 37:159, and it is the verse's final word: whatever they say, He is beyond it.

**Why Partners and Offspring Are Rejected Together**

The verse pairs two errors that seem different — taking jinn as partners and attributing children to God — because they share a root. Both diminish God by placing Him in relation to other beings as an equal or a kin. A partner is a peer who shares one's domain; a child is one's own kind, of one's own substance. Both deny God's absolute uniqueness. The verses that follow will state this uniqueness positively: He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, without consort, Creator of all things (v. 101); there is no god but He (v. 102); sight does not comprehend Him (v. 103). Verse 100 clears away the errors so that verses 101–103 can state the truth.

**The Contemporary Reach of the Verse**

Literal belief in jinn-partners and divine daughters has faded from most societies, but the structure of the error persists. Wherever spiritual beings, forces, or powers are credited with independent control over human fate — luck, fate, "the universe," ancestral spirits, energies to be appeased — the verse's diagnosis applies: partners have been made for God from among His creatures, without knowledge. And wherever God is imagined as a being among beings, with a family, a nature shared by others, or a domain shared with rivals, the verse's response applies: glory be to Him; He is exalted above what they describe. The believer's task is the one Abraham performed and the verse commands — to see through the created to the Creator and to declare Him free of every likeness.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:101

> **˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and earth. How could He have children when He has no mate? He created all things and has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of everything.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Positive Statement after the Negation**

Verse 100 rejected the partners and offspring attributed to God. Verse 101 states, positively, why such attributions are impossible: *badīʿu al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* — "the Originator of the heavens and the earth." The verse opens with a divine name and proceeds to a tightly reasoned argument. It is one of the Qur'an's most philosophically precise verses, and it addresses the claim of divine sonship — Christian and pagan — at its root.

**The Name *Badīʿ***

*Badīʿ* comes from *badaʿa*, to originate, to bring into existence without precedent or model — the root of *bidʿah*, an innovation with no prior example. As a divine name it means the One who creates absolutely, from nothing, without any pattern to follow or material to use. It also means, as the source commentary notes, the One who is Himself unique, unprecedented, without peer. The two meanings converge: the One who originates everything is Himself originated by nothing and resembled by nothing. The name appears here and in 2:117, in both cases followed by the denial of offspring:

> "˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth" (2:117)

The heavens and the earth — the totality of created reality — were originated by Him without precedent. This establishes the context for the question that follows: the One who brought all things into being from nothing does not need or have the means for offspring.

**"How Should He Have a Child When He Has No Consort?"**

*Annā yakūnu lahu waladun wa lam takun lahu ṣāḥibah* — "how could He have a child when He has no consort?" The word *ṣāḥibah* means a female companion, a mate, a wife. The argument is simple and, within its terms, decisive. In the world of creatures, offspring arise from the union of male and female of the same kind. God has no mate. There is no female counterpart to God, no being of His kind with whom He could produce offspring. Therefore He cannot have a child in any sense analogous to the one the claim implies.

Al-Zamakhsharī develops the point: God transcends all species. A consort must be of the same species as her mate; but God is not a member of any species — "There is nothing like Him, for He ˹alone˺ is the AllHearing, All-Seeing" (42:11). The very concept of a consort for God is incoherent, and so the concept of a child for Him is incoherent. The jinn said the same when they heard the Qur'an: "˹Now, we believe that˺ our Lord—Exalted is His Majesty—has neither taken a mate nor offspring," (72:3).

**"And He Created All Things"**

*Wa khalaqa kulla shay'* — "and He created everything." This clause completes the argument from a second direction. Everything other than God is created by God. A child of God would have to be either created — in which case it is a creature, not a child in the sense of sharing God's nature — or uncreated — in which case there would be two uncreated beings, which contradicts "He created all things." There is no third option. Whatever exists besides God is His creation, and a creature cannot be His offspring. Jesus, the angels, Ezra, the goddesses — all fall under "all things" and all are created.

The source commentary adds a further consideration from al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī. Begetting is a bodily process: it requires that a part of the parent be separated and joined to the mate. God has no body and no parts; nothing can be separated from Him. And God creates by fiat — "Be, and it is" (2:117; 3:47; 6:73; 36:82) — not by a process of gestation and birth. His mode of bringing things into being is creation, not procreation. The Qur'an says of Jesus specifically: "He created him from dust, then said to him," (3:59).

**"And He Is Knower of All Things"**

*Wa huwa bi-kulli shay'in ʿalīm* — "and He is of all things Knowing." The verse closes with knowledge, and the commentators find the closing apt. God's knowledge of all things means that He knows the truth of what they attribute to Him and will hold them to account for it. It also completes the picture of a Being who needs nothing: one who knows everything and has created everything has no lack that a child could fill. Human beings desire children for companionship, for help, for continuation after death, for a share in the future. None of these motives applies to the One who is eternal, self-sufficient, all-powerful, and all-knowing. The Qur'an says: "To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" (4:171) and "There is none in the heavens or the earth who will not return to the Most Compassionate in full submission" (19:92–93).

**The Structure of the Argument**

The verse's reasoning can be laid out in steps. God is the Originator of all things without precedent (premise 1). A child requires a consort of the same kind; God has no consort and no kind (premise 2). Everything other than God is His creation, so nothing can share His nature (premise 3). God knows all things and lacks nothing, so He has no motive for offspring (premise 4). Therefore the attribution of a child to God is impossible on every ground: metaphysical (no consort, no kind), logical (created vs. uncreated), and teleological (no need). The verse compresses all of this into a single sentence.

**The Verse and Christian Doctrine**

The verse's argument was directed, in the first place, at the Arab claim of divine daughters, but it also addresses the Christian claim of divine sonship — a claim the Qur'an confronts in many places (4:171; 5:17, 72–75, 116–117; 9:30–31; 19:34–36, 88–93; 112:3). Christian theologians responded that they did not mean physical begetting, and the Qur'an's own language acknowledges that 'Son of God' was used by some in a sense not intended literally ("We are the children of Allah and His most beloved!" (5:18)). But the Qur'an's position is that any use of 'son' for God — whether literal or as a claim of shared divine nature — compromises His uniqueness, and it insists on the language of servant instead. Jesus is described as "truly a servant of Allah" (19:30) and as "a Word from Him" whose "name will be the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary" (3:45) — a creature brought into being by God's command, honored above most of creation, but a creature. The verse's argument from "He created all things" is meant to apply to every version of the claim.

**"Badīʿ" and the Believer's Wonder**

Beyond its polemical function, the verse's opening name is an invitation to wonder. God is the *Badīʿ* — the One who originated the heavens and the earth with no model, no material, no predecessor. Every act of human making uses existing materials and follows existing patterns. God's making does neither. The believer who reflects on this understands why no partner or child can be ascribed to Him: the Originator of all is in a category of one. The verse asks the hearer to hold this uniqueness clearly in mind, so that the imagination's tendency to picture God as a greater version of a creature — with kin, companions, and needs — is corrected at its source.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:102

> **That is Allah—your Lord! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. ˹He is˺ the Creator of all things, so worship Him ˹alone˺. And He is the Maintainer of everything.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Conclusion of the Argument**

After the signs of creation (vv. 95–99), the rejection of partners and offspring (v. 100), and the demonstration that God can have no child (v. 101), verse 102 draws the conclusion: *dhālikumu Allāhu rabbukum* — "that is God, your Lord." The demonstrative gathers everything described — the Cleaver of the seed and the dawn, the Maker of the stars, the Sender of rain, the Originator without consort — and says: this is your Lord. The verse is a summary creed and a command, and it functions as the hinge between the sūrah's argument and its practical demand.

**"That Is God, Your Lord"**

The phrase *dhālikumu Allāh* appeared at verse 95 and recurs in 10:3, 32; 35:13; 39:6; 40:62, 64 — always after a description of God's acts in creation. It answers the question "Who is God?" not with an abstract definition but by pointing at what He does. The One who splits the seed and sends the rain — *that* is God. And He is "*your* Lord" — the *rabb* who owns, sustains, and governs you, the hearers. The possessive is personal: the God being described is not a philosophical principle but the Lord of each person listening.

**"There Is No God but He"**

*Lā ilāha illā huwa* — the first half of the *shahādah*, the foundational statement of Islam. The verse places it here as the conclusion that the whole preceding passage has been building toward. If God alone does what verses 95–99 described, and if no partner or child can be ascribed to Him (vv. 100–101), then there is no god but He. The statement is not asserted arbitrarily; it is reached.

The formula negates and affirms. *Lā ilāha* — there is no god, no object worthy of worship, no being to whom one should turn in ultimate dependence. *Illā huwa* — except Him. Everything the idolaters worshipped falls under the negation; the One Creator alone stands in the exception. Abraham's confession (vv. 78–79) had this shape; so does this verse.

**"Creator of All Things"**

*Khāliqu kulli shay'* — "Creator of every thing." The phrase repeats the substance of verse 101 ("He created all things") in the form of a name. Everything that exists other than God is His creation — the heavens and the earth, the jinn and the angels, human beings and their circumstances. The universality is absolute: *kulli shay'*, "every thing," without exception.

The source commentary notes that this phrase became a focus of theological debate. The Ashʿarites read "Creator of all things" as including human acts: God creates the actions of human beings, who "acquire" (*kasb*) them and are responsible for them. The Muʿtazilites argued that human acts are the creation of human beings themselves, and pointed to the very next words — "so worship Him" — as evidence: it would be purposeless, they held, for God to command an act He had already created. Al-Rāzī records both positions. The mainstream Sunnī view, which the Ashʿarites and Māturīdites articulated in different ways, holds that God is the Creator of all things including human acts, while human beings possess real choice and real responsibility; the verse's "Creator of all things" and its "so worship Him" are both true, and the mystery of their relation is not resolved by denying either.

For the ordinary reader, the phrase's practical meaning is clear enough: nothing exists, happens, or is done except by God's creative power, and so nothing else deserves the reliance and worship that belong to Him.

**"So Worship Him"**

*Fa'ʿbudūh* — "so worship Him." The particle *fa-* ("so," "therefore") marks the command as a consequence. Because He is your Lord, because there is no god but He, because He is the Creator of all things — therefore worship Him. The whole argument of the sūrah has been leading to this imperative. Knowledge of God is not an end in itself; it obligates. The one who knows that God alone creates and sustains, and who then worships something else, has contradicted his own knowledge.

The word *ʿibādah* (worship) is broad. It includes the rites — prayer, fasting, pilgrimage — but extends to every act done in obedience and love of God: seeking His pleasure in work, in family, in speech, in the use of wealth. The Qur'an says that human beings and jinn were created for nothing else (51:56). The command here is the purpose of creation, stated as the conclusion of the argument from creation.

**"And He Is Guardian over All Things"**

*Wa huwa ʿalā kulli shay'in wakīl* — "and He is over all things a Trustee." The word *wakīl* means one entrusted with the management and protection of affairs — a guardian, an agent, a disposer. God is the *Wakīl* of all things: everything is in His charge, managed by Him, protected by Him. The verse has already used the word negatively of the Prophet ﷺ (v. 66: "I am not a guardian over you"); here it is affirmed of God. The Prophet ﷺ is not the guardian; God is.

The name gives the command "worship Him" its ground of trust. To worship God is to entrust oneself to Him, and the verse assures the worshipper that the One he entrusts himself to is the Trustee of all things. Nothing is outside His management; nothing can befall the one who relies on Him except by His disposal. The believers said at Uḥud, when threatened with an overwhelming army: "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Trustee (*wakīl*)" (3:173) — and the Prophet ﷺ taught these words as what Abraham said in the fire (al-Bukhārī 4563).

**The Verse as a Complete Confession**

Verse 102 contains, in five clauses, a complete statement of faith. Identification: that is God, your Lord. Exclusivity: there is no god but He. Attribute: Creator of all things. Obligation: so worship Him. Trust: He is Guardian over all things. A believer who understands these five clauses has understood the essential message of the sūrah — indeed, of the Qur'an. Everything else is elaboration.

**Why the Command Comes Here**

The placement of "so worship Him" is instructive. It comes after ninety-nine verses of argument, sign, story, and warning — not before. The Qur'an does not begin with demands; it begins with evidence, and it makes the demand when the evidence has been laid out. This is a model for how faith is to be taught: first the signs, then the reasoning, then the conclusion, then the obligation. The command to worship is not a bare imposition; it is what the honest mind arrives at when it has followed the signs to their Author.

**Worship as the Answer to the Sūrah's Question**

The sūrah opened with the question implicit in its first verse: why do those who disbelieve set up equals to the God who created the heavens and the earth? Verse 102 gives the answer they should have given: there is no god but He; worship Him. The verses between have removed every excuse — the idols do nothing, the celestial bodies set, the jinn are created, no child is possible. What remains is the One Creator and the single appropriate response. The verse names both.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:103

> **No vision can encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision. For He is the Most Subtle, All-Aware.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Transcendence of the One to Be Worshipped**

Verse 102 commanded worship of God, the Creator of all things. Verse 103 guards against a misunderstanding that worship might invite: that the One worshipped is a being who can be seen, located, and encompassed like the idols. *Lā tudrikuhu al-abṣār* — "sights do not perceive Him." The verse is one of the Qur'an's central statements about divine transcendence, and it has been the subject of sustained theological reflection.

**The Verb *Adraka***

*Yudriku* (from *adraka*) means to reach, to attain, to overtake, to grasp, to perceive comprehensively. The word implies not mere seeing but encompassing — taking in the whole of a thing. When one says that sight "*adraka*" an object, one means that it has grasped it fully, taken its measure. The verse denies that any sight does this to God. The plural *abṣār* (sights, faculties of vision) generalizes: no eye, no visual faculty, of any creature, comprehends Him.

**"But He Comprehends All Sight"**

*Wa huwa yudriku al-abṣār* — "and He perceives the sights." The same verb is turned around. Sights do not grasp Him; He grasps all sights. God perceives every eye, every act of seeing, every thing that is seen, and every faculty by which anything is seen — including the subtlest realities that no eye reaches. The verse thus asserts a total asymmetry: God is the Perceiver of all, perceived comprehensively by none. He is not an object among objects that a creature might inspect; He is the One from whom nothing, including the act of inspection itself, is hidden.

**The Debate over Seeing God**

The source commentary gives careful attention to the theological debate this verse occasioned. The Muʿtazilites held that the verse proves God cannot be seen at all, in this world or the next. Al-Zamakhsharī, the great Muʿtazilite commentator, argued that human sight attaches only to forms and bodies; God has no form or body; therefore He cannot be an object of sight in any circumstance. On this view, the verse is a flat denial of the vision of God.

The Ashʿarites and the scholars of ḥadīth held that the righteous will see God in the Hereafter, and they read the verse accordingly. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī explain that the verse denies *idrāk* — comprehensive perception, encompassing — not vision as such. The believers in Paradise will see their Lord, but they will not encompass Him; their sight will not take His measure or grasp His totality, just as their knowledge, though real, does not encompass Him: "He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them, but they cannot encompass Him in ˹their˺ knowledge" (20:110). Sight can be real without being comprehensive. Al-Rāzī further observes that the second clause — "He comprehends all sight" — shows that God is not absolutely beyond perception, since He perceives Himself; and that "sights do not comprehend Him" denies that *all* sights do so, not that *any* sight ever can.

The scriptural support for the vision of God in the Hereafter is substantial:

> "looking at their Lord" (75:22–23)

> "Those who do good will have the finest reward and ˹even˺ more" (10:26) — "more" (*ziyādah*) being explained by the Prophet ﷺ as the vision of God's face (Muslim 181).

> "Undoubtedly, they will be sealed off from their Lord on that Day" (83:15) — implying that the righteous will not be veiled.

And the ḥadīth, transmitted through many chains:

> "You will see your Lord on the Day of Resurrection as you see the moon on the night it is full, and as you see the sun when there are no clouds before it; you will not be crowded in seeing Him." (al-Bukhārī 554, 7434; Muslim 633)

The consensus of Sunnī theology, following these texts, is that the believers will see God in the Hereafter with a real vision, without modality, without encompassing, and without God being contained in any direction or place. The verse denies encompassing; it does not deny the vision the other texts affirm. In this world, however, the vision is not granted, as Moses learned when he asked and was told, "When his Lord appeared to the mountain, He levelled it to dust and Moses collapsed unconscious" (7:143); al-Jalālayn and others hold that the vision is for the next life only.

**Further Readings**

The source commentary records other perspectives. Some suggested that God will grant the righteous a new faculty — a "sixth sense" — by which they will see Him (al-Rāzī). Sufi commentators such as Ibn ʿAjībah and al-Baqlī suggested that human beings may see God through a vision granted by God Himself — that God sees Himself through them — so that the seer sees not by his own faculty but by a light from the Seen. Some Shīʿī commentators, following reports from the Imams, read "sight" as the imagination or the vision of the heart, which cannot encompass God in His totality. The Sufis speak similarly of the "eye of the heart" as the faculty by which God is known. These readings converge on the verse's essential point: whatever mode of perceiving God is granted to creatures, it does not encompass Him.

**"And He Is the Subtle, the Aware"**

*Wa huwa al-laṭīfu al-khabīr* — "and He is the Subtle, the Aware." The two names explain the two preceding clauses. *Al-Laṭīf* is the Subtle: the One so fine, so beyond the grossness of bodies, that physical sight cannot perceive Him — and, in another sense, the Gentle and Kind, who reaches His servants with benefits in ways they do not perceive. *Al-Khabīr* is the Aware: the One who knows the inner reality of all things, including the subtle realities no eye reaches. Al-Zamakhsharī draws the connection: God is subtle, so He is not perceived by physical vision; but He Himself possesses the essential reality of perception and so comprehends all sights and all subtle things.

The pairing of *al-Laṭīf* and *al-Khabīr* occurs several times (22:63; 31:16; 33:34; 67:14), and the source commentary notes that it indicates a relationship between subtlety and knowledge: the One who is Himself beyond gross perception is the One who perceives even the subtlest thing. Luqmān taught his son: "˹Even˺ if a deed were the weight of a mustard seed—be it ˹hidden˺ in a rock or in the heavens or the earth—Allah will bring it forth" (31:16). The subtle Knower reaches what nothing else reaches.

**The Practical Meaning of the Verse**

For worship, the verse establishes the proper posture. The One worshipped cannot be seen, imaged, located, or encompassed. This is why Islam forbids images of God, rejects any physical representation of the divine, and prays toward a direction (the Kaʿbah) without imagining that God is *in* that direction. The idolaters worshipped what they could see; the believer worships the One who sees him and whom he cannot see. This is the meaning of the Prophet's ﷺ definition of *iḥsān*: "to worship God as though you see Him; for if you do not see Him, He sees you" (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8). The second half of that definition is this verse: you do not see Him; He sees you.

For hope, the verse — read with the texts on the vision of God — offers the believer the greatest of all promises: that in Paradise he will see the Lord he worshipped unseen. The Prophet ﷺ said that when the people of Paradise have entered, God will ask if they want anything more, and they will say, "Have You not brightened our faces, admitted us to Paradise, and saved us from the Fire?" Then the veil will be removed, "and they will not have been given anything more beloved to them than looking at their Lord" (Muslim 181). The vision that this world denies, the next world grants — without encompassing, as the verse says, but real.

**The Balance of the Verse**

The verse holds transcendence and presence together. God is not seen — He is beyond every sight. God sees — nothing escapes Him. He is Subtle — beyond grasp. He is Aware — grasping all. A believer who forgets the first half falls into anthropomorphism, imagining God as a being who can be pictured. A believer who forgets the second half falls into deism, imagining a God so remote that He does not see. The verse forbids both. The One who cannot be comprehended is the One from whom nothing is hidden, and the worshipper lives between these truths: unable to see, always seen.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:104

> **Indeed, there have come to you insights from your Lord. So whoever chooses to see, it is for their own good. But whoever chooses to be blind, it is to their own loss. And I am not a keeper over you.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Sight to Insight**

Verse 103 said that sight (*abṣār*) does not comprehend God. Verse 104 uses the same root for a different faculty: *qad jā'akum baṣā'iru min rabbikum* — "there have come to you insights from your Lord." *Baṣā'ir* is the plural of *baṣīrah*, inner vision, insight, the perception of the heart. The wordplay is deliberate. Physical sight cannot reach God; but God has sent *insights* — proofs, clarifications, illuminations — by which the heart may perceive what the eye cannot. What the eye is denied, the heart is given.

**What the "Insights" Are**

The commentators identify the *baṣā'ir* in complementary ways. Al-Ṭabarī glosses them as guidance — the vision of the heart that leads to the truth of religion. Al-Zamakhsharī calls insight the "light of the heart" from which all real vision derives. Ibn ʿAjībah speaks of the "eye of the heart." In the immediate context, the insights are the arguments and signs the sūrah has laid out: the seed and the dawn, the stars and the rain, the single soul, the refutation of partners and offspring, the affirmation of the One Creator. Each is a *baṣīrah* — something that makes the truth visible to the inner eye. The Qur'an calls itself *baṣā'ir* in 7:203 and 45:20: "This ˹Quran˺ is an insight for humanity—a guide and mercy for people of sure faith"

The plural is significant. Not one insight but many — as the sūrah has said, "thus do We vary the signs" (vv. 46, 65, 105). God has provided illumination from many directions, so that a person who misses one may catch another.

**"From Your Lord"**

The insights come *min rabbikum* — from your Lord. They are not human speculation or the Prophet's ﷺ invention; they are sent by the One who sustains the hearer. This gives them authority and also intimacy: the Lord who feeds you with rain has also sent you light for your heart. The phrase connects to verse 102 ("that is God, your Lord") — the Lord just described as Creator of all things is the sender of these insights.

**"So Whosoever Sees Clearly, It Is to the Benefit of His Own Soul"**

*Fa-man abṣara fa-li-nafsih* — "so whoever sees, it is for himself." The verb *abṣara* means to see, to perceive — here, with the inner eye, to grasp the insights and accept the truth. The one who does so benefits himself alone. The construction *li-nafsih* — "for his soul," "for himself" — is the Qur'an's standard way of saying that the reward of faith accrues to the believer, not to God, who needs nothing, and not to the Prophet ﷺ, who gains nothing personally from anyone's belief. Al-Ṭabarī: he shall reap the reward of it.

**"And Whosoever Is Blind, It Is to Its Detriment"**

*Wa man ʿamiya fa-ʿalayhā* — "and whoever is blind, it is against it." The verb *ʿamiya* means to be or become blind — here, spiritually: to fail to perceive the insights, to refuse them. The consequence is *ʿalayhā* — against his soul. He harms only himself. The pair *li-* ("for") and *ʿalā* ("against") frames the two outcomes with perfect symmetry: what one does with the insights redounds entirely to oneself, for good or ill.

The opposition of seeing and blindness is one of the sūrah's recurring images (v. 50: "Have they not travelled throughout the land so their hearts may reason, and their ears may listen"; 11:24; 13:16; 35:19; 40:58). In every case it refers to spiritual perception, as the Qur'an makes explicit: "Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind" (22:46). The idolaters had perfect eyesight; they saw the seed and the dawn and the stars; they were blind to what these showed.

**The Principle of Personal Consequence**

The verse states a principle that runs throughout the Qur'an: the consequences of belief and disbelief fall on the one who chooses.

> "So whoever chooses to be guided, it is only for their own good" (10:108; 17:15; 39:41)

> "And whoever does evil, it is to their own loss" (41:46; 45:15)

This principle has two implications. First, God is not benefited by faith or harmed by disbelief. The Prophet ﷺ transmitted God's words: "O My servants, you cannot reach harm to Me so as to harm Me, nor can you reach benefit to Me so as to benefit Me" (Muslim 2577). The command to believe is for the believer's sake. Second, no one else bears the consequence of one's choice. The blind man's blindness is against himself alone; he cannot blame his ancestors, his leaders, or his society, and none of them will bear his burden (6:164).

**"And I Am Not a Keeper over You"**

*Wa mā ana ʿalaykum bi-ḥafīẓ* — "and I am not a keeper over you." The speaker is the Prophet ﷺ, as al-Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿAjībah confirm; the shift to the first person marks his voice within the divine address. The word *ḥafīẓ* means a guardian, a watcher, one who keeps and preserves. The Prophet ﷺ disclaims this role over the people. He is not their keeper — not responsible for making them see, not accountable for their blindness, not empowered to compel their vision. The disclaimer echoes verse 66 ("I am not a guardian over you") and recurs in 4:80, 11:86, and 42:48. Its implication, as Ibn ʿAjībah notes, is that God, not the Prophet ﷺ, is their Keeper.

The placement of this disclaimer after the statement of personal consequence is logical. If seeing benefits the seer alone and blindness harms the blind alone, then the Prophet ﷺ — who neither gains from the one nor loses from the other — is simply the one through whom the insights came. He conveyed; they choose; God keeps.

**The Verse's Structure**

The verse moves in three steps. The gift: insights have come from your Lord. The choice and its consequence: whoever sees benefits himself; whoever is blind harms himself. The limit of the messenger: I am not your keeper. The movement is from God's provision, through human responsibility, to the Prophet's ﷺ role — which is to say, the whole structure of guidance. God gives; human beings respond; the Prophet ﷺ delivers and does not compel.

**Insight and the Believer's Cultivation**

The verse also implies a task. Insights have come; they must be *seen*. Seeing with the heart is not automatic; it requires attention, sincerity, and the removal of what blinds — arrogance, desire, imitation of ancestors. The Qur'an says that God's signs are for "those who reflect" (13:3; 16:11; 30:21; 39:42), and reflection is an act. The believer cultivates *baṣīrah* by reading the Book with attention, looking at creation as the sūrah has taught, and turning to God for the light the heart needs. The Prophet ﷺ prayed: "O God, place light in my heart, and light in my sight, and light in my hearing" (al-Bukhārī 6316; Muslim 763). The light in the heart is the *baṣīrah* of this verse.

**The Verse for the Caller to God**

Finally, the verse is a charter for everyone who conveys the truth. Your task is to convey the insights God has sent. Whether they are received is not in your control and not on your account. Those who see benefit themselves; those who refuse harm themselves; and you are not their keeper. This frees the caller from the two errors the Prophet ﷺ was guarded against throughout this sūrah: despair when the message is refused, and coercion to force its acceptance. He is a bearer of insight, not a keeper of souls. The keeping belongs to God.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:105

> **And so We vary our signs to the extent that they will say, “You have studied ˹previous scriptures˺,” and We make this ˹Quran˺ clear for people who know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Method Named Again**

*Wa kadhālika nuṣarrifu al-āyāt* — "and thus do We diversify the signs." The verb *ṣarrafa* (to turn about, to present in varied forms) has appeared in verses 46 and 65, and the sūrah has just exemplified it: the signs of creation (vv. 95–99), the refutation of partners and offspring (vv. 100–101), the creed (v. 102), the transcendence of God (v. 103), the insights given (v. 104). Each approaches the same truth from a different angle. The verse pauses to say why the Qur'an works this way.

**Two Purposes**

The verse states two purposes, of which the second is straightforward and the first requires explanation.

The second: *wa li-nubayyinahu li-qawmin yaʿlamūn* — "and that We may make it clear for a people who know." The variation of signs serves clarity. A single argument may fail to reach a given mind; many arguments, from many directions, leave the truth exposed on every side. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the phrase refers to the various proofs of God's Oneness presented throughout the sūrah, each designed to remove doubt. "A people who know" — the phrase of verse 97 — are those who receive the clarification, because they bring to it the knowledge and honesty it requires.

**"Lest They Should Say, 'You Have Studied'"**

The first purpose is stated as: *wa li-yaqūlū darasta* — literally, "and that they may say, 'You have studied.'" The phrase has puzzled readers, because it seems to say that God varies the signs *in order that* the idolaters may make this accusation. The commentators resolve this in several ways.

One reading, followed in the translation ("*lest* they should say"), takes the *lām* as expressing consequence rather than purpose, or understands an implicit negation: the signs are varied so thoroughly that the accusation "you learned this from others" becomes untenable. Another reading takes the phrase at face value as a statement of what will in fact happen: God varies the signs, and the outcome — foreseen and, in the sense of the divine decree, willed — is that the obstinate will respond by saying "As for the believers, it has increased them in faith and they rejoice" while the sincere will find clarity. This is the Qur'anic pattern in which the same revelation guides some and hardens others (2:26; 9:124–125; 17:82). Both readings are transmitted, and both make the same point: the varied presentation of signs exposes the deniers' response as an excuse.

**The Accusation**

*Darasta* — "you have studied," "you have learned by reading." The idolaters claimed that the Prophet ﷺ had acquired his material by studying with the People of the Book, reading their scriptures, or learning from knowledgeable foreigners. The Qur'an records the accusation in several forms:

> "And We surely know that they say," (16:103)

> "˹These revelations are only˺ ancient fables which he has had written down, and they are rehearsed to him morning and evening" (25:5)

> "This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but a fabrication which he made up with the help of others" (25:4)

The accusation appears also in 6:25, 8:31, 16:24, 23:83, 27:68, 46:17, 68:15, and 83:13 in the form "legends of the ancients." Variant readings of this verse — *dārasta* ("you have studied with others," "you have engaged in mutual study") and *darasat* ("they [the signs] have been studied," or "these are old, worn-out things") — preserve the same charge in different forms.

**Why the Accusation Fails**

The verse's placement answers the accusation by juxtaposition. The signs just presented — the splitting seed, the dawn, the stars, the rain, the single soul, the refutation of divine offspring, the transcendence of God beyond sight — are not the sort of thing learned from a rabbi or a monk. They are drawn from the natural world visible to everyone, arranged with a precision and reasoned with a force that no known source in Arabia provided. The very variety of the signs (*taṣrīf*) defeats the charge: if the Prophet ﷺ had studied with a human teacher, his material would bear that teacher's stamp and be limited to that teacher's knowledge; instead it ranges over creation, history, theology, and law with a consistency and comprehensiveness that points to a single, superhuman source.

The Prophet ﷺ was also known to be unlettered (7:157; 29:48: "You ˹O Prophet˺ could not read any writing ˹even˺ before this ˹revelation˺, nor could you write at all"). He had lived forty years among the Makkans without any reputation for learning, had made only brief journeys outside Arabia, and had no known teacher. The claim that he had "studied" was not a serious explanation but a way of avoiding the implication of what he brought.

**"For a People Who Know"**

The verse ends by naming the audience for whom the clarification is effective: *qawm yaʿlamūn*, "a people who know." The contrast with the accusers is implicit. The accusers do not know; they assume, and their assumption is that a man like themselves could not have received revelation, so they invent a human source. Those who know weigh the signs and recognize their origin. The two responses to the same varied presentation — the accusation and the recognition — sort people into the two categories the sūrah has been distinguishing throughout.

**The Broader Principle**

The verse teaches something about the reception of truth generally. The same evidence produces opposite reactions depending on the disposition of the one who receives it. To the sincere, the variety of the Qur'an's signs is illuminating; to the obstinate, it is suspicious — "where did he get all this?" The Qur'an does not adjust its method to placate the obstinate; it presents the signs fully and lets the reactions reveal the hearts. This is why the verse can say, without contradiction, that the signs are varied both "that they may say 'you have studied'" and "that We may make it clear for a people who know." The one presentation does both, because the difference lies in the recipients.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse invites the reader to place himself. When he encounters the Qur'an's arguments — from creation, from history, from reason — does he receive them as clarification, or does he reach for an explanation that lets him avoid their force? The accusation "you have studied" has modern descendants: "he borrowed from earlier religions," "it reflects its cultural environment," "these ideas were in the air." Each may contain a grain of observation, but each functions as the Makkan charge functioned: to avoid engaging the signs themselves. The verse says that the signs have been varied precisely so that this avoidance is exposed, and so that the one who knows may see clearly.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:106

> **˹O Prophet!˺ Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord—there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—and turn away from the polytheists.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Instruction after the Proofs**

Having presented the varied signs (v. 105), the sūrah tells the Prophet ﷺ what to do now: *ittabiʿ mā ūḥiya ilayka min rabbik* — "follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord." The command is simple and returns to the definition of the Prophet's ﷺ role given in verse 50: "I follow only what is revealed to me." After all the argument, the essential thing is unchanged: follow the revelation.

**"Follow That Which Has Been Revealed unto Thee"**

The verb *ittabaʿa* means to follow closely, to walk in the track of. The Prophet ﷺ is to follow the revelation — to shape his belief, conduct, and message by it, adding nothing and omitting nothing. This is the source of his authority and the limit of it. He does not follow his own preference, the desires of the idolaters (v. 56), or the pressures of his situation; he follows what has come to him from his Lord. The command is repeated in similar words in 10:109 ("And follow what is revealed to you and be patient until God gives judgment") and 33:2 ("And follow that which is revealed to you from your Lord").

The phrase "from your Lord" (*min rabbik*) grounds the revelation's authority in the relationship it comes from. It is not merely "what has been revealed" but "what has been revealed *from your Lord*" — from the One who sustains and guides you. Following it is therefore not submission to an external rule but fidelity to the One who has been faithful to him.

**"There Is No God but He"**

*Lā ilāha illā huwa* — inserted in the middle of the command, between "follow" and "turn away." The placement is deliberate. The reason to follow the revelation is that it comes from the only God; the reason to turn from the idolaters is that they worship others than the only God. The *shahādah* is the hinge on which both halves of the command turn. It also summarizes the content of the revelation the Prophet ﷺ is told to follow: whatever else it contains, its center is this.

**"And Turn Away from the Idolaters"**

*Wa aʿriḍ ʿan al-mushrikīn* — "and turn away from the idolaters." The verb *aʿraḍa* means to turn one's side to something, to disregard, to withdraw attention from. This is the third time the sūrah has given a form of this instruction (v. 68: turn away from those who mock the signs; v. 70: leave those who take religion as play; v. 91: leave them to their vain discourse). After the signs have been presented and the proofs varied, if the idolaters persist, the Prophet ﷺ is not to wear himself out over them.

The turning away is not hostility, and it is not the end of conveying. The Prophet ﷺ continued to preach in Makkah for years after this verse. The instruction concerns his inner posture and his priorities: do not be consumed by their rejection, do not chase after them, do not let their obstinacy divert you from following the revelation. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the turning away means not engaging in fruitless dispute with those who have shown they will not accept the truth, and continuing with one's own duty. Verse 107 will give the theological reason: had God willed, they would not have associated partners; it is not in your hands.

**The Structure of the Command**

The verse contains a positive command (follow), a creed (no god but He), and a negative command (turn away). Read as a unit, it says: hold to the revelation, because its God is the only God, and do not be diverted by those who reject Him. This is the whole of the Prophet's ﷺ practical instruction, and it has a permanent application. The believer, too, is to follow what has been revealed, to hold the *shahādah* at the center, and to decline to be drawn into endless contention with those who reject it. His energy is for the truth, not for the argument.

**Turning Away as Dignity and as Mercy**

The command to turn away preserved the Prophet's ﷺ dignity and, in a sense, was a mercy to the idolaters. Dignity: the messenger of God does not beg or plead with those who mock; he states the truth and continues on his way. Mercy: continued confrontation with the obstinate hardens them further, while withdrawal leaves them space to reflect. Many of the Makkans who were unmoved by argument were moved later by the Prophet's ﷺ conduct, by the steadfastness of the believers, and by events. The turning away was not abandonment; it was the wisdom of knowing when speech has done what it can.

**Between "Follow" and "Turn Away"**

There is a discipline in the verse that the caller to God must learn. Two opposite temptations beset anyone who conveys the truth to those who reject it. The first is to compromise the message to make it acceptable — which the verse forbids by saying "follow what has been revealed." The second is to become so absorbed in fighting the rejecters that one's own path is neglected — which the verse forbids by saying "turn away." The middle way is fidelity to the revelation combined with detachment from the outcome. The Prophet ﷺ walked it, and the verse maps it.

**Not Abrogated**

Some scholars held that the command to "But once the Sacred Months have passed, kill the polytheists ˹who violated their treaties˺ wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them on every way" was abrogated by the later verses commanding fighting (9:5). The stronger view, held by many, is that there is no abrogation here. The verse describes the posture of the caller toward those who reject the message — a posture that remains valid in every age and circumstance — and not a ruling about warfare. Turning away from disputation is compatible with any legal ruling about relations with hostile powers; the two operate at different levels. The Prophet ﷺ turned away from the idolaters' mockery in Makkah and continued to do so, in the sense of not being diverted by it, throughout his life.

**The Verse as a Daily Instruction**

The verse can be read as a program for the believer's day. Follow what has been revealed: begin from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and measure choices by them. There is no god but He: keep the center in view. Turn away from the idolaters: do not let those who reject the truth — whether through mockery, pressure, or the sheer weight of a culture that ignores God — set the terms of one's inner life. The believer who does these three things has done what the Prophet ﷺ was commanded here, and the next verse will tell him why he need not carry the burden of the rest.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:107

> **Had Allah willed, they would not have been polytheists. We have not appointed you as their keeper, nor are you their maintainer.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reason behind "Turn Away"**

Verse 106 commanded the Prophet ﷺ to turn away from the idolaters. Verse 107 gives the reason: *wa law shā'a Allāhu mā ashrakū* — "and had God willed, they would not have associated partners." The idolaters' *shirk* exists within God's will. He could have prevented it — could have created them without the capacity to err, or compelled them to believe — and He did not. Their state is therefore not a failure of the Prophet's ﷺ effort, and it is not within his power to change. The verse relieves him of a burden by telling him where the matter actually rests.

**"Had God Willed, They Would Not Have Ascribed Partners"**

The statement is a fundamental one in the Qur'an's teaching about the divine will, and it is repeated in various forms (2:253; 5:48; 6:35, 112, 137, 149; 10:99; 11:118; 16:9, 93; 32:13; 42:8). The most direct parallel is 10:99: "Had your Lord so willed ˹O Prophet˺, all ˹people˺ on earth would have certainly believed, every single one of them" Verse 35 of this sūrah said the same: "had God willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance."

The verse teaches that nothing happens outside God's will — including disbelief. This does not mean God approves of *shirk*; He has forbidden it, condemned it, and warned of its punishment throughout this sūrah. It means that God has willed to create human beings with genuine choice, and has willed not to override that choice by compulsion. The *shirk* of the idolaters is their own act, freely chosen and fully culpable; and it takes place within a world that God has willed to be one in which such choice is possible. The two truths — divine will and human responsibility — are held together, not collapsed into either determinism or the denial of God's sovereignty.

**The Idolaters' Misuse of This Truth**

The Qur'an records that the idolaters themselves invoked the divine will as an excuse: "Will, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated others with Him ˹in worship˺ or made anything unlawful" (6:148; 16:35). The same words that this verse states as a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ, the idolaters used as a defense — and the Qur'an rejects their use of it: "Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us" (6:148). The difference is in the purpose. The verse states God's will to relieve the Prophet ﷺ of responsibility for what he cannot control. The idolaters invoked it to relieve themselves of responsibility for what they *could* control — their own choice. The first is truth; the second is evasion. God's will encompasses human choice; it does not abolish it.

**"We Have Not Made Thee a Keeper over Them"**

*Wa mā jaʿalnāka ʿalayhim ḥafīẓan* — "and We have not made you a keeper over them." The word *ḥafīẓ* is the word of verse 104. There the Prophet ﷺ said it of himself; here God says it to him. God has not appointed him to watch over the idolaters' hearts, to preserve them from error, or to answer for their choices. His appointment is as messenger, warner, and bringer of good news (v. 48) — not as keeper.

**"Nor Art Thou Their Guardian"**

*Wa mā anta ʿalayhim bi-wakīl* — "nor are you over them a trustee." The word *wakīl* is the word of verse 66 ("I am not a guardian over you") and of verse 102 ("He is Guardian over all things"). The Prophet ﷺ is not their *wakīl*; God is the *Wakīl* of all things. The two words together — *ḥafīẓ* and *wakīl* — cover both aspects of responsibility: keeping (preserving from harm) and managing (disposing of affairs). Neither belongs to the Prophet ﷺ with respect to the idolaters. Both belong to God.

**The Pattern of Disclaimers**

This is the fourth time in the sūrah that the Prophet's ﷺ responsibility for the idolaters' choices has been disclaimed (vv. 52, 66, 104, 107), and the pattern will continue (v. 135; cf. 4:80; 10:108; 17:54; 25:43; 39:41; 42:6, 48; 50:45; 88:21–22). The repetition shows how important the point was — both for the Prophet's ﷺ peace and for the correct understanding of prophethood. The Prophet ﷺ cared so intensely for his people that the Qur'an had to tell him again and again: you are not their keeper. Each disclaimer was a lifting of weight from a heart that kept picking it up.

**How Verses 104–107 Fit Together**

The four verses form a coherent statement about responsibility. Insight has come from God (104a). Whoever sees or is blind does so for or against himself (104b). The Prophet ﷺ is not their keeper (104c). The signs are varied for those who know (105). The Prophet ﷺ must follow the revelation and turn from those who reject it (106). Their rejection is within God's will, and the Prophet ﷺ is neither keeper nor guardian over them (107). The message is layered: God provides, individuals choose and bear the consequence, God's will encompasses all, and the messenger's role is bounded. Within these bounds the Prophet ﷺ is free to do his work without despair.

**The Theological Balance**

The verse walks a line that Islamic theology worked hard to articulate. On one side is the error of denying God's comprehensive will — imagining that human beings act in a domain God does not govern, so that their disbelief is a defeat of His purpose. The verse forbids this: had He willed, they would not have associated. On the other side is the error of denying human responsibility — imagining that because God wills all, the idolaters are not culpable. The Qur'an forbids this in 6:148 and throughout. The mainstream position, expressed by al-Ṭaḥāwī and others, is that God's will encompasses everything, that human beings have real choice and real accountability, and that the relation between these is known to God and not fully to us. The believer affirms both and refuses to sacrifice either to a system.

**The Verse for Anyone Who Cares for Another's Faith**

The verse applies to every believer who longs for someone else's guidance — a parent for a child, a friend for a friend, a teacher for a student — and who is tempted to feel that the other's refusal is his own failure, or to resort to pressure to produce a result. The verse says: had God willed, they would have believed; you are not their keeper or guardian. This is not indifference; it is truth, and it makes sustained love possible. The one who knows he is not the keeper can keep loving and keep conveying without being crushed. The one who thinks he is the keeper will burn out, or will try to force what cannot be forced. The Prophet ﷺ, who loved his people more than anyone has loved a people, was told this verse for exactly that reason.

**"They Would Not Have Ascribed Partners"**

The verse's first clause also contains, read carefully, a rebuke to the idolaters. God's will could have prevented their *shirk* — and it did not, because He willed to leave them their choice and to test them by it. Their *shirk*, therefore, is neither necessary nor excusable; it is what they did with the freedom they were given. The consolation to the Prophet ﷺ is at the same time a verdict on them: it was in your hands, and you chose this. The verse that lifts the burden from the messenger places it squarely on those who rejected him.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:108

> **˹O believers!˺ Do not insult what they invoke besides Allah or they will insult Allah spitefully out of ignorance. This is how We have made each people’s deeds appealing to them. Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Restraint on the Believers**

The preceding verses instructed the Prophet ﷺ to turn away from the idolaters. This verse instructs the believers in a specific form of restraint: *wa lā tasubbū alladhīna yadʿūna min dūni Allāh* — "and do not insult those whom they call upon besides God." The verb *sabba* means to revile, to abuse, to curse. The believers are forbidden from cursing the idols.

**The Occasion**

Al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, and others record the circumstances. The Muslims in Makkah, in their zeal, used to revile the idols of the Quraysh — perhaps, as al-Zamakhsharī suggests, after the revelation of 21:98, which described the idols and their worshippers as fuel for Hell. The idolaters retaliated by reviling God. The leaders of Quraysh went to Abū Ṭālib and proposed a truce: let Muhammad's followers stop cursing our gods, and we will stop cursing his God. The Prophet ﷺ initially replied that he would agree only if they testified that there is no god but God; they refused. The verse was then revealed, instructing the believers to cease reviling the idols — not as a concession to the idolaters, but so that the believers would not be the cause of God being reviled.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported as saying: "They said, 'O Muhammad, either you stop insulting our gods or we will insult your Lord.' So God forbade them to insult their idols, lest they insult God out of enmity, without knowledge."

**"Lest They Should Revile God out of Enmity, without Any Knowledge"**

*Fa-yasubbū Allāha ʿadwan bi-ghayri ʿilm* — "so that they revile God in transgression, without knowledge." The word *ʿadw* means enmity, hostility, transgression of limits. The idolaters' reviling of God would be an act of hostile transgression, committed "without knowledge" — in ignorance of what they were doing and of whom they were insulting. The believers are forbidden to provoke this.

Al-Rāzī raises a question: the Makkans believed in Allāh as the supreme God, so how would they revile Him? He suggests that they may have reviled Him indirectly — by cursing the Prophet ﷺ who spoke in His name, or by invoking Fate against divine causality, or by uttering blasphemies in anger they would not have uttered in calm. Whatever the form, the verse's concern is clear: the believers must not become the occasion of God's name being abused.

**The Principle: Weighing Consequences**

The verse establishes a principle of enormous importance in Islamic ethics: an act that is permissible or even praiseworthy in itself may be forbidden if it leads to a greater evil. Reviling idols is, in the abstract, a true statement about false gods — they *are* worthless. But if reviling them provokes the idolaters to revile God, then the act has produced a harm greater than any benefit it brought. The jurists formulated this as *sadd al-dharā'iʿ* (blocking the means to evil) and as the rule that "warding off harm takes precedence over securing benefit." Al-Qurṭubī states the rule derived from this verse: whatever is a means to what is forbidden is itself forbidden, even if it is a means to something good.

The Prophet ﷺ applied the same principle when he said:

> "Among the major sins is a man's cursing his parents." They asked, "How does a man curse his parents?" He said, "He reviles another man's father, so that man reviles his father; and he reviles his mother, so that man reviles his mother." (al-Bukhārī 5973; Muslim 90)

The one who initiates the chain bears responsibility for what it produces. The believers who cursed the idols would bear a share in the idolaters' cursing of God.

**Wisdom in Calling to God**

The verse also teaches something about the manner of *daʿwah*. The source commentary draws the parallel with 20:44, where Moses and Aaron are commanded to speak to Pharaoh — "Speak to him gently, so perhaps he may be mindful ˹of Me˺ or fearful ˹of My punishment˺." (20:44). Provocation entrenches; gentleness opens. The one who insults what another holds sacred does not persuade him; he inflames him, and closes the door that argument might have opened. The Qur'an commands calling "Invite ˹all˺ to the Way of your Lord with wisdom and kind advice, and only debate with them in the best manner" (16:125). Reviling is not the best way, and the verse forbids it not merely because of its consequences but because it does not serve the purpose of bringing people to God.

This does not mean the believer may not state that idols are false. The whole sūrah does so, in argument after argument. There is a difference between demonstrating the falsehood of an object of worship and hurling abuse at it. The first is what Abraham did (vv. 74–81); the second is what the verse forbids. The distinction is between reasoned refutation, which respects the hearer's intelligence, and insult, which attacks his feelings and provokes retaliation.

**"Thus Have We Made the Deeds of Every Community Seem Fair unto Them"**

*Kadhālika zayyannā li-kulli ummatin ʿamalahum* — "thus have We made attractive to every community their deeds." The verse steps back to a general observation. Every people finds its own ways attractive — its religion, its customs, its practices. The idolaters were attached to their idols not through reasoned conviction but because their way of life had been made to seem fair to them. This is why insulting their gods provoked such a fierce reaction: one was attacking something they loved.

The Qur'an speaks of deeds being "made fair" in over a dozen places. Sometimes the agent is unnamed (6:122; 9:37; 13:33; 40:37; 47:14); sometimes it is Satan (6:43; 8:48; 15:39; 16:63; 27:24; 29:38); and sometimes, as here, it is God (cf. 10:12; 27:4; 41:25). The commentators explain the attribution to God in several ways. He makes deeds seem fair by granting prosperity or respite, which people take as approval (3:178; 7:95; 23:55–56). He allows the natural attachment people feel toward their inherited ways (2:170; 5:104; 7:70). And He does this as a test — the attachment to one's own ways is part of the trial of faith, which requires overcoming it when truth arrives. Verse 107 said that God willed to leave the idolaters their choice; this verse says that the attractiveness of their ways is part of the conditions in which that choice is made.

The general truth is applicable to everyone. Each community — including the community of believers — finds its own practices fair. The believer must recognize that his attachment to his ways does not by itself prove they are right, and that the idolaters' attachment to theirs explains their resistance without justifying it. This recognition breeds humility in oneself and understanding toward others.

**"Then unto Their Lord Shall Be Their Return"**

*Thumma ilā rabbihim marjiʿuhum* — "then to their Lord is their return." Whatever seems fair now will be judged then. The attractiveness of a community's ways in this life is not the measure of their worth; the return to God is. The formula "then to their Lord is their return" appears throughout the sūrah (vv. 36, 60, 62, 164) and keeps every observation about this world tethered to the next.

**"And He Will Inform Them of That Which They Used to Do"**

*Fa-yunabbi'uhum bi-mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — "To Allah you will all return, and He will inform you of what you used to do" The formula of verse 60, repeated in many places (5:105; 9:94, 105; 10:23; 29:8; 31:15; 39:7; 62:8). On that Day, the deeds that seemed fair will be shown as they were. The idolaters who reviled God in enmity, and the believers who provoked them — each will be informed. The verse's closing thus applies its principle to both sides: God will judge the idolaters for their *shirk* and their blasphemy, and He will judge the believers for the wisdom or foolishness with which they conveyed the truth.

**The Verse's Permanent Relevance**

Few verses of the Qur'an are more directly relevant to religious life in plural societies. Muslims live among people of other faiths and none, whose sacred objects, figures, and beliefs the Qur'an regards as false. The verse forbids reviling them — not because they are true, but because reviling provokes retaliation against what Muslims hold most sacred, closes hearts to the message, and does not serve the purpose of bringing people to God. The believer may argue, demonstrate, and invite; he may not insult. This restraint is not weakness; it is the discipline of one who cares more about God's name being honored than about the satisfaction of abusing an idol.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:109

> **They swear by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a sign were to come to them, they would certainly believe in it. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Signs are only with Allah.” What will make you ˹believers˺ realize that even if a sign were to come to them, they still would not believe?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Oath and Its Emptiness**

*Wa aqsamū bi'llāhi jahda aymānihim* — "and they swore by God with the utmost of their oaths." The phrase *jahda aymānihim* means the most strenuous, most solemn form of oath they could muster. The Makkans swore by God — whom they acknowledged as the supreme deity — that if only a miraculous sign came to them, they would believe. The swearing was emphatic; the sincerity was not.

The Qur'an records this pattern of solemn oaths from disbelievers and hypocrites in several places, always in the service of deception or excuse:

> "They swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a warner were to come to them, they would certainly be better guided than any other community" (35:42)

> "They swear by Allah their most solemn oaths that if you ˹O Prophet˺ were to command them, they would certainly march forth ˹in Allah" (24:53)

The oath is a way of making a demand sound like a promise. "Give us a sign, and we will believe" sounds reasonable. The verse exposes what it actually is.

**The Reported Occasion**

Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Wāḥidī record a report about the verse's occasion. The Quraysh, having heard the Prophet ﷺ recite the accounts of Moses' staff and Jesus' raising of the dead, said: "You tell us that Moses had a staff with which he struck the rock and water flowed, and that Jesus raised the dead, and that Thamūd had a she-camel. Bring us a sign like these, and we will believe you." The Prophet ﷺ asked what sign they wanted; they asked that Mount Ṣafā be turned to gold. He began to supplicate for this, and Gabriel came to him and said: "If you wish, Ṣafā will become gold; but if they then do not believe, God will punish them as He has never punished anyone; or if you wish, We will leave the door of repentance and mercy open to them." The Prophet ﷺ chose the latter, and this verse was revealed.

The report illuminates the following verse (v. 110) as well, and it fits the pattern established in verses 8 and 37: the great signs demanded by the idolaters were withheld not from inability but from mercy, since their rejection after such a sign would have sealed their destruction.

**"Say: Signs Are with God Alone"**

*Qul innamā al-āyātu ʿinda Allāh* — "Say: Signs are only with God." The restrictive particle *innamā* ("only") locates the signs entirely with God. The Prophet ﷺ does not possess them, cannot produce them, and does not decide when they come. This was stated in verse 37 ("God is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know") and is a consistent Qur'anic principle:

> "It was not for any messenger to bring a sign without Allah" (13:38; 40:78)

The answer disposes of the demand in a single stroke. The Makkans were, in effect, trying to negotiate with the Prophet ﷺ over what God alone controls. He tells them where to direct their demand — and, implicitly, that God has already sent the sign He chose to send: the Qur'an itself, the "clear proof" of verse 57.

**"What Will Make You Realize That, Even If They Were to Come, They Would Still Not Believe?"**

*Wa mā yushʿirukum annahā idhā jā'at lā yu'minūn* — "and what would make you perceive that, if they came, they would not believe?" The address shifts — to the believers, according to most commentators, or to the Prophet ﷺ. The believers may have hoped that a great sign would convert the idolaters; some reports say they urged the Prophet ﷺ to ask for it. The verse tells them: how do you know that, if the sign came, they would believe? The implied answer, and the explicit statement of verses 110–111, is that they would not.

The Arabic admits two readings. With *annahā* ("that they"), the sense is as translated: what would make you realize that they would not believe? With *innahā* ("indeed they"), the clause becomes a separate statement: "And what would make you perceive [what is in their hearts]? Indeed, if the signs came, they would not believe." Both readings converge on the same verdict.

**Why Signs Do Not Produce Faith in the Obstinate**

The verse states what the sūrah has argued from its opening (vv. 4, 7, 25, 35, 37): faith is not a mechanical response to evidence. A person who has decided not to believe will not be moved by any sign, because he will find a way to explain it away — as the Makkans dismissed the Qur'an as 'sorcery' (v. 7) and would have called a mountain of gold an illusion. The obstacle is not a lack of evidence but a disposition of the heart. The Qur'an says of Pharaoh's people, who saw the greatest signs of any nation: "But when Our enlightening signs came to them, they said, 'This is pure magic.'" (27:13). "And, although their hearts were convinced the signs were true, they still denied them wrongfully and arrogantly." (27:14). Inner conviction and outward rejection coexisted. A sign persuades the mind; it does not compel the will.

The history of the Prophet's ﷺ own signs confirms this. The moon was split (54:1–2), and the Makkans said, "Passing magic." The Qur'an was recited, and they said, "Legends of the ancients." The Night Journey was described, and they mocked. Those who believed did so on the basis of the Qur'an and the Prophet's ﷺ character; those who refused would have refused anything.

**The Mercy in the Refusal**

Read with the report about Mount Ṣafā, the verse shows God's mercy in withholding what the idolaters demanded. Had the sign come and they had rejected it — as the verse says they would — their punishment would have followed at once, as it did for every nation that rejected a manifest sign (v. 8; 17:59: "And We gave Thamûd the shecamel as a clear sign, but they wrongfully rejected it"). By not sending the sign, God kept the door open, and many of those very Makkans walked through it years later. The verse that seems to describe their hopeless obstinacy is, in its context, part of the reason they were given time to change.

**The Verse for the Believer**

The verse guards the believer against a form of impatience: the wish that God would produce some overwhelming demonstration that would settle every argument and convert every skeptic. The verse says that such demonstrations do not convert the unwilling and that signs are, in any case, God's to give. The believer's task is to convey the signs that have been given — the Qur'an, creation, the prophetic example — and to trust God with the hearts. It also guards him against the reverse error in himself: making his own faith conditional on signs. The one who says "I would believe if only..." has made the idolaters' oath. Faith is a response to what God has already shown, not a bargain for what He has not.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:110

> **We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Completing the Answer**

Verse 109 asked what would make the believers realize that the idolaters would not believe even if a sign came. Verse 110 gives the divine account of why: *wa nuqallibu af'idatahum wa abṣārahum* — "and We turn their hearts and their sights." The verse describes the inner state of those who have rejected the truth once and continue to reject it, and the divine action that corresponds to that state.

**The Verb *Qallaba***

*Nuqallibu* comes from *qallaba*, to turn over, to turn about repeatedly, to flip — the root of *qalb*, the heart, which is so named because it turns. To "turn the hearts and sights" is to move them from one state or thought to another, so that they do not settle on the truth. The source commentary connects the verb to two well-known ḥadīths:

> "The heart of the son of Adam is between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful, as one heart; He turns it (*yuqallibuhu*) however He wills." Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "O God, Turner of hearts (*muqallib al-qulūb*), turn our hearts to Your obedience." (Muslim 2654)

> The Prophet ﷺ used to say frequently: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." When asked why, he said: "There is no heart but that it is between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful; if He wills, He makes it upright, and if He wills, He turns it aside." (al-Tirmidhī 2140; Ibn Mājah 3834)

Al-Rāzī notes that although the ḥadīths concern the believer and the Prophet ﷺ while the verse concerns the disbelievers, together they teach God's complete power over the inner life of human beings.
