The heart is not autonomous; it turns, and God is the Turner. This is why the believer's constant prayer is for firmness.

**"Hearts and Sights"**

*Af'idah* (sg. *fu'ād*) is a word for the heart with connotations of burning or intense feeling — the heart as the seat of perception and emotion. *Abṣār* are the sights — physical and inner. The verse names both faculties by which truth is received: the inner perception of the heart and the perception of the eye (or the insight that verse 104 called *baṣīrah*). Both are turned away, so that neither the evidence before the eyes nor the recognition within the heart produces faith.

**"As They Did Not Believe in It the First Time"**

*Kamā lam yu'minū bihi awwala marrah* — "just as they did not believe in it the first time." This clause is the verse's key. The turning of hearts is not arbitrary; it corresponds to (*kamā*, "just as") their initial refusal. When the truth first came — the Qur'an, the Prophet's ﷺ call — they rejected it. That first rejection was their free act. The subsequent turning of their hearts is the consequence: having refused the truth when it was clear, they are left in a state where it no longer appears clear to them. God turns their hearts *as* they turned from Him.

This is the principle stated in many places: "So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate" (61:5); "There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase" (2:10); and, in this sūrah, the sealing of hearts (v. 46) and the making of deeds seem fair (v. 108). Al-Zamakhsharī connects the verse to these passages on the sealing of hearts. The disbelievers' incapacity to perceive is the outcome of their own choice, ratified by God. Had they believed the first time, their hearts would have been turned toward guidance instead.

The phrase also answers the question of verse 109 precisely. Why would a sign not make them believe? Because their hearts have been turned by their first refusal, and a second sign would meet the same disposition that rejected the first. The problem is not the evidence but the condition of the receiver — a condition they brought upon themselves.

**"And We Shall Leave Them to Wander Confused in Their Rebellion"**

*Wa nadharuhum fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn* — "and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly." The verb *dhara* means to leave, to let be — the same verb the sūrah has used for the Prophet's ﷺ leaving of the mockers (vv. 70, 91, 112). God leaves them. He does not compel them to believe, does not cut short their lives to end their wandering, and does not interfere with the path they have chosen. The word *ṭughyān* means transgression, overstepping bounds, rebellion — the state of one who has exceeded all limits. The verb *ʿamiha* means to wander blindly, confused, without direction — as a person lost in the dark.

The phrase appears in 2:15 of the hypocrites ("God mocks them and prolongs them in their transgression while they wander blindly"), and the idea recurs in 7:186, 10:11, and 23:75. Al-Rāzī explains that "leaving" them means neither interfering with their choice nor ending their respite. This is the same divine patience the sūrah has described repeatedly (vv. 12, 58, 67): God delays, gives time, and lets those who wander continue to wander — which is both a mercy (they may yet turn) and a judgment (their wandering deepens).

**The Theological Balance**

The verse has been read in different ways by the theological schools. The Ashʿarites saw in it evidence of God's direct control over hearts. The Muʿtazilites read it as describing God's punishment for prior disbelief: He "turns their hearts" in the sense of withdrawing His grace and leaving them to the consequences of their choice. The mainstream position, reflected in the verse's own structure ('*as* they did not believe the first time'), holds both: God's turning of hearts is real and sovereign, and it responds to what human beings do with their freedom. The one who refuses light is left in darkness; the one who seeks light is given more (47:17: "As for those who are ˹rightly˺ guided, He increases them in guidance and blesses them with righteousness"). Neither the sovereignty nor the responsiveness is denied.

**The Verse as Warning**

For the reader, the verse is a warning about the consequences of first refusals. The state it describes — hearts and sights turned, wandering in confusion — is not the state in which anyone begins. It is reached by a sequence: the truth comes; it is refused; the refusal becomes habit; the heart is turned; the truth, when it comes again, no longer registers. The verse warns against the first step, because the later ones follow from it. The Prophet ﷺ described this process:

> "Trials will be presented to hearts as a reed mat is woven, stick by stick. Any heart that absorbs them will have a black spot placed in it, and any heart that rejects them will have a white spot placed in it, until there are two kinds of hearts: one white like a smooth stone, which no trial will harm as long as the heavens and earth endure; and the other black and dusty like an overturned vessel, which does not recognize good or reject evil." (Muslim 144)

The "overturned vessel" (*mujakhkhiyan*) is a heart turned upside down — the *taqlīb* of this verse.

**The Believer's Response**

The correct response to the verse is the Prophet's ﷺ prayer: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." The believer who understands that hearts turn, and that God is the Turner, does not rest in his present faith as a secure possession. He asks for firmness, guards against the first refusals that begin the turning, and responds to every new truth with acceptance rather than resistance — so that his heart is turned toward guidance, and not, as the verse describes, away from it.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:111

> **Even if We had sent them the angels, made the dead speak to them, and assembled before their own eyes every sign ˹they demanded˺, they still would not have believed— unless Allah so willed. But most of them are ignorant ˹of this˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Hypothesis Pushed to Its Limit**

Verse 109 said that if a sign came, the idolaters would not believe. Verse 111 tests this claim against the most overwhelming signs imaginable: *wa law annanā nazzalnā ilayhimu al-malā'ikata wa kallamahumu al-mawtā wa ḥasharnā ʿalayhim kulla shay'in qubulan* — "and even if We sent down to them the angels, and the dead spoke to them, and We gathered before them every thing, face to face." Three signs, each exceeding what any people had ever been shown.

**The Three Signs**

*The angels sent down.* The Makkans had demanded this (v. 8: "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"; 25:7, 21). The verse imagines it granted: angels descending visibly, confirming the Prophet ﷺ. Even this would not suffice. Verses 8–9 explained one reason — an angel visible to human beings would have to take human form, and the confusion would remain. This verse states the deeper reason: the obstacle is not the absence of angels but the disposition of the hearts (v. 110).

*The dead speaking.* The idolaters denied the resurrection; they said "there is nothing but our life in this world" (v. 29). Suppose the dead rose and spoke to them, testifying to what they had seen. Would they believe? The verse says no. Sūrah 13:31 makes the same point: "If there were a recitation that could cause mountains to move, or the earth to split, or the dead to speak" (13:31) — even then. The demand for the dead to speak was made explicitly by the deniers (44:36: "Bring ˹back˺ our forefathers, if what you say is true").

*All things gathered before them.* *Ḥasharnā ʿalayhim kulla shay'in qubulan* — "We gathered before them every thing, face to face." The word *qubulan* means facing, confronting, in plain view; al-Jalālayn and al-Ṭabarī also record the reading "in groups," "in droves." The image is of all creation assembled before them as witnesses — every creature, every sign, every proof — presented face to face. Even this totality would not move them.

**"They Would Still Not Believe"**

*Mā kānū li-yu'minū* — "they would not be such as to believe." The construction (*mā kānū li-*) is emphatic: it was not in them to believe; belief was not something they were going to do. The verse thus confirms verse 109's verdict and grounds it in verse 110's diagnosis. Hearts that have been turned by their own refusal do not respond to signs, however great.

**"Unless God Wills"**

*Illā an yashā'a Allāh* — "except that God should will." The exception is crucial and prevents the verse from being read as a statement of absolute impossibility. Nothing is beyond God's will. He could will their belief, and if He did, they would believe — with or without the angels and the dead. The verse says that the signs by themselves would not produce faith; only God's will produces it, and He grants it according to His wisdom. This is the principle stated in 10:100: "It is not for any soul to believe except by Allah" Faith is not manufactured by evidence; it is granted by God to the one who turns toward Him.

The exception also holds open the door that the rest of the verse might seem to close. Some of these very Makkans did believe later — not because angels descended but because God willed it, working through the Qur'an, the Prophet's ﷺ example, the passage of time, and their own eventual turning. Abū Sufyān, Khālid, ʿIkrimah, Ṣafwān — none of them saw the dead speak; all of them came to faith when God willed. The verse's "unless God wills" is the space in which their conversion happened.

**"But Most of Them Are Ignorant"**

*Wa lākinna aktharahum yajhalūn* — "but most of them are ignorant." The word *jahl* means ignorance — not merely lack of information but the state of not knowing what matters, acting without knowledge, the opposite of *ḥilm* (forbearance grounded in understanding). The verse closes by naming the idolaters' fundamental condition. Their demand for signs was itself a sign of ignorance: they did not understand that faith comes by God's will and the heart's turning, not by spectacle. They imagined that belief was a transaction — show us and we will pay — and did not know that the currency was their own sincerity, which they had already refused to spend.

The phrase "most of them" is careful. Not all. Among the idolaters were those who would come to know. The Qur'an's judgments on groups are almost always qualified in this way (v. 37: "most of them do not know"; v. 116: "most of those on earth"), leaving room for the exceptions God wills.

**The Argument of Verses 109–111**

The three verses form a single argument. The idolaters swear that a sign would make them believe (109a). The Prophet ﷺ answers that signs are God's alone (109b). The believers are warned not to assume a sign would work (109c). God explains that the idolaters' hearts have been turned by their first refusal and that they are left to wander (110). And He states that even the greatest conceivable signs would not produce faith without His will, because most of them are ignorant of what faith requires (111). The sequence moves from the idolaters' claim, through its refutation, to the theology that explains why the refutation holds.

**The Nature of Faith Illuminated**

The verse teaches something about faith that is easy to miss. Faith is not the conclusion of a proof that any rational being must accept once shown. If it were, the angels and the speaking dead would compel it. Faith is a response of the whole person — mind, heart, and will — to God's signs, and it requires that the person be willing. The unwilling can always resist, because no evidence removes the freedom to deny. This is why the Qur'an addresses the will as much as the mind: it commands, warns, invites, and reminds, and not only argues. And it is why the Qur'an insists that faith is by God's will: He alone can turn the heart that the person has left in His hands.

**The Believer's Gratitude**

The verse should produce in the believer not contempt for the ignorant but gratitude for his own faith. He did not believe because he was cleverer or saw greater signs than the Makkans who refused. He believed because God willed it — 'unless God wills' — and turned his heart when he turned toward Him. The Qur'an says: "Rather, it is Allah Who has done you a favour by guiding you to the faith, if ˹indeed˺ you are faithful" (49:17). The one who knows that his faith is a gift will guard it, thank for it, and pray, as the Prophet ﷺ did, that the Turner of hearts keep it firm.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:112

> **And so We have made for every prophet enemies—devilish humans and jinn—whispering to one another with elegant words of deception. Had it been your Lord’s Will, they would not have done such a thing. So leave them and their deceit,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Opposition as a Law of Prophethood**

*Wa kadhālika jaʿalnā li-kulli nabiyyin ʿaduwwan* — "and thus have We made for every prophet an enemy." The verse states a rule. The opposition the Prophet ﷺ faced in Makkah was not unique to him or a sign of his failure; it was the condition of every prophet before him. Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus — each had enemies who mocked, plotted, and persecuted. Al-Bayḍāwī notes that the verse presents this as a divine arrangement with a purpose: the prophets are tested by opposition, the truth is clarified by contrast with falsehood, and the sincere are distinguished from the insincere by how they respond.

The parallel verse is 25:31: "Similarly, We made enemies for every prophet from among the wicked, but sufficient is your Lord as a Guide and Helper" The second sentence there supplies what this verse implies: the enemy is real, and God is sufficient against him.

**"Satans from among Mankind and Jinn"**

*Shayāṭīna al-insi wa'l-jinn* — "satans of humans and jinn." The word *shayṭān* (from a root meaning to be far, or to burn) denotes a rebellious, malicious being who turns others from good. It usually refers to Iblīs and the evil jinn. This verse — with 2:14, 2:102, and 114:6 — establishes that human beings can also be satans: those who set themselves against God's religion and its messengers, who whisper doubt, and who lead others astray, are satans in the full sense, whatever their species.

The source commentary records the saying of Mālik ibn Dīnār: "The satans among human beings are more severe against me than the satans among the jinn; for when I seek refuge in God, the jinn-satan departs from me, but the human satan comes to me and drags me openly into sin." The observation is acute. The whispering jinn can be repelled by remembrance of God; the human satan — the friend who mocks piety, the colleague who normalizes wrong, the public voice that ridicules faith — persists, and his influence operates through social pressure that remembrance alone does not dissolve. The verse names both so that neither is underestimated.

Abū Dharr reported that the Prophet ﷺ asked him, "Have you sought refuge in God from the satans of men and jinn?" He asked, "Are there satans among men?" The Prophet ﷺ said, "Yes, and they are worse than the satans of the jinn" (Aḥmad 21257, with weakness in its chain, but its meaning is confirmed by this verse).

**"Who Inspire Each Other with Flowery Discourse in Order to Deceive"**

*Yūḥī baʿḍuhum ilā baʿḍin zukhrufa al-qawli ghurūran* — "some of them inspire others with gilded speech, in delusion." The verb *awḥā* means to communicate subtly, to suggest, to inspire — the same root as *waḥy*, revelation. Its use here is pointed: as God inspires His prophets with truth, the satans inspire one another with falsehood. The word *zukhruf* means gold ornament, gilding — anything made to look precious by a decorative surface. *Zukhruf al-qawl* is speech gilded to seem beautiful, wise, or true while being hollow. The purpose is *ghurūr* — deception, delusion, the false confidence a mirage produces.

The description fits every form of seductive falsehood: the eloquent argument against faith, the polished mockery, the sophisticated case for indulgence, the persuasive rationalization of wrong. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the satans whisper beautiful but vain words to one another and to others in order to lead astray. The jinn-satans inspire the human ones with objections and doubts; the human ones dress them in rhetoric and spread them. The Qur'an elsewhere describes Satan's promise as "nothing but delusion" (4:120; 17:64) and warns against being deluded about God "Be mindful of your Lord, and beware of a Day when no parent will be of any benefit to their child, nor will a child be of any benefit to their parent" (31:33; 35:5).

The verse teaches discernment. Beautiful speech is not a mark of truth. Some of the most damaging falsehoods are the most elegantly expressed. The believer learns to look beneath the gilding to the substance, asking not "is this well said?" but "is this true, and where does it lead?"

**"Had Thy Lord Willed, They Would Not Have Done So"**

*Wa law shā'a rabbuka mā faʿalūh* — "and had your Lord willed, they would not have done it." The formula of verse 107, applied now to the satans' deception. God could have prevented it; He did not, because the existence of opposition and the test it provides are part of His design for human life. The satans act by their own choice and are fully culpable; and their action falls within a world God has willed to contain such trials. The believer is thus told two things at once: the enemy is real and accountable, and the enemy is not outside God's control.

**"So Leave Them and That Which They Fabricate"**

*Fa-dharhum wa mā yaftarūn* — "so leave them and what they invent." The instruction of verses 70, 91, and 106 is repeated. The Prophet ﷺ is not to be consumed by the satans' campaign; he is to leave them and their inventions — the false religion, the gilded arguments, the fabricated objections — and continue with his own work. The source commentary connects this to verse 108: aggressive confrontation may only harden resistance, while steady conveyance of the truth leaves the door open.

"Leaving" is not passivity. It is the refusal to be drawn onto the enemy's ground — to fight gilded speech with gilded speech, or to answer mockery with mockery. The Prophet ﷺ left them and kept reciting the Qur'an, praying, teaching, and living the truth. Over time, this was more effective than any counter-campaign could have been: the gilded speech wore thin, and the plain truth endured.

**The Enemy Named and Its Method Exposed**

The verse gives the believer a map of what he is up against. There is an enemy — this is a law, not an accident. The enemy operates through both invisible whisperings and visible human agents. Its method is beautiful speech designed to deceive. Its existence is within God's will, so it is not to be feared as an independent power. And the response is to leave it and hold to the truth. Each element is practical. The believer who knows there will be enemies is not shaken when they appear. The one who knows they include human beings is not naïve about the source of the pressure he feels. The one who knows their weapon is gilded speech examines eloquence critically. The one who knows they act by God's leave does not despair. And the one who knows the response is to leave them does not exhaust himself in fruitless combat.

**The Comfort in the Verse**

Finally, the verse places the Prophet ﷺ — and every believer who suffers opposition for the truth — in the company of all the prophets. "Every prophet" had an enemy. To be opposed for God's sake is to walk the road that Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus walked. The opposition is not evidence against the truth of one's cause; it is, in a sense, evidence for it, since falsehood does not attract satans' enmity. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The most severely tried of people are the prophets, then the next best, then the next best" (al-Tirmidhī 2398). The verse is that ḥadīth's foundation, and its consolation.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:113

> **so that the hearts of those who disbelieve in the Hereafter may be receptive to it, be pleased with it, and be persistent in their evil pursuits.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Continuation of the Sentence**

Verse 113 continues the sentence begun in verse 112 and describes the effect of the satans' gilded speech: *wa li-taṣghā ilayhi af'idatu alladhīna lā yu'minūna bi'l-ākhirah* — "and so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline toward it." The pronoun "it" refers to the flowery discourse of the previous verse. The satans inspire one another with deceptive speech, and the hearts of the deniers lean toward that speech.

**"Incline Toward It"**

The verb *ṣaghā* means to incline, to lean toward, to listen attentively — as one inclines the ear to a voice one wants to hear. The word *af'idah* (hearts, in the sense of the seat of perception and feeling) was used in verse 110. The hearts of the deniers are drawn to the gilded speech because it says what they want to hear: that there is no Hereafter, that religion is play, that their ways are fine, that the Prophet ﷺ is a poet or a madman. The inclination is not forced; it is the natural attraction of a heart to what flatters its existing desires.

**"Those Who Believe Not in the Hereafter"**

The deniers are identified by a single feature: they do not believe in the Hereafter. The source commentary notes that belief in the Hereafter is treated by the commentators as one of the foundations of all religious seriousness (cf. v. 92). One who believes he will stand before God and answer for his deeds cannot afford to be seduced by beautiful lies; one who denies the accounting has nothing to guard against. The verse thus identifies the vulnerability that the satans exploit: the absence of belief in consequences.

**"And Be Content with It"**

*Wa li-yarḍawh* — "and that they may be pleased with it." Beyond inclining, the hearts settle into satisfaction. The gilded speech becomes their conviction; they are content with it, at ease in it. This is the state that verse 108 described — deeds "made to seem fair" — and that verse 110 described — hearts turned. The deniers are not tormented by doubt; they are comfortable. Al-Rāzī notes that this contentment is itself the deepest form of misguidance: the one who is troubled may yet seek, but the one who is satisfied does not.

**"And So Commit That Which They Commit"**

*Wa li-yaqtarifū mā hum muqtarifūn* — "and that they may commit what they are committing." The verb *iqtarafa* means to commit, to perpetrate, to acquire — usually of wrong deeds. The sequence is complete: the heart inclines to the false speech, becomes content with it, and acts on it. Inclination becomes conviction, conviction becomes conduct. The satans' work bears fruit in what the deniers do.

The phrase "what they are committing" is deliberately unspecified, encompassing everything the sūrah has described: the *shirk*, the mockery, the persecution of believers, the invented prohibitions, the rejection of the Prophet ﷺ. All of it is the outcome of hearts that inclined to gilded speech and rested content in it.

**The Structure of the Three Purposes**

The verse gives three purpose clauses, each introduced by *li-* ("so that"): that the hearts may incline; that they may be content; that they may commit. Grammatically, these are the purposes of the satans' inspiration in verse 112 — this is what the deceivers intend. But they are also, on a deeper reading, within the divine ordering described in verse 112 ("thus have We made for every prophet an enemy"). The satans' purpose and God's purpose coincide in outcome while differing utterly in intention: the satans intend destruction; God intends a test whose result reveals the hearts. The Qur'an holds this doubleness throughout: what the enemy does in malice, God permits in wisdom.

**The Theological Discussion**

The source commentary notes the debate this verse generated. Al-Rāzī and the Ashʿarites read it as evidence that God exercises control over human inclinations toward belief or disbelief: the "so that" clauses describe what God brings about. The Muʿtazilites read the verse as describing a punishment: God allows the deniers' rejection to entrench itself, so that disbelief begets more disbelief, and the absence of immediate punishment gives them a false confidence. The two readings differ in emphasis but agree on the phenomenon: hearts that have rejected the truth become increasingly inclined toward falsehood, content in it, and productive of wrong. Whether one calls this God's decree or the natural consequence of choice that God permits, the practical warning is the same.

**The Psychology of the Verse**

The verse describes a process that can be observed in any life. A person hears an argument that excuses what he wants to do. He inclines toward it — not because it is sound but because it is convenient. He rests in it; it becomes "what he thinks." And he acts on it, committing what the argument permitted. The satans' gilded speech is effective not because it is compelling but because the heart it addresses is already leaning. The verse locates the root of the process in the denial of the Hereafter: the heart that does not fear consequences has no reason to resist a convenient lie.

This is why the Qur'an's insistence on the Hereafter is not a separate doctrine from its moral teaching but the foundation of it. Belief in the accounting is the immune system of the soul. Where it is present, gilded speech is examined; where it is absent, gilded speech is embraced.

**The Believer's Protection**

The verse implicitly teaches the believer how to be protected from what it describes. First, by holding firmly to belief in the Hereafter, so that no argument that excuses wrong can find purchase. Second, by examining the inclinations of his own heart: when he finds himself drawn to a view because it is convenient rather than because it is true, he recognizes the *ṣaghw* the verse warns of. Third, by guarding against contentment with his own state — the believer is never fully "content" in the sense of the verse, because he knows he is accountable and may be wrong. And fourth, by attending to the link between conviction and conduct: what he allows himself to believe, he will eventually do.

**The Verse in Its Sequence**

Verses 112–113 together explain the mechanism of opposition to the prophets. There are enemies (112a). They are satans, human and jinn (112b). They spread gilded speech (112c). This is within God's will (112d). The Prophet ﷺ should leave them (112e). Their speech finds hearts that do not believe in the Hereafter (113a). Those hearts incline, are content, and act (113b–d). The whole process is laid bare, from the source of falsehood to its fruit in deeds, and the Prophet ﷺ is told that his part is to leave them to it and continue with the truth. The next verse will state what the truth is that he holds to: the Book, sent down and expounded, against which no other judge is needed.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:114

> **˹Say, O Prophet,˺ “Should I seek a judge other than Allah while He is the One Who has revealed for you the Book ˹with the truth˺ perfectly explained?” Those who were given the Scripture know that it has been revealed ˹to you˺ from your Lord in truth. So do not be one of those who doubt.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prophet's Rhetorical Question**

*A-fa-ghayra Allāhi abtaghī ḥakaman* — "Shall I then seek other than God as a judge?" The question is rhetorical and the answer is no. The verse gives the Prophet ﷺ his response to the whole campaign of verses 109–113: the demands for signs, the gilded speech of the satans, the contentment of the deniers. His answer is that he already has the only Judge he needs.

The word *ḥakam* means an arbiter, a judge, one whose decision settles a dispute. The Makkans wanted the Prophet ﷺ to accept some other standard of proof — a miracle of their choosing, the approval of their elders, the verdict of the crowd. He asks whether he should seek any judge other than God. The question recalls verse 57 ("judgment belongs to God alone") and applies it: God has already judged, by sending the Book.

**"When It Is He Who Has Sent Down unto You the Book, Expounded"**

*Wa huwa alladhī anzala ilaykumu al-kitāba mufaṣṣalan* — "while He is the one who has sent down to you the Book, detailed." The word *mufaṣṣal* is the passive participle of *faṣṣala*, the verb of verses 55, 97, 98, and 126: set out in detail, made distinct, expounded. The Book has been sent down with its contents detailed — its teachings, its proofs, its laws, its distinctions between truth and falsehood. Given such a Book, why seek another judge?

The commentators draw out two senses, both of which the source commentary notes. First, as al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zamakhsharī explain, the verse answers the demand for a miraculous sign: the Qur'an itself is the sign — the evidentiary miracle (*muʿjizah*) of inimitable language and content (2:23–24; 10:38; 17:88). To ask for another sign is to seek a judge other than the one God has already provided. Second, as al-Bayḍāwī and al-Rāzī add, the verse answers the need for a standard of truth: why should anyone need another way to distinguish right from wrong when God has sent a Book in which the distinction is expounded? The Book is both the proof and the criterion.

**The Qur'an as the Basis of Judgment**

The verse connects judgment (*ḥukm*) to the Book, a connection the Qur'an makes repeatedly (2:213; 3:23; 4:105; 5:43–49). Most such passages are Madinan and concern the use of scripture to judge between people in worldly disputes. This verse is Makkan and concerns the more basic question of what standard settles the truth of religion itself. The answer is the same in both contexts: the Book God sent down. From this verse and its parallels, Islamic thought derived the principle that revelation is the ultimate criterion — the *ḥakam* — in matters of faith and law, and that no human judgment may override it. Verse 57's "judgment belongs to God alone" and this verse's "shall I seek a judge apart from God" are the Qur'anic roots of the doctrine.

**"Those unto Whom We Have Given the Book Know That It Has Been Sent Down from Thy Lord in Truth"**

*Wa'lladhīna ātaynāhumu al-kitāba yaʿlamūna annahu munazzalun min rabbika bi'l-ḥaqq* — "He commands them to do good and forbids them from evil, permits for them what is lawful and forbids to them what is impure, and relieves them from their burdens and the shackles that bound them" The People of the Book — Jews and Christians — are cited as witnesses. Their own scriptures, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zamakhsharī explain, support the truth of the Prophet's ﷺ mission, either because they describe him (7:157; 61:6) or because the Qur'an's message accords with the essential teachings of the Torah and the Gospel. Those among them who were honest recognized the Qur'an's origin: the Qur'an records such recognition (2:146: "Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children"; 5:83: "When they listen to what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears for recognizing the truth"; 13:36; 28:52–53).

The verse thus adds a second witness to the first. The Book's own detailed clarity is one proof; the recognition of it by those who possessed earlier revelation is another. The Makkans, who had no scripture, were being told that those who did have one knew what the Qur'an was. Sūrah 10:94 makes the same appeal: "If you ˹O Prophet˺ are in doubt about ˹these stories˺ that We have revealed to you, then ask those who read the Scripture before you"

This does not mean all the People of the Book accepted the Prophet ﷺ; the Qur'an is clear that many did not, and that some concealed what they knew (v. 91; 2:146; 3:71). It means that the knowledge was there, among them, and that the honest among them bore witness to it.

**"So Be Not among the Doubters"**

*Fa-lā takūnanna min al-mumtarīn* — "so do not be among the doubters." The imperative is second person singular, addressed grammatically to the Prophet ﷺ, as in 2:147, 3:60, 10:94, and 11:17. The commentators — al-Bayḍāwī and al-Rāzī — explain that the address, though singular, is meant for the Prophet's ﷺ community and for all who hear, as is common in the Qur'an. The Prophet ﷺ did not doubt; the command establishes for everyone that, given the Book's clarity and the witness borne by the People of the Book, doubt has no ground.

There is also a way in which the command speaks to the Prophet ﷺ directly and appropriately. He had just been told to leave the deniers and their gilded speech (v. 112). The pressure of sustained rejection, mockery, and sophisticated argument could, in any human being, generate at least a moment's unease. The verse says: do not be among the doubters — you have the Book, detailed, and the witnesses who know. Hold to it.

**The Structure of the Verse**

The verse has three movements. The rhetorical question: shall I seek another judge? The ground: God has sent the Book, expounded. The confirmation: the People of the Book know it is true. And the conclusion: do not doubt. Each movement builds on the last. The Prophet ﷺ needs no other judge because he has the Book; the Book is not merely his claim but is recognized by those with prior scripture; therefore doubt is groundless.

**The Verse for the Believer's Standard**

The verse gives the believer his standard. When he faces the modern equivalents of the Makkan demands — "prove it in the way we accept," "meet our criteria," "satisfy the consensus of the age" — the verse's question applies: shall I seek a judge apart from God? He has the Book, expounded. This is not obscurantism; the Book itself commands reason, reflection, and evidence, and the sūrah has been a sustained exercise in all three. It is the recognition that the final criterion of religious truth is what God has revealed, and that no human court sits above it. The believer submits his judgment to the Book; he does not submit the Book to the judgment of those who reject it.

**A Possible Madinan Origin**

Some commentators note that this verse may have been revealed in Madīnah, where engagement with the People of the Book was constant, and placed here by the Prophet's ﷺ direction. Al-Zamakhsharī lists it among the possibly Madinan verses of the sūrah. Whether or not that is so, its function in this place is clear: after the account of the satans' deception and the deniers' contentment, it states the Prophet's ﷺ unshaken position — one Judge, one Book, no doubt.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:115

> **The Word of your Lord has been perfected in truth and justice. None can change His Words. And He is the All-Hearing, All- Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Completeness of the Word**

Verse 114 affirmed that God has sent down the Book, expounded, and that there is no judge apart from Him. Verse 115 describes the quality of that Book: *wa tammat kalimatu rabbika ṣidqan wa ʿadlan* — "and the Word of your Lord has been completed in truth and justice." The verb *tamma* means to be complete, to be fulfilled, to reach perfection. The Word of the Lord is complete — nothing is lacking in it, and nothing needs to be added.

**"The Word of Thy Lord"**

*Kalimat rabbik* — "the Word of your Lord." The commentators offer two readings that the source commentary presents together. Al-Ṭabarī takes it as referring to the Qur'an as a whole: God has completed His revelation; the Book is whole and perfect. This parallels 6:154, where the Book given to Moses is described as 'complete' (*tamāman*), and 9:32 and 61:8, where God promises that He "will ˹certainly˺ perfect His light" (61:8) — understood as His guidance. On this reading, the verse answers those who demanded something more than the Qur'an: the Word is complete; there is nothing further to send.

The majority — al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī in another place, al-Zamakhsharī — take "the Word" collectively as all that God has said in the Qur'an: His commands, prohibitions, promises, threats, reports, and judgments. Each is "complete" in the sense that it will be fulfilled: His reports are true, His promises will come to pass, His threats will be carried out, His rulings are just. Sūrah 7:137 uses the same expression of God's promise to the Children of Israel being fulfilled, and 11:119 of His word that Hell will be filled. On this reading, the verse assures the Prophet ﷺ that everything God has said in the Book — including the promise of his vindication and the warning to his enemies — will be realized.

**"In Truth and Justice"**

*Ṣidqan wa ʿadlan* — "in truthfulness and justice." Al-Bayḍāwī explains the pairing precisely. The Word is complete in *ṣidq* — truth — in that its reports, its accounts of the past, its descriptions of God and the unseen, and its promises are all perfectly true; nothing in it is false or will fail. And it is complete in *ʿadl* — justice — in that its commands, prohibitions, and judgments are perfectly just; nothing in it is unfair or disproportionate. The two words cover the two functions of speech: informing and directing. God's informing is entirely true; His directing is entirely just.

This is a claim no human text can make. Human reports contain errors; human laws contain injustices. The verse asserts that the Word of God is free of both. This is the foundation of the Muslim's confidence in the Qur'an: not merely that it is authoritative but that it is *true* in all it says and *just* in all it requires.

**"None Alters His Words"**

*Lā mubaddila li-kalimātih* — "there is no changer of His words." The phrase appeared in verse 34, where it assured the Prophet ﷺ that God's promise of help to the messengers could not be altered. It recurs in 10:64 and 18:27, and 10:15 states the Prophet's ﷺ own inability to alter the Qur'an. The meaning is twofold. God's decrees cannot be changed by anyone: what He has promised will happen; what He has threatened will come; no power can revise it. And God's revealed words cannot be corrupted: the Qur'an, unlike earlier scriptures whose custodians altered and concealed (v. 91), is preserved by God Himself — "It is certainly We Who have revealed the Reminder, and it is certainly We Who will preserve it" (15:9).

The second sense grounds the Qur'an's textual integrity. The Prophet ﷺ could not change it (10:15; 69:44–47). His Companions memorized and recorded it. It has been transmitted, letter for letter, by uninterrupted mass transmission for fourteen centuries. This is the fulfilment of "none alters His words," and it is one of the reasons the Qur'an can serve as the "judge" of verse 114: a judge whose rulings could be tampered with would be no judge.

**"And He Is the Hearing, the Knowing"**

*Wa huwa al-samīʿu al-ʿalīm* — "and He is the Hearing, the Knowing." The two names close the verse and undergird its claims. God hears — every word spoken by the deniers, every gilded phrase of the satans (v. 112), every oath sworn falsely (v. 109), and every prayer of the believers. God knows — the truth of every matter, the justice of every ruling, the outcome of every promise. A Word that is complete in truth and justice must issue from One who hears and knows everything; otherwise it could not be complete. And a Word that none can alter is guarded by One who hears any attempt and knows any alteration.

The pairing also carries a note of warning and of comfort. Warning to the deniers: He hears what you say about His Word and knows what you intend. Comfort to the Prophet ﷺ: He hears your prayers and knows your situation; His Word to you — of help, of vindication — is complete, and none can alter it.

**The Verse as the Ground of Trust**

Verses 114–115 together form the foundation of the Prophet's ﷺ stability in the face of everything the preceding verses described. He needs no judge but God (114a). God has sent the Book, expounded (114b). The People of the Book recognize it (114c). He must not doubt (114d). The Word is complete in truth and justice (115a). None can alter it (115b). God hears and knows (115c). This is what the believer stands on when the satans of men and jinn spread their gilded speech: a Word that is complete, true, just, unalterable, and issued by the All-Hearing, All-Knowing. Against such a foundation, the flowery discourse of the deniers is what verse 112 called it — deception.

**Application: Reading the Qur'an as Complete**

The verse shapes how the believer approaches the Qur'an. He does not read it looking for gaps to fill with other authorities; it is complete. He does not suspect its reports; they are true. He does not resent its commands; they are just. He does not fear that it has been corrupted; none alters His words. And he does not imagine that any human judgment — his own or anyone's — sits above it. This posture is not credulity; it is the appropriate response to a Word from the One who hears and knows all things, and it is the posture the sūrah has been cultivating since its first verse. The ninety-nine verses of argument preceding this one were the reasons; this verse is the resting place.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:116

> **˹O Prophet!˺ If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah’s Way. They follow nothing but assumptions and do nothing but lie.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Warning against the Majority**

*Wa in tuṭiʿ akthara man fi'l-arḍi yuḍillūka ʿan sabīli Allāh* — "and if you obey most of those on the earth, they will lead you astray from the way of God." The verse states a principle that runs against a deep human instinct: the instinct to assume that what most people believe and do is right. The Qur'an says the opposite. Most of those on earth, if followed, lead away from God's path.

**"Most of Those on Earth"**

The phrase is sweeping. Not 'most of the Makkans' or 'most of the idolaters' but 'most of those on the earth.' In the Prophet's ﷺ time, the majority of humanity was idolatrous, and even among the People of the Book, most had strayed from the pure teaching of their prophets. The Qur'an repeats this assessment in many forms: "most of them do not believe" (2:100; 26:8, 67, 103), "most of them are ignorant" (6:111), "most of them do not know" (6:37; 7:187), "And many of them are ˹still˺ rebellious" (5:59; 57:16, 26), "˹Only˺ a few of My servants are ˹truly˺ grateful" (34:13). The sūrah has qualified its judgments with "most of them" throughout, and here it makes the principle explicit.

The Prophet ﷺ is warned in several places not to obey the disbelievers, hypocrites, and sinners (18:28; 25:52; 33:1, 48; 68:8, 10; 76:24; 96:19). This verse generalizes: the majority as such is not a reliable guide.

**Why the Majority Misleads**

The verse gives the reason: *in yattabiʿūna illā al-ẓanna wa in hum illā yakhruṣūn* — "they follow nothing but conjecture, and they only surmise." Two words define the epistemic condition of the majority.

*Ẓann* is conjecture, supposition, opinion held without certain knowledge — belief that may be true or false but is not grounded in proof. The Qur'an consistently attributes erroneous religion to *ẓann* (6:148; 10:66; 38:27; 45:24; 53:23, 28), and declares that "˹And˺ surely assumptions can in no way replace the truth" (10:36; 53:28). Even those among the People of the Book who did not know their scripture are said to follow *ẓann* (2:78), as are those who imagine that Jesus was crucified (4:157).

*Kharṣ* is guessing, estimating — the word used for estimating the yield of a palm tree before harvest. *Yakhruṣūn* means they merely guess; they make claims about God, religion, and the unseen with no basis but estimation. The Qur'an uses the word for the idolaters' assertions about God (10:66; 43:20) and curses "the guessers" (51:10).

The verse's diagnosis is that most people do not arrive at their beliefs by knowledge. They inherit them, absorb them from their environment, adopt them because they are convenient, or guess. A belief so held is not made true by being widely shared. A million conjectures do not add up to one proof. This is why the majority misleads: not because numbers are inherently wrong, but because the majority's beliefs are typically formed without the knowledge that would make them reliable.

**The Context: Food and Idolatrous Custom**

Al-Ṭabarī and others note that the verse directly precedes a discussion of dietary law (vv. 118–121), and some connected the warning to a specific pressure: the idolaters' invitation to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers to eat what had been slaughtered for their idols, or their argument for eating carrion. Al-Suyūṭī and al-Zamakhsharī record the idolaters' claim: "You eat what you kill, but you do not eat what God kills?" — meaning that an animal that died by itself was "killed by God" and therefore more fitting to eat than one slaughtered by human hands. The argument had a surface plausibility — it was *zukhruf al-qawl*, gilded speech (v. 112) — and it was the view of the majority around the Prophet ﷺ. The verse warned him not to be swayed by it.

Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī give the broader reading: most people follow their whims or their fathers' customs rather than guidance, and following them leads astray. Both readings hold; the specific occasion illustrates the general rule.

**The Principle in Islamic Thought**

The verse became a foundational text for a principle that Islamic scholars articulated in many forms: truth is not determined by numbers. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said: "The *jamāʿah* (the community of truth) is what accords with the truth, even if you are alone." Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: "Follow the paths of guidance, and the fewness of those who travel them will not harm you; and beware of the paths of misguidance, and do not be deceived by the multitude of those who perish." The Prophet ﷺ foretold that Islam "began as a stranger and will return to being a stranger as it began, so glad tidings to the strangers" (Muslim 145). The believer measures his position against the truth, not against the crowd.

**Not a License for Contrarianism**

The verse does not teach that the majority is always wrong or that being in a minority is a mark of truth. The Qur'an also commands the believer to hold to the community (3:103) and warns against departing from "And whoever defies the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them and follows a path other than that of the believers, We will let them pursue what they have chosen, then burn them in Hell—what an evil end" (4:115). The Prophet ﷺ commanded adherence to the *jamāʿah*. The verse's target is specific: obedience to "most of those on earth" in matters of religion, where the majority follows conjecture. It does not concern practical decisions where collective experience is valuable, nor the consensus of those who possess knowledge, which Islamic law treats as authoritative. The distinction is between the many who conjecture and the few who know; the verse says follow knowledge, whatever the number who hold it.

**The Psychological Weight of the Verse**

The pull of the majority is among the strongest forces acting on belief. It operates not through argument but through the felt sense that "everyone" cannot be wrong, that dissent is presumptuous, and that safety lies in conformity. The Prophet ﷺ faced this in its most extreme form: a lone man against his entire city, his entire tribe, and — as the verse says — most of those on earth. The verse gave him the intellectual ground on which to stand: the many were conjecturing; he had knowledge from his Lord (v. 114). Every believer who has held to a truth against social pressure knows the weight the verse lifts.

**The Verse for the Present**

In every age, "most of those on earth" hold views that a believer cannot share — about God, about right and wrong, about the purpose of life. The pressure to conform has never been greater than in an age of mass communication, where the majority's opinion is broadcast continuously and dissent is visible and costly. The verse's counsel is unchanged: do not obey the majority in matters of the way of God; ask whether they follow knowledge or conjecture; and hold to what has been revealed. The next verse will give the assurance that makes this possible: God knows best who is astray and who is guided — and it is His knowledge, not the crowd's, that decides.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:117

> **Indeed, your Lord knows best who has strayed from His Way and who is ˹rightly˺ guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ground of Confidence**

Verse 116 warned that following the majority leads astray, because the majority follows conjecture. Verse 117 supplies the alternative to conjecture: *inna rabbaka huwa aʿlamu man yaḍillu ʿan sabīlih* — "indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way." Against the guesses of the many stands the knowledge of God. He knows — with certainty, in every case — who is astray and who is guided. The believer's confidence rests not on numbers but on this knowledge.

**"Thy Lord Knows Best Those Who Stray from His Way"**

The construction *huwa aʿlamu* — "He is most knowing," "He knows best" — is emphatic. God's knowledge of who is astray is not approximate or general; it is complete and particular. He knows each person who has left His way, how far he has strayed, why, and whether he will return. The phrase "from His way" (*ʿan sabīlih*) picks up the "way of God" of verse 116: the path from which the majority leads astray is God's path, and God knows precisely who has left it.

The implication for verse 116 is direct. The majority may be confident, articulate, and unanimous; they may regard the believer as the one who has strayed. God knows otherwise. His knowledge, not their opinion, is the measure. This is the same assurance given in verse 53 ("Does God not know best those who are thankful?") and verse 58 ("God knows best the wrongdoers"). The sūrah returns again and again to God's knowledge as the answer to human misjudgment.

**"And He Knows Best the Rightly Guided"**

*Wa huwa aʿlamu bi'l-muhtadīn* — "and He is most knowing of the guided." The parallel clause completes the picture. God knows the astray; He also knows the guided. The believers in Makkah were few, despised, and regarded by the majority as foolish or deluded. God knew them as the guided. Their status did not depend on the crowd's recognition; it was known to the One whose knowledge is the only knowledge that finally matters.

The pairing of the two clauses also implies that God will act on His knowledge. He who knows the astray will judge them; He who knows the guided will reward them. The verse is thus both a comfort and a warning, according to which category the hearer belongs to.

**The Verse as the Resolution of the Preceding Passage**

Verses 109–117 have traced a sequence: the idolaters' demand for signs (109), the turning of their hearts (110), the futility of even the greatest signs (111), the satans of men and jinn with their gilded speech (112), the hearts that incline to it (113), the Prophet's ﷺ refusal of any judge but God (114), the completeness of God's Word (115), and the warning against the majority (116). Verse 117 is the resolution. In all this confusion — false oaths, turned hearts, deceptive speech, majority pressure — one thing is fixed: God knows who is astray and who is guided. The Prophet ﷺ can rest in that.

**Knowledge against Conjecture**

The verse's key contrast is with the *ẓann* and *kharṣ* of verse 116. The majority conjectures; God knows. This is the whole difference between the two parties. Human beings, even sincere ones, see partially; they may judge a person guided who is astray, or astray who is guided. Only God sees the heart, the whole course of a life, and the end. The verse therefore removes the final judgment of who is on the right path from human hands entirely — including the believer's own. He is not to judge himself guided on the basis of self-assurance, nor to judge others astray on the basis of appearance. He is to hold to God's way as best he knows it and leave the knowing to God.

**Two Practical Consequences**

First, the verse frees the believer from the need for the majority's approval. If God knows best who is guided, the crowd's verdict is not decisive. The Prophet ﷺ was told this in the face of a city's rejection; the believer applies it in the face of whatever social disapproval his faith incurs. What matters is God's knowledge, and God's knowledge is not swayed by numbers.

Second, the verse restrains the believer from arrogance toward those who differ. If God knows best who is astray, the believer does not have final knowledge of anyone's ultimate state. He may — must — judge that *shirk* is astray, that the Qur'an is guidance, that God's way is the right way; the verse does not counsel relativism. But he does not know who will die in which state, and he does not know the hearts. Many of the "astray" majority of Makkah became the guided within a decade. The believer's certainty about the path coexists with humility about persons, and the verse supports both.

**The Pattern of "Knows Best"**

The formula "your Lord knows best" (*rabbuka aʿlam*) is one of the Qur'an's recurring reassurances, appearing in contexts of dispute, rejection, and uncertainty (16:125; 17:25, 54, 55, 84; 28:56, 85; 53:30, 32; 60:10; 68:7). In every case it does the same work: it removes the final verdict from human contention and places it with God. This is not an evasion of argument — the sūrah has argued at length — but the acknowledgment that after all argument, the truth about persons is known to God alone. Sūrah 68:7 uses the exact phrasing of this verse in a similar context of the Prophet ﷺ being called mad by his people: "Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has gone astray from His way, and He is most knowing of the guided."

**The Comfort of Being Known**

For the believer who holds to God's way against the current, the verse offers the deepest form of comfort: he is *known*. The majority may misjudge him, mock him, or ignore him. God knows him — knows that he is among the guided, knows what it costs him, knows his sincerity. The Prophet ﷺ, standing alone against most of those on earth, was told that his Lord knew best the guided. So is every believer who stands where he stood. The knowledge that matters is not the world's opinion but God's, and God's knowledge is perfect.

**Transition to the Dietary Verses**

The verse closes the section on rejection and majority pressure and opens onto a concrete application (vv. 118–121): the question of what may be eaten, on which the idolatrous majority pressed the believers with gilded arguments. Verses 116–117 have prepared the ground. Do not follow the majority; God knows who is astray and who is guided. Now, in the matter of food, the sūrah will show what following God's way rather than the crowd's looks like in practice.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:118

> **So eat only of what is slaughtered in Allah’s Name if you truly believe in His revelations.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Principle to Practice**

The sūrah has spent over a hundred verses establishing *tawḥīd* and the authority of revelation. Now it turns to a concrete matter of daily life: *fa-kulū mimmā dhukira ismu Allāhi ʿalayh* — "so eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned." The particle *fa-* ("so," "therefore") links the command to what precedes: because God alone is the Judge (v. 114), because His Word is complete (v. 115), and because the majority follows conjecture (v. 116), the believers should eat according to God's rule and not the idolaters' customs.

The turn to food is not a descent from lofty theology to trivial detail. In Arabia, food was the arena in which idolatry was most visibly practiced: animals slaughtered for idols, meat dedicated to deities, taboos invented in the gods' names (vv. 136–140). The question of what one eats and in whose name it is slaughtered was a question of whom one worships. The sūrah's name — *al-Anʿām*, the Cattle — comes from this section, and the section is the practical test of everything the sūrah has taught.

**"Eat of That over Which the Name of God Has Been Invoked"**

The rule is stated positively: eat what has had God's name mentioned over it. The commentators explain the scope. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī note that some took it as a general condition for all food — that one should mention God's name over whatever one eats, which the Prophet ﷺ taught as a practice ("Say *bismillāh*, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is near you," al-Bukhārī 5376; Muslim 2022). But the primary reference, as al-Rāzī explains, is to meat: an animal is lawful to eat when God's name has been invoked at its slaughter. This excludes carrion, over which no name was invoked because it was not slaughtered, and it excludes what was slaughtered in the name of idols (2:173; 5:3; 16:115).

The invocation of God's name at slaughter (*tasmiyah*) is, with the ritual method of slaughter, what makes meat *ḥalāl*. The Qur'an mentions the invocation in 5:4 (over hunting animals), 22:28, 22:34, and 22:36 (over sacrificial animals), and 6:121 will state the negative form of this verse's command: "Do not eat of what is not slaughtered in Allah"

**The Meaning of the Invocation**

Why does saying God's name over an animal matter? The commentators give several reasons that together form a theology of eating. First, the invocation acknowledges that the animal's life belongs to God and that taking it is permitted only by His leave. The slaughterer says *bismillāh, Allāhu akbar* — "in the name of God, God is greatest" — declaring that he acts by God's authority, not his own. Second, it dedicates the act to God alone, excluding any other name. The idolaters slaughtered in the names of their gods; the believer slaughters in God's name, and the meat is thereby distinguished from theirs. Third, it makes the ordinary act of obtaining food an act of remembrance. The believer cannot eat meat without God's name having been spoken over it, and so his table is connected to his faith.

The Qur'an makes the connection to *tawḥīd* explicit in 22:34: "For every community We appointed a rite of sacrifice so that they may pronounce the Name of Allah over the sacrificial animals He has provided for them" The invocation over food is a practice of *tawḥīd*.

**"If You Are Believers in His Signs"**

*In kuntum bi-āyātihi mu'minīn* — "if you are believers in His signs." The conditional gives the command its force. Eating what has God's name over it — and, by implication, refusing what does not — is a consequence of believing in His signs. One who believes in God's signs follows His rule about food; one who follows the idolaters' rule has, in that matter, not believed. The verse thus makes the dietary practice a test of faith.

The phrasing also answers the idolaters' argument, recorded in the commentaries on verse 116: "Do you eat what you kill and not what God kills?" The idolaters urged the believers to eat carrion. The verse says: if you believe in God's signs, eat what His name was invoked over — which carrion was not. The believers' abstention from carrion, far from being an inconsistency, was the mark of their faith.

**The Occasion**

Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Wāḥidī record the background from Ibn ʿAbbās and others. The idolaters came to the Muslims and said: "You claim to worship God, yet you eat what you slaughter and do not eat what God has caused to die" — arguing that an animal that died naturally was killed by God and therefore more fitting to eat. Some reports say the argument came from Persian Zoroastrians via the Quraysh, who wrote to them for material to use against the Prophet ﷺ. The verses 118–121 were revealed in response, affirming the rule and exposing the argument as the gilded speech of satans (v. 121). Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī record the report from Ibn ʿAbbās (Abū Dāwūd 2819; al-Tirmidhī 3069, graded ḥasan).

**Eating as an Act of Faith**

The verse turns eating into an act of faith. This is characteristic of Islam, which does not divide life into sacred and secular but brings every act under God's rule. The Prophet ﷺ said that the believer is rewarded even for the food he puts in his wife's mouth (al-Bukhārī 56; Muslim 1628). The rule about invoking God's name is one instance of this. The believer eats what God has permitted, in the manner God has prescribed, with God's name upon it — and his meal is thereby distinguished from the idolater's meal, though the food may look the same.

**The Positive Formulation**

It is notable that the verse commands eating ("eat of...") rather than only forbidding. The Qur'an's dietary law is, in the first place, a permission: eat of the good things (2:168, 172; 5:88; 7:160). The prohibitions are few and specific — carrion, blood, swine, what was dedicated to other than God, and what was not properly slaughtered (2:173; 5:3; 6:145; 16:115). The verse opens the door before verse 121 marks its limits. The idolaters had invented elaborate taboos (vv. 136–140); the Qur'an sweeps them away and replaces them with a simple rule: what has God's name over it is yours to eat.

**Preparation for What Follows**

Verse 118 states the rule; verse 119 will ask why anyone would refuse what God has permitted; verse 120 will command the abandonment of sin, outward and inward; and verse 121 will forbid eating what God's name was not invoked over and expose the satanic origin of the contrary argument. The four verses together apply the sūrah's teaching on revelation and majority to a single question, and they show that following God rather than the crowd is not an abstraction but a matter of what is on one's plate.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:119

> **Why should you not eat of what is slaughtered in Allah’s Name when He has already explained to you what He has forbidden to you—except when compelled by necessity? Many ˹deviants˺ certainly mislead others by their whims out of ignorance. Surely your Lord knows the transgressors best.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question of Refusal**

Verse 118 commanded eating what has God's name over it. Verse 119 asks why anyone would not: *wa mā lakum allā ta'kulū mimmā dhukira ismu Allāhi ʿalayh* — "and what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned?" The question is directed at those who hesitated — whether believers made uncertain by the idolaters' arguments, or the idolaters themselves who refused what was slaughtered in God's name while eating carrion and what was slaughtered for idols. The form "what ails you" (*mā lakum*) expresses surprise at an irrational refusal.

The verse thus balances verse 118. That verse addressed the pressure to eat what was forbidden (carrion); this one addresses the opposite error — refusing what was permitted. Both errors come from following the crowd or one's own scruples rather than God's clear rule. The Qur'an guards against unwarranted prohibition as firmly as against unwarranted permission; verses 140 and 143–144 will condemn the idolaters for forbidding what God allowed.

**"When He Has Expounded for You That Which He Has Forbidden You"**

*Wa qad faṣṣala lakum mā ḥarrama ʿalaykum* — "and He has detailed for you what He has forbidden you." The verb *faṣṣala* (to detail, set out distinctly) is the verb of verses 55, 97, 98, 114, and 126. God has detailed what is forbidden; whatever is not in that detailed list is permitted. This is a foundational principle of Islamic law: the default in matters of food — and, more broadly, in worldly matters — is permission, and prohibition requires a specific text. The Prophet ﷺ said: "What God has permitted in His Book is lawful, what He has forbidden is unlawful, and what He was silent about is a concession" (al-Tirmidhī 1726; Ibn Mājah 3367).

Al-Ṭabarī understands the "detailed" prohibitions as those set out in 5:3, which lists carrion, blood, swine, what was dedicated to other than God, and animals killed by strangling, blow, fall, goring, or predators unless slaughtered in time. Al-Qurṭubī raises the chronological problem: 5:3 was revealed in Madīnah, and this verse in Makkah. He suggests either that the verb is to be understood as future — "He will detail for you" — or that the reference is to the Makkan detailing in 6:145, which lists carrion, blood, swine, and what was dedicated to other than God. Either way, the point stands: God has specified the forbidden, and it is a short list.

**"Unless You Are Compelled Thereto"**

*Illā mā'ḍṭurirtum ilayh* — "But whoever is compelled by extreme hunger— not intending to sin—then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" Even the forbidden becomes permitted under compulsion — when one is starving and nothing else is available. The exception is stated in every list of dietary prohibitions (2:173; 5:3; 16:115; 6:145), and it established the legal principle of *ḍarūrah* (necessity): "necessities render the prohibited permissible," within the limits of what the necessity requires. The verse's placement of the exception here, within a passage rebuking those who refused permitted food, sharpens its point: God has permitted even the forbidden in extremity — and you refuse the permitted in ordinary circumstances? The refusal is exposed as doubly irrational.

The exception also reveals the character of God's law. It is not a system of taboos indifferent to human welfare; it is a guidance that accounts for human need. The prohibitions protect; the exception protects when the prohibition would harm. The Qur'an says of the one compelled: "But if someone is compelled by necessity —neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful" (2:173).

**"Indeed, Many Lead Astray through Their Own Caprices, without Any Knowledge"**

*Wa inna kathīran la-yuḍillūna bi-ahwā'ihim bi-ghayri ʿilm* — "and indeed, many lead astray by their desires, without knowledge." The verse identifies the source of the confusion about food: not God's law, which is clear, but human caprice. The word *ahwā'* (desires, whims) is the word of verse 56, where the Prophet ﷺ refused to follow the idolaters' desires; *bi-ghayri ʿilm* (without knowledge) is the phrase of verse 100, where partners and offspring were attributed to God without knowledge. The idolaters who argued for carrion, and who forbade certain cattle in the names of their gods (vv. 138–140), were leading people astray by their own caprice, dressed up as religion.

Al-Qurṭubī connects the phrase to those who tried to persuade the believers that carrion — "killed by God" — was better than what human hands slaughtered. The argument was caprice without knowledge: it sounded pious but rested on nothing God had revealed. It is the "conjecture" and "surmise" of verse 116 applied to a concrete case.

The verb *yuḍillūna* is read by some as *yaḍillūna* — "many go astray by their desires" — rather than "lead astray." Both readings are transmitted, and both are true: those who follow caprice go astray themselves and lead others with them.

**"Surely Thy Lord Is He Who Knows Best the Transgressors"**

*Inna rabbaka huwa aʿlamu bi'l-muʿtadīn* — "indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors." The formula of verse 117 is applied to a specific category: the *muʿtadūn*, those who overstep bounds — the root is *ʿadā*, to transgress, the source of *ʿudwān* (aggression, enmity). In matters of food, the transgressors are those who cross God's limits in either direction: permitting what He forbade or forbidding what He permitted. God knows them. Their arguments may be gilded and their numbers large, but He knows precisely who has overstepped His bounds.

The closing thus places the whole question of food within the frame of divine knowledge and judgment. The believer who eats what God permitted and refuses what He forbade is not merely following a rule; he is honoring limits set by One who knows the transgressors and will hold them to account.

**The Verse's Teaching on Religious Scruple**

The verse addresses a temptation that afflicts the pious as much as the impious: the tendency to forbid oneself what God has permitted, out of excessive scruple, inherited custom, or the desire to seem more devout. The Qur'an regards this as a real error, not a harmless excess. It asks, "Will you not eat ˹your offerings˺?" (37:91). It tells the Prophet ﷺ elsewhere, "Why do you prohibit ˹yourself˺ from what Allah has made lawful to you, seeking to please your wives" (66:1). And it condemns those who "Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants" (7:32). God's law is the measure; adding to its prohibitions is as much a departure from it as subtracting from them.

**Knowledge as the Criterion**

The verse turns on the contrast between God's detailing (*faṣṣala*) and human caprice "without knowledge." What God has detailed is known; what people add or remove by whim is not knowledge but desire. The believer's task in matters of food, and in every matter of religious practice, is to hold to what has been detailed — to know the limits God has set — and to be suspicious of every rule, however pious it sounds, that cannot be traced to His Word. This is the practical application of verses 114–117: God is the Judge, His Word is complete, the majority conjectures, and God knows best. In the matter of food, that means: eat what He permitted, avoid what He forbade, and do not let caprice — one's own or the crowd's — add or subtract.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:120

> **Shun all sin—open and secret. Indeed, those who commit sin will be punished for what they earn.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Command of Complete Scope**

In the middle of the passage on food, the sūrah places a command of total breadth: *wa dharū ẓāhira al-ithmi wa bāṭinah* — "and leave the outward of sin and its inward." The word *ithm* means sin, offense, that which incurs guilt — from a root suggesting slowness or falling behind, as sin holds a person back from good. The command is to abandon it in both its dimensions: the outward (*ẓāhir*) and the inward (*bāṭin*).

**Outward and Inward Sin**

The commentators explain the pairing in several complementary ways, all of which the source commentary records.

The most straightforward, from al-Bayḍāwī and al-Sulamī: outward sin is what is committed publicly, where people can see; inward sin is what is committed in secret, where only God sees. The command forbids both — the sin one hides from people no less than the sin one commits openly. This closes the door to the hypocrisy that avoids public wrong while indulging private wrong. The Prophet ﷺ warned of "people who will come on the Day of Resurrection with good deeds like the mountains of Tihāmah, and God will make them scattered dust... they are people who, when they are alone with what God has forbidden, violate it" (Ibn Mājah 4245).

A second reading, also from al-Bayḍāwī: outward sin is that committed with the limbs — the hand, the tongue, the eye — and inward sin is that committed in the heart — envy, arrogance, malice, hypocrisy, the love of what God hates. This reading extends the prohibition into the interior life. The Qur'an holds people accountable for the heart: "Allah will not hold you accountable for unintentional oaths, but for what you intended in your hearts" (2:225); "Indeed, all will be called to account for ˹their˺ hearing, sight, and intellect" (17:36). Al-Ṭabarī adds that inward sin may include the *intention* to sin — the settled resolve, even before the act.

A third reading, recorded by al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī from early authorities, takes both terms as referring to sexual sin specifically, by analogy with 6:151 and 7:33, where "indecencies, outward and inward" (*fawāḥish*) are understood in this sense. On this reading, outward sin is open fornication and inward sin is the taking of secret paramours — a practice tolerated in pre-Islamic Arabia (cf. 4:25; 5:5). Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī observe, however, that the verse's language is general and gives no indication of restriction to one kind of sin; and al-Ṭabarī adds that if it were to be tied to a specific matter, the surrounding context would suggest the transgression of dietary law rather than sexual sin.

A fourth, from the Sufi commentators (al-Sulamī): outward sin is seeking the goods of this world for their own sake, and inward sin is seeking even the goods of Paradise as one's ultimate aim — both of which distract from God Himself. This reading takes the verse to its furthest interior reach: any attachment that displaces God, however refined, is a form of inward sin.

**Why the Command Appears Here**

The placement between verses 119 and 121 — both about food — is not accidental. The passage has been exposing the idolaters' caprice in matters of eating: their invented prohibitions, their argument for carrion, their slaughter in the names of idols. Verse 120 steps back and states the principle behind all of this: leave sin entirely. The idolaters' dietary errors were sins; some were outward (eating what was slaughtered for idols), some inward (the caprice and arrogance that produced the errors). The believer is to abandon all of it.

The placement also teaches something about the relationship between the specific and the general in the Qur'an. A rule about food is embedded in a command about the whole moral life, so that the believer does not treat dietary law as a set of isolated taboos but as one application of the total commitment to leaving what God has forbidden. Eating what God's name was not invoked over is not a small technical fault; it is *ithm*, and the same disposition that abandons all sin will abandon it.

**"Surely Those Who Commit Sin Shall Be Recompensed"**

*Inna alladhīna yaksibūna al-ithma sa-yujzawna bi-mā kānū yaqtarifūn* — "indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit." The verb *kasaba* (to earn, acquire) treats sin as something one accumulates — a debt one builds up. The verb *iqtarafa* (to commit) is the verb of verse 113. The recompense is certain (*sa-*, "will surely be"), and it corresponds to what was committed (*bi-mā*).

The clause gives the reason for the command. Sin is not left behind at death; it is earned, recorded, and repaid. The idolaters' contentment with their ways (v. 113) rested on the assumption that there would be no reckoning. The verse states that there will be. This connects to the closing of verse 108 ("He will inform them of what they used to do") and to the whole sūrah's insistence on the Hereafter.

**The Interior Life in Islamic Ethics**

The verse's inclusion of "inward sin" establishes a principle that distinguishes Islamic ethics from mere legalism. It is not enough to conform outwardly; the heart must be purified. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart." (al-Bukhārī 52; Muslim 1599)

And:

> "God does not look at your bodies or your forms, but He looks at your hearts." (Muslim 2564)

The scholars of the inner life — al-Ghazālī above all — built their science on this verse and its like. The "inward sins" they catalogued — pride, envy, ostentation, love of status, hatred, suspicion, greed — are as forbidden as theft and fornication, and more dangerous because they hide. The verse commands their abandonment with the same word it uses for outward sin: *dharū*, leave.

**The Two Directions of Vigilance**

The verse asks the believer to watch in two directions. Outward: what do my hands do, what does my tongue say, what do my eyes look at, what do I eat? Inward: what does my heart harbor, what do I resolve in secret, what do I love and hate, what do I do when no one sees? The first vigilance protects one's conduct; the second protects one's soul. A person may perfect the first and neglect the second, and be, in God's sight, corrupt. The verse forbids this division.

**Leaving Sin as a Practice**

The command is *dharū* — leave, abandon, let go. Sin is pictured as something one holds and can release. This is encouraging: the verse does not command the impossible task of never having sinned, but the possible one of letting go of what one holds. Every believer sins; the Prophet ﷺ said, "All the children of Adam are sinners, and the best of sinners are those who repent" (al-Tirmidhī 2499). The command is to release the sin — to stop, to turn, to repent — outwardly and inwardly. And the promise of verses 12 and 54 stands behind it: God has prescribed mercy upon Himself for those who repent and reform. The recompense the verse warns of is for "those who earn sin" and keep it; those who leave it find the door of verse 54 open.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:121

> **Do not eat of what is not slaughtered in Allah’s Name. For that would certainly be ˹an act of˺ disobedience. Surely the devils whisper to their ˹human˺ associates to argue with you. If you were to obey them, then you ˹too˺ would be polytheists.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Negative Rule**

Verse 118 stated the rule positively: eat what has God's name over it. Verse 121 states it negatively: *wa lā ta'kulū mimmā lam yudhkari ismu Allāhi ʿalayh* — "He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah" Together, the two verses draw the line. What was slaughtered with God's name invoked is lawful; what was not is forbidden. This covers, as al-Jalālayn and al-Ṭabarī explain, both meat slaughtered in the names of idols or by pagan rites (2:173; 5:3; 16:115) and carrion, over which no name was invoked because no slaughter took place.

**"Truly It Is Iniquity"**

*Wa innahu la-fisq* — "and indeed, it is *fisq*." The word *fisq* denotes transgression, going out from obedience — as the date-skin (*fisq*) splits away from the fruit (discussed at v. 49). Al-Ṭabarī glosses it as a clear sin and an act of disobedience. The eating of what God's name was not invoked over is not a minor infraction; it is *fisq*. The pronoun "it" may refer to the act of eating or to the food itself — 6:145 uses *fisq* for "what was dedicated to other than God" — and both senses hold.

The severity of the word reflects the stakes. In the Makkan context, the food question was a question of allegiance. To eat what was slaughtered for idols was to participate in idol worship; to eat carrion on the idolaters' argument was to accept their reasoning over God's rule. Both were departures from obedience.

**The Legal Question of Forgotten Invocation**

The verse raised a question the jurists debated: what of an animal slaughtered by a Muslim who forgot, or neglected, to say God's name? The source commentary summarizes the positions. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī held that such meat is lawful whether the omission was inadvertent or deliberate, reasoning that the verse's primary target is what was slaughtered for other than God or died without slaughter, and that the Muslim's slaughter carries God's name implicitly — al-Shāfiʿī cited the ḥadīth of ʿĀ'ishah in which people asked about meat brought by recent converts who may not have said God's name, and the Prophet ﷺ replied, "Say God's name over it yourselves and eat" (al-Bukhārī 2057).
