Abū Ḥanīfah and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal held that inadvertent omission is excused — since "God has excused my community for forgetfulness" — but deliberate omission renders the meat unlawful, on the plain sense of this verse. The difference is real, but all schools agree that the invocation is at least strongly required and that meat slaughtered in the name of other than God is forbidden.

**"Indeed, the Satans Inspire Their Friends to Dispute with You"**

*Wa inna al-shayāṭīna la-yūḥūna ilā awliyā'ihim li-yujādilūkum* — "and indeed, the satans inspire their friends to argue with you." The verse names the source of the carrion argument: the satans of verse 112, human and jinn, who inspire (*yūḥūna*, the same verb as in v. 112) their allies (*awliyā'*, friends, partisans) to dispute with the believers. Al-Ṭabarī explains the general sense: those who engage in disingenuous debate about God's law encourage and incite one another.

The commentators also record specific identifications. Some reports name Persian Zoroastrians allied with Quraysh who formulated the carrion argument — "you eat what you kill but not what God kills" — and sent it to the Makkans to use against the Prophet ﷺ (al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī). Others name a group of Jews who argued similarly (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī). Al-Wāḥidī reports that the argument seemed persuasive to some of the Companions, and that this verse was revealed to settle the matter. Most commentators hold the general reading: whoever the specific disputants were, the verse exposes their argument as satanic inspiration.

The exposure is instructive. The carrion argument had the marks of *zukhruf al-qawl* (v. 112) — it was pious-sounding ("what God kills"), plausible on its surface, and designed to make the believers doubt a clear rule. The verse teaches that such arguments, however clever, come from the enemy, and that their purpose is not truth but *jidāl* — contentious dispute intended to unsettle.

**"And If You Obey Them, You Are Surely Idolaters"**

*Wa in aṭaʿtumūhum innakum la-mushrikūn* — "and if you obey them, you are indeed idolaters." The verse closes with its most striking statement. To obey the satans' friends in this matter — to eat carrion on their argument, or what was slaughtered for idols at their invitation — is *shirk*. Not merely sin, not merely *fisq*, but association of partners with God.

Why? Because obedience in matters of lawful and unlawful is a form of worship. To accept a rule about what may be eaten from any authority other than God is to take that authority as a legislator alongside God — which is precisely what the Qur'an means by taking 'lords besides God.' The Qur'an says of the People of the Book: "They have taken their rabbis and monks as well as the Messiah, son of Mary, as lords besides Allah, even though they were commanded to worship none but One God" (9:31), and when ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim objected that they did not worship them, the Prophet ﷺ explained: "Did they not forbid what God permitted, and you forbade it; and permit what God forbade, and you permitted it?" He said, "Yes." The Prophet ﷺ said: "That is your worship of them" (al-Tirmidhī 3095). The principle is exactly this verse's: to obey a creature in permitting what God forbade or forbidding what God permitted is to make that creature a partner with God in legislation.

**The Weight of the Verse**

The verse establishes that the question of lawful and unlawful is not peripheral to *tawḥīd* but central to it. The right to declare what is permitted and forbidden belongs to God alone; this is part of what it means that "judgment belongs to God alone" (v. 57) and that one seeks no judge but Him (v. 114). Whoever arrogates that right to himself, or grants it to another, has committed a form of association. The idolaters of Makkah did this systematically — inventing prohibitions on cattle and crops in their gods' names (vv. 136–140) — and the verse tells the believers that following them in it, even in the single matter of carrion, would place them in the same category.

This is why the source commentary notes that the verse, though occasioned by a specific dispute, has "general application." Every age produces authorities — cultural, political, intellectual — that claim to define right and wrong independently of revelation, and every age produces arguments as gilded as the carrion argument for accepting their definitions. The verse's warning stands: obedience to such authorities against God's clear rule is not a small compromise; it touches the root of faith.

**The Structure of Verses 118–121**

The four verses form a unit. Eat what has God's name over it, if you believe in His signs (118). Why would you refuse what God permitted, when He has detailed what is forbidden — and even that is permitted in necessity? Many mislead by caprice without knowledge (119). Leave sin, outward and inward (120). Do not eat what God's name was not invoked over; it is *fisq*; the satans inspire their friends to dispute with you; obeying them is *shirk* (121). The unit moves from permission to prohibition, from the specific rule to the general principle behind it, and from the food itself to the theology of legislation. It applies everything the sūrah has taught — the exclusive judgment of God, the danger of the majority, the gilded speech of satans — to a matter as concrete as a meal.

**The Believer's Discipline**

The practical discipline the verse instills is care about what one eats and — more deeply — care about whom one obeys in defining what is lawful. The believer says God's name at slaughter, avoids what was slaughtered for other than God, refuses carrion, and — when confronted with arguments for abandoning these rules, however sophisticated — recognizes their source. He does not obey the satans' friends. In doing so, he preserves not merely his diet but his *tawḥīd*.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:122

> **Can those who had been dead, to whom We gave life and a light with which they can walk among people, be compared to those in complete darkness from which they can never emerge? That is how the misdeeds of the disbelievers have been made appealing to them.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Parable of Two Persons**

After the legal passage on food, the sūrah returns to its deepest concern — the difference between guidance and misguidance — through a parable. *A-wa man kāna maytan fa-aḥyaynāhu wa jaʿalnā lahu nūran yamshī bihi fī al-nās ka-man mathaluhu fī al-ẓulumāti laysa bi-khārijin minhā* — "Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one whose likeness is in the darknesses, not emerging from them?" The question is rhetorical, and the answer is obvious: they are not alike. Compare 35:22 ("the living and the dead are not equal") and 39:22.

**Death and Life as Spiritual States**

The verse uses "dead" and "life" metaphorically. Elsewhere in the sūrah — verse 95, "He brings forth the living from the dead" — the language refers to physical creation or resurrection. Here, as al-Ṭabarī and the commentators agree, it refers to spiritual awakening. The disbeliever is "dead" — unresponsive to truth, insensible to the signs, incapable of the movement of faith. God "gives him life" through guidance; he becomes responsive, seeing, moving toward God.

The metaphor is thoroughly Qur'anic. "Respond to Allah and His Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life" (8:24). "You certainly cannot make the dead hear ˹the truth˺" (27:80; 30:52). The sūrah itself said, "Only those who hear will respond; as for the dead, God will resurrect them" (v. 36). The disbeliever is not merely wrong; he is, in the dimension that matters most, not alive. And faith is not merely a change of opinion; it is a resurrection.

**"A Light by Which to Walk Among Mankind"**

Having been given life, the believer receives a light — *nūr* — by which he walks among people. Al-Ṭabarī explains the light as religious guidance, or the Qur'an specifically. Al-Rāzī reads the one given life as a person whose soul God has prepared to receive revelation, and the light as revelation itself.

Light is the Qur'an's central symbol for guidance and revelation (5:15; 7:157; 14:1; 42:52; 64:8). The phrase "by which to walk among mankind" is significant: the light is not for private contemplation but for living — for moving through the world of people, making decisions, distinguishing right from wrong in ordinary life. The believer walks through the same world as the disbeliever, but he sees it. Compare 57:28: "through which Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace, brings them out of darkness and into light by His Will, and guides them to the Straight Path" And the repeated formula: God "Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light" (2:257; 5:16; 14:1; 57:9; 65:11).

**"One Who Is in Darkness from Which He Does Not Emerge"**

The contrast: one whose condition (*mathaluhu*, his likeness, his case) is to be in *al-ẓulumāt* — the darknesses, plural — and not emerging from them. The plural echoes verse 1 of the sūrah, where God "made the darknesses and the light": darkness is many, light is one. The disbeliever is not in one darkness but in layers — ignorance, caprice, tradition, arrogance, the whispering of satans. And he does not emerge; the phrase *laysa bi-khārijin minhā* pictures a settled condition, not a passing moment.

The two states are not merely different; they are incommensurable. One walks with light; the other cannot find his way out. The verse asks, "Is the one like the other?" — the same form of question used in verse 50 ("Are the blind and the seeing equal?"). To pretend they are equal is to deny the obvious.

**The Occasion of Revelation**

The verse is general, but the commentators record occasions. The best known concerns Ḥamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the Prophet's uncle, and Abū Jahl, his fiercest enemy. According to the report in al-Rāzī and al-Wāḥidī, Abū Jahl insulted the Prophet ﷺ; Ḥamzah, a powerful and respected man returning from a hunt, was told of it, went to Abū Jahl, struck him with his bow, and declared his Islam. The verse was revealed about the two: Ḥamzah, who had been dead and was given life and light, and Abū Jahl, who remained in darkness and never emerged — he died at Badr in his disbelief. Ḥamzah died a martyr at Uḥud, "the lord of martyrs."

Other reports name ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who opposed Islam violently and then became its pillar (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭūsī); ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, an early Companion who was tortured for his faith (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī); or the Prophet ﷺ himself (al-Rāzī). Whatever the specific occasion, the pattern is the same: a person who was in darkness was brought to light, and the difference between what he was and what he became is the difference the verse names.

**"Thus for the Disbelievers, What They Used to Do Was Made to Seem Fair"**

*Kadhālika zuyyina li-l-kāfirīna mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — "thus was made fair-seeming to the disbelievers what they used to do." The verse closes by explaining why the one in darkness does not emerge: his condition has been made attractive to him. He does not perceive the darkness as darkness. His deeds seem good to him; his way seems right. This is the *tazyīn* the sūrah has mentioned at verses 43 and 108 and will mention again at 137 — the beautification of evil that follows persistent choice of it, whether attributed to Satan or, as here, in the passive, to God's decree following human choice.

The clause explains the tragedy of the disbeliever. He is not in darkness unwillingly; he has come to like it. The Qur'an asks elsewhere, "Are those whose evil-doing is made so appealing to them that they deem it good ˹like those who are rightly guided˺" (35:8). And warns: "˹They are˺ those whose efforts are in vain in this worldly life, while they think they are doing good" (18:103–104).

**The Believer's Gratitude**

The verse should produce in the believer a specific gratitude. He was dead; he was given life. He was in darkness; he was given light. He did not do this for himself — the verbs are God's: *aḥyaynāhu*, *jaʿalnā lahu*. The Prophet ﷺ taught a supplication that echoes this: "O God, place light in my heart, light in my hearing, light in my sight, light on my right, light on my left, light before me, light behind me, light above me, light below me — and make me light" (al-Bukhārī 6316; Muslim 763). The believer who understands verse 122 asks for more of the light he has been given, knowing its source.

**The Psychology of Emergence**

The verse also suggests why emerging from darkness is difficult. The darknesses are plural and layered; the condition has been made attractive; the one within does not perceive his need. The person in darkness must first recognize that he is in darkness — and this recognition is itself a beginning of light, a grace. This is why the Qur'an insists that guidance is God's gift, and why the believer, seeing another in darkness, does not despise him but remembers that he himself was once dead, and prays for the other's life as his own was given.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:123

> **And so We have placed in every society the most wicked to conspire in it. Yet they plot only against themselves, but they fail to perceive it.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pattern in Every Town**

*Wa kadhālika jaʿalnā fī kulli qaryatin akābira mujrimīhā li-yamkurū fīhā* — "and thus We placed in every town the great ones of its guilty, that they might plot therein." The verse generalizes from Makkah to every community: in each, the leading opponents of the prophet are the town's *akābir* — its great ones, chiefs, the powerful — who are also its *mujrimūn*, its guilty, criminal ones. The word *akābir* is the plural of *akbar*, "greater"; these are the people of rank, wealth, and influence.

Al-Ṭabarī explains that the verse refers to those who stand in strong opposition to a prophet who comes to their community. Compare 25:31: "Thus did We make for every prophet an enemy from among the guilty" — the same *kadhālika*, the same *mujrimīn*. The verse belongs to a Qur'anic pattern: the notables (*al-mala'*) of Noah's people (7:60), of Hūd's (7:66), of Ṣāliḥ's (7:75), of Shuʿayb's (7:88), and of Pharaoh's court (7:109; 10:75, 83) are consistently the front line of rejection. The commentators (al-Jalālayn, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī) draw the general conclusion: it is most often the powerful who resist a prophet most stubbornly — Abū Jahl of the previous verse being the Makkan example.

**Why the Powerful Resist**

The reasons are structural. A prophet's message threatens the existing order — its religion, its hierarchy, its sources of legitimacy and revenue. Those who benefit most from the order have most to lose. The Makkan chiefs controlled the Kaʿbah's pilgrimage economy, the tribal alliances, and the prestige that came with custodianship of the idols. Monotheism threatened all of it. Beyond material interest, there is pride: the great man does not easily accept instruction from one he regards as socially beneath him — which is why the Makkans objected that the Qur'an was not sent down to "If only this Quran was revealed to a great man from ˹one of˺ the two cities" (43:31). And there is the habit of command: the powerful are used to defining what is true and good for others, and a revelation that defines these independently of them is an intolerable rival.

The Qur'an's consistent observation is that "Whenever We sent a warner to a society, its elite would say," (34:34). The followers of the prophets, by contrast, were typically the weak and poor — a fact the Makkans held against the Prophet ﷺ (verses 52–53), and which Heraclius, in the famous ḥadīth, recognized as a mark of true prophethood: "the followers of the messengers are the weak" (al-Bukhārī 7).

**"That They May Plot Therein"**

*Li-yamkurū fīhā* — "so that they may plot there." The *lām* has been read as a *lām* of consequence (they end up plotting) or of purpose within the divine wisdom (God places them there, and their plotting serves a purpose in His plan — testing the believers, distinguishing truth from falsehood, and bringing on them the consequences of their choice). *Makr* is scheming, contrivance — the secret planning of harm. The Makkan chiefs' *makr* is recorded in the Qur'an: "And Allah is the best of planners" (8:30).

**"But They Only Plot Against Themselves"**

*Wa mā yamkurūna illā bi-anfusihim wa mā yashʿurūn* — "they plot only against themselves, but they fail to perceive it" (6:123). This is the verse's turn. The plotters imagine they are harming the prophet and his followers. In reality, every plot rebounds on the plotter. "But evil plotting only backfires on those who plot." (35:43). The Makkan chiefs plotted, and their plotting led them to Badr, where Abū Jahl and the others who had schemed against the Prophet ﷺ were killed — the plot had circled back.

The source commentary places this in what it calls the Qur'an's "moral reflexivity": actions return to their doer. "They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it" (2:9); "they mislead none but themselves" (3:69); "Whatever you ˹believers˺ spend in charity, it is for your own good—as long as you do so seeking the pleasure of Allah" (2:272); "And whoever commits a sin—it is only to their own loss" (4:111). The consequences of one's deeds may fall on others in this life, but in the Hereafter — and in the deepest sense even here — they fall on oneself alone. The plotter damages his own soul with every scheme, and builds his own punishment.

**"Though They Are Unaware"**

*Wa mā yashʿurūn* — "and they do not perceive." The plotters do not sense that the plot is against themselves. This is the mark of the darkness of verse 122: the one in darkness does not know he is in darkness; the plotter does not know he is the victim. The verse's closing repeats the theme of self-deception that runs through the sūrah — the beautification of deeds (v. 122), the not-perceiving (2:9, 12), the thinking one is doing well while losing everything (18:104).

**The Divine Wisdom in the Arrangement**

The verse says God "made" (*jaʿalnā*) the great ones among the guilty in every town. This is not an endorsement of their crime but a statement of the divine ordering that permits it. The commentators explain: God, in His wisdom, allows the opposition to a prophet to be led by the powerful, so that the truth's victory — when it comes — is manifestly God's, not the product of human power; so that the believers are tested and refined; and so that the plotters receive the consequences of their free choice. The arrangement also ensures that faith is never simply a matter of following the strong. Had the powerful embraced every prophet, people would have followed them out of deference rather than conviction. Their opposition makes faith a choice against the grain — and therefore a real choice.

**The Consolation and the Warning**

For the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, the verse is consolation: what you face in Makkah is not unique; every prophet faced the same from the same kind of people; and their plots will fall on their own heads. For the powerful of every age, it is a warning: the position of "great one" does not protect from being counted among the "guilty," and the schemes of the great are as self-destructive as any other sin — more so, because the great have more with which to scheme.

**A Contemporary Reflection**

The verse describes a pattern still observable. Movements that call for truth and justice against entrenched interest tend to be resisted first and hardest by those who hold the interest. The resistance is often sophisticated — the *makr* of the powerful is rarely crude — and often presented as defense of order, tradition, or the common good. The verse teaches the believer not to be surprised by this, not to mistake rank for rightness, and to trust that plots against truth are, in the end, plots against the plotters.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:124

> **Whenever a sign comes to them, they say, “We will never believe until we receive what Allah’s messengers received.” Allah knows best where to place His message. The wicked will soon be overwhelmed by humiliation from Allah and a severe punishment for their evil plots.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Demand Escalates**

Throughout the sūrah, the disbelievers have demanded signs (vv. 37, 109). Verse 124 records what they say when a sign actually comes: *wa idhā jā'athum āyatun qālū lan nu'mina ḥattā nu'tā mithla mā ūtiya rusulu Allāh* — "and when a sign comes to them, they say: We will never believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God." They do not accept the sign that came (cf. vv. 4, 25, 111). Instead, they raise a new demand — not for a sign to be shown to them, but for a sign to be *given* to them, as it was given to the messengers. They want prophethood itself, or at least its miracles, for themselves.

Al-Jalālayn, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Rāzī explain the demand: the disbelievers said, in effect, "Why should Muhammad receive revelation and not we? We will not believe until revelation comes to us as it came to him and the prophets before him." Compare 17:90–93 ("We will not believe in you until you cause a spring to gush forth... or you bring God and the angels before us... or you ascend into heaven, and we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book we can read") and 74:52 ("Rather, every one of them desires to be given scrolls spread open").

**The Occasion**

Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī report that the verse was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, the wealthy chief of Makhzūm, who said: "If prophethood were true, I would have more right to it than Muhammad, for I am older than he and have more wealth and children." Abū Jahl is also reported to have said, "We competed with Banū ʿAbd Manāf in honor, and when we were neck and neck, they said: 'We have a prophet who receives revelation from heaven.' By God, we will never believe in him until revelation comes to us as it comes to him."

The demand exposes the true objection. It was not that the sign was insufficient; it was that the *wrong person* had received it. The Makkan chiefs measured worthiness by wealth, lineage, and age, and by their measure the orphan Muhammad ﷺ ranked below them. This is the objection of 43:31: "If only this Quran was revealed to a great man from ˹one of˺ the two cities"

**"God Knows Best Where to Place His Message"**

*Allāhu aʿlamu ḥaythu yajʿalu risālatah* — "God knows best where He places His message." The answer is decisive and brief. The choice of a messenger is God's, made by His knowledge, not by human standards of rank. The verse does not argue that Muhammad ﷺ was wealthy or noble enough; it denies that wealth and nobility are the relevant criteria at all. God places His message where He knows it belongs.

The principle corrects a deep error. The Qur'an repeatedly rejects worldly status as a marker of spiritual standing. "We ˹alone˺ have distributed their ˹very˺ livelihood among them in this worldly life and raised some of them in rank above others so that some may employ others in service" (43:32). "It is not your wealth or children that bring you closer to Us" (34:37). When the Israelites objected to Saul as king because "How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been blessed with vast riches" the answer was: "Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature" (2:247). The Prophet ﷺ was chosen not for his fortune but for his character — "And you are truly ˹a man˺ of outstanding character" (68:4) — and for what God alone knows of a soul's fitness to bear His word.

The verse also forecloses the demand to receive revelation oneself. Prophethood is not acquired; it is bestowed. No one attains it by desire, wealth, or effort. The disbelievers' condition — "until we are given the like" — is therefore not a serious condition but an evasion; they have set a bar that God's wisdom will never meet for them, and so have guaranteed their own unbelief.

**"Humiliation Before God and a Severe Punishment"**

*Sa-yuṣību alladhīna ajramū ṣaghārun ʿinda Allāhi wa ʿadhābun shadīdun bi-mā kānū yamkurūn* — "there will befall those who committed crimes humiliation from God and a severe punishment for what they used to plot." The word *ṣaghār* is smallness, abasement, humiliation — the precise opposite of the *akābir*, the "great ones," of the previous verse and of the greatness the Makkan chiefs claimed. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the contrast: those who demanded prophethood because of their worldly greatness will receive, from God, smallness. Their honor was before people; their humiliation will be before God.

The punishment is "for what they used to plot" — connecting to verse 123. The demand for a sign of their own was itself part of the *makr*, a scheme to discredit the Prophet ﷺ; and the scheme rebounds as humiliation and punishment.

**The Theology of Divine Selection**

The verse touches a principle central to Islamic theology: God's freedom in choosing whom He wills for His purposes. "Your Lord creates and chooses whatever He wills—the choice is not theirs" (28:68). "Allah selects messengers from both angels and people, for Allah is truly All-Hearing, All-Seeing" (22:75). This freedom is not arbitrary; it is exercised by knowledge — *aʿlamu*, "knows best." God knows the hearts, the capacities, the fitness of each soul, and places His message accordingly. The human observer sees only externals — wealth, age, tribe — and judges by them; God sees what the externals conceal.

This has a practical implication for how believers regard one another. Rank in God's sight is by *taqwā* (49:13), not by any worldly measure. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Many a disheveled, dust-covered person, turned away from doors, if he were to swear by God, God would fulfill his oath" (Muslim 2622). The Makkan chiefs' error — judging worthiness by status — is an error believers can fall into among themselves, and the verse warns against it.

**The Pattern of Envy**

Beneath the demand lies envy. The chiefs could not bear that Muhammad ﷺ had been given what they had not. The Qur'an names this: "Or do they envy the people for Allah" (4:54). Envy of God's distribution is a rejection of God's wisdom — it says, in effect, that God placed His gift wrongly. The verse's answer, "God knows best where to place His message," is also the answer to all envy: God's distribution of every gift is by knowledge, and objection to it is objection to Him.

**The Sign That Was Rejected**

The verse opens with "when a sign comes to them." The Qur'an itself was the sign, and it came. The Makkans' response — demanding more, demanding it for themselves — demonstrates the principle of verse 111: signs do not produce faith in those who have resolved not to believe. The sign is sufficient; the resistance lies in the demand's motive, which is pride and envy rather than a genuine search for truth. The believer learns to examine his own conditions for belief: whether they are honest requests for clarity or, like the Makkans', disguised refusals.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:125

> **Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens their heart to Islam. But whoever He wills to leave astray, He makes their chest tight and constricted as if they were climbing up into the sky. This is how Allah dooms those who disbelieve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Guidance as Expansion of the Breast**

*Fa-man yuridi Allāhu an yahdiyahu yashraḥ ṣadrahu li-l-islām* — "so whoever God wishes to guide, He expands his breast for submission." The verb *sharaḥa* means to open, widen, lay open — as one opens meat by cutting, or opens a subject by explaining it (whence *sharḥ*, commentary). The *ṣadr*, breast, is in Qur'anic anthropology the seat of thoughts, intentions, faith and disbelief — the housing of the heart. God "Indeed, they enfold ˹what is in˺ their hearts, ˹trying˺ to hide it from Him" (5:7; 8:43; 11:5). To expand the breast for Islam is, as al-Bayḍāwī says, to make the soul receptive to truth and to remove whatever impedes acceptance.

The image is used of the Prophet ﷺ — "Have We not uplifted your heart for you ˹O Prophet˺," (94:1), often linked to the opening and cleansing of his heart — and of Moses' prayer, "Uplift my heart for me," (20:25). Compare 39:22: "Can ˹the misguided be like˺ those whose hearts Allah has opened to Islam, so they are enlightened by their Lord"

**The Prophet's Description of the Expanded Breast**

The commentators (al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭūsī) record that when this verse was revealed, the Companions asked how the breast is expanded, and the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "It is a light that God casts into the heart of the believer, so that it is expanded and opened for it." They asked, "Is there a sign by which it is known?" He said: "Yes — turning toward the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it comes."

The ḥadīth is transmitted by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, and others; its chains are discussed, but its meaning is confirmed by the whole Qur'an. The expansion is a light — the light of verse 122. Its signs are practical: orientation toward the Hereafter, detachment from the world's illusion, and readiness for death. The person whose breast is expanded is recognizable not by ecstasy but by the direction of his life.

**Misguidance as Constriction**

*Wa man yurid an yuḍillahu yajʿal ṣadrahu ḍayyiqan ḥarajan ka-annamā yaṣṣaʿʿadu fī al-samā'* — "and whoever He wishes to lead astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were climbing up into the sky." Two words describe the tightness. *Ḍayyiq* is narrow. *Ḥaraj* is intensely constricted — al-Ṭabarī notes that *ḥaraj* also denotes a dense thicket of trees so tangled that nothing can enter, evoking a woodland so choked that light cannot penetrate. The breast of the one led astray is such a thicket; faith finds no room in it.

"As if he were climbing to the sky": the image conveys the impossible and the suffocating. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ṭabarī explain that climbing into the sky is beyond human capacity, so faith is likewise impossible for one whose breast God has constricted. Modern readers notice that the image also describes the physical reality of ascent: the higher one climbs, the thinner the air, the tighter the chest, the harder the breath. The Qur'an's picture of a breast constricted "as if climbing into the sky" corresponds to what a climber experiences at altitude — a correspondence many commentators have remarked on as a sign of the Qur'an's precision.

The form *yaṣṣaʿʿadu* (from *taṣaʿʿada*) intensifies: not merely climbing but laboring upward, struggling against resistance. The one led astray, faced with faith, struggles as though against gravity itself; every step toward belief is a strain, and he falls back.

**The Breast in Islamic Anthropology**

The source commentary notes that the breast's expansion and constriction relate not only to the physical body but to what Islamic thought calls the subtle body — the inner dimension that transcends the physical yet affects it. Ordinary language preserves this: one speaks of an 'expansive' mood and of a 'tightness in the chest' under anxiety. The Qur'an uses the constriction of the breast for the prophets' distress at rejection (11:12; 15:97; 26:13). Here the constriction is the inability to receive truth. The fifth Imam Muḥammad al-Bāqir is reported to have described it vividly: for one who has not attained truth, it is as if the heart has left its place and risen into the throat; when he attains truth, it settles back (al-Ṭūsī).

**The Question of Divine Will**

The verse attributes both guidance and misguidance to God's will. This is stated throughout the Qur'an (v. 35; 32:13; 14:4; 74:31) and was discussed at verses 39 and 110. The commentators' balance holds here. God's will is not arbitrary: al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Ṭūsī read the expansion as an act of divine kindness (*luṭf*) and perhaps a reward for prior openness to guidance, and the constriction as a consequence of prior rejection. The *kadhālika*, "thus," in the final clause indicates that the constriction is a punishment following disbelief: the person who refuses faith finds his breast narrowed, which makes later faith harder still — a descending spiral in which initial rejection produces a state that entrenches rejection (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭūsī).

Ibn Taymiyyah's formulation: God guides by His grace those who turn to Him, and leaves to their own choice those who turn away, and the leaving is itself just, for they chose it. The verse's two halves describe what happens to a soul under each divine response. The believer prays, "Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us" (3:8), because he knows that the expansion is a gift that can be withdrawn.

**"Thus Does God Heap Defilement upon Those Who Do Not Believe"**

*Kadhālika yajʿalu Allāhu al-rijsa ʿalā alladhīna lā yu'minūn* — "This is how Allah dooms those who disbelieve" (6:125). *Rijs* is filth, defilement, abomination — used of idols and wine (5:90) and of the state of the hypocrites (9:125). Al-Jalālayn and al-Qurṭubī explain it as punishment, including the punishment of giving Satan authority over them — contrast 15:42 and 16:99, where Satan has no authority over believers. The unbeliever's inner state is not neutral; it becomes defiled, and the defilement is itself the beginning of punishment. One commentator remarks that there is no punishment more severe than obliviousness to truth (al-Qushayrī).

**Practical Wisdom**

The verse gives the believer a diagnostic and a discipline. The diagnostic: does my breast expand toward the truth or tighten against it? When a verse or a command reaches me, do I open or resist? The discipline: to seek the expansion by the means the Prophet ﷺ named — turning toward the Hereafter, detaching from illusion, preparing for death. These are not consequences only; they are also causes. The one who practices them finds his breast widening. And the one who feels the constriction should recognize it as a warning — the first sign of the thicket forming — and should hurry to God before it closes. The Companions' question, "Is there a sign by which it is known?", is the right question, and the Prophet's answer is the believer's daily examination.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:126

> **That is your Lord’s Path—perfectly straight. We have already made the signs clear to those who are mindful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"This Is the Path of Thy Lord"**

*Wa hādhā ṣirāṭu rabbika mustaqīmā* — "and this is the path of your Lord, straight." The demonstrative *hādhā*, "this," points back: to the Qur'an, to the religion the sūrah has been expounding, to the *islām* for which the breast is expanded in the previous verse, or — as al-Ṭabarī suggests — to the whole exposition of guidance and misguidance that has preceded. All are one thing: the way God has laid out. The verse names it *ṣirāṭ rabbika*, "the path of your Lord" — His path, belonging to Him, leading to Him.

The *ṣirāṭ mustaqīm* is the Qur'an's central image for religion. It is what the believer asks for in every prayer: "Guide us along the Straight Path," (1:6). A *ṣirāṭ* is a broad, clear highway, not a winding track; *mustaqīm* is straight, upright, without deviation. The image conveys that God's way is direct — the shortest distance between the servant and his Lord — and that it is one, unlike the many crooked paths that branch off it (6:153, coming later in the sūrah: "So follow it and do not follow other ways, for they will lead you away from His Way").

**The Word "Mustaqīmā"**

The adjective appears in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*): "this is the path of your Lord — in a state of being straight." Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the construction emphasizes the straightness as the path's essential and enduring condition, not an incidental description. The path does not become straight; it *is* straight, always. It is the observer's vision, not the path, that may be crooked.

The "straightness" has several dimensions. It is straight in doctrine: pure *tawḥīd*, without the deviation of *shirk* in either direction. It is straight in law: the balance between the idolaters' arbitrary prohibitions and the libertine's dismissal of all limits — the point made in the food passage just concluded. It is straight in ethics: the abandonment of sin outward and inward (v. 120). And it is straight in its destination: it leads to the Abode of Peace (v. 127).

**The Placement**

The verse is placed after the great parable of light and darkness (v. 122) and the description of the expanded and constricted breast (v. 125). Having shown what guidance and misguidance are internally, the sūrah now names guidance externally: it is a path — objective, laid down, walkable. The internal expansion of the breast and the external straight path correspond: the expanded breast is what allows one to see and walk the path; the path is what the expanded breast is opened toward. Neither is complete without the other. A person may have an inner openness but no clear way to walk; a person may have the way before him but a breast too tight to enter it. God gives both to whom He guides.

**"We Have Expounded the Signs"**

*Qad faṣṣalnā al-āyāti* — "We have indeed detailed the signs." The verb *faṣṣala*, to separate into distinct parts, to expound in detail, has been a refrain in the sūrah (vv. 55, 97, 98, 114, 119). God has not left the path vaguely marked; He has explained its signs distinctly — in creation, in revelation, in the arguments the sūrah has deployed against idolatry, in the rules it has given about food. The straightness of the path is matched by the clarity of its signposting.

The past-tense *qad faṣṣalnā*, "We have already detailed," conveys completion. The exposition is done; the responsibility now lies with the hearer. This is the constant Qur'anic position: God has established the proof (*ḥujjah*), and what remains is the human response. "Still it transpired so Allah may establish what He had destined—that those who were to perish and those who were to survive might do so after the truth had been made clear to both" (8:42).

**"For a People Who Take Heed"**

*Li-qawmin yadhdhakkarūn* — "for a people who remember." The verb *tadhakkara* is to recall, to take to heart, to be reminded. The signs are detailed for those who *remember* — the same verb-class as *dhikr*, remembrance. The formula recurs in the sūrah with variations: "for a people who know" (v. 97), "for a people who understand" (v. 98), and now "for a people who take heed." Each names a faculty required to benefit from the signs: knowledge, understanding, and — here — remembrance.

Why remembrance? Because the truth of *tawḥīd* is not new information but something the human being already knows in the depth of his nature (*fiṭrah*) and has forgotten. The Qur'an calls itself a "reminder" (*dhikr*, *tadhkirah*) more often than a teaching. The signs are detailed so that those who are willing to remember will recognize what they had forgotten. The straight path is not foreign; it is the way home, and the one who "takes heed" recognizes the road.

**The Restriction Is Not Exclusion**

"For a people who take heed" does not mean the signs were detailed only for some and withheld from others. They are detailed for all; they *benefit* those who take heed. The rain falls on all ground; it produces growth in the receptive soil. The Prophet ﷺ compared guidance to rain falling on different kinds of land — some absorb and grow, some hold water for others, some are hard and yield nothing (al-Bukhārī 79; Muslim 2282). The signs are the rain; the "people who take heed" are the receptive earth.

**The Believer's Response**

The verse invites two responses. The first is gratitude: the path is straight and the signs are detailed — the believer is not left to guess. The second is vigilance: since the path is straight, any deviation is the walker's, not the road's. The Companion Ibn Masʿūd said: the Prophet ﷺ drew a straight line and said, "This is the path of God," then drew lines to its right and left and said, "These are paths, on each of which is a satan calling to it," and recited 6:153 (Aḥmad 4142; al-Nasā'ī in al-Kubrā). The believer walks the line and refuses the branches, remembering — *yadhdhakkarūn* — what he was made for.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:127

> **They will have the Home of Peace with their Lord, Who will be their Guardian because of what they used to do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Destination of the Straight Path**

Verse 126 named the path; verse 127 names where it ends. *Lahum dāru al-salāmi ʿinda rabbihim* — "for them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord." The pronoun "them" refers to "the people who take heed" of the previous verse — those who received the signs, remembered, and walked the straight path. Their destination is *dār al-salām*.

**The Meanings of "Dār al-Salām"**

*Dār* is an abode, a dwelling, a home. *Salām* is peace, safety, soundness, freedom from every defect and harm. The phrase has been understood in several ways, which the source commentary records.

Most commonly, it is Paradise — the Garden God has prepared for His friends as a reward for the hardships they endured and the good they did (al-Ṭabarī). The Qur'an uses 'the Abode of the Hereafter' in the same sense (v. 32; 2:94; 16:30), and 13:22–24 identifies "the ultimate abode" (13:22) as Gardens of Eden, where the angels greet the inhabitants with "Peace be upon you for your perseverance." (13:24). Paradise is the abode of peace because there is no fear, grief, weariness, enmity, or death there: "There they will never hear any idle or sinful talk — only good and virtuous speech." (56:25–26); "Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be: Peace" (33:44).

Second, since *al-Salām* is a Name of God — "He is Allah—there is no god except Him" (59:23) — *dār al-salām* has been read as "the Abode of God," the house that belongs to Him and to which He invites (Ibn ʿAjībah, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). Compare 10:25: "And Allah invites ˹all˺ to the Home of Peace and guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path" — where the same pairing of the straight path and *dār al-salām* appears as here in verses 126–127.

Third, *salām* may simply describe the Abode's quality — a place characterized by peace (al-Rāzī) — or by the greeting "Peace" that fills it (Ibn ʿAjībah; cf. 10:10).

All three converge. Paradise is the abode of peace because it is God's abode, and God is Peace; and because everything in it is sound and safe; and because its language is the greeting of peace.

**"With Their Lord"**

*ʿInda rabbihim* — 'with their Lord,' in His presence, in His keeping. The phrase indicates both location and status: the Abode is in God's proximity, and it is already reserved for them in His knowledge. It also contains the Garden's highest blessing — nearness to God. The commentators note that the greatest joy of Paradise is not its gardens but the vision of God and His pleasure: "Allah has promised the believers, both men and women, Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever, and splendid homes in the Gardens of Eternity, and—above all— the pleasure of Allah" (9:72). The Sufi commentators press this: Ibn ʿAjībah distinguishes the Garden of Gnosis (*maʿārif*) from the Garden of Ornaments (*zakhārif*), and says whoever enters the former has no longing for the latter, since nearness to God makes one independent of all else. He also suggests that some souls enter a foretaste of the Abode of Peace before death — the state of inner peace granted to those who have found rest in God.

**"And He Shall Be Their Protector"**

*Wa huwa waliyyuhum* — "Who will be their Guardian because of what they used to do" (6:127). The word *walī* is protector, guardian, patron, close friend. God is the *walī* of the believers: "Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light" (2:257) — the same movement as verse 122. The sūrah earlier asked, "Shall I take as protector other than God?" (v. 14), and rejected every other *walī* (vv. 51, 70). Here the true *walī* is affirmed for those who took no other.

The contrast with the surrounding verses is deliberate. Verses 121 and 128 speak of the satans and "their friends" (*awliyā'*) — the disbelievers who took satans as patrons. Verse 127 speaks of the believers, whose *walī* is God. Everyone has a *walī*; the question is who. Those who took satans as patrons will be gathered with them in the Fire (v. 128); those whose patron was God will be with Him in the Abode of Peace.

**"Because of That Which They Used to Do"**

*Bi-mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — "on account of what they used to do." The reward is connected to deeds. This does not mean that deeds purchase Paradise — the Prophet ﷺ said, "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They asked, "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said, "Not even I, unless God envelops me in His mercy" (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816). It means that deeds are the cause God has appointed, the condition He has set, the means by which His mercy is reached. The *bā'* is the *bā'* of causation, not of price. The same phrase closes verses about punishment — "for what they used to do" — and here closes a verse about reward: the symmetry establishes that the Hereafter answers to this life in both directions.

**The Term in Later Usage**

The source commentary notes the resonance of *dār al-salām* in Islamic civilization. It became a name for Baghdad under the ʿAbbāsids, for the city of Dar es Salaam in East Africa, and is sometimes used as synonymous with *dār al-islām*. The wide use reflects the term's aspiration: to build on earth some image of the peace promised in the Hereafter.

**Peace as the Fruit of the Path**

The verse teaches what the straight path produces: peace. The disbeliever's state, as the previous verses described it, is darkness, constriction, defilement, and self-destructive plotting — the opposite of peace. The believer's state, even amid the hardship of Makkah, is oriented toward peace, and its full realization awaits him with his Lord. The Islamic greeting — *al-salāmu ʿalaykum* — is a daily rehearsal of the destination. Every time believers exchange it, they wish each other the Abode of Peace, and remind each other whose *walī* they have.

## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:128

> **˹Consider˺ the Day He will gather them ˹all˺ together and say, “O assembly of jinn! You misled humans in great numbers.” And their human associates will say, “Our Lord! We benefited from each other’s company, but now we have reached the term which You appointed for us.” ˹Then˺ He will say, “The Fire is your home, yours to stay in forever, except whoever Allah wills to spare.” Surely your Lord is All-Wise, AllKnowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Scene of Gathering**

*Wa yawma yaḥshuruhum jamīʿan* — "and the Day He gathers them all together." The verse opens onto the Day of Judgment, where all — jinn and humans, misleaders and misled — stand together. The sūrah has returned to this scene repeatedly (vv. 22, 30, 94), each time exposing a different aspect of the disbelievers' condition. Here it exposes the alliance between the satans of the jinn and their human partisans, mentioned in verses 112 and 121, and brings it to judgment.

**"O Company of Jinn! Many Among Mankind Have You Claimed"**

*Yā maʿshara al-jinni qad istakthartum min al-ins* — "from the evil of the lurking whisperer—" The verb *istakthara* means to take or acquire much, to seek to increase. God addresses the jinn directly: you have gathered a great number of humans — led them astray, made them your followers. Al-Ṭabarī connects this to verse 112: the jinn led many astray through gilded speech, and through whispering (114:4–6).

Al-Rāzī makes an important clarification: 'claimed' does not mean the jinn possessed humans or controlled their wills. The jinn called and tempted; humans responded. Satan's own testimony on that Day confirms it: "I did not have any authority over you. I only called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves." (14:22). The responsibility remains human. The jinn's 'taking many' is the result of many freely following.

**"Our Lord! We Have Profited from Each Other"**

*Wa qāla awliyā'uhum min al-insi rabbanā istamtaʿa baʿḍunā bi-baʿḍ* — "and their friends among mankind will say: Our Lord, we benefited from one another." The human partisans of the jinn speak — the jinn are silent, as the misleaders typically are at judgment. Their confession is remarkable in its honesty: we used each other.

How did they profit from one another? Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī explain both sides. Humans profited from the jinn by the false assurances they received — the pre-Islamic Arab who entered a valley would call on its jinn for protection (72:6), and felt safer for it; humans consulted soothsayers who relied on jinn, and gained a sense of knowing the unseen; and, more broadly, humans gained from the jinn the pleasure of the sins the jinn made attractive to them. The jinn profited from humans by the greatness, power, and authority attributed to them — beings called upon and feared are magnified by the calling and fearing — and by the satisfaction of leading astray.

The confession describes every corrupt alliance. Each party gains something from the other: the misleader gains followers and status; the follower gains permission, pleasure, and the comfort of company. Neither gains anything real. And on the Day of gathering, the mutual profit is revealed as mutual ruin.

**"We Have Reached Our Term Which Thou Hadst Appointed"**

*Wa balaghnā ajalanā alladhī ajjalta lanā* — "and we have reached our term which You appointed for us." The *ajal* is the appointed term — either the end of earthly life or the Day of Judgment itself (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī). The speakers acknowledge that the term God set has arrived; their time of mutual profit is over. The statement is one of resignation and recognition: what God appointed has come, and there is no appeal. The sūrah opened with the two appointed terms (v. 2); here the second has been reached.

**"The Fire Is Your Abode"**

*Qāla al-nāru mathwākum khālidīna fīhā* — "He will say: The Fire is your dwelling, abiding therein." The word *mathwā* — a place of staying, a lodging — contrasts with the *dār* of the previous verse. The believers have a *dār*, a home; the disbelievers have a *mathwā*, a place where they are held. The Abode of Peace with their Lord, versus the Fire as lodging: the two destinations set side by side.

**"Except as God Wills"**

*Illā mā shā'a Allāh* — "except what God wills." This exception, attached to eternal punishment, has occupied the commentators. Several understandings are offered. Some take it as referring to the interval between death and the Fire — the period in the grave and at the gathering — during which they are not yet in the Fire (al-Ṭabarī reports this). Some take it to refer to the sinful monotheists who will be removed from the Fire by intercession and God's mercy, after being punished for their sins — a doctrine firmly established by ḥadīth (al-Bukhārī 7439; Muslim 183), though these are not disbelievers. Some take it as an assertion of God's sovereignty — an affirmation that the eternity of the Fire is by His will and under His power, not a necessity binding Him (al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī), like the exception in 11:107–108. Ibn Kathīr surveys the views and inclines to the reading that the exception affirms divine sovereignty and that the eternity of the disbelievers' punishment is established by many decisive texts. Whatever the specific referent, the clause reminds the hearer that even at the threshold of Hell, the matter is in God's hands — a fitting note, since the verse ends with His wisdom and knowledge.

**"Truly Thy Lord Is Wise, Knowing"**

*Inna rabbaka ḥakīmun ʿalīm* — "your Lord is Wise, Knowing." The judgment is not arbitrary. It is issued by One who knows every detail of the alliance — who tempted whom, who responded, what each gained — and whose wisdom places each in the place he chose. The pairing of *ḥakīm* and *ʿalīm* answers any objection to the sentence: it is just because it is issued by perfect knowledge and perfect wisdom.

**The Nature of Jinn-Human Alliance**

The verse treats the jinn's misleading of humans as a real phenomenon. Islamic theology affirms the existence of the jinn as a created order with free will, some believing and some not (72:11, 14). The disbelieving jinn — the satans — whisper, tempt, and are called upon by those who seek their aid. Pre-Islamic Arabia's soothsayers, its valley-guardians, its magical practices, all involved traffic with jinn. The verse's warning extends to every age in which people seek benefit from unseen powers other than God — through divination, sorcery, or the invocation of spirits — and to the subtler traffic in which a person lets the whispered suggestion govern him. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever goes to a soothsayer and believes what he says has disbelieved in what was sent down to Muhammad" (Aḥmad 9536; Abū Dāwūd 3904).

**The Lesson**

The verse's most piercing moment is the human confession: *istamtaʿa baʿḍunā bi-baʿḍ*, "we profited from each other." The alliance seemed mutually beneficial in the world; it was mutually destructive in truth. The believer examines his alliances by this standard: what am I gaining from this relationship, and what is it gaining from me, and would either of us wish to say so before God? An alliance whose profits could not be confessed at the gathering is one to leave now, before the term arrives.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:129

> **This is how We make the wrongdoers ˹destructive˺ allies of one another because of their misdeeds.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Principle Behind the Scene**

Verse 128 showed the jinn and their human friends gathered together for judgment, confessing their mutual profit. Verse 129 states the principle: *wa kadhālika nuwallī baʿḍa al-ẓālimīna baʿḍan bi-mā kānū yaksibūn* — "and thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others, because of what they used to earn." The alliance was not accidental. It is a law of God's ordering that wrongdoers are drawn to one another and given over to one another, as a consequence of their own earning.

**The Range of "Nuwallī"**

The verb *nuwallī* (from *wallā*, form II of the root *w-l-y*) has a wide semantic range, and al-Ṭabarī records three meanings that fit the verse, all of which the source commentary preserves.

First: God makes the wrongdoers *supporters* of one another in this life. Like attracts like; the corrupt find the corrupt, form alliances, and reinforce each other — the jinn and their human friends, the Makkan chiefs and their followers, every company of the guilty. The Qur'an says, "they encourage what is evil, forbid what is good, and withhold ˹what is in˺ their hands" (9:67), and of the believers by contrast, "The believers, both men and women, are guardians of one another" (9:71).

Second: God makes them *follow* one another into the Fire — as one group enters, another follows, "Whenever a group enters Hell, it will curse the preceding one until they are all gathered inside, the followers will say about their leaders," (7:38). The alliance of the world becomes the succession of the Hereafter: those who followed each other in sin follow each other into punishment.

Third: God gives some wrongdoers *authority* over others — He sets tyrants over wrongdoing peoples, so that the oppressor and the oppressed are both wrongdoers, and each is the other's punishment. This reading is supported by a saying attributed to several early authorities: "As you are, so will you be governed." Al-Ṭabarī and others report Ibn ʿAbbās' comment that God, when He wills good for a people, gives them righteous rulers, and when He wills otherwise, sets over them the worst among them. Al-Qurṭubī cites the saying of Mālik ibn Dīnār: "I read in some of the books of wisdom: I am God, King of kings; the hearts of kings are in My hand; whoever obeys Me, I make them a mercy to him; whoever disobeys Me, I make them a punishment to him. So do not occupy yourselves with cursing kings, but repent to Me and I will turn them toward you."

All three meanings are within the verb, and the commentators accept that the verse may intend all of them together. Wrongdoers ally in this world, are set over one another as punishment, and follow one another into the Fire.

**"Because of That Which They Used to Earn"**

*Bi-mā kānū yaksibūn* — "for what they used to earn." The alliance and its consequences are a result of deeds. God does not arbitrarily consign the wrongdoers to one another; they earned it. Their choices drew them together, their sins made them fit companions, and the oppression they suffer at one another's hands is the return of what they themselves earned. This is the moral reflexivity of verse 123 applied to the social order: the plotter's plot rebounds on him, and the wrongdoer's wrong returns to him through other wrongdoers.

**The Social Law**

The verse describes a law of human society that observation confirms. Corruption is not solitary; it networks. The corrupt official finds corrupt partners; the criminal finds accomplices; the propagandist finds an audience that wishes to be deceived. And corrupt societies produce corrupt leadership — not as an external punishment imposed from nowhere, but as the natural fruit of the soil. A people whose values are dishonest will elevate dishonest rulers, and then suffer under them. The verse names this as divine ordering (*nuwallī*, "We make allies") — God's law is at work in the social consequence, just as it is at work in the physical.

The corollary is the path of reform. If the wrongdoers' domination of one another is "Will to torment a people, it can never be averted, nor can they find a protector other than Him" then the remedy is to change what is earned. The Qur'an states this as a general law: "state ˹of favour˺ until they change their own state ˹of faith˺" (13:11). Mālik ibn Dīnār's counsel — do not busy yourselves cursing the rulers, but repent — follows directly from this verse.

**The Contrast with the Believers' Alliance**

Verse 127 said of the believers, "He is their Protector (*walī*)." Verse 129 says of the wrongdoers that God "makes them allies" (*nuwallī*) of one another. The same root; opposite conditions. The believers' patron is God; the wrongdoers' patrons are each other. The one alliance ends in the Abode of Peace; the other in mutual recrimination in the Fire — "They will turn on each other, throwing blame." (37:27). To have God as *walī* is to be freed from dependence on the alliances of the corrupt.

**The Hereafter Dimension**

The verse also connects to the scene of verse 128 in a more direct way. The human partisans of the jinn said, "We benefited from each other" (6:128). Verse 129 answers: yes, and this mutual profiting was itself something God permitted as a consequence of your earning, and it will continue — you will be together in the Fire, allies still, but with no profit. The company one kept in sin is the company one keeps in punishment. "Close friends will be enemies to one another on that Day, except the righteous," (43:67).

**Practical Guidance**

The verse instructs the believer in the choice of companions and alliances. Since wrongdoers are given over to one another, to enter the company of wrongdoers is to enter the mechanism the verse describes. The Prophet ﷺ said: "A person is on the religion of his close friend, so let each of you look to whom he takes as a close friend" (Abū Dāwūd 4833; al-Tirmidhī 2378). And: "The example of a righteous companion and a bad companion is like the bearer of musk and the one who blows the bellows" (al-Bukhārī 5534; Muslim 2628). The believer seeks the company of those whose *walī* is God, and avoids the alliances of those who are given over to one another.

It also instructs him in how to read the injustices of his time. When wrongdoers dominate wrongdoers, the believer does not conclude that God is absent; he recognizes verse 129 at work, and turns to the only reform that reaches the root — the reform of what is earned.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:130

> **˹Allah will ask,˺ “O assembly of jinn and humans! Did messengers not come from among you, proclaiming My revelations and warning you of the coming of this Day of yours?” They will say, “We confess against ourselves!” For they have been deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life. And they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question at Judgment**

The scene of verse 128 continues. Having addressed the jinn alone, God now addresses both orders together: *yā maʿshara al-jinni wa al-insi a-lam ya'tikum rusulun minkum yaquṣṣūna ʿalaykum āyātī wa yundhirūnakum liqā'a yawmikum hādhā* — "O assembly of jinn and mankind, did not messengers come to you from among you, relating to you My signs and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?" The question is rhetorical; it establishes that the proof (*ḥujjah*) was delivered. Before the sentence of verse 128 is carried out, the record is read: messengers came, signs were related, the Day was foretold.

**The Two Functions of the Messengers**

The messengers did two things. They "related My signs" (*yaquṣṣūna ʿalaykum āyātī*) — conveyed revelation, explained God's evidences in creation and scripture. And they "warned you of the meeting of this your Day" (*yundhirūnakum liqā'a yawmikum hādhā*) — announced the Judgment that is now taking place. The phrase "this your Day" is pointed: the Day they were warned of is the Day on which they now stand. The warning has become the reality; there is no longer any room for the doubt the sūrah has repeatedly recorded (vv. 29, 31).

**Messengers to the Jinn?**

The question "did not messengers come to you *from among yourselves*" is addressed to both jinn and humans, and it raised for the commentators the question of whether the jinn had messengers of their own kind. The source commentary records the range of opinion.

Some — al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī — accept the literal sense: there were messengers among the jinn, jinn sent to jinn, just as human messengers were sent to humans. Others — Ibn Kathīr prominently — hold that prophethood and messengership were confined to human beings, citing 57:26, which places prophethood among the progeny of Noah and Abraham, and noting that the jinn who heard the Qur'an (46:29–32; 72:1–13) returned to their people as *warners* (*mundhirīn*), not as messengers, and called them to follow a human prophet. On this view, "Did messengers not come from among you" (6:130) is addressed to the two orders jointly, and the messengers were from among one of the two — a usage Arabic permits, as when God says He brings forth pearls and coral "Out of both ˹waters˺ come forth pearls and coral" (55:22) though they come from only one. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Thaʿlabī note that jinn may function as warners among their kind, and al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Zamakhsharī allow that they may serve as "messengers of the human messengers" — bearers of the message to their own people.

What is not disputed is that the jinn are morally accountable, that they received God's message, and that they will be judged. The jinn are created to worship God (51:56), are addressed by revelation (55:33; 72:1–2), undergo judgment (37:158; 41:25; 46:18), and may enter the Fire (7:38, 179; 11:119; 32:13) or Paradise. Sūrah al-Raḥmān addresses jinn and humans together throughout, with the refrain "Which of your Lord's favors will you deny?"

**"We Bear Witness Against Ourselves"**

*Qālū shahidnā ʿalā anfusinā* — "they will say: We testify against ourselves." The confession is complete. Faced with the record, they cannot deny that messengers came. They admit it — against their own interest, with no defense. Compare 7:37: "and they will confess against themselves that they were indeed disbelievers" And 67:8–11: the keepers of Hell ask, "Did a warner not come to you" and they answer, "Yes, a warner came to us, but we denied... Had we listened or reasoned, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze. And they will confess their sin."

The confession serves the justice of the judgment. God does not punish on His testimony alone, though His testimony suffices; He brings the sinners to testify against themselves, so that the sentence is acknowledged by those who receive it. This is the verse that follows (131): God does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are unwarned. The confession proves they were warned.

**"The Life of This World Deluded Them"**

*Wa gharrat-humu al-ḥayātu al-dunyā* — "and the life of this world deceived them." The verse pauses the courtroom scene to state, in the narrator's voice, why they ended here. Not because the messengers failed; not because the signs were unclear; but because the world deceived them. The verb *gharra* is the verb of verse 70 ("whom the life of the world has deluded") and verse 112 (the "delusion" of gilded speech). The world's deception is its promise of permanence, its immediate pleasures that crowd out the distant reckoning, its status and wealth that seem to be real goods. The sūrah has said, "The life of this world is nothing but play and diversion" (v. 32); those who took the play for reality were deceived by it.

**"They Bear Witness Against Themselves That They Were Disbelievers"**

*Wa shahidū ʿalā anfusihim annahum kānū kāfirīn* — the confession is restated with its content made explicit: they testify that they were disbelievers. The repetition is emphatic. On that Day, there will be no one to blame. The deniers will name their own denial, with their own mouths — or, as other verses indicate, with their limbs when their mouths are sealed (36:65; 41:20–21).

**The Theology of the Proof**

The verse establishes a principle central to Islamic theology: no one is punished without having received the message. "And We would never punish ˹a people˺ until We have sent a messenger ˹to warn them˺" (17:15). The rhetorical question — "did not messengers come to you?" — is asked so that the answer, given by the accused themselves, closes the case. Divine justice requires that the proof be established before the sentence, and the verse shows the proof being verified at the end, in the presence of those who received it.

**The Warning for the Living**

The verse's power for the living reader lies in the phrase "this your Day." The Day is future for the reader; it is present for the speakers in the verse. The reader is being shown a scene in which people like himself — who heard messengers, who were warned — confess that they heard and were warned, and that the world deceived them. The verse invites the reader to give his testimony *now*, while it can still be a testimony of faith rather than a testimony against himself. The messengers have come; the signs have been related; the Day has been announced. What remains is not to be deceived by the world before the term of verse 128 arrives.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:131

> **This ˹sending of the messengers˺ is because your Lord would never destroy a society for their wrongdoing while its people are unaware ˹of the truth˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reason for Sending Messengers**

*Dhālika an lam yakun rabbuka muhlika al-qurā bi-ẓulmin wa ahluhā ghāfilūn* — "that is because your Lord would not destroy the towns for wrongdoing while their people were heedless." The demonstrative *dhālika*, "that," refers to the sending of messengers described in the previous verse. Why did messengers come to jinn and humans, relating signs and warning of the Day? Because God does not destroy a people for their wrongdoing while they are *ghāfilūn* — heedless, unaware, uninformed. He warns first. The messengers are the warning.

**Two Readings of "Bi-Ẓulmin"**

The phrase *bi-ẓulmin* can attach to two different parts of the sentence, and the commentators record both readings.

The first and preferred reading (al-Bayḍāwī, al-Jalālayn, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī): God would not destroy the towns *for their wrongdoing* while their people were heedless — that is, He does not punish wrongdoing before the wrongdoers have been made aware, through messengers, that what they do is wrong and what its consequences are. Heedlessness here means ignorance of the message: a people who have not been reached by a prophet's warning are not destroyed for their errors. This is the principle of 17:15: "And We would never punish ˹a people˺ until We have sent a messenger ˹to warn them˺"

The second reading (al-Ṭabarī records it): God would not destroy the towns *unjustly* — that is, it would be an injustice on God's part to destroy people before warning them, and God does not do injustice. On this reading, *bi-ẓulmin* describes what the destruction would be if it were unwarned, and the verse affirms God's justice. The Qur'an repeats that God does not wrong people: "Allah never wronged them, but they wronged themselves" (3:117; 10:44; 29:40; 30:9).

Both readings arrive at the same doctrine. Punishment follows warning; God's justice requires that the proof be established before the sentence.

**"While Their People Were Heedless"**

*Wa ahluhā ghāfilūn* — "while its people are heedless." *Ghaflah* is heedlessness, inattention, the state of not being aware. The verse specifies that destruction does not come upon the heedless — upon those who have not been awakened to what is at stake. Once messengers have come and warned, heedlessness is no longer innocent; it is willful. But before the warning, it is a condition God does not punish with destruction.

The condition tells us something about the nature of accountability in Islam. Accountability is proportional to knowledge. The Qur'an says, "All good will be for its own benefit, and all evil will be to its own loss" (2:286), and the Prophet ﷺ said that the pen is lifted from the child until maturity, the sleeper until he wakes, and the insane until he recovers (Abū Dāwūd 4403) — all cases where awareness is absent. Verse 131 extends the principle to communities: they are not destroyed until awakened.

**The Question of Those Never Reached**

The verse bears on the theological question of those who never received a prophet's message — the *ahl al-fatrah*, the people of the interval between prophets, and those in remote lands. The mainstream Sunni position, grounded in this verse and 17:15, is that such people are not punished for disbelief in a message they never received; various ḥadīth indicate they will be tested on the Day of Judgment (Aḥmad 16301, the ḥadīth of the four who will plead excuse — the deaf man, the imbecile, the senile man, and the one who died in the interval). Al-Ghazālī and others developed this into a careful account of the degrees of "reaching": a distorted or defamed report of the message does not constitute the message reaching a person. The verse's principle stands behind all such discussions: God does not destroy the heedless.

**The Pattern of Destroyed Towns**

The verse's language — "destroy the towns" (*muhlika al-qurā*) — evokes the Qur'anic accounts of communities destroyed for rejecting their prophets: the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, Midian, Pharaoh. In every case, the pattern the verse describes holds: a messenger came, warned clearly and repeatedly, was rejected, and only then did destruction fall. "Your Lord would never destroy a society until He had sent to its capital a messenger, reciting Our revelations to them" (28:59). The destroyed towns were not heedless when destroyed; they were informed and defiant.

**The Verse in Its Context**

Verses 128–130 showed the judgment of jinn and humans, with the accused confessing that messengers came. Verse 131 explains why the confession matters: it proves they were not heedless. God's justice is vindicated in the very moment of sentencing. This is the sūrah's manner throughout: not merely to declare the punishment but to show its justice, so that the hearer understands that what awaits the disbeliever is not arbitrary wrath but the consequence of an informed choice.

**The Mercy in the Principle**

The verse is often read as a statement of justice, but it is equally a statement of mercy. God could, in absolute sovereignty, do as He wills with His creatures; He has bound Himself — "He has prescribed mercy upon Himself" (v. 12, 54) — not to destroy without warning. The sending of every prophet is an act of this mercy: a warning before the fall, an offer before the sentence. The Prophet ﷺ described himself in this role: "My likeness and the likeness of what God sent me with is that of a man who came to a people and said: I have seen the army with my own eyes; I am the naked warner; so save yourselves!" (al-Bukhārī 6482; Muslim 2283). The naked warner — the one who strips off his garment and waves it from a hilltop to signal danger — is the figure verse 131 requires: no destruction without him.

**Implications for the Believer**

Two implications follow. First, since God does not punish the heedless, those who have received the message bear a responsibility the heedless do not. The believer who knows the Qur'an cannot claim *ghaflah*. His accountability is that of the warned. Second, the verse establishes the importance of conveying the message. If God's justice operates through warning, then those who carry the warning — the prophets and, after them, their inheritors — participate in the mechanism of divine justice and mercy. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Convey from me, even a single verse" (al-Bukhārī 3461). Every act of conveying extends the warning that verse 131 makes the precondition of judgment.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:132

> **They will each be assigned ranks according to their deeds. And your Lord is not unaware of what they do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Degrees for All**

*Wa li-kullin darajātun mimmā ʿamilū* — "and for all are degrees from what they did." The "all" (*kullin*) embraces everyone mentioned in the preceding scene: jinn and humans, believers and disbelievers, misleaders and misled. Each has a rank corresponding to his deeds. The word *darajāt* — degrees, steps, ranks — is the plural of *darajah*, a step of a staircase. The image is of a scale of ascent and descent on which every soul is placed exactly where its works have brought it.

The commentators note that *darajāt* is used for both the ranks of Paradise and the depths of Hell, though the Qur'an sometimes uses *darakāt* (descending steps) for the latter — "Surely the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire—and you will never find for them any helper—" (4:145). Here the single word covers both: the believers have degrees of reward, the disbelievers degrees of punishment, and within each group the degrees are as various as the deeds.

**The Principle of Differentiation**

The verse establishes that the Hereafter is not binary. It is not merely Paradise or Fire, but Paradise with its levels and Fire with its depths. The Qur'an states this repeatedly: "They ˹each˺ have varying degrees in the sight of Allah" (3:163); "Allah has elevated in rank those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who stay behind ˹with valid excuses˺" (4:95); "They will have elevated ranks, forgiveness, and an honourable provision from their Lord" (8:4); "But whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done good, they will have the highest ranks" (20:75); "Each ˹of the two groups˺ will be ranked according to what they have done so He may fully reward all" (46:19, the identical phrase); "Allah will elevate those of you who are faithful, and ˹raise˺ those gifted with knowledge in rank" (58:11).

The Prophet ﷺ described the degrees of Paradise: "In Paradise there are a hundred degrees that God has prepared for those who strive in His way; between each two degrees is the distance between heaven and earth" (al-Bukhārī 2790). And concerning the reciter of the Qur'an: "It will be said to him: Recite and ascend, and recite as you used to recite in the world, for your station is at the last verse you recite" (Abū Dāwūd 1464; al-Tirmidhī 2914). The degrees are earned; they correspond to deeds.

**Justice in the Degrees**

The principle answers a question that a simple Paradise/Fire scheme would leave open: are all believers equal, and all disbelievers equal? The verse says no. The believer who strove all his life is not placed with the one who believed at the last hour, though both are saved; the disbeliever who led thousands astray is not placed with the one who merely followed, though both are lost. "It has already been multiplied for all, but you do not know." (7:38) — "Let them bear their burdens in full on the Day of Judgment as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge" (16:25). Verse 128's jinn who "claimed many" will bear more than those they claimed.

This is divine justice at its most precise. Nothing is lost; nothing is rounded. "Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it" (99:7–8). The degrees are the visible structure of this precision.

**"From What They Did"**

*Mimmā ʿamilū* — "from what they did." The *min* may be causal (because of what they did) or partitive (degrees drawn from their deeds, constituted by them). Either way, the rank is a function of the work. This is the same principle that closed verse 127 ("because of what they used to do") and verse 129 ("because of what they used to earn"). The sūrah insists on it: the Hereafter is the harvest of this life, and the harvest is measured.

The source commentary notes that elsewhere the Qur'an speaks of God raising some in degrees without explicit reference to their deeds — Abraham (v. 83), or the trial of verse 165, where degrees are a test. Both are true. In this world, degrees are distributed by divine wisdom as a trial; in the Hereafter, degrees are assigned by divine justice as a recompense. The worldly degree is a question; the otherworldly degree is the answer.

**"And Thy Lord Is Not Heedless of What They Do"**

*Wa mā rabbuka bi-ghāfilin ʿammā yaʿmalūn* — "and your Lord is not heedless of what they do." The verse ends with the word *ghāfil*, echoing the *ghāfilūn* of the previous verse. People may be heedless of their wrongdoing (v. 131); God is never heedless of it. The negation is emphatic — *mā ... bi-ghāfilin*, with the intensifying *bā'*. Not for a moment, not in a single deed, is God unaware.

The formula appears throughout the Qur'an (2:74, 85, 140, 144, 149; 3:99; 11:123; 14:42; 23:17; 27:93). Its function is twofold. To the wrongdoer, it is a warning: whatever you conceal, whatever you think escaped notice, is recorded and will be weighed. "Do not think ˹O Prophet˺ that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do" (14:42). To the believer, it is consolation: your struggle, your patience, your unseen good deeds, are not forgotten. "As for those who believe and do good, We certainly never deny the reward of those who are best in deeds" (18:30).

**The Degrees as Motivation**

The doctrine of degrees is one of the Qur'an's chief motivations for striving. If all believers received the same reward, there would be little reason to exceed the minimum.
