Because there are degrees, every additional good deed raises one's station; every night prayer, every charity, every restrained anger, every word of remembrance is a step. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The people of Paradise will see the people of the upper chambers above them as you see a bright star far off on the horizon, because of the difference in rank between them" (al-Bukhārī 3256; Muslim 2831). The Companions asked whether these were the prophets' stations, and he said, "No — by Him in Whose hand is my soul — they are men who believed in God and affirmed the messengers." The chambers are open to ordinary believers who strove.

**The Believer's Application**

The verse asks the believer to hold two things together. First, humility: whatever his degree, it is 'from what he did,' and what he did was enabled by God; there is no ground for boasting. Second, aspiration: the degrees are real and ascending, and God is not heedless of a single step. He should therefore compete — "So let whoever aspires to this strive ˹diligently˺" (83:26) — not in the world's degrees, which are a trial, but in the degrees the verse names, which are the recompense. And he should never imagine that any effort is wasted or any deed unseen; the last clause forbids the thought.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:133

> **Your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, Full of Mercy. If He wills, He can do away with you and replace you with whoever He wills, just as He produced you from the offspring of other people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Names Together**

*Wa rabbuka al-ghaniyyu dhū al-raḥmah* — "and your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy." The verse opens by pairing two divine attributes whose conjunction is the key to everything that follows. God is *al-Ghanī* — free of all need, independent of everything, rich in the absolute sense. And He is *dhū al-raḥmah* — the Possessor of Mercy. He needs nothing from His creatures, and yet He shows them mercy. The two together define the character of the warnings the sūrah has delivered: they come from One who gains nothing by being obeyed, and who warns purely for the sake of the warned.

**The Name al-Ghanī**

*Ghanī* means free from need, self-sufficient, rich. Applied to God, as the source commentary explains, it does not refer to material wealth but to ontological fullness: God's being is complete in itself and depends on nothing. Every other being is *faqīr*, poor, dependent — "It is you who stand in need of Allah, but Allah ˹alone˺ is the Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy" (35:15). The Name appears frequently (2:263, 267; 4:131; 10:68; 14:8; 22:64; 31:26; 57:24; 64:6), and in 47:38 it is set directly against human poverty: "Here you are, being invited to donate ˹a little˺ in the cause of Allah"

Islamic philosophy gave this Name its most rigorous expression. Ibn Sīnā distinguished the Necessary Being (*wājib al-wujūd*), whose existence is by its own essence and cannot not be, from contingent beings (*mumkin al-wujūd*), whose existence is borrowed and could equally not be (al-Rāzī draws on this). God is the only Necessary Being; all else is contingent and therefore, in the deepest sense, has no existence of its own. This is the philosophical face of what the Qur'an says simply: "To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth" (2:116, 255; 4:171). *Al-Ghanī* is the One whose being is His own; everything else has its being from Him.

**The Consequence: God Needs Nothing from Us**

The theological implication for the sūrah's argument is stated by al-Bayḍāwī: God does not need human beings to accept His message. Their faith does not enrich Him; their disbelief does not diminish Him. "If you disbelieve, then ˹know that˺ Allah is truly not in need of you, nor does He approve of disbelief from His servants" (39:7). "Surely Allah is not in need of ˹any of˺ His creation" (29:6). The Prophet ﷺ transmitted from his Lord: "O My servants, you cannot reach My harm so as to harm Me, and you cannot reach My benefit so as to benefit Me... If the first of you and the last of you, the humans and the jinn among you, were as pious as the most pious heart among you, that would add nothing to My kingdom" (Muslim 2577).

This changes the character of the warnings. Since God needs nothing, the warnings of verses 130–131 are entirely for the benefit of those warned. They are not the demands of a needy sovereign but the counsel of a merciful One. Hence the second attribute.

**The Name Dhū al-Raḥmah**

Al-Rāzī explains that God is "Possessor of Mercy" in the most universal and perfect sense: He gives existence to all creatures without needing any of them — the giving is pure mercy, since nothing compels it. And the conjunction of the two Names indicates that all mercy belongs to Him: no creature is merciful except by a share of His mercy, since every creaturely quality is borrowed from Him. The Prophet ﷺ said that God created mercy in a hundred parts, kept ninety-nine with Himself, and sent one part down to earth, "and from that one part creatures show mercy to one another, so that the mare lifts her hoof from her foal for fear of hurting it" (al-Bukhārī 6000; Muslim 2752).

The pairing thus constitutes a small theology of the sūrah's message. God, who needs nothing, warns out of mercy. To reject the warning harms only oneself.

**"If He Will, He Can Remove You"**

*In yasha' yudhhibkum wa yastakhlif min baʿdikum mā yashā'* — "If He wills, He can do away with you and replace you with whoever He wills" (6:133). The independence of God is now made concrete. He can remove the addressees — from life, from the earth, from existence — and replace them with others. There is no necessity in their continuation. The Qur'an says the same elsewhere: "If it is His Will, He can remove you altogether, O humanity, and replace you with others" (4:133). Hūd warned his people: "But if you turn away, I have already delivered to you what I have been sent with" (11:57). And: "We surely destroyed ˹other˺ peoples before you when they did wrong, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs but they would not believe" (10:13–14).

The verb *istakhlafa*, "cause to succeed," shares its root with *khalīfah*, the vicegerent of verse 165. Human beings are successors — each generation inherits the earth from the previous one, and holds it on trust. The verse reminds the Makkans that their tenure is not permanent and not deserved; God placed them and can replace them.

**"Just as He Brought You into Being from the Progeny of Another People"**

*Ka-mā ansha'akum min dhurriyyati qawmin ākharīn* — "as He produced you from the descendants of another people." The proof of God's ability to replace them is their own existence: they themselves are the replacements of earlier peoples. The Makkans descended from generations before them, many of whom were destroyed for their wrongdoing — ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others whose ruins the Makkans knew. God brought the Makkans forth from the progeny of others; He can bring others forth from theirs. The argument is from the observed to the possible: what God has already done once, He can do again.

The verb *ansha'a* — to produce, raise up, originate — is the verb of verse 98 ("He produced you from a single soul") and verse 141 ("He produced gardens"). Each generation is a fresh production, held in being by the Producer. None is self-sustaining; none is necessary.

**The Link to What Precedes**

Verses 130–131 established that God sends messengers before destroying any people. Verse 133 explains the spirit of this: not that God needs the warnings heeded, but that He is merciful and does not wish destruction. The mention of replacement then makes the stakes concrete. The Makkans are not indispensable. If they reject the warning, the mercy that sent it does not preclude the justice that removes them and gives their place to others — as happened with the peoples before them, and as happened, in the event, with the Makkan chiefs themselves, who were replaced by the very believers they persecuted.

**The Practical Wisdom**

The verse trains the believer in two attitudes. Toward God: he serves One who needs nothing, and so his service is a gift to himself, not a favor to God; this dissolves pride in worship. Toward himself and his community: he holds his position on the earth as a successor whose tenure is not guaranteed — a trust that may be withdrawn — and this dissolves complacency. And the pairing of the two Names gives him the right picture of every command and prohibition he has received: it comes from One who could remove him without loss to Himself, and instead warns him out of mercy.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:134

> **Indeed, what you have been promised will certainly come to pass. And you will have no escape.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Certainty of the Promise**

*Inna mā tūʿadūna la-āt* — "indeed, what you are promised is surely coming." The verse is short and its force is entirely in its certainty. Three emphases stack: *inna*, "indeed"; the *lām* of affirmation on *la-āt*; and the active participle *āt*, "coming," which in Arabic conveys imminence — not "will come" someday but "is on its way," already in motion. What is promised is the Day of Judgment, the resurrection, the reckoning, the degrees of verse 132, and the possible removal of verse 133 — everything the sūrah has warned of.

The verb is *tūʿadūna*, "you are promised" or "you are threatened" — the root *w-ʿ-d* covers both the promise of good and the promise of harm. To the believers, what is coming is the Abode of Peace; to the disbelievers, what is coming is the Fire. The single word holds both, and the verse's certainty applies to both.

**"And You Cannot Thwart It"**

*Wa mā antum bi-muʿjizīn* — "and you are not able to frustrate [it]." The verb *aʿjaza* means to render incapable, to escape, to outrun, to frustrate. The active participle *muʿjizīn* describes those who would slip away from God's grasp or defeat His purpose. The negation is emphatic (*mā ... bi-*). No one can escape what is coming, delay it, outrun it, or defeat it. The Qur'an says the same in many places: "Nor have you any protector or helper besides Allah" (29:22); "But those who strive to discredit Our revelations, they will be the residents of the Hellfire" (22:51); "Imagine if His torment were to overcome you by night or day—do the wicked realize what they are ˹really˺ asking Him to hasten" (10:50).

**The Promise That Is True**

The source commentary gathers the Qur'an's insistence that God's promise is true: "So be patient, for the promise of Allah certainly is true" (4:122; 10:4, 55; 18:21; 30:60; 31:33; 35:5; 40:55, 77; 45:32; 46:17). This is not a rhetorical flourish but a doctrinal cornerstone. God's promise is true because God does not lie — "He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together on the Day of Judgment—about which there is no doubt" (4:87) — and because His power guarantees fulfillment. A human promise may fail through dishonesty or inability; God's promise can fail through neither. The disbelievers' whole strategy, as the sūrah has exposed it, is to treat the promise as a fable (v. 25), to demand it hastened (v. 57–58), to imagine it will not come (vv. 29–30). Verse 134 answers all of this in a single sentence.

**The Logic of the Verse**

The verse follows verse 133 closely. God is self-sufficient and merciful; He can remove you and replace you. Someone might think: perhaps He will not; perhaps we will continue as we are. The verse forecloses this: what you are promised is coming, and you cannot prevent it. Whether the promised thing is destruction in this world or judgment in the next, it will arrive on schedule, and no human effort — no plotting (v. 123), no alliance (v. 129), no demand for signs (v. 124) — can prevent it.

The logic also connects to God's self-sufficiency. Because God needs nothing, He is not bargaining. There is no negotiation in which the disbelievers might offer something to avert the promise. A needy sovereign might be bought off; the Self-Sufficient cannot be. The promise therefore stands absolutely.

**The Delay Is Not Cancellation**

The verse addresses the most common misreading of God's patience. The Makkans had been warned for years; nothing had happened; they concluded nothing would. The Qur'an repeatedly corrects this: "And Allah will never fail in His promise" (22:47). "Do not think ˹O Prophet˺ that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do" (14:42). The Prophet ﷺ said: "God gives respite to the wrongdoer until, when He seizes him, He does not let him go" — and he recited, "Such is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong" (al-Bukhārī 4686; Muslim 2583, citing 11:102). Delay is a mercy, not a reprieve.

**The Verse as Consolation**

For the believers under persecution in Makkah, the verse is also consolation. What *they* were promised — the Abode of Peace (v. 127), their Lord as Protector, the vindication of truth — is coming too, and no one can thwart it. The Makkan chiefs' power seemed permanent and the believers' situation hopeless; the verse says that the promise is on its way and the powerful cannot stop it. Within a decade, the promise arrived in the world: the persecutors were defeated and the persecuted entered Makkah in triumph. The full promise awaits the Hereafter.

**The Word "Āt"**

A note on the participle. Arabic uses the active participle for what is present or imminent. The Qur'an uses *āt* for the Hour ("Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him in worship˺" 40:59; 22:7) and for God's command ("God's command is coming, so do not seek to hasten it," 16:1). The choice conveys that the promised thing is not a distant possibility but a present certainty that has not yet arrived — like a traveler already on the road. The believer lives in expectation of what is already approaching; the disbeliever lives in denial of it. Neither changes its arrival.

**The Practical Stance**

The verse produces a particular stance in the one who accepts it: sober readiness. Since what is promised is coming and cannot be prevented, the only rational response is to prepare for it — to be among those for whom the promise is the Abode of Peace rather than the Fire. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The intelligent one is he who takes account of himself and works for what comes after death; the incapable (*ʿājiz*) is he who follows his desires and hopes in God" (al-Tirmidhī 2459). The word *ʿājiz* is from the same root as *muʿjizīn*: the one who imagines he can frustrate God's promise is himself the incapable one. The intelligent recognize the promise as certain and act.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:135

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O my people! Persist in your ways, for I ˹too˺ will persist in mine. You will soon know who will fare best in the end. Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Say" — The Prophet's Declaration**

*Qul yā qawmi iʿmalū ʿalā makānatikum innī ʿāmil* — "Say: O my people, work according to your position; indeed I am working." The Prophet ﷺ is instructed to address the Makkans as "my people" — a form of address that retains kinship and concern even in confrontation, the address the prophets before him used to their peoples (Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Shuʿayb all say *yā qawmi*). He is not disowning them; he is telling them where matters stand.

**"Work According to Your Ability"**

*Iʿmalū ʿalā makānatikum* — literally, "work upon your station/position," understood as "according to your ability, your capacity, your way." The imperative here is not a permission but, as al-Ṭabarī says, a warning and a threat (*tahdīd*). It means: continue as you are, do your utmost, exhaust your capacity in opposing this message — and see where it leads. The form is used elsewhere when the outcome is already certain and the addressee is being left to demonstrate the futility of his course: "He is certainly AllSeeing of what you do" (41:40); "Persist in your ways, for I ˹too˺ will persist in mine" (39:39).

The construction concedes nothing to the opponents' cause; it concedes only that they are free to pursue it. It is the confidence of one who knows the end. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the contrast between "your position" — their station of power, wealth, and hostility — and the Prophet's "I am working" on his own station of obedience and message-bearing. Each works from where he stands; the results will show which station was real.

**"I, Too, Am Working"**

*Innī ʿāmil* — "Why has no ˹other˺ sign been sent down to him from his Lord" a doer. The Prophet ﷺ does not merely wait for the opponents' downfall; he works. The mission continues — calling, warning, reciting, enduring. The Qur'an elsewhere pairs this with waiting: "I too am waiting with you" (9:52; 10:20, 102). Working and waiting together: the Prophet ﷺ does what is his to do and leaves the outcome to God.

The clause is also a model of the believer's posture in a hostile environment. He does not despair, retreat, or match hostility with hostility; he works. The quiet certainty of *innī ʿāmil* — "I am working" — is a stronger response to opposition than any argument.

**"Soon You Shall Know Whose End Is the Abode"**

*Fa-sawfa taʿlamūna man takūnu lahu ʿāqibatu al-dār* — "so you will come to know for whom is the final outcome of the Abode." The *ʿāqibah* is the end, the final result, the ultimate outcome. 'The Abode' (*al-dār*) is the permanent Abode of the Hereafter — the *dār al-salām* of verse 127 — though the phrase also carries the sense of 'the final outcome in this abode,' the world, since the Qur'an speaks of the good end in both. Compare "The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous." (7:128; 11:49; 28:83) and "It is they who will have the ultimate abode" (13:22) — "How excellent is the ultimate abode!" (13:24).

The phrase "you will know" (*sawfa taʿlamūn*) is a refrain of the Qur'an addressed to deniers (6:67; 11:39; 26:49; 39:39; 40:70; 102:3–4). It appeals to the future as the arbiter. The dispute between the Prophet ﷺ and his people will not be settled by argument alone; it will be settled by outcome. And the outcome, the verse implies, is not in doubt — it is only not yet visible to them.

**"Surely the Wrongdoers Will Not Prosper"**

*Innahu lā yufliḥu al-ẓālimūn* — "indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper." The verse ends by naming the outcome. *Falāḥ* is success, prosperity, attainment of what is sought — the word of the call to prayer, "come to *falāḥ*." The wrongdoers will not attain it. The formula closes verse 21 of the sūrah ("the wrongdoers will not prosper") and appears at 12:23, 28:37, and elsewhere. Its repetition here, at the end of the section on the alliance of wrongdoers and the destination of the Abode, brings the argument to its point: the outcome of the Abode belongs to those who did not wrong, and the wrongdoers — whatever their present position — will not reach it.

The word *ẓālimūn* also identifies the opponents precisely. Their opposition to the Prophet ﷺ is not merely intellectual disagreement; it is *ẓulm*, wrongdoing — the placing of things where they do not belong, the worship of what is not God, the rejection of what is true. The sūrah has called *shirk* "Never associate ˹anything˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺, for associating ˹others with Him˺ is truly the worst of all wrongs" (31:13) and "the wrongdoers" its practitioners throughout.

**The Structure of the Challenge**

The verse belongs to a category the Qur'an uses frequently: the challenge that leaves the matter to time. The Prophet ﷺ does not threaten the Makkans with his own power — he has none. He tells them to continue and see. This is a form of argument available only to one who is certain, and it functions as a sign in itself. When the Makkans heard an unarmed, persecuted man tell them, calmly, "Work as you can; I am working; you will know," they were hearing a confidence that had no worldly basis. Its only basis was the truth of what he carried. History confirmed him: within years, the Makkans knew.

**The Ethical Dimension**

There is also an ethical teaching in the verse's restraint. The Prophet ﷺ is not told to curse his people, to wish them harm, or to gloat over their coming defeat. He is told to say: work, I am working, you will know. The address "my people" persists. The verse teaches the believer how to stand firm without becoming bitter — to hold the truth with certainty while leaving the outcome, and the judgment of persons, to God. The Prophet ﷺ demonstrated this at the conquest of Makkah, when those who had "worked according to their ability" against him for twenty years stood before him defeated, and he said: "Go, for you are free."

**A Reflection for the Present**

The verse remains a resource for anyone who holds the truth in a setting that rejects it. The temptation is either to abandon the work under pressure or to spend one's energy fighting the opponents on their terms. The verse's alternative: do your work; let them do theirs; the end will show. This is not passivity — *innī ʿāmil* is emphatic activity — but a freedom from the need to win every immediate contest. The final outcome of the Abode is not decided by who prevails in the argument today; it is decided by who was right and who did right, and "the wrongdoers will not prosper."

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:136

> **The pagans set aside for Allah a share of the crops and cattle He created, saying, “This ˹portion˺ is for Allah,” so they claim, “and this ˹one˺ for our associate-gods.” Yet the portion of their associate-gods is not shared with Allah while Allah’s portion is shared with their associate-gods. What unfair judgment!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Section on Invented Religion**

With this verse the sūrah opens the section from which it takes its name — the exposure of the idolaters' practices concerning cattle (*anʿām*) and crops (vv. 136–150). Having established God's exclusive right to legislate (vv. 114–121), the sūrah now shows in detail what the idolaters did with the right they usurped: they invented a religion of shares, taboos, and infanticide, and ascribed it to God. The section is the concrete evidence for the sūrah's charge that idolatry is not merely false belief but false law.

**The Practice of Dividing Shares**

*Wa jaʿalū li-Llāhi mimmā dhara'a min al-ḥarthi wa al-anʿāmi naṣīban* — "and they assigned to God, of what He created of tillage and cattle, a portion." Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr describe the practice: the Makkans divided their harvests and herds into shares, one for God and one for their idols (their "partners," *shurakā'*). The share for God was distributed to guests and the poor; the share for the idols was spent on their custodians, sacrifices, and shrines. Compare 16:56: "And they assign to what they do not know a portion of what We have provided them."

The verse's phrasing already indicts the practice. The crops and cattle are what *He created* (*dhara'a*, to sow, scatter, bring forth in multitude). They are assigning to God a share of what is entirely His, as though He were one claimant among several. And they are assigning to "partners" a share of what those partners did not create and cannot use.

**"Or So They Claim"**

*Bi-zaʿmihim* — "by their claim," "according to their assertion." The verb *zaʿama* denotes a claim without foundation, an assertion that may be false. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the phrase marks the practice as invented: there was no divine command for this division; it was their own device, which they nonetheless treated as religious duty. The word recurs in verse 138 with the same function. The Qur'an uses it to strip a practice of its claimed authority: "this is God's," they say — but it is only their *zaʿm*.

**The Asymmetry of the Shares**

The verse's central observation is an asymmetry that betrays the idolaters' real allegiance. *Fa-mā kāna li-shurakā'ihim fa-lā yaṣilu ilā Allāh, wa mā kāna li-Llāhi fa-huwa yaṣilu ilā shurakā'ihim* — "what is for their partners does not reach God, but what is for God reaches their partners."

The commentators (al-Jalālayn, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAbbās via Mujāhid and others) explain the mechanics. When the shares were divided, if anything from the idols' share happened to fall into God's share — some grain blown across, some animal straying — they would take it back and restore it to the idols' share. But if anything from God's share fell into the idols' share, they left it there. Similarly, if God's share of a crop failed while the idols' share flourished, they took from God's share to make up the idols'; if the idols' share failed, they did not touch God's to make it up. If they were in need, they ate from God's share and not from the idols'. Their justification was that "God is rich and does not need it, while our gods are poor" (al-Jalālayn) — a reasoning that, as al-Ṭabarī notes, betrayed a greater loyalty to the idols than to God.

The asymmetry reveals the heart. In the abstract, the idolaters acknowledged God as the greatest deity — the sūrah has recorded that they admitted He created the heavens and earth (cf. 29:61; 31:25). In practice, when interests collided, the idols won. Their actual devotion — measured not by what they said but by what they did when something had to give — was to the partners. The verse exposes the truth of every divided loyalty: what one truly worships is what one protects when the shares are in conflict.

**"Evil Indeed Is the Judgment They Make"**

*Sā'a mā yaḥkumūn* — "evil is what they judge." The verb *ḥakama*, to judge, to decide, is the verb of verse 57 ("judgment belongs to God alone") and verse 114 ("shall I seek other than God as judge?"). The idolaters have usurped the role of judge — deciding how creation should be divided between God and gods — and their judgment is evil. It is evil in its premise (that God has partners), in its practice (the invented shares), and in its bias (favoring the partners against God). The verdict *sā'a mā yaḥkumūn* recurs in the Qur'an for the idolaters' assigning daughters to God while wanting sons for themselves (16:59) and for their assumption that the righteous and the wicked will be treated alike (45:21). Each is a case of human judgment overriding divine truth.

**The Deeper Diagnosis**

The verse's diagnosis extends beyond ancient Arabia. Wherever human beings acknowledge God in principle but arrange their actual lives around other loyalties — wealth, status, nation, ideology, self — the asymmetry of verse 136 reappears. What belongs to the other loyalties is guarded; what belongs to God is negotiable. Time for God is the first cut when schedules collide; money for God is the first economy; obedience to God is the first compromise. The verse names this pattern as *shirk* in practice, whatever the professed belief.

It also exposes a specific rationalization: "God does not need it." True in itself — God is *al-Ghanī*, the verse before last said so — but false as a reason for shortchanging Him. God does not need our worship; we need to worship Him. The idolaters used a true premise about God to justify a false practice toward Him, and the Qur'an, having just affirmed the premise (v. 133), condemns the practice.

**The Function of Exposure**

The Qur'an's method in this section is exposure through detail. It does not merely say "their religion is false"; it describes the religion — its shares, its rules, its exceptions — so that its arbitrariness is visible. A practice described precisely often refutes itself. Who could believe that the Creator of the crops wanted His share to be the one that could be raided when the idols' share ran short? The description makes the answer obvious. This is the sūrah's confidence: truth needs only to be set beside falsehood in clear light for the difference to appear.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:137

> **Likewise, the pagans’ evil associates have made it appealing to them to kill their own children—only leading to their destruction as well as confusion in their faith. Had it been Allah’s Will, they would not have done such a thing. So leave them and their falsehood.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Crops to Children**

The previous verse exposed the idolaters' division of crops and cattle. This verse turns to something far graver: *wa kadhālika zayyana li-kathīrin min al-mushrikīna qatla awlādihim shurakā'uhum* — "and likewise their partners made fair-seeming to many of the idolaters the killing of their children." The *kadhālika*, "likewise," connects the two: the same "partners" that received the shares of the harvest also beautified infanticide. The corruption of religion in small things (shares of grain) and in the gravest thing (the murder of one's own children) comes from a single source.

**Who Are the "Partners" Here?**

The word *shurakā'* in this verse has been understood in two ways, as the source commentary records. First, the idols and false deities: the idolaters believed their gods commanded or approved the killing of children (al-Jalālayn), and so the idols, as objects of their belief, "made it fair." Second, the satans who whisper: the real agents behind the idols are the satans of verses 112 and 121, who inspire the idolaters through whispering to kill their children (al-Ṭabarī and others). Both are true on different levels. The idol is the face; the satan is the force. Al-Zamakhsharī also notes that "partners" may refer to the human custodians and priests of the idols who instituted and encouraged these practices — the "human satans" of verse 112 — since they are called partners as the idolaters made them partners in legislation.

**The Practice of Infanticide**

The pre-Islamic Arabs killed their children in two main circumstances. The most notorious was female infanticide: burying infant daughters alive, out of shame at having daughters or fear that they would be captured in raids and bring dishonor (16:57–59; 81:8–9). The second was killing children of either sex from fear of poverty, especially in famine (6:151; 17:31). A third form, which some commentators mention here, was the vow to sacrifice a child to the idols — as ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the Prophet's grandfather, had vowed to sacrifice a son and was redeemed by a hundred camels.

The Qur'an's response to female infanticide is among its most searing passages: "He hides himself from the people because of the bad news he has received" (16:58–59). And on the Day of Judgment: "and when baby girls, buried alive, are asked" (81:8–9). The Prophet ﷺ made abolition of the practice a condition of the women's pledge (60:12), and said: "Whoever has a daughter and does not bury her alive, nor insult her, nor prefer his son over her, God will admit him to Paradise" (Abū Dāwūd 5146).

**"Made It Seem Fair"**

*Zayyana* — the verb of beautification, of verses 43, 108, and 122. The verse's psychological insight is that the killing of one's own children — an act against the deepest instinct — could be made to seem *good*. The father who buried his daughter believed he was protecting his honor; the parent who killed in famine believed he was being prudent; the one who sacrificed to the idol believed he was being pious. Each had been persuaded that an atrocity was a virtue. This is the ultimate power of *tazyīn*: not merely to make a sin attractive, but to make it appear as duty. The Prophet ﷺ described the reversal of values that follows from it: "There will come upon people years of deceit, in which the liar is believed and the truthful is disbelieved, the treacherous is trusted and the trustworthy is thought treacherous" (Ibn Mājah 4036).

**"That They May Ruin Them and Confound Them in Their Religion"**

*Li-yurdūhum wa li-yalbisū ʿalayhim dīnahum* — "in order to destroy them and to confuse for them their religion." Two purposes, and the *lām* may be of purpose or consequence. *Ardā* is to bring to ruin, perdition. *Labasa* is to confuse, to make obscure by mixing — the verb of verse 9 ("We would have confused for them what they confuse") and 82 ("do not mix their faith with wrongdoing"). The satans' aim in beautifying infanticide was twofold: to destroy the idolaters — in this world through the loss of their children, in the next through punishment — and to confound their religion.

Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Ṭabarī explain "their religion" as the original religion of the Arabs — the monotheism of Abraham and Ishmael, which the Arabs had inherited and progressively corrupted. Infanticide was a corruption of that religion: a practice foreign to Abraham's way, mixed into it until the Arabs could no longer distinguish the inherited truth from the imported falsehood. The verse thus presents pre-Islamic idolatry not as an original religion but as a confusion — Abrahamic monotheism overlaid with satanic additions until the whole was obscured.

**"Had God Willed, They Would Not Have Done So"**

*Wa law shā'a Allāhu mā faʿalūh* — the formula of verse 112 (and vv. 35, 107). God permitted this in His wisdom, as He permits all human evil, without approving it. The phrase is not an excuse for the idolaters but a reminder to the Prophet ﷺ that the corruption he sees is within God's knowledge and plan, not beyond His control. It also refutes the idolaters' own use of divine will as justification — "had God willed, we would not have associated" (v. 148) — by placing the will where it belongs: as a permission of free choice, not a command of the thing chosen.

**"So Leave Them and That Which They Fabricate"**

*Fa-dharhum wa mā yaftarūn* — "so leave them and what they invent." The Prophet ﷺ is told to leave them — not to abandon the call, but to cease grieving over their obstinacy and to leave their judgment to God, as in verses 70, 91, and 112. The word *yaftarūn*, "they fabricate," names infanticide and the whole system that beautified it as *iftirā'* — a lie invented against God. This is the charge of verse 21 ("who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against God?"), now brought to its most terrible instance: the invention of a religion that murders children in God's name.

**The Verse's Reach**

The verse's principle outlives its occasion. Whenever a society persuades itself that killing its children is honorable, prudent, or pious — whatever form the killing takes and whatever the argument for it — verse 137 identifies the source of the persuasion and its purpose: to ruin and to confound. The Qur'an's alternative is stated later in the sūrah: "Do not kill your children out of poverty; We provide for you and for them" (v. 151). Trust in the Provider is the antidote to the fear that satans exploit. And the verse's naming of infanticide as a *religious* corruption — a confusion of *dīn* — warns that atrocities are most dangerous when they wear the garment of duty.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:138

> **They say, “These cattle and crops are reserved—none may eat them except those we permit,” so they claim. Some other cattle are exempted from labour and others are not slaughtered in Allah’s Name—falsely attributing lies to Him. He will repay them for their lies.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Invented Taboos**

The verse catalogues three categories of the idolaters' invented prohibitions concerning cattle (*anʿām*) and crops (*ḥarth*). Each is presented as a claim (*zaʿm*) and a fabrication (*iftirā'*), and the verse ends with the promise of recompense. The exposition continues the method of verse 136: describe the practice precisely, and let its arbitrariness condemn it.

**"These Cattle and Crops Are Sacrosanct"**

*Wa qālū hādhihi anʿāmun wa ḥarthun ḥijrun lā yaṭʿamuhā illā man nashā'u bi-zaʿmihim* — "and they say: these are cattle and tillage that are *ḥijr*; none may eat them except whom we will — by their claim." The word *ḥijr* means forbidden, restricted, walled off — from the root of *ḥajara*, to prevent, to enclose (whence *ḥujrah*, a room, and *al-Ḥijr*, the enclosure beside the Kaʿbah). The idolaters designated certain animals and crops as *ḥijr*: set apart, untouchable, except by those they permitted.

Who was permitted? Al-Ṭabarī offers two understandings. The animals may have been dedicated to the idols and reserved for their service — prohibited to ordinary people, permitted to those the idolaters chose. Or the restriction was by sex: permitted to men, forbidden to women (verse 139 confirms this pattern). Al-Qurṭubī records that "whom we will" referred to the custodians of the idols — the priests and attendants of the shrines, who alone could eat what was dedicated. In each case, the criterion for who could eat was human will (*man nashā'u*), not divine command. The verse's "by their claim" (*bi-zaʿmihim*) marks it as invention.

**"Cattle Whose Backs Are Forbidden"**

*Wa anʿāmun ḥurrimat ẓuhūruhā* — "and cattle whose backs are forbidden." These were animals that could not be ridden or made to carry loads — set free, exempt from labor, as an act of devotion. The commentators (al-Jalālayn, al-Ṭabarī) connect these to the four institutions named in 5:103: the *baḥīrah* (a she-camel whose ear was slit after bearing a certain number of young, and which was then left unridden and unmilked except by guests), the *sā'ibah* (an animal set free by vow, never to be used), the *waṣīlah* (a ewe that bore twins of both sexes, whose male was spared from sacrifice), and the *ḥām* (a stallion camel that had sired a certain number, whose back was declared forbidden). The Prophet ﷺ identified ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy, a chief of Khuzāʿah, as the one who first instituted these practices, and said he saw him "dragging his intestines in the Fire" (al-Bukhārī 3521; Muslim 2856) — the man who introduced idolatry and its taboos to Arabia.

**"Cattle Over Which They Do Not Invoke the Name of God"**

*Wa anʿāmun lā yadhkurūna isma Allāhi ʿalayhā* — "and cattle over which they do not mention the Name of God." Al-Qurṭubī explains this as animals slaughtered in the names of the idols, in place of God's Name; others take it more simply as animals slaughtered without invocation, or animals over which God's Name was deliberately not spoken — during the pilgrimage rites, for example, or when riding — as an act of devotion to the idols. The verse links back to the food passage (vv. 118–121): the idolaters, who argued for eating carrion, also withheld God's Name from their own slaughter. Their dietary practice was inverted at both ends — eating what God forbade and withholding His Name from what He permitted.

**"Fabricating Against Him"**

*Iftirā'an ʿalayh* — "as a fabrication against Him." The accusative is a *mafʿūl lahu* or *ḥāl*: they did all this by way of fabrication, ascribing it to God. This is the decisive charge. The idolaters did not present these taboos as their own customs; they presented them as religion — as God's will. The *ḥijr* animals were sacred *to God*; the freed camels were freed *for God*; the withholding of His Name was *piety*. The Qur'an's response is the word *iftirā'*: invention, falsehood forged in God's Name. Al-Ṭabarī notes that some held these practices to have been inspired by the satans the idolaters took as partners — the verse before said as much — but the idolaters bore responsibility for accepting the inspiration and attributing it to God.

**"Soon Will He Recompense Them"**

*Sa-yajzīhim bi-mā kānū yaftarūn* — "He will recompense them for what they used to fabricate." The verse closes with the promise that recurs in the section (vv. 139, 120). The recompense is for the fabrication — not merely for the practices, but for the lie about God that gave them authority. This locates the sin precisely. It is not that the idolaters ate or abstained wrongly; it is that they legislated in God's Name without His permission, which is the crime the sūrah has been building toward since verse 57 ("judgment belongs to God alone").

**The Anatomy of Invented Religion**

The verse gives a portrait of how false religion works. It takes what God created and permitted (cattle, crops) and overlays it with human restrictions. It presents these restrictions as sacred. It reserves exceptions for a privileged class (the custodians, the men). It accumulates detail — this animal free, that one forbidden, this one for men only — until the system acquires the solidity of tradition. And it defends the system as ancestral religion (vv. 148, 2:170). The Qur'an's response cuts through the accumulated detail to the single question: did God command this? If not, it is *iftirā'*.

The Qur'an's own dietary law is the inverse of this. It is few in its prohibitions (v. 145 will list them: carrion, blood, swine, what was dedicated to other than God), universal in its application (no privileged class, no distinction of sex), and grounded in explicit revelation. The contrast between the two systems is the contrast between religion received and religion invented.

**The Continuing Application**

The verse's warning is not confined to cattle. Whenever human beings forbid what God permitted and present the prohibition as piety — whenever religious authority accumulates restrictions without revealed basis and defends them as tradition — the pattern of verse 138 recurs. The Prophet ﷺ warned against it: "The most sinful of Muslims is one who asks about something that was not forbidden, and it is forbidden because of his asking" (al-Bukhārī 7289; Muslim 2358) — a warning against the appetite for prohibition itself. Islam's principle is that in matters of ordinary life, the default is permission, and prohibition requires proof. Verse 138 is one of the foundations of that principle.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:139

> **They ˹also˺ say, “The offspring of this cattle is reserved for our males and forbidden to our females; but if it is stillborn, they may all share it.” He will repay them for their falsehood. Surely He is All-Wise, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sex-Based Taboo**

The verse describes the most revealing of the idolaters' invented rules: a distinction by sex in what could be eaten. *Wa qālū mā fī buṭūni hādhihi al-anʿāmi khāliṣatun li-dhukūrinā wa muḥarramun ʿalā azwājinā* — "and they say: what is in the bellies of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives." The "cattle" are the sacred animals of verse 138 — the *baḥīrah* and *sā'ibah* especially. "What is in their bellies" is, on the primary reading (al-Bayḍāwī, al-Jalālayn), their offspring: when one of these sacred animals gave birth, the live young could be eaten only by men. Some understood the phrase as the animals' milk, which also came "from their bellies" — the Qur'an uses the same expression for milk in 16:66 and 23:21 (al-Qurṭubī records this). Al-Ṭabarī allows that both offspring and milk may be intended, with the exception about stillbirth applying to the offspring alone.

**"Exclusively for Our Males"**

*Khāliṣatun li-dhukūrinā* — "pure for our males," "reserved exclusively." *Khāliṣ* is unmixed, pure, exclusive. Men had exclusive right. "Forbidden to our wives" — *azwāj*, which most commentators understood as women generally, though some reports specify daughters (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī). The rule was gendered: sacred food for men, prohibition for women.

**"But If It Be Stillborn, Then All Shall Have a Share"**

*Wa in yakun maytatan fa-hum fīhi shurakā'* — "and if it is dead, then they are all partners in it." If the young was born dead — a carcass — then women could eat it too. The rule collapses into absurdity at this point, and the Qur'an records it precisely so that the absurdity is visible. What was sacred and reserved for men when alive became common property when dead. The women were permitted the carrion and denied the fresh meat. The rule had nothing to do with holiness and everything to do with privilege: men took the good, women received the remainder.

This detail also exposes the incoherence of the idolaters' position on carrion. They argued (v. 118–121) that carrion should be eaten because "God killed it." Here they permitted carrion to women while reserving the properly slaughtered young for men. Their principles bent to whatever served the powerful.

**The Verse as Social Critique**

Beneath the dietary detail is a critique of the pre-Islamic treatment of women. The same society that buried its daughters (v. 137) and would not let women eat the sacred meat is exposed as one that used religion to entrench male privilege. The Qur'an's response across its revelation was to dismantle this: to declare that "The believers, both men and women, are guardians of one another" (9:71), that "Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds" (16:97), that women inherit (4:7), that the buried daughter will be asked for what sin she was killed (81:8–9). Verse 139 is one of the early exposures of the system the Qur'an would replace.

The Qur'an's own dietary law contains no distinction by sex. What is lawful is lawful for all; what is forbidden is forbidden to all. The contrast with verse 139 is deliberate and instructive: revealed law does not make food a marker of social hierarchy.

**"Soon Will He Recompense Them for That Which They Ascribe"**

*Sa-yajzīhim waṣfahum* — literally, "He will recompense them their description." The word *waṣf* means describing, characterizing, attributing. Al-Ṭabarī explains: their *description* of these things as lawful or forbidden — their attribution of these rules to God, their false characterization of His law. The recompense is for the *ascription*: for saying "this is God's law" when it was their own invention. The phrase parallels "what they used to fabricate" in verse 138 and names the same crime from another side. In verse 138 they *invented*; in verse 139 they *described* — and the description was a lie about God. Compare 16:116: "This is lawful, and that is unlawful,"

**"Truly He Is Wise, Knowing"**

*Innahu ḥakīmun ʿalīm* — the verse closes with the two Names that governed the judgment scene at verse 128. God is Wise: His recompense is measured, fitting, and just. God is Knowing: He knows exactly what they ascribed, why, and with what motive — the privilege behind the piety. The Names also contrast with the idolaters' lawmaking: their rules were neither wise (they collapsed into absurdity) nor knowing (they were "without knowledge," v. 140). God's law proceeds from wisdom and knowledge; theirs from caprice and interest.

**The Broader Lesson About Religious Rules**

The verse teaches how to test a claimed religious rule. Does it serve the interests of those who promulgate it? Does it collapse into incoherence under examination? Does it distribute burdens and privileges by category rather than by God's revealed word? The idolaters' rule fails every test: it served men, it collapsed at the stillbirth exception, and it was gendered without any revealed basis. The believer learns from this to distinguish what God has revealed from what human beings have added in His Name, and to be especially suspicious of rules that happen to benefit their authors.

**The Divine Method of Refutation**

Note again the Qur'an's method. It does not argue at length against the rule; it states the rule fully, including its exception, and pronounces recompense. The rule refutes itself once stated. This is the confidence of truth before falsehood: falsehood, described accurately, is its own refutation. The Qur'an's willingness to describe the idolaters' practices in their own terms — rather than caricaturing them — is itself a form of fairness, and it makes the judgment "He is Wise, Knowing" credible. The One who describes accurately before He judges is the One whose judgment can be trusted.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:140

> **Lost indeed are those who have murdered their own children foolishly out of ignorance and have forbidden what Allah has provided for them— falsely attributing lies to Allah. They have certainly strayed and are not ˹rightly˺ guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict on the Section**

Verses 136–139 described the idolaters' practices; verse 140 pronounces the verdict. *Qad khasira alladhīna qatalū awlādahum safahan bi-ghayri ʿilmin wa ḥarramū mā razaqahumu Allāhu iftirā'an ʿalā Allāh* — "lost indeed are those who killed their children foolishly, without knowledge, and forbade what God provided them, as a fabrication against God." The two gravest charges are gathered: infanticide (v. 137) and the invented prohibitions (vv. 136, 138–139). Both are declared *khusrān* — loss.

**"Lost Indeed"**

*Qad khasira* — "they have surely lost." The verb *khasira* is commercial: to lose in a transaction, to suffer a loss of capital. The sūrah has used it before: "those who lose their souls" (vv. 12, 20, 31). The idolaters, in their own view, were gaining — protecting honor, husbanding resources, practicing piety. The verse says they were losing: losing their children, losing the provision God gave them, and losing their souls. The commentators explain the loss as twofold — they lose their way in this world and face perdition in the Hereafter. The loss of a child killed for fear of poverty is a loss with no compensation; the loss of provision forbidden by invented rule is a loss self-inflicted; and the loss of the soul for the lie against God is the total loss.

**"Foolishly, Without Knowledge"**

*Safahan bi-ghayri ʿilm* — "in foolishness, without knowledge." *Safah* is foolishness, lightness of mind, the opposite of *rushd* (sound judgment) and *ḥilm* (forbearance, maturity). Al-Bayḍāwī explains the foolishness: they killed their children from fear of poverty or shame, not knowing that it is God who provides for them and their children — as verse 151 will say, "We provide for you and for them." Their action was based on a false calculation: that a child is a cost, that provision is fixed and must be divided, that honor is preserved by murder. Every premise was ignorance.

Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī record the specifics: the northern tribes of Rabīʿah and Muḍar especially were known for killing daughters, either from fear of capture and dishonor or from fear of the burden of supporting them. The verse names their motive as *safah* — not malice, but folly. This is important. The idolaters were not monsters who enjoyed killing; they were fools who believed a lie about provision and honor. The Qur'an's remedy is therefore knowledge: the knowledge that God provides, that daughters are a gift, that honor is in *taqwā*.

**"And Make Forbidden That Which God Has Provided Them"**

*Wa ḥarramū mā razaqahumu Allāh* — "and forbade what God provided them." The second charge. God gave them cattle and crops as *rizq*, provision — a gift for their sustenance. They forbade it to themselves and to others by invented rule. This is ingratitude compounded by presumption: ingratitude in refusing the gift, presumption in claiming the authority to refuse it in God's Name. The sūrah asked earlier, "Why should you not eat what God's Name has been invoked over, when He has detailed to you what He forbade?" (v. 119). The idolaters forbade what He permitted, which is as much a violation as permitting what He forbade — perhaps more, since it wears the mask of piety.

**"Fabricating Against God"**

*Iftirā'an ʿalā Allāh* — the third occurrence of the charge in this section (vv. 137, 138, 140). The prohibitions were not merely customs; they were presented as God's law. This is the heart of the crime and the reason the verse pronounces total loss. To sin is to disobey God; to fabricate against God is to make Him the author of the sin — to attribute one's own invention to His command. "Who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against God?" (v. 21, 93, 144). The one who kills his child in famine sins gravely; the one who kills his child believing his god commands it, and teaches this as religion, has done something worse: he has made his sin into worship.

**"They Indeed Have Gone Astray, and Were Not Rightly Guided"**

*Qad ḍallū wa mā kānū muhtadīn* — "they have gone astray and were not guided." Two statements, negative and positive. They strayed — left the path; and they were never on it — were not among the guided. The second denies them even the past: their whole condition, not just a lapse, was misguidance. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the emphasis: the doubled statement removes any ambiguity about their state. They did not err from a position of guidance; they were astray throughout.

This connects to verse 137's diagnosis that their religion was a confusion (*labs*) of the Abrahamic inheritance. They believed they were following Abraham; the verse says they were never on his path. Straying and not being guided are the same fact stated twice, because the idolaters' claim to be guided needed a double denial.

**The Verse and the Sanctity of Children**

The verse became, as the source commentary notes, one of the scriptural foundations for the prohibition of killing children in Islamic law, including the general prohibition of abortion. The classical schools differed on the permissibility of early termination in exceptional circumstances — before the ensoulment traditionally placed at 120 days, and where necessary to preserve the mother's life — but all agreed that the killing of children from fear of poverty or shame, which is what the verse names, is among the gravest sins. The Prophet ﷺ, asked which sin is greatest, listed: "That you set up a rival to God while He created you; then that you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you; then that you commit adultery with your neighbor's wife" (al-Bukhārī 4477; Muslim 86). The order — *shirk*, then infanticide — mirrors this section of the sūrah: fabrication against God, then the killing of children.

**Provision as the Answer to Fear**

The verse's implicit teaching is that fear of poverty is a form of ignorance. The idolaters killed because they did not know the Provider. The Qur'an's response throughout is to teach the Provider: "There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah" (11:6); "Do not kill your children for fear of poverty" (17:31). Note the order in 17:31 — "for them and for you" — the child's provision is mentioned first, as though to say: the child is not a drain on your provision but a bearer of his own. The one who knows this cannot kill from fear. The one who does not know it is *safīh*, and his foolishness is deadly.

**The Continuing Warning**

The verse warns every age against two errors that recur in new forms: the sacrifice of children to fear or convenience, and the invention of religious prohibitions without revealed basis. Both, the verse says, are loss; both are done "without knowledge"; both, when ascribed to God, are fabrication. The remedy for both is the same: knowledge of God as Provider and as sole Legislator.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:141

> **He is the One Who produces gardens—both cultivated and wild — and palm trees, crops of different flavours, olives, and pomegranates— similar ˹in shape˺, but dissimilar ˹in taste˺. Eat from the fruit they bear and pay the dues at harvest, but do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Creator's Provision Against Invented Prohibition**

After exposing the idolaters' division and forbidding of crops and cattle, the sūrah returns to the One who created them. *Wa huwa alladhī ansha'a jannātin maʿrūshātin wa ghayra maʿrūshāt* — "and He it is who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised." The emphatic *huwa alladhī*, "He is the One who," reclaims what the idolaters had parceled out. They divided the crops between God and their partners; the verse says *He* produced all of them. They forbade some of the cattle and crops; the verse says: eat. The logic is that the Creator alone has the right to regulate what He created, and He has regulated it by permission, not by the idolaters' taboos (al-Ṭūsī draws this connection explicitly).

**The Catalogue of Gardens**

The verse enumerates. *Maʿrūshāt* — trellised — are vines raised on supports, like grapevines; *ghayr maʿrūshāt* — untrellised — are plants that stand on their own or spread on the ground. Then the date palm (*al-nakhl*), the staple of Arabia; then *al-zarʿ mukhtalifan ukuluh* — "crops of diverse produce," grains and vegetables of varying yield, taste, and kind; then olives and pomegranates, *mutashābihan wa ghayra mutashābih* — "resembling and not resembling," alike in some respects (leaf, shape) and different in others (taste, fruit).

The verse is nearly identical to verse 99, and the commentators refer the reader there. The repetition is purposeful. Verse 99 presented the gardens as signs of God for "a people who believe"; verse 141 presents them as provision against the idolaters' prohibitions. The same creation serves as proof of the Creator and as refutation of those who forbid His gifts. The phrase "like unto one another and yet not alike" recurs to emphasize the deliberate variety of creation — from one water and one soil, God brings forth endless difference, which no idol did and no human rule can regulate.

**"Eat of Their Fruit When They Grow"**

*Kulū min thamarihi idhā athmar* — "Eat from the fruit they bear and pay the dues at harvest" (6:141). The command to eat is direct, addressed to all — no reserved shares, no forbidden categories, no distinction of sex. It is the command of verse 118 — to "eat only of what is slaughtered" (6:118) — applied to the produce of the earth. The Qur'an's default is permission: "Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan" (2:168). The idolaters' *ḥijr* is answered by God's *kulū*.

**"And Pay the Due Thereof on the Day of Its Harvest"**

*Wa ātū ḥaqqahu yawma ḥaṣādih* — "and give its due on the day of its harvest." Here the verse attaches to the permission its condition: a *ḥaqq*, a right, a due, belongs in the harvest and must be given. The idolaters gave shares to idols; the believers give a due to those who have a right to it — the poor and needy.

The commentators discuss the nature of this due, as the source commentary records. Al-Jalālayn and al-Ṭabarī describe it as a portion given to the needy at harvest time — perhaps a tenth. Some (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī report the view) identify it with the *zakāh* on produce, which the Prophet's Sunnah fixed at a tenth for rain-watered crops and a twentieth for irrigated ones (al-Bukhārī 1483). Others (al-Bayḍāwī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) hold that since this verse is Makkan and *zakāh* was formally established in Madinah, the verse commands a general charity at harvest — the handfuls given to those who come by, the gleanings left for the poor — distinct from the later fixed *zakāh*. The Twelver tradition, on a report from the fourth or fifth Imam, understands it as a few handfuls of grain given at reaping, distinct from *zakāh* (al-Ṭūsī, al-Ṭabrisī). Some hold that the fixed *zakāh* abrogated the unspecified due of this verse; others that both remain — the fixed obligation and the recommended generosity at harvest.

The phrase "on the day of its harvest" is significant on any reading. Giving is tied to the moment of receiving. Before the produce is stored, sold, or counted, a share goes to those in need. This trains the heart to see the harvest as God's gift with a right attached, not as private gain to be taxed later. The Prophet ﷺ practiced and commanded this: he would order that the gleaners be allowed their share, and he told the assessors of dates to "leave a third; if not a third, then a quarter" for the owners' generosity and the needs of passers-by (Abū Dāwūd 1605; al-Tirmidhī 643).

**"But Be Not Prodigal"**

*Wa lā tusrifū* — "and do not be excessive." *Isrāf* is going beyond the proper limit, in any direction. The commentators apply it here in two ways. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Jalālayn: do not be excessive in giving — do not give away so much of the harvest that you and your dependents are left without; compare 17:29, "Do not be so tight-fisted, for you will be blameworthy" A report says the verse was revealed when Thābit ibn Qays harvested his palms and gave away everything, leaving his family with nothing. Al-Ṭabarī: do not be excessive in consumption or wastefulness in a way that would prevent you from giving the due — the prodigal who consumes everything has nothing left for the *ḥaqq*. Both apply. The verse commands a balance: eat, give, but neither eat nor give to excess.

There is a third sense that fits the section: the idolaters' prohibitions were themselves *isrāf* — an excess in the other direction, forbidding what God permitted. Al-Rāzī notes that *isrāf* includes transgressing the limit in matters of lawful and unlawful, and that the idolaters' arbitrary taboos were a form of it. The verse thus corrects both excesses: the excess of forbidding (the idolaters) and the excess of consuming or giving without measure.

**"Truly He Loves Not the Prodigal"**

*Innahu lā yuḥibbu al-musrifīn* — "He does not love the excessive." The formula appears at 7:31 ("There is no doubt that whatever ˹idols˺ you invite me to ˹worship˺ are not worthy to be invoked either in this world or the Hereafter") and the prodigal are named among the people of the Fire (40:43). God's love is withheld from excess because excess is disorder — a violation of the measure (*qadar*) by which He created all things (54:49). The balanced use of provision — enough for oneself, a due for others, no waste — is the pattern the verse commends.

**The Verse's Program**

Verse 141 sets out, in one sentence, an economy of provision: God creates; humans eat; a due is given to the needy at the moment of harvest; excess is avoided. Against the idolaters' economy — shares to idols, taboos for women, privilege for custodians, children killed from fear of scarcity — the Qur'an's economy is one of gratitude, generosity, and measure. The one who lives by it does not fear poverty (because the Provider is known), does not hoard (because the due is given), and does not waste (because excess is unloved). This is what it means to receive the gardens as God's gift rather than as material for invented religion.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:142

> **Some cattle are fit for labour, others are too small. Eat of what Allah has provided for you and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Certainly, he is your sworn enemy.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Gardens to Cattle**

Verse 141 reclaimed the gardens and crops for their Creator; verse 142 does the same for the cattle. *Wa mina al-anʿāmi ḥamūlatan wa farshan* — "and of the cattle, [He produced] bearers of burden and *farsh*." The verse continues the verb *ansha'a* ("He produced") from the previous verse: just as He brought forth the diverse crops, He brought forth the livestock in their diverse uses. The idolaters had declared certain cattle's backs forbidden (v. 138); the verse says God made some cattle precisely *for* burden. They had reserved certain animals' offspring for men (v. 139); the verse says God made cattle for all to eat.

**"Some for Burden"**

*Ḥamūlah* — from *ḥamala*, to carry — denotes animals that bear loads and riders: camels chiefly, and horses, mules, and donkeys, the large livestock (al-Ṭabarī). The Qur'an elsewhere counts this among God's signs: "And they carry your loads to ˹distant˺ lands which you could not otherwise reach without great hardship" (16:5–7). The idolaters' *ḥām* — the stallion whose back was declared forbidden — was a refusal of this purpose.

**"And Some for Slaughter" — The Word Farsh**

*Farsh* is from a root meaning to spread out, and the commentators, as the source records, read it in several ways that together display the animal's usefulness. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zamakhsharī: animals laid out for slaughter — the sheep and goats that are "spread" on the ground to be killed, as opposed to the camels that stand for slaughter. Al-Zamakhsharī also: animals whose hides become *furush*, spread coverings, rugs, and furnishings; al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī note that sheep in particular were understood here, because their skins and wool were spread as bedding. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī: animals that are ridden, since the rider spreads himself astride the beast — so that *farsh* would be small riding animals as against the *ḥamūlah* of large pack animals. Some also understood *farsh* as animals too small to carry burdens — those that are "low to the ground."

The multiplicity is not confusion but richness. The single word gathers the animal's gifts: meat, hide, wool, bedding, transport. The Qur'an repeatedly presents these as signs of God's beneficence: "And there is certainly a lesson for you in cattle, from whose bellies We give you ˹milk˺ to drink, and in them are many other benefits for you, and from them you may eat" (23:21); "And out of their wool, fur, and hair He has given you furnishings and goods for a while" (16:80); "Do they not see that We singlehandedly created for them, among other things, cattle which are under their control" (36:71–72); and their beauty: "They are also pleasing to you when you bring them home and when you take them out to graze" (16:6).

**"Eat of That Which God Has Provided You"**

*Kulū mimmā razaqakumu Allāh* — "eat of what God has provided you." The command repeats verse 141's *kulū* and verse 118's. Three times in the space of a few verses the Qur'an commands eating — against a system of invented abstentions. The phrase "what God has provided" (*mā razaqakum*) is the same phrase used in verse 140's charge: they "forbade what God provided them." The verse restores the provision to its purpose. Compare 16:114: "So eat from the good, lawful things which Allah has provided for you, and be grateful for Allah"

**"And Follow Not the Footsteps of Satan"**

*Wa lā tattabiʿū khuṭuwāti al-shayṭān* — "and do not follow the footsteps of Satan." The identical pairing — eat what God provided; do not follow Satan's footsteps — appears in 2:168, and the commentators connect the two passages. *Khuṭuwāt* are steps, footprints: the path Satan lays down, step by step. The image is of gradual leading — Satan does not present the destination but only the next step. The idolaters' taboos were Satan's footsteps: one invented rule, then another, then the sacralizing of the whole, then the killing of children — each step following the one before, until a whole religion of fabrication had been built. Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah glossed "the footsteps of Satan" as "his works" and "his acts of disobedience," and Mujāhid specified vows of sin — such as the vows by which the *sā'ibah* and *baḥīrah* were consecrated.

The placement of the warning after the command to eat is precise. Satan's footsteps, in this context, are not leading toward gluttony but toward *prohibition* — toward forbidding what God permitted. This inverts the common assumption that Satan only tempts to indulgence. He also tempts to false abstinence, false piety, invented rules — and this temptation is more dangerous because it feels like virtue. The Prophet ﷺ warned against both directions: he refused to permit a Companion to fast every day, pray all night, and abstain from marriage, saying, "Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me" (al-Bukhārī 5063; Muslim 1401).

**"Truly He Is a Manifest Enemy unto You"**

*Innahu lakum ʿaduwwun mubīn* — "Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray ˹in this life˺ nor suffer ˹in the next˺" The enmity is established from the beginning of human history: Satan's refusal to bow to Adam, his temptation in the Garden, his expulsion with the words "But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in, and We said," (2:36; 7:24; 20:123). The Qur'an repeats the warning insistently (2:208; 7:22; 12:5; 17:53; 28:15; 35:6; 36:60; 43:62). The word *mubīn*, "manifest, clear," indicates that the enmity is not hidden; Satan has declared it — "I will certainly mislead them all," (38:82). One who follows the footsteps of a declared enemy has been deceived not about the enemy's intentions, which are open, but about the nature of the steps, which are disguised as wisdom or piety.

**The Verse's Logic**

The verse presents a simple binary: eat what God provided, or follow Satan's footsteps. There is no third option, because to abstain from God's provision on the basis of an invented rule is not neutral — it is following a path God did not lay. The idolaters imagined that their taboos were extra piety, a way of being more careful than required. The verse says they were steps on the enemy's path. This is a principle of wide application: additions to God's religion that present themselves as extra devotion are, when they have no basis in revelation, departures from it. "The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger of Allah and the fulfilment of His Word through Mary and a spirit ˹created by a command˺ from Him" (4:171; 5:77).

**Practical Application**

The verse shapes a believer's relation to God's gifts. He receives them — food, transport, clothing, the whole usefulness of the animal world — as *rizq*, provision, and uses them with gratitude and without invented scruple. He is alert to the "footsteps": the gradual, plausible steps by which something permitted comes to be treated as forbidden, or something forbidden as permitted. And he remembers that the one laying the steps is an enemy — declared, manifest, and patient — who is as content to lead a person into false abstention as into false indulgence, so long as the person leaves the path God laid.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:143

> **˹Allah has created˺ four pairs: a pair of sheep and a pair of goats—ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Has He forbidden ˹to you˺ the two males or the two females or what is in the wombs of the two females? Tell me with knowledge, if what you say is true.”—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Eight Pairs"**

*Thamāniyata azwāj* — "eight pairs" or "eight mates." The phrase continues the grammatical thread from verse 142: God produced of the cattle burden-bearers and *farsh* — eight kinds. The word *zawj* means one member of a pair, a mate; "eight *azwāj*" are eight individuals forming four pairs: the male and female of sheep, goats, camels, and oxen (al-Jalālayn). These four species — *ḍa'n* (sheep), *maʿz* (goats), *ibil* (camels), *baqar* (cattle) — are the *anʿām*, the livestock from which the sūrah takes its name, and the animals around which the idolaters' taboos revolved. Compare 39:6: "He creates you in the wombs of your mothers ˹in stages˺, one development after another, in three layers of darkness"

This verse names the first two pairs: "of sheep, two, and of goats, two" — a male and female of each. Verse 144 names the remaining two pairs, camels and oxen. The verses are a matched set, each with the same interrogation.

**The Interrogation**

*Qul ā-al-dhakarayni ḥarrama ami al-unthayayni ammā ishtamalat ʿalayhi arḥāmu al-unthayayn* — "Say: Is it the two males He forbade, or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain?" The Prophet ﷺ is instructed to put the question that exposes the idolaters' system. Their taboos, as verses 138–139 described, fell variously on males, on females, on offspring. The question forces the matter to its logical elements. Every one of these animals is either male or female or in the womb. Which of the three did God forbid?

If God forbade the males, then every male sheep and goat should be forbidden — but the idolaters ate males freely. If He forbade the females, every female should be forbidden — but they ate females too. If He forbade what the wombs contain, then all offspring should be forbidden — but they ate offspring, with their arbitrary exceptions. Their actual practice — this particular she-camel after her fifth young, that stallion after ten sirings, this offspring for men only — corresponded to none of the three exhaustive categories. The question has no answer that fits their practice, and so their practice is shown to have no principle. The commentators describe the questioning as mockery (*tahakkum*) targeting the arbitrariness of the prohibitions.

**The Logical Method**

The argument is a disjunctive elimination. The categories are exhaustive (male, female, unborn); the idolaters' taboos are consistent with none; therefore the taboos have no basis in the categories of creation. This is the same form of reasoning Abraham used against the celestial bodies (vv. 76–78) — the systematic exhaustion of alternatives — and the same the sūrah has used throughout. The Qur'an does not merely assert that the idolaters are wrong; it constructs a demonstration that a reasonable person cannot evade.

The argument also makes a theological point implicitly. God's law follows the structure of creation: it deals with kinds, not with arbitrary individuals. If God had forbidden something in the cattle, it would be a category — as He did in fact forbid a category, swine (v. 145). The idolaters' taboos, falling on particular individuals by accidents of birth-order and vow, bear no relation to the kinds God created, and so cannot be His law.

**"Tell Me with Knowledge, If You Are Truthful"**

*Nabbi'ūnī bi-ʿilmin in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — "inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful." The demand is for *ʿilm*, knowledge — proof, evidence, a source. The idolaters had claimed these taboos were God's will; the Prophet ﷺ asks them to produce the knowledge on which the claim rests. This is the recurring demand of the sūrah: "Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us?" (v. 148); "Bring your witnesses" (v. 150). And it is the recurring diagnosis: the idolaters act "without knowledge" (vv. 100, 108, 119, 140, 144), following conjecture (vv. 116, 148).

The conditional "if you are truthful" (*in kuntum ṣādiqīn*) implies its own answer. They are not truthful — not because they are lying about their beliefs, but because their claim that God forbade these things is a falsehood attributed to God. The only truthful answer to "which did He forbid?" is "we do not know; we inherited these rules and ascribed them to Him."

**The Sheep and Goats First**

Why begin with sheep and goats rather than camels, the most prized? Perhaps because sheep and goats were the most common and most frequently subject to the taboos of *waṣīlah* (the ewe whose twin male was spared). Perhaps because the argument gains force by starting with the humble animals: if the idolaters cannot justify their taboos on a sheep, they cannot justify them on a camel. The pairing — small livestock in this verse, large in the next — also gives the interrogation a rhythm: the same question asked twice, so that the absence of an answer is heard twice.

**The Broader Principle**

The verse establishes a method for evaluating any claimed religious prohibition: ask for its basis in knowledge. Not "is this our custom?" or "did our fathers do this?" but "did God forbid it, and how do you know?" A prohibition that cannot answer this question is not religion; it is *zaʿm* (v. 136, 138), claim. The believer applies this test to the rules he inherits and the rules he is offered, and holds only what can answer. The Prophet ﷺ said: "To Him belongs whatever is before us, and whatever is behind us, and everything in between" — and he recited, "And your Lord is never forgetful" (19:64) (al-Ḥākim, al-Bazzār; al-Dāraquṭnī 4396 similar). The silence of revelation is permission, and the one who fills the silence with prohibitions must answer verse 143's question.

**The Spirit of the Challenge**

The challenge is sharp but not unfair. It gives the idolaters every opportunity: three categories, an invitation to inform, a condition of truthfulness. If they had knowledge, they could produce it. The verse's confidence is that they cannot — and history records no answer. The taboos of the *baḥīrah* and *sā'ibah* vanished with the coming of Islam, not because they were forbidden by force, but because, once the question was put, no one could say why they had ever been observed.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:144

> **and a pair of camels and a pair of oxen. Ask ˹them˺, “Has He forbidden ˹to you˺ the two males or the two females or what is in the wombs of the two females? Or were you present when Allah gave you this commandment?” Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah to mislead others without ˹any˺ knowledge? Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Pair of Pairs**

*Wa mina al-ibili ithnayni wa mina al-baqari ithnayn* — "and of camels, two, and of oxen, two." The verse completes the eight mates of verse 143: camels and cattle, male and female of each. The camel was the most valuable animal in Arabia and the center of the most elaborate taboos — the *baḥīrah*, *sā'ibah*, and *ḥām* of 5:103 were all camels. The interrogation is repeated word for word: which did He forbid — the two males, the two females, or what their wombs contain? The repetition is deliberate. The idolaters' silence on the sheep and goats is now compounded by their silence on the camels and oxen. There is no category in which their taboos find a principle.

**"Or Were You Present When God Enjoined This upon You?"**

*Am kuntum shuhadā'a idh waṣṣākumu Allāhu bi-hādhā* — "or were you witnesses when God commanded you this?" This is the new element, and it shifts the argument from logic to epistemology. Verse 143 asked *what* God forbade and demanded knowledge. Verse 144 asks *how they could know*. There are only two ways to know what God has commanded: by direct witness of the commanding, or by report from a messenger. The idolaters rejected the messenger — they denied Muhammad's prophethood and, in effect, the possibility of revelation reaching them. So, al-Rāzī reasons, unless they were personally present when God issued the command, they have no means of knowing it. And they were not present. Therefore their claim to know that God forbade these animals is empty.

The question exposes the idolaters' inconsistency. They demanded the strongest proof from the Prophet ﷺ — an angel, a written book descending, a sign like Moses' — while claiming, for their own taboos, a divine origin they could not possibly have witnessed. They applied the severest skepticism to revelation and none at all to inherited custom. The verb *waṣṣā* — to enjoin, to charge solemnly — is the verb used for God's actual commandments in verses 151–153 ("this He has enjoined upon you"). The contrast is pointed: God's true enjoining is about to be recited; the idolaters' claimed enjoining is a thing they never witnessed.

**"Who Does Greater Wrong Than One Who Fabricates a Lie Against God"**

*Fa-man aẓlamu mimmani iftarā ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban* — "so who is more wrongdoing than one who invents a lie against God?" The rhetorical question is the sūrah's refrain (vv. 21, 93) and the Qur'an's (7:37; 10:17; 11:18; 18:15; 29:68; 61:7). Having demonstrated that the idolaters' taboos have no basis in the categories of creation and no possible source in knowledge, the verse names what they are: a lie invented against God. And it ranks this lie as the greatest wrong — greater than any other, because it corrupts the source of all right and wrong. Theft misappropriates property; murder destroys a life; but the fabrication of religion in God's Name misrepresents God Himself and misleads all who trust the fabrication.

**"That He May Lead Men Astray Without Knowledge"**

*Li-yuḍilla al-nāsa bi-ghayri ʿilm* — "in order to lead people astray without knowledge." The fabricator does not merely err privately; he propagates.
