The invented taboos of ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy and his successors misled generations of Arabs. The phrase "without knowledge" may attach to the fabricator (he leads astray though he has no knowledge) or to those led (they follow without knowledge); both are true. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as describing the leader: he misleads on the basis of nothing but his own invention. The result is the scene of verse 128: many claimed, following those who claimed to speak for God.

This is why the Qur'an treats religious fabrication with such severity. The one who invents a rule in God's Name and teaches it acquires the burden of everyone who follows it: "Let them bear their burdens in full on the Day of Judgment as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge" (16:25). The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever calls to misguidance has upon him sin like the sins of those who follow him, without diminishing their sins in any way" (Muslim 2674).

**"Truly God Guides Not Wrongdoing People"**

*Inna Allāha lā yahdī al-qawma al-ẓālimīn* — "And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people" The verse closes with a formula found throughout the Qur'an (2:258; 3:86; 5:51; 9:19, 109; 28:50; 46:10; 61:7; 62:5). The fabricators are *ẓālimūn* — the word of "who does greater *ẓulm*" a clause earlier — and God does not guide those who persist in *ẓulm*. The statement is both a judgment and an explanation. A judgment: they are left in their misguidance. An explanation: this is why, despite the clarity of the argument in verses 143–144, they do not accept it — persistent wrongdoing has closed them to guidance. The Qur'an's consistent teaching is that guidance requires a receptive heart, and *ẓulm* — especially the *ẓulm* of lying about God — destroys receptivity.

**The Structure of the Two Verses**

Verses 143–144 together form a complete refutation. They enumerate the animals (all four species, both sexes, and the unborn). They ask which God forbade (no answer fits). They demand knowledge (none is produced). They ask about the source of knowledge (no witness, no accepted messenger). They name the result (fabrication against God). They state its purpose and effect (leading people astray). And they pronounce the consequence (no guidance for such wrongdoers). Nothing is left unaddressed. This is the Qur'an's method of *ḥujjah* — conclusive argument — which verse 149 will name explicitly: "to God belongs the conclusive argument."

**The Standing Lesson**

The verse's question — "were you present when God enjoined this?" — remains the sharpest test of any claimed divine rule. Religion is knowledge of God's will, and that knowledge comes only through what God has actually revealed. Whatever cannot be traced to revelation — however old, however widely observed, however pious it seems — is not known to be God's will, and to declare it so is to fabricate. The verse thus protects religion from accretion and the believer from the burden of rules God never gave. Ibn Taymiyyah made this a principle: acts of worship are established only by revealed text, and whatever is added in God's Name without it is innovation, however sincere its practitioners. Verse 144 is among the foundations of that principle.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:145

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to eat except carrion, running blood, swine—which is impure—or a sinful offering in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—then surely your Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Revealed Answer**

After demolishing the idolaters' taboos, the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to state what revelation actually forbids. *Qul lā ajidu fī mā ūḥiya ilayya muḥarraman ʿalā ṭāʿimin yaṭʿamuhu illā...* — "Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, except..." The framing is precise and instructive. The Prophet ﷺ does not say "I forbid" or "I permit"; he says "I do not find in what was revealed to me." He is the transmitter of a law he did not make. This is exactly the source of authority the idolaters lacked (v. 144): revelation, received and reported. And the formulation is limiting — "I do not find *anything* forbidden *except*" — which establishes the default of permission and confines prohibition to what is named.

**The Four Prohibitions**

First, *maytah* — carrion, an animal that died without proper slaughter, whether by natural death, disease, strangling, falling, goring, or predation (as 5:3 details). This is the prohibition the idolaters had argued against with their "what God killed" sophistry (vv. 118–121); the verse states it plainly as revealed.

Second, *dam masfūḥ* — "blood poured forth," flowing blood, the liquid blood drained from an animal at slaughter. The qualifier *masfūḥ* is significant: it restricts the prohibition to shed, flowing blood, and excludes the blood that remains in the meat and organs after draining, which is permitted. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Two kinds of dead things and two kinds of blood have been made lawful for us: the two dead things are fish and locusts, and the two bloods are liver and spleen" (Ibn Mājah 3314; Aḥmad 5723). The source commentary notes the distinction between the liquid blood and the organs.

Third, *laḥm khinzīr* — 'the flesh of swine,' with the parenthetical *fa-innahu rijs* — 'for it is defilement.' Only this prohibition receives an explicit reason in the verse. *Rijs* is filth, impurity, abomination — the word used for idols (22:30) and for the state of the disbelievers (v. 125). The pig is declared impure in itself, and the jurists extended the prohibition from its flesh to all its parts, since "flesh" is the primary but not exclusive referent and the reason given (defilement) applies to the whole animal.

Fourth, *fisqan uhilla li-ghayri Allāhi bihi* — "a sinful thing over which other than God was invoked," meaning an animal slaughtered as an offering to an idol or in any name other than God's. The verse calls this *fisq* — transgression — the word of verse 121 ("indeed it is *fisq*"). This is the category the idolaters practiced most freely, and it is the one that touches *tawḥīd* directly.

**The Same List Elsewhere**

The four prohibitions appear in 2:173, 5:3, and 16:115 with the same core content. 5:3, revealed late in Madinah, elaborates the categories of carrion (strangled, beaten, fallen, gored, partly eaten) and adds what was sacrificed on stone altars and divided by arrows. The consistency across the Makkan and Madinan periods shows that the dietary law was fixed from early on; only its detail was expanded.

**Is the List Exhaustive?**

The verse's "I do not find... except" led some — notably ʿĀ'ishah and Ibn ʿAbbās in certain reports, and the Ẓāhirī school — to hold that only these four are forbidden by revelation, and that other prohibitions are matters of dislike, not unlawfulness. The majority, however, hold that the verse is a statement of what was revealed *at that time* (it is Makkan) and that later revelation and the Sunnah added further prohibitions: the Prophet ﷺ forbade "every beast with fangs and every bird with talons" (Muslim 1934), domestic donkeys at Khaybar (al-Bukhārī 4199), and other categories. Al-Jalālayn and al-Qurṭubī note the additions from the Sunnah. Both positions agree on the verse's central thrust: the prohibitions are few and specific, and the idolaters' elaborate taboos are not among them.

Al-Qurṭubī records that some considered this verse to have been revealed, or recited, at ʿArafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage — a possible Madinan context for what is otherwise a Makkan verse — but the majority hold it Makkan and note that its wording ("I do not find") fits the earlier period.

**"But Whosoever Is Compelled by Necessity"**

*Fa-mani iḍṭurra ghayra bāghin wa lā ʿādin fa-inna rabbaka ghafūrun raḥīm* — "but whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then your Lord is Forgiving, Merciful." The exception repeats that of 2:173 and 5:3 and applies verse 119's principle ("except what you are compelled to"). One who faces starvation may eat of the forbidden to preserve life. The conditions: *ghayr bāghin* — not desiring it, not seeking it out, not eating from appetite; *wa lā ʿādin* — not transgressing, not exceeding the amount necessary. The jurists derived from this the maxim that necessity is measured by its extent (*al-ḍarūrah tuqaddaru bi-qadarihā*): one eats what averts death, no more. Some early authorities read *bāghin* and *ʿādin* as referring to rebels and highwaymen — those in unlawful travel — who would not benefit from the concession; but the majority read the terms as describing the manner of eating.

The exception closes with two Names: *Ghafūr* (Forgiving) and *Raḥīm* (Merciful). God forgives what necessity compelled and shows mercy in permitting it. The law bends toward life. This is the opposite of the idolaters' law, which killed children from fear of scarcity and forbade food to women; God's law permits even the forbidden to save a life.

**The Theology of the Verse**

Three principles emerge. First, permission is the default and prohibition is the exception; the burden of proof lies on the one who forbids. Second, prohibition comes only from revelation — "what has been revealed to me" — not from custom, priesthood, or human authority. Third, the law is for human welfare and yields to necessity. Together these define the Islamic approach to the lawful and the forbidden and stand as the constructive answer to the idolaters' system: where they had many taboos, from human sources, applied without mercy, Islam has few prohibitions, from God, applied with mercy.

**The Wisdom in the Prohibitions**

The commentators have reflected on the reasons for the four. Carrion is diseased or decayed and its blood retained; flowing blood is a medium of impurity and disease; swine is declared *rijs* in itself; and what is offered to other than God is forbidden not for its substance but for its dedication — because eating it is participation in *shirk*. The first three concern the body; the fourth concerns the soul. Islamic law protects both. But the believer's obedience does not depend on knowing the reasons; he abstains because God forbade, and the reasons, where known, are confirmations rather than conditions. Ibn Taymiyyah observed that God forbade nothing but what harms and permitted nothing but what benefits, whether or not the harm and benefit are apparent to us.

**The Verse in Daily Life**

The verse governs a Muslim's daily table. He does not eat carrion, blood, pork, or what was dedicated to other than God; he does not add to these prohibitions from his own invention; he does not treat the permitted as suspect; and in genuine necessity, he eats what preserves life without appetite or excess, trusting the Forgiving and Merciful. The simplicity of the rule is its mercy. A religion that had multiplied dietary taboos as the idolaters did would have made every meal an anxiety; verse 145 makes every meal a gift with four exceptions.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:146

> **For those who are Jewish, We forbade every animal with undivided hoofs and the fat of oxen and sheep except what is joined to their backs or intestines or mixed with bone. In this way We rewarded them for their violations. And We are certainly truthful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Why the Jewish Law Is Mentioned Here**

Having stated the four prohibitions of Islamic law (v. 145), the sūrah turns to a different, more restrictive dietary law — that imposed on the Jews. *Wa ʿalā alladhīna hādū ḥarramnā kulla dhī ẓufur* — "and to those who are Jews We forbade every [animal] possessing *ẓufur*." The purpose is twofold. It anticipates an objection: if God's law is as simple as verse 145 says, why did the Jews have so many prohibitions? The verse answers: those were a specific recompense for specific disobedience, not the original or universal law. And it contrasts with the idolaters' taboos: the Jewish prohibitions were at least genuinely revealed — "We forbade" — whereas the idolaters' were invented. Revealed restriction, even as punishment, is God's; invented restriction is fabrication.

**"Every Animal with Claws"**

*Dhī ẓufur* — literally "possessor of a nail/claw/talon." The commentators differ on the exact reference. Many (al-Jalālayn, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) understood it as animals with undivided toes or hooves — camels, ostriches, and the like — since Leviticus 11 forbids camels (which chew the cud but do not divide the hoof) and animals that "walk on their paws." Others took *ẓufur* in its more common sense of claw or talon and understood the prohibition to cover all beasts and birds of prey — which, as the source commentary notes, became part of Islamic dietary law too, through the Sunnah's prohibition of fanged beasts and taloned birds (Muslim 1934). The Qur'an's phrasing is general enough to embrace both readings, and the Jewish law in fact forbade both categories.

**The Fat of Oxen and Sheep**

*Wa mina al-baqari wa al-ghanami ḥarramnā ʿalayhim shuḥūmahumā illā mā ḥamalat ẓuhūruhumā awi al-ḥawāyā aw mā ikhtalaṭa bi-ʿaẓm* — "and of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fats, except what their backs carry, or the entrails, or what is mixed with bone." The Jews were forbidden the fat (*shaḥm*) of cattle and sheep — specifically the suet, the pure fat around the kidneys and internal organs — with three exceptions: the fat on the back (which is intermingled with meat), the fat adhering to the entrails (*ḥawāyā*, the intestines), and the fat mixed with bone (the tail fat, the fat of the ribs, and marrow). This corresponds closely to Leviticus 3:9–10 and 7:23–25, which forbid the fat covering the entrails and kidneys and reserve it for burning as an offering.

The precision of the verse's description of a law contained in the Torah — from a Prophet ﷺ who could not read it — is itself notable. The commentators point to such passages as evidence of the Qur'an's divine origin: its knowledge of the details of prior scripture, without access to the texts, is one of the arguments of verse 114 ("those to whom We gave the Book know it is sent down from your Lord with truth").

**Does the Prohibition on Fat Apply to Muslims?**

The jurists answered no. The verse explicitly restricts the prohibition to "those who are Jews," and the Prophet ﷺ himself dealt with fat as lawful. Al-Qurṭubī records that Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī cited the report from Khaybar in which a Companion took a bag of fat from the spoils and the Prophet ﷺ let him keep it (al-Bukhārī 3153; Muslim 1772) — at the very siege where he established other prohibitions (donkeys, fanged beasts). The Prophet ﷺ also condemned the Jews for circumventing the fat prohibition: "May God curse the Jews; when God forbade them the fat, they melted it, sold it, and consumed its price" (al-Bukhārī 2236; Muslim 1581). The condemnation is not of the Muslims eating fat but of the Jews evading their own law by legal fiction — a warning against every such evasion.

**"Thus Did We Recompense Them for Their Willful Disobedience"**

*Dhālika jazaynāhum bi-baghyihim* — "that We recompensed them for their *baghy*." *Baghy* is transgression, rebellion, willful wrongdoing, oppression. The restrictive law was a punishment. This is stated more fully in 4:160: "We forbade the Jews certain foods that had been lawful to them for their wrongdoing, and for hindering many from the Way of Allah," And 3:93: "All food was lawful for the children of Israel, except what Israel made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed" — showing that the original law was permissive and the restrictions came later, in response to conduct. Al-Zamakhsharī glosses the *baghy* simply as their wrongdoing; al-Ṭabarsī specifies their mistreatment of the needy and their consumption of usury and unlawful wealth, which 4:161 mentions alongside the prohibition.

The principle is that law can function as discipline. God, in His wisdom, sometimes imposes restriction not because the thing restricted is evil in itself but because the people need the discipline of restriction. The Jewish dietary law was, on this reading, a yoke placed on a rebellious people — which is why the Qur'an describes the Prophet ﷺ as one who "relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them" (7:157). The Muslim community, spared these restrictions, is not thereby superior in itself but is under a lighter covenant — and warned by the Jewish example of what *baghy* can bring.

**"And Surely We Are Truthful"**

*Wa innā la-ṣādiqūn* — "and indeed We are truthful." The verse closes with an affirmation that God speaks truth in what He has just said — about the Jewish law, about its cause, and about the four prohibitions of the previous verse. The affirmation answers two audiences. To the Jews who might deny that their restrictions were a punishment, claiming them as original law or a mark of election: God is truthful in His account. To the idolaters who claimed their taboos were divine: God is truthful in what He actually forbade, and the contrast with their fabrications is complete. The phrase echoes verse 143's challenge — "tell me with knowledge, if you are truthful" — and supplies the answer: the idolaters cannot claim truthfulness; God does.

**The Comparative Lesson**

The verse gives the Muslim reader a comparative view of dietary law across the Abrahamic revelations. Before the Torah: permission, except what Jacob forbade himself. Under the Torah: extensive prohibition, as discipline. Under the Qur'an: return to near-original permission, with four prohibitions. The trajectory is from freedom, through corrective restriction, back to freedom under a final law that has learned from the discipline. The idolaters' taboos sit outside this trajectory altogether: neither original permission nor revealed discipline, but invention.

**A Reflection on Discipline and Freedom**

The verse teaches that restriction is not intrinsically pious and freedom not intrinsically lax. God restricted the Jews because of their *baghy* and freed the Muslims by His mercy. The measure of a law is not its severity but its source and its fit to the people it governs. A believer who understands verse 146 does not envy stricter systems as though they were holier, nor despise the discipline God imposed on others; he receives his own law as the mercy it is, and takes care not to earn, by *baghy*, a heavier one.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:147

> **But if they deny you ˹O Prophet˺, say, “Your Lord is infinite in mercy, yet His punishment will not be averted from the wicked people.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Who Denies, and What**

*Fa-in kadhdhabūka* — "so if they deny you." The pronoun "they" is read by the commentators as referring to the Jews of the previous verse, who might deny the account of their dietary restrictions as a punishment, or to the idolaters, who deny the whole message; al-Ṭabarī allows both. The Prophet ﷺ is told how to answer denial: not with argument — the argument has been given — but with a statement of two attributes held in balance.

**"Your Lord Is Possessed of Vast Mercy"**

*Fa-qul rabbukum dhū raḥmatin wāsiʿah* — "Your Lord is infinite in mercy, yet His punishment will not be averted from the wicked people." (6:147). The word *wāsiʿah* — vast, wide, all-encompassing — describes a mercy of which God says: "I will ordain mercy for those who shun evil, pay alms-tax, and believe in Our revelations" (7:156). The verse begins with mercy, and the source commentary explains why. The Jews, al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī note, argued that God's mercy was so vast that He would not punish them for their disobedience — "The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days" (2:80); "We are the children of Allah and His most beloved" (5:18). The Prophet ﷺ is told to affirm the premise: yes, your Lord's mercy is vast. The affirmation is not grudging. God's mercy is the first thing said about Him in this response, as it is the first thing said about Him in every sūrah's opening.

The vastness extends even to the deniers, in a specific sense. God's mercy is shown to them in that He does not punish immediately; He gives respite, sends warnings, holds back the consequence so that they may repent. The delay the deniers mistake for indifference is itself mercy — the theme of verse 134 and of "Your Lord is the All-Forgiving, Full of Mercy" (18:58).

**"But His Might Will Not Be Averted from the Guilty People"**

*Wa lā yuraddu ba'suhu ʿani al-qawmi al-mujrimīn* — "and His might will not be turned back from the guilty people." *Ba's* is might, severity, punishment, the force of God's judgment — the word of verse 43 ("when Our might came to them") and 65. The passive *lā yuraddu*, "is not repelled," indicates that nothing and no one can turn it aside once it comes: no intercessor, no argument about mercy, no claim of election. And it falls on *al-qawm al-mujrimīn* — "the guilty people," the criminals — the term of verses 55, 123, and 124.

The second clause corrects the misuse of the first. Vast mercy does not mean the absence of judgment. The Jews' reasoning — 'God is merciful, therefore we will not be punished' — takes a true premise to a false conclusion, because it ignores that God is also just and that His mercy has a structure: it reaches those who turn to it. "I will ordain mercy for those who shun evil, pay alms-tax, and believe in Our revelations" (7:156). The mercy is vast; the criminals exclude themselves from it by persisting in crime.

**The Balance of Hope and Fear**

The verse states in a single breath what Islamic spirituality calls the balance of *rajā'* (hope) and *khawf* (fear). Mercy is vast: this forbids despair. Might is not averted: this forbids presumption. The Prophet ﷺ said: "If the believer knew what punishment is with God, no one would hope for His Paradise; and if the disbeliever knew what mercy is with God, no one would despair of His Paradise" (Muslim 2755). And: "Were God to punish the inhabitants of His heavens and earth, He would punish them without wronging them; and were He to show them mercy, His mercy would be better for them than their deeds" (Abū Dāwūd 4699). The believer holds both. The verse teaches the Prophet ﷺ to teach both, and to teach them in this order — mercy first, then might — because the deniers' error was to keep the first and drop the second.

**The Verse as a Model of Response**

The verse also models how to answer religious presumption. The presumer says, "God is merciful; He will not punish me." The wrong answer is to deny God's mercy — this is false and drives the person to despair. The right answer, which the verse gives, is to affirm the mercy fully and then to state what the presumer omits: the mercy does not shield the persistent criminal. This is truthful, complete, and merciful in itself — it leaves the door open while warning of what lies outside it. Al-Ṭabarī summarizes: God's vast mercy should not lead the wrongdoers to think His might will be indefinitely turned from them.

**The Place of the Verse in the Section**

Verses 145–146 stated two laws: the Muslim four prohibitions and the Jewish restrictions imposed as punishment. Verse 147 anticipates the response of denial and answers it with the two attributes that govern all law: mercy, which is the source of the law's permissions and its leniency (the exception for necessity in verse 145, the lightening of the burden in Islam), and might, which is the guarantee of the law's seriousness (the punishment of *baghy* in verse 146, the recompense promised to the fabricators throughout the section). Every law of God is mercy to those who accept it and a warning to those who reject it. The verse names both in the compass of a sentence.

**The Name Dhū Raḥmah Again**

The verse repeats the description of verse 133, *dhū al-raḥmah*, now intensified: *dhū raḥmatin wāsiʿah*. The sūrah returns to God's mercy insistently — "He has prescribed mercy upon Himself" (vv. 12, 54); "your Lord is Self-Sufficient, Possessor of Mercy" (v. 133); here "Possessor of vast mercy." The insistence is itself an argument: a book that returns to divine mercy this often, even while warning of divine might, is not the book of a harsh God. The warnings are set within the mercy, not against it. The believer who reads the sūrah's severe passages should read them as the verse instructs — as the "might" of One whose mercy is vast, held back as long as mercy allows, and falling only on those who make themselves *mujrimīn* by refusing it.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:148

> **The polytheists will argue, “Had it been Allah’s Will, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated others with Him ˹in worship˺ or made anything unlawful.” Likewise, those before them rejected the truth until they tasted Our punishment. Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? Surely you follow nothing but ˹false˺ assumptions and you do nothing but lie.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Idolaters' Last Defense**

Having been refuted on the substance of their taboos (vv. 136–145), the idolaters retreat to a philosophical defense. *Sa-yaqūlu alladhīna ashrakū law shā'a Allāhu mā ashraknā wa lā ābā'unā wa lā ḥarramnā min shay'* — "those who associate will say: Had God willed, we would not have associated, nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." The future tense *sa-yaqūlu*, "they will say," indicates a prediction: the Qur'an anticipates the argument before it is made, or foretells its repetition. The argument is: everything happens by God's will; we practice idolatry and our taboos; therefore God willed them; therefore they are legitimate — or at least we are not responsible.

The same argument appears in 16:35 ("Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything besides Him") and 43:20 ("Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them"). Al-Bayḍāwī notes that the argument aims to present their practices as part of a revealed or divinely intended order.

**Why the Argument Fails**

The argument's premise is, in one sense, true. The Qur'an itself says, "Had God willed, they would not have associated" (v. 107), and "Had God willed, they would not have done so" (v. 137). Ibn ʿAjībah acknowledges this: on one level, the idolaters' statement is accurate. God's will encompasses all that occurs; nothing happens outside it.

But the conclusion does not follow. God's *will* (*mashī'ah*) that something occur is not God's *approval* (*riḍā*) of it, nor His *command* (*amr*). God wills — in the sense of permits, in His creative decree — that human beings choose freely, including that they choose wrongly; He does not thereby command or approve the wrong choice. The theologians distinguish the *irādah kawniyyah* (the creative, existential will, by which all things come to be) from the *irādah sharʿiyyah* (the legislative will, by which God commands and loves). The idolaters' practices fall under the first — God permitted them to exist — but not the second — God did not command or approve them. To argue from the first to the second is to confuse permission with sanction.

The confusion is exposed by its consequences. If "God willed it" legitimated whatever occurs, then every crime would be legitimate; the murderer could say "had God willed, I would not have killed." No one accepts this reasoning in ordinary life — the idolaters themselves punished theft and murder. They reserved the argument for their religion alone, which shows it was not a principle but an evasion.

The deeper answer is the one the source commentary draws out: God is capable of altering their practices by force, but refrains in order to leave them free to choose. Their statement "had God willed, we would not have done it" is true precisely because God willed to give them choice — and therefore the responsibility for the choice is theirs. The argument that was meant to remove responsibility actually confirms it.

**"Those Who Were Before Them Had Similarly Denied"**

*Kadhālika kadhdhaba alladhīna min qablihim ḥattā dhāqū ba'sanā* — "thus denied those before them, until they tasted Our might." The argument is not new. Earlier peoples used it — the same fatalist excuse for the same idolatry — and it did not save them. They "tasted" (*dhāqū*) God's might, the vivid verb the Qur'an uses for experiencing punishment (3:106; 4:56; 6:30; 7:39; 8:35). The argument had no effect on the outcome. This is the empirical refutation: whatever the argument's theoretical appeal, the record shows that those who relied on it perished.

The word *kadhdhaba*, "denied," is significant. The Qur'an classifies the fatalist argument as *denial* — not as a sincere philosophical position but as a form of rejecting the messengers. The one who says "God willed my idolatry" is using God's Name to deny God's message.

**"Do You Have Any Knowledge That You Can Produce for Us?"**

*Qul hal ʿindakum min ʿilmin fa-tukhrijūhu lanā* — "Say: Do you have any knowledge that you can bring out for us?" The demand of verses 143–144 repeated: produce your evidence. Al-Bayḍāwī and Ibn Kathīr explain: do you have any proof that God approved your idolatry and prohibitions, that He commanded them, that they are His religion? The argument from divine will is not knowledge; it is an inference from the fact that things happened to the claim that God sanctioned them — and that inference is invalid. Knowledge of what God approves comes only from revelation, which they rejected.

**"You Follow Naught but Conjecture, and You Merely Surmise"**

*In tattabiʿūna illā al-ẓanna wa in antum illā takhruṣūn* — "you follow nothing but conjecture, and you do nothing but guess." The diagnosis of verse 116 exactly: *ẓann* and *khurṣ*, conjecture and guesswork. The fatalist argument, which sounds like theology, is unmasked as conjecture — a guess about God's approval dressed as an inference from God's power. The idolaters had no knowledge of what God approved; they surmised that whatever they did must be approved, since it happened. The Qur'an's word for this is *kharṣ*: estimation, the guessing of a quantity one cannot measure.

**The Theological Legacy**

This verse became a central text in Islamic theology's treatment of free will and predestination. The Jabriyyah (compulsionists) held that human acts are entirely God's and humans have no real agency — a position the Qur'an here puts in the mouth of the idolaters and condemns. The Qadariyyah and Muʿtazilah, reacting, held that humans create their own acts independently — a position other verses (v. 107, 137, 149) exclude. The mainstream Sunni position, articulated by al-Ashʿarī, al-Māturīdī, and refined by Ibn Taymiyyah, holds both: God's will encompasses all that occurs, and human beings truly choose and are truly responsible. The apparent tension is resolved by the distinction between God's creative and legislative will, and by the recognition that God's willing of human freedom is what makes human responsibility real. Verse 148 stands as the Qur'an's own rejection of fatalism-as-excuse: God's will is not an alibi.

The Prophet ﷺ addressed the same confusion. When the Companions asked, "Since everything is written, why should we work?" he answered: "Work, for everyone is eased toward that for which he was created" — and recited, "As for one who gives and fears God and believes in the best, We will ease him toward ease" (al-Bukhārī 4949; Muslim 2647). The decree does not remove the work; it is realized through the work.

**The Practical Warning**

The verse warns believers against the same evasion in subtler forms. "It was written" as an excuse for sin; "God willed it" as a reason not to change; "this is my nature" as a defense of a vice — each is verse 148's argument in new dress. The believer affirms the decree without using it as an alibi: he attributes his good to God's enabling and his sin to his own choice, seeks forgiveness for the latter, and never says of his wrongdoing, "had God willed, I would not have done it," as though that settled the matter. The idolaters said it, and tasted God's might.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:149

> **Say, “Allah has the most conclusive argument. Had it been His Will, He would have easily imposed guidance upon all of you.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Argument That Ends Arguments**

*Qul fa-li-Llāhi al-ḥujjatu al-bālighah* — "Say: To God belongs the conclusive argument." The idolaters produced no knowledge, only conjecture (v. 148). Against their conjecture stands God's *ḥujjah* — proof, argument, demonstration — which is *bālighah*: reaching its goal, conclusive, decisive. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Ṭūsī explain: the argument that is clear and incontrovertible, that reveals all opposing arguments as false, and that achieves its purpose of establishing truth and removing doubt. The word *bālighah* is from *balagha*, to reach, arrive at; a *ḥujjah bālighah* is one that arrives — that gets all the way to certainty and leaves the opponent nothing to say.

The definite article and the prepositional structure (*li-Llāhi al-ḥujjah*) convey exclusivity: the conclusive argument is God's, not theirs. Whatever arguments the idolaters advance — the fatalist excuse, the appeal to ancestors, the demand for signs — are not *ḥujjah* but *ẓann*. God alone has proof.

**What Is God's Conclusive Argument?**

The commentators identify it in several ways that complement each other. Ibn ʿAjībah and al-Bayḍāwī: the argument is constituted by the messengers and the revelation they brought. God sent prophets, gave them signs, revealed books, and explained the truth so clearly that no one can claim ignorance — "˹All were˺ messengers delivering good news and warnings so humanity should have no excuse before Allah after ˹the coming of˺ the messengers" (4:165). The messengers *are* God's argument; after them, the human being has no argument left.

Al-Rāzī and others add: the argument is also the evidence in creation and in reason. The sūrah has argued from the heavens and the earth (v. 1), from the growth of seed and the succession of night and day (vv. 95–99), from the logic of Abraham's search (vv. 76–79). These are God's arguments too, available to everyone with sight and intellect. The seventh Shīʿī Imam Mūsā al-Kāẓim is reported to have said: "God has two arguments against mankind: an outward one and an inward one. The outward is the messengers, prophets, and imams; the inward is the intellects" (al-Kāfī). The formulation captures a truth accepted across the traditions: God has established His proof both by sending revelation from outside and by placing reason within.

The phrase *ḥujjat Allāh* became a term of art in Islamic thought for certain, irrefutable proof. Shāh Walī Allāh of Delhi titled his great work on the rationale of the Sharīʿah *Ḥujjat Allāh al-Bālighah*, taking the phrase from this verse. Twelver Shīʿīs call their Imams "proofs of God" (*ḥujaj Allāh*). In every usage, the sense is the same: a demonstration from God that settles the matter.

**The Connection to Abraham**

Verse 83 said of Abraham: "That was Our argument (*ḥujjah*) which We gave to Abraham against his people." Abraham's demonstration — the systematic elimination of star, moon, and sun as gods — was a *ḥujjah* given by God. Verse 149 generalizes: God possesses the conclusive argument, and He gives it to His messengers to deploy. The sūrah's own argumentation — including the interrogation of verses 143–144 — is an instance of the *ḥujjah bālighah*, and its effect on the idolaters (silence, then evasion into fatalism) demonstrates its conclusiveness.

**"Had He Willed, He Could Surely Have Guided You All"**

*Fa-law shā'a la-hadākum ajmaʿīn* — "so had He willed, He would have guided you all together." The verse answers the idolaters' fatalist argument with its own correct form. They said: "had God willed, we would not have associated." The Qur'an replies: yes — had He willed, He would have guided all of you, by compulsion, leaving no one in error. He did not so will. Why?

The source commentary records two lines of interpretation. Some (Ibn ʿAjībah, Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī) read the verse as indicating that God's will is to guide some and not others — since not all are guided, and God could have guided all, it follows that He willed the guidance of some only; this is supported by verses on God's misleading (2:26; 6:125; 74:31). Others (al-Ṭūsī, and the mainstream of those who emphasize responsibility) read it as indicating that God, though capable of guiding all by force, chose not to compel, because He willed to make human beings responsible (*mukallaf*) — to leave them free to accept or reject guidance, so that the Hereafter's judgment would be just. Compare verse 35: "Had God willed, He would have gathered them all to guidance."

Al-Ṭūsī's argument is instructive: if God compelled people to belief or unbelief, He would have no *ḥujjah* against the disbelievers — they could truthfully say, as the idolaters of verse 148 falsely said, that God made them disbelieve. The conclusive argument requires that people be free. So the two halves of the verse are connected: God's argument is conclusive *because* He did not compel; His refraining from forced guidance is what makes the argument, and the judgment, just.

The two lines of interpretation need not conflict. God wills to guide those who turn to Him and leaves in error those who turn away — and this is both a real distinction in His will (the first reading) and a consequence of human choice within His decree (the second). The verse denies only that God's not compelling everyone gives anyone an excuse.

**The Logic of the Two Verses**

Verses 148–149 form a tight exchange. The idolaters: "God willed our idolatry, so we are not responsible." The Qur'an: "Have you knowledge of that? No — only conjecture. The knowledge is God's; the conclusive argument is His. And yes, He could have compelled you all to guidance — He chose not to, so that your choice would be real and His argument against you complete." The idolaters' appeal to divine will is turned around: divine will established the freedom that makes them responsible, and established the proofs that leave them without excuse.

**The Believer's Confidence and Humility**

The verse gives the believer both. Confidence: the truth he holds rests on the conclusive argument — the messengers, the revelation, the evidence of creation and reason — and no counterargument can stand against it. He need not fear debate; he need not win every exchange; the *ḥujjah* is God's and it has already arrived. Humility: he was not guided by his own superiority. Had God willed, He could have guided all; that the believer was guided is God's gift, and he holds it with gratitude, not pride. He prays, as the sūrah has taught, to be kept on the path, knowing that guidance was given and can be withheld.

**The Verse in Daʿwah**

Finally, the verse shapes how the believer calls others. He presents God's argument — the proofs of revelation and reason — as fully and clearly as he can, because the argument is conclusive and deserves full presentation. But he does not imagine that his presentation compels belief, because "had He willed, He would have guided you all" — and He willed instead that hearts be free. The caller's task is to convey the *ḥujjah*; the response belongs to the hearer and the guidance to God.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:150

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Bring your witnesses who can testify that Allah has forbidden this.” If they ˹falsely˺ testify, do not testify with them. And do not follow the desires of those who deny Our proofs, disbelieve in the Hereafter, and set up equals with their Lord.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Demand for Evidence**

The section on the idolaters' taboos closes with a last challenge. *Qul halumma shuhadā'akumu alladhīna yash-hadūna anna Allāha ḥarrama hādhā* — "Say: Bring here your witnesses who testify that God forbade this." The escalation is deliberate. Verse 143 asked for knowledge; verse 144 asked whether they were present; verse 148 asked whether they had any knowledge to produce; verse 150 asks for witnesses. Every possible source of evidence has now been requested: logic, presence, knowledge, testimony. The idolaters can produce none.

The word *halumma* — "come, bring" — is an emphatic summons, used in Arabic to call someone to come forward with something. The Prophet ﷺ is instructed to demand, publicly, that the idolaters produce anyone who can testify that God forbade the cattle and crops they had made taboo (vv. 136, 138–139, 143–144). It is the language of a court: the claim has been made; let the witnesses be called.

**The Standard of Testimony**

The demand reflects a principle of Islamic epistemology and law: a claim requires evidence, and the burden lies on the claimant. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies" (al-Bayhaqī 21201; al-Tirmidhī 1341 similar). The idolaters claimed that God forbade certain things; they must prove it. That God did *not* forbid something needs no proof — the default is permission (v. 145: "I do not find... anything forbidden except"). This distribution of burden protects the freedom God gave and guards against the multiplication of prohibitions on the strength of assertion alone.

**"Then If They Bear Witness, Do Not Bear Witness with Them"**

*Fa-in shahidū fa-lā tash-had maʿahum* — "then if they testify, do not testify with them." The verse anticipates that some may come forward — false witnesses who will swear that God forbade these things. The Prophet ﷺ is told: do not join their testimony; do not lend it credence; do not act as though their oath makes it true. False testimony does not become true by being sworn. The commentators note that the verse presupposes the idolaters' witnesses would be lying, since no true witness to a divine prohibition could exist where none was revealed.

The instruction has a general force: a believer does not confirm a falsehood because others assert it, however many or however confident they are. The majority of verse 116 may swear to a thing; the believer does not swear with them. Testimony is a serious act — the Qur'an forbids concealing it (2:283) and commands standing firm in it "Stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives" (4:135) — and false testimony is among the greatest sins: the Prophet ﷺ, listing the gravest sins, sat up from reclining and said, "And false testimony! And false speech!" and repeated it until the Companions wished he would stop (al-Bukhārī 2654; Muslim 87).

**"And Do Not Follow the Caprices of Those Who Deny Our Signs"**

*Wa lā tattabiʿ ahwā'a alladhīna kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā* — "and do not follow the desires of those who deny Our signs." The verse shifts from testimony to following. Even if the Prophet ﷺ does not join their testimony, he might be pressured to accommodate their practices — to compromise, to tolerate the taboos as harmless custom. The verse forbids this. Their claims are *ahwā'*, caprices, whims — the word of verses 56 and 119 — and the caprices of those who deny God's signs are not to be followed in anything. The prohibition on following the caprices of the deniers recurs throughout the Qur'an (2:120, 145; 5:48–49; 13:37; 42:15; 45:18), always in the context of pressure to bend revelation toward what others want.

**The Three Descriptions**

The verse describes those whose caprices are not to be followed with three attributes. They *deny Our signs* — reject the revelation and the evidences. They *believe not in the Hereafter* — deny resurrection and judgment. They *ascribe equals unto their Lord* — commit *shirk*, setting up rivals to God. The source commentary identifies the last two as their central religious errors, and the sūrah has been built around them: the denial of the Hereafter (vv. 29–32) and the association of partners (throughout). The three together define the idolaters' condition and explain why their caprices are worthless as a guide: one who denies the signs, the Hereafter, and God's uniqueness has no standard by which to judge anything, and his preferences reflect only desire.

**"Ascribe Equals unto Their Lord"**

*Wa hum bi-rabbihim yaʿdilūn* — "and they make equals to their Lord." The verb *ʿadala* here means to set something as equal, to equate — the verb of verse 1: "yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord." The sūrah returns, in this closing verse of its section on invented law, to the phrase with which it began. The inclusion forms a frame: the sūrah opened by charging the disbelievers with *ʿadl* (making equals) despite God's creation of the heavens and earth, and now, having shown in detail how their invented religion works, it repeats the charge. Their taboos on cattle and crops are the concrete expression of setting up equals to God — because to legislate in His Name without His word is to make oneself, or one's idols, His equal in the right to command.

**The Section's Conclusion**

Verses 136–150 have accomplished a complete treatment of invented religion. They described its practices (shares, taboos, sex-based rules, infanticide); exposed their arbitrariness (which sex, which category?); demolished their claimed source (were you present? bring your witnesses?); stated the true law in its simplicity (four prohibitions); explained the different law of the Jews (recompense for rebellion); answered the fatalist defense (God's will is not an alibi); and asserted God's conclusive argument. Verse 150 closes the case by demanding witnesses and forbidding accommodation.

What follows — verses 151–153 — is the positive counterpart: the commandments God actually enjoined, recited by the Prophet ﷺ in place of the fabrications. The transition is marked by the parallel: the idolaters cannot produce witnesses that "God forbade this"; the Prophet ﷺ will now say, "Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden." The false prohibitions are cleared away so that the true ones can be heard.

**The Enduring Discipline**

The verse trains the believer in two refusals. He refuses to confirm as God's law what cannot be shown to be God's law — he does not "bear witness with them," however many they are. And he refuses to follow the caprices of those who have rejected the standards of truth — he does not shape his religion to accommodate the preferences of those who deny its foundations. Both refusals require firmness, and the verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ in the singular, as though to say: even if you stand alone, do not testify with them and do not follow them. The believer who inherits this instruction inherits also the confidence of verse 149 that makes it bearable: the conclusive argument is God's.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:151

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Come! Let me recite to you what your Lord has forbidden to you: do not associate others with Him ˹in worship˺. ˹Do not fail to˺ honour your parents. Do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for you and for them. Do not come near indecencies, openly or secretly. Do not take a ˹human˺ life—made sacred by Allah—except with ˹legal˺ right. This is what He has commanded you, so perhaps you will understand.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The True Prohibitions**

Against the idolaters' fabricated taboos, the Prophet ﷺ now recites what God actually forbade. *Qul taʿālaw atlu mā ḥarrama rabbukum ʿalaykum* — "Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you." The summons *taʿālaw* — "come up, come here" — answers the *halumma* of verse 150. They were told to bring their witnesses; now they are invited to hear the genuine law. The verb *atlu*, "I recite," marks the source: this is not the Prophet's opinion but recited revelation — the *ʿilm* the idolaters lacked.

Verses 151–153 form what the commentators call the *waṣāyā al-ʿashr*, the ten commandments of the Qur'an — not identical to the Decalogue of Moses, but overlapping with it and closing with the same theme of the one path. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "In Sūrah al-Anʿām are the clear verses (*muḥkamāt*), the Mother of the Book" — and recited these three verses (al-Ḥākim 3232). ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Who among you will pledge to me on three verses?" and recited 6:151–153, then said, "Whoever fulfills them, his reward is with God; and whoever falls short in any of them and God takes him to account in this world, it is his expiation; and whoever is deferred to the Hereafter, his matter is with God — if He wills He punishes him and if He wills He pardons him" (al-Ḥākim 3233; cf. al-Bukhārī 18 for the parallel pledge). Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said these verses are the opening of the Torah: "In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful: Say, come, I will recite..."

**First: Ascribe Nothing as Partner unto Him**

*Allā tushrikū bihi shay'ā* — "that you associate nothing with Him." The first prohibition is *shirk*, in every form. The sūrah has catalogued the forms: idols (v. 74), celestial bodies (vv. 76–78), jinn (v. 100), invented sons and daughters (v. 100), invented law (vv. 136–150). "Nothing" (*shay'ā*) — not an idol, not a star, not a spirit, not a saint, not a desire, not a legislator. The prohibition is placed first because every other prohibition depends on it: the one who associates partners with God has no ground for any other obligation, since he has divided the source of obligation.

Grammatically, the clause "that you associate nothing" could be read as the content of what is forbidden ("He forbade you: that you associate") or as a new command following the recitation ("I recite what He forbade — [and I command]: do not associate"). Both yield the same meaning. The construction shifts, in the following clauses, from what is forbidden to what is commanded (kindness to parents), which shows that "what your Lord has forbidden" is being used loosely for "what your Lord has enjoined," positive and negative together.

**Second: Be Virtuous Toward Parents**

*Wa bi-l-wālidayni iḥsānā* — "And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺," The pairing of *tawḥīd* with kindness to parents recurs throughout the Qur'an (2:83; 4:36; 17:23; 31:14). Al-Rāzī explains the logic: after God, no one has a greater claim on a person than his parents, who were the means of his existence and cared for him when he could not care for himself. The debt to God is followed immediately by the debt to those through whom God brought one into being. The word *iḥsān* — excellence, doing beautifully — asks more than obedience or maintenance; it asks that the treatment be beautiful. The Prophet ﷺ, asked who most deserves good companionship, said, "Your mother," three times, and then, "your father" (al-Bukhārī 5971; Muslim 2548). And: "The pleasure of the Lord is in the pleasure of the parent, and the anger of the Lord is in the anger of the parent" (al-Tirmidhī 1899).

**Third: Slay Not Your Children for Fear of Poverty**

*Wa lā taqtulū awlādakum min imlāq* — "Do not kill your children for fear of poverty" *Imlāq* is destitution, poverty — the actual poverty of the parent (17:31 uses *khashyata imlāq*, "for fear of poverty," the anticipated poverty). After the duty of children to parents comes the duty of parents to children: not to kill them. The verse addresses the practice of verses 137 and 140 and gives the reason that dissolves it: *naḥnu narzuqukum wa iyyāhum* — "We provide for you and for them." The order here is "you and them"; in 17:31 it is "them and you." The commentators note the difference: here the poverty is actual, so the parents' provision is mentioned first (you are fed, and so will they be); there the poverty is feared, so the children's provision is mentioned first (they bring their own provision). In both cases the answer to fear is the Provider.

**Fourth: Approach Not Indecencies, Outward or Inward**

*Wa lā taqrabū al-fawāḥisha mā ẓahara minhā wa mā baṭan* — "and do not approach indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden." *Fawāḥish* (singular *fāḥishah*) are gross indecencies — most often sexual sins (4:15, 22; 17:32), but here, as the source commentary notes, more likely all serious moral transgressions. The command is not "do not commit" but "do not approach" (*lā taqrabū*): stay away from the paths that lead there, the situations, the preliminaries — as 17:32 says of fornication, "It is truly a shameful deed and an evil way" The distinction of outward and inward repeats verse 120; al-Rāzī explains its point: one who avoids sin in public but commits it in private shows that his motive was fear of blame, not obedience to God. The believer is the same in secret as in the open.

**Fifth: Slay Not the Soul Save by Right**

*Wa lā taqtulū al-nafsa allatī ḥarrama Allāhu illā bi-l-ḥaqq* — "and do not kill the soul that God has made sacred except by right." Human life is *ḥarām*, inviolable, by God's decree. The exception "by right" (*bi-l-ḥaqq*) covers lawful execution under due process — for murder, for waging war against society (5:33), and the other cases the Prophet ﷺ enumerated: "The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in one of three cases: a life for a life, the married adulterer, and the one who abandons his religion and separates from the community" (al-Bukhārī 6878; Muslim 1676). Outside such right, killing is among the gravest sins: "whoever kills a soul, other than for a soul or corruption on earth, it is as if he had killed all mankind" (5:32). The prohibition follows the prohibition on killing children as the general follows the particular: no soul, child or adult, may be killed except by right.

**"This He Has Enjoined upon You, That Haply You May Understand"**

*Dhālikum waṣṣākum bihi laʿallakum taʿqilūn* — "that He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand." The verb *waṣṣā* — to enjoin, to charge as a last testament — is the verb the idolaters were asked about in verse 144: "were you present when God *enjoined* this?" Here is the true enjoining. The verse ends with *taʿqilūn*, "that you may use reason." The five commandments of this verse — *tawḥīd*, parents, children, indecency, life — are the foundations of any rational moral order; a society that violates them destroys itself. Al-Rāzī observes that the five commands of this verse pertain to outward conduct and the four of the next to matters more hidden; and that this verse's ending "that you may understand" fits commands whose rationality is evident, while the next verse's "that you may remember" fits commands that require recalling one's obligations, and the third verse's "that you may be reverent" fits the summary command to follow the one path.

**The Structure of the Ten**

The commandments of verses 151–153 are conventionally counted as ten: (1) no *shirk*; (2) kindness to parents; (3) no infanticide; (4) no indecency; (5) no unlawful killing; (6) protection of the orphan's property; (7) just measure and weight; (8) just speech; (9) fulfillment of God's covenant; (10) following the straight path. They move from God to family to society to the self's integrity and back to God. They are the positive counterpart to everything the sūrah has exposed as fabrication, and they were recited in Makkah — before there was a Muslim state to enforce them — as the moral constitution of the community that would come.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:152

> **And do not come near the wealth of the orphan—unless intending to enhance it—until they attain maturity. Give full measure and weigh with justice. We never require of any soul more than what it can afford. Whenever you speak, maintain justice—even regarding a close relative. And fulfil your covenant with Allah. This is what He has commanded you, so perhaps you will be mindful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Table**

Verse 151 gave five commandments concerning God, family, and life. Verse 152 gives four more concerning property, commerce, speech, and covenant — the obligations that hold a society together in its transactions. Al-Rāzī's observation that these concern more hidden matters is apt: the misuse of an orphan's wealth, the shaving of a measure, the shading of testimony, the quiet breach of a pact are sins that often escape notice. The verse brings them under the same *waṣiyyah* as the great prohibitions.

**Sixth: Approach Not the Orphan's Property**

*Wa lā taqrabū māla al-yatīmi illā bi-llatī hiya aḥsanu ḥattā yablugha ashuddah* — "and do not approach the orphan's property except in the way that is best, until he reaches his full strength." The orphan (*yatīm*) — a minor who has lost his father — is the paradigm of the vulnerable person whose rights depend on the conscience of others. His property is in a guardian's hands, and no one is watching but God. The verse says: do not *approach* it — the same verb as for indecencies — except *bi-llatī hiya aḥsan*, "with that which is best." Al-Ṭabarī explains the exception: the guardian may manage the property to preserve and grow it (investing rather than letting it dwindle), and a poor guardian may take a modest, reasonable amount for his labor, as 4:6 permits ("whoever is poor, let him consume reasonably"), while the rich guardian should abstain. The repetition of this command verbatim in 17:34 signals its weight.

"Until he reaches his full strength" (*ashudd*) — al-Rāzī explains this as the age at which knowledge and judgment are sufficiently developed; it is a qualitative threshold, assessed by testing the orphan's competence (4:6: "test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you find in them sound judgment, release their property to them"), not merely a number of years. The Prophet ﷺ counted "consuming the orphan's property" among the seven destructive sins (al-Bukhārī 2766; Muslim 89), and the Qur'an describes those who do so as "eating fire into their bellies" (4:10).

**Seventh: Observe Fully the Measure and the Balance with Justice**

*Wa awfū al-kayla wa al-mīzāna bi-l-qisṭ* — "and give full measure and weight with justice." Commerce is the daily interface between people, and its integrity depends on the honesty of measures. The command is to *fulfill* (*awfū*) the measure and the balance — to give the full amount, neither less (which cheats the buyer) nor, by implication, taking more than due (which cheats the seller). *Qisṭ* is equity, fairness — the exact balance. The theme recurs (7:85; 11:84–85; 17:35; 26:181–182; 55:8–9) and an entire sūrah opens with it: "but give less when they measure or weigh for buyers" (83:1–3). Shuʿayb's people were destroyed in part for this sin. The believer's honesty in the marketplace is a religious act as much as his prayer.

**"We Task No Soul Beyond Its Capacity"**

*Lā nukallifu nafsan illā wusʿahā* — "We do not burden a soul except to its capacity." The clause is placed immediately after the command about measures, and the commentators explain its position: absolute precision in weighing is beyond human capacity — a grain more or less is inevitable — so God requires the honest effort, not superhuman exactness. The principle is general: it appears in 2:286, 7:42, 23:62, and 65:7, and is a foundational doctrine of Islamic law. Every obligation in the ten commandments — and in the whole religion — is within human reach. God does not command the impossible. This makes the covenant fair and the failure inexcusable: no one can say the commands were beyond him.

**Eighth: When You Speak, Be Just, Even Against a Kinsman**

*Wa idhā qultum fa-ʿdilū wa law kāna dhā qurbā* — "and when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a relative." The command governs speech in general and testimony in particular. Al-Rāzī reads it broadly: speak with truth and integrity always — in judgment, in testimony, in report, in praise and blame. The hardest test of just speech is kinship: the temptation to testify for one's relative, to shade the truth for one's tribe, was the ruling ethic of pre-Islamic Arabia ("support your brother, right or wrong"). The verse cuts this: justice in speech even when a kinsman is on the other side. Compare 4:135: "Be maintainers of justice, witnesses for God, even against yourselves or parents or relatives." And 5:8: "Let not hatred of a people cause you to be unjust; be just — that is nearer to God-consciousness." The Prophet ﷺ redefined the tribal maxim: "Support your brother whether he is the wrongdoer or the wronged." They asked, "We support him when he is wronged, but how when he is the wrongdoer?" He said, "You restrain him from wrongdoing; that is supporting him" (al-Bukhārī 6952).

**Ninth: Fulfill the Pact of God**

*Wa bi-ʿahdi Allāhi awfū* — "and God's covenant, fulfill." The *ʿahd* of God is understood by al-Ṭabarī as the whole of what God has enjoined and forbidden — the covenant of obedience implied in creation and made explicit in revelation. It includes the primordial covenant of 7:172 ("Am I not your Lord?"), the covenant of the believers to obey, and every oath and vow sworn in God's Name. Compare 2:40 ("fulfill My covenant and I will fulfill yours") and 13:20 ("those who fulfill the covenant of God and do not break the pact"). The command closes the transactional section with the transaction that underlies all others: the servant's pledge to his Lord. One who keeps faith with God keeps faith with the orphan, the customer, and the truth; one who breaks it will break the rest.

**"This He Has Enjoined upon You, That Haply You May Remember"**

*Dhālikum waṣṣākum bihi laʿallakum tadhakkarūn* — "that He has enjoined upon you, that you may remember." The refrain repeats with a changed ending. Verse 151 said "that you may understand"; verse 152 says "that you may remember." Al-Rāzī suggests the fit: the commands of this verse are ones people know but forget under pressure — the guardian forgets the orphan's right when he needs money, the merchant forgets the measure when the margin is thin, the witness forgets justice when his brother is accused. They need not new understanding but remembrance. The commandments are given so that in the moment of temptation the believer *remembers*.

**The Coherence of the Verse**

The four commands share a structure: each concerns a situation where one party has power over another and could abuse it without detection — the guardian over the orphan, the seller over the buyer, the speaker over the truth, the servant over his own promise. In each, justice depends on inner integrity, not external enforcement. This is why the verse belongs with the "inward" commands: it addresses the conscience where no one watches. And this is why it ends with remembrance: the conscience is kept alive by recalling, again and again, that God sees the measure, the testimony, and the orphan's coin.

**The Practical Program**

The verse yields a daily ethic: guard the property of the vulnerable as you would your own; give full measure in every exchange, of goods, of labor, of time; speak the truth though it costs your kin; and keep every promise made in God's Name, beginning with the promise of obedience. These are not lofty ideals but ordinary disciplines, and the verse reminds the believer that they are within his capacity — "We task no soul beyond its capacity" — so that he has no excuse for neglecting them.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:153

> **Indeed, that is My Path—perfectly straight. So follow it and do not follow other ways, for they will lead you away from His Way. This is what He has commanded you, so perhaps you will be conscious ˹of Allah˺.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Tenth Commandment: The One Path**

*Wa anna hādhā ṣirāṭī mustaqīman fa-ttabiʿūh* — "and that this is My path, straight, so follow it." The ten commandments close with the command that gathers the other nine: follow the path. The demonstrative "this" (*hādhā*) refers to what has just been recited — the commandments of verses 151–152 — and, more broadly, to the whole religion of which they are the summary. It is called *ṣirāṭī*, "My path," in God's own voice: the path belongs to Him, leads to Him, and is defined by Him. The adjective *mustaqīman* stands, as in verse 126, as a circumstantial description: this is My path in its state of straightness, always straight.

The commentators (al-Rāzī and most others) understand the path specifically as the religion of Islam as brought by the Prophet ﷺ — the Qur'an and his Sunnah — while acknowledging that in its essence it is the one religion of all the prophets, the *dīn* of Abraham that verse 161 will name. Compare 5:15–16: "through which Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace, brings them out of darkness and into light by His Will, and guides them to the Straight Path"

**"And Follow Not Other Ways"**

*Wa lā tattabiʿū al-subula fa-tafarraqa bikum ʿan sabīlih* — "and do not follow the ways, for they will separate you from His way." The contrast is between *ṣirāṭ* — singular, the highway — and *subul* — plural, the paths, the byways. God's way is one; the alternatives are many. And the alternatives *separate* (*tafarraqa*) — scatter, disperse, divide. The verb is significant: the other paths do not merely lead elsewhere; they fragment. Those who leave the one path do not arrive at a single alternative but at countless ones, each further from the others and from the source.

The "other ways" have been identified by the commentators as the paths of idolatry, of Judaism and Christianity in their departures from the original monotheism, of innovation (*bidʿah*), of the desires (*ahwā'*), and of the satans who call to each of them. Mujāhid said: "the innovations and the doubts." All are covered. Any way other than the one God laid is a *sabīl* that separates.

**The Ḥadīth of the Line**

The verse's image was made concrete by the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Masʿūd reported:

> The Messenger of God ﷺ drew a line for us with his hand and said: "This is the path of God, straight." Then he drew lines to its right and to its left and said: "These are the paths; upon each of them is a satan calling to it." Then he recited: "And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow the ways, for they will separate you from His way." (Aḥmad 4142; al-Nasā'ī, *al-Kubrā* 11174; al-Ḥākim 3241, who graded it sound)

The drawing makes the verse visible: one line, and many branching from it, each with its caller. The believer's task is to stay on the one line and to recognize the callers on the branches for what they are. Jābir reported a similar drawing in which the Prophet ﷺ said of the side lines, "These are the paths of Satan," and of the middle line, "This is the path of God" (Ibn Mājah 11).

**The Two Pronouns**

The verse shifts from "My path" (*ṣirāṭī*) to "His way" (*sabīlih*). God speaks in the first person and then refers to Himself in the third. The commentators note that this *iltifāt* (grammatical shift) adds solemnity: "My path" expresses the intimacy of God's address; "His way" expresses the majesty of the One whose way it is. The path is both personal and absolute.

**"This He Has Enjoined upon You, That Haply You May Be Reverent"**

*Dhālikum waṣṣākum bihi laʿallakum tattaqūn* — "that He has enjoined upon you, that you may be God-fearing." The third refrain, with the third ending. Verse 151: "that you may understand." Verse 152: "that you may remember." Verse 153: "that you may have *taqwā*." The progression is one of ascent. Understanding the commandments is the first stage; remembering them under pressure is the second; and *taqwā* — the settled disposition of God-consciousness that keeps one on the path without needing to reason it out each time — is the goal. The one who has *taqwā* does not stand at every fork weighing the branches; he walks the line because he fears and loves the One who drew it.

**The Unity of the Ten**

Verses 151–153 form a unit that Islamic tradition has treated as the Qur'an's fundamental moral charter. They begin with the One God and end with the one path — *tawḥīd* in belief at the start, *tawḥīd* in practice at the end. Between them lie the obligations to parents, children, life, the vulnerable, commerce, speech, and covenant. The unit says: worship One, walk one way, and everything between follows. Ibn Masʿūd said: "Whoever wishes to look at the testament of the Messenger of God ﷺ, on which is his seal, let him read: 'Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you' to 'that you may be reverent'" (al-Tirmidhī 3070; al-Ṭabarānī). The Prophet's testament — his *waṣiyyah* to his community — is these three verses.

**The Sociology of the Verse**

The verse contains a warning about religious division that the sūrah will develop in verse 159. The mechanism it names — following the many paths leads to fragmentation — is observable in history. Communities that abandon the revealed path for human devisings do not arrive at a unified alternative; they splinter, and each splinter claims the truth. The remedy is not a new human unity but return to the one *ṣirāṭ*. "And hold firmly to the rope of Allah and do not be divided" (3:103). The rope and the path are the same thing: what God gave, not what people constructed.

**The Believer's Daily Practice**

The verse gives the believer his bearings. He asks, of any teaching or practice, whether it is on the line or on a branch — whether it is God's path or one of the *subul*. He is suspicious of novelty in religion, not from rigidity but because the branches are where the callers stand. He recites, seventeen times a day at least, "Guide us along the Straight Path," (1:6), and this verse tells him what he is asking for: the one way God enjoined, in the ten commandments and everything that flows from them. And he knows that the request is answered by walking: *fa-ttabiʿūh*, "so follow it." The path is straight; the following is the believer's part.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:154

> **Additionally, We gave Moses the Scripture, completing the favour upon those who do good, detailing everything, and as a guide and a mercy, so perhaps they would be certain of the meeting with their Lord.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn to the Torah**

After reciting God's commandments, the sūrah turns to the Book in which those commandments were earlier given. *Thumma ātaynā Mūsā al-kitāb* — "then We gave Moses the Book." The Torah is invoked here for several reasons. It shows that the ten commandments just recited are not a novelty but the continuation of what God gave Moses — the same moral law, revealed to the same human nature. It prepares the argument of verses 155–157, that the Makkans can no longer plead ignorance of revelation. And it positions the Qur'an (v. 155) as the successor to the Torah in a single line of guidance.

The word *thumma*, "then," has puzzled the commentators, since the Torah preceded the Qur'an. The explanation: *thumma* here marks sequence in recitation or in the order of discourse, not in time — "then [know that] We gave Moses..." — or it connects to a more distant reference, such as verse 84's account of Abraham's line and the prophets who followed. Al-Zamakhsharī and others read it as sequence of narration: having stated the commandments, the sūrah now goes on to say something about the earlier Book.

**"Complete for Those Who Would Be Virtuous"**

*Tamāman ʿalā alladhī aḥsana* — "as a completion for the one who did good." The phrase has several readings. Al-Ṭabarī: the Torah was given as a completion of God's favor upon those who did good — the righteous among the Israelites, who received in it the perfection of guidance. Others: it was given as a completion upon Moses himself, who "did good" in his obedience and mission, and to whom God completed His blessing by revealing the Book. Others read *alladhī* generically: complete for whoever does good — that is, the Torah is a complete provision for anyone who follows it in virtue. All three converge: the Torah was a complete gift to those who received it well.

The word *tamām*, completion, echoes verse 115: "the Word of your Lord is completed (*tammat*) in truth and justice." The same completeness is ascribed to the Qur'an there and to the Torah here. God's books are complete for their purposes.

**"An Exposition of All Things"**

*Wa tafṣīlan li-kulli shay'* — "and a detailing of everything." The Torah expounded in detail what its people needed — law, narrative, guidance, warning. The word *tafṣīl* is from the root of *faṣṣala*, the verb the sūrah has used for God's detailing of the signs and for the Qur'an as *mufaṣṣal* (v. 114). 'All things' is understood as all things needed for religion and law, not literally every fact — the same sense in which the Qur'an is "an explanation of all things, a guide, a mercy, and good news for those who ˹fully˺ submit." (16:89). The parallel descriptions, as the source commentary notes, indicate that the Qur'an regards the Torah as a genuine, detailed revelation of the same kind as itself.

**"A Guidance and a Mercy"**

*Wa hudan wa raḥmah* — "as a guide and a mercy" (6:154). The two words that will describe the Qur'an in verse 157 ("a clear proof—a guide and mercy" (6:157)). The Torah guided — showed the way — and was mercy — a gift for the welfare of those who received it. The Qur'an says of it elsewhere: "Indeed, We revealed the Torah, containing guidance and light, by which the prophets, who submitted themselves to Allah, made judgments for Jews" (5:44), and "And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guide for the Children of Israel" (17:2). The Qur'an's respect for the Torah as a revealed book is consistent and explicit, even as it charges its custodians with concealment and distortion (2:75, 79; 5:13).

**"That Haply They Might Believe in the Meeting with Their Lord"**

*Laʿallahum bi-liqā'i rabbihim yu'minūn* — "that they might believe in the meeting with their Lord." The Torah's purpose, like the Qur'an's, was to produce faith in the encounter with God — the resurrection, the judgment, the standing before Him. This is stated as the culmination of the Book's descriptions: complete, detailed, guiding, merciful — *in order that* they believe in meeting their Lord. All of scripture's completeness and detail serve this end. The "meeting with God" is the sūrah's persistent theme (vv. 30, 31, 94, 130), and the verse establishes that it was the Torah's theme too. Some have claimed the Hebrew Bible lacks a clear doctrine of resurrection; the Qur'an says the Torah was given to produce faith in the meeting with God, and the Prophet ﷺ affirmed that Moses and all the prophets taught the Hereafter.

**The Torah's Continuing Validity**

The source commentary draws out an implication: the verse presents the Torah as a valid source of guidance and a path to virtue, an idea made explicit in 5:43–45, where the Jews are told to judge by what God revealed in the Torah. The Qur'an does not present itself as abolishing the earlier books but as confirming them (*muṣaddiq*) and serving as a guardian over them (*muhaymin*, 5:48) — correcting where they were distorted, completing where they were partial, and superseding in law where God willed. The moral core — the commandments of verses 151–153 — is common to both.

**The Argument the Verse Prepares**

The placement of the verse is strategic. The Makkans had been saying, in effect, "We were not sent a book; the Jews and Christians were." Verse 154 acknowledges this — yes, Moses was given a complete Book — and verse 155 answers: and now you have been given one. The excuse is being removed step by step. By describing the Torah in the same terms as the Qur'an (complete, detailed, guidance, mercy), the verse also establishes that what the Makkans are receiving is not a lesser thing but the same kind of gift — indeed, the final form of it.

**The Believer's Attitude Toward Earlier Revelation**

The verse shapes how a Muslim regards the Torah and, by extension, the Gospel. He believes they were revealed by God — this is an article of faith (2:136, 285). He honors Moses as one of the greatest messengers, mentioned more often in the Qur'an than any other. He regards the moral law of the Torah as God's law, confirmed in the Qur'an. He does not consider the earlier books as available in their pristine form, and takes the Qur'an as the criterion for what in them is preserved. And he sees in the succession of books — Torah, Gospel, Qur'an — a single mercy unfolding, so that his own scripture is not a rupture with the past but its completion. The verse's language — *tamām*, *tafṣīl*, *hudā*, *raḥmah* — teaches him to speak of the Torah with the respect the Qur'an itself shows.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:155

> **This is a blessed Book We have revealed. So follow it and be mindful ˹of Allah˺, so you may be shown mercy.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"And This Is a Blessed Book"**

*Wa hādhā kitābun anzalnāhu mubārak* — "and this is a Book We have sent down, blessed." The demonstrative *hādhā*, "this," turns from the Torah of the previous verse to the Qur'an — the Book now being recited. The verse is brief but dense with meaning. Three things are said about the Book: it is *kitāb*, a scripture, of the same kind as what Moses received; it is *anzalnāhu*, "We sent it down," from God, not composed by a man; and it is *mubārak*, blessed.

**The Meaning of "Mubārak"**

*Barakah* is blessing in the sense of abundant, lasting, increasing good — the root suggests permanence and increase, as water gathers and stays in a *birkah*, a pool. A *mubārak* thing is one in which God has placed lasting good that grows and spreads. The Qur'an is *mubārak* in several senses the commentators elaborate. It is blessed in its content: guidance, law, wisdom, healing (17:82). It is blessed in its effects: those who follow it find their lives, communities, and hearts filled with good. It is blessed in its permanence: it has been preserved (15:9) and will be recited until the end of time. And it is blessed in its increase: the more one studies it, the more it yields — its meanings do not exhaust. The word is used of the Qur'an at 21:50 ("this is a blessed reminder We have sent down") and 38:29 ("a blessed Book We have sent down to you, that they may reflect on its verses"). The description sets it apart from every human book, whose good is finite and whose relevance fades.

**The Parallel with the Torah**

The verse's description of the Qur'an as "sent down" and "blessed" parallels the Torah's description in the previous verse as complete, detailed, guidance, and mercy. The parallel is the point. The Makkans acknowledged that the Jews and Christians had a book from God (v. 156). Verse 155 says: here is yours — of the same kind, from the same Sender, with the same purpose. The two verses together form the premise for the argument of verses 156–157: every excuse is now removed.

**"So Follow It"**

*Fa-ttabiʿūh* — "so follow it." The same imperative as verse 153's "follow it" concerning the straight path. The Book and the path are one: to follow the Book is to walk the path. The command is not merely to believe in the Book, to honor it, or to recite it, but to *follow* it — to make it the guide of action. The idolaters had followed their fathers, their caprices, the majority, the satans' inspirations; the Qur'an offers a different object of following. Al-Ṭabarī: act by what is in it, hold what it permits as lawful and what it forbids as forbidden.

**"And Be Reverent"**
