*Wa ittaqū* — "and have *taqwā*." The second command. *Taqwā* is the guarding of oneself against God's displeasure — the settled consciousness of Him that shapes conduct. It was the goal named in verse 153 ("that you may be reverent"); here it is commanded directly alongside following the Book. The two go together: one follows the Book *with* God-consciousness, not mechanically; and one's God-consciousness is given content and direction *by* the Book. Without the Book, *taqwā* has no map; without *taqwā*, the Book is a text one reads but does not live.

**"That Haply You May Receive Mercy"**

*Laʿallakum turḥamūn* — "that you may be shown mercy." The result of following and reverence is mercy — God's mercy in this world and the next. The verse ends where verse 154 ended for the Torah: with mercy. The Torah was "a guidance and a mercy"; the Qur'an is followed "that you may receive mercy." The same gift, offered again.

The word *laʿalla*, "that haply," "so that perhaps," does not express doubt on God's part but hope and expectation from the human side: follow, and you may hope for mercy. It also preserves the freedom the sūrah has insisted on. The mercy is not automatic; it is offered to those who follow and revere. The Prophet ﷺ said: "No people gather in one of the houses of God, reciting the Book of God and studying it among themselves, but that tranquility descends upon them, mercy covers them, the angels surround them, and God mentions them to those who are with Him" (Muslim 2699). The mercy the verse promises begins in the gathering around the Book.

**The Simplicity of the Verse**

The verse is one of the shortest in this part of the sūrah, and its brevity is a kind of eloquence. After the long exposure of the idolaters' fabricated religion and the recitation of the true commandments, the verse says, in effect: here is the Book; follow it; fear God; receive mercy. It is a complete program in a sentence. Everything the sūrah has argued for — *tawḥīd*, the Hereafter, the exclusive authority of revelation, the rejection of invented law — is realized by the one act of following this blessed Book with a God-conscious heart.

**The Believer's Relationship to the Book**

The verse defines that relationship in three verbs. The Book is *sent down* — so it is received, not made; the believer approaches it as a gift from above, not as a text to be judged. It is to be *followed* — so it is a guide, not a decoration; its function is realized in action. And it is followed *with reverence* — so it is approached with the heart, not only the mind. Ibn Masʿūd said: "The bearer of the Qur'an should be known by his night when people sleep, by his day when people eat, by his sorrow when people rejoice, by his weeping when people laugh, by his silence when people chatter, and by his humility when people boast." The follower of the blessed Book is marked by it.

**Blessing as Evidence**

Finally, the description *mubārak* invites verification. A book's blessing is visible in its fruits. The Qur'an transformed the Arabs of the seventh century from a fragmented, idolatrous, infanticidal society into a civilization; it has been memorized entire by millions across fourteen centuries; it continues to guide, console, and reform lives daily. The commentators considered this manifest *barakah* one of the signs pointing to the Book's origin — for no human composition has shown such lasting, increasing good. The verse's claim, "this is a blessed Book," is one the reader can test by following it.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:156

> **You ˹pagans˺ can no longer say, “Scriptures were only revealed to two groups before us and we were unaware of their teachings.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Excuse Removed**

The verse gives the first of two reasons why the blessed Book was sent down to the Arabs: *an taqūlū innamā unzila al-kitābu ʿalā ṭā'ifatayni min qablinā* — "lest you say: The Book was only sent down upon two groups before us." The construction *an taqūlū* is understood as "lest you should say" or "so that you would not say" — the Book was revealed to forestall this excuse. God, in His justice, does not punish without warning (v. 131) and does not leave a people with a plausible plea of ignorance. The Qur'an removes the plea in advance.

**"Two Groups Before Us"**

*Ṭā'ifatayn* — "two groups, two parties": the Jews and the Christians, who received the Torah and the Gospel. The Arabs knew of these scriptures; they lived alongside Jewish tribes in Yathrib and Khaybar and Christian communities in Najrān, Syria, and Abyssinia. They could have said — and the verse anticipates that they would have said — that God's revelation had been addressed to others: to the Children of Israel, in Hebrew, in a foreign land, in a foreign age. "We were never sent a book; how could we be held to what we never received?" Compare 28:47: "Also so they would not say, if struck by an affliction for what their hands have done" And 35:42, where the Arabs swore that if a warner came to them they would be more guided than any nation.

**"And We Were Indeed Heedless of Their Study"**

*Wa in kunnā ʿan dirāsatihim la-ghāfilīn* — "and we were, of their study, indeed heedless." *Dirāsah* is study, reading, learning — the root of *madrasah*. The excuse continues: even if the earlier books contained guidance for us, we were unaware of their study. Ibn Kathīr and al-Zamakhsharī understand this as the Arabs' inability to read the Torah and Gospel — books in languages they did not know, held by communities they did not belong to, studied in ways they had no access to. The word *ghāfilīn*, heedless, recalls verse 131: God does not destroy a people "while they are heedless." The Arabs' anticipated plea was precisely that they were heedless — through no fault of their own — of what the two groups studied.

The plea would have had some force. It is true that the Arabs had no scripture in their own tongue and no access to the study of the Jewish and Christian books. A just God, the sūrah has insisted, does not hold people to what they could not know. So what is God's answer? Not to deny the premise, but to remove it: He sends them a Book in their own language (v. 157: "a clear proof from your Lord"). The excuse is not refuted; it is made obsolete.

**The Logic of Divine Justice**

The verse displays the principle of verse 149 — "Allah has the most conclusive argument" (6:149) — in operation. God's argument is conclusive because He anticipates and removes every excuse. Had the Arabs been left without revelation, they could have pleaded verse 156. So He sent revelation. Had it been in a language they could not understand, they could have pleaded incomprehension. So He sent it "in a clear Arabic tongue" (26:195). Had it been given to a stranger, they could have pleaded distrust. So He sent it through one of their own, whom they knew as *al-Amīn*, the trustworthy. Step by step, the ground for excuse is removed until the only thing left is the choice. "And We would never punish ˹a people˺ until We have sent a messenger ˹to warn them˺" (17:15) — and the messenger has been sent to them, with a Book, in their tongue.

**The Verse as an Insight into Human Nature**

The verse also reveals something about how people reason about their religious failures. The excuse it anticipates is one of comparison and displacement: "Others were given what we were not; we cannot be blamed for lacking it." The move shifts responsibility from the self to circumstance. The Qur'an takes the move seriously enough to answer it — but the answer is that circumstance has now changed, and the excuse that was once available is available no longer. The person who continues to use it after the Book has come is not pleading ignorance but choosing it.

**The Word "Innamā"**

The excuse is introduced with *innamā*, 'only': "Scriptures were only revealed to two groups before us and we were unaware of their teachings." (6:156). The restrictive particle expresses the idolaters' view of revelation as a possession of particular peoples — a Jewish thing, a Christian thing, not a universal gift. The Qur'an's response, across its revelation, is that God's guidance is not the property of any people: "We surely sent a messenger to every community, saying," (16:36); "There is no community that has not had a warner" (35:24). The two groups were not the only recipients in history, and they are certainly not the last. The Arabs' own descent from Abraham through Ishmael, and their possession of the Kaʿbah, made them heirs of a revelation older than either group's — a point the sūrah makes in its treatment of Abraham (vv. 74–83, 161).

**Preparing Verse 157**

Verse 156 removes the excuse of not having received; verse 157 will remove the excuse's boastful twin — "had we received, we would have done better." The two are paired because they are the two forms the same evasion takes: self-pity ("we were never given a chance") and self-flattery ("we would have excelled if given one"). Both dissolve when the Book actually arrives, because then the person is tested and his conduct, not his claims, shows what he would do.

**The Contemporary Echo**

The verse's excuse survives in modern forms: "Religion was for another age, another culture; we cannot be expected to know or follow it." The verse's answer holds: the Book has been sent down, it is available, it is clear, and its availability ends the plea. What the reader does with it is the test that verse 156 was revealed to make possible.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:157

> **Nor can you say, “If only the Scriptures had been revealed to us, we would have been better guided than they.” Now there has come to you from your Lord a clear proof—a guide and mercy. Who then does more wrong than those who deny Allah’s revelations and turn away from them? We will reward those who turn away from Our revelations with a dreadful punishment for turning away. Waiting for the Apocalypse?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Excuse: The Boast**

*Aw taqūlū law annā unzila ʿalaynā al-kitābu la-kunnā ahdā minhum* — "or lest you say: Had the Book been sent down upon us, we would have been better guided than they." The second anticipated excuse is not a plea of deprivation but a boast of hypothetical superiority. The Arabs looked at the Jews and Christians — their divisions, their departures from their own scriptures — and said: had *we* been given a book, we would have done better. The same boast is recorded in 35:42: "They swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a warner were to come to them, they would certainly be better guided than any other community"

The boast is a familiar human posture. It costs nothing to claim virtue in a situation one has not faced. The idolaters could assert their superior fitness for revelation indefinitely, so long as revelation did not come. Its arrival would end the claim by testing it.

**"Now There Has Come unto You a Clear Proof from Your Lord"**

*Fa-qad jā'akum bayyinatun min rabbikum wa hudan wa raḥmah* — "in a clear Arabic tongue" The answer to both excuses at once. The Book has come. It is a *bayyinah* — a clear proof, a manifest evidence: the Qur'an itself, in clear Arabic (al-Ṭabarī; 26:195), understandable to those who claimed they could not study the foreign books. It is "a guidance and a mercy" — the exact words used for the Torah in verse 154, so that the Arabs have received precisely what the two groups received, and cannot say theirs is lesser. And it is "from your Lord" — from the One they acknowledged as their Lord, addressed to them.

The test the boast invited has now been set. "Had we been given a book, we would be better guided" — here is the Book; be better guided. The verse's construction makes the challenge explicit: your claim is now falsifiable, and your conduct falsifies or confirms it.

**"So Who Does Greater Wrong Than One Who Denies the Signs of God and Turns Away from Them?"**

*Fa-man aẓlamu mimman kadhdhaba bi-āyāti Allāhi wa ṣadafa ʿanhā* — "so who is more wrongdoing than one who denies God's signs and turns away from them?" The rhetorical question of verses 21, 93, and 144 in a new form. There, the greatest wrong was to fabricate a lie against God; here, it is to deny His signs and turn from them after they have come. The two are the same crime from opposite sides: fabricating what God did not say, and rejecting what He did say. Compare 32:22: "And who does more wrong than the one who is reminded of Allah"

The verb *ṣadafa* means to turn aside, to turn away — and also, transitively, to turn *others* away. Ibn Kathīr and al-Zamakhsharī read it here in the second sense: the idolaters not only rejected the signs themselves but worked to turn others from them — the "they forbid it and keep away from it" of verse 26. The wrong is thus compounded: personal rejection plus obstruction of others. This is the conduct of the "great ones among the guilty" (v. 123), who plotted to keep their people from the message.

The question's force lies in the context. Those who boasted they would be better guided than the two groups, once given the Book, deny it and turn others away. Their wrong is therefore greater than the two groups' failures they had criticized — because they had claimed superiority and been given the means to prove it, and instead had done worse.

**"Soon Shall We Recompense Those Who Turn Away from Our Signs with a Terrible Punishment"**

*Sa-najzī alladhīna yaṣdifūna ʿan āyātinā sū'a al-ʿadhābi bi-mā kānū yaṣdifūn* — "We will recompense those who turn away from Our signs with an evil punishment for what they used to turn away." The verb *ṣadafa* appears three times in the verse's second half — *ṣadafa*, *yaṣdifūna*, *yaṣdifūn* — hammering the charge. The punishment is "for their turning away": the recompense matches the crime. They turned from the signs; the punishment is the consequence of that turning. *Sū' al-ʿadhāb* — "the evil of punishment," the worst of it — is reserved for those who, having been given the clear proof, not only rejected it but repelled others from it.

**The Two Excuses Together**

Verses 156–157 have closed both doors. The plea "we were not given a book" is answered by the giving. The boast "we would have done better" is answered by the giving and the resulting test. What remains is the conduct: those who follow the Book receive the mercy of verse 155; those who deny it and turn others away receive the punishment of verse 157. The Qur'an's justice is displayed in its thoroughness — no excuse is left standing — and its mercy in its patience: the excuses were anticipated and answered before punishment, not after.

**The Human Lesson**

The verse teaches a general truth about hypothetical virtue. Claims about what one *would* do in circumstances one has not faced are worthless as evidence of character; only conduct in the actual circumstance counts. The Arabs' boast was tested by the Book's arrival, and most of the Makkan leadership failed the test they had invited. The believer applies this to himself: not "I would be steadfast if tested" but the steadfastness he actually shows when tested; not "I would follow the truth if it were clear" but his following of the truth that is already clear before him. The Book has come; the hypothetical has become actual; and the measure is response.

**Denying and Turning Away as Distinct Sins**

The verse distinguishes two acts: *kadhdhaba* (denying) and *ṣadafa* (turning away). One may deny inwardly without acting; one may turn away — and turn others away — as an active policy. The punishment is specified "for their turning away," which the commentators note indicates the gravity of the active obstruction. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever calls to guidance has a reward like the rewards of those who follow him, without diminishing their rewards in any way; and whoever calls to misguidance has sin like the sins of those who follow him" (Muslim 2674). The one who turns others from the signs bears the weight of every one he turned. This is why the verse's warning falls with such severity on the leaders of Makkah: they did not merely disbelieve; they blocked the road.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:158

> **Are they awaiting the coming of the angels, or your Lord ˹Himself˺, or some of your Lord’s ˹major˺ signs? On the Day your Lord’s signs arrive, belief will not benefit those who did not believe earlier or those who did no good through their faith. Say, “Keep waiting! We too are waiting.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**What Are They Waiting For?**

*Hal yanẓurūna illā an ta'tiyahumu al-malā'ikatu aw ya'tiya rabbuka aw ya'tiya baʿḍu āyāti rabbik* — "Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or that your Lord should come, or that some of the signs of your Lord should come?" The Book has come (v. 157); the proof is clear; the excuses are gone. What more are the deniers waiting for? The verse names three things — and each is an event after which faith is no longer possible.

The angels' coming: the disbelievers had demanded to see angels (vv. 8–9, 111). But the angels come to the disbeliever only at death — to take his soul — or at the Day of Judgment. Al-Ṭabarī reads the verse's 'angels' as the angels of death: the idolaters, in effect, are waiting for their own deaths. The Lord's coming: the coming of God for judgment on the Last Day, "and your Lord comes ˹to judge˺ with angels, rank upon rank" (89:22), which the sūrah's audience had scoffed at (2:210; 16:33). Some of the Lord's signs: the great portents of the end — the signs of the Hour. In each case, the deniers are waiting for the very thing that ends the possibility of choosing.

**The Sign After Which Faith Does Not Avail**

*Yawma ya'tī baʿḍu āyāti rabbika lā yanfaʿu nafsan īmānuhā lam takun āmanat min qablu aw kasabat fī īmānihā khayrā* — "the day some of the signs of your Lord come, faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before, or earn good in its faith." The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) identify the decisive sign, on the authority of the Prophet ﷺ, as the rising of the sun from the west:

> "The Hour will not come until the sun rises from its place of setting; and when it rises and the people see it, all of them will believe — and that is when faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before." Then he recited this verse. (al-Bukhārī 4635; Muslim 157)

And: "Three things, when they appear, faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before: the rising of the sun from its setting-place, the Dajjāl, and the Beast of the Earth" (Muslim 158). The principle is that of 4:18 and 10:90–91 (Pharaoh's belief as he drowned): repentance and faith are accepted only while the veil of the unseen remains. Once the unseen becomes seen — at death for the individual, at the great signs for the world — belief is no longer belief in the unseen but acknowledgment of the obvious, and it earns nothing. The Prophet ﷺ said: "God accepts the servant's repentance as long as the death-rattle has not reached his throat" (al-Tirmidhī 3537; Ibn Mājah 4253).

**"Or Earn Some Goodness in Its Belief"**

The verse names two things that will not avail after the sign: faith that was not held before, *and* good works that were not earned before in a state of faith. The second clause addresses the believer who had faith but did no good — who deferred his repentance and his righteous deeds. After the sign, he cannot begin. Ibn Kathīr explains: the disbeliever's new faith will not be accepted, and the believer who had been negligent will not be able to make up what he neglected. The verse thus warns both: the one without faith, to believe now; the one with faith, to earn good now. Both windows close at the same moment.

**The Foolishness of Waiting**

The verse's rhetorical question exposes the irrationality of the deniers' demand for overwhelming signs. They wanted certainty before believing — an angel, God Himself, a cosmic portent. But certainty of that kind is exactly what removes the value of belief. Faith is meaningful because it is chosen in the presence of evidence but the absence of compulsion; that is what makes it a moral act and a test. To demand compulsion is to demand the end of the test — and when the test ends, so does the possibility of passing it. The deniers were, without knowing it, asking for their own foreclosure. Compare 43:66 and 47:18: "Once it actually befalls them, will it not be too late to be mindful"

**"Say: Wait! We, Too, Are Waiting"**

*Quli intaẓirū innā muntaẓirūn* — "Say: Wait; indeed we are waiting." The verse ends with the command of verse 135's spirit: work as you will, we are working; wait as you will, we are waiting. The "we" is the Prophet ﷺ and the believers (or, some say, God speaking with royal plural). The believers also wait — but for a different thing. The deniers wait for the signs that will end their chance; the believers wait for the promise that will vindicate their faith. Both waits end on the same Day, with opposite results. Al-Rāzī reads the command as a threat: wait for what you are waiting for, and see. The formula recurs (7:71; 9:52; 10:20, 102; 11:122; 20:135; 52:31), always with this double edge — patience for the believer, warning for the denier.

**The Theology of the Closed Door**

The verse establishes a doctrine of great practical weight: the acceptance of faith and repentance has a term. God's mercy is vast (v. 147) and His door is open — but open *in this life*, before death and before the great signs. After that, the matter is judgment, not repentance. This is not a limitation on mercy but its structure: mercy that could be claimed after the test would make the test meaningless, and God's justice to those who believed in the unseen requires that those who waited for the seen not be equated with them. "They are not equal" (32:18).

**The Urgency the Verse Creates**

The verse is one of the Qur'an's strongest arguments against procrastination in faith and repentance. Every deferral assumes that the door will still be open tomorrow. The verse says the door closes — at a moment no one knows, by death or by sign. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Hasten to good deeds before seven things: do you await anything but poverty that makes you forget, or wealth that makes you rebel, or illness that corrupts, or old age that weakens, or death that comes suddenly, or the Dajjāl — the worst absent thing awaited — or the Hour, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter?" (al-Tirmidhī 2306). The one who has understood verse 158 does not wait. He believes now, and earns good in his faith now, because "now" is the only time in which either avails.

**The Believer's Waiting**

Finally, the verse dignifies the believer's own waiting. He is not waiting idly or anxiously; he is waiting in the confidence of verse 134 — "what you are promised is surely coming" — and in the activity of verse 135 — "I am working." His waiting is *intiẓār* in the positive sense: expectation, readiness, the posture of one who has prepared and awaits the arrival. The deniers' waiting is the posture of one who has not prepared and imagines the arrival will never come.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:159

> **Indeed, you ˹O Prophet˺ are not responsible whatsoever for those who have divided their faith and split into sects. Their judgment rests only with Allah. And He will inform them of what they used to do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Warning Against Division**

*Inna alladhīna farraqū dīnahum wa kānū shiyaʿan lasta minhum fī shay'* — "indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects, you are not of them in anything." Verse 153 warned that following the many paths "separates you from His way" (*tafarraqa*). Verse 159 names those who have done exactly that: they *farraqū* — divided, split apart — their religion, and became *shiyaʿ* — factions, sects, parties, each following its own leader. The Prophet ﷺ is told he has nothing to do with them.

**Two Readings of "Farraqū"**

The majority reading is *farraqū*, "they divided": they broke their religion into pieces, accepting some parts and rejecting others, or splitting into groups each claiming the whole. A second reading, transmitted from ʿAlī and Ḥamzah among the reciters and noted by al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Zamakhsharī, is *fāraqū*, "they separated from" — they left their religion altogether, abandoning it. Both readings describe departures from the one path: division within it, or departure from it. Al-Ṭabarī accepts both as sound.

**Who Are They?**

The commentators offer several identifications, which the source commentary records and which are not mutually exclusive. First, the Jews and Christians, who divided into sects after their prophets and differed over their books (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) — the Qur'an says of them, "They did not split ˹into sects˺ out of mutual envy until knowledge came to them" (42:14; 3:19; 98:4). Second, the idolaters, with whom the sūrah has been chiefly engaged, who differed among themselves over which partners to worship — idols, stars, jinn, angels (al-Rāzī) — each tribe with its own god and rite. Third, the people of innovation (*bidʿah*) and doubt within the Muslim community who would come later (al-Ṭabarī reports this from Abū Hurayrah and others). The verse is general enough to include all who fragment the religion God gave.

**The Ḥadīth of the Sects**

The commentators (al-Zamakhsharī among them) cite in connection with this verse the Prophet's prediction:

> "The Jews divided into seventy-one sects, and the Christians into seventy-two sects, and my community will divide into seventy-three sects — all of them in the Fire except one." They asked, "Which one, O Messenger of God?" He said: "That which follows what I and my Companions are upon." (al-Tirmidhī 2641; Abū Dāwūd 4597; Ibn Mājah 3992)

The ḥadīth confirms that the verse's warning is not confined to earlier communities. Division is a danger to the Muslim community too, and the safeguard is the same one the verse implies: adherence to what the Prophet ﷺ brought, without addition or subtraction.

**"Thou Hast Nothing to Do with Them"**

*Lasta minhum fī shay'* — "you are not of them in anything." Al-Ṭabarī explains: you are free of them and their division; you are not answerable for them; you are commanded to leave them rather than to fight them. The statement disowns the Prophet's connection to any sectarian path. He is on the one *ṣirāṭ*; the sects are on the *subul*; there is no overlap. For the believer, the statement is a standard: to be "of" the Prophet ﷺ is to be on the undivided path; to join a faction that divides religion is to step outside what he was "of."

Some early authorities held that this verse was abrogated by the "verse of the sword," on the understanding that it commanded leaving the disbelievers unfought. The stronger view is that it is not abrogated: it is a statement of the Prophet's non-responsibility for the sectarians' choice and non-participation in their division — a statement that remains true regardless of the rules of warfare.

**"Their Matter Rests with God Alone"**

*Innamā amruhum ilā Allāh* — "their affair is only to God." The Prophet ﷺ is not to be consumed by the sects — not to adjudicate every quarrel, not to grieve over every division, not to take on himself the outcome. God will handle it. This is the release granted at verses 66, 69, 70, 107, and 112: your task is to convey; the judgment is God's.

**"Then He Will Inform Them About That Which They Used to Do"**

*Thumma yunabbi'uhum bi-mā kānū yafʿalūn* — "then He will inform them of what they used to do." On the Day of Judgment, God will show each faction what it actually did — not what it claimed, not what its leaders taught, but the truth of its deeds and the reality of its divisions. The formula recurs at 5:14, 5:48, and 6:108, always in the context of religious difference. The divisions that seem so important in this world — each sect certain of its rightness — will be resolved not by argument but by God's disclosure.

**The Nature of Sectarian Division**

The verse and its context permit a diagnosis of what sectarianism is. It is *farraqū dīnahum* — dividing *the religion*, treating the one path as a set of separable pieces to be selected among. It produces *shiyaʿ* — parties defined by loyalty to a leader or a distinctive doctrine rather than to the whole of what God revealed. It is the natural endpoint of following the *subul*, the many paths of verse 153. And it is condemned not because difference of opinion is forbidden — the Companions differed on many matters without becoming *shiyaʿ* — but because *shiyaʿ* make loyalty to the party the criterion of truth, and this is a form of the *shirk* in legislation the sūrah has exposed throughout.

The Qur'an's alternative is stated positively elsewhere: "And hold firmly to the rope of Allah and do not be divided" (3:103); "He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah, and what We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, ˹commanding" (42:13). Unity is not uniformity of opinion but common adherence to the one revealed path, with disagreement within it conducted as brotherhood rather than faction.

**The Believer's Application**

The verse gives the believer a test for his religious affiliations. Does his group hold to the whole of the revealed religion, or select from it? Does it define itself by adherence to God's Book and the Prophet's way, or by loyalty to a leader, a slogan, a distinctive? Does it regard other Muslims on the same path as brothers, or as enemies? The Prophet ﷺ was told he had nothing to do with those who divide; the believer who wishes to be "of" him keeps to the undivided path, treats sectarian partisanship as the danger the verse names, and leaves the judgment of the factions to God, who will inform them.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:160

> **Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold. But whoever comes with a bad deed will be punished for only one. None will be wronged.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Arithmetic of Mercy**

After warning of judgment and division, the sūrah states the principle by which deeds are weighed. *Man jā'a bi-l-ḥasanati fa-lahu ʿashru amthālihā wa man jā'a bi-l-sayyi'ati fa-lā yujzā illā mithlahā wa hum lā yuẓlamūn* — "whoever comes with a good deed shall have ten of its like; and whoever comes with an evil deed shall be recompensed only with its like; and they will not be wronged." The verse expresses a double standard — not a double standard of justice, but a standard of justice for evil and a standard of bounty for good. Evil is repaid exactly; good is multiplied.

**"Whosoever Brings a Good Deed"**

*Man jā'a bi-l-ḥasanah* — "whoever comes with a good deed." The verb *jā'a bi-*, "comes with, brings," pictures the Day of Judgment: the servant arrives before God carrying what he did. He does not merely have a record; he *brings* the deed, as one brings goods to a market. A *ḥasanah* is a good deed, a beautiful act — any act of obedience, from the declaration of faith to the removal of a stone from the road.

**"Ten Times the Like Thereof"**

*ʿAshru amthālihā* — "ten of its likes." The reward is tenfold. The Prophet ﷺ explained this in the ḥadīth transmitted from his Lord:

> "God has written down the good deeds and the evil deeds, then explained them: whoever intends a good deed and does not do it, God writes it with Him as a complete good deed; and if he intends it and does it, God writes it with Him as ten good deeds up to seven hundred times, up to many times more. And whoever intends an evil deed and does not do it, God writes it with Him as a complete good deed; and if he intends it and does it, God writes it as one evil deed." (al-Bukhārī 6491; Muslim 131)

The ḥadīth shows that ten is the minimum multiplier, not the only one. Al-Rāzī and others note that 'ten' should not be read as a precise arithmetical factor but as an indication that good is multiplied many times over — the Qur'an elsewhere gives seven hundred for charity (2:261) and "Only those who endure patiently will be given their reward without limit" for patience (39:10). Ten is the floor of divine generosity; the ceiling is unknown. The mention of ten specifically may reflect the sūrah's earlier theme of completeness — ten being the number of fullness in Arabic reckoning — or may simply be the base from which "Allah multiplies ˹the reward even more˺ to whoever He wills." (2:261).

**"Whosoever Brings an Evil Deed Shall Be Recompensed Only with the Like Thereof"**

*Fa-lā yujzā illā mithlahā* — "he is not recompensed except with its like." One evil deed, one recompense — no more. The restrictive *illā*, "except," is emphatic: God does not multiply evil. This is justice in its purest form: the punishment equals the crime, never exceeds it. Compare 40:40: "Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like; but whoever does righteousness, male or female, while a believer — those will enter Paradise, provided for without account." And 28:84; 27:89.

Al-Zamakhsharī states the principle: the multiplication of good manifests divine bounty (*faḍl*); the exact recompense of evil manifests divine justice (*ʿadl*). God deals with His servants by both, and the verse shows how they are apportioned: bounty toward their good, justice toward their evil — and never the reverse.

**"And They Shall Not Be Wronged"**

*Wa hum lā yuẓlamūn* — "None will be wronged." (6:160). No one will receive less good than he earned or more punishment than he deserved. The clause guarantees the accounting. It applies to both parties: the doer of good will not have his reward diminished; the doer of evil will not have his punishment inflated. "And if it is a good deed, He will multiply it many times over and will give a great reward out of His grace" (4:40).

**The Theology of the Verse**

The verse resolves a question that has troubled every moral tradition: how can a finite life earn infinite Paradise, and how can finite sin merit Hell? The Qur'an's answer has two parts. On the side of reward, God multiplies — He gives "from Himself," beyond what was earned, so that Paradise is not purchased by deeds but granted by bounty on the occasion of deeds. This is why the Prophet ﷺ said none enters Paradise by his deeds alone, "unless God covers me with His mercy" (al-Bukhārī 5673). On the side of punishment, God is exact — no one receives more than his like — and the eternity of Hell, for those who earn it, corresponds to the eternity of the disbelief they would have persisted in had they lived forever (the commentators' explanation), or to the gravity of *shirk* as an offense against the Infinite. In either case, the verse's guarantee holds: they are not wronged.

**The Psychology of the Verse**

The verse is designed to produce hope without complacency. The tenfold multiplication encourages the servant: every small good is worth ten, so nothing good is negligible, and the balance can be tipped by deeds that seem minor. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not belittle any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face" (Muslim 2626). At the same time, the exact recompense of evil warns: nothing evil is overlooked, and one evil deed cancels — in weight — one good deed, but not ten. The believer who understands the arithmetic works to fill his scale with good, knowing that God's generosity makes the filling easier than it would be under strict equivalence.

**The Verse After the Warning**

The placement is merciful. Verse 157 promised terrible punishment for those who turn away; verse 158 warned that the door will close; verse 159 disowned the sectarians. Verse 160 now says: but the accounting, when it comes, is weighted toward mercy. The one who brings even a little good is met with multiplication. This is the sūrah's manner throughout — severity followed by mercy, warning followed by encouragement — reflecting the God who "has prescribed mercy upon Himself" (v. 12, 54) and whose "mercy precedes His wrath" (al-Bukhārī 7404; Muslim 2751).

**The Practical Program**

The verse yields a simple practice: multiply the *ḥasanāt*. Since each is worth at least ten, the believer seeks them everywhere — in worship, in kindness, in honest work, in restraint from sin (which itself is written as a good deed), in the intention to do good even when unable. And since each *sayyi'ah* is worth exactly one, he does not despair when he falls: one repentance, one good deed, outweighs it. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Whoever comes with 'there is no god but God' will have ten of its like" — the smallest good, the greatest multiplication. The verse turns the moral life from a fearful ledger into an opportunity, and that is its intent.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:161

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Surely my Lord has guided me to the Straight Path, a perfect way, the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prophet's Declaration**

The sūrah moves toward its close with a series of declarations the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to make. *Qul innanī hadānī rabbī ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm* — "Say: Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path." The statement is personal and definite. After a hundred and sixty verses of argument against the idolaters, the Prophet ﷺ does not say "I have concluded" or "I have chosen" but "my Lord has guided me." Guidance is God's act; the Prophet ﷺ is its recipient. This is the humility that the sūrah has modeled since Abraham's "unless my Lord guides me, I shall be among the people astray" (v. 77).

**Five Descriptions of One Reality**

The verse names the path by five descriptions that the Qur'an regularly associates: a straight path, an upright religion, the creed of Abraham, *ḥanīf*, and not of the idolaters. Each illuminates the others.

*Ṣirāṭ mustaqīm*, the straight path: the image of verses 126 and 153 — the one direct highway to God, as against the many byways. It is what every Muslim asks for in every unit of prayer (1:6).

*Dīnan qiyaman*, an upright religion: *qiyam* (a variant of *qayyim*) means standing straight, firmly established, correct, sustaining. The religion is upright in itself — without crookedness — and upholding of those who follow it, providing what they need to stand. The phrase appears at 9:36, 12:40, 30:30, 30:43, and 98:5. In 30:30 it is tied to the *fiṭrah*: "That is the Straight Way, but most people do not know"

*Millata Ibrāhīm*, the creed of Abraham: *millah* is a religious way, a creed, a community's belief. The Qur'an repeatedly identifies the religion of Muhammad ﷺ with that of Abraham (2:130, 135; 3:95; 4:125; 16:123). The identification is central to the sūrah, which devoted verses 74–83 to Abraham's discovery of *tawḥīd* by reason and his rejection of his people's idols. The Makkans claimed Abraham as their ancestor and the Kaʿbah as his house; the verse tells them that his actual religion is the one they are rejecting.

*Ḥanīfan*, a *ḥanīf*: one who inclines away from falsehood toward truth — from the root *ḥ-n-f*, to incline. The word is used of Abraham almost exclusively (2:135; 3:67, 95; 4:125; 6:79; 16:120, 123) and, in a few verses, as a command to the Prophet ﷺ and his community (10:105; 22:31; 30:30). The *ḥanīf* is the natural monotheist, who turns from every idol to the One by an inclination built into his nature. Pre-Islamic Arabia knew a few such figures — Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Waraqah ibn Nawfal in his early years, and others — who rejected idolatry and sought Abraham's religion; the Prophet ﷺ before his call was understood in tradition to have lived as a *ḥanīf*. The word also distinguishes Abraham's way from Judaism and Christianity as they had developed: "Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian" (3:67).

*Wa mā kāna mina al-mushrikīn*, "and he was not of the idolaters": the negative that seals the positive. Abraham's way excludes *shirk* entirely. The phrase is the exact echo of verse 79, where Abraham himself said, "I have turned my face as a *ḥanīf* to Him who created the heavens and the earth, and I am not of the idolaters." The sūrah began its Abraham section with this confession and ends its argument with the Prophet ﷺ affirming the same.

**Why Abraham at the End?**

The sūrah's argument against the idolaters has been comprehensive: the signs of creation, the fate of earlier nations, the logic of *tawḥīd*, the exposure of invented law. But its most persuasive figure for a Makkan audience was Abraham. The Makkans revered him; they traced their lineage and their sanctuary to him. To show that the religion Muhammad ﷺ brought is Abraham's religion — and that the Makkans' idolatry is a departure from it — was to turn their own heritage against them. The verse accomplishes this in a sentence. The Prophet ﷺ is not introducing a foreign faith; he is restoring the creed of the Makkans' own father.

**The Unity of Religion**

The verse's five descriptions together express a doctrine: true religion is one. It is the straight path, always the same; the upright religion, established in human nature; the creed of Abraham, taught to the prophets; the *ḥanīf* way, inclining from falsehood; and the rejection of *shirk*, its defining negation. Muhammad ﷺ did not found a new religion but was guided to the one that had always existed. "He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah, and what We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, ˹commanding" (42:13). The verse is the sūrah's answer to sectarian division (v. 159): the remedy is the one religion of the *ḥanīf*.

**The Believer's Confession**

The verse is spoken in the first person, and every believer who recites it makes it his own: "my Lord has guided me to a straight path." It is a confession of gratitude (guidance received, not achieved), of identity (the creed of Abraham, not a sect), and of exclusion (not of the idolaters — no partners, in worship or in law). The Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and verses 162–163 in his opening supplication for prayer (Muslim 771), so that the Muslim's daily worship begins with the declaration the sūrah's argument concludes with: I have been guided to the straight path, the religion of Abraham, and I am not of those who associate.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:162

> **Say, “Surely my prayer, my worship, my life, and my death are all for Allah—Lord of all worlds.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Statement of Total Devotion**

*Qul inna ṣalātī wa nusukī wa maḥyāya wa mamātī li-Llāhi rabbi al-ʿālamīn* — "Say: Indeed my prayer, my sacrifice, my living, and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds." The sūrah's long argument against idolatry closes, as the source commentary observes, not with a further argument but with a declaration — simple, uncompromising, and complete. Four things are named — worship, rite, life, and death — and all four are consecrated to God alone. Nothing is left over for partners.

**"My Prayer"**

*Ṣalātī* — my prayer, the ritual prayer, the central act of worship. The Prophet ﷺ declares it is for God — directed to Him, performed for His sake, offered to no other. The idolaters also prayed, but their prayer at the House was "nothing but whistling and clapping" (8:35), directed to idols alongside God. The believer's prayer is *li-Llāh*, for God, exclusively.

**"My Sacrifice"**

*Nusukī* — my *nusuk*. The word has a range, which al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī record: it can mean religious rites generally — any act of devotion that draws one near to God (whence *manāsik*, the rites of pilgrimage, and *nāsik*, a devout worshipper) — or, more specifically, ritual sacrifice, the slaughter of an animal as an act of worship. In the context of the sūrah, which has been concerned since verse 118 with slaughter and the invocation of God's Name over it, the specific sense is prominent (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The idolaters slaughtered in the names of their gods and withheld God's Name from their animals (v. 138); the Prophet ﷺ declares that his sacrifice is for God. Compare 108:2: "So pray and sacrifice to your Lord ˹alone˺" — the same pairing of prayer and sacrifice as the two great outward acts of worship.

The pairing is significant. Prayer is the worship of the body and tongue; sacrifice is the worship of wealth and possession. Between them they cover what a person is and what a person has. Both are for God.

**"My Living and My Dying"**

*Maḥyāya wa mamātī* — my life and my death. The declaration expands from the specific acts of worship to the whole of existence. Al-Zamakhsharī explains: all one's actions in life, and one's death itself, are for God — done for His pleasure. Al-Qurṭubī: for drawing near to Him. Ibn ʿAjībah: with all consideration of self removed from one's actions.

"My living is for God" means that every act of life — eating, working, marrying, resting, speaking — is oriented toward Him, so that the whole of life becomes worship. The Prophet ﷺ taught that even the morsel a man puts in his wife's mouth is charity (al-Bukhārī 56), and that "in the sexual relation of one of you there is charity" (Muslim 1006) — because the believer's ordinary acts, done with right intention, are for God. "My dying is for God" means that death, too, is His — accepted as His decree, met in His obedience, and, at its highest, given in His cause. The martyr's death is the fullest sense of "my dying is for God"; but every believer who dies in submission dies for Him.

The two words also embrace the full span of human existence. There is nothing before life or after death that is one's own to give; life and death together are the totality. The Prophet ﷺ gives the totality.

**"For God, Lord of the Worlds"**

*Li-Llāhi rabbi al-ʿālamīn* — the object of the devotion is named with the title of the Fātiḥah's opening: God, the Lord of all worlds. The title is the reason for the devotion. Since He is the Lord of everything, everything belongs to Him, and to devote everything to Him is not excess but accuracy. The idolaters divided their devotion among many lords; the Prophet ﷺ gives his to the one Lord of all, because there is no other.

**The Verse as a Definition of Islam**

The verse is the fullest single statement of what *islām* — submission — means. It is not merely the performance of certain rites but the orientation of the whole self, in every act and at every moment, toward God. This is the *iḥsān* the Prophet ﷺ defined as "worshipping God as though you see Him" (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8) — a consciousness that does not switch off between prayers. The declaration makes no distinction between sacred and secular: the same *li-Llāh* covers prayer and living. This is why Islamic ethics extends to every domain of life — commerce, family, politics, eating — and why the sūrah could move without transition from theology to dietary law. All of it is for God.

**The Verse in the Prophet's Practice**

The Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and the next as part of the opening supplication of his night prayer, together with Abraham's declaration in verse 79 (Muslim 771; al-Qurṭubī records the practice). The Muslim who follows him begins his standing before God by declaring that his prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are God's. The declaration is not only a statement but a consecration: by saying it, the worshipper places himself, at the beginning of the prayer, in the condition the verse describes.

**The Contrast with Divided Devotion**

The verse is the resolution of the sūrah's central contrast. From verse 1 — "yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord" — the sūrah has exposed divided devotion: shares for God and shares for partners (v. 136), slaughter for God and slaughter for idols, allegiance to God and allegiance to ancestors, majority, and satans. Against all of this the verse sets a devotion that is undivided in its object (God alone), undivided in its scope (prayer, sacrifice, life, death), and undivided in its ground (He is Lord of the worlds). There is nothing left to give to a partner, because everything has been given to the One.

**The Practical Aspiration**

For the believer, the verse is both a description of the goal and a means toward it. Few live in the constant state the verse describes; but the daily recitation of it — in prayer, in the opening of the night vigil — trains the intention. The believer asks himself, of each act: is this for God? And he learns to make it so, by intention, until the exceptions grow fewer. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Deeds are according to intentions" (al-Bukhārī 1; Muslim 1907). The verse is the intention that makes all deeds worship.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:163

> **He has no partner. So I am commanded, and so I am the first to submit.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"He Has No Partner"**

*Lā sharīka lah* — "no partner has He." The declaration of verse 162 is completed by the negation that defines it. God, Lord of the worlds, to whom prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are given, has no *sharīk* — no associate, no partner, no one who shares in His lordship or His right to worship. The phrase is the negative face of *tawḥīd*, as "for God, Lord of the worlds" is its positive face. The two together form the complete confession: everything for Him, nothing for anyone else.

*Lā sharīka lah* is the phrase the pilgrims proclaim in the *talbiyah* — "Here I am, O God, here I am; here I am, You have no partner, here I am" — the cry with which the Prophet ﷺ entered the rites of the pilgrimage (al-Bukhārī 1549; Muslim 1184). The pre-Islamic Arabs had a corrupted *talbiyah*: "Here I am, You have no partner — except a partner who is Yours; You possess him and what he possesses" (Muslim 1185 records the Prophet's rebuke of this). The Qur'an's *lā sharīka lah* strips the exception. There is no partner, not even one "who belongs to God." This is the whole difference between the religion of Abraham and the religion of the Makkans, contained in the presence or absence of a clause.

**"This I Am Commanded"**

*Wa bi-dhālika umirtu* — "and with that I have been commanded." The Prophet ﷺ does not present his undivided devotion as a personal choice or spiritual achievement but as obedience to a command. He was commanded to devote everything to God and to affirm that He has no partner. This locates the authority: the declaration is not the Prophet's invention (which would make it one more *sabīl*) but God's command (which makes it the *ṣirāṭ*). It also models the believer's posture: *tawḥīd* is not merely a conclusion one reaches but a command one obeys. "And I am commanded to be the first of those who submit ˹to His Will˺" (39:12) — the same construction.

**"And I Am the First of Those Who Submit"**

*Wa anā awwalu al-muslimīn* — "and I am the first of the *muslimīn*." The phrase has been understood on several levels, all of which the source commentary presents.

On the plainest level, the Prophet ﷺ was the first of his community and his time to submit — the first Muslim of the final dispensation, before any Companion. The phrase recurs at verse 14 ("I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit") and 39:12. This sense is real: he preceded all in this *ummah*, and led by example.

On a deeper level, al-Rāzī reads "first" as denoting rank rather than time: the Prophet ﷺ is foremost in submission — his surrender to God's will and decree is the most complete of any human being's. In the context of verses 162–163, which express total devotion, "first" means "most perfect in this devotion." Others submit; he submits most fully, and is therefore first in the order of submission.

On the level of Islamic metaphysics, some commentators connect the phrase to the doctrine of the Muhammadan Reality (*al-ḥaqīqah al-Muḥammadiyyah*) or Muhammadan Light — the teaching that the Prophet's spiritual reality preceded all creation, so that he was, in truth, the first to submit before any other being. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I was a prophet while Adam was still between spirit and body" (al-Tirmidhī 3609; Aḥmad 16623). On this reading, "I am the first of those who submit" is literally true in the order of being, not only in the order of history.

The plain sense suffices for the verse's purpose, and the other senses deepen it without contradicting it. In every sense, the Prophet ﷺ is the model: the first to submit, the foremost in submission, and the one whose submission others follow.

**The Word "Muslimīn"**

The verse ends with the name of the religion's adherents: *al-muslimīn*, those who submit. The word is not sectarian; the Qur'an applies it to Noah (10:72), Abraham (2:131), Jacob's sons (2:133), Joseph (12:101), Moses' followers (10:84), the disciples of Jesus (3:52), and all who submitted to God in every age. To be *muslim* is to be one who has surrendered to God alone — which is exactly what verses 162–163 describe. The Prophet ﷺ is the first *muslim* of his time and the foremost of all, and the community he founded takes its name from the condition these verses define.

**The Close of the Argument**

Verses 161–163 form the sūrah's peroration. The long case against idolatry — from the creation of heavens and earth (v. 1), through Abraham's search (vv. 74–79), the signs of nature (vv. 95–99), the exposure of invented law (vv. 136–150), the ten commandments (vv. 151–153) — resolves into a personal creed: I have been guided to the straight path, the religion of Abraham; my prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are for God; He has no partner; this I was commanded; I am the first of those who submit. Everything the sūrah has argued is contained in these words. The argument was for the mind; the creed is for the heart and the will.

**The Believer's Recitation**

Since the Prophet ﷺ recited these verses at the opening of prayer, every Muslim can make them the opening of his own. Their recitation is a renewal of the covenant of verse 152 — "fulfill the pact of God" — in its most concentrated form. The one who says, with attention, "my living and my dying are for God, He has no partner, this I was commanded, and I am of those who submit," has said what the whole sūrah exists to teach, and has placed himself, for that moment, exactly where the sūrah wishes him to stand.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:164

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Should I seek a lord other than Allah while He is the Lord of everything?” No one will reap except what they sow. No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of your differences.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rhetorical Refusal**

*Qul a-ghayra Allāhi abghī rabban wa huwa rabbu kulli shay'* — "Say: Shall I seek other than God as a lord, while He is the Lord of all things?" The verse stands as the third of the closing declarations, and it takes the form of the sūrah's characteristic rhetorical question — the form of verse 14 ("Shall I take as protector other than God?") and verse 114 ("Shall I seek other than God as judge?"). The three questions together cover the three relationships in which one might be tempted to turn elsewhere: protection, judgment, and lordship. In each, the answer is the same and for the same reason.

The reason is stated: *wa huwa rabbu kulli shay'* — "while He is the Lord of everything." *Rabb* is lord, master, sustainer, the one who owns, nurtures, and governs. If God is the Lord of all things — of every star the idolaters worshipped, every idol they carved, every jinn they feared, every ancestor they followed — then to seek another lord is to seek, as lord, something that is itself under His lordship. The question has no rational answer except "no." Compare 7:140, where Moses asks his people, "Shall I seek for you a god other than God, while He has favored you above the worlds?" Only ignorance of God's universal lordship, the source commentary observes, could make the seeking of another lord conceivable.

**The Occasion**

Some commentators report that the verse responded to an invitation from the Makkans: they proposed that the Prophet ﷺ return to their religion, or that he worship their gods for a time and they would worship his, and they would bear the consequences — "˹Just˺ follow our way, and we will bear ˹the burden of˺ your sins" (29:12). The verse answers both the invitation and the offer of indemnity: I will not seek another lord; and no one can bear another's burden.

**"No Soul Does Evil, Save Against Itself"**

*Wa lā taksibu kullu nafsin illā ʿalayhā* — "and no soul earns except against itself." The verb *kasaba*, to earn, is used here for earning evil (as the context requires and as *ʿalayhā*, 'against it,' indicates). Whatever wrong a soul earns falls on that soul. This is the principle of moral reflexivity that the sūrah has stated at verse 123 ("they plot only against themselves, but they fail to perceive it" (6:123)) and 129 and that runs through the Qur'an: wrongdoers wrong themselves (2:57; 3:117; 7:160; 10:44); deceivers deceive themselves (2:9); "Whatever you ˹believers˺ spend in charity, it is for your own good" (2:272). The consequences of an act may touch others in this world, but the moral weight of it — its effect on the soul's destiny — rests with the doer alone.

**"And None Shall Bear the Burden of Another"**

*Wa lā taziru wāziratun wizra ukhrā* — "and no bearer of burden bears the burden of another." The image is of a load (*wizr*) carried on the back; each carries his own. The principle appears at 17:15, 35:18, 39:7, and 53:38, and it is among the most consequential doctrines of Islamic theology. It excludes inherited guilt: no one is born bearing another's sin. It excludes vicarious atonement: no one can take another's burden upon himself, and no one can lay his burden on another. It excludes the tribal ethic in which the tribe answers for the individual and the individual for the tribe. And it excludes the Makkans' offer to bear the Prophet's sins if he followed them — an offer the Qur'an exposes as empty: "And they will surely be questioned on Judgment Day about what they used to fabricate" (29:13) — the additional burden being for misleading others, which is their own sin, not a transfer of the misled's.

The principle establishes the individual as the unit of moral accountability. Each soul stands before God alone: "And each of them will return to Him on the Day of Judgment all alone" (19:95). "˹It is˺ the Day no soul will be of ˹any˺ benefit to another whatsoever, for all authority on that Day belongs to Allah ˹entirely˺" (82:19). The Prophet ﷺ said to his own family: "O Fāṭimah, daughter of Muhammad, ask me what you will of my wealth, but I cannot avail you anything against God" (al-Bukhārī 2753; Muslim 206). If the Prophet ﷺ could not carry his daughter's burden, no one carries anyone's.

The doctrine does not exclude intercession by God's leave (2:255) nor the multiplication of reward through others' benefit (a righteous child's prayer, knowledge left behind, ongoing charity — Muslim 1631). These are additions to one's own account by God's grace, not transfers of another's burden. Nor does it exclude the leader's bearing the burden of those he misled — which is his own sin of misleading. The principle is precise: no one bears the guilt of another's act.

**"Then unto Your Lord Is Your Return"**

*Thumma ilā rabbikum marjiʿukum* — "then to your Lord is your return." The verse turns from the principle to its enforcement. All will return to God — the same Lord of all things named at the verse's opening. The sūrah has said this repeatedly (vv. 36, 60, 62, 108); it now says it as the seal of the closing declarations. The return is the moment at which each soul's own burden is weighed.

**"And He Will Inform You of That Wherein You Differed"**

*Fa-yunabbi'ukum bi-mā kuntum fīhi takhtalifūn* — "To Allah you will all return, then He will inform you ˹of the truth˺ regarding your differences" The religious differences between the Prophet ﷺ and the idolaters — and among the sects of verse 159 — will be settled not by further argument but by God's disclosure. The formula recurs (5:48; 2:113; 10:93; 45:17). Its placement here, at the end of a sūrah that has been one long argument, is a kind of closure: the argument has been made, the proof established (v. 149); what remains, for those who still differ, is the Day on which God Himself will show what was true.

**The Verse's Structure**

The verse moves through the whole of the moral order in one sentence. Lordship: God alone is Lord of all things. Responsibility: each soul earns for itself alone. Non-transferability: none bears another's burden. Return: all come back to the Lord. Disclosure: He resolves every difference. This is the architecture of Islamic accountability, and it stands opposed at every point to the idolaters' system — with its many lords, its tribal collective guilt, its bargains of indemnity, and its denial of return.

**The Practical Weight**

The verse frees and burdens the believer at once. It frees him from carrying what is not his: he is not guilty for his ancestors' sins, his tribe's crimes, or his neighbor's choices; he cannot be held for what he did not do. And it burdens him with what is his: no one will carry his load; no intercessor can substitute for his own repentance; no bargain can transfer his account. He stands alone before the Lord of all things, with his own earning. This is why the closing declarations — I have been guided, my life and death are for God, He has no partner, I seek no other lord — are in the first person singular. Each soul must say them for itself.

---
## Sūrah al-Anʿām 6:165

> **He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth and elevated some of you in rank over others, so He may test you with what He has given you. Surely your Lord is swift in punishment, but He is certainly AllForgiving, Most Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Verse**

The sūrah that opened with "Praise be to God, who created the heavens and the earth" closes with the human being's place on that earth. *Wa huwa alladhī jaʿalakum khalā'ifa al-arḍ* — "and He it is who made you vicegerents of the earth." The emphatic *huwa alladhī*, "He is the One who," matches the openings of verses 97, 98, 99, and 141, each of which reclaimed a domain of creation for its Creator. Here the domain is human society itself: its succession, its hierarchy, its trial. The last word of the sūrah is about how one lives, under God, among others, on the earth He made.

**"Vicegerents upon the Earth"**

*Khalā'if* is a plural of *khalīfah* — successor, deputy, representative, one who comes after and stands in place of another. The word has two Qur'anic senses, both active here. The first is succession: each generation succeeds the one before, inheriting the earth from those who have passed and holding it until they pass in turn. The Qur'an uses the term for communities that replaced destroyed ones (7:69, 74; 10:13–14, 73) and, in 24:55, for the promise that the believers will be made *khalā'if* on the earth if they believe and do good. Al-Ṭabarī and most commentators take this sense as primary: you succeed those before you — earlier nations, earlier generations — and others will succeed you (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī). This links to verse 133: God brought you forth from the progeny of others and can replace you.

The second sense is representation: the human being is God's *khalīfah* on earth, as Adam was appointed (2:30) — a steward holding the earth on trust, charged to manage it according to its Owner's will. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī note that the addressees have inherited this position. Both senses converge in the verse's teaching: you are here temporarily, as successors, and you are here responsibly, as deputies. Neither permanence nor ownership is yours. The word became the title of the Muslim ruler — the caliph — but the verse addresses all: *jaʿalakum*, "He made *you*," every human being.

**"And Raised Some of You by Degrees Above Others"**

*Wa rafaʿa baʿḍakum fawqa baʿḍin darajāt* — "and He raised some of you above others in degrees." The degrees here, as the source commentary argues, are worldly — not the degrees of the Hereafter (v. 132), since what follows ("that He may try you") applies to this life, where the test is, not to the next, where the recompense is. The commentators specify: degrees of provision and wealth (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī), of rank and nobility (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī), of intellect and ability (al-Rāzī), of strength, health, beauty, influence, and every other worldly endowment.

The verse states a fact everyone observes and many resent: people are not equal in what they are given. The Qur'an neither denies the inequality nor treats it as injustice. It attributes it to God — "He raised" — and gives its purpose in the next clause. Compare 43:32: "We have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and raised some of them above others in degrees, so that some may employ others in service; and the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate." And 16:71; 17:21.

**"That He May Try You in That Which He Has Given You"**

*Li-yabluwakum fī mā ātākum* — "in order to test you in what He has given you." This is the verse's center. The differences in worldly degree are not rewards or punishments; they are the material of a test. The word *balā'* is trial, testing — putting something to proof to reveal its nature. Each person is tested *in what he was given*: the rich in his wealth, the poor in his poverty, the powerful in his power, the weak in his weakness, the intelligent in his intellect, the healthy in his health.

The commentators describe the two directions of the test. Al-Zamakhsharī: those given more are tested in their gratitude, humility, generosity, and justice toward those given less — will they share, will they be fair, will they remember the Giver? Al-Sulamī: those given less are tested in their patience, contentment, trust, and freedom from envy — will they accept God's apportionment, will they strive honorably, will they emulate the nobler rather than resent them? Neither position is the safer. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Every community has its trial, and the trial of my community is wealth" (al-Tirmidhī 2336). And also: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires" (al-Bukhārī 6487; Muslim 2822). Both ends of the scale are tested, and the test is the same: what do you do with what you were given?

This reframes every worldly circumstance. Nothing one has is simply one's own; it is "what He has given" — a loan under test. Nothing one lacks is simply deprivation; it is also "what He has given" — a different test. The verse dissolves both the arrogance of the fortunate and the despair of the unfortunate by placing both under the same purpose. Al-Tustarī adds a consolation: the hardships one suffers in this life should not be regarded as punishment but as purification and expiation — every hardship except the hardening of the heart, which alone is a true affliction.

**"Truly Thy Lord Is Swift in Retribution"**

*Inna rabbaka sarīʿu al-ʿiqāb* — "indeed your Lord is swift in punishment." The verse turns to the outcome of the test. For those who fail — who receive without gratitude, who use their degree to oppress, who respond to their lack with rebellion — retribution is swift. Al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Zamakhsharī apply this to the ungrateful and disobedient in the face of God's gifts. 'Swift' (*sarīʿ*) does not contradict God's patience; it means that when the term comes, the reckoning is immediate, and that the whole of life, however long it seems, is short before the Day. "They truly see this ˹Day˺ as impossible, but We see it as inevitable." (70:6–7).

**"And Truly He Is Forgiving, Merciful"**

*Wa innahu la-ghafūrun raḥīm* — "and indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful." The sūrah's last words are mercy. For those who pass the test — who are grateful, who approach God through obedience, who repent of what they fail in (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī) — God is Forgiving of their shortcomings and Merciful in His acceptance. The juxtaposition of "And ˹remember, O Prophet,˺ when your Lord declared that He would send against them others who would make them suffer terribly until the Day of Judgment" and "Forgiving, Merciful" (also at 7:167) holds fear and hope in a single breath, as the commentators observe: the possibility of irreversible judgment is always near, and God's forgiveness is always available. The verse does not let the reader rest in either alone.

The order matters. Retribution is stated first and mercy last, so that the sūrah ends on mercy — as it began with praise and returned, at verses 12 and 54, to "He has prescribed mercy upon Himself." The Sūrah of the Cattle, with all its warnings, its exposures, its scenes of judgment, closes with the Names *Ghafūr* and *Raḥīm*. This is the God it has argued for from its first verse: One, without partner, Lord of all things, swift when He seizes, and forgiving and merciful in His essence.

**The Sūrah's Frame**

Verse 1 and verse 165 enclose the sūrah. The first: God created the heavens and the earth, made the darknesses and the light, and yet people ascribe equals to Him. The last: God made human beings successors on the earth, raised them in degrees to test them, and is swift in retribution and forgiving and merciful. Between them lies the whole argument — creation as proof, prophecy as guidance, judgment as certainty, invented law as fabrication, the ten commandments as the true path, and the closing creed of total devotion. The frame says: the God who made the world is the God who placed you in it and will judge how you lived. The sūrah's 165 verses are the exposition of that sentence.

**The Believer's Departure from the Sūrah**

The reader who has followed the sūrah from beginning to end leaves it with a clear picture of his situation. He is a successor on an earth he does not own, holding gifts he did not make, placed at a degree he did not choose, under a test whose purpose he now knows. He has been shown the signs, warned of the Day, taught the commandments, and given the creed. His Lord is swift when the term comes and forgiving as long as it has not. What remains is what verse 135 named: to work. And what the last words promise is that the One for whom he works is *Ghafūr*, *Raḥīm* — Forgiving, Merciful — so that the work is done in hope.
